1 
Culture and the Psychology Curriculum 
Foundations and Resources 
Walter J. Lonner, Kenneth D. Keith,  and David Matsumoto 
Introduction In 2013, an American Psychological Association (APA) Task Force on Undergraduate Education in Psychology established “Guidelines for the Undergraduate Psychology Major.” The guidelines included comments on teaching diversity. They wrote that the task force 
is mindful of the importance of diversity as an outcome of quality undergraduate education in psychology. The term diversity encompasses human, sociocultural, socio- historical, and sociopolitical diversity in its many forms, including race, ethnicity, gender identity/ expression, sexual orientation, age, religious affiliation, health and disability status, national identity and immigration status, and social class, among other socio- cultural differences and distinctions. (See http:// www. apa.org/ ed/ precollege/ about/ psymajor- guidelines.pdf) 
These are commendable goals— goals that can be, and to some extent have been, transferred globally. As cross- cultural psychologists, we obviously agree with them and applaud the APA’s intentions. We belong to a growing international network of culture- oriented psychologists who firmly believe in and endorse such initiatives. Culture is as important as genes in understanding human thought and behavior. In the context of this Handbook and in keeping with the title of this chapter, we wish to suggest ways that 
 
 
4 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
psychology instructors might use a rapidly expanding body of information and resources in this domain to help convey to their students a number of perspectives that culture- oriented psychologists have contributed to help shape a more complete and inclusive psychology. 
Until the early 1970s, curricular offerings that focused on the relations between culture and psychology were rarely found in colleges and universities in the United States and, we assume, the world. Fortunately, the situation has changed substantially, year by year and decade by decade. Currently, many universities offer such courses, and numerous textbooks in the area have appeared (e.g., Berry, Poortinga, Breugelmans, Chasiotis, & Sam, 2011; Heine, 2012; Keith, 2018; Laungani, 2007; Matsumoto, 2001; Matsumoto & Juang, 2013; Rich, Gielen, & Takooshian, 2017; Shiraev & Levy, 2012). Additionally, a variety of handbooks, such as this one, now in its second edition, have updated research results found in thousands of studies. Edited books have also appeared over the years, and these will be mentioned in the following pages. The three- volume Encyclopedia of Cross- Cultural Psychology (Keith, 2013) is an authoritative guide to concepts, contributors, and a specialized vocabulary. Journals such as the Journal of Cross- Cultural Psychology (JCCP, inaugurated in 1970) and Culture and Psychology (1995) have flourished. Many academic psychologists will choose one or more of these books and related resources for their courses, sometimes borrowing proven syllabi from colleagues. However, most may want to develop their own syllabi or seek additional sources of material for their own courses, perhaps for the first time. 
Inevitably, anyone who teaches in this area will have to deal, at least cursorily, with all of the foundational topics covered in this Handbook. All components of this book, either singly or in some combination, could easily be the sole focus in an entire course with a bulging bibliography that, in many topical areas, can be traced to Ancient Greece. Having taught relevant courses and written books on these topics over the years, the authors of all chapters in this book have frequently tackled the challenges of studying other cultures with alacrity and authority. These experts are excited to pass on to others what they have learned and to encourage the inclusion of culture in the curriculum. 
A number of American psychologists have recently endorsed various efforts to increase the coverage of ethnic diversity, largely (but not exclusively) from the United States’ base of multiculturalism in the psychology curriculum. Chronologically, several such efforts are Richmond, Broussard, Sterns, Sanders, and Shardy (2015); Hall, Yip, and Zarate (2016); Fuentes and Shannon (2016); Gurung and colleagues (2016); and Takooshian, Gielen, Plous, Rich, and Velayo (2016). The last article focuses on internationalizing the psychology curriculum, which is consistent with our intent in this chapter. Takooshian et al. provide an overview of various ways that psychology students can increase their international awareness. These include engaging in cross- cultural research, especially in teams; study or work abroad; attending conferences; and joining organizations at (usually) low student rates. The International Association for Cross- Cultural Psychology (IACCP), for example, is particularly interested in student membership. Additionally, 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  5 
Keith (2012) recounts a variety of factors from more than four decades of college teaching that should be taken into account when teaching about culture. This includes the culture of the classroom— such factors as the diversity of the students, the nature of the instructor and his or her experiences with other cultures and the broader world, and the extent to which faculty from diverse backgrounds are included in the instruction. 
For many years, all the contributors to this book have taught courses that focus on culture and especially culture in a global sense. This small but expanding nucleus of academic psychologists has enjoyed teaching about the interrelations between culture and psychology and has been encouraged by the progress made in the field during the past half- century. As part of that nucleus, our experiences give us some confidence in imparting knowledge about the hybridization of culture and psychology. As academic psychologists with lengthy careers, we have frequently taught culture- oriented classes and seminars, developing syllabi and carefully selecting appropriate texts and journal articles, often making them available in university libraries for mandatory reading. The group with which we tend to identify— the IACCP— has about 750 members from more than 75 countries. The IACCP, unlike the APA, has never developed a coherent set of guidelines for psychology education. Perhaps it should have. But, in the absence of such a mandate, we present in this chapter a perspective that primarily embodies the nature and scope of cross- cultural psychology, with questions that aid teachers of a culture- oriented psychology in framing and developing their courses. 
We hope to aid the teaching of a more globally sensitive psychology by providing an overview of various perspectives needed to prepare syllabi or lectures for culture- oriented classes and by contributing to a general psychology program that can be used in any psychological curriculum. Through these efforts, we hope to provide instructors with a set of overarching, guiding questions that they may address as they develop and implement courses in this area. Despite the myriad of topics that can be covered and the multiplicity of individual differences among teachers in style, pedagogy, methodology, and knowledge, we believe that all teachers need to deal with, at some level, a few questions that implicitly or explicitly frame how they understand and thus teach culture- oriented material in psychology. The three questions that seem to embody the main issues are: 
 1. What is culture? How teachers and researchers define culture will affect how they teach and study it. Definitions of culture on which all can agree remain elusive. Yet we believe that teachers and researchers need to have their own working definitions of culture and make them explicit because those definitions inevitably influence how one thinks, studies, and teaches about culture. Descriptions of various perspectives concerning the association between culture and psychology all influence definitions of culture and are discussed later. 
 2. What is the relation between culture and psychological processes and behaviors? A  typical way for teachers and researchers to understand this connection is that culture causes psychological processes and behaviors. This perspective tends to see 
6 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
culture as a macro- social phenomenon that has a top- down influence on individuals. This perspective is implied in such language as “cultural influences on” aggression, cognition, emotion, perception, social behavior, learning, personality and so many other topical dimensions in psychology. Another viewpoint is of reverse causation— that individual behaviors are produced as adaptations to an environment, and culture is later extrapolated as a result of the behavioral adaptations. Yet another viewpoint is that culture and individual psychological processes mutually constitute each other in each ontology. Which perspective teachers adopt frames how they teach culture- oriented psychology. The various perspectives discussed later also reflect how the field has wrestled with this question. 
 3. How are human psychological processes and behaviors constituted? This is essentially the age- old nature– nurture question. Are any psychological processes or behaviors produced by an innate, biologically based source? Or are all behaviors learned in development and thus culturally constructed? If some behaviors are biologically based and some culturally constructed, which are the former and which the latter? Do psychological or behavioral universals exist, and if so, how are they constituted? We discuss later the issue of psychological universals because this issue is directly related to this question (see also Chapter 8 by Heidi Keller and Chapter 12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang on approaches that integrate innate, biological substrates with cultural learning). 
We also provide teachers with some practical assistance. Appendix A  lists and describes associations and organizations that focus in various ways on the interplay between culture and psychology. Also, Unit 11 in the Online Readings in Psychology (located at https:// scholarworks.gvsu.edu/ orpc/ ), publishes a list of academic units in numerous countries that focus on culture. The Online Readings contain more than 100 articles that many have found invaluable in the teaching of cross- cultural psychology. We consider these offerings to be major resources, adding to our efforts to help enrich psychology education by taking a global perspective. 
Our effort should not be construed as tantamount to producing a “cookbook” of teaching in this area. As with basic courses and lectures in any branch of psychology, there is no perfect or uniform way to teach about the myriad culture- oriented topics and perspectives that are spread across the entire spectrum of the discipline. There is too much topical variation and too many individual differences in the styles and experiences of instructors to expect academic uniformity. Instead, we wish to provide teachers of culture with a solid corpus of guiding questions, information, and resources that should be helpful in many facets of a psychological curriculum. We begin with an overview and description of various approaches to understanding the relation or interaction between culture and psychology, which provides a framework for teachers to find their own answers to the three questions we posed earlier.
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  7 
The Landscape of Multiple Culture- Oriented Psychologies One way to begin to address the three questions posed earlier is to identify, acknowledge, and understand the various perspectives that exist regarding the admixture of culture and psychology. These perspectives are embodied to a large extent in the various subdomains of culture- oriented psychology, which include cross- cultural psychology, cultural psychology, indigenous psychology, psychological anthropology, and multiculturalism, each of which addresses our three questions in slightly— sometimes profoundly— different ways. These subdomains emerged, in large part, in response to different evolutions of thought in regard to our three questions. We believe that teachers of a culture- oriented psychology should have a basic understanding and background of the various perspectives as they deal with the questions we have posed. Defining and discussing the various approaches that in some way involve the admixture of culture and psychology usually starts with some historical facts. 
Historical Highlights Beginning with its ancient roots, the discipline of psychology gradually separated from philosophy to become a respectable science. It embraced the study of a wide range of topics that touched the lives of all humans. During most of its modern history, the basic tenets of psychological science and its standard menu of important topics became known as “mainstream” psychology (hereafter without the customary quotation marks). Despite obviously knowing about differences in customs, languages, and so forth around the world, major theorists and practitioners in psychology were largely attuned to WEIRD audiences— Western, Educated people from the Industrialized countries and who were Rich and mainly Democratic (Henrich, Heine, & Norenzayan, 2010). Some writers have estimated that about 80% of psychologists who have ever lived came from the United States, Canada, and Great Britain and its geopolitical extensions, along with Germany and other Western European countries. Moreover, an even greater percentage of psychological research has come from such disproportionate segments of the world’s population (Arnett, 2008). Similar imbalances are captured by the acronym WASP— Western Academic Scientific Psychology. 
A comprehensive inquiry into the history and development of cross- cultural psychology might begin with Chapter 2, by Michael Harris Bond, in this volume, or the fore-word to Keith’s three- volume Encyclopedia of Cross- Cultural Psychology (Lonner, 2013). (The latter is available free of charge as a pdf article; see IACCP.org). Earlier contributions (Jahoda, 1970, 1982, 1992, 2011; Jahoda & Krewer, 1997; Klineberg, 1980)  trace the beginnings of psychological interest in cultures other than one’s own. Additional historical and essentially pre- 1980 perspectives on cross- cultural psychology would be enriched by reading all the chapters in volume 1 in the six- volume Handbook of Cross- Cultural Psychology 
 
 
 
8 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
(Triandis et al., 1980), as well as a selection of the enormous number of references spread across the 51 chapters that comprise that set of seminal books. A four- volume set of books is a compendium of numerous previously published book chapters and journal articles considered to be foundational and canonical to cross- cultural psychology (Sam & Berry, 2017). Unit 1 in the Online Readings in Psychology and Culture (ORPC), which as noted earlier was designed specifically for teaching, provides additional information of historical interest (see IACCP.org; Lonner, 2015). 
Among the main points made in these historical snapshots and analyses is that the term “culture” and the phenomena it represents have been around for centuries and that efforts to use culture to help explain diversity in human thought and behavior are not new. Another important strand of thoughtful reflection contained in these perspectives is that a definition of cross- cultural psychology with which everyone agrees remains slippery (recall Question 1 posed earlier). While definitional difficulties and allegiances will likely remain ongoing matters of debate and discussion, and some critics will continue to question the importance or veracity of cross- cultural psychology, perhaps the most important thing to keep in mind is that “what cross- cultural psychology is called is not nearly as important as what it does— to ensure the broadest range of psychological topics be explored within the broadest possible spectrum of ethnicity and culture and by diverse methodologies” (Segall, Lonner, & Berry, 1998, p. 1102). 
A comprehensive review of the world’s psychological literature during the past century would show that many psychologists have been interested in culture, ethnicity, or national origin as “determinants” or at least as intervening variables (Lonner & Adamopoulos, 1997) in explaining human thought and behavior (recall Question 2). Indeed, even the father of modern experimental psychology, Wilhelm Wundt, is an ac-knowledged pioneer in this area because of his interest in Volkerpsychologie, as gener-ously witnessed by the 10 volumes he published under that title from 1900 to 1920 (see, e.g., Wundt, 1916). 
Perhaps the first “traveling” and dedicated pioneer in exploring possible relations between culture and basic psychological processes was W.  H. R.  Rivers. Around the turn of the twentieth century, Rivers (1901), of Cambridge University, led an expedition consisting of both psychologists and anthropologists that gathered seminal data from sites in the South Pacific and on the east coast of India. 
Considering all of psychology’s history, if one wanted to find journal articles that to some extent involved “culture” or other descriptors used to characterize people who share a common heritage, language, or destiny (such as an “ethnic group”), the task would be rather easy. Despite the preponderance of research that has focused on relatively healthy and wealthy white people from industrialized societies as “subjects” in psychological research, it is nearly certain that any psychological topic one can imagine has been involved somehow and in varying degrees of sophistication in studies that included individuals from diverse cultural and psycholinguistic groups.
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  9 
With just a few notable exceptions during the first two- thirds of the twentieth century there was no pattern or coherent program of research guiding these excursions. “Sabbatical opportunism” and “jet- set research” prevailed for years. This usually meant that an inquisitive and energetic psychologist, typically from the United States or some other Western country, would travel to some exotic corner of the world during an aca-demic leave lasting a few weeks to several months and, inter alia, “test” some principle or examine some theory of interest. Returning to the comforts of home, he (occasionally she) would characteristically write a report and submit it to some accommodating if not enthusiastically welcoming journal and thus earn some credit in helping to expand psychology’s vistas. 
Although such reports may have been noteworthy at the time, sustained efforts to develop a strategy of systematic research were scarce. There were few books on methodology, organizations of like- minded people, or other sources of support for such efforts. Moreover, psychologists who engaged in cross- cultural efforts were frequently viewed as rather odd creatures who tended to eschew orthodox and routine academic pursuits while living and working in the periphery or “lunatic fringe” of the discipline. The prevailing opinion among academic psychologists was that “culture” as a respectable thing to study belonged to anthropologists. (That opinion is still held by some, especially those who may view psychology as a “natural” science, whose “laws” of behavior transcend culture, just as “laws” of learning or human development are often believed to be phylogenetically robust.) The epitome of a culture- bound and culture- blind psychology would hold that culture amounts to nothing more than a little “noise” in an otherwise pristine set of basic principles that work everywhere on the planet. 
The Big Change The picture of isolated and disconnected cross- cultural research changed radically in the mid- to late 1960s when several strands of relatively independent efforts took place and then converged. During that active period, the modern era of culture- oriented psychology grew quickly. The year of 1966 was especially meaningful to the senior author, for both personal and professional reasons. In early February, while working in Germany, he met his bride- to- be and married her less than 3 months later in Basel, Switzerland. Romance aside, unknown to him at the time, two publications that year turned out to be highly important in the development of cross- cultural psychology. One of them was a journal article that proved to be influential in the development of cross- cultural research methodology (Frijda & Jahoda, 1966), and the other was to become a classic comparative study of cultural influences on visual perception that involved nativist and empiricist perspectives as well as elements of anthropological and psychological theory (Segall, Campbell, & Herskovits, 1966). Slightly earlier, a noteworthy event was a meeting at the University of Nigeria in Ibadan during the Christmas and New Year period of 1965– 66. Attracting about 100 well- known and primarily social psychologists, the meeting was 
 
10 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
designed to serve as a forum in which various social psychological perspectives could be discussed with respect to their cultural generalizability— or lack thereof— and their theoretical underpinnings. Those in attendance also developed ways to collaborate in the future. For instance, they agreed to keep in touch with each other through the irreg-ularly appearing Cross- Cultural Social Psychology Newsletter, with Harry Triandis serving as its first editor. (The direct descendant of the Newsletter is the quarterly Cross- Cultural Psychology Bulletin, with William K. Gabrenya currently serving as editor.) John W. Berry initiated a second activity that involved development of a Directory of Cross- Cultural Researchers. Originally containing a little more than 100 entries and published in 1968 in the International Journal of Psychology, the intent of that directory was to encourage cooperation and collaboration in various kinds of psychological research throughout the world. The Directory was updated in 1970, 1973, and twice in the 1980s; its most recent updating was done in 1998. The third significant activity was the development in 1968 and 1969, and then the inaugural publication in 1970, of the quarterly JCCP, with Lonner serving as its founding editor. The JCCP became the first psychology journal in the world with “culture” or “cross- cultural” in its title. Initially a quarterly publication, its influence and growth continues. Its fiftieth anniversary is being celebrated this year (2019) and it is now published 10 times a year. 
The three activities just described combined to form a catalyst in 1971– 72. At the initiative of the late John L. M. B. Dawson, the inaugural meeting of the IACCP was held in August 1972, at the University of Hong Kong, where Dawson was head of the department of psychology. That meeting brought together about 110 psychologists (and a handful of anthropologists and psychiatrists) who knew about each other’s work but with few exceptions had not yet met each other. At that time, the IACCP became an association of scholars, with officers, a constitution, and all the other trappings of a full- fledged (albeit small) professional organization (see Dawson & Lonner, 1974). Jerome Bruner was the IACCP’s first president, and Dawson served as its first secretary- general. This convergence of events marked the first time that cross- cultural psychology was institutionalized and became “official” and sanctioned by a group of like- minded scholars. It instantly became associated with three publications:  JCCP, the Cross- Cultural Social Psychology Bulletin, and the ongoing publication of the selected proceedings of most of the IACCP conferences. IACCP conferences, either internationally or regionally, have been held in about 30 different countries. 
All of these developments form such a coherent historical picture that it has earned archival status. Recently, the Cummings Center for the History of Psychology (CCHP), located at the University of Akron, in Ohio, added the IACCP Archives to its holdings. Covering a wide range of topics and historical artifacts, the Center is an informative place to visit for beginning and advanced students, as well as teaching faculty. Fortunately, many of the holdings of the still- developing IACCP Archives are also available online at CCHP.org.
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  11 
The events just described serve as a brief overview of the way cross- cultural psychology developed at the organizational level. For this volume, the more important issue concerns how the enterprise can be understood at the scientific and conceptual levels. Those levels involve an assortment of methodological and epistemological matters in an attempt to explicate culture’s connection to human behavior (recall the guiding questions posed earlier). Our attention now turns briefly to those considerations, which essentially entail multiple approaches to the psychological coverage of culture and in some ways the cultural study of psychology. At the same time, these approaches cover different perspectives in addressing the three questions posed earlier. Much greater detail appears in the chapters to follow as well as in the other topical chapters. 
Cross- Cultural Psychology Why does it matter? There are many reasons why cross- cultural psychology is important. Who would disagree, for instance, that learning about other cultures is of great benefit, if for no other reason than that such knowledge may prepare anyone for more effective intercultural interaction? Similarly, who would not argue that the exploration and understanding of other cultures or ethnicities is one of the hallmarks of an educated person, especially in our increasingly globalized and troubled world? Most importantly, why should psychologists not want to expand their thinking and research, thereby adding to a more solid base by “consulting all that is human” (which was the leitmotif accompanying the founding of the JCCP in 1970)? Studying the world beyond one’s borders is important in its own right (Cole, 1984) and provides insight into who we are as a species in a vast universe, where we came from, and where we may be going. For cross- cultural psychologists, however, the main scientific reason for the origination and continuation of cross- cultural psychology has been to extend the range of variation of psychological functioning. It has been described as “psychology writ large” as it has expanded its reach throughout the world. Students need to be reminded of the limitations imposed by the fact that modern psychology is largely a Western academic affair that has basked in the glow of scientifically respectable research characterized by the legacy of logical positivism. Ultimately, the globalization of psychology is an overarching goal of cross- cultural psychology (Berry, 2013). 
The late Gustav Jahoda (1970) put the situation in colorful perspective when he commented on psychology’s constrained borders. He said that this narrowness reminds one 
of Parson Thwackum in Tom Jones [Henry Fielding’s humorous 1749 novel about a commoner raised among the English nobility], who said, “When I mention religion, I mean the Christian religion; and not only the Christian religion, but the Protestant religion, and not only the Protestant religion but the Church of England.” 
 
 
12 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
This might well be suitably transposed as “When I mention a psychological subject, I mean a subject from a western industrialized culture; and not only from a western industrialized culture, but an American; and not only an American, but a college student.” No doubt this is unfair, reflecting as it does on the amount of work that has been done in the United States. Nonetheless, the excessive concentration on such an odd (as far as humanity at large is concerned) population makes one wonder about the range of application of the “laws” experimentally derived in this manner. (p. 2) 
In short, the great majority of what is known about the psychological functioning of human beings has come from a massive amount of research and theory that originated in the “highly psychologized” world, or the “first world” of psychology (Moghaddam, 1987). Nearly half a century ago, culturally oriented scholars proclaimed that relatively little was known, psychologically, about vast portions of the rest of the world. This is still true, but the gap is narrowing. 
Standard Methodological Paradigm While Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver of this Handbook provides an overview of research methods used in culture- comparative research, we assert here that extending the range of variation, as noted earlier, is often given as the main reason for the advent of cross- cultural psychology. This usually means going to cultures other than one’s own to investigate the robustness or generalizability of psychological findings that many, in the absence of disconfirming or conflicting evidence, consider to be true and invariant. Because the vast majority of psychological research has been conducted in the highly industrialized Western world by psychologists who have infrequently experienced other cultures in depth, these efforts usually involved going to non- Western and relatively “unpsychologized” (unstudied) parts of the world. However, for more general purposes, the definition of cross- cultural psychology provided by Berry, Poortinga, Breugelmans, Chasiotis, and Sam (2011) is useful and commonly accepted. They said that cross- cultural psychology is “the study of similarities and differences in individual psychological functioning in various cultural and ethnocultural groups; of ongoing changes in variables reflecting such functioning, and of the relationships of psychological variables with sociocultural, ecological and biological variables” (p. 5). Matsumoto and Juang (2013) offered a more concise definition: Cross- cultural research “tests the cultural parameters of psychological knowledge” (p. 4). 
The standard (but certainly not the only) methodological protocol in cross- cultural psychology is the “transfer, test, and discovery” procedure. This involves (1)  selecting some psychological principle, test, or model that has worked respectably well in the originating culture; (2) “testing” what has been selected for study in one or more other cultures (this is, of course, synonymous with extending the range of variation or testing the parameters) to see to what extent it generalizes elsewhere; and (3)  discovering 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  13 
(possibly) factors or elements in other cultures that were not present in the originating culture in which the psychological concept was promulgated. This procedure has most of the elements that characterize mainstream psychology and especially the oft- cited “gold standard” of routine psychological investigations. What seems to be evident in the orthodox cross- cultural research protocol is that cultures (or elements within them) are treated as independent (or quasi- independent) variables. Because cultures cannot be “manipulated” (which is, of course, a key element in the definition of an independent variable as traditionally understood), this part of the procedure is of paramount importance and is a reduction or assumption that bothers some scholars (see later discussion). Thus “Mother Nature” is viewed as a quintessential expert in experimental design (recall Question 3 posed earlier). The different “experimental conditions” or “independent variables” she has created are called “cultures,” with people who are somehow recognized as “different” from the people of some other culture whose participation was central to the original body of information. 
At its base, cross- cultural psychology should perhaps be viewed not as a “field” or separate discipline but as a special method of scientific inquiry. With it comes a set of unique methodological circumstances or problems that require careful attention. For instance, the selection of samples must be done carefully, and various problems associated with equivalence (of language, procedures, measurement, etc.) must be addressed. Of course, those who design and carry out routine mainstream psychological research must also be attentive to problems associated with sample selection and its implications, as well as the nature of the tasks or conditions presented to participants. So must they be concerned about ethics. However, in cross- cultural research, the situation is usually much more complicated, time- consuming, and controversial. 
We do not have space in this chapter to discuss all the components associated with solid cross- cultural methodology (see Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver for more details). However, if cross- cultural psychology is, as some suggest (see later in this chapter), “nothing more” than an extension of standard empiricist/ positivist inquiry, then the only substantial difference between psychological orthodoxy and cross- cultural psychology’s quest to establish universals or regularities in human thought and behavior are those special factors that make this line of research rather challenging in the overlapping realms of scientific reasoning, methods of inquiry, and logistics. 
Some psychology instructors may want to build an entire culture- oriented course around the numerous conceptual and methodological hurdles that confront cross- cultural psychologists and, in so doing, learn more about the results of substantive research. Chronologically, Brislin, Lonner, and Thorndike (1973); Triandis et al. (1980); van de Vijver and Leung (1997); Matsumoto and Yoo (2006); van de Vijver, Chasiotis, & Breugelmans (2011); Lonner (2015), and, of course, He and van de Vijver (Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver) can be visited for discussions of the evolution of advances in cross- cultural research methodology. Additionally, a special issue of the JCCP provides a current overview of the status and advances in the methods that are used in culture- comparative 
14 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
research (Fischer & Poortinga, 2018a). An article in that issue summarizes the status of contemporary culture- comparative research (Fischer & Poortinga, 2018b) and, in so doing, suggests ways that research in this area can be improved. 
In summary, in less than half a century, research carried out by cross- cultural psychologists has gone from relatively simple comparative studies involving few researchers and cultures to highly sophisticated approaches that frequently involve extensive collaboration among researchers in dozens of countries (see later discussion). On that score, the reader might be interested in reading an overview of noteworthy changes and developments in cross- cultural psychology during the first fifty years of the Journal of Cross- Cultural Psychology, the flagship publication in cross- cultural psychology (Lonner, 2019). The increasing sophistication of cross- cultural psychology and its breadth and depth of topical coverage is one of the more important contributions to the discipline of psychology during the past half century. Appendix A features descriptions of numerous associations and organizations that have emerged over the years. Concomitant with this growth and continuing maturation, cultural neuroscience recently entered the landscape of comparative inquiry (see Chapter 21 by Joan Y. Chiao and Katherine D. Blizinsky as well as Sasaki & Heejung, 2017). 
Cultural Psychology 
It is the dilemma of psychology to deal as a natural science with an object that creates history. 
— Ernest E. Boesch (1971) 
Cultural analysis is intrinsically incomplete. And, worse than that, the more deeply it goes the less complete it is. 
— Clifford Geertz (1973) 
Having briefly explained the essence of cross- cultural psychology, we now turn to its closest sibling, cultural psychology. Cultural psychology, which neophytes sometimes confuse or conflate with cross- cultural psychology, boasts a strong network of accomplished scholars who tend to be closer in their scholarly proclivities to cultural anthropologists than to cross- cultural psychologists. While cultural psychology does not have its own international organization, its proponents belong to various associations and scholarly groups. These include the IACCP and the International Society of Cultural Activity Research (ISCAR). They also tend to contribute to certain specialized journals, such as Psychology and Culture (see Appendix A). Given their mutual and total dedication to the psychological study of culture, it can be difficult to pinpoint where cross- cultural psychology ends and cultural psychology begins, or vice versa. In fact, according to recent surveys, at least one- third of all culture- oriented psychologists identify with both cultural and cross- cultural psychology. Also, Jerome Bruner and Gustav Jahoda, the inaugural and first full- time presidents, respectively, of IACCP, represented a combination of 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  15 
both approaches and were also fond of cultural anthropology (see Cole, 1984 for a lucid statement about the importance of studying culture). Moreover, while cross- cultural psychology has an agenda with which most of its adherents agree (basically, and generally, to examine the cultural generalizability of psychological laws and theories by using diverse methodologies that permit comparisons), those who primarily identify with cultural psychology do not seem to have a uniform procedure in their approach(es) to the study of other cultures, nor do they have a program of specific goals guiding their efforts. They believe in “thick description” and tend to be skeptical about universals (recall Question 3 posed earlier). They decry hegemony and prefer hermeneutics (deep and detailed interpretation and not psychometric assessment and testing)— or, if you will, idiographic over nomothetic ways to gather information and explain it. However, it is unlikely that any of cultural psychology’s dedicated adherents would be bothered by its lack of a pristine methodological or goal- directed identity. In fact, they tend to welcome healthy discourse in their quest to understand how persons and cultures work in their mutually constitutive ways. 
It may be accurate to say that cultural psychologists view themselves and their efforts as broadly ecumenical in both conceptualizing and conducting research or in writing essays or commentaries that concern the centrality of culture in understanding the behavior of human beings in their specific contexts. Broadly stated, and noted earlier, if cross- cultural psychology is a “quantitative” (nomothetic) and comparative enterprise that seeks to broaden (mainstream) psychology’s reach in “etic” ways, then cultural psychology thrives on “qualitative” and idiographic “emic” research that strives for depth and meaning: meaning that must be grounded in the context of the culture and its various unique symbols, icons, folk tales, and the Yin and Yang of everyday life— not disjointed artifacts of contrived realities as represented in tightly controlled experimental conditions that are studied at one point in history. When one considers such clever phrases as “Kultur als externe seele” (Culture as external soul), one knows that he or she is not in a laboratory setting! The senior author of this chapter is a dedicated cross- cultural psychologist, but, after hundreds of hours discussing culture with one eminent cultural psychologist— the late Swiss- born Ernest Boesch, along with his Thai wife, Supanee— his views of culture and what it means to others changed dramatically (see Lonner & Hayes, 2007). Cultural psychology is drenched in history and philosophy and arguably predates cross- cultural psychology by a generation or two. Cross- cultural psychology’s primary aim is to broaden the scope of the discipline. While part of the distinction between the two may be a simple matter of breadth (cross- cultural psychology) versus depth (cultural psychology), we recommend caution in extracting truly radical differences between the two. We have no quarrel with either approach and in fact vigorously endorse them. 
The following abridged self- description of the journal most closely associated with cultural psychology, Culture and Psychology, captures the essence of its intentions. Inaugurated in 1995, the masthead policy of that journal highlights several key points that have guided their efforts:
16 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Culture in its various forms— semiotic mediation, situated activity, dialogical nature of the self and its environment, social representing of human living— is present in each and every moment in our human lives. The science of cultural psychology unites psychology, anthropology, sociology, and history into a general science of cultural being. Its focus is on basic understanding of the psychology of human beings: their identity, social conduct, intra- and intersubjective experiences, emotions, and everyday creativity. 
Earlier in this chapter, we pointed out that cross- cultural psychology should be characterized primarily by what it does and not by some facile definition. We accord cultural psychology the same respect by saying that it, too, should be identified by what it does and, more precisely, by how it views relationships between the individual and his or her culture. With regard to what cultural psychology does today, many cultural psychologists do, in fact, conduct culturally comparative research in cross- cultural designs (akin to cross- cultural psychology). With regard to how cultural psychology views relationships between individuals and culture, Miller (1997) commented that the core perspective of cultural psychology is that culture and individual behavior are inseparable components of the same phenomenon (recall Question 2 posed earlier). Miller noted that this perspective contrasts with the tendency, particularly in early work in cross- cultural psychology, for culture and psychology to be somewhat dichotomized and understood as discrete phenomena, with culture conceptualized and used as a sort of independent variable that affects the “dependent variable” of individual behavior. The late Ernest Boesch, mentioned earlier, the founder of symbolic action theory (Boesch, 1991), was, like other cultural psychologists, strongly critical of treating culture as an “independent variable” and thus as something completely outside the person. He was also critical of applying a positivist or natural science template to efforts to understand people from other cultures. In an important article, Boesch (1996) wrote about what he called cross- cultural psychology’s seven “flaws” (more accurately, challenges), which range from the conceptual and methodological to the philosophical. A biographical sketch of Boesch and a presentation of several of his highly respected articles appeared in a book designed to honor his contributions (Lonner & Hayes, 2007). And a special issue of the journal Culture and Psychology, edited by Jaan Valsiner (vol. 3, no. 3 September, 1997), is de-voted to Boesch’s ideas and to reflections by others about his influence. 
As noted earlier, cultural psychology is not a unified field. Several of the more productive scholars in the various cultural orientations have their own distinctive views of the differences between cross- cultural psychology and cultural psychology. For instance, Cole (1996, p. 104) delineated the main characteristics of what he thinks constitutes cultural psychology: 
 • It emphasizes mediated action in a context.  • It insists on the importance of the “genetic method” understood broadly to include 
historical, ontogenetic, and microgenetic levels of analysis.
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  17 
 • It seeks to ground its analysis in everyday life events.  • It assumes that mind emerges in the jointly mediated activity of people. Mind, then, is 
in an important sense, “co- constructed” and distributed.  • It assumes that individuals are active agents in their own development but do not act 
in settings entirely of their own choosing.  • It rejects cause– effect, stimulus– response, explanatory science in favor of a science 
that emphasizes the emergent nature of mind in activity and that acknowledges a central role for interpretation in its explanatory network. 
 • It draws upon methodologies from the humanities as well as from the social and biological sciences. 
We strongly encourage teachers of psychology to take great pains to explain the approaches these two leading international communities of scholars take in studying other cultures. Numerous entries in the Encyclopedia of Cross- Cultural Psychology (Keith, 2013) explain the differences between these two psychological perspectives that both hope to enrich psychology further by explaining how culture and its myriad forms around the world influence the lives of all humans. The views of several cultural psychologists, including Richard Shweder (Shweder & Sullivan, 1993) and Jaan Valsiner (2007), will enrich any course in psychology, especially at more advanced levels in psychology education. 
We end this section with a quote from the late cultural psychologist, Ernest Boesch: 
The relationship between cultural and cross- cultural psychology is not one of either- or, one of simply choosing to be the one or the other, because at their appropriate place, each is needed. (See Lonner & Hayes, 2007, p. 257) 
Indigenous and Ethnic Psychology Indigenous psychology and ethnic psychology, for our purposes in this chapter, may well be synonymous. Together with cross- cultural and cultural psychology, indigenous psychology might be called the third point of a “golden triad” of efforts to explain the unsettled marriage between psychology as an academic discipline and culture as a phenomenon that all humans share, but in a menagerie of forms throughout the world. Nearly two decades ago, Patricia Greenfield (2000) wrote about these three approaches to culture. Her article is well worth reading in preparation for a discussion of the sometimes very different views taken by scholars who share the same goal of expanding the ways that culture- oriented psychologists view the fuzzy concept of culture. 
Cross- cultural psychologists espouse methodological pluralism and an openness to various efforts that hope to explain both similarities and differences in human thought and behavior. Yet, perhaps because of the methods and concepts it typically uses, this area of inquiry is questioned by those who claim that it is nothing more than Western conceptual and methodological hegemony pretentiously playing the game of scientific 
 
18 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
reductionism using unsuspecting psychological “subjects” as pawns. Harsh as that characterization may sound, one can read analyses of the cross- cultural psychological effort by individuals representing either cultural psychology or even mainstream psychology and emerge with the impression that cross- cultural psychology “doesn’t get it” and is an enterprise beset with “perilous problems” in a complex world populated by “moving cultures” (Hermans & Kempen, 1998). One such suspicious quarter is championed by individuals who represent what its adherents call “indigenous psychologies” or the “indigenization of psychology.” The goal of this approach, according to its proponents, is not to abandon science, objectivity, the experimental method, and a search for universals (characteristics that they claim define cross- cultural psychology) but to provide a more rigorous science that is firmly grounded in human understanding. Interestingly, espoused and encouraged by both “militant” indigenously oriented researchers and dedicated cross- cultural psychologists, this movement, as articulated by Kim (1995) has much in common with cultural psychology. 
Consider a definition of the indigenous psychologies approach (recall Question 2 posed earlier): 
culture is not viewed as a variable, quasi- independent variable, or category (e.g. individualistic or collectivistic), or a mere sum of individual characteristics. Culture is an emergent property of individuals interacting with their natural and human environment. Culture is defined as a rubric of patterned variables . . . (and a) process definition of culture (is that it) represents the collective utilization of natural and human resources to achieve desired outcomes. (Kim, Park, & Park, 2000, p. 67, emphasis in original) 
Indigenous psychology is frequently championed by psychologists who, many think, have been overlooked by the juggernaut of Western psychology with its powerful connections to the highly industrialized world. Indigenous psychologists tend to ground their research on their own terms, eschewing scientific hegemony from the outside world. This deeply “emic” approach is especially popular among the “first peoples” of North America as well as among Asian groups. 
Cultural psychologists would likely have no difficulty with these foregoing comments, and cross- cultural psychologists would nod their heads in approval. Perhaps the only factor with which cultural psychologists may quarrel is that proponents of the indigenous approach freely use many aspects of mainstream psychology to search for meaningful within- culture patterns of thought and behavior. For instance, several researchers who identify with indigenous psychology have used standard survey and questionnaire techniques that are as common as toothpaste in Western psychology in efforts to help understand the nature and structure of personality (itself a Western term) in other societies. Perhaps the only way to enter the pasture of a truly universal psychology is through the gates of potentially multiple paths patrolled and described by indigenous perspectives. 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  19 
Thus, the sum of indigenous psychologies (i.e., all that survives Procrustean tests in other cultures conducted by, for, and from within those cultures) is that elusive and oft- cited goal of a universal psychology. 
Psychological Anthropology The discipline of anthropology is at the core of the cultural sciences. Having been around for at least as long as psychology, anthropology is broadly the study of humankind, including human origins and variations. Cultural scholars in other fields will benefit directly and indirectly from the insights provided by a large number of influential anthropologists. Like psychology, the field of anthropology is subdivided into fairly discrete branches. One of these branches is psychological anthropology, a title first proposed by Frances Hsu (1972) to replace the earlier subdiscipline of culture and personality. Two decades ago, one of its leading proponents defined psychological anthropology as “anthropological investigations that make use of psychological concepts and methods” (Bock, 1994, p. iv). Bock insisted that an anthropology “that takes account of individuals must make use of ideas from neighboring disciplines,” an idea with which cross- cultural psychologists as well as cultural psychologists would heartily agree. The field of psychological anthropology is clearly and intentionally a hybrid animal. The esteemed psychologist Donald T. Campbell and the anthropologist Raoul Naroll— prominent scholars in their respective disciplines— explain the “mutual methodological relevance of anthropology and psychology” (Campbell & Naroll, 1972). That chapter provides a methodological and conceptual bridge between these two important fields. 
Psychological anthropologists have guided cross- cultural efforts in psychology in important ways. The study of culture and dreams, culture and mental illness, cognitive anthropology, the development of children, innovations in field research such as systematic observation in naturalistic settings, and many other orientations have proved to be immensely instructive to cross- cultural psychologists. The pioneering “Six Cultures” project, spearheaded by the late Beatrice and John Whiting, was a wide- ranging examination of child development carried out under the aegis of psychological anthropology (Whiting & Whiting, 1975). Even if we had the space to do so in this chapter, we would not want to attempt a complete presentation of this branch of anthropology. We primarily want to point out that psychological anthropologists have much to offer scholars in neighboring fields and that their efforts have informed numerous efforts in cross- cultural psychology and especially cultural psychology. 
Although it is not explicitly an association devoted to psychological anthropology, the Society for Cross- Cultural Research (see Appendix A), which has held its conferences only in the United States, attracts many who strongly identify with this anthropo-logical subfield. Two journals, Ethos and Cross- Cultural Research, publish many articles by psychological anthropologists. Finally, while it may not be entirely appropriate to mention it in this context, the journal Transcultural Psychiatry (which began in 1956 as the Transcultural Psychiatric Research Review) publishes articles and reviews that are 
 
20 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
consistent with psychological anthropology. That periodical is of primary interest to ethnopsychiatrists and others, including many cross- cultural and cultural psychologists in the mental health field, who are interested in understanding social and cultural determinants of psychopathology and psychosocial treatment of mental disorders and conditions. The only organizational structures with which it is obviously affiliated are the broad international psychiatric and clinical psychology communities. The Human Relations Area Files (HRAF) constitute a valuable resource for culture- oriented research. The Files, inaugurated in 1937, were the brainchild of anthropologist George Peter Murdock. The main Files are located at Yale University, with other institutions in the United States and elsewhere housing them (see Appendix A for further information). 
Multiculturalism, Polyculturalism, Intercultural Psychology (“Culture- Mixing”) The term “multiculturalism” has most frequently been used in highly ethnically (culturally) diverse nations, such as Canada and the United States, two of the most ethnically diverse nations in the world. It is sometimes difficult to differentiate among multicultural psychology, cultural, and cross- cultural psychology, especially when academic programs tout multiculturalism as their emphasis but often use the same texts and publish in the same journals as the other two groupings. For instance, Heine’s (2012) text, Cultural Psychology, is as useful to cross- cultural psychologists as it is to cultural psychologists. On the other hand, those who strongly identify with multiculturalism tend to focus on the ills, problems, and issues that face the plethora of ethnic groups in pluralistic nations. Social justice, prejudice, bias, discrimination, stereotyping, inequalities in education and employment, and other social problems are examples of the topics most frequently visited by multiculturalists (see Berry, 2017). The APA has been quite active in multiculturalism. The influential Handbook of Multicultural Psychology (Leong, 2014) as well as Berry (in press) are excellent sources of information in this area. A chapter in volume 1 of that two- volume set is devoted to the teaching of multicultural psychology (Dunn & Hammer, 2014). 
An extremely active area under the rubric of multiculturalism involves acculturation psychology (Sam & Berry, 2016; see also Chapter 20 by Colleen Ward and Ágnes Szabó in this volume) and intercultural relations. Some curricular perspectives in psychology may want to focus only on this domain of theory and research. The ongoing project titled Mutual Intercultural Relations in Pluralistic Societies (MIRIPS) is especially relevant (Berry, 2017). A description of this 17- nation project is available online at http:// www.victoria.ac.nz/ cacr/ research/ mirips. 
Berry (in press) noted that the domain of multiculturalism at the societal level includes the actual presence of cultural diversity, social equity, and social cohesion in culturally plural societies, and the policy orientations that a society takes in these issues. At the psychological level, the study of multiculturalism includes attitudes toward diversity and equity, and the degree to which individuals are willing to change in order to accommodate this diversity and accept equity. 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  21 
Another example of this hybridization is in the area of counseling that involves counselors from one cultural or ethnic group and clients who have different cultural or ethnic backgrounds. The first edition of Counseling Across Cultures (Pederson, Lonner, & Draguns, 1976)  was published under the assumption that it would be used in the training of counselors throughout the world. Over the years, it became clear that counseling, as known in the industrialized West, is largely a North American field. Because of this, the seventh edition was explicitly designed primarily for use with ethnic and immigrant clients in the United States and Canada (Pedersen, Lonner, Draguns, Trimble, & Scharron- del Rio, 2016). However, Gerstein et  al.’s (2009) edited text, International Handbook of Cross- Cultural Counseling: Cultural Assumptions and Practices Worldwide, contains numerous chapters from professionals in many countries. 
Consider also the concept of polyculturalism, a relatively new term closely related to both indigenous psychology and especially multiculturalism (recall Question 2 posed earlier). According to its proponents, polyculturalism 
assumes that individuals’ relationships to cultures are not categorical but rather are partial and plural; it also assumes that cultural traditions are not independent, sui generis lineages but rather are interacting systems. Individuals take influences from multiple cultures and thereby become conduits through which cultures can affect each other. (Morris, Chiu, & Liu, 2015) 
Morris et al. proposed the term as an alternative to traditional perspectives, such as cultural and cross- cultural psychology, because of their limitations. Polycultural thinking is obviously more important whenever different cultures or ethnic groups interact frequently, such as in widespread migration and, therefore, integration and adaptation. In short, cultures affect each other in a dynamic myriad of adaptation, adjustment, and integration. See Rosenthal and Levy (2000) for a detailed discussion of the various ideological approaches to improving intergroup attitudes and relations in pluralistic societies. Polemics and research on culture mixing, another term that has recently stepped surfaced, was the focus of a recent special issue of the JCCP (Hao, Dongmei Li, Peng, Peng, & Torelli, 2016). (In this volume, see also Chapter 2 by Michael Harris Bond, and Chapter 19 by Ying- yi Hong and Siran Zhan for discussions about polyculturalism.) 
A developing new perspective, intercultural psychology, is a subfield whose proponents examine how individuals who were socialized in one culture reestablish their lives in another culture. The concept of “culture mixing” is obviously linked to intercultural psychology. Berry (in press), as noted earlier, assembled a bibliography for these various perspectives. Intercultural psychology and culture mixing are especially appropriate in the ongoing crises in immigration and acculturation. The psychology of acculturation has become a field almost on its own. Colleen Ward and Ágnes Szabó, in Chapter 20, cover that burgeoning area. 
This section has presented an all- too-brief overview of several different yet in some ways strikingly similar perspectives in psychology that focus on culture as a crucial factor 
22 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
in the development of humans. As mentioned earlier, we presented this material because of our belief that teachers of a culture- oriented psychology should have a basic understanding of the various current perspectives that elaborate relations between culture and psychology. At the same time, knowledge of those perspectives can inform teachers of their own perspective, and this material helps teachers address the three questions we posed at the beginning of this chapter. Together, this should help them understand how they comprehend (and thus teach) culture- oriented psychology, along with the strengths and weaknesses of their approaches. 
We close this discussion about the bouquet of psychology and culture endeavors with a noteworthy tale. At the Twenty- second International Conference of the IACCP in 2014, in Reims, France, a special 2- hour symposium was on the program. Titled “On the Road to Half a Century of Cross- Cultural Psychology: Foundations, Current Status, and Forecasts,” it featured six psychologists, each of whom had been involved in the field for about 50 years (see Roland- Lévy, Denoux, Voyer, Boski, & Gabrenya, 2016). The short presentations by these seasoned scholars appear in the first unit of their book, in a section labeled “Diversity in Theories.” Easily printable as pdf documents, this group of presentations would be excellent references for class discussion. Toward the end of the symposium, it was pointed out that while all participants were devoted cross- cultural psychologists, most were also active in one or more of the other perspectives mentioned earlier. “It’s a Big Tent now,” became an instant mantra. Meaning, of course, that all of these stems in the bouquet grow and flourish, in similar and often convergent ways, under the same celestial roof that is home to more than seven billion souls. 
The Ongoing Search for Psychological Universals In the introduction to this chapter, we noted that one issue that teachers of a culture- oriented psychology have to deal with is the question of how human psychological processes and behaviors are constituted (recall Questions 2 and 3 posed earlier). This issue, in turn, raises questions about the existence of psychological universals and permeates differences among the multiple approaches to the study of culture and psychology described in the previous section. It is inevitable that any broad- banded psychological endeavor, such as a theory, that features the concept of culture will, at some point, be obliged to consider the matter of psychological universals. We assert that it would be impossible to conduct research or to teach culture- centered courses that either explicitly or implicitly compare or contrast different cultures in any psychological topic without considering universals. Even if a scholar dismisses universals as a useful concept, he or she should be compelled to explain the reasons for taking that stance. It is axiomatic that anything that is not absolutely a human universal (the facticity of life and its certain end, for example) must be understood on both culture- general and culture- specific terms. 
 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  23 
The “etic– emic dilemma” (sometimes called the “insider– outsider debate”) usually enters conversations about universals or their absence. Borrowed from psycholinguis-tics, where phonetics involve universal speech utterings and phonemics deal with culture- specific sounds (Pike, 1967), cross- cultural psychologists use the suffixes of etics and emics to explore the extent to which they need to be concerned with a universal (etic) comparative base (see Berry, 1969, and virtually any book that focuses on cross- cultural research methods). 
This section provides an overview of ongoing contemporary perspectives that have been prominent in the study of universals. Following that, several examples of research and scholarship that tend to rely on universalistic thinking will be briefly summarized. Table 1.1 depicts a general framework that succinctly covers three “isms”:  absolutism, relativism, and universalism. 
In Table 1.1 the absolutism quadrant represents “hardliners” who hold that to study one person in one culture is to study all persons in all cultures, which, ipso facto, is to ig-nore all cultural factors and to assume homogeneity in methods. The relativism quadrant represents cultural psychology, and the universalism quadrant represents cross- cultural psychology. The no- no quadrant has little meaning unless one entertains a sort of scientific nihilism. See Fontaine (2011) for a more detailed discussion of the absolutism- relativism- universalism debate. 
Another useful perspective in looking at universals was proposed nearly 70 years ago by Aberle, Cohen, Davis, Levy, and Sutton (1950). They asserted that several “functional prerequisites” must be met if a society is to remain a “going concern.” They noted that “A comparative social science requires a generalized system of concepts which will enable the scientific observer to compare and contrast large bodies of concretely different social phenomena in consistent terms” (p. 100). These societal prerequisites adjust over time in response to environmental and other circumstances (Hermans & Kempen, 1998). The prerequisites state that functioning societies maintain a system of roles and statuses, have higher and lower statuses, exercise a gender- and age- based division of labor, provide for the socialization of children and others, have a shared cognitive organization and world- view, normalize the expression of emotion (see Chapter  12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang), and do something concrete about behavior that the society deems abnormal and disruptive. These posited universals, albeit at a high level of abstraction, were central to

a widely cited article by Berry (1969) titled “On Cross- Cultural Comparability.” Because cross- cultural psychology is identified strongly with making comparisons in an effort to understand differences and similarities in human behavior among people in different societies (cultures), these prerequisites form a base from which to work. 
Universal Aspirations in Culture- Oriented Psychology When the modern movement in cross- cultural psychology was approaching its adolescence, Lonner (1980) proposed the existence of seven levels, or types, of universals: simple, variform (variations of simple, but not total uniformity), functional, diachronic, ethologically oriented, systematic behavioral, and “cocktail party.” That proposal, which was a chapter in the seminal Handbook of Cross- Cultural Psychology (Triandis et al., 1980), served as a useful explanatory scheme for a decade. It was then surpassed by the work of anthropologist Donald Brown (1991). In an unprecedented tour- de- force book- length compendium of many efforts to explain the nature and scope of universals, Brown built a solid case for the continued study of universals and offered a new question: “given the inherent tendency for disparate peoples to develop disparate cultures, how on earth can some things be the same everywhere” (p. 88). In  chapter 6 of his book, Brown discussed the nature of “Universal People” (UP) and provided informative examples. The UP, for example: 
 • name things and develop taxonomies that are fundamental to UP cognition  • have language and employ gestures, especially with their hands  • are moved by sexual attraction  • have distinct patterns of preparing for birth  • have groups which they define by locality  • develop a pattern for socialization; children aren’t left alone to grow up on their own  • differentially develop ways of assigning prestige  • have divisions of labor, minimally based on sex and age  • have families with relationships defined by their members  • have governments and leaders. 
Brown described many other characteristics of UP that are worthy of lively classroom discussion. That book, with its extensive annotated bibliography, is highly recommended for its clarity and thoroughness and would serve as a guide to the many scholarly discussions centered on human universals. Brown disavowed culture as the paramount factor in shaping human behavior, but he asserts that it can be on par with genes, for example, in defining what constitutes humanness. That’s all the more reason to promote the study of human behavior across the globe. 
Some 20 years later, Norenzayan and Heine (2005) offered a fresh look at psychological universals. A central concern they addressed was to reject absolutistic thinking, which, much more than relativistic or even universalistic thinking, had been common 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  25 
in psychological methodology for decades— which is a major reason why the call for a more culture- oriented psychology emerged with a flourish about 50 years ago. The main problem involves the level of abstraction used in research. At high levels of abstraction (e.g., all people eat and drink, show aggression, play games, etc.), results would be too diffuse to be of any benefit. Conversely, if the level of abstraction is too low (e.g., a strange and particularistic aspect of behavior), establishing some pattern or even a near- universal would be difficult if not impossible. 
For these reasons, Norenzayan and Heine advocated finding a methodology that is sensitive to levels and employs a decision- tree analysis. They proposed “three levels of universals and one case of non- universal that can be observed cross- culturally” (p. 772). Using a mental “toolbox” analogy (Cole, 1996)  and decision flowchart, the process involves existential, functional, and accessibility universals and the nonuniversal case (see Figure 1.1). 
In mainstream psychology, especially in the field of psychometrics and psychological testing, researchers have developed thousands of ways to measure traits, abilities, interests, values, and other constructs of human action. The vast majority of these efforts have tacitly assumed that accessibility universals were at the core of their culture- comparative research. As explained by Norenzayan and Heine (2005),
