cultures (it is also a functional universal); and c) it is accessible to the same degree across cultures. (p. 772) 
Many cross- cultural psychologists have been similarly engaged in a quest to discover a logical semblance of order out of immense and often bewildering (to outsiders) variations in human behavior (Lonner, 2011). This involves searching for a dichotomy, trichotomy, taxonomy, pattern, structure, or stage- oriented sequence of development, morality, abnormality, or any other popular way to categorize, describe, and measure the range of behavior in some domain of interest. Some sort of coherent organization would presumably open the door leading to the interpretation of behavior. Because categorizing and counting are features of universal cognition, these propensities have frequently been used to create order in human thought and behavior, much like what Mendeleyev did when he developed the Table of Chemical Elements, what Linnaeus accomplished with binomial nomenclature in botany, and what Kraepelin contributed when he introduced his taxonomy of psychopathology. 
Closer to our conceptual home, the anthropologist Ruth Benedict searched for regularities in the “great arc of potentialities” in personality described in her famous book, Patterns of Culture (Benedict, 1934). (Note that the title she chose was not “dis-jointed elements of culture.”) A  member of the then- popular Culture and Personality School, Benedict believed that there are patterns of behavior shared by all members of a culture as a function of the demands of unique environmental factors. The ancients did similar things, and so did the pseudoscientists a century or more ago when they developed “theories” such as astrology, phrenology, or physiognomy. Still proposing numerous ways to devise ways to order patterns of thought and behavior, for culture- oriented psychologists the concepts of introversion and extraversion are among the more salient examples. To say that Jesse is an introvert is to say a lot, but it also says little when great deviations in expected behavior are easy to find. Furthermore, if used in extremis, they can lead to hurtful and malicious stereotyping. In cross- cultural psychology, quite a number of explanatory structures have been advanced, with undoubtedly more to come. Likewise, to say that Abdul (or Elizabeth) has many close friends because he (or she) is from a collectivistic (or individualistic) society may be too broad a brush in explaining the behavior of individuals. The higher the level of abstraction, such as an entire country, the more unlikely it is to find total commonality at the lowest level (the individual). 
The existence of psychological universals has implications for how teachers (and researchers) think about how human behavior is constituted and the relative contributions of biological (i.e., nature) and cultural (i.e., nurture) factors (recall Question 3). The study of psychological universals will no doubt continue unless, of course, a completely culture- free psychology emerges sometime in the future. At that hypothetical point, the debate surrounding absolutism, relativism, and universalism will be abated, and a truly pancultural psychology will have settled the argument. Until that highly improbable time arrives, the culture- oriented perspectives in psychology, and indeed all of psychology, 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  27 
will have to work through the uncertainties that exist in the complex world involving a witch’s brew mixture of human mind, thought, culture, and behavior. 
How Have Researchers Documented the Link Between Culture and Psychology? One issue for teachers (and researchers) to grasp is how scientific methods have empirically linked culture with psychological processes and behaviors. Over the years, the field has come far from merely documenting cultural differences in a variety of psychological processes and behaviors to developing sophisticated ways of quantifying the relationship between culture and psychology. Perhaps more than any other effort in psychology, dimensionalizing, categorizing, pigeonholing, and in general searching for “patterns” in various psychological domains has been a strong emphasis in culture- comparative research (and in cultural psychology itself, as exemplified in the popular area of trying to unravel patterns or dimensions of self; see Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith on cultural dimensions and Chapter 17 by Amir Rosenmann and Jenny Kurman, on culture and self). In a wide- ranging class in cross- cultural psychology, it would be beneficial and productive to devote time to explain and discuss a sample of ways that cross- cultural psychologists have developed to empirically link, and thus help explain, how culture influences human behavior. In fact, the theoretical frameworks of teachers (and researchers) on this fundamental question concerning the relationship of culture and psychology will undoubtedly frame how one teaches (and conducts studies); thus, addressing this underlying question is one of paramount importance for all scholars. 
Fortunately, there has been a distinct progression of such methods to do so. Lonner (1975) noted that there were three eras in cross- cultural psychology. These eras brought an increase in the sophistication of methods (see also Chapter 2 by Michael Harris Bond, this volume). Some three decades later, Matsumoto and Yoo (2006) made a similar observation when they noted an evolution in cross- cultural research methods, which obviously included a variety of ways to help explain complex relations between mind and culture. Matsumoto and Yoo identified three generations (phases) of cross- cultural research. The first phase utilized simple cross- cultural comparisons, where similarities and differences between (usually) two cultures were measured by using a range of assessment devices usually developed by Western psychologists. The second phase featured the identification of meaningful dimensions of cross- cultural variability. Three examples of activities in this phase are Hofstede’s so- called work- related values, including individualism– collectivism; Schwartz’s circumplex of values; and the development of the NEO- PR- R, a tool to measure personality factors. These developments were notable to the field because they provided ways that allowed researchers to quantify cultures— and individuals within and across cultures— which in turn allowed for their operationalization in research. These developments facilitated the evolution of the third phase of cross- cultural research 
 
 
28 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
identified by Matsumoto and Yoo, which has been concerned with making further advances in the field. This phase especially addressed the cultural attribution fallacy— that country names were simply replaced with dimension labels. As noted earlier in this chapter, a recent special issue of the JCCP (Fischer & Poortinga, 2018a) addresses a number of important methodological challenges and their solutions. 
The following sections are brief descriptions of these three popular ways to dimensionalize common aspects of behavior at both the personal level and the group, or culture, level. More complete and comprehensive descriptions of these topics exist; here, we briefly describe their contributions to an empirical science linking culture and psychology for teachers. 
Cultural Dimensions One of the major questions that has plagued theory and research on culture and psychology concerns the question of how to understand cultures along meaningful dimensions of variability so that those dimensions can be used to understand the interactions between culture and psychology in more significant ways. Fortunately, the past few decades have produced several major ways to do so, which we briefly introduce here (see also Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith, this volume, for an extended discussion). The development of these dimensions has been important not only for theory building, but also empirically because they provided researchers with culture- level data with which to empirically link data concerning psychological processes and behaviors on the individual level in mediation, moderation, or multilevel analyses. For this reason, they have been an incredibly useful development in the evolution of cross- cultural studies and in thinking about, and thus teaching, a globalizing psychology. 
Individualism– Collectivism and the Hofstede Dimensions The dichotomy (or continuum) of individualism– collectivism has been used for decades in a great variety of scholarly efforts in the social sciences. Its origins date back to German philosophies under the archaic rubrics of Gemeinschaft (individualism) and Gesellschaft (society, community or “the collective”). It is among the most widely used dichotomies in culture- related and international discourse and scholarship (see Kagitçibasi, 1997; Triandis, 1995). Countless research projects have used individualism– collectivism as a primary intervening or moderator variable, making it among the most widely used bifurcations in the history of psychological excursions into the cultural and behavioral repertoire. 
At the societal level, the dichotomy (or continuum) of individualism– collectivism is a dominant explanatory construct, whereas at the individual level the dichotomy (or continuum) of introversion– extraversion is an analogous and equally dominant explanatory construct in terms of its ubiquitous application in its respective area. However, individualism– collectivism’s influence as a sort of one- stroke “life raft” explanatory construct in research will likely fade, albeit slowly. Still, a solid understanding 
 
 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  29 
of individualism– collectivism and how it has been used in culture- oriented studies is currently essential. In Hofstede’s well- known scheme of work- related values, individualism– collectivism is the most dominant of the five values associated with his work. Introduced in 1980, Hofstede’s other values are power– distance, uncertainty avoidance, and masculinity– femininity (Hofstede, 1980, 2001). A fifth value, long- term versus short- term orientation, was added some years later (see iaccp/ orpc.org). The Hofstede dimensions have primarily been used to measure values at the level of cultures, or regions within cultures or countries. For instance, a grouping of countries in the industrialized Western world (e.g., the United States, Canada, Australia, and Germany) form a cluster at the individualism pole, while various non- Western and Asian countries cluster at the collectivism pole. 
Social Axioms A more recent idea that, like Aberle et al.’s scheme mentioned earlier, operates at the highly abstract cultural level is Leung and Bond’s Social Axioms Theory (Leung & Bond, 2004, 2010; see also Chapter 2 by Michael Harris Bond). Social axioms are generalized beliefs about people, groups, institutions, the physical environment, the spiritual world, and various categories of social events. These generalized beliefs are encoded in the form of assertions about relationships between entities. The axioms and a brief explanation of each are 
 • Social cynicism: A negative assessment of human nature, biased views against some groups of people, mistrust of social institutions, and a belief that people disregard ethical means in achieving their ends. 
 • Social complexity: A belief that there are multiple ways of achieving a given outcome, as well as a belief that a given person’s behavior is inconsistent from situation to situation. 
 • Reward for application: A belief that effort, knowledge, careful planning, and the in-vestment of various resources and hard work will lead to positive results. 
 • Religiosity (originally called Spirituality): Belief in the existence of a supernatural being and the beneficial social functions of religious institutions and practice. 
 • Fate control: A belief that life events are determined by grand external forces, but also a reassuring belief that there are some ways for people to influence the impact of such forces. 
Tight vs. Loose Cultures First proposed by a Finnish anthropologist (Pelto, 1968), the construct and theory of cultural tightness and looseness proposed a continuum that can be useful to assess the degree to which social entities such as corporations and organizations are “tight” (rule- governed, with little tolerance for deviations) as opposed to “loose” (few strongly enforced rules and greater tolerance for deviations). The theory has usually been applied to the structures and policies of large organizations, but it can be used for any aggregate social entity, such 
 
 
30 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
as universities, city councils, or political organizations (Gelfand, Nishii, & Raver, 2006; Gelfand et al., 2011). The tightness– looseness continuum can be contrasted with other country- level attributes such as values, personality structures, and social axioms. For instance, intuitively, individualism correlates positively with “looseness” and collectivism with “tightness.” Harrington and Gelfand (2014) employed the construct in an analysis of various dimensions that characterize the 50 United States. 
The Schwartz Value Structure Assessing values, both individually and collectively, has a long history in psychology and other social sciences. In recent years, this assessment has been accomplished with the use of the Schwartz Value Scale (SVS). The SVS, in questionnaire format, has been a fruitful way to measure values at the societal level (Schwartz, 1992, 2006; Tormos, Vauclair, & Dobewall, 2017). The SVS espouses a circumplex (wheel) of nine values, arranged under four higher order categories:  Openness (Hedonism, Stimulation, Self- Direction), Self- Transcendence (Universalism, Benevolence), Conservation (Tradition, Conformity, and Security), and Self- enhancement (Achievement, Power and Security). All of these values are posited as pan- cultural. 
Personality Traits Major culture- oriented contributions during the past few decades concern studies documenting the universality of personality traits (see also Chapter  13 by Jüri Allik and Anu Realo). The emergence of a universal pattern of personality traits represented a popular way to dimensionalize human behavior, but primarily at the individual level (as opposed to the cultural level, which the dimensions described previously describe). The primary method to assess personality traits across cultures utilizes the so- called “Big Five” device. With a lengthy history in the popular (and indispensable to psychology) area of personality assessment, the NEO- PI- 3 and its earlier versions were designed to measure 30 personality traits, or factors, that are grouped under five superordinate domains: Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. Since these factors are deemed as universal as biophysical markers such as height, weight, and skin color, the NEO- PI- 3 has, since its inception, been one of the more widely used measures of personality in cross- cultural psychology (Allik et al., 2017; Allik & McCrae, 2004). Researchers in this areas often collaborate in multicultural strategies that involve the NEO- PE (de Raad et al., 2014; McCrae et al., 2005). 
Aside from cultural dimensions and personality traits, there are multiple other ways to “assess” culture on the individual and cultural levels (e.g., self- construal scales). There are also experimental manipulations that can be and have been used. They primarily involve the technique of priming to demonstrate the “effects” of culture on psychological processes and behaviors (for a review, see Matsumoto & Yoo, 2006). All of these methodologies and their associated theoretical implications can and should be considered by teachers of a culture- oriented psychology in order to understand better 
 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  31 
the relation between culture and psychology and to address the three questions posed in the introduction to this chapter. 
Advances in Conceptualizing Methodologies The methods just described, along with numerous other ways to dimensionalize behavior, have been instrumental in the third phase of the evolution in cross- cultural assessment that Matsumoto and Yoo (2006) noted. The main characteristic of this phase is a striking improvement in understanding complex interactions between, for instance, individualism– collectivism scores at the cultural level and self- construals at the individual level (Markus & Kitayama, 1991). Hence, the construct of an independent– interdependent sense of self entered the field in a big way. Likewise, Nisbett’s (2003) treatise on Eastern (holistic) versus Western (analytic) thought provided yet another dichotomy that has been used in countless studies, frequently including dozens of cultures/ countries and contributing authors (also see Chapter 11 by Qi Wang and Sawa Senzaki for more discussion about the analytic- holistic perspective). 
The great expansion of the cyberworld has played a significant role in the evolution of studies in the third phase. Until about 1990, and especially before the advent of the ubiquitous Internet, collaboration between scholars in different countries was rather slow and plodding. It was unusual for more than about three or four psychologists to work on the same project and to publish their research. During the past two decades, there has been a striking increase in collaboration (see Lonner, 2019). It is now common to read journal articles with dozens of co- authors, most of whom have never banged on a regular typewriter and patiently awaited routine and infinitely slower “snail mail.” Many of these cyberteam workers have never met each other. The Internet, Facebook, Twitter, Skype, Wiki, and other marvels of the cyberworld have revolutionized the kind of research that employs scales or tests designed to measure values, personality, or any other psychological attributes to determine if they provide a universal template in a great variety of cultures. Of course, this type of research methodology also has implications for the depth of knowledge about culture and psychology generated. 
There are hundreds of other ways to measure things in psychology, a scientific discipline that is drawn to the measurement and analysis of a great assortment of human mental facilities. Alternatively, it is a discipline that strives to understand the “enigmatic other”— a phrase used by cultural psychologist Ernest Boesch to help describe how difficult it is to plumb the depths of the complex human psyche and how it is manifested in a cacophony of culture- based alterations. Alas, space does not permit us to continue with additional examples of how such activities can be used in psychology classes. However, in teaching psychology, a productive class activity could involve searching the literature for various means that cross- cultural psychologists have used in their efforts to help understand both societal and individual differences and similarities throughout the world. The other chapters in this Handbook can be the first step in such a search. 
 
32 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Cultural Coverage in Introductory Psychology Texts It is important to discuss the nature and scope of cultural coverage in introductory psychology texts (IPTs) for they usually give students their first real taste of psychology as a science. IPTs have always been natural bellwethers of the discipline. Their authors attempt to capture the contemporary tenor of psychological knowledge, theory, and applications. The texts they produce are then used in one of the most popular undergraduate courses in the United States, Canada, and other countries around the world, many in translated and abridged editions. The authors of IPTs do an admirable job of introducing psychology to more than 2 million students per year worldwide. The texts are colorful, attractive, and nicely organized. Academic psychologists surely know of these texts, none of which has ever had a title such as Introduction to Psychology in the Western World. Many instructors also teach about culture in other courses, especially developmental and social psychology (see Smith & Best, 2009). In short, these fixtures in beginning courses capture the elementary essence of contemporary psychology and influence the many students who choose psychology for further study. But how many of them do a credible job of introducing students to the world beyond their borders? 
Early psychology texts rarely, if ever, mentioned culture; culture does not appear, for example, in James’s (1892/ 1961) Psychology: The Briefer Course; in Ladd’s (1894) Primer of Psychology; or in Titchener’s (1910) A Textbook of Psychology. As the discipline matured and the world became more diverse and globalized, psychologists began to expand their horizons. While some earlier psychologists went across the grain and considered other cultures, as explained earlier in this chapter, it wasn’t until the mid- to late 1960s that an increasing number of psychologists began to include culture as a powerful factor in their thinking and research. The explosion of culture- oriented research half a century ago should have led to a large increase in cultural coverage in IPTs. Cush and Buskist (1997) even went so far as to proclaim that future IPTs would be replete with culture coverage. Unfortunately, they were wrong— but not entirely. For example, 1 year later, Miller and Gentile (1998) found that cross- cultural psychology was among the least important topics within the discipline to be covered. 
In the late 1980s, Elke Rumple (now Murdock), a graduate student from Germany, conducted a detailed examination of the extent to which culture was mentioned in 35 IPTs. She found a paucity of culture coverage (see Lonner, 1989). Twenty years later, that project was replicated with a sample of 40 IPTs. Although there was a clear increase in cultural coverage in those texts, and while some texts (e.g., Myers & DeWall, 2015) now specifically mention cross- cultural issues and research, the changes have not been as striking as Cush and Buskist (1997) predicted (Griggs & Jackson, 2013; Lonner & Murdock, 2008). Similar findings have been reported for a sample of social psychology texts used in Canada (Scott & Safdar, 2016). 
 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  33 
There are several possible reasons why the inclusion of culture in IPTs has not been as generous as expected. Prominent reasons are (1) some authors’ limited familiarity with relevant culture- saturated books and journal articles; (2)  limited space in IPTs, where only the basics in the growing field of psychology can be covered; (3) the authors’ belief that relatively immature students are not yet ready for the complexity of culture coverage; and (4) the implicit assumption that the study of culture belongs to the private domain of anthropology or perhaps in other courses in the instructor’s department. On the other hand, we can say with confidence that the coverage of culture, generally, in psychology books, journal articles, and conferences is here to stay. Every corner of psychological research, theory, and its various applications has not only found culture, but it is also often featured in a great variety of psychological outpourings. A mere trickle half a century ago, now research employing culture as a powerful factor in affecting thought and behavior has grown into a sizeable river. 
We believe that the introductory psychology course as taught at the reader’s college or university should increase its important role in serving as an excellent starting point in incorporating culture in understanding psychology. At the very least, it would be informative— and a good project for energetic students— to assess the nature and scope of psychology education as it pertains to culture and ethnicity at the local level. 
Closing Comments The inclusion of culture in the psychology curriculum has increased dramatically since the discipline broke from philosophy to become a valuable and indispensable mainstay in modern life. In psychology’s early days, culture was only rarely mentioned, and, in the earliest texts introducing psychology (the now- ubiquitous “intro psych” texts), culture as a vital factor in shaping human behavior was almost completely avoided. However, over the years, the situation changed dramatically. The mid- 1960s mark the period when culture was no longer either marginalized or dismissed as a real force in psychological theory, research, and applications (Lonner, 2013). An explosion of books, journals, organizations, conferences, research projects, and other activities that feature culture has occurred. This Handbook and similar resources involving hundreds of culture- oriented psychologists attest to this remarkable growth. 
All of these developments have resulted in the assimilation of culture as an important part of the curricular offerings in psychology, but not in a uniform manner. For instance, the presence of culture in most of the currently available basic psychology texts remains quite variable. Most of them mention culture in more or less significant ways, but with still wide variations among the 40– 50 extant texts. While some introductory texts (e.g., Myers & DeWall, 2015) pay much more attention to culture than others, some have sparse coverage. Curiously, no broad- banded text introducing psychology to vast 
 
34 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
numbers of new students has ever emphatically featured culture throughout its pages. It may be that the inclusion of culture in a very busy and expanding discipline has reached (or is nearing) its asymptote. Compensating for this limited coverage in basic texts, the past 30 years have produced a striking increase in the number of texts that are entirely devoted to culture- oriented research. Some of these texts were mentioned previously. A logical assumption to make is that the more culture- oriented texts there are, the less pressure there is for IPT authors to include culture in their efforts to cover the expanding range of topics in an increasingly popular discipline. 
Nevertheless, we consider it imperative to include culture and its linkage to all psychological topics. In a shrinking and troubled world, the more that students know about cultural influences on thought and behavior, the more able they will be when they reach the real world. 
We began this chapter by posing three questions that we believe teachers of a culture- oriented psychology should pose to themselves to aid them in framing and developing their courses. Subsequently, we provided a background that we believe can help teachers address those questions and be useful in thinking about, developing, and administering various courses in a standard psychology curriculum. This chapter may help instructors as they outline and organize course syllabi and activities, prepare for lectures, or assign readings. The authors of this chapter can attest to the great challenges and even greater enjoyment in teaching about the myriad factors out there— beyond our perceived geographic and cognitive borders— that affect the lives, thoughts, and behavior of people throughout the world. We believe that a psychology that does not include the power of culture in shaping the lives of people everywhere is an incomplete discipline as well as a dangerous exercise in ethnocentric thinking. Psychology instructors must be mindful not only of the teaching of culture, but also of the culture of teaching (Keith, 2012). We hope that the information and details provided in this chapter will prove helpful to all who give culture the serious attention it deserves in psychology education. 
We end this overview with the suggestion to use Appendix A when searching for additional resources in the planning of curricular efforts. A second and closely related list of resources for scholarship and teaching in the area of cross- cultural psychology is found in Unit 11 (Teaching Cross- Cultural Psychology) of the Online Readings in Psychology and Culture (https:// scholarworks.gvsu.edu/ orpc/ ). This list contains the names, locations, and contact information for centers, units, and committees in (usually) departments of psychology at many colleges and universities in numerous countries. Syllabi for teaching courses in this area as well as information that may lead to cooperation and collaboration are included. These units are rich sources of information, including course syllabi, reading lists, and other aids that can be helpful for instruction in both undergraduate and graduate programs (see IACCP.org).
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  35 
Appendix A Resources: Associations and Organizations A number of associations and organizations that focus exclusively or largely on the interface between psychology and culture have emerged over the years. While complete information about them can easily be found on the Internet, brief descriptions of the scope of these resources are provided here. Many of these resources involve hundreds of psychologists who occasionally or routinely teach in the culture and psychology area. With a little effort, useful course syllabi can be found and requested. 
Alphabetical Order of Curricular Resources at the Association and Organizational Level American Psychological Association (APA). Established in 1892, it currently has about 118,000 members. With a great many activities, it has about 70 publications, mostly journals. While none of them is expressly devoted to culture, most publish culture- related articles. 
The APA’s organizational structure includes four entities that are relevant resources for our purposes:  • Division 2: The Society for the Teaching of Psychology (STP) is the only exclusively 
teaching- oriented division (Division 2) of the APA. The STP exists to advance understanding of psychological science by promoting excellence in the teaching and learning of the discipline. In recent years, the STP has extended its cultural reach through committees on diversity and international relations and through expanded educational programming at international psychology conferences. On its webpage (teachpsych.org/ ), STP provides such free- access teaching materials as syllabi for cross- cultural psychology courses. The STP also publishes a journal, Teaching of Psychology, in support of its mission. 
 • Division 45: The Society for the Psychological Study of Culture, Ethnicity, and Race encourages research on ethnic minority issues and the application of psychological knowledge to United States ethnic minority issues. The division promotes public welfare through research and encourages professional relationships among psychologists who share these concerns and interests. It publishes the quarterly journal Cultural Diversity and Ethnic Minority Psychology and the division newsletter, Focus, which is published two to three times per year. The Teaching Resources section of the newsletter contains documents that pertain to any aspect of teaching the study of culture, ethnicity, and race. It aims to catalog syllabi, activities, demonstrations, videos, PowerPoint presentations, and related resources to help instructors develop and improve course offerings. It encourages colleagues to also 
 
 
 
36 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
submit classroom activities, annotated bibliographies, film guides, lab manuals, advising aids, textbook compendiums, and other relevant instructional materials. All submissions are reviewed by volunteers serving on the Teaching Resources team. 
 • Division 52: International Psychology promotes global perspectives seeking to develop culturally inclusive, contextually informed psychological science. The division aims to support international connections, multicultural research and practice, and global application of psychological principles to public policy. Division 52 publishes a quarterly journal, International Perspectives in Psychology: Research, Practice, Consultation, and an online newsletter, International Psychology Bulletin. This division often sponsors symposia and other events at annual APA conventions that are valuable for the teaching of culture- related topics. 
 • The Committee on International Relations in Psychology (CIRP) is primarily concerned with the advancement of international relations and the promotion of culture- oriented research and scholarship. The CIRP sponsors an annual award that recognizes distinguished and enduring lifetime contributions to the international cooperation and advancement of knowledge in psychology. 
See www.apa.org for complete details of these four resources. Asian Association of Social Psychology (AASP). As noted in its website, the mis-
sion of this association is to provide scholars in Asia and the Pacific with a collaborative forum for capability building and the discussion, promotion, and publication of their research. Its main outlet for such research is the Asian Journal of Social Psychology. It also publishes a newsletter and an e- journal, the Journal of Pacific Rim Psychology. The AASP, formed in 1995, promotes research on Asian traditions, philosophies, and ideas that have scientific merit and practical applications, and expands the boundary, substance, and direction of social psychology by supplementing and integrating Western psychology’s focus on intraindividual processes with a broader and more holistic view from Asian culture and society. It also sponsors conferences and other activities. The AASP website is http:// asiansocialpsych.org. 
Gesellschaft für Kulturpsychologie (Society for Cultural Psychology). Paraphrasing its website, this organization was founded in Salzburg, Austria in 1986, where it still has its seat today. Its membership includes a confederation of largely German- speaking psychologists who are active both in scientific research and teaching as well as in different fields of applied psychology. It is internationally oriented and interested in interdisciplinary cooperation. The society’s objectives are the advancement of theoretical, empirical, and applied cultural and cross- cultural psychology as well as the promotion of relevant ideas in these fields. The journal, Psychology and Culture, is tied to the society in terms of overall purpose but is not its official publication. Its website (in German, but with an English version), is http:// www.kulturpsychologie.de. 
Human Relations Area Files (HRAF). As noted by HRAF on its website, the files are a compilation, indexing, and distribution of a collection of ethnographic and other 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  37 
texts that are indexed by culture and subject, from 400 member institutions located in more than 30 nations. HRAF indexes the information in its collection of ethnography by culture and subject. OWC is an acronym for the Outline of World Cultures, a systematic listing of the cultures of the world; an OWC code, or OWC number, is a culture identification code. The OWC number is a four- character alphanumeric ID derived from the classification scheme presented in the Outline of World Cultures. Each distinct culture in the list of Cultures Covered in eHRAF is assigned an OWC number, and text on that culture has been indexed using that OWC. OCM stands for “Outline of Cultural Materials,” a thesaurus- like listing of subject descriptors used to index the texts included in the eHRAF Collections. An OCM code, or OCM number, is a three- digit numeric code for a subject descriptor that is described in the Outline of Cultural Materials. The OCM lists approximately 80 broad terms and more than 700 narrower terms that are used to index the texts at the paragraph level. Both the OWC and OCM lists are available in the Web version of HRAF. An untold number of research projects have used HRAF to help develop hypotheses, coordinate research, aid in the completion of dissertations, and so forth. HRAF encourages teachers to use the Files in their classes. Because they are available online, their use in classes can be easily accessed (see http:// hraf.yale.edu/ ). 
International Academy of Intercultural Research (IAIR). This interdisciplinary organization was officially established in 1997. The main impetus for its existence was the realization that culture- oriented research was going on in a number of disciplines and that members of these disciplines could benefit from an exchange of different points of view. Psychology, Education, Communications, Anthropology, Sociology, and Marketing, among other academic orientations, are represented by both the main organizing com-mittee and the entire operation of the International Journal of Intercultural Relations, founded in 1976. The IAIR holds biennial conferences in different parts of the world. Complete details can be found at www.interculturalacadecy.org. 
International Association of Applied Psychology (IAAP). Created in 1919 by Édouard Claparède under the name of International Association of Psychotechnics (Association Internationale de Psychotechnique), it is among the oldest psychological associations in the world. The present name was adopted in 1955. International Congresses of Applied Psychology (ICAP) are organized every 4 years. It sponsors two journals: Applied Psychology: An International Review and Health and Well- Being. It is organized around 18 divisions. Each division has an online section, and the division is linked often to a specialized journal. The IAAP Handbook of Applied Psychology has been one of its main publications. IAAP is not specifically focused on culture, but its title and history clearly welcome cross- cultural research. Many of its members and officers have been active in culture- oriented research. Its website is http:// iaapsy.org/ . 
International Association for Cross- Cultural Psychology (IACCP). Inaugurated in 1972, IACCP’s exclusive focus is to promote and implement cross- cultural research in psychology. Among the Association’s goals is to promote the inclusion of culture in psychology and to help achieve a global psychology. It has about 750 members from 
38 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
more than 80 countries. It sponsors both international and regional conferences. Its of-ficial publications include the Cross- Cultural Psychology Bulletin, the Journal of Cross- Cultural Psychology (inaugurated in 1970 at Western Washington State College [now Western Washington University] and published by Sage Publications), and the e- book, Online Readings in Psychology and Culture. The latter was launched in 2001 at Western Washington University (it is now hosted by Grand Valley State University in Michigan) and was designed to be a major pedagogical aid. The home page for IACCP includes a link to Unit 11, the Teaching of Cross- Cultural Psychology. Please see IACCP.org for complete details. 
International Committee of Psychology Educators (ICOPE). The aim of the International Council of Psychology Educators (incorporated in New South Wales, Australia) is to advance psychology education around the world. The structure of ICOPE, founded in 2008, includes a full membership category of psychology educators and an affiliate membership of psychology students. The association builds on the ICOPE conferences initiated by Victor Karandashev and the late Sherri McCarthy in 2008 and on associated publications. The website for the organization is http:// www.psychliteracy.com/ icope- inc/ . 
International Society for Cultural and Activity Research (ISCAR) was founded in 2002 with the merging of two organizations formed in the earlier 1980s: the International Society for Cultural Research and Activity Theory and the Conference for Sociocultural Research. It is focused on sociocultural theory and its application to practice, and it has connections with several publications, including Ethos and Mind, Culture, and Activity: An International Journal, which is associated with the Laboratory of Comparative Human Cognition. 
International Union of Psychological Science (IUPsyS). The largest psychological organization in the world, the IUPsyS represents more than 1  million members from more than 80 countries, members of national psychology organizations worldwide, and 17 affiliate organizations. Founded in 1950, it sponsors international meetings every 4 years. Not specifically focused on culture- oriented psychology, its main concern is the advancement of psychology as a basic and applied science. The quarterly International Journal of Psychology, inaugurated in 1966, is its official publications. For further details, visit its website at www.iupsys.net. 
L’Association Internationale pour la Recherche Interculturelle (ARIC). Founded in Geneva in 1984, ARIC is devoted to intercultural research and related activities. It is multidisciplinary and is exclusively a Francophone association. With a Bulletin and annual conferences, it is an obvious site for research and education in countries and regions where French is the main or only language (especially France, Quebec, and Switzerland). Its website is http:// www.aric- interculturel.com. 
Society for Cross- Cultural Research (SCCR). As excerpted from its website, SCCR is a multidisciplinary organization. Its members all share a common devotion to the conduct of cross- cultural research. SCCR members are professionals and students 
CulTure and The PsyChology Curr iCulum  |  39 
from the social science fields of psychology, anthropology, sociology, and related fields including education, family studies, social work, human development, psychiatry, communications, ethnic studies, and business. A distinguishing characteristic of the Society, compared with other academic organizations, is that it is fundamentally interdisciplinary and provides members the opportunity to network with scholars from a wide variety of approaches to cross- cultural and comparative research. Since its founding in 1971, SCCR has hosted conferences that offer members and participants the opportunity to know each other better, form productive and lasting relationships, and provide genuine support to their fellow colleagues and students. Its quarterly journal, Cross- Cultural Research, publishes articles spread across many disciplines. SCCR is academi-cally linked to the Human Relations Area Files. SCCR’s website (http:// www.sccr.org/ ) contains links to many international resources, including those involved with teaching. 
Sociedad Interamericana de Psicologia, Inc. (SIP). Also known as the InterAmerican Society of Psychology, SIP was founded in Mexico City by a group of behavioral scientists in 1951. SIP is a member of the International Union of Psychological Sciences (IUPsyS), a division of the International Council of Scientific Unions. Through these groups, SIP is connected to international organizations such as UNESCO. The leadership of SIP includes members from North, Central, and South America and the Caribbean. The official languages of SIP are Spanish, English, Portuguese, and French. Its official publication is the InterAmerican Journal of Psychology, published three times a year. It accepts manuscripts from all areas of psychology and in all of the listed languages. Active members receive this publication and have electronic access to its bul-letin, InterAmerican Psychology: Bulletin. Among its goals is to contribute to international understanding by means of an enlarged understanding of cultural differences and communicating across national boundaries. SIP is active in many areas. For further information, see www.sipsych.org for complete details. 
Society for Intercultural Education, Training and Research (SIETAR). Founded in 1974, SIETAR is an international network for trainers and researchers in the area of international and cross- cultural communication. With more than 3,000 members worldwide, it draws together a network of national and regional networks. SIETAR was the publisher of the International Journal of Intercultural Relations until it was taken over by the IAIR (see earlier listing). Its website is www.sietarusa.org.
