Levels of Analysis Before examining the various dimensions of nation- level variance that have been identified, we need to consider the arguments for and against relying on dimensions to explain cultural differences. This involves a consideration of what might be the major purpose of cross- cultural psychology. What is it that we wish to explain? If our goal is to explain the differences that are found between the behaviors of individuals, that task has been extensively addressed by personality psychologists (see also Chapter 13 by Jüri Allik and Anu Realo). There are indeed modest differences between the average personality profiles of different nations (McCrae, Terracciano et al., 2005a; McCrae, Terracciano et al., 2005b), but there is much greater variance between individuals within a given nation (Poortinga & van Hemert, 2001), and to explain these differences we must undertake individual- level analyses. Conversely, if our goal is to understand the differences between predominant patterns of behavior in different regions or nations of the world, we must treat those higher level entities as units. If we try to understand global variation in terms of individual differences, we become entangled in what has variously been called Simpson’s paradox or the ecological fallacy (Robinson, 1950). 
The ecological fallacy is the belief that the relationship between two variables that is found in two or more samples will also be found if those samples are pooled. To understand this common misunderstanding better, consider some examples. Subjective well- being is found to be highest in the richest nations on earth (Diener, Diener, & Diener, 1995). However, at the individual level, the richest persons in most nations are not found to be the happiest (Diener & Biswas- Diener, 2002). In US elections, Republicans usually win the less wealthy states, and Democrats tend to win the richer states. Yet, at the individual level, those who vote Republican have tended to be wealthier than Democratic voters (Gelman, Park, Shor, Bafumi, & Cortina, 2008). These paradoxical effects occur because the causal factors influencing the correlations that are found at each level of analysis differ from one another. For instance, in relation to subjective well- being, we know that rich nations are able to afford a broader range of facilities and that this will enhance the well- being of many citizens. However, rich citizens will be indifferent to these resources because they can already control access to whatever facilities they desire. 
Of course, nations are not either wholly wealthy or completely impoverished. We can test the way in which subjective well- being and personal wealth are related to one another across the full range of levels of national wealth. Diener and Diener (1995) came close to doing this, but they focused on self- esteem rather than personal wealth. Across 31 nations, they found that the individual- level correlation between well- being and self- esteem grew stronger the more individualistic was the nation. As we shall see, nation- level individualism and national wealth are strongly correlated with one another. Thus, we can say that nation- level wealth moderates the relation found between individual- level variables of interest. More recent studies (e.g., Fischer & Boer, 2011) have addressed this kind of issue through the use of multilevel modeling, which can concurrently address 
 
70 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
the contribution of individual- level and nation- level components of effects. For the moment, I focus more simply on the utility of characterizing nations in ways that are useful to cross- cultural psychologists. 
Defining Cultural Contexts What Do We Mean by Culture? In the preceding discussion, wealth was used as an indicator of nation- level differences. Whether we can consider wealth to be an attribute of national culture depends on how we choose to define the concept of culture. After more than a century of debate, we have no consensual definition (Brown, Dickins, Sear, & Laland, 2011), but most authors would agree to treat it as an attribute of an entity shared across individuals. This could entail shared patterns of behavior, shared values, shared beliefs, shared ways of thinking about oneself and others, and so forth. Within this range of definitions, wealth is most certainly an attribute of culture since money is an abstract entity that has long since lost its relation to gold or any other physical entity that might have objective value. Money has a shared meaning because we are all socialized to believe it to be real and to allow our lives to be regulated on the basis of that shared belief. Nonetheless, most authors treat wealth as not falling within the definition of culture, arguing that it should be controlled statistically if we are to understand the relation between key cultural entities such as nations and the psychological phenomena that occur within them. 
The decision to discount wealth is particularly unfortunate because wealth satisfies many definitions of culture rather better than do some of the other candidates with which we may wish to characterize nations. Preferred bases for defining cultures have most frequently been based on attributes with known relevance to the prediction of individual behaviors, such as values, beliefs, and self- construals. If scores on these types of psychological attributes are aggregated to the nation level, they can portray the average endorse-ment of, for instance, a specific set of values, sometimes referred to as a citizen mean (Smith, Fischer, Vignoles, & Bond, 2013). 
However, in order to treat such averages as indicators of national culture, we need to know how much variability there is within a population. Does the average score reflect cultural homogeneity, or are there evident cultural differences between regions, occupations, genders, age groups, and so forth? Recent studies indicate that variance in values is much greater between individuals than between nations (Fischer & Schwartz, 2011), so if we wish to define cultures in terms of value priorities, we need to know more about how individuals relate their own values to those that are endorsed by others around them. Such an approach is by no means impossible. For instance, Schwartz (2014) proposes that 
[s] ocietal culture is a latent hypothetical construct. It cannot be observed directly, but can be inferred from its manifestations. The rich complex of meanings, 
 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  71 
beliefs, practices, symbols, norms and values prevalent among people in a society are among the manifestations of the underlying culture. They are not culture itself. (p. 6) 
In Schwartz’s view, the lack of consensus on values in a nation occurs because individuals are exposed to varying combinations of the differing institutional processes that comprise a society as a whole. Thus, by surveying a suitable set of manifestations of the underlying culture across a range of adequately representative samples we can come closest to defining the dimensions along which large groups vary. As Rohner (1984) helpfully summarized the issue some years ago, nations are not cultures, but nations have cultures. We can characterize nations in terms of prevailing values, attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors and, by so doing, identify relevant aspects of their cultures. 
Measuring Cultural Contexts If we wish to define the culture of a nation or some other large entity, we need to have some kind of yardstick against which each entity can be evaluated. Many cross- cultural studies have been conducted that compare samples from just two nations. By themselves, such studies can tell us little about cultural differences, although they may do so to some extent if they are designed in ways that enable them to draw on dimensions of nation- level variation that have been previously established. To define nation- level dimensions, one requires nation- level data from many nations, and these data must treat each nation as a single case, not as a series of individual cases. 
Hofstede (1980) was the first to realize that, to create defensible measures of dimensions of variation between nations, one must analyze the structure of aggregated item scores from one’s survey at the nation level. Computing a massive, multinational, individual- level factor analysis and then importing the dimensions thus defined to the nation level would render one vulnerable to the ecological fallacy. Nation- level means for individual items may factor together in different ways from those found in individual- level analyses, and they do so often (though not always) (Leung & Bond, 2007). 
Factor analyses and allied procedures require an adequate number of cases to ensure validity, and it is clear that, at the nation level, the available number of cases falls far short of what is typically recommended. However, nation- level means differ from individual- level means since each is based on aggregation of a substantial number of individual- level responses. Consequently, data from 30 or 40 nations have usually been treated as providing an adequate basis for defining their dimensions. We can best evaluate how problematic is this restricted sampling by examining the extent to which different studies are found to replicate the dimensions of variation that are identified. As we shall see, substantial replicability of dimensions is indeed found. In the next section, I examine in turn the best known studies whose authors have sought to define and measure dimensions of cultural variation, broadly following the historical sequence of their conduct. In subsequent 
 
72 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
sections, I consider how we may now be best able to use the nation- level dimensions that have been identified to explain different effects. 
The Search for Culture- Level Dimensions The Hofstede Project The study undertaken by Hofstede (1980) has become very well- known and has greatly influenced the subsequent development of cross- cultural research as well as forming the basis of many types of training programs focused on the development of cross- cultural interaction skills. In essence, Hofstede drew on a global databank of responses to morale surveys completed by employees of the IBM company. After extensive exploratory investigations, he was able to generate equivalent samples for each sampled nation by including only servicing and marketing employees and then controlling for differences in age, gender, and function. He next conducted nation- level factor analyses of specific groups of item means, which led him to define four nation- level dimensions of variance across the 50 nations and three regions for which he judged there to be an adequate number of individual cases. 
The definition of two dimensions— power distance and uncertainty avoidance— was based on Hofstede’s prior belief that hierarchy and stress were important aspects of organizational functioning. Relevant items were selected from the survey and subsequently shown to factor together at the nation level. The other two dimensions— individualism– collectivism and masculinity– femininity— were defined on the basis of factor analysis of 14 items identifying a range of work motives. Scores for collectivism and power distance were found to correlate strongly with one another, but Hofstede argued that it was beneficial to keep them separate. National wealth was shown to correlate positively with individualism and negatively with power distance. 
In more recent publications, the sample of nations for which scores are provided has been substantially increased (Hofstede, 2001; Hofstede, Hofstede, & Minkov, 2010). However, the additional scores are derived from different samples, and their value in comparison to the 1980 scores has been estimated by a complex adjustment procedure whose validity has not been evaluated (http:// geerthofstede.com/ research- and- vsm/ vsm- 2013). Sufficient studies have now been completed that we can examine in turn the definition and predictive validity of each of his original four dimensions. 
Individualism– Collectivism Hofstede (2001) defines individualistic societies as those in which individuals are separate from their social context, whereas in collectivistic societies individuals are inseparable from their social context. The items actually defining individualism– collectivism were ratings evaluating desirable aspects of one’s job. Nations scoring high on individualism had strong loadings on having “personal” time, freedom, and challenge. Nations scoring high 
 
 
 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  73 
on collectivism had stronger loadings on use of skills, good environmental conditions, and opportunities for training. Hofstede reasoned that these latter items imply dependence on others and therefore exemplify aspects of collectivism. Later commentators (e.g., Smith et al., 2013) have noted the tenuous connection between the items defining this dimension and the ways in which Hofstede himself and numerous other authors (e.g., Triandis, 1995)  have conceptualized individualism– collectivism as a dimension of culture. Nonetheless, scores on this dimension correlate with numerous other national- level indices even after controlling for wealth (Hofstede, 2001) and have been shown to predict a broad variety of cross- cultural effects (Kirkman, Lowe, & Gibson, 2006; Taras, Kirkman, & Steel, 2010). The meta- analysis conducted by Taras et  al. identified no less than 892 effects linking individualism– collectivism with dependent variables. Noting the risks of interpreting effects at different levels of analysis due to the ecological fallacy, they report separate summaries of effects obtained in studies at individual and nation levels. The mean size of 771 individual- level effects was 0.19, whereas for 87 nation- level effects it was 0.47. 
Power Distance Power distance was defined by Hofstede on the basis of employees’ perceptions of their superiors’ managerial style. Given its strong correlation with the dimension of individualism– collectivism, researchers have less often employed it as an independent predictor of effects. Taras et al. reported the mean of 164 individual- level effects as .15 and the mean of 71 nation- level effects as 0.45. 
Uncertainty Avoidance Uncertainty avoidance was defined by Hofstede on the basis of three items referring to the belief that rules should not be broken, the expectation that one may change jobs in the coming years, and the level of reported nervousness and tension at work. Taras et al. obtained a mean of 73 individual- level effects as .15, and a mean of 56 nation- level effects as .26. 
Masculinity– Femininity The masculinity- femininity dimension was derived by Hofstede from the same factor analysis that yielded the individualism– collectivism dimension. It is defined in terms of a contrast between work motives favoring recognition and achievement versus work motives favoring good relations with others and an agreeable living area. This dimension has proved much less attractive to researchers, perhaps due to ambivalence about the gendered naming of the dimension, and despite the further attempts of Hofstede (1998) to provoke interest in it. Taras et al. obtained a mean of 196 individual- level effects as .19, and a mean of 44 nation- level effects as .15. 
Overall, the Taras et al. meta- analysis indicates substantial predictive validity at the nation level, particularly for the associated dimensions of collectivism and power distance. 
 
 
 
74 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
However, many of the studies included small numbers of sampled nations, and the dependent measures varied greatly. Furthermore, in contrast to the correlations reported by Hofstede (2001), the meta- analytic results did not control for wealth. Nonetheless, the range of studies included in the analysis indicates the large and lasting impact of the Hofstede project. While some critics have derided the value of identifying dimensions (McSweeney, 2002), others have accepted the challenge to mount studies in which measures were purposively designed ahead of data collection and sampling was more fully representative. 
In designing such studies, it was particularly important to achieve greater clarity as to what aspects of national cultures are being tapped. Hofstede’s measures include items referring to aspects of values, beliefs, perceived behaviors, motives, and emotions. Measures with this degree of heterogeneity suffer from two major weaknesses. First, we cannot specify with any precision exactly what is the nature of the differences that have been identified. Second, we do not know to what extent the words used in these measures have equivalent meanings when translated into different languages. Subsequent researchers have sought to address these problems more thoroughly. 
Values as the Basis of Dimensions Subsequent to Hofstede’s project, the principal basis on which researchers have sought to characterize differences between the cultures of nations has been through surveys of the values endorsed as guiding principles in one’s life by samples of individuals located in a range of different nations. The measures first employed asked respondents how important various attributes and phrases are as guiding principles, following the pioneering work in this field of Rokeach (1973). From these data, Schwartz (1992) identified a series of broad domains of values relevant to aspects of interpersonal living and undertook individual- level analyses within each of the samples of students and teachers whom he had surveyed in order to determine whether values can be classified in terms of these broad themes and whether these themes have a consistent structure across cultures. Inconsistent structure would imply that given values do not have equivalent meaning across samples. Schwartz then retained those items from his initial surveys that gave stronger evidence of equivalence. 
Following the procedure pioneered by Hofstede (1980), he next prepared nation- level scores for individual value items and determined the ways in which these item means related to one another at this level of analysis (Schwartz, 1994). Using smallest space analysis, he identified three dimensions of variation:  autonomy (subdivided between intellectual autonomy and affective autonomy) versus embeddedness, egalitarianism versus hierarchy, and mastery versus harmony. 
More recent studies have employed versions of the Portrait Values Questionnaire (Schwartz et al., 2001). In this measure, respondents are asked to rate how similar they are to a series of persons espousing differing types of values. This survey format is more readily understood by respondents. Schwartz’s values data have also been analyzed using 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  75 
more conventionally popular techniques such as factor analysis (Schwartz & Boehnke, 2004), and more fine- grained distinctions between types of individual- level values have been proposed (Schwartz, Cieciuch, Vecchione, et al., 2012). However, Schwartz’s three basic dimensions of nation- level variation continue to prove replicable. Schwartz (2004, 2009) has used multidimensional scaling to generate plots positioning up to 77 nations and eight global regions in terms of autonomy– embeddedness, egalitarianism– hierarchy and mastery– harmony. 
In considering the way in which Schwartz’s analysis positions particular nations, it is important to take account of a major methodological issue that arises when conducting surveys. Respondents from different parts of the world differ in the extent to which they tend to answer questions positively (Smith, 2004). Acquiescence and other types of distinctive responding are discussed more fully in the response style section later in this chapter, but, for the moment, we should note that both Hofstede and Schwartz addressed this problem by standardizing their nation- level means. This increases confidence in the validity of the scores obtained. A further check on validity can be obtained by comparing the scores obtained from the two projects. Despite the differences in the populations sampled, the dates at which data were collected, and the nature of the measures used, autonomy– embeddedness correlates with individualism– collectivism at .64 and with power distance at −.52 (Smith et al., 2013). Other dimensions correlate with one another less strongly, but with significant overlap. The relationships between nation- level indices identified in different studies are more fully summarized by Smith et al. (2013). 
As wealth is a key component of nation- level culture, it is important to clarify its relation with nation- level cultural dimensions. Hofstede (2001) addressed this issue by controlling for wealth when computing correlations with other indices. Schwartz (2007) addressed the issue more directly by testing hypotheses about the relation over time between national wealth and scores for his dimensions. National wealth in 1993 is postdicted by autonomy values and egalitarian values measured around 1995. Increase in wealth between 1993 and 2004 is predicted by the measure of autonomy values obtained around 1995. Thus, there is some evidence of mutual influence between nations’ wealth and their levels of autonomy values. This issue has been further addressed by Fischer and Boer (2011) who showed that autonomy values were a stronger predictor than wealth of nation- level indices of well- being. Schwartz (2007) has reported further tests of the extent to which his dimensions could predict changes in objective nation- level indices. Across 75 nations, autonomy and egalitarian values measured in 1995 predicted increases in indices of democratization from 1995 to 2002, even when controlling for national wealth. These values also predicted a decrease in family size from 1985 to 2001. Contrasts in values between 55 nations were also significantly predictive of amounts of foreign direct investments, even after controlling for differences in wealth (Schwartz, 2009). Investments were stronger from nations high in autonomy and mastery (e.g., Anglo nations) than in nations low on these dimensions and stronger where nations have 
76 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
similar levels of egalitarianism. These results indicate substantial predictive validity for the Schwartz measures. 
Schwartz’s measures have provided an advance on those reported by Hofstede because they are more precisely specified, tap a broader range of nations, and were collected more recently. However, they are based on sets of responses from students and school teachers, and these populations may not fully represent nations as a whole. There is also no compelling reason why values should be preferred as the basis for defining cultural differences rather than beliefs, norms, behaviors, or self- construals. Further studies sampling these alternative bases of cultural differences are considered later in this chapter, but first we examine additional studies that have focused on values. 
The GLOBE Project The group of researchers calling themselves the GLOBE (Global Leadership and Organizational Effectiveness) project (House, Hanges, Javidan, Dorfman, & Gupta, 2004)  sought to develop and amplify the achievements of Hofstede’s project and to advance understanding of cultural variations in effective leadership. In relation to cultural differences, they developed two sets of measures, one focused on values and one focused on perceived behaviors, which they described as “practices.” Business managers working in three specified industries were sampled within 62 nations. While Hofstede defined his dimensions of cultural variation inductively, the GLOBE researchers defined in advance the nine dimensions of cultural variation that they wished to examine. Many of these dimensions were conceptualized on the basis of Hofstede’s work, with each of his dimensions operationalized as either one (power distance; uncertainty avoidance) or two newly specified dimensions (in- group collectivism and institutional collectivism; assertiveness and gender egalitarianism as representations of the opposing poles of masculinity– femininity). Three further dimensions were specified: performance orientation, humane orientation, and future orientation. 
The GLOBE researchers considered culture to be “conceptual- emergent” (Kozlowski & Klein, 2000). In other words, they focused not on individuals’ reports about themselves, but on their perceptions of relevant aspects of their cultural context. By doing so, they assumed that cultural context is to be considered not as an aggregation of individuals, but as an aggregate of shared perceptions about behavior— in other words, norms. For their measure of values, they designed items that asked how others in one’s society should behave. For their measure of practices, they used items focused on the perceived behaviors of those in one’s society. Thus, this project characterized nations along 18 dimensions: nine describing one’s society as it is perceived to be and nine describing it as one believes it should be. In many cases, these two types of measures proved to negatively correlated: respondents saw their society as unlike how they would like it to be. 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  77 
The GLOBE- Hofstede Debate The GLOBE measures were strongly criticized by Hofstede (2006) who argued that there is an important distinction to be made between one’s own personal values and generalized opinions as to how others ought to behave. For instance, an individual might personally favor assertion and ambition while believing that society as a whole should be tolerant and accepting. Which of these measures is preferable as an indicator of culture would depend on one’s conceptualization of culture. Hofstede (2006) believed that personal values provide a more secure basis upon which to define cultural differences, while the GLOBE researchers responded that “cultural dynamics go beyond mathematical averages of what is desirable to individual actors” (Javidan, House, Dorfman, Hanges, & Sully de Luque, 2006, p. 900). What is certain is that the GLOBE measure of in- group collectivism values is not significantly correlated with either Hofstede’s individualism– collectivism or with Schwartz’s autonomy– embeddedness. 
In contrast, some of the GLOBE measures of the behaviors perceived to be typical in one’s society do correlate much more strongly with the equivalent measures from Hofstede and Schwartz. For instance, their measure of in- group collectivism practices correlates at .82 with Hofstede’s collectivism and at .66 with Schwartz’s embeddedness. This further enhances confidence that measures of this dimension of cultural variance can be replicated. For other dimensions, the match is more problematic. The GLOBE measure of Uncertainty Avoidance is negatively correlated at −.62 with Hofstede’s measure of the same name. This contrast is most probably because of the very different items used to define this concept in the two studies. Hofstede’s items highlight the experience of uncertainty, while the GLOBE items focused on the presence of rules and procedures in society. 
The differing methods used and results obtained from Hofstede’s and GLOBE’s large- scale projects have generated substantial controversy as to how to measure cultural differences most validly. This confrontation has been beneficial as it highlights the areas in which the procedures to be used require clearer justification (Smith, 2006). In further contrast to the nation- level analyses of individual items scores employed by Hofstede and Schwartz, the GLOBE researchers determined the structure of their scales through the use of individual- level analyses. This procedure would only yield valid nation- level scores if the structure of their dimensions is isomorphic (i.e., the same at both levels). While the isomorphic structure of Schwartz’s dimensions has been established (Fischer, 2012), this was not tested in the GLOBE data. Opinions differ as to the extent to which this invalidates their measures (Peterson & Castro, 2006; Hanges & Dickson, 2006). The GLOBE researchers also used an improved method of correcting for response style, but this added care does not appear to have affected their results substantially. 
The GLOBE data augmented our knowledge of cultural dimensions by having sampled a different and more precisely specified segment of society, through greater recency, and especially through testing the utility of different types of measure. The 
 
78 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
measures of perceived behaviors have proved especially valuable by indicating convergence with prior measures based on personal values. 
The World Values Survey In all of the studies thus far surveyed in this chapter, researchers involved have themselves designed the measures that they employed. Practical contingencies have also dictated that their samples have been potentially unrepresentative of the nations as whole that they surveyed, even though their samples from different nations were in most cases equivalent to one another. Concurrent with these projects has been the progressive development of large- scale opinion surveys that are based on representative national samples. The most extensive and publicly available of these has been the World Values Survey (WVS; www.worldvaluessurvey.com), which has great potential for remedying deficiencies in the sampling employed in other studies. However, the use of WVS data to define cultural dimensions has its own limitations. Decisions as to what items are to be included in the surveys have, at least until recently, been based on criteria unrelated to the priorities of cross- cultural psychologists. This has constrained the possibility of defining measures on the basis of an adequate number of conceptually related items. Nonetheless, several groups of researchers have identified dimensions of nation- level variation that are derived from WVS data, and it is important to examine their relation to those found in less adequately representative samples. 
The Inglehart Project Commencing in the 1980s, WVS focused primarily on political attitudes, and these were surveyed in just a few nations. Successive WVS waves have been expanded to cover more than 80 nations and a much broader content of items. The principal initiator of the project was Inglehart (1997), and his primary focus was on documenting and understanding cultural change in terms of a trend toward post- materialism. Nation- level factor analysis of selected WVS items yielded two dimensions that were summarized as exemplifying reliance on traditional authority versus rational- legal authority and values emphasizing survival versus self- expression. Successive data collections have indicated a trend in many nations toward increased endorsement of rational- legal authority and self- expression. The items defining these dimensions are a mixture of attitudes, beliefs, and values, but, in these analyses, no correction is made for cultural differences in response style. It is difficult to know how much this inattention affects the structure of the factors obtained. Nonetheless, scores on rational- legal authority and self- expressiveness correlate strongly with wealth, Hofstede’s individualism, and Schwartz’s autonomy measures (Inglehart & Oyserman, 2004), as well as with Bond et al.’s measures of (2004) societal cynicism and dynamic externality beliefs. 
In more recent analyses (Inglehart & Welzel, 2005; Welzel, 2014), continuing increases in nation- level self- expression values are interpreted in terms of the emancipation of individuals to act in an autonomous manner dependent upon the modernization 
 
 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  79 
of societies in terms of factors such as increased wealth, urbanization, and greater opportunities for education. However, it is unclear whether the items used by these authors to define the dimension measuring change are valid across all cultures. Bomhoff and Gu (2012) showed that, in nation- level analyses of WVS data from East Asian societies, the items used by Inglehart and Welzel to define self- expressive values do not factor together in the way that they do in data from Western societies. While reliance on the global samples afforded by WVS data facilitates the testing of generalizations about societies as a whole, it risks losing the distinctiveness of specific regions. 
Trust One of the items defining Inglehart and Welzel’s dimension of self- expressiveness is based on responses to the statement, “You have to be very careful about trusting people,” with permitted responses being, “most people can be trusted” or “you have to be careful.” This comes closer to being a belief than a value, but improved formulations of the phrasing of this term have made it possible to define a cultural dimension based on aspects of trust. Trust in those whom one does not know is seen by Welzel (2014) as an important precondition for the enhancement of emancipative values and economic growth. Trusting strangers will become more possible in circumstances where one is protected by the rule of law and in less turbulent environments. Early results showed that generalized trust was correlated with Hofstede’s individualism even when controlling for national wealth (Allik & Realo, 2004). Muethel and Bond (2013) found that, across 42 nations, generalized trust was indeed higher where the rule of law is endorsed, but low collectivism was an even stronger predictor. However, these results leave open the question of whether out- group trust is independent of respondents’ level of in- group trust. 
In more recent WVS waves, six questions relating to trust have been included, each asking about trust in a different category of persons. This makes it possible to define trust more precisely in terms of separate dimensions of in- group trust and out- group trust. Welzel and Delhey (2015) showed that, across 76 nations, out- group trust was predicted by a knowledge index summarizing nation- level intellectual resources (e.g., education, information technology, etc.) even when they controlled for in- group trust and for individualism. Thus, measures of out- group trust can provide a behaviorally relevant nation- level dimension of beliefs with greater precision than those identified in earlier studies of individualism– collectivism. 
Parental Values Another set of 10 questions included within recent waves of the WVS asked parents what values they wish to encourage within their children. Bond and Lun (2014) showed that, across 55 nations, parental goals could be summarized in terms of two dimensions. The first of these, self- directedness versus other- directedness, was found to correlate with wealth and Schwartz’s autonomy versus embeddedness values. The second dimension, civility versus practicality, was correlated with Schwartz’s egalitarianism versus harmony 
 
 
80 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and with low societal cynicism beliefs. High scores on self- directedness and civility socialization norms were found to predict subjective well- being of respondents across 50 nations (Lun & Bond, 2016). Identification of these dimensions and of their linkage with established dimensions of variation between nations has potential for strengthening links between aspects of developmental psychology and nation- level characterizations of culture. 
Long- Term Orientation In addition to the four dimensions identified in his 1980 study, Hofstede (2001) postulated a fifth dimension of cultural variation which he defined as long- term orientation. This was based on his interpretation of the dimension called “Confucian Work Dynamism” first identified by the Chinese Culture Connection (1987). This dimension contrasted East Asian nations that strongly endorsed values such as thrift, persistence, and protecting one’s public face with nations from other parts of the world where these values were less strongly endorsed. More recently, Minkov and Hofstede (2012) have factor analyzed WVS items with conceptual content similar to the original definition of long- term orientation from 38 nations. Two factors were found, of which the first correlated strongly with the original scores for Confucian Work Dynamism as well as with Inglehart’s scores for secular or nontraditional values. Further examination of this dimension will be required. 
Beliefs as Another Basis for Dimensions The strong emphasis on using values as the basis for defining cultural dimensions has led some researchers to explore whether difference in beliefs may account for additional variance between cultures. Beliefs have to do with what is seen as true or false, in contrast to the distinction between what is desirable or undesirable that is tapped by measures of values. In an early study, Smith, Trompenaars, and Dugan (1995) surveyed beliefs in internal versus external locus of control among employees in 43 nations using Rotter’s (1966) well- known locus of control scale. This scale includes a diverse set of items, and, after individual- level standardization, multidimensional scaling identified three nation- level factors. The first factor tapped belief in personal efficacy versus belief in the efficacy of politicians. Across the nations sampled by Smith et al., scores on this factor correlated strongly with Schwartz’s scores for mastery. The second factor tapped belief in personal efficacy versus belief in the need to depend on others. Scores on this factor correlated strongly with Schwartz’s scores for autonomy and Hofstede’s scores for individualism. Thus there is evidence that some types of belief vary across nations in ways that parallel the types of values that are endorsed in those nations. Belief in personal efficacy is strong in nations favoring individualism and autonomy. 
A more systematic investigation was undertaken by Leung, Bond, de Carrasquel, et al. (2002). Drawing on a collection of more than 200 folk sayings and proverbs from different cultures, they formulated a model of generalized beliefs, which they described as “social axioms.” Five individual- level dimensions of axioms were first identified by 
 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  81 
sampling five nations and later shown to be replicable across 41 nations (Leung & Bond, 2004). When these data were analyzed at the nation- level, just two factors were identified (Bond et al., 2004). The first of these, dynamic externality, combined items from four of the five factors identified at the individual level. The majority of these items comprised beliefs in reward for application and endorsement of religiosity. Scores on this factor were high in nations scoring on Schwartz’s embeddedness, as well as Hofstede’s collectivism and power distance, GLOBE’s in- group collectivism practices, and low wealth. The second factor was societal cynicism, and scores on this factor were less strongly correlated with the results of the preceding studies but were associated with low mean scores for life satisfaction derived from the WVS. 
The studies of social axioms were conducted on an inductive basis, seeking to identify the structure of beliefs without predicting what dimensions might emerge. A contrary approach was adopted by Owe et al. (2013), who designed and tested the validity of a measure of contextualism, which they defined as the belief component of the overall concept of collectivism. This was defined as the belief that, in order to understand a person, one needs knowledge of his or her context. Contextualism was predicted to be stronger in collectivist cultures than in individualist cultures. Nation- level scores on this measure derived from adults in 35 nations were shown to correlate significantly with GLOBE in- group collectivism as well as with indices of in- group favoritism, greater trust of in- groups than out- groups, and higher levels of perceived corruption. In an advance on the methods used in earlier studies, these effects were shown to remain significant even when measures of collectivism based on values measures were controlled. 
The studies of beliefs thus add to the evidence for a single conglomerate dimension of national variance defined by collectivism, power distance, collectivist behaviors, beliefs in dynamic externality, and low wealth. It was Triandis (1995) who first identified individualism– collectivism as a cultural syndrome and argued for the development of separate measures of self- perceptions, relations with others, goals, and norms for this syndrome. Certainly, the correlations between the measures thus far, surveyed in the range between .5 and .7, explain no more than a maximum of 50% of variance between them. While this shows an impressive degree of convergence, it does not exclude the distinctive usefulness of each of these separate measures. As we have seen, Owe et al.’s (2013) measure of contextualism can explain variation between nations that is additional to that tapped by measures based on values. The contrasting results from the individual- and nation- level analyses of social axioms also underline the usefulness of analyzing the same data concurrently at two levels. While reward for application and religiosity are separate factors at the individual level, they come together at the nation level. This provides evidence for the heterogeneity of nations. In a nation high on dynamic externality, there are persons high on religiosity and persons high on reward for application, but the individual- level analysis indicates that they are likely to be different persons.
82 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Social Norms as a Further Basis for Dimensions The finding that variance in values is much greater at the individual level than at the nation level has encouraged researchers recently to give greater attention to the role of social norms in guiding the behaviors of individuals within differing cultural contexts (Gelfand & Harrington, 2015; Morris & Liu, 2015). As social norms are by definition more contextualized than individual attributes such as values and beliefs, to study them cross- culturally one must either select a specific norm for study or else focus on the process of norm adherence in itself. Matsumoto et al. (2008) took the former path, surveying norms concerning the expression of emotion by students in 32 nations. Respondents were asked what they should do if they experienced each of seven different emotions in various different social settings, which were defined in terms of who was present and whether the setting was public or private. Overall citizen means for expressiveness were significantly greater in nations scoring higher on Hofstede’s individualism. However, after controlling for overall expressiveness, it appeared that this result was largely due to greater expression of happiness and surprise and less expression of sadness. There were no significant links between individualism and expression of anger, contempt, disgust, or fear. There was, however, greater individual- level variability in emotional expression within the more individualistic nations, which suggests greater salience of norms in the more collectivistic nations. This is consistent with the results of the meta- analysis by R. Bond and Smith (1996), who compared the results of conformity studies using the Asch experimental paradigm in 17 different nations. Conformity was strongest in the samples from Asia, Africa, and Latin America, which score high on Hofstede’s collectivism and on Schwartz’s embeddedness. 
The research procedure that was employed in studying social axioms has also been employed in studying social norms. In other words, rather than studying culture- specific beliefs or norms, general underlying themes are extracted that have universal relevance. In relation to norms, the focus has been on the extent to which adherence to norms is a mandatory requirement. Gelfand et al. (2011) hypothesized that in more challenging environments, cultures would evolve in which behaviors were more tightly constrained, whereas in more equable contexts cultures would be more loose, with individuals accorded greater latitude in how they could behave. Across 33 nations, these authors found that perceived tightness was associated with Hofstede’s collectivism and power distance, Schwartz’s embeddedness, and Bond et al.’s (2004) fate control and reward for application, as well as with many objective indices of challenging environments. Respondents also completed a more detailed survey asking which behaviors would be appropriate or inappropriate in a range of different contexts. These data confirmed that respondents in the cultures perceived as tight were indeed more restricted in the range of behaviors seen as appropriate to a given context. 
The studies of social norms amplify the characterization of nation- level differences in terms of values and beliefs. Norms specify required behaviors rather more closely than do values or beliefs. A  meta- analysis by Morling and Lamoureux (2008) further 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  83 
underlined the link between overt behavioral differences and cultural dimensions. These authors examined contrasts in cultural products such as advertisements, song lyrics, and newspaper articles, finding more collectivist content in the nations that score higher on collectivism. 
Dimensions Based on Self- Construals The ways in which individuals perceive themselves has long been thought of as a key aspect of cultural difference. Following Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) pioneering formulation, construing oneself as relatively independent of others has been seen as characteristic of members of individualist cultures, whereas construing oneself as interdependent with others has been seen as characteristic of members of collectivistic cultures. However, self- construal has until recently been thought of as an attribute of individuals rather than as providing a basis for describing cultures. Aggregation of individual- level scores for self- construal has yielded confusing and misleading mean scores for nations (Oyserman, Coon, & Kemmelmeier, 2002), principally because of the poor psychometric properties of the self- construal measures that have most frequently been used (Schimmack, Oishi, & Diener, 2005; Smith et al., 2013). 
Vignoles et  al. (2016) have sought to remedy this situation, drawing on prior conceptualizations of self- construal but developing more adequate measures. Scales defining seven different aspects of individual- level self- construal (listed later) were formulated, with some items keyed toward one end of the dimension and other items keyed toward the opposing end of the dimension, thereby reducing the extent of measurement artifacts due to acquiescent responding. This measure was first tested by sampling students from 16 nations. Improved versions of items tapping the seven dimensions were then administered to adults within 55 cultural groups in 33 nations, thus overcoming the excessive reliance in earlier studies on contrasts between East Asian and North American samples. The choice to collect more than one sample from some of the nations sampled was deliberate and served to acknowledge the presence of substantial diversity within particular nations. Factor analyses confirmed that a seven- dimensional representation of self- construal was superior to a simple division between independence and interdependence. 
Importantly for the present purpose, multilevel modeling indicated that sample- level means obtained for the seven dimensions of self- construal were isomorphic with the individual- level means and could therefore be used to characterize the samples from which the data were drawn. To reduce confusion as to levels of analysis, Vignoles et al. (2016) refer to their sample- level scores as defining “cultures of self.” The seven identified dimensions were named as difference (versus similarity), self- direction (versus dependence on others), self- expression (versus harmony), self- containment (versus connectedness to others), consistency (versus variability), self- reliance (versus dependence on others), and self- interest (versus commitment to others). Across the 33 nations sampled, the first four of these dimensions were significantly correlated with latent scores for 
 
84 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
individualism– collectivism based on means from Hofstede’s (2001), Schwartz’s (2009), House et al.’s (2004), and Owe et al.’s (2013) data. The other three dimensions of cultures of self were unrelated to individualism– collectivism. Scores for cultures of self also showed significant relations with indices of human development and of religious heritage. 
The recent study by Vignoles et al. (2016) offers much greater precision in measuring the dimension of variation that has dominated research over the past several decades but it also indicates options for more fully exploring alternative dimensions that may prove to be of equal importance. 
Limitations and Potential Uses Having enumerated the currently available descriptions of cultural dimensions, it is important to consider their limitations and then to consider how best to take account of them as a guide to their present and future uses. Table 3.1 provides a summary of key attributes of the larger scale studies that have been discussed in this chapter, highlighting some of their relative strengths and weaknesses. 
Limitations Three key issues have dominated debates about the characterization of cultural dimensions. The first of these concerns the extent to which respondents whose data are used to define those dimensions are actually able to make valid responses to the survey questions that are addressed to them. The second has to do with response styles as a threat to the validity of measurement. Finally, we have noted already that there is substantial evidence for the heterogeneity of large- scale entities such as nations and that internal variation is therefore likely to attenuate the strength of any associations to be found between nation- level scores and dependent measures. 
Respondents as Reliable Informants Survey items typically ask respondents to describe themselves or those around them. Heine, Lehman, Peng, and Greenholz (2002) have argued that items of this type do not provide any comparison standard against which to anchor one’s ratings. If no reference group is provided, respondents are likely to make widely varying assumptions as to how to make comparisons, with a resultant loss of validity. Heine et al. showed that by asking respondents to make ratings with reference to other nationalities or with reference to one’s own nationality yielded strikingly different mean scores. The effects obtained by Heine et al. are probably much stronger than the variation among respondents to cross- national surveys because respondents are often not told that their responses will be compared with those from other nations. Nonetheless, reference group effects are a serious problem, although opinions differ as to whether they are more acute in relation to self- descriptions or to descriptions of others (Hofstede, 2006; Javidan et al., 2006). 
 
 
 
 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  85 
The most direct way of addressing this problem has been Schwartz et al.’s (2001) development of the personal values questionnaire, in which the objects of comparison are precisely specified. Another option is to draft survey items in contextually specific formats, for instance by keying them to one’s family rather than to one’s group or to leaving the context completely unspecified. Another preferable procedure is provided by testing the nomological net of mean scores on one’s measure, with particular attention

Response Styles There is substantial diversity both between individuals and between samples from different cultural groups in the propensity to respond to surveys using Likert- type response scales with distinctive response styles (Johnson, Shavitt, & Holbrook, 2011). Possible response styles include tendencies toward acquiescence, extreme responding, and moderate responding. Smith (2004) compared indices of acquiescence derived from nation- level projects such as those of Hofstede (2001), Schwartz (2009), and House et al. (2004) and found strong correlations between the nations within each sample that scored high on acquiescence. Although the mean scores obtained in these projects were not invalidated because in each of them the researchers had used methods controlling for acquiescence, the presence of consistent effects indicates that scores obtained in studies that did not control for response style (e.g., Bond et al., 2004; Inglehart & Oyserman, 2004; Welzel, 2014) could be problematic. There is a continuing debate about whether response style can be considered as a valid attribute tapping the ways in which members of particular cultural groups wish to communicate with one another or whether it is better thought of as a measurement artifact that should be controlled (Fischer, 2004; Smith, 2011; and Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver). 
As a first step in clarifying cultural variations in response style in relation to different types of response mode, Smith et al. (2016) compared the contexts in which acquiescence and extremity were strongest when responding to Likert response scales and when responding to a version of Schwartz’s (2001) portrait values questionnaire. Using the sample means provided by Vignoles et al. (2016), they found that, with Likert scale responses, acquiescence was greatest in cultures of self that scored high on harmony and similarity with others. With Schwartz’s measure, acquiescence was strongest in cultures of self that scored high on self- reliance and self- consistency. Extremity was greatest in groups high on self- reliance and self- consistency when using either type of response mode. Thus, there are distinctive types of response style with both response modes. The argument in favor of controlling for response style is thus enhanced. 
The Diversity of National Cultures National cultures provide a context within which individuals decide how to behave. However, there are numerous more specific contexts that may be more salient to individuals at any given point in time, such as one’s family, friendship group, work setting, or local community. The norms of these more immediate groupings may frequently provide guides for how best to think and act (Gelfand & Harrington, 2015; Morris & Liu, 2015). In studying national cultures, we assume that the assemblage of values, beliefs, and cultures of self that prevail within these smaller groups constitute variations on overall themes that are sustained by attributes that are common to nations as a whole, 
 
 
dimens ions of CulTural VariaT ion  |  87 
such as language, climate, laws, educational systems, predominant religions, and so forth. Whether these elements do in fact have sufficient communality to support their predictive validity is an empirical question. 
Future Uses In this chapter, the focus has been primarily on how contexts that are operationalized as national cultures can be described, and, to some extent, what independent correlates of those descriptions have been identified. The related question of how nations come to differ in the ways that have been described has not been addressed, although there is a growing literature relevant to that issue (e.g., Fincher, Thornhill, Murray, & Schaller, 2008; Georgas, van de Vijver, & Berry, 2004; Chapter 4 by Evert Van de Vliert and Dejun Tony Kong). The remaining question has to do with how best to benefit from the existence of measures of national culture. 
There are many aspects of human behavior that are universal, although these universals may be expressed in somewhat different ways within different cultural groups. A major task for cross- cultural psychologists is to provide frameworks that can explain the incidence of these variations. Dimensions of national culture are well suited to this purpose because the great majority of cross- cultural studies to date have involved sampling from two or more nations or cultural groups. If it can be shown that variation between such groups is uniquely associated with scores on relevant cultural dimensions, this can exclude the numerous alternate reasons why two or more samples may differ from one another. The greater the number of sampled groups included in a study, the better is the chance of choosing between alternative explanations. 
Since there are frequently variations in the behavior of individuals, it is important that nation- level tests for explanations of cultural differences should control for individual- level variability. The way forward therefore lies through multilevel modeling of the effects to be explained. Several of the more recent studies already cited in this chapter used such methods, although this important aspect of their design was not highlighted (Bond & Lun, 2013; Lun & Bond, 2016; Smith et al., 2016; Vignoles et al., 2016; Welzel & Delhey, 2015). As an instance of the effects often obtained through multilevel modeling, the nation- level correlates of generalized trust obtained by Muethel and Bond (2013) were found even after controlling for individual- level correlates of trust. 
Such a pattern of results is not always obtained. In their study of generalized trust across 31 European nations, Gheorghiu, Vignoles, and Smith (2009) found that when a nation- level predictor based on collectivism was taken into account, individual- level predictors of trust were no longer significant. Thus, in this case, national- level contrasts outweighed individual variability. 
Multilevel modeling can give us a much clearer understanding of cultural differences. For instance, Becker et al. (2012) studied variations in the motive for distinctiveness across 21 cultural groups. Theorizing based on the proposals of Markus and Kitayama (1991) has led most writers to expect that members of individualistic cultures 
 
88 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
would favor distinctiveness, while members of collectivist cultures would not. Becker et al. found that the motive for distinctiveness was actually equally strong in both types of culture. However, those in individualistic cultures favored distinctiveness based on personal difference and separateness, while those in collectivist cultures favored distinctiveness based on holding key roles in their groups. These effects were predicted much more strongly by respondents’ cultural contexts than by their personal values and beliefs. 
Becker et al. (2014) obtained similar results in relation to motives related to self- esteem. Being able to control one’s life was a stronger predictor of self- esteem in more individualistic cultures, but doing one’s duty was a stronger predictor of self- esteem in more collectivistic cultures. In this study, these effects also depended on the cultural context more than on the values and beliefs of individual respondents. The results of these studies illustrate some of the ways in which one can make good use of nation- level dimensions of culture when one has access to an adequate number of culturally varied samples. 
Conclusion While the conceptualization and measurement of cultural dimensions was seen by many as holding great promise in earlier times, a variety of critics have found reason to favor alternative approaches to the study of culture. Some prefer qualitative or indigenous approaches, while others find the fluid and dynamic nature of culture to be better addressed through individual- level experimentation, as illustrated by other chapters in this handbook. The case for retaining culture- level dimensions rests on the continuing flow of significant effects that have been reported by researchers working within that tradition, particularly as more valid measures have been devised. 
The principal limitations to making greater use of dimensions in cross- cultural research are twofold. First, one needs to sample many nations in order to do adequate studies. With the advent of databases such as the WVS, this requirement is less of an impediment that it used to be. Second, there is uncertainty as to whether we yet have the best dimensions of cultural variation. This chapter has shown that, despite our best efforts, most measures of dimensions continue to cluster around the basic contrast between rich individualistic nations and less rich collectivistic nations. Alternative measures have been proposed, but they have yet to show their predictive value. The field is ripe for further development.

Cold, Heat, Wealth, and Culture 
Evert Van de Vliert and Dejun Tony Kong 
Many civilizations have worshipped the Sun or the Earth— and for good reasons. If the Sun would shine from farther away or closer up, humankind would freeze to death in the cold or burn to death in the heat. If the Earth would not spin around the Sun and around its own tilted axis, its inhabitants would freeze to death in one hemisphere with eternal winter or burn to death in the opposite hemisphere with eternal summer. Indeed, the Sun’s radiation and the Earth’s rotation support life. Conversely, all living species on our planet must carefully navigate between climatic cold and heat. These adaptations are particularly relevant to humans who feed on plants and animals. As a notable consequence, few of our ancestors have migrated to arctic or desert regions where livability is highly problematic. Elsewhere, our ancestors have created lots of practices and artifacts, including money, to meet basic needs during cold winters or hot summers. So pervasive are these adaptations that we have come to disconnect them from ambient temperatures. 
This chapter concentrates on population- level connections between thermal climate and societal culture— the shared system of needs and stresses and embedded behavioral goals, means, and outcomes at the place of residence (Van de Vliert, 2013a). We first describe Hofstede’s (1980) early discovery of some mysterious connections between a country’s distance from the equator and the national culture of its inhabitants. Hofstede speculated that the latitudinal gradient of average temperatures might be ultimately accountable for the latitudinal gradients of cultural individualism and power differences (see also Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith for a review of Hofstede’s work). Inspired by recent work (Van Lange, Rinderu, & Bushman, 2017a), we refine that early climate– culture speculation by addressing the broader puzzle of latitudinality. The remaining sections then review and generalize latitude- related evidence of climato- economic pressures on cultural individualism and political democracy as components of freedom and on four other 
 
 
94 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
cultural characteristics with sufficient sample sizes in both latitudinal hemispheres: corruption and aggression as antisocial characteristics; trust and creativity as prosocial characteristics. 
A Mysterious Discovery Cold, heat, and culture have in common the spatial characteristic that they vary along the north- south axis of the Earth in a remarkable fashion. Cold extremes and some cultural characteristics increase, whereas heat extremes and other cultural characteristics decrease, toward the north and south poles. As a case in point, back in the 1970s, Hofstede (1980) detected that cultural individualism steeply increases, whereas power differences steeply decrease, at higher latitudes with colder winters and cooler summers. For example, compared to the Guatemalans and the Malaysians at lower latitudes, the Danes and the New Zealanders at higher latitudes appeared to place much more value on cultural individualism and power equality. This is a mystery because geographic latitude— an imaginary line connecting locations at a given distance from the equator— has descriptive rather than explanatory relevance. 
Confronted with this mystery, Hofstede (1980, 2001) argued that thermal climate might be at the beginning of a causal chain toward individualism and egalitarianism because colder environments are more problematic and harder to cope with. In countries with colder winters and cooler summers, survival and population growth are more dependent on human intervention in nature, with the complicating effects that there is more need for technology, more technological momentum for change, more questioning of group rules and authority, and more two- way teaching and learning. In subtropical and tropical climates, by contrast, there is less need for human intervention and for technology, leading to a more static society in which boundaries between in- groups and out- groups are more persistent, authority is questioned less, and teachers are increasingly experienced as omniscient and powerful. It was only decades later that others, to which we now turn, started to refine Hofstede’s seminal speculations about latitudinal gradients of cold, heat, and culture. 
Latitudinal Gradients of Cold and Heat The most recent understanding of the latitude- related impact of climate on culture is that average temperature and seasonal variation in temperature jointly help shape the evolution of societal functioning (Gailliot, 2014; Van Lange et al., 2017a). Average temperature as such is an inaccurate determinant because it ignores the bipolarity of thermal livability. Clearly, 4°C and 40°C both pose existential problems, so that larger seasonal variations around the same mild average temperature have larger impacts on societal functioning (Van de Vliert & Tol, 2014). Also, higher latitudes have both lower averages and larger variations in temperature over the course of the year. These shortcomings of average temperature as a predictor of culture can be overcome by 
 
 
 
Cold, heaT, WealTh, and CulTure  |  95 
concentrating on winter and summer deviations from a biologically optimal point of reference. 
Current climate– culture research adopts 22°C (~72°F) as a benchmark from which measurements of societal livability are made. This temperature is the approximate midpoint of the individual ranges of comfortable temperatures (Parsons, 2003) and the temperature preferred by tourists (Bigano, Hamilton, & Tol, 2006). Also, existential needs for nutrition and health are met more easily in climates with temperatures varying around a base range of, say, 17°C to 27°C (Cline, 2007; Parker, 2000; Van de Vliert, 2009). Thus, climates are more demanding to the extent that their winter temperatures are colder than 22°C (cold demands) and their summer temperatures hotter than 22°C (heat demands). 
Indices for cold and heat deviations from 22°C, and for total temperature deviations from 22°C, are available for at least 232 independent countries and dependent territories (Van de Vliert, 2013c; http:// www.rug.nl/ staff/ e.van.de.vliert/ projects). These indices reveal that the present- day Earth offers humans and the plants and animals they feed on larger cold deviations from 22°C (mean [M] = 30.94, standard deviation [SD] = 25.97) than heat deviations from 22°C (M = 21.28, SD = 7.61). Additionally, these indices reveal that the latitudinal gradient of cold demands (r = .89, p < .001) is much steeper than the latitudinal gradient of heat demands (r = −.51, p < .001), so that the total of the current thermal demands increases from the equator toward the poles. By implication, compared with latitudinal decreases in heat demands, latitudinal increases in cold demands provide potentially more convincing explanations of latitudinal gradients of culture, at least within the context of the present Sun- Earth system. 
Latitudinal Gradients of Culture Back to the 1970s and to Hofstede’s (1980) mysterious discovery. Across 40 countries, cultural individualism (r = .75, p < .001) and power differences (r = −.65, p < .001) were not only oppositely associated with absolute latitude; they were also negatively associ-ated with each other (r = −.67, p < .001). More specifically, cultural individualism and power differences loaded on the same bipolar factor, which seemed to make little sense and therefore led Hofstede to treat them as if they represent distinct dimensions instead of opposite poles of the same dimension. Four decades onward, it has slowly but surely become clear how we should interpret and understand cultural individualism and power differences as opposite ends of one and the same dimension— freedom (Van de Vliert, 2013a). 
Cultural individualism refers to freedom from the constraint of social discrimination; that is, freedom from identifying and maintaining sharp boundaries between in- groups and out- groups, between “us” and “them.” There is more individualism and less in- group– out- group discrimination where there are fewer external threats to one’s in- groups and thus less necessity of group defense (Brewer, 1999; Richter & Kruglanski, 2004; Triandis, 1995) and where there is less competition for scarce resources through coalitional activity (Bugental, 2000). Similarly, yet differently, power equality refers to 
 
96 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
freedom from the constraint of superordination and subordination where members of a society discriminate less between higher- ups and lower- downs. Power equality maximizes freedom from hierarchical discrimination by minimizing “the provision (or possible revision) of benefits (e.g., protection, resources) or limitation of costs (e.g., aggression) by the more dominant individual in return for the compliance or deference of the less dominant individual” (Bugental, 2000, p. 201). 
So, cultural differences in individualism versus collectivism and in power equality versus inequality are both “daughters” of the “mother” dimension of differences in freedom from having to continuously and carefully scan the social environment for interactional requirements. However, this one- dimensional perspective of freedom from social constraints complicates rather than simplifies the biogeographic puzzle. Freedom from positive discrimination of in- group members, freedom from negative discrimination of out- group members, freedom from obedience to authority, and freedom from mutiny and rebellion all increase with distance from the equator. What on Earth is going on? Why do populations at different latitudes acquire, value, and practice distinct algorithms of personal freedom from social constraint? Are these algorithms generalizable to freedom from other social constraints, such as values and practices dealing with corruption, aggression, trust, creativity, and more? Are cold and heat— and tools to handle cold and heat— playing parts? 
The Broader Puzzle of Latitudinality Latitudinal gradients in living species have been well- documented for centuries. Most notably, biologists are familiar with (a)  the Bergmann effect— the increase of body size at higher latitudes, (b) the Allen effect— the decrease of surface- to- volume ratio at higher latitudes, and (c)  the Forster effect— the smaller numbers of animal and plant species at higher latitudes, commonly referred to as the latitudinal gradient in biodiversity (Harcourt, 2015). Similarly, just like biodiversity in nonhuman species, linguistic diversity in humans decreases at higher latitudes (Nettle, 1998, 1999), whereas economic wealth increases at higher latitudes (Parker, 2000; Theil & Galvez, 1995; Van de Vliert, Kluwer, & Lynn, 2000; Williamson & Moss, 1993; Zuleta, 2012). Despite all this work on latitudinality, surprisingly little use has been made of the informative value of the opposite directions of distances from the equator in the northern and southern hemispheres. 
Borrowing from “Hell on Earth? Equatorial Peaks of Heat, Poverty, and Aggression” (Van de Vliert & Daan, 2017), we propose that latitudinal gradients of cold and heat are more plausible origins of latitudinal gradients of culture to the extent that these gradients (a)  occur in the northern hemisphere, (b)  replicate in the southern hemisphere, and (c)  reverse their downward or upward sloping direction at a near- equatorial turning point. Table 4.1 illustrates, for Hofstede’s (2001) 50 countries and three regions, how the prevalences of thermal demands and cultural freedom increase at more northern latitudes north of the equator but decrease at more northern latitudes south of the equator. What are the odds that this is a coincidence or that an ecological condition other than 
 
Cold, heaT, WealTh, and CulTure  |  97 
thermal climate must be held accountable for this remarkable north– south reversal of culturally anchored freedom? 
Perhaps it may be wiser to think somewhat broader and deeper about the near- equatorial reversal points of the latitudinal gradients of cultural freedom in Table 4.1. These oppositely sloping northern and southern gradients of discrimination between in- groups and out- groups (cultural individualism) and between higher- ups and lower- downs (power differences) imply the existence of equatorial peaks of social constraints. If one thinks of them as equatorial troughs of freedom from social- psychological constraints, they elegantly match the pit of abject poverty that economists call the equatorial Grand Canyon of wealth (Parker, 2000; Theil & Galvez, 1995). Therefore, it is not inconceivable that national wealth mediates and modifies the impact of thermal climate on societal culture, an idea that has come to be known as the climato- economic theory of culture (Van de Vliert, 2009, 2013a). 
Climato- Economic Pressures on Cultural Freedom An incomplete and, in fact, painfully misleading story has it that climate determines culture. For more than 25 centuries, scientists have told that story over and over again (Feldman, 1975; Jankovic, 2010; Sommers & Moos, 1976). Ibn Khaldun, for example, observed that “the more emotional people were in the warmer climes with the prudes in the frigid North” (Harris, 1968, p.  41). At the beginning of the twentieth century, proponents of the geographical school similarly argued how climate determines who we are and what we do (Sorokin, 1928; Tetsuro, 1971), sometimes with horrifying overtones of the superiority of some races and inferiority of others (Huntington, 1945; Taylor, 1937). As so often, the psychological truth is more complex.
