automatic reaction to the self, it appears to be a multifaceted construct that corresponds to different domains such as “social self,” “academic self,” or “intellectual self.” With too many implicit associations with the self in specific contexts, it is difficult to be reliably activated, measured, and compared across cultures (e.g., Falk, Heine, Takemura, Zhang, & Hsu, 2015). 
Construct bias can also be caused by differential appropriateness of the behaviors associated with the construct in the different cultures. Take intelligence for example. Western intelligence tests tend to focus on reasoning and logical thinking (such as the Raven’s Progressive Matrices). When Western individuals are asked which characteristics they associate with an intelligent person, skilled reasoning and knowing much are frequently mentioned. In addition, social aspects of intelligence are mentioned. The latter aspects are even more prominent in everyday conceptions of intelligence in non- Western groups. Data from Nso people of Cameroon and other parts of Africa supported that, in non- Western countries, children’s engagement of cognition goes beyond the school- oriented domain with which intelligence is commonly associated in the United States and Europe, and it is more relevant when they are participants in cultural communities (Nsamenang, 2006). Finally, poor sampling of all the relevant behaviors indicative of the construct can give rise to construct bias. Poor sampling can also come from another source. For instance, a removal of large proportions of biased items targeting one construct would lead to construct underrepresentation. 
Method Bias Method bias is a general term for bias stemming from sampling, instrument character-istics, and administration. Sample bias stems from differences in sample characteristics that have a bearing on the target measures. Sample bias is more likely to threaten cross- cultural comparisons when the cultures examined differ in more aspects; such a larger cultural distance will often increase the number of alternative explanations for cross- cultural differences to be considered. A typical case in point is to confound respondents’ education attainment with IQ. A usual practice in cross- cultural comparisons of using convenience samples of university students as matching samples may be challenged on the grounds of significant differences in university education quality and enrolment rates, which can introduce selection biases in the sampling process. 
Instrument bias usually involves incomparability of instruments due to differential stimulus familiarity (mainly in cognitive testing) and differential response styles (in personality and survey research). Instrument bias is a common source of bias in cognitive tests. Analyzing response patterns of an assessment to be used for a specific reading disability in Zambia, Hein et al. (Hein, Reich, Marks, Thuma, & Grigorenko, 2016) found that Zambian students’ low level of acquaintance with standardized testing and lack of previous test exposure resulted in more missing responses to questions of written stimuli, open- ended questions, and questions requiring action responses. This example illustrates how stimulus familiarity could challenge the ecological validity of an assessment and 
 
researCh meThods  |  171 
endanger comparisons of test scores across cultures. Response styles, defined as the systematic tendency of respondents to endorse certain response options on some basis other than the target construct, may impact valid cross- cultural comparisons. For instance, van Herk, Poortinga, and Verhallen (2004) found that acquiescent and extreme response styles in self- report of purchasing intentions, although probably representing valid individual and cultural differences that are difficult to “turn off ” (He & van de Vijver, 2015a), lead to errors in estimates in volume of sales. 
Administration bias can be caused by differences in the physical, technical, or so-cial environmental administration conditions. For example, when interviews are held in the houses of respondents, physical conditions (e.g., ambient noise, presence of others) are difficult to control in cross- cultural studies, which subsequently influences how respondents answer questions (e.g., He & van de Vijver, 2016). Technical environmental aspects involve administration modes. For example, Gnambs and Kasper (2015), in a meta- analysis of survey experiments, found significantly more disclosure of socially undesirable behaviors in computerized surveys than in paper- and- pencil surveys. Similarly, Aquilino, Wright, and Supple (2000) reported reduced bystander effects in reporting sensitive behaviors with computer- assisted self- administrated interviewing compared with paper- and- pencil surveys. Examples of social environmental conditions are individual (vs. group) administration, amount of space between testees (in group testing), or class size (in educational settings). Other sources of administration bias are ambiguity in the test instructions and/ or testing guidelines or a differential application of these instructions. A final source of administration bias is communication problems between the respondent and the tester/ interviewer. For example, the interventions of interpreters may influence the measurement outcome. 
Item Bias This type of bias is commonly induced by poor item translation, ambiguities in the original item, low familiarity/ appropriateness of the item content in certain cultures, and influence of cultural specifics, such as nuisance factors or differential connotations associated with the item wording. Poor item translation can either be caused by translation errors or by “genuine” linguistic idiosyncrasies. Even translations that are linguistically correct may still be of low quality from a psychological point of view. In a 43- country comparative project on health behavior in school- aged children, Schnohr et al. (2016) found that the frequency of “fair” as one of the four response options in self- rated health showed a large cross- cultural variation, and a qualitative survey of the back- translation revealed that this word has very different meanings across cultures: the word had a negative connotation in 25 cultures, a positive connotation in 10 cultures, and a neutral connotation in nine cultures. Item bias can also stem from idiomatic expressions or poorly translatable words, such as the well- known German term “Zeitgeist,” which has no one- to- one English translation, and the English “distress,” which does have an equivalent in many languages. 
 
172 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
On Detecting and Dealing with Bias There are several routes by which to approach bias (cf. Poortinga & Van der Flier, 1988) once it is detected in the design, implementation, and analysis phase of a cross- cultural study. A first option is to ignore bias. At first sight, it may seem paradoxical to mention this option because ignoring bias cannot be considered as a real way of dealing with it. We mention it here because of its popularity in the early days of cross- cultural research. Many cross- cultural studies are reported in the literature in which there is no analysis of bias and in which observed cross- cultural differences are interpreted at face value. From a methodological perspective, this “hit- and- run” approach is hardly defensible; it may indeed be one of the determinants of the slow theoretical progress in cross- cultural psychology. Second, bias can be seen as an indicator that an instrument is inadequate for cross- cultural comparison; once bias is detected, a researcher can decide to refrain from making such comparisons. Such an approach is prudent though highly restrictive. Bias may be unavoidable, particularly in the comparison of highly dissimilar cultural groups (e.g., differential testwiseness in comparing pupils from highly different educational systems). Third, bias can be seen as providing important clues about cross- cultural differences. In this approach, bias refers to cultural specifics, whereas instruments (or parts thereof) that do not show bias point to universals. A comparison of biased and unbiased aspects of an instrument yields important clues about cross- cultural differences. Fourth, an attempt can be made to reduce bias. 
Among the perspectives on how to deal with bias just presented, the last three perspectives are of more value. It should be noted that absolute cross- cultural comparability (free of bias) and ecological validity of studies are not always compatible. In fact, they are competing goals. Removing biased elements to achieve better comparability may result in construct underrepresentation and loss of cultural- specific richness of the construct, which jeopardizes the ecological validity; whereas striving for ecological validity means retaining cultural specifics that are hardly comparable with other cultures. We propose that advancing the field of cross- cultural psychology requires a better integration of these perspectives and rigorous procedures in research methods. In the following paragraphs, we outline strategies to detect and deal with bias at the design/ implementation stage and at the data analysis stage of a cross- cultural study. In the first stage, potential bias should be avoided as much as possible by an adequate design and standardized implementation; in the second stage, various psychometric methods can be used to detect bias and even correct for bias in scores. 
Design and Implementation Stage Table 6.2 presents a brief overview of strategies that target different types of bias. In the design of a cross- cultural study, a well- known method to avoid or reduce bias is cultural decentering, which focuses on the common elements across cultures (e.g., words and concepts that are specific to one particular language or culture are eliminated). 
 
 
 
researCh meThods  |  173 
Alternatively, when the convergence approach is used to deal with construct bias, instruments are independently developed in different cultures (languages), and all instruments are then translated and administered to subjects in all these cultures. 
We pay special attention to the design and selection of instruments in minimizing bias. The choice of instrument has to be approached from a broader perspective than the availability of existing instruments. Three options in instrument choice are available in a cross- cultural study: adoption, adaptation, and assembly (van de Vijver & Leung, 1997). Adoption means using the original of a measure and applying a close translation of an instrument in another culture. However, it can only be used when the items in the source and target language versions have an adequate coverage of the construct measured and the response formats are appropriate in various cultures (Harkness, 2003). Adaptation is a combination of a close translation of certain stimuli and modifications of other stimuli; an adaptation is preferred when adoption of all stimuli is inadequate on conceptual (e.g., concept or theory- driven), language (e.g., linguistic or pragmatic- driven), cultural (e.g., terminological or norm- driven), and psychometric (familiarity or format- driven) grounds (Van de Vijver & He, 2016). For instance, the English word “friend” can indicate both a male and a female person, whereas various languages use gender- specific words for male and female friends, such as French (“ami” and “amie”) and German (“Freund” and “Freundin”), and adaptation from English to other language needs to take care of

174 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
the language specifics. Nowadays, adaptation has become more frequently used, and the term has become the de facto standard in working with tests in multiple languages. The change of word signifies the change of emphasis in the process of working with multiple language versions from a linguistic to a multidisciplinary perspective in which, in addition to language, cultural information and psychological knowledge about the target constructs are viewed as essential in preparing stimulus materials for a new cultural con-text. Assembly refers to the compilation of a new measure when neither adoption nor adaptation is suitable. An assembly can maximize the cultural appropriateness of an instrument, but it renders numerical comparisons of scores across cultures impossible. The choice of an instrument depends on the target cultures and research aims. Adoption is preferred if the goal is to compare scores across cultures directly, whereas adaptation and assembly are better to maximize the ecological validity of the instrument. In particular, when construct bias constitutes a real threat to a direct comparison, the assembly of a new instrument is called for (cf. F. M. Cheung et al., 1996). Initiated by the International Test Commission, a committee with members from various international psychological associations, has formulated Guidelines that specify recommended practices in test translations/ adaptations. The latest guidelines are provided in Appendix 6.1. 
In the implementation of a cross- cultural study, extensive training of testers and the standardization of test administrations, to be specified in a test manual, is an important tool in reducing bias. When cultures are close to each other, such standardization may go a long way to prevent the emergence of unwanted score differences. Yet, when the cultural distance between the groups is large, it may not suffice, and additional steps need to be taken to ensure ecological validity. This requires working with nonstandard samples or methods of data collection. For example, local informants can be asked to judge the accuracy of an instrument, local surveys can be held, or instruments can be administered in a nonstandard way to examine whether the questions- as- responded- to are the questions- as- intended. 
Data Analysis Stage Once data have been collected, various psychometric methods are available to detect bias and demonstrate levels of equivalence. The utilization of factor analysis at the scale level and DIF analysis at the item level are discussed here. 
Exploratory Factor Analysis Procedure Both exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) can be used to check construct bias, whereas CFA is also capable of detecting item bias. EFA is preferred when the underlying structure of a construct is unclear or when long instruments are administered in many cultures. The rationale to use EFA (and various other dimensionality- reducing techniques) to study equivalence is that identical constructs are measured in all cultures if the structure of an instrument, as displayed in these techniques, is the same across cultures. So, the identity of the number of factors and 
 
 
 
researCh meThods  |  175 
factor loadings reflects structural equivalence. Comparisons of multiple cultures can be conducted either in a pairwise or in a one- to- all manner (i.e., each culture is compared to the combined solution). Target rotations are used to evaluate factor congruence by means of the computation of Tucker’s phi coefficient. This coefficient tests to what extent factors are identical across cultures. Values of Tucker’s phi above .90 are usually considered to be adequate and above .95 to be excellent (van de Vijver & Leung, 1997). Similarly, a multidimensional scaling (MDS), as an exploratory approach, can place items into a multidimensional space that generates a graphical display of the interrelations between items: items that are close together in the space have a similar meaning, and items that are placed far away from each other have dissimilar meanings (Borg & Groenen, 2005). 
Confirmatory Factor Analysis Procedure Multiple- group CFA is a more frequently used method to test the level of equivalence. This analysis uses covariance matrix information to test hierarchical models. For example, to examine whether the same one- factor model holds in various cultures, a series of nested models are usually tested. The configural invariance model, which specifies that the same latent construct with the same indicators, is the baseline model. In the measurement weights model (metric invariance), factor loadings are constrained to be equal across cultures. In the intercept invariance model (scalar invariance), items are constrained to have the same latent mean across cultures, which can be used to detect item bias. A satisfactory fit of the intercept invariance model provides evidence that there is no bias. The level of comparability can be inferred from the fit indexes in each model and the comparisons of fit indexes from different models, depending on the numbers of groups involved and the nature of the data (i.e., continuous or categorical) (e.g., G. W. Cheung & Rensvold, 2002; Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014, 2016). 
New Developments in Equivalence Procedures In large- scale cross- cultural comparisons that involve dozens of cultures, the hierarchical models in conventional multiple group CFA may not always yield sound estimates (e.g., Byrne & van de Vijver, 2010). Furthermore, it is argued that the constraints in the conventional testing are overly strict (Muthén & Asparouhov, 2012) and it is rather difficult to find scalar equivalence. Alternative methods, such as partial invariance, exploratory structural equation modeling, Bayesian approximate invariance, and alignment, have been proposed in the literature and are actively researched within the large- scale assessment community. 
Partial invariance means that only a subset of parameters (factor loadings and/ or item intercepts) is constrained to be invariant, and the other subset of parameters is allowed to vary across countries. Subsequently, the invariant subset can be compared across cultures (Byrne, Shavelson, & Muthén, 1989). 
Exploratory structural equation modeling relaxes the constraints in multigroup CFA models by fixing fewer loadings at zero (allowing small- sized cross- loadings) and 
 
 
176 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
allowing for much more variation in factor loadings across cultures. For example, using exploratory structural equation modeling where they could not find a good fit in a CFA, Bowden, Saklofske, van de Vijver, Sudarshan, and Eysenck (2016) reported a good fit in a large- scale study of the three- factor structure of personality as measured by the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire. 
Instead of constraining the parameters of loadings and/ or intercepts to be exactly the same across cultures, Bayesian approximate invariance testing allows small differences in these parameters across cultures (Muthén & Asparouhov, 2012; van de Schoot et al., 2013). In operational terms, one can specify the pair- wise differences in each parameter (loadings and/ or intercepts) across cultures to follow a zero mean and a very small variance (.01 or .05) distribution in a way that allows some flexibility in these parameters. It is suggested that if the model with such specifications fits well, approximate invariance is supported, and the comparisons of scale scores are acceptable (Davidov et al., 2015). 
Alignment estimates group- specific factor means and variances without requiring full measurement invariance (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2014). Alignment favors the simplest model with the fewest noninvariant parameters. In a sense, alignment can be viewed as exploratory, in that it incorporates a simplicity function similar to the rotation criteria used in EFA to discover the most optimal measurement invariance pattern and to estimate the factor mean and variance parameters in each group. Given its recent introduction, the applications are not numerous. De Bondt and van Petegem (2015) used the Bayesian approximate invariance test with alignment optimization in evaluating the psychometric quality of an overexcitability scale, in which they showed the superiority of this combined approach compared with conventional CFA with modification indexes. All in all, these new approaches seem promising in advancing our field, yet the implications of using these new approaches on the validity of cross- cultural comparisons await further investigation. 
Differential Item Functioning DIF analysis aims to identify biased items (Zumbo, 1999). Quantitatively, DIF can be modeled with item responses via contingency tables (i.e., Mantel- Haenszel statistics) and regression models (i.e., logistic regression with binary responses); the common ground for these methods is to match and compare groups by conditioning on the total score. Item response theory (IRT)- based DIF analysis is a latent variable modeling approach that evaluates differences in response probability between cultures, conditional on some measure of the latent dimension. DIF detection is most often carried out in data measuring unidimensional constructs and between a reference and a focal culture, while various extensions are being developed to accommodate multidimensional constructs and more cultural groups. In the measurement model of constructs, items exhibiting large effect sizes of DIF can then be freely estimated, resulting in partial invariance (Cees & Khurrem, 2014). The identification of sources of anomalies in cross- cultural research at the item level is of obvious relevance, both theoretical and practical, but its 
 
researCh meThods  |  177 
implementation has met with major difficulties. First, it is often difficult to comprehend why an item is biased. Second, results of different procedures for identifying bias often do not always show the same results (e.g., Fortin Morales, van de Vijver, & Poortinga, 2014). Convergence of bias statistics has been studied from several perspectives using different quantitative approaches (e.g., IRT and Mantel- Haenszel approach) and various qualitative evidences (e.g., from cognitive interviewing with respondents and expert judgment). Once the biased items are detected in a DIF analysis, qualitative and mixed- methods studies may shed light on the sources of item bias and inform future survey design and implementation (e.g., Benítez & Padilla, 2014). 
Future Developments In the first edition of this volume, the major methodological challenge was described as the integration of cultural psychology and cross- cultural psychology (van de Vijver, 2001). The historically sharp distinction between the noncomparative, qualitatively oriented cultural psychology and the comparative, quantitatively oriented cross- cultural psychology has become much less pronounced. Qualitative comparative and quantitative one- culture studies are more common today. In our view, an integration of perspectives is still a major task in the coming period, but this integration no longer refers to the distinction between cultural and cross- cultural psychology. The central task will be the integration of emic and etic methods (Cheung et al., 2011) and qualitative and quantitative methods (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2007). The two distinctions are related in cross- cultural research. The need for integration starts from the idea that it is very common in cross- cultural psychology to find that the basic psychological structure is invariant across cultures but that a close inspection often shows that cultures can differ in their manifestations of these universal structures (Berry, Poortinga, Breugelmans, Chasiotis, & Sam, 2011). In emic– etic parlance, this means that the basic structure is universal (etic) but manifestations can be emic; extraversion is universal, but some behaviors associated with extraversion could be culture- specific. Examples of such integrative studies, which typically feature first qualitative stages followed by quantitative stages, come from the personality domain (e.g., F. M. Cheung et al., 1996; Fetvadjiev et al., 2015; Zeinoun, Daouk- Öyry, Choueiri, van de Vijver, 2017). The main methodological task ahead of us is to develop more sophisticated ways of integrating such qualitative and quantitative data. Some work in this area has been conducted, known in the mixed- methods liter-ature as triangulation (Denzin, 2012). Currently available procedures are mainly developed in quantitative approaches, known as multitrait- multimethod designs, and do not include qualitative data unless these are quantified. However, we must ask if the future of mixed methods is really dependent on triangulation. It may well be that qualitative and quantitative methods will continue to be mainly used where they are strongest: obtaining a description or finding the structure of a complex reality using qualitative procedures (ethnographic research comes to mind here) and verifying or testing a structure using 
 
178 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
quantitative procedures (using statistical tests). The question is, then, not so much how both procedures can address the same question, but how both types of evidence can complement each other. Clearly, more work is needed here. 
In light of the challenges exemplified by studies using a single approach, a combined approach taking into consideration both methodological rigor and cultural sensitivity may be preferred (Cheung et al., 2011). A combined approach involves an integrated and balanced treatment of culturally universal and specific aspects that takes place through the use of a combination of etic and emic measurements or the use of mixed methods. An example can be found in a study by Suryani et al. (Suryani, van de Vijver, Poortinga, & Setiadi, 2012), which started with a qualitative study on the indigenous characteristics of Indonesian leadership. The authors developed a local questionnaire to tap into indigenous characteristics of leadership and administered it to managers in Indonesia. Two styles were identified: benevolent paternalism and transformational leadership. Next, a local questionnaire, based on the qualitative study, and the leadership questionnaire from the GLOBE project were jointly administered to another group of Indonesian managers. The results showed that Indonesian leadership had one component involving a more local, modernization dimension (as identified in the indigenous study) and another more universal person- versus team- oriented leadership dimension (as identified in the GLOBE project). For constructs with a presumably universal applicability (e.g., leadership, work- related values, management styles), such a questionnaire- based approach is feasible, and a combined emic- etic perspective can help to draw ecologically valid conclusions. 
A second challenge is the refinement of equivalence procedures in the quantitative paradigm. The appreciation of the shortcomings of extant procedures, even very modern ones, comes from large- scale projects. Projects that involve dozens of countries often use structural equation modeling to assess equivalence. When using CFA, often seen as the best possible procedure, it turns out to be impossible to find support for scalar invariance. Yet more detailed analyses often fail to find sources of the lack of invariance. Procedures like exploratory structural equation modeling and Bayesian structural equation modeling show the same problem to a somewhat lesser extent. With the current statistical procedures, it is virtually impossible in large- scale studies to tease apart models that incorrectly specify identical parameters across cultures (and should be modified) and models that are fairly identical across cultures that show a poor fit due to statistical procedures that are overpowered. There is a trend in the statistical literature to relax assumptions and allow some variation in parameters of factor analytic models across cultures, such as some differences in factor loadings or intercepts (“approximate invariance”) (Davidov, Meuleman, Cieciuch, Schmidt, & Billiet, 2014). However, it is as yet unclear to what extent such innovations can “salvage” the scalar invariance approach. It will be interesting to explore very different approaches. Large- scale projects could be analyzed from a different perspective. For example, rather than testing the null hypothesis that a scale is invariant across all cultures, we can test targeted hypotheses about confounding differences. An example of such a question would be: To what extent are cross- cultural differences in self- reported professional attitudes and practices influenced by response 
researCh meThods  |  179 
styles (He & Van de Vijver, 2015b), or to what extent are cross- cultural differences in attitudes toward citizen rights influenced by the proportion of immigrants in a country (Davidov et al., 2016)? Sources of invariance are then not identified post hoc, as is done in conventional statistical procedures, but are included in the statistical modeling procedure. The feasibility of this approach hinges on the successful cooperation of substantive and methodological experts. 
A common thread in this section on future developments is the need for combining different types of expertise in cross- cultural studies. The term “translation” has been largely replaced by “adaptation,” to signify that developing an instrument in a new language is more than just a linguistic endeavor (Hambleton, Merenda, & Spielberger, 2005). Among other things, cultural expertise is needed to understand why specific questions will (or will not) work in a new context. These joint efforts are not only relevant for translating/ adapting instruments, but will also enhance all stages of a study, from conceptualization, to design and instrument choice, to analysis procedures. Going beyond our disciplinary boundaries seems to be the main challenge ahead of us. 
Appendix 6.1 
On the initiative of the International Test Commission, a committee with members from various international psychological associations has formulated Guidelines that specify recommended practices in test translations/ adaptations. Presented here is the updated 2010 version (see also van de Vijver, 2016). 
(a) Aim and domains covered Aim “the objective was to produce a detailed set of guidelines for 
adapting psychological and educational tests for use in various different linguistic and cultural contexts” (ITC, nd) 
Domains covered 
1. Cultural context 2. Technicalities of instrument development and adaptation 3. Test administration 4. Documentation and interpretation 
(b) Guidelines Context C.1  Effects of cultural differences which are not relevant or important to the main 
purposes of the study should be minimized to the extent possible. C.2  The amount of overlap in the construct measured by the test or instrument in the 
populations of interest should be assessed. Test Development and Adaptation D.1  Test developers/ publishers should insure that the adaptation process takes full 
account of linguistic and cultural differences among the populations for whom adapted versions of the test or instrument are intended. 
 
 
180 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
D.2  Test developers/ publishers should provide evidence that the language use in the directions, rubrics, and items themselves as well as in the handbook are appropriate for all cultural and language populations for whom the test or instrument is intended. 
D.3  Test developers/ publishers should provide evidence that the choice of testing techniques, item formats, test conventions, and procedures are familiar to all intended populations. 
D.4  Test developers/ publishers should provide evidence that item content and stimulus materials are familiar to all intended populations. 
D.5  Test developers/ publishers should implement systematic judgmental evidence, both linguistic and psychological, to improve the accuracy of the adaptation process and compile evidence on the equivalence of all language versions. 
D.6  Test developers/ publishers should ensure that the data collection design permits the use of appropriate statistical techniques to establish item equivalence between the different language versions of the test or instrument. 
D.7  Test developers/ publishers should apply appropriate statistical techniques to (1) establish the equivalence of the different versions of the test or instrument, and (2) identify problematic components or aspects of the test or instrument which may be inadequate to one or more of the intended populations. 
D.8 Test developers/ publishers should provide information on the evaluation of validity in all target populations for whom the adapted versions are intended. 
D.9  Test developers/ publishers should provide statistical evidence of the equivalence of questions for all intended populations. 
D.10  Nonequivalent questions between versions intended for different populations should not be used in preparing a common scale or in comparing these populations. However, they may be useful in enhancing content validity of scores reported for each population separately. 
Administration A.1 Test developers and administrators should try to anticipate the types of 
problems that can be expected, and take appropriate actions to remedy these problems through the preparation of appropriate materials and instructions. 
A.2 Test administrators should be sensitive to a number of factors related to the stimulus materials, administration procedures, and response modes that can moderate the validity of the inferences drawn from the scores. 
A.3 Those aspects of the environment that influence the administration of a test or instrument should be made as similar as possible across populations of interest. 
A.4 Test administration instructions should be in the source and target languages to minimize the influence of unwanted sources of variation across populations.
researCh meThods  |  181 
A.5 The test manual should specify all aspects of the administration that require scrutiny in a new cultural context. 
A.6 The administrator should be unobtrusive and the administrator- examinee interaction should be minimized. Explicit rules that are described in the manual for administration should be followed. 
Documentation/ Score Interpretations I.1 When a test or instrument is adapted for use in another population, 
documentation of the changes should be provided, along with evidence of the equivalence. 
I.2 Score differences among samples of populations administered the test or instrument should not be taken at face value. The researcher has the responsibility to substantiate the differences with other empirical evidence. 
I.3 Comparisons across populations can only be made at the level of invariance that has been established for the scale on which scores are reported. 
I.4 The test developer should provide specific information on the ways in which the sociocultural and ecological contexts of the populations might affect performance, and should suggest procedures to account for these effects in the interpretation of results.
