The Role of Emotions in Socialization Processes Across Cultures 
Implications for Theory and Practice 
Heidi Keller 
Darwin (1872) described emotions as pan- human phenomena with adaptive value. From an evolutionary perspective, emotions have evolved to coordinate responses to situations that represented adaptive problems (e.g., Cosmides & Tooby, 2000). Therefore, emotions are regarded as biologically based and not learned differently in each culture (Darwin, 1872). It is generally assumed that infants are born with a repertoire of basic emotions although the presumed number varies. Carol Izard (1991), for example, describes eight universally recognizable emotions in terms of facial expressions (joy, disgust, sadness, anger, pain, interest, fear, surprise) that would emerge during the first six months of life. Paul Ekman (1972) conceived of six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise; he later added contempt as a seventh emotion; e.g., Ekman, 1992) that are expressed through a combination of muscle contractions (action units) in the face and can be analyzed with the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). Part of these conceptions of emotion is the assumption that emotional experience and expression are consonant. Irenäus Eibl- Eibesfeldt (1984, 2004)  further extended the universality claim regarding the social regulatory function of emotional expressions with a documentation of what he called the “universal grammar of human behavior,” as, for example, in the emotional expression of the “greeting face” (lowered head, wide open eyes, and open mouth) that is displayed in the presence of small babies. 
 
 
210 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
On the other hand, there is a long tradition of cultural differences reported by anthropologists who observed unique emotions and emotional regulations in different parts of the world. In her book, Coming of Age in Samoa, Margaret Mead (1928/ 1961) writes about her experiences of living in a small village on the island of Ta’u in Samoa. She came there in 1925 to discover whether adolescence is the biologically primed phase of emotional turbulence that it was considered in the Euro American culture or whether it varies along with cultural norms and values. During her 9- month stay, she interviewed 68 young women between the ages of 9 and 20. Distinct rules of conduct governed social life and development so that standing out from the community is not wanted and pride is an emotion that is particularly devaluated, regarded as being a major failure. However, individuality is expressed and encouraged in singing and dancing without reference to appropriate behavior according to age and status. 
Gregory Bateson, an English anthropologist, social scientist, linguist, and ecologist, traveled as a student during the 1930s to the Iatmul in New Guinea and later to Bali. Although he is mainly known for his contributions to systems theory and cybernetics, he also acted as a visual anthropologist (together with his wife of that time, Margaret Mead) and used photography and film to describe, for example, the life of the Bajoeng Gede people in Bali. He documented how Balinese mothers ignored the emotional expressions of their children when the children got too excited, a regulation that is apparently different from European or Euro American middle- class emotion regulation patterns. 
The anthropologist Jean Briggs published her book, Never in Anger: Portrait of an Eskimo Family (1970), after having lived for almost 2 year with the Utku Inuit people on the Arctic coast during the 1960s. She described the particularly unique emotional control governing social encounters. She wrote, among many other things, about the cultural construction of the vocabulary of emotion and the emotional underpinnings of attachment in her award- winning book, Inuit Morality Play: The Emotional Education of a Three- Year- Old (1998). 
Without going into details of methodological differences between these two perspectives— the universalist and the culturally specific perspectives on emotions— they may also express fundamental differences in research orientation. Universalists, especially those with an ethological background, look for the occurrence of phenomena where frequency and other contextual parameters are less important. Face- to- face contact between infants and caregivers, for example, occurs in all cultural communities, yet the prevalence and interactional embodiment vary widely, signifying different conceptions of caregiving and socialization strategies (Keller, 2007; Keller, Schölmerich, & Eibl- Eibesfeldt, 1988). Cultural anthropologists are mainly interested in the singularity and specificity of local phenomena, rarely comparing cultural contexts (e.g., Greenfield, 2004; Rogoff, 2003). 
The conceptual framework on which the remainder of this chapter is based embraces the inextricable interrelationship of biology and culture (i.e., universal and specific dimensions of emotions and their expressions). Biological predispositions for the experience and display of emotions interact with cultural influences to produce a 
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  211 
human’s behavioral repertoires (Matsumoto & Hwang, 2011; see also Chapter  12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang). Emotions are interwoven with the conception of the self and therefore crucial for developing competence in context, a view that has already been detailed by Mead, Bateson, and Briggs. 
In the following paragraphs, the role of emotions in early social interactions in different cultural environments will be discussed based on the existing literature and our own research program. It must be noted that there is a disparity of information favoring Western middle- class families coming from the overwhelming body of existing researchers as well as research participants. Information about other cultural environments is scarce and often sketchy. Yet there is enough evidence to conclude that the Western way is not universal and representative for the world’s population; on the contrary, it may even be regarded as an outlier in the world’s orchestra (Arnett, 2008; Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, 2010). Attachment theory as the main developmental socioemotional theory will be placed into perspective with respect to different socialization pathways. 
In order to discuss different developmental pathways and compare different cultural contexts, it is important to lay out our understanding of emotion and culture first (for a more extensive discussion see Keller & Kärtner, 2013). 
The Conception of Emotion There is no consensus on the definition of emotion in the literature. Therefore, the conception that is vital to this chapter will be briefly outlined. We conceive of emotions as mental states that intertwine feeling with cognitive and motivational states. Therefore, emotions involve different components, such as subjective experience, expressiveness, psychophysiological changes, and behavior. It is assumed that emotions evolved to motivate and coordinate behaviors that were adaptive in the ancestral environment (Panksepp, 1982). “The emotions are specialized modes of operation shaped by natural selection to adjust the physiological, psychological, and behavioral parameters of the organism in ways that increase its capacity and tendency to respond adaptively to the threats and opportunities characteristic of specific kinds of situations” (Nesse, 1990, p.  268). Emotional repertoires are based in universal predispositions that are shaped in an organism’s interactions with the environment and especially with other people of particular phenotypic appearances (Griffiths & Scarantino, 2009). For example, it can be assumed that stranger anxiety (i.e., a 1- year- old child’s experience and expression of distress when confronting a stranger) is evolutionarily primed since strangers may be potentially dangerous and threatening. Stranger anxiety may develop in the behavioral repertoire when infants’ social encounters are restricted to a few consistent caregivers, as is the case in Western middle- class families. It may not develop when infants are regularly exposed to many people, both familiar and nonfamiliar, as in Ivorian Beng society (Gottlieb, 2004). Moreover, the appearance 
 
212 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
of stranger anxiety seems to depend on the exclusivity and emotional intensity of attachment relationships, as the comparison of Western middle- class and North West Cameroonian Nso farming village babies reveals (Otto, 2014). These different forms of regulation depend on the ecosocial structure of the environments, which may provide more or less opportunities for the display of particular emotions based in norms and conventions regulating social encounters. Even if there are biologically innate nonverbal displays for the expression of specific emotions, as Tracy and Matsumoto (2008) have demonstrated for pride and shame, it can be expected that the expression may differ with practice. Sociocultural norms and conventions also modulate the intensity of expressions of the same emotions. 
Culture selects from the phylogenetically evolved universal repertoire and reinforces particular emotional agendas that are actively acquired during the first years of life as part of social regulatory processes. The same predispositions are thus canalized and shaped in meaningful social encounters to form adaptive patterns in the respective environment— as are all developmental tasks and phenomena (Keller & Kärtner, 2013). Since environments, their affordances, constraints, and challenges are vastly different, the same behavioral solution would not have adaptive value everywhere, and humankind would not have survived with a fixed emotional repertoire. 
Emotions are thus closely interwoven with experiences, evaluations, and regulations of self, relationships, and situations. Thus, the sociocultural context constitutes the meaning and the expression of emotions (Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Matsumoto, 1989; Mesquita, 2001, 2007; see also Chapter 12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang). 
The Conception of Culture Culture also has been conceptualized in numerous ways over the past decades (see e.g., Jahoda, 2012; Spencer- Oatey, 2012). A  common core is the reference to shared ideas, beliefs, and attitudes; that is, the representational part and shared behaviors, the actional part of culture (Greenfield & Keller, 2004). The basis for similarities and differences in cultural ideas and behaviors is the similarity of contexts and living conditions. Evolutionary theory and cultural/ cross- cultural psychology and anthropology concur in relating culture to the affordances and constraints of a particular context. Based on physical and geographical parameters, social structures like household composition and definition of family are contingent on these parameters and are reflected in norms, values, and beliefs as well as in behavioral regulations. These processes have always to be situated within historical, sociopolitical contexts (Bronfenbrenner, 1977; Cole, 2002; Marey- Sarwan, Keller & Otto, 2015; Vicedo, 2013). Thus, culture is constructed and co- constructed in dynamic processes along these different dimensions. It can be regarded as a representation of contextual information that is acquired during ontogeny (Keller, 2007; LeVine, 1974, 1988; Weisner, 1987; Whiting, 1963), which thus qualifies it as the primary mode of human adaptation (Greenfield & Keller, 2004; Rogoff, 2003). In order to understand 
 
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  213 
culturally shaped human psychology, it is therefore crucial to contextualize empirical studies in ethnographic accounts of respective environments (Hay, 2015; Gaskins, 2014). Sociodemographic milieus can be regarded as a proxy for environmental ethnographies (Keller, 2007; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). 
Defining Cultural Environments Culture thus can be regarded as rooted in sociodemographic milieus that are formed by the interplay of several dimensions. The organizational element is the degree of Western- type formal education, situated in classrooms with trained adult teachers and an explicit educational agenda. This type of education differs substantially from nonformal or incidental education that is situated in everyday routines and practices aimed at the acquisition of local knowledge as well as religious training (e.g., the Jewish jeshiva).1 
The degree of formal education is related to the fertility rate of individuals on a worldwide scale (Cochrane, 1979). The higher the degree of formal education, the later the birth of the first child and the lower the number of offspring. The acquisition of higher formal education extends income- generating activities as a basis of family foundation and procreation. The degree of formal education also influences the household composition and thus the definition of family. More formally educated individuals live predominantly in two- generation households and nuclear families. Less formally educated individuals tend to live in multigenerational households and family clans. The family organization reflects moreover the economic base of the individual and family. On average, more educated individuals tend to live in more prosperous and economically affluent milieus than formally less educated families. Formal education, age at first birth, number of children in the household, and household composition form sociodemographic milieus in which particular norms, values, beliefs, and behavioral conventions (i.e., cultures) have developed. Different sociodemographic milieus are thus regarded as the foundation of different cultures. However, culture is a dynamic conception and underlies processes of change along with environmental changes so that it is transmitted, created, and co- created between and across generations (Moscovici, 1984). 
This conception definitely excludes countries or societies as units of cultural or cross- cultural analysis. Countries host multiple sociodemographic milieus that necessitate different adaptive patterns and therefore different cultures. 
Our existing psychological knowledge is mainly based on one particular sociodemographic milieu:  Western middle- class. Formal education is usually highly 
1. Formal education is not considered here as being superior to nonformal education; it is a different mode of education with different goals and different topics. Moreover, formal education may look very different in different locations (Döge & Keller, 2012; Gernhardt, Lamm, Keller & Döge, 2014). 
 
214 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
coincident with late parenthood, fewer offspring, and individualized parenting aimed at “bringing out the best” of a unique child (Keller, 2015; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). Children are primarily raised in nuclear families with few family responsibilities. Life is situated within the anonymous, large- scale reality of Western postindustrialized, knowledge societies (Keller, Zach, & Abels, 2005). This context represents a very small part of the world’s population, presumably less than 5%. Research results originating from this population, however, are generalized to the world’s population in general in theory and practice. This practice has come under serious criticism during the past few years (Arnett, 2008; Henrich, Heine, & Norenzayan, 2010). 
Obviously, there are other sociodemographic milieus on this planet, and their respective cultural contexts are largely understudied. One context that is particularly relevant for our discussion refers to the dense social network of traditional farming village communities. Economy is usually subsistence- based with little economic diversity among multigenerational households and clans. The population is small- scale, with person- to- person interactions as the prevalent social mode. Formal education, if at all available, is basic or restricted. The social organization is often characterized by hierarchical family systems based on age, gender, and communal work. Reproduction starts early, spacing is often dense, and many children are born. Childcare is distributed as a communal responsibility (Keller & Chaudhary, 2017). This ecocultural context is estimated to represent around 30– 40% of the world’s population. Moreover, it is the environment from which modern city life has evolved (LeVine & LeVine, 2016) and defines the background of most migrants into Western societies. 
These two types of environments— Western middle- class families and non- Western traditional subsistence- based farming communities— and their respective cultural models can be regarded as prototypes from which variations and combinations arise (Keller, 2007). One hybrid type that has received increasing attention in the past is urban middle- class individuals/ families from non- Western countries. They have a high formal education equal to their Western middle- class peers, yet they occupy an intermediate position between the Western middle- class and the rural farming life with respect to age at first birth, number of children, and household organization (Kağitcibaşi, 2007; Keller, 2007; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). Mode of subsistence also has an impact on cultural patterns of adaptation, as variation from the farmer’s model has been reported with respect to foragers (Hewlett, 2004), nomadic herders (Casimir, 2010), and fishermen (Uskul, Kitayama, & Nisbett, 2008). Nevertheless, they all differ substantially from the Western middle- class cultural model. These different environmental contexts are associated with different socialization strategies and educational agendas in line with different conceptions of competence associated with environmental affordances and constraints. Emotions and emotional regulations are enacted very differently in these environments in line with the overarching conceptions of the self, personhood, and relationships (Morelli et al., 2017).
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  215 
Children’s Learning Environment in Western Middle- Class Families Becoming a competent member of the Western middle- class world is based on a cultural model promoting individuality, self- determination, and (individual) freedom of choice. These values pertain to an autonomous self. A middle- class mother from Los Angeles2 talks about her 3- month- old son in an interview: “Yes, he is an independent being. He is completely different from me and his father There has been really something completely new created.” 
The focus is on independent mental states, choice, individual preferences, self- maximization, and self- fulfillment. As another middle- class mom from Los Angeles refers to her 3- month- old baby girl: “my baby is now becoming more interested in the world. She is, you know, developing her memory and you know the side of the brain and she wants to look around, she is very interested.” 
This cultural script can be conceptualized as psychological autonomy (Keller, 2012; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). This mode of defining autonomy has consequences for the defini-tion of relatedness. Relatedness in this worldview must mean that separate, self- contained individuals establish self- selected relations with others that are defined and negotiated from the point of view of individual psychological autonomy (Keller & Kärtner, 2013). 
Infants’ early social experiences are based on exclusive dyadic encounters with an adult caregiver, mainly the mother. The major interactional mode is face- to- face exchange, with contingent responsiveness and mirroring of the baby’s (facial) signals. Contingent responsiveness means prompt and adequate reactions to any subtle visual and vocal infant signal, so that infants can experience the causality of their behavior (Blehar, Lieberman, & Ainsworth, 1977; Stern, 1985; Keller, Lohaus, Völker, Cappenberg, & Chasiotis, 1999; see also the conception of intuitive parenting: Papousek & Papousek, 1995). Affect mirroring means mirroring the facial emotional displays that are a nonverbal, external reflection of the baby’s inner state (Gergeley & Watson, 1999). A middle- class mother from Berlin explains: “Well, I  think it’s, uhm, most important to have eye contact so that the baby can see your facial expressions, hear your voice.” As soon as babies’ waking times increase during the so- called 2- month shift, face- to- face contact between mother and baby increases significantly. Smiling into the baby’s face also increases significantly between 6 and 8 weeks of age, as does the baby’s smiling at his or her mother’s face (Kärtner, Holodynski, & Wörmann, 2013). Thus, babies become attuned to a distal interactional style. The experience and expression of emotions is encouraged and regarded as instantiation of the independent self (Shweder & Bourne, 1982), thus promoting autonomy 
2. The interview and conversational examples that are presented in short excerpts in the following paragraphs are part of different research projects of the Culture and Development lab at Osnabrück University (for a summary, see Keller, 2007; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). 
 
216 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and individualistic competence. In particular, positive emotions like joy, happiness, and excitement should be maximized, and negative ones minimized (Friedlmeier, Corapci, & Cole, 2011). “You need to smile, darling,” is the desperate wish of a Berlin middle- class mother when her baby is about to start fussing. Especially when there are others present, like a research team, babies should present themselves— and thus also their mothers— at their best through smiling and cooing, as this short transcript of another Berlin middle- class mother demonstrates: 
Oh sweetie, what is the matter? Hm? [Are you] bored, or what? Baby starts crying Sweetie. Hm? [tststs] [tststs] Hm? Hm? What an impression are you making in the movie. (Baby continues fussing) Hm? So? (Baby quiets down with pacifier) You can look friendly. Hm? 
Western middle- class mothers (caregivers) want their babies to express a positive at-titude toward the world in general: “Enjoying life, uh? You are enjoying life, uh?” says a Los Angeles mother to her 3- month- old baby daughter with an expression of happiness herself. It is obvious that mothers are verbalizing infants’ inner states, emotions, intentions, and preferences. Mentalizing is regarded as a necessary parenting quality for children’s healthy development in Western middle- class families (Meins et  al., 2002; Fonagy, 1999) by adding a verbal track to affect mirroring. 
In this way, babies learn first and primarily about themselves. Only later, at about 2 years of age, do they understand that others may be different from themselves and have other preferences (i.e., preferring to eat broccoli over crackers; e.g., Gopnik & Meltzoff, 1994). Young children can recognize others’ internal (emotional) states as different from their own after they are able to recognize themselves in the mirror as an indicator of the development of a separated, categorial self (e.g., McDonald & Messinger, in press; but see Kärtner, Keller, & Chaudhary, 2010a). This is exactly the developmental science represented in Western textbooks, but it reflects solely the cultural model of the Western middle- class, with its emphasis on psychological autonomy. 
The intensive dyadic social encounters that babies experience during the first year of life are supplemented with artifacts like toys that further emphasize cultural messages. The use of children’s books is an important tool with which children can be socialized to the emotional values of their sociocultural milieu. Accordingly, Euro American preschoolers prefer excited smiles over calm expressions and perceive them as happy in picture books (Tsai, Louie, Chen, & Uchida, 2007a). Children draw themselves in line 
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  217 
with the prevailing cultural conception of the self. German preschoolers from middle- class families draw themselves generally as big figures with smiling faces (Gernhardt et al., 2014). 
Thus, facial emotional expressiveness is a centerpiece of early communication and interactional exchanges, with positive emotional displays being the gold standard of a happy child. 
It is within this cultural milieu that attachment theory has been developed (Bowlby, 1951; Ainsworth, 1977). Attachment theory can be considered as the major theory of socioemotional development to date which claims universal validity. However, it conceptualizes solely the Western middle- class perspective, with its child- centered view, the necessity of contingent visual/ vocal responsiveness and mentalizing, and the open expression of emotionality as the basis for the development of a secure attachment relationship for all children. This view has been criticized as ignoring the vast cultural diversity that characterizes human socialization strategies, emotional experience, and expressiveness and thus conceptions of the self. Margaret Mead had already pointed to this deficit in Bowlby’s conception at the very onset of attachment theory (Mead, 1954; for a detailed discussion see Vicedo, 2018). Despite impressive collections of different socialization agendas and strategies (e.g., Gottlieb, 2014; Gottlieb & DeLoache, 2017; Harwood, Miller, & Lucca Irizarry, 1995; Keller & Bard, 2017; Lancy, 2015; LeVine & LeVine, 2016; Otto & Keller, 2014; Quinn & Mageo, 2013; Senft & Senft, 2017; Vicedo, 2013), attachment researcher amazingly still come to the conclusion that, despite this variability, attachment theory is “a universally applicable account of the bond between caregivers and infants based on evolutionary and ethological considerations” (Mesman et al., 2016a). 
Varieties in Children’s Learning Environments and Their Consequences for Emotion Socialization Anthropologists have repeatedly described conceptions of the mind that do not focus on individual mental states as discussed in the Western literature (e.g., Barrett, Lewis, & Haviland- Jones, 2016; Duranti, 2008; Everett, 2009, 2014; Schieffelin & Ochs, 1986). The conception of the self includes others; others and the self are not separated. This conception values cooperation, conformity, obligation, modesty, and respect as the basic motifs of social regulation. These values necessitate different socialization strategies with different emotional markers. We have proposed the cultural model of hierarchical relatedness to capture this way of being and living that is adaptive in rural, subsistence- based communities, in particular in farming villages in non- Western societies. Relatedness defined in this way necessitates also a different mode of autonomy, one that can be characterized as action autonomy. Autonomy is not primarily focused on the individual’s mind and his or her free will, decision over choices, and the primacy of the subjective 
 
218 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
perspective, but instead on action responsibility for the social system, which yet equally necessitates independent/ autonomous functioning (Keller, 2012; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). 
Socialization strategies emphasizing hierarchical relatedness and action autonomy are quite different from the Western middle- class philosophy. Babies are carried on the back or hips of others almost all day. They thus experience being in synchronous motion with others, prompting a feeling of a communal self that sets the stage for integration into a network of different roles and responsibilities. Face- to- face exchange and emotional facial expressiveness with an emphasis on uniqueness and exclusiveness does not support these goals. Instead, babies learn to watch others and observe what they are doing. 
Caregiver’s attention is distributed and co- occurring with other activities like household chores or farming. It is not exclusively directed toward the infant and particularly not toward the child’s face. Thus, the visual attention may be on peeling vegetables or washing dishes, but the bodily attention is on the baby, who is constantly monitored for his or her bodily expressions. Contingent responsiveness to body signals is enacted in breastfeeding, changing body positions, and other bodily adjustments (Chapin, 2013). 
Along with distributed attention goes distributed care. Different caregivers cooperate in child care, so that children often do not become exclusively attached to one particular caregiver. 
A Northwest Cameroonian Nso farming mother has explained her philosophy in an interview: 
mother: No . . . I’m just thinking the child should not grow up only in the world of herself and the mother. 
interviewer: Okay. mother: You need to bring in other people into her life because you cannot just 
grow up with your child. There are moments, for instance, if she [the mother] dies now, the child will find it difficult now getting closer to another person. 
High mortality rates and the strains of the daily workload in a challenging environment clearly necessitate socialization strategies that are substantially different those of from Western middle- class families. Caring for a baby is a social commitment undertaken by several others, mostly other children (alloparenting or multiple caregiving) who know how to care for a baby without exploring the baby’s inner world or interpreting facial signals. 
Gabriel Scheidecker (2016) has significantly contributed to our knowledge of multiple caretaking with a case study from Madagascan villages. He observed (among other things) all the social encounters of children between 3 and 41  months with all their social partners. He reported that during the first months of life, infants are in physical contact with their mothers about 50% of the time, which drops to almost 0% at 2 years. However, face- to- face contact and maternal smiling are almost nonexistent. Mothers breastfeed and carry infants; all other social encounters take place in interactions with 
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  219 
other children, mainly with the group of children aged to 5 years, the “peer group” in his terminology. 
Conformity, modesty, and respect are also apparent in emotional disclosure. Discouragement of emotional expressiveness has been observed in many sub- Saharan rural environments like that of the Gusii in Kenya (LeVine et al., 1994), the !Kung in Botswana (Barr, Konner, Bakeman, & Adamson, 1991), and the Cameroonian Nso (e.g., Kärtner, Keller, & Yovsi, 2010b), but also in rural areas of other continents like that of the Indian Gujarati villagers (Abels et al., 2005). In many of these rural communities, open facial expression of emotions is regarded as disruptive and contradicting to social mores. Emotional expressiveness would impair the social rank order (the inequality between higher and lower ranking, older and younger individuals), with moral and conventional implications. It may also be subject to the evil eye taboo. Negative emotions are regulated in an anticipatory fashion through breastfeeding before an infant starts crying (Rothbaum, Pott, Azuma, Miyake, & Weisz, 2000), which fosters the perception of communion and the blurring the ego– other boundary. If infants display signs of negative emotions openly, the social reaction may be harsh, as the following short transcript of a Cameroonian Nso woman with her 3- month- old baby indicates: 
baby: [Fusses.] mother: Ship (.) Ship. Terrible. baby: [Cries.] mother: Take! Take! (.) See! See! No! (.) No! (.) No! Don’t cry again! (.) We don’t cry 
in Mbah! [name of market place across street] Terrible::: They don’t cry in Mbah! [angry] Stop fast! 
The discourse style is quite different from the Western middle- class model: there is no question asking, but instead instructions and commands; there is open criticism and even scolding, with ongoing references to the social group and the behavioral conventions customary to this group (“We do not cry in Mbah!”). 
Positive emotions are not reciprocated from adults, and infants quickly learn proper facial displays. Nso babies’ waking times also increase at 2  months of age, indicating the two- month shift, yet face- to- face contact between mother and baby, smiling of the mother at the baby’s face, and the baby’s smiling at his or her mother’s face do not increase (Kärtner et al., 2010b; Kärtner, 2013). Thus, infants learn to display neutral faces. Nso mothers strongly emphasize that it is an important socialization goal for children during the first 3 years of life to learn to control their emotions (Keller & Otto, 2009). 
The consequence of this socialization strategy is evident in 1- year- old children’s reactions to strangers. Stranger anxiety is assumed to be a universal reaction emerging at about 8  months of age (“8  months anxiety”) when children have formed specific attachments to one or a few significant others. Confrontations with a stranger are therefore part of increasing stress for 1- year- old infants in a laboratory procedure 
220 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
to assess children’s quality of attachment (the Strange Situation Procedure). However, Cameroonian Nso children or Ivorian Beng children, for example, do not show any signs of stranger anxiety (Gottlieb, 2014; Keller & Otto, 2009; Otto, 2014). In an experiment, when a strange woman came into a Nso compound and picked up a 1- year- old child who had just been breastfed by the mother and turned away from the mother, most of the children picked up reacted with a blank face while stretching their arms toward the strange woman. This reaction is considered to characterize a good child and proper conduct. Being emotionally neutral and receptive of the care of different persons is the culturally valued image of a good child (Otto, 2014). 
This baby behavior and this mode of parenting is not in line with the presumptions of attachment theory for the development of secure attachment relationships. On the contrary, the explicit emphasis of training and control as valuable parenting qualities would figure as intrusiveness and the warranted symbiosis between baby and caretakers would be classified as a clinical picture of enmeshment. Moreover, the distribution of caretaking for a baby to different persons, and particularly the significant role of other children, would not match Western caregiving morals (Keller & Chaudhary, 2017). These examples underline the cultural/ contextual specificity of adaptive reaction patterns since it certainly would not be advisable for Western middle- class babies to embrace strangers and separate from the mothers without loud protests. Whereas in Western middle- class families socialization processes are framed and regulated through emotional expressiveness, in particular positive emotionality, emotional neutrality is prevalent in many non- Western rural traditional communities where socialization processes are framed and regulated by social roles and conventions. These are basically differently organized socialization processes. 
Emotional self- effacement is not only part of social regulation in farming villages, but it also characterizes social encounters in many urban families, especially in Asian cultures. In line with the values of social respect and modesty, often rooted in religions like Confucianism, Buddhism, or Hinduisms, East Asians value calm over excited emotional states and expressions/ displays. Jeanne Tsai and colleagues (Tsai et al., 2007a; Tsai, Miao, Seppala, Fung, & Yeung, 2007b), for example, describe Taiwanese values promoting ideal affect as calm happiness, and Taiwanese children preferred calm happiness (smiling with the mouth closed) in the expressions of picture book figures compared to the excited happiness that US children preferred (smiling with open mouth and display of teeth). Interestingly, it was shown that, across cultures, exposure to story books altered children’s preferences. Thus, children exposed to an exciting (or calm) book will alter their preference for excited (or calm) activity. Tsai and colleagues (2007a) conclude that this shows that children are largely malleable in their emotions and suggests that it takes a period of time for cultural values to become ingrained. 
Culture supplies meanings to the accessibility of different emotion themes. Meanings and practices of different cultural contexts thus give rise to systematic cultural variation in emotional experience (Kitayama, Mesquita, & Karasawa, 2006). Table 8.1 
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  221 
summarizes different socialization strategies. However, it must be emphasized that these two strategies are not the endpoles of one dimension or exhaustive of worldwide variety. 
Different Conceptions of Parental Love and Warmth Mothers’ inclination for the preference (or not) of distributed caretaking is rooted in their living environment. The Nso mother referred to earlier explained that multiple caretaking is a necessity in order to ensure continuing childcare in case the mother dies (Otto, 2008). The strains of the daily duties of a farming or foraging woman do not leave room for an exclusive, time- consuming mother– child relationship— and state- regulated and supported maternal or paternal leaves do not exist. This does not, however, imply that Nso women, like other traditionally living villagers, do not love their children. Love in the Cameroonian Nso is expressed through body contact, in line with the preferred mode of interaction. Being in close proximity and sharing bodily rhythms is considered expressing love and warmth. In line with the focus on action over verbalizing and mentalizing in Nso social regulations, doing something for the child, like cooking and preparing food, is another expression of love and warmth. Love is not expressed through looking and talking. Talking about feelings would be considered as grossly inappropriate and immature behavior.

222 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
These action- related conceptions of warmth, love, and attachment are also shared by educated urban dwellers in non- Western countries. Studies comparing Chinese and other South East Asian urban families with European American ones confirmed different modes of warmth and love. Especially preparing and providing food plays a special role as an emotional investment (see, e.g., Chaudhary, 2013, for Indian families). On the Internet platform Bento on March 14, 2016, young people with an Asian migration background listed “things that you only know if you have Asian roots.” Among the comments: 
As soon as you get into to your parents place, they will ask you whether you are hungry and want to eat something. Then they present you five different dishes. 
It would be considered as very strange to tell your parents that you love them or hug each other. 
Charissa Cheah and colleagues (Cheah, Li, Zhou, Yamamoto, & Leung, 2015) interviewed Chinese immigrant and European American mothers concerning their conceptions of warmth in the parent– child relationships. Both groups found warmth equally important, yet they had different ideas regarding its expression. Chinese immigrant mothers’ responses were interpreted as reflecting a cultural emphasis on nurturance and instrumental support, whereas European American mothers’ responses reflected the Western cultural focus on more direct and outward demonstrations of warmth. This same difference was also found in a comparative study of middle- class mothers from Beijing and Los Angeles in interactional situations with their 3- month- old babies. Following are brief examples from the transcripts of these conversations. The Beijing mothers’ contributions were instrumental in referring to themselves as helping the child: “Mommy will help you move . . . ” “Let mommy get your rattle, let mommy find your rattle.” Los Angeles mothers, on the other hand, asked the child whether she or he wanted help and encouraged the child to do things for her- or himself: “Would you like some help?” “Can you make it go again? Broom Broom. Get it, you can get it. You can get it, I know you can” (Keller & Demuth, 2007). Beijing mothers express their love and care through helping the infant, whereas the LA mother supports her child’s individuality with praise and by instilling pride in the child’s own achievements. 
Also feeding is regarded as a sign of parental love and affection in many cultural communities. Contrary to the Western middle- class belief of the importance of early independent eating, mothers from many different non- Western (urban as well as rural) communities understand feeding the child as a sign of affection and care. The Indian cultural psychologist Nandita Chaudhary discusses on her Facebook site (July 2, 2017) reasons why Indian parents feed their children: “The third reason, and perhaps the most intense, is that the act of feeding another person (child or other loved one, someone in need) is an act of affection; and if you have cooked it, well, that’s a double dose of it!!”
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  223 
Focal Emotions Cultural environments do not only differ in the expression and intensity of emotions; socialization strategies may be centered on different focal emotions. In Western middle- class families, joy, happiness, and excitement (positive emotionality) seem to be organizing socialization processes, as we have argued before. Heidi Fung, for example, has described the emphasis on shame in Taiwanese families’ socialization practices as compared to the emphasis on positive emotionality and praise in European American families (Fung, 1999). Birgitt Röttger- Rössler and colleagues (Röttger- Rössler, Scheidecker, Jung, & Holodynski, 2013; Röttger- Rössler, Scheidecker, Funk, & Holodynski, 2015) have studied the socialization of emotions in long- term field observations of 12 months each in three different societies: the Minangkabau in Indonesia, the Bara in Madagascar, and the Tao in Taiwan. These three groups share a common affiliation with the West Austronesian language family yet differ vastly in their economy, social structure, and religious orientation. These authors were interested in children’s acquisition of categorial emotion knowledge, how emotions become expressed and regulated, and which cultural transmission practices are related to differences in these domains. Their multimethod assessments comprised the documentation of the indigenous emotional vocabularies, the documentation of emotional episodes in real- life situations, interviews concerning socialization practices, cultural models of emotions, and others addressing children as well as adults. They could present evidence that the Indonesian Minangkabau emphasize “shame,” while the Madagascan Bara emphasize “fear” and the Taiwanese Tao “anxiety” as focal socializing emotions. The Cameroonian Nso expect shame and guilt in the emotional repertoire of children long before German middle- class mothers expect these emotions to be present in their children (Keller & Otto, 2009). 
Finally, cultural environments differ in the regulatory function that is assigned to different emotions. 
An interesting case study is presented in a documentary film by Donata Elschenbroich and Otto Schweitzer (1995). They observed transition into kindergarten in Japanese institutions and could observe that children were rather abruptly separated from their mothers and simply handed over to a daycare teacher. The children burst into tears, which was accepted and appreciated. The teachers explained that the crying indicated that the children were attached to their mothers; this was highly valued and the teachers believed that they could learn to know the children through their crying and consequently better care for them. This practice is directly opposite to German ideas about quality pedagogy, which is aimed at minimizing children’s distress and negative emotionality. Transition into daycare is organized as a smooth passage, usually with the mother spending decreasing amounts of time over a period of several weeks with the child in the institution. A  particular adult kindergarten teacher serves as a reference person who familiarizes the child with the institution and the group. This attachment theory– based program is designed to prevent the experience and expression of negative 
 
224 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
affect in the child (Laewen & Andres, 2011). Thus, cultures differ remarkably with respect to the emotions that they deem central in framing and structuring socialization processes. 
Outlook and Implications In the previous paragraphs, the role of emotions in socialization strategies of families in different cultural contexts has been highlighted exemplarily. In particular, two contexts were addressed: Western urban middle- class families representing the cultural model of psychological autonomy/ psychological relatedness and rural subsistence- based families in non- Western societies representing the cultural model of hierarchical relatedness/ action autonomy. We added also examples from urban middle- class families from non- Western societies, especially from South East Asia, that combine psychological autonomy in some segments of their lives with hierarchical relatedness in other segments of their lives or who experience multiple other possible combinations of the two prototypical models (Keller, 2007, 2012; Keller & Kärtner, 2013). 
Emotions have been discussed with respect to the prevalence and centrality of particular emotions (focal emotions) in socialization strategies, culture- specific meaning systems, and cultural conventions of emotional expressiveness. It is obvious that, based on universal predispositions, emotional experience and emotional expressions may be differently shaped in different environments so that different phenotypic appearances emerge. It is, however, common practice to apply the Western middle- class understanding of emotional experience, expression, and socioemotional regulation on a worldwide scale— in research as well as in practice. For example, East Asian mothers are often characterized as lower in warmth and harsher in their parenting strategies than European American mothers. These ethnocentric evaluations are based on comparative studies using instruments that are operationalizing the Western philosophy and/ or evaluating practices according to one (the Western) meaning system. Cheah and colleagues (2015) discuss these comparisons as relying especially on physical and verbal expressions of love that may not capture the pivotal role of instrumental care– related expressions in other cultures. Instruments often use Likert like scales that cannot capture the meaning behind certain practices. 
Cheung and Elliott (2016) discuss cultural variations in the meaning and measurement of sensitivity based on studies with participants from Singapore. They used the Emotional Availability scale (EA; Biringen, 2008)  that has been described as valid in different cultural contexts based on comparative studies. Cheung and Elliott (2016) conclude tentatively that the inconsistencies they found may relate to the weight of the affective component in the scale, especially in reference to positive emotions and the affective quality of dyadic interactions expressed “by warm smiles and giggles, interested eye contact, and comforting and playful physical contact” (Biringen, 2008, p. 24). The local Singaporean interaction style differs in that displays of positive affect are not frequent 
 
The role of emoTions in soCial izaT ion ProCesses  |  225 
occurrences in day- to- day parent– child interactions (for a greater discussion, see Cheung & Elliott, 2016). The culturally important dimensions may not be assessed at all using Western tools, even if they are translated and back- translated as cultural adaptations. 
Answering the same questions similarly also does not prove construct validity. For example, Cameroonian Nso farming women, Indian farming women from Gujarat, and German middle- class women all indicated that breastfeeding is very important for babies during the early phase of their lives. Yet they had very different meaning sets in which their opinions were embedded. The farming women thought of the nutritional value and the permanent availability of nutrition due to bodily proximity, whereas the urban Western women thought of the special dyadic situation affording face- to- face contact that facilitated the emotional bonding processes (Keller, 2013; see also the importance of warmth discussed earlier). 
Interpreting the behaviors and ideas in one cultural model with the standards of another cultural model is unscientific and unethical. It is unscientific because of the incomplete and superficial assessment of the existing literature or simply due to ignorance of its relevance, as is often the case, for example, in attachment research (for an example, see Mesman, van IJzendorn, & Sagi- Schwartz, 2016). It is unethical for the same reasons, with yet wider implications for clinical and educational practice. Migrants from rural ecocultural milieus that adhere to a model of hierarchical relatedness with its respective emotional regulations are often evaluated and interpreted as having emotional deficits, as being poor parents who are not interested in the well- being of their children because they do not display the explicit and verbal (hugging, kissing) affection that the Western model deems normal. There are ample examples in books dealing with migrants from an applied perspective where one can read about the “lack” of mentalizing ability of many migrants (e.g., different chapters in Brisch, 2016) or the bland affect and emotional noninvolvement that is diagnosed in migrant parents. Action by child protection services often follows, such as taking children out of their family and other measures that are highly inappropriate and that deteriorate family life and hinder children’s development (e.g., Chaudhary & Valsiner, 2015). 
Getting to know the different emotional repertoires of different cultural environments and finding a way to maneuver between them or develop ways to combine them is a challenging task for many migrants, especially for those who already have been socialized in their culture of origin (first and 1 1/ 2 generations), but also for following generations. Tensions with first- generation parents and grandparents are inevitable for the next generations (see Röttger- Rössler, 2016). On the other hand, maintaining cultural values (especially family- related values of community, respect, and responsibility) and the language of origin has been associated with better integration in terms of educational attainments, health, well- being, and other societal factors. The so- called immigrant paradox points to the fact that the generations following migrants are less adjusted and have more personal and social problems when they give up their culture of origin and become assimilated into the new culture (Garcia Coll & Marks, 2012).
226 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Emotions are central to human life. They define the quality of and give meaning to our existence (Zalta, 2012). This is what humans share across borders, cultures, and races. How this quality is defined and what constitutes meaning is bound to cultural models that groups of humans share (e.g., those who live in similar sociocultural milieus). And there are certainly also individually unique features, since emotional experience and expression are constructed and co- constructed during ontogeny just as all human characteristics are, even if there is a universal and inborn base. The recognition of these differences is the moral responsibility of basic scientists as well as of practitioners from different domains such as pediatrics, family law, counseling and therapy, and education in different parts of the world.

Basic Processes 
 
9 
Gender and Culture 
Deborah L. Best and Angelica R. Puzio 
One of the more striking variations observed when traveling in different countries is that some societies emphasize the differences between women and men, while other societies show less interest in such diversity. Highlighting sex differences leads to the expectation that gender must be an important determinant of human behavior. However, it is essential to remember that, anatomically and physiologically, human males and females are much more similar than different. Consequently, they are mostly interchangeable with regard to social roles and behaviors, with childbearing being the fundamental exception. As classic and more recent cross- cultural research related to gender is reviewed, the reader may be surprised to see how little difference gender makes when considered against the broad background of variability in psychological characteristics across cultural groups. Yet, as will be apparent in the discussion, women continue to experience marked inequalities in social, educational, and economic domains. The status of the gender groups is unequal in all cultures that have been studied, with men enjoying higher status than women (Leaper & Bigler, 2011). 
This chapter concerns gender in the cross- cultural context, extending from the individual to the cultural level and examining topics such as gender roles and stereotypes, relationships between men and women, the roles of biology and socialization, and theories of gender role development. The focus is upon the general areas of developmental, personality, and social psychology that deal with how males and females view themselves and one another, as well as the way they should and do interact. Before reviewing the literature, some basic gender- related terms will be defined to avoid conceptual confusion. 
 
 
236 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Definitions of Gender- Related Concepts 
 • Sex refers to the anatomical and physiological differences between males and females, particularly in regard to chromosomal, hormonal, and reproductive dissimilarities. 
 • Gender is also used to distinguish the female and male members of the human species but with emphasis on sociocultural and psychological meaning that is assigned to biological differences between the sexes. 
 • Gender roles refer to the social roles, including familial, occupational, and recreational activities, which men and women occupy with differential frequency. 
 • Gender role ideology designates beliefs concerning appropriate relationships between the genders, varying along a dimension ranging from a traditional, male- dominant or anti- female view to a modern, egalitarian, or feminist view. 
 • Gender stereotypes refer to the psychological traits and behaviors that are believed to occur with differential frequency in the two gender groups (i.e., men are more “aggressive,” women are more “emotional”). Stereotypes provide support for traditional gender role assignments and may serve as socialization models for children. 
 • Masculinity– femininity represents the degree to which men and women adhere to traits that have been socially prescribed as masculine or feminine. 
 • Gender identity refers to an individual’s internal understanding of themselves as female or male. 
 • Cisgender describes the correspondence of gender identity and birth- assigned sex cat-egory (e.g., an individual who was labeled “male” at birth and identifies as a man). 
 • Transgender, gender queer, and non– gender conforming are terms used to describe gender identities that do not correspond to the traditional male– female dichotomy. Transgender is often used to describe a lack of correspondence between gender identity and birth- assigned sex category (e.g., an individual who was labeled “male” at birth and identifies as a woman), whereas gender queer and non– gender conforming refer to a multitude of gender identities that exist between or beyond traditional gender binaries. 
With these definitions in mind, the discussion now turns to the individual and the role of gender in cross- cultural context. Cross- cultural studies of gender are concerned with both the degree to which psychological processes and behaviors are relatively invariant across cultures as well as how they vary systematically with cultural influences. 
Developmental Influences: Biological Aspects Having seen the influence of gender on the behavior and relationships of adults, it is natural to wonder about the development of gender- related beliefs and behaviors and the role of biological and cultural influences across ontogeny. The next sections give an overview 
 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  237 
of the more biological aspects of development followed by a discussion of the cultural and socialization aspects of gender development (see also Chapter 7 by Harry W. Gardiner and Chapter 8 by Heidi Keller for extended discussions of culture and development). 
Biological Determinism and Sexual Dimorphism Researchers studying gender differences in behavior often cite similarities across cultures as support for the role of genes and hormones, implying complete genetic or biological determinism or essentialism. Biological determinism assumes that any biological influence or bias always leads to an irreversible sex difference, making biology both the necessary and sufficient cause of sex differences. However, biology is neither. The long- standing nature– nurture controversy within developmental psychology has shown that biology does not cause behavior and that such thinking is quite naïve. Rather, cross- cultural research supports the notion that genetic and environmental factors interact in a dynamic system (Lerner, 2015). 
Sex chromosomes or sex hormones are neither necessary nor sufficient to cause behaviors; they simply change the probability of occurrence of certain behaviors (Hoyenga & Hoyenga, 1993; Lickliter & Honeycutt, 2003). The gene– behavior pathway is bidirectional (Gottlieb, 1983, 2007), and, somewhat like people inherit genes, they may “inherit” environments by living close to parents and family (Figure 9.1). 
Brain imaging techniques have shown that as humans acquire new experiences and gain new knowledge, the environment continually shapes and reshapes the brain across the lifetime. However, the notion that genes and biology determine gender- differentiated cognition and behaviors, although incorrect, is still very much alive (Vidal, 2012). 
In addition to overstating and misinterpreting the role of genetic factors in the conception of sex differences, biological determinism also postulates that the sexes fall into dimorphic categories (i.e., distinctly male and female). Current research disputes this claim, instead supporting the notion that sex- differentiation operates on a continuum rather than a dichotomy. For example, research exploring the degree to which male and female brains are structurally differentiated regarding gray and white matter has found

little within- sex consistency (Joel et  al., 2015). Increases in public and academic discourse surrounding intersex, transgender, gender queer, and gender non– conforming individuals has also given visibility to a nondichotomous understanding of the sexes (Tate, Youssef, & Bettergarcia, 2014). Growing evidence suggests that sex differentiation is the result of multiple co- acting genetic and sociocultural factors, and such differentiation occurs outside of a restrictive male– female binary. Despite an increasingly nuanced understanding of sexual dimorphism, some relatively consistent physiological differences exist and are noted here. 
Brain Structures When looking at cortical brain structures, Knickmeyer and colleagues (2014) found that sex differences vary across development. Some sex differences in brain structure are stable across the lifespan. Others are not present in the neonate but arise during childhood and/ or adolescence. Some sex differences are present during periods with high circulating gonadal steroids (e.g., neonate, adult, not during childhood), and other sex differences are unique to the neonate. Sexual dimorphism of the brain reflects the dynamic interplay of the biological (e.g., prenatal, neonatal, pubertal hormones; sex- chromosomes) and the experiential (e.g., parental expectations and interactions; physical hazards; culturally influenced lifestyle) (Rutter, Caspi, & Moffitt, 2003). Indeed, cortical structure varies in a complex, highly dynamic way across the human lifespan. 
Physical Differences Compared with females, at birth males are about a ½- pound heavier and have a higher activity level (Campbell & Eaton, 1999; Eaton & Enns, 1986), a higher basal metabolism, more muscle development, and a higher pain threshold (Rosenberg & Sutton- Smith, 1972). Males have larger brain size and advanced motor development while females have more advanced sensory development (Fausto- Sterling, García Coll, & Lamarre, 2011) and greater average brain cortical maturity (Thordstein, Lofgren, Flisberg, Lindecrantz, & Kjellmer, 2006). The groups overlap for these small sex differences, and many disappear over time. During the preadolescent years (ages 3– 10), there are few gender differences in morphology or hormonal states, but those that are observed are consistent with the sexual dimorphism that is found later (Tanner, 1961, 1970). By adulthood, males attain greater height and have a more massive skeleton, higher muscle- to- fat ratio, higher blood oxygen capacity, more body hair, and different primary and secondary sex characteristics (D’Andrade, 1966; Janssen, Heymsfield, Wang, & Ross, 2000; Tanner, 1961). A number of these anatomical and stamina- related differences are thought to be related to the longer growth period of boys and the hormonal changes that appear after age 8 (Ember, 1981). However, these differences only hold within populations, not between, and they apply only to group means rather than individual comparisons (Munroe & Munroe, 1975/ 1994). Many women are stronger and more active than many men, and parental and cultural expectations can amplify or diminish such sex differences. 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  239 
The body of literature on sexual dimorphism suggests that while biology is not destiny, biological influences are certainly important contributors to the development of gender differences. The term “biological” is often used to refer to genes— in this case sex chromosomes— but “biological” should also include the influence of an organism’s prenatal and postnatal environments, and often the activities in those environments are culturally determined. For example, length of sleep bouts, which are usually considered to be biologically regulated, are modified by culturally determined demands on mothers’ time. Indeed, the development of infants’ sitting and walking are influenced by culturally defined childcare practices (Super & Harkness, 1982). 
Transgenderism, Gender Nonconformity, and Intersexuality Although sexual development and sexuality are not the focus of this chapter (see Hines, 2013, for an excellent review of these topics), sexual development, which shapes gender development, has a number of biological influences, including sex chromosomes, gonads, sex hormones, and internal and external genitalia that combine with physical, social, and emotional experience to result in culturally defined gender categories. These categories are often simplified into female, male, and sometimes intersex, although “nature” does not determine where each category begins and ends. The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (2015) notes that intersex individuals “do not fit the typical definitions for male or female bodies.” Such variations may include ambiguous genitalia, as well as chromosomal genotype and sexual phenotype that differ from XY- male and XX- female, and these variations are independent of gender identity and sexual orientation. Genes by themselves do not determine or “cause” gender development, but they have a complex interaction with culture and the physical environment, a dynamic system that develops across the lifespan (Salk & Hyde, 2012). 
Increasing evidence suggests that both sex and gender can manifest in non- dimorphic ways, with social and academic visibility on the rise for intersex and transgender individuals (Coulter, Kenst, Bowen, & Scout, 2014). Typically, humans are assigned to binary male and female gender categories at birth based on anatomical differences in genitalia, and subsequent gender socialization practices mirror these rigid categorizations. However, some intersex conditions (e.g., androgen insensitivity syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia) may make categorization difficult. 
Although most individuals develop a gender identity that corresponds with their birth- assigned sex, some do not. Those who feel that their internal sense of gender does not match their assigned sex category are often referred to as existing on the “transgender spectrum,” although the way individuals label nonconforming expressions of gender are determined by both individual and cultural factors. Cultures around the world vary in the levels of tolerance and recognition given to these individuals. In many societies, such as the United States, transgender people face considerable discrimination, harassment, and violence (Bradford, Reisner, Honnald, & Xavier, 2013) despite growing social awareness of 
 
240 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
transgender experiences. In other cultures, nonbinary expressions of gender are woven into cultural practices and histories. For example, hijras, which refers to gender nonconforming or “third gender” people in India and Pakistan, once occupied traditional roles of dancing and performing at various cultural ceremonies, although this is less common today (Goel, 2016). A growing body of research surrounding transgender and gender nonconforming individuals suggests that gender identity and birth- assigned sex do not always align. 
Sociobiology, Evolutionary Psychology, Economic Anthropology Looking at the interplay between biology and environment, sociobiologists (e.g., Daly & Wilson, 1978; Wilson, 1975), evolutionary psychologists (e.g., Buss, 1990a; Kenrick & Luce, 2000; Nisbett, 1990), and economic anthropologists (Fry, 1987)  suggest that some behavioral mechanisms have evolved in response to selection pressures. Diversity in gender roles reflects the fact that different circumstances trigger different behavioral responses, each of which are biologically prepared. 
For example, Gilmore (1990) proposes that the male macho behavior pattern is an adaptation to extreme risk associated with economic necessities. The dramatic difference in gender roles between two South Pacific islands, Truk and Tahiti, illustrate Gilmore’s hypothesis. Trukese males are competitive, violent fighters, and sexually promiscuous while females are expected to be submissive and protected by the men. In contrast, Tahitian men are not interested in material pursuits or in competition and are expected to be passive and submissive while the women are generally known to be sexually active. Gilmore (1990) accounts for these variations by pointing out dramatic differences in obtaining food. Tahitians fish in a protected lagoon where there is little risk and fish are plentiful. Trukese must fish in the open ocean with the genuine possibility of not returning after a day at sea. Thus, the macho style may be an adaptation to danger that encourages Trukese men to face great peril. 
Evolutionary theory has made the assumption that different behaviors are adaptive for males and females, and it has been used to explain differences that are found between the sexes. For example, evolutionary theory is used as an explanation for gender differences in parental investment and in the number of desired sexual partners. Evolutionary sexual selection is used to explain gender differences in aggression (Buss, 1989, 1990b). While these explanations are appealing, support for these conceptions has been mixed (Pedersen, Putcha- Bhagavatula, & Miller, 2011). 
Developmental Influences: Cultural/ Socialization Aspects Cultural Influences Even though biological factors may impose predispositions and restrictions on development, sociocultural factors are important determinants of development (Best & Williams, 
 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  241 
1993; Keller & Kärtner, 2013; Munroe & Munroe, 1975, 1994; Rogoff, Gauvain, & Ellis, 1984). Culture has profound effects on behavior, prescribing how babies are delivered, how children are socialized, how they are dressed, what is considered intelligent behavior, what tasks children are taught, and what roles adult men and women will adopt. The scope and progression of children’s behaviors, even behaviors that are considered biologically determined, are governed by culture. Cultural universals in gender differences are often explained by similarities in socialization practices while cultural differences are attributed to differences in socialization. Unfortunately, this is an oversimplified view of how gendered behaviors develop. 
One of the best known, though often questioned, examples of cultural diversity in gender- related behaviors is Margaret Mead’s classic study of three tribes in New Guinea (Mead, 1935, 1949). Mead reported that, from a Western viewpoint, these societies created men and women who are both masculine and feminine and who reversed the usual gender roles. More recent studies have found cultural groups that differ from traditional gender roles. Aka and Bofi foragers of Central Africa have relatively egalitarian gender roles, positive evaluations of female and male children, fathers who are highly involved with infants, and both parents are involved in net hunting and other subsistence activities (Fouts, 2008). Similarly, among the Murik of Papua New Guinea, the composition of gender emphasizes maternal qualities for both males and females (Barlow, 2013). Murik men value and express maternal qualities of caregiving and feeding others, and the role of caregiver is considered to be one of power, independence, and resourcefulness. Giving food, whether as a daily activity or in a ritual, is an act of proximity- seeking, the hallmark of attachment. 
Interestingly, the pervasive nature of sex differences in behaviors were poignantly illustrated in the Israeli kibbutz, established in the 1920s, where there was a deliberate attempt to develop egalitarian societies (Rosner, 1967; Snarey & Son, 1986; Spiro, 1956). Initially, there was no sexual division of labor among members of this society. Both women and men worked in the fields, drove tractors, and worked in the kitchens and laundries. However, as time went by and the birthrate increased, it was soon discovered that women could not undertake many of the physical tasks of which men were capable. Women soon found themselves in the same roles from which they were supposed to have been emancipated: cooking, cleaning, laundering, and teaching and caring for children. The kibbutz attempts at equitable division of labor seemed to have little effect on the children. Carlsson and Barnes (1986) found no cultural or sex differences between kibbutz- raised children and Swedish children regarding how they conceptualized typical female and male gender role behaviors nor in their gender- typed self- attributions, though they were more liberal than urban Israeli adolescents (Kulik, 1998). 
Socialization of Boys and Girls For boys and girls, many behavioral differences are attributed to differences in socialization, the intertwined physical, social, and emotional experiences that create culturally 
 
 
242 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
guided embodiment (Thelen, 2008). Barry, Bacon, and Child (1957) examined socialization practices in more than 100 societies and found that boys are generally raised to achieve and to be self- reliant and independent, while girls are raised to be nurturant, responsible, and obedient. However, Hendrix and Johnson (1985) reanalyzed these data and did not replicate the male– female difference in socialization. Indeed, the instrumental- expressive components were not polar opposites but were orthogonal, unrelated dimensions with similar emphases in the training of boys and girls. 
In their meta- analysis of 158 studies on North American parents’ differential socialization of boys and girls, Lytton and Romney (1991) found the only significant effect was for the encouragement of gender- typed behaviors. In the 17 additional studies from other Western countries in their analysis, there was a significant sex difference for physical punishment, with boys receiving a greater portion than girls. Differential treatment of boys and girls decreased with age, particularly for disciplinary strictness and encouragement of gender- typed activities. 
In an excellent review of the literature on parenting of girls and boys, Leaper (2002) pointed out several differential practices not examined in earlier studies. Mothers respond more contingently to infant sons than daughters, perhaps because boys are more irritable, and this response pattern encourages sons to develop greater emotional self- regulation. Mothers are generally more verbally stimulating than fathers, and they talk more to daughters than to sons. Parents discuss emotional experiences with daughters more than with sons, and they are more likely to talk about sadness with daughters and anger with sons. 
Overall, these socialization findings suggest that there may be subtle differences in the ways that boys and girls are treated by parents. In research, these differences are not consistently significant, perhaps due to the categories used to quantify behaviors. Even if parents do not differentiate between daughters and sons due to biological differences or preexisting preferences, the same parental treatment may affect girls and boys differently. 
Task Assignment Examination of children’s learning environments in various cultural groups yields a better understanding of how cultural differences in socialization processes affect children’s development. Learning environments were investigated in the classic Six Culture Study (Edwards & Whiting, 1974; Minturn & Lambert, 1964; Whiting & Edwards, 1973) which examined aggression, nurturance, responsibility, and help and attention- seeking behaviors of children aged 3– 11 in Okinawa, Mexico, the Philippines, India, Kenya, and the United States. Fewer gender differences were found in the three samples (United States, the Philippines, Kenya) where both boys and girls cared for younger siblings and performed household chores. In contrast, more differences were found in the samples (India, Mexico, Okinawa) where boys and girls were treated dissimilarly and girls were asked to assume more responsibility for siblings and household tasks. Indeed, the fewest 
 
gender and CulTure  |  243 
gender differences were found in the American sample, in which neither girls nor boys were assigned many childcare or household tasks. 
Gaskins (2015) points out that when European American parents do assign children tasks, it is not because they need their help but because parents think children should work in order to learn responsibility and independence. Bradley (1993) examined children’s labor in 91 Standard Cross- Cultural Sample cultures (Murdock & White, 1969) and found that children younger than 6 years perform little work whereas children older than 10 years perform work much like that of same gender adults. Both boys and girls do women’s work (e.g., fetching water) more frequently than men’s (e.g., hunting), and children tend to do work that adults consider demeaning or unskilled. Women monitor children’s labor, which socializes them and helps the mother. Along with providing care in parents’ old age, children’s labor is one of the important benefits of having children (Trommsdorff, 2009). 
These findings are consistent with research in the United States (Etaugh & Liss, 1992) which indicated that girls did more chores than boys, with more than half of the girls having kitchen- related tasks, and some girls babysat. Boys were more likely to take out the trash or have no chores, and no boys babysat. Recently, Giles and colleagues (Giles, Cantin, Best, Tyrrell, & Gigler, 2014) found that African American and Hispanic fifth- graders had more household chores and filial responsibilities than European American children, and minority girls had more chores than boys. Although all minority children were involved in caring for younger siblings, girls spent twice as much time in sibling care as boys. 
Using similar methodology, Cameron and Best (2015) investigated children’s home responsibilities in Turkey, which traditionally has emphasized gender differences. However, over recent years, Turkey has been moving toward more gender equality, although collectivist and patriarchal characteristics are still apparent (Kağıtçıbaşı, 1996). Fifth- grade girls reported more household responsibilities (e.g., preparing meals, cleaning) than boys, and, interestingly, for some types of activities, boys reported more caregiving for younger siblings. Although Turkish culturally based gender roles may be shifting, increased home responsibilities have affected girls and boys in distinct ways, with boys reacting more negatively to their new responsibilities (Figure 9.2). 
Caregiving Weisner and Gallimore (1977) analyzed data from 186 societies and found that mothers, female adult relatives, and female children are the primary caregivers of infants. However, when those infants reach early childhood, responsibilities are shared among both sex peer groups. Sibling caregivers are a predominant source of socialization in societies where 2- to 4- year- olds spend more than 70% of every day with their child nurses. Children 5– 11 years old, usually girls, regularly provide daytime care for infant siblings, particularly after the infant reaches 5  months of age (Levine et  al., 1994). Mothers in such societies spend much of their time in various productive activities, such as gardening,
