gender and CulTure  |  245 
animal care, and spinning, and they are not devoted exclusively to mothering (Greenfield, 1981; Minturn & Lambert, 1964) although children in all cultures see mothers as responsible for children. Indeed, attachment theory emphasized the centrality of the mother– child dyad as the basis for normal social development, and mothers do spend more time with infants than do other caregivers even when multiple caregiving is commonplace (Tronick, Morelli, & Ivey, 1992). Girls’ greater interest in and interactions with babies begins in the late preschool years and continues into adulthood (Blakemore, 1998). 
Moreover, in 20% of 80 cultures surveyed (Katz & Konner, 1981; West & Konner, 1976), fathers were rarely or never near their infants. Father– infant relationships were close in only 4% of the cultures, but, even when close, fathers spent only 14% of their time with their infants and gave only 6% of the actual caregiving. In most societies, play characterized paternal interactions with children (Munroe & Munroe, 1994). In a recent nine- country study (China, Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, the Philippines, Sweden, Thailand, and the United States), mothers had significantly more progressive, modern attitudes toward childrearing and education and fathers’ had more authoritarian attitudes, but the differences were small (Bornstein, Putnick, & Lansford, 2011). Looking at the role of fathers, their absence has been associated with violent or hypermasculine behaviors (Gronseth, 1957; Katz & Konner, 1981; Lynn & Sawrey, 1959; Segall, 1988; Stolz, 1954; Whiting, 1965). A recent longitudinal study of 15,293 families in the UK’s Millennium Cohort Study across children’s first 7 years of life indicated a robust relation between father absence and both girls’ and boys’ problem behaviors (Flouri, Narayanan, & Midouhas, 2015). 
Fathers in North American cultures spend less time with children and also pay less attention to female offspring than to males and encourage gender- typed activities more than mothers (Lytton & Romney, 1991). Mothers are equally important as caretakers of sons and daughters, but fathers tended to be more important as caretakers of sons (Rohner & Rohner, 1982) (Figure 9.3). 
Mackey and Day (1979) observed parents and children in public places in 10 different cultures and found that girls were more often in groups that had no adult males while boys were frequently found in all- male groups and mixed- gender ones, and these differences intensified with age. Fathers of child and adolescent girls show less interested attention to them, do fewer activities with them, and put less effort into promoting their cognitive/ intellectual development, which may lead to girls developing less interest and ability in traditionally male domains or careers (Bronstein, 2006). 
Peers Throughout childhood and adolescence, peers play an important role in socialization. Peer influence increases as children grow older, helping to structure the transition between childhood and adulthood (Edwards, 1992). Analysis of peer interactions of 2- to 10- year- olds from the Six Culture Study and six additional samples (Edwards, 1992; Edwards & Whiting, 1993) showed a cross- culturally universal and robust tendency for 
 
246 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
same- gender preference to emerge after age 2. By middle childhood, gender segregation is found frequently. Edwards speculates that same- gender attraction may be motivated by a desire for self- discovery, making same- gender agemates the best mirrors. Agemates resemble the child in abilities and activity preferences, but they also provide the greatest opportunity for competition and conflict. 
Play, a frequent component of peer interaction, may be an important activity in which gender is socially learned in early childhood (Leaper & Friedman, 2007). Mean level gender differences in toy choices and gender- typed play, whereby boys typically engage in more action- oriented activity and girls in more affiliative and domestically oriented activity, have been demonstrated cross- culturally. Such differences exist even in Nordic cultures known for their highly egalitarian views on gender (Nelson, 2005). 
Preadolescents and adolescents have more confidence in relating to own- gender versus other- gender peers, and this gender- based relationship efficacy may serve a role in gender segregation (Zosuls, Field, Martin, Andrews, & England, 2014). Although gender segregation seems to be the rule, it is not a universal pattern (Montgomery, 2010). Even in the gender segregated Kipsigis of rural Kenya, middle childhood girls and boys are not separated and do not seem to prefer their own- gender playmates (Harkness & Super, 1985). Indeed, in the hunter- gatherer !Kung and Efe societies, children frequently play in multiage and multisex groups (Konner, 2005).

Adolescent initiation rites found in many cultures are designed to detach the initiate from the family; to socialize them to culturally appropriate sexuality, dominance, and aggression; to create peer group loyalty; and to solidify political ties. Collective rituals are more common for boys than girls and are found more frequently in “warrior” societies which emphasize gender differences in men’s and women’s activities (Edwards, 1992). Although Western education has begun to change initiation rites, vestiges remain. 
Education Educational settings also greatly influence children’s behaviors. Observations of fifth- graders in Japan and in the United States indicate that teachers in both countries paid more attention to boys, particularly negative attention, and the greater attention was not attributable to off- task or bad behavior (Hamilton, Blumenfeld, Akoh, & Miura, 1991). 
Parental beliefs about academic performance can also have profound impact on children’s achievements. Serpell (1993) found that education was considered more important for Zambian boys than girls, and fathers assumed responsibility for arranging schooling even though mothers were primarily responsible for childcare. In China, Japan, and the United States, mothers expect boys to be better at mathematics and for girls to be better at reading (Lummis & Stevenson, 1990) although they perform equally well in some aspects of both disciplines. 
In an extensive 12- year study of more than 700 European American children, Simpkins, Fredricks, and Eccles (2015) found support for their expectancy- value model of children’s achievement- related activities and choices in sports, instrumental music, mathematics, and reading. Parents’ perceptions of their children’s abilities influenced their children’s sense of their own abilities, particularly in sports and reading. Fathers had greater predictive influence on children’s math abilities, and parents of boys valued instrumental music less than sports. Boys’ ability self- concepts, value beliefs, and participation in sports and math were higher than girls’ and were lower than girls’ in reading and music. Interestingly, children showed gender- stereotyped patterns of expectancy and value in all areas, with boys having higher ability beliefs and values for sports and math and girls having higher ability beliefs and values in reading and music. Parents’ beliefs about sports and music were similar to their children’s, but beliefs about reading and math did not differ for sons and daughters. Some of the traditional cultural beliefs regarding differential educational expectations and opportunities for girls and boys are changing in concert with changes in women’s roles and increases in economic development and globalization. 
The literature reviewed echoes the broader maxim that development does not exist in isolation; multiple, co- acting contexts interact to produce gender- typed behaviors. The influence of culturally varied socialization practices reveals that gender is constructed not only through biology, but also through children’s interactions with peers, family, and caregivers, as well as other educational and nation- specific contexts. 
 
248 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Cross- Cultural Theories of Gender- Related Learning Most theories of gender role learning emphasize gender information readily available in the culture even though the theories were devised primarily in the United States.1 Each theory can be adapted to explain cross- cultural patterns of development. As Leaper and Friedman (2007) note, theories of gender development are often complementary despite differing levels of emphasis on social and cognitive influences. 
Social Cognitive Learning Theories Social learning theories (Bandura, 1969; Bussey & Bandura, 1984; Mischel, 1970) consider gender role development to be the result of cumulative experience. Parents, teachers, peers, media, and other socialization agents shape children’s gender- related behaviors through the respective reinforcement and punishment of gender- appropriate and inappropriate behaviors, modeling, expectations, toy choices, and other differential treatment of boys and girls. Research in the United States has shown same- sex and opposite- sex parents react differently to their children, with fathers showing more differential behavior than mothers (Maccoby & Jacklin, 1974). Meta- analysis supports the notion that parental attitudes influence children’s development of gender schemas (Tenenbaum & Leaper, 2002); however, such findings have not been replicated successfully across cultures (e.g., Israel, Kulik, 2002; Japan, Korea, Sagara & Kang, 1998). The few studies conducted in other countries (Mexico, Bronstein, 1984; Sweden, Lamb, Frodi, Hwand, Frodi, & Steinberg, 1982; Australia, Russell & Russell, 1987; Israeli kibbutzim, Sagi, Lamb, Shoham, Dvir, & Lewkowicz, 1985) do not always show consistent differential parental treatment of boys and girls. 
Halpern and Perry- Jenkins (2016) asked white working- class, dual- earner parents in the United States about their gender ideology and gendered behaviors across the first year of parenthood and in a 6- year follow- up when their children’s gender role attitudes were assessed. When mothers engaged in more traditional feminine behaviors (e.g., housework, childcare), girls had more knowledge of feminine gender stereotypes and boys had less knowledge of masculine stereotypes, and children were more interested in gender- traditional careers. Although fathers’ behavior and ideology had little influence on girls’ views, fathers with more egalitarian ideology had sons with fewer stereotypes about the other gender. 
Best and her colleagues (Best, House, Barnard, & Spicker, 1991) observed parents and their preschool children in public parks and playgrounds in France, Germany, and Italy and found that parent– child interactions varied across both gender and country. 
1. Although psychoanalytic theory was quite influential in early studies of cross- cultural gender differences (see: Burton & Whiting, 1961; Freud, 1939; Mead, 1949; Munroe & Munroe, 1974; Munroe, Munroe, & Whiting, 1981), it has received little recent attention and will not be reviewed in this chapter. 
 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  249 
Italian and French parents and children were more interactive than were German parent– child dyads, and French and Italian children showed and shared more objects with their fathers than mothers, with the pattern reversed for German children. These interactional differences may be related to the cultural differences in gender stereotype learning discussed later. Perhaps female characteristics are learned earlier by German children as a result of greater interaction with mothers than fathers, a pattern that was not found in the other countries. 
While there is substantial cross- cultural evidence that social forces play an important part in gender role learning, social learning by itself does not provide a sufficient explanation. Differential treatment of boys and girls varies greatly across cultures and is not consistently tied to differential behavior (Bronstein, 1984; Lamb et al., 1982; Russell & Russell, 1987). Tasks assigned to children, as well as role models in the larger culture, provide opportunities for them to learn differential roles and behaviors (Halimi, Consuegra, Struyven, & Engels, 2016). The salient aspects of culture that contribute to children’s gender role learning and behaviors should be systematically addressed. 
Cognitive Developmental Theories Another prominent theory of gender role learning, cognitive developmental theory (Kohlberg, 1966; Martin, Ruble, & Szkrybalo, 2002; Ruble, 1987), emphasizes the role of external forces on children’s developing gender role orientation. The impact of these factors, however, is governed by the child’s emerging cognitive structures. In particular, cognitive developmental theorists stress the importance of understanding how children synthesize and integrate gender knowledge from the social world into their personal concepts of gender (Martin et al., 2002). Cognitive developmental theory proposes that children progress through stages of learning in which they process gender- relevant information with increasing cognitive complexity as they age. 
Slaby and Frey (1975) identified four stages in the development of American children’s understanding of gender. Initially, children do not distinguish between the sexes, but in the second stage they begin to use gender categories based on superficial physical characteristics. In the latter two stages, achieved by age 4½ to 5 years, children develop “gender constancy”— the understanding that gender is stable across time and is consistent. Martin, Ruble, and Szkrybalo (2002) posit that the development of gender constancy may be indicative of a period in which children become particularly susceptible to integrating and consolidating gender- relevant information into their growing understanding of gender- appropriate behavior. 
In testing cognitive developmental theory, Munroe, Shimmin, and Munroe (1984) expected to find cultural differences in progression through the gender stages related to the degree to which societies emphasize distinctions between males and females. Contrary to expectation, these culture- specific predictions were not supported. Children in the sex- differentiating cultures of Kenya and Nepal did not attain gender classification at an earlier age than did children in Belize and Samoa. In fact, Kenyan children reached 
 
250 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
this stage at an older age than did Samoan children, and Nepalese children did not differ from the other groups. As predicted, the latter stages, which depend on cognitive structural factors, showed little variation across cultures. Munroe and Munroe (1982) suggest that gender understanding develops slowly in cultures where young children have little contact with male figures, as in more traditional cultures in which childcare is almost completely a maternal responsibility. 
Bussey (1983) has found that gender constancy is not an important antecedent for the development of sex- typed behaviors. For boys, there is a two- process model that involves acceptance of masculine behavior and rejection of feminine behavior. There is a one- process model for girls that involves acceptance of same- sex behavior without rejection of other- sex behavior. Hence, it is acceptable for young girls to be “tomboys” but not for boys to be “sissies.” 
Taken as a whole, these findings indicate the dominant contribution of cognitive developmental factors and the concomitantly small contribution of culture- specific factors in the development of gender concepts. 
Gender Schema Theory A variant of cognitive developmental theory and social cognitive learning theory has evolved, gender schema theory (Bem, 1981, 1983; Liben & Signorella, 1980, 1987; Signorella, Bigler, & Liben, 1993). A scheme is a set of ideas used for organizing infor-mation, filtering new information, and directing cognitive processing. If a child has a strong gender scheme, new information congruent with the culturally- defined gender stereotype is easily learned, assimilated, and further solidifies the stereotype. Gender schemes regulate behaviors to conform to cultural definitions of masculinity and femininity. Gender schema theory assumes that the primacy of the gender concept within a particular culture serves as a basis for organizing information (Jacklin, 1989), though there is little evidence for this assumption from cultures other than the United States 
Social Role Theory Although it does not propose developmental mechanisms, social role theory is often used as an explanation for cultural differences in gender roles. The theory suggests that the gender division of labor in a society is based on biological differences between women and men (e.g., size, strength, childbearing) and leads to psychological and behavioral gender differences (Eagly & Wood, 2016). Over time, men’s roles have become more dominant and women’s more subordinate, and differential traits, such as aggression and nurturance, have evolved to support these differential roles. Contrary to social role theory’s cross- cultural predictions, across an array of psychological attributes, cognitive abilities, and physical measures, gender differences are larger in cultures with more gender egalitarianism (Schmitt et al., 2016). 
Overall, theories of gender role development have emphasized the importance of culture through parents, peers, and other socialization agents as well as through 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  251 
children’s gendered experiences. Unfortunately, many of those theories have been derived from mostly Western studies, with only occasional recognition of cultural variations and nuances (Halimi et al., 2016). Gender role learning is embedded within children’s social, cultural, and historical contexts (Bussey & Bandura, 1999; Elder, 1998), suggesting that future research should examine gender development in more diverse cultural settings. 
Gender Differences in Male and Female Behaviors Together, biological and cultural influences lead to differences in the behaviors of males and females, and four areas where cross- cultural gender differences have been found will be reviewed briefly here: nurturance, aggression, proximity to adults, and self- esteem. 
Nurturance In the Six Culture Study, Edwards and Whiting (1980) found that, between ages of 5 and 12, gender differences in nurturance were most consistent in behavior directed toward infants and toddlers rather than in behavior directed toward mothers and older children. Since infants elicit more nurturant behavior than do older children, girls who spent more time with infants demonstrated more nurturance than boys who were not engaged in as much infant interaction. Blakemore (1998) found that by 3 years of age, white American girls showed more interest in and nurturance toward babies than did boys. Children, especially boys, who had younger siblings were less interested in interacting with babies than were children without younger siblings. Furthermore, boys of parents with more traditional gender role attitudes showed less interest in and nurturance than girls, but there was no gender difference for children of parents with egalitarian attitudes. 
Even subtle factors, such as parental attitudes, do influence the development of children’s gender role attitudes and behaviors. In their classic study, Barry, Bacon, and Child (1957) found that, compared with boys, girls were socialized to be more nurturant (82% of cultures), obedient (35% of cultures), and responsible (61% of cultures). Boys, on the other hand, were socialized to be more achieving (87% of cultures) and self- reliant (85% of cultures) than girls. In 108 cultures, Welch, Page, and Martin (1981) found more pressure for boys to conform to their roles than girls, who also had greater role variability. More recent studies continue to find differences in how mothers and fathers treat girls and boys (Blakemore, Berenbaum, & Liben, 2009). 
Aggression Cross- cultural studies of prepubertal children have consistently shown that boys have higher levels of aggression, competitiveness, dominance- seeking, and rough- and- tumble play than do girls (Ember, 1981; Freedman & DeBoer, 1979; Strube, 1981). Examining data from the Six Culture Study and additional African samples, Whiting and Edwards (1988) found sex differences in aggression and dominance, but, unlike their earlier 
 
 
 
 
252 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
findings, aggression did not decrease with age and was more physical among the oldest boys. Omark, Omark, and Edelman’s (1975) playground observations in Ethiopia, Switzerland, and the United States showed that boys were more aggressive than girls, and Blurton Jones and Konner’s (1973) had similar findings in four !Kung Bushmen villages and in London. In their observations in four nonindustrial cultures, Munroe and his colleagues (Munroe, Hulefeld, Rodgers, Tomeo, & Yamazaki, 2000) found more frequent aggression in boys than girls (Figure 9.4). 
While both boys and girls segregated by sex, aggregation by sex was associated most strongly with episodes of aggression by boys. A recent study of 7- to 10- year- olds found that boys reported being more physically aggressive than girls in nine countries (China, Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Kenya, the Philippines, Sweden, Thailand, United States), but there was no consistent gender difference in relational aggression (Lansford, et al., 2012) 
The Six Culture Study indicated that mothers generally react similarly to boys’ and girls’ aggression, but there was some evidence of differential aggression training in Okinawa and the United States which suggested that fathers may play an important role in socializing aggression in boys (Minturn & Lambert, 1964). Indeed, Japanese boys and girls who experience conflicts with fathers show higher levels of physical aggression toward their peers (Kawabata & Crick, 2016). 
Acceptance of aggression is similar for males and females in Western European countries, but there are gender differences in the forms of aggressive acts. Males initially are more restrained, but, when they act, they are more direct and use physical violence (Card, Stucky, Sawalani, & Little, 2008; Ramirez, 1993), while females are more likely to use indirect aggression, shouting, and verbal attacks (Burbank, 1987). and Lundell (2002) suggest that parents are more tolerant of boys’ acting out behaviors. As a result, boys learn that aggression is a way to communicate and externalize problems when in conflict with their same- gender peers (Kawabata & Crick, 2016). Moving to the other end of the spectrum, Boehnke and colleagues (Boehnke, Silbereisen, Eisenberg, Reykowski, & Palmonari, 1989) examined the development of prosocial motivation in school children from West Germany, Poland, Italy, and the United States. By age 12, but not before, girls demonstrated more mature motives in their responses to hypothetical situations which provided opportunity for prosocial action. 
Proximity to Adults and Activity Observing the play of 5- to 7- year- olds in eight cultures (Australian Aboriginal, Balinese, Ceylonese, Japanese, Kikuyu, Navajo, Punjabi, Taiwanese), Freedman (1976) found that boys ran in larger groups, covered more physical space, and did more physical and unpredictable activities while girls were involved in more conversations and games with repeated activities. Girls are usually found closer to home (Draper, 1975; Munroe & Munroe, 1971; Whiting & Edwards, 1973). A recent study of children in two locations in England found that boys had greater mobility than girls and became independent much earlier. Girls managed to attain similar independence from adults by traveling in groups, a form of collective independence (Brown, Mackett, Gong, Kitazawa, & Paskins, 2008). Mikkelsen and Christensen (2009) found similar patterns using GPS- tracking and a rolling mobile phone survey in a suburban area of Copenhagen and two villages in Jutland, Denmark. 
Task assignment (Whiting & Edwards, 1973) and behavioral preferences may contribute to these gender differences in proximity to adults (Draper, 1975). Boys tend to interact more with other boys while girls tend to interact more with adult females (Blurton Jones & Konner, 1973; Omark et al., 1975; Whiting & Edwards, 1973). 
Children’s drawings reflect a gender segregation similar to that seen in play, with boys drawing more pictures of boys and girls of girls (Freedman, 1976). Perhaps reflecting gender differences in what children like, boys in nine cultures drew more vehicles, monsters, and violence themes than did girls, who drew more flowers. A recent study of 6- to 12- year- olds in 13 countries found that boys drew more vehicles, weapons, and sports than girls, and girls used more colors than boys (Alter- Muri & Vazzano, 2014). There was no difference between boys and girls for inclusion of animals or bugs in their images. Overall, there were few geographic differences. 
Self- Esteem and Self- Efficacy Beliefs There has been considerable debate in recent years regarding gender differences in self- esteem, or the degree to which an individual feels satisfied with him- or herself. According to past research, girls seem less satisfied with being girls than boys are with being boys (Burns & Homel, 1986; Kling, Hyde, Showers, & Buswell, 1999), and boys perceive themselves to be more competent than girls (van Dongen- Melman, Koot, & 
 
 
254 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Verhulst, 1993). However, such research has been criticized for reflecting the experiences of white, middle- class children and adolescents in the United States (Greene & Way, 2005). More recent work suggests that gender role ideology, rather than gender itself, may explain observed differences in girls’ and boys’ self- esteem in white samples. For example, black girls in the United States have higher self- esteem than white girls, and this difference may be due to variation in gender stereotypes between the racial groups (Buckley & Carter, 2005; Jones, Buque, & Miville, 2018). It is important to note that despite the growing complexity within self- esteem research, girls’ dissatisfaction with being girls may not be consistently manifested in lower self- esteem. Rather, girls may begin to process their lower social status in relation to boys through beliefs regarding self- efficacy (Bussey & Bandura, 1999; Wood & Eagly, 2010). Indeed, compared with boys, adolescent girls in Nepal, the Philippines, and Australia had lower opinions of their physical and mathematical abilities, but girls in Australia and Nigeria felt more competent in reading (Watkins & Akande, 1992; Watkins, Lam, & Regmi, 1991). Nigerian boys believed they were more intelligent than did girls (Olowu, 1985). In a recent study, 5- year old girls in the United States were less likely to label themselves as “really, really smart” in comparison to their male peers, downplaying their intelligence before reaching the first grade (Bian, Leslie, Murphy, & Cimpian, 2018). Although variation in self- esteem and other self- efficacy measures may occur throughout early development in correspondence with varying socialization practices, gender differences in self- esteem appear to plateau during adulthood in most cultures (Diener & Diener, 2009). 
In sum, differences between boys and girls in nurturance, aggression, and mobility are robust and consistently found across cultures (Ember, 1981), while self- esteem and self- efficacy differences are less consistent. Culture shapes the social behaviors of children by selecting the company they keep and the activities that engage their time. Such experiences can maximize, minimize, or even eliminate gender differences in social behaviors. 
Gender Roles and Stereotypes Within the context of cultural stereotypes about male– female differences, gender roles and knowledge develop. Research in the United States indicates that, as early as 2 years of age, children use gender labeling with people (Martin et al., 2002) and stereotype objects as masculine or feminine (Thompson, 1975; Weinraub et al., 1984). By age 3– 4, children use stereotypic labels “accurately” with toys, activities, and occupations (Edelbrook & Sugawara, 1978; Guttentag & Longfellow, 1977; Liben & Bigler, 2002). 
Similar gender stereotyping of toys is found in Africa, where girls play with dolls and boys construct vehicles and weapons (Bloch & Adler, 1994). By age 4– 5, Sri Lankan village children demonstrate gender differences in play similar to those found with British children (Prosser, Hutt, Hutt, Mahindadasa, & Goonetilleke, 1986). Boys exhibit more negative behaviors and more fantasy object play while girls display more fantasy 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  255 
person play. Even though cultural factors determine the content of children’s play, only a few types of play behaviors seem to be culturally specific. 
Development of Gender- Trait Stereotypes Research in the United States indicates that children acquire knowledge of gender- trait stereotypes somewhat later than stereotypic knowledge of toys and occupations (Best et  al., 1977; Reis & Wright, 1982; Williams & Best, 1990a). Using the Sex Stereotype Measure (SSM) to assess children’s knowledge of adult- defined stereotypes, research conducted with European American children revealed a consistent pattern of increasing knowledge from kindergarten through high school, similar to a typical learning curve. The most dramatic increases in stereotype knowledge occurred in the early elementary school years, with scores reaching a plateau in the junior high years (Figure 9.5). 
African American children’s scores increased with age but were lower than those of the European American children, perhaps reflecting subcultural variation in stereotype content and knowledge. 
Cross- Cultural Findings Williams and Best and their colleagues (1990a) administered the SSM II to 5- , 8- , and 11- year- olds in 25 countries. Across all countries, the percentage of stereotyped responses rose from around 60% at age 5 to around 70% at age 8 (Figure 9.6).

Strong, aggressive, cruel, coarse, and adventurous were consistently associated with men at both age levels, and weak, appreciative, softhearted, gentle, and meek were consistently associated with women. Both male and female scores were unusually high in Pakistan and relatively high in New Zealand and England. Scores were atypically low in Brazil, Taiwan, Germany, and France. Although there was variation between countries in the rate of learning, there was a general developmental pattern in which the acquisition of stereotypes begins prior to age 5, accelerates during the early school years, and is completed during the adolescent years. 
Boys and girls learned the stereotypes at the same rate, although there was a tendency for male stereotype traits to be learned somewhat earlier than female traits. In 17 of the 24 countries studied, male stereotype items were better known than female items. Germany was the only country where there was a clear tendency for the female stereotype to be better known than the male. In contrast, female stereotype items were learned earlier than male items in Latin/ Catholic cultures (Brazil, Chile, Portugal, Venezuela) where the adult- defined female stereotype is more positive than the male (Neto, Williams, & Widner, 1991; Tarrier & Gomes, 1981). 
In predominantly Muslim countries, 5- year- olds associated traits with the two sexes in a more highly differentiated manner, and they learned the stereotypes, particularly the male items, at an earlier age than in non- Muslim countries. Children in predominantly Christian countries were slower in their initial learning of the stereotypes, perhaps reflecting the less- differentiated nature of the adult stereotypes, particularly in Catholic countries.

gender and CulTure  |  257 
Using a combined measure of traits and roles, Albert and Porter (1986) examined the gender stereotypes of 4- to 6- year- olds in the United States and South Africa and found stereotyping increased with age. South African children stereotyped the male role more than did US children, but there were no country differences for the female role. South African children from liberal Christian and Jewish backgrounds stereotyped less than children from more conservative religious groups. In the United States, religious background was not a factor. 
Looking at older children, 11– 18 years of age, Intons- Peterson (1988) found that Swedish children attributed more instrumental qualities to women than did American children. Gender stereotypes were more similar in Sweden than in the United States, perhaps reflecting Swedish cultural philosophy. Surprisingly, in Sweden, ideal occupational choices did not overlap; young Swedish women were interested in service occupations, such as flight attendant, hospital worker, and nanny, and young Swedish men were interested in business occupations. In contrast, ideal occupations for the sexes overlapped in the United States with both groups listing doctor, dentist, attorney, and business executive as their top choices. Considering the similarities found across diverse countries and the differing measures used, gender stereotypes appear to be universal, with culture modifying rate of learning and minor aspects of content. These findings are consistent with the general pancultural model of gender stereotypes discussed previously and suggest that pan- cultural stereotypes could be considered to be variform universals (Lonner, 1980). 
An interesting new line of research has shown the “math is for boys” stereotype among American elementary school boys and girls (Cvencek, Meltzoff, & Greenwald, 2011) and German elementary school girls (Steffens, Jelenec, & Noacket, 2010). Interestingly, even in Singapore, where both boys and girls equally excel in math, children associate math with boys, perhaps due to exposure to Western media and parents’ stereotypical views of academic subjects (Cvenceka, Meltzoff, & Kapur, 2014). 
Gender at the Individual Adult Level Gender Role Ideology In virtually all human groups, women have greater responsibility for “domestic” activities while men have greater responsibility for “external” activities. Wood and Eagly (2009) point out that the gender roles ascribed to women and men in most societies are in no way random and originate in biosocial realities of human development. In particular, gender role ideology originates from attributions about biological differences between the sexes, primarily the fact that women bear and often nurse offspring (Huber, 2007; Williams & Best, 1990b). Social change has brought about new conceptions of women’s and men’s labor roles, with men engaging in more domestic activities and women in more external, particularly economic, activities in some cultures. The gender division of labor 
 
 
258 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
will be reviewed later in the chapter while here the beliefs and attitudes about appropriate role behaviors for the two sexes will be discussed. 
Most researchers classify gender role ideologies along a continuum ranging from traditional to modern. Traditional ideologies assert that men are more “important” than women in their cultural context and that it is proper for men to control and dominate women. In contrast, modern ideologies represent a more egalitarian view, sometimes labeled a feminist position, in which women and men are equally important, and dominance of one gender over the other is rejected. 
Gender roles have been studied extensively in India, where contemporary Indian culture juxtaposes traditional and modern ideologies. When male and female Indian and American university students were asked what qualities women in their culture should and should not possess, Indian students expressed more traditional views than American students. Women in both groups were more modern, or liberal, than were men (Agarwal et al., 1992; Rao & Rao, 1985). This finding echoes research in the United States, as Eagly, Diekman, Johannesen- Schmidt, and Koenig (2004) found that women were more likely to endorse egalitarian views toward gender than men. Other predictors of modern or egalitarian sex role ideologies in Indian women include coming from a nuclear family, having an educated mother, and working in professional or career- oriented disciplines (Ghadially & Kazi, 1979). 
Similarly, education and professional managerial work are strong predictors of sex role attitudes for both Japanese and American women (Suzuki, 1991). American women with jobs, no matter what sort, had more egalitarian attitudes than women without jobs. In contrast, Japanese women with career- oriented professional jobs were more egalitarian than all other women, with or without jobs. Interestingly, Sugihara and Katsurada (2002) found that gender ideologies may be shifting toward a more egalitarian model in Japan, as men and women were equally likely to describe themselves as having both masculine and feminine attributes. 
Gibbons, Stiles, and Shkodriani (1991) capitalized on a unique research opportunity and studied attitudes toward gender and family roles among adolescents from 46 different countries attending schools in the Netherlands. Countries of origin were grouped into two categories based on Hofstede’s cultural values:  the wealthier, more individualistic countries and the less wealthy, more collectivistic countries. Students from the second group of countries had more traditional attitudes than students from the first group of countries, and girls generally responded less traditionally than boys. Recent work supports the notion that countries with greater wealth and individualism are more likely to support egalitarian views toward men’s and women’s roles in society (Hofstede, 2001). Surprisingly, however, Davis and Robinson (1991) found that women with more education and with employed husbands in the United States, Great Britain, Germany, and Austria were less favorable toward gender equality than were less- educated women with no male wage earner.
gender and CulTure  |  259 
In a larger study of 33 nations, Yu and Lee (2013) found that, in societies with fewer impediments for women, there was more approval for mothers being employed outside the home but lower levels of support for gender equality in the home. They pointed out that when there is a reduction in barriers for women, a society may become more liberal in one aspect of gender ideology and more conservative on another. Indeed, the relation between the division of labor and beliefs about appropriate gender role behaviors is quite complex. In a number of sex role ideology studies, Americans served as a reference group and were usually found to be more liberal, suggesting that Americans may be unusual in this respect. However, Williams and Best (1990b) did not find this to be true in their 14- country study of sex role ideology with university students. The most modern ideologies were found in European countries (the Netherlands, Germany, Finland, England, Italy). The United States was in the middle of the distribution, and the most traditional ideologies were found in African and Asian countries (Nigeria, Pakistan, India, Japan, Malaysia). Generally, women had more modern views than men, but not in all countries (e.g., Malaysia and Pakistan). However, there was high correspondence between men’s and women’s scores in a given country. Overall, the effect of culture was greater than the effect of gender. 
Before concluding that observed variations between countries are due to cultural factors, the variations must be shown to relate to cultural comparison variables. Williams and Best (1990b) found a substantial relationship between men’s and women’s sex role ideology and economic- social development; that is, sex role ideology tended to be more modern in more developed countries. Sex role ideology also was more modern in more heavily Christian countries, in more urbanized countries, and in countries in the higher latitudes. 
Gender Stereotypes Related to sex role ideology, and often used as justifications for those beliefs, are gender stereotypes, the psychological traits believed to be more characteristic of one gender than the other. In their research, Williams and Best (1990a) presented the 300 person- descriptive adjectives from the Adjective Checklist (ACL; Gough & Heilbrun, 1980) to university students in 27 countries2 and asked them to indicate whether, in their culture, each adjective was more frequently associated with men, more frequently associated with women, or not differentially associated by gender. There was substantial agreement across all 27 countries concerning the psychological characteristics differentially associated with men and with women (Figure 9.7). 
Male and female stereotypes differed most in the Netherlands, Finland, Norway, and Germany and least in Scotland, Bolivia, and Venezuela. Stereotypes of men and women

In each country, the high agreement male- and female- stereotype items were scored using an affective meaning scoring system, and in all countries the male- stereotype items were more active and stronger than the female- stereotype items. Interestingly, there was no pan- cultural effect for favorability, with the male stereotype being more positive in

gender and CulTure  |  261 
some countries (e.g., Japan, South Africa, Nigeria) and the female stereotype in others (e.g., Italy, Peru, Australia). Using a second scoring system (Transactional Analysis ego states) indicated that in all countries the Critical Parent and Adult ego states were more characteristic of men while the Nurturing Parent and Adapted Child ego states were more characteristic of women, and the Free Child ego state was not differentially associated. A third scoring system based on 15 psychological needs revealed that, across all countries, dominance, autonomy, aggression, exhibition, and achievement were associated with men while nurturance, succorance, deference, and abasement were associated with women. A reanalysis of the stereotype data in terms of the Five Factor Model of personality revealed that the pan- cultural male stereotype was higher in Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Openness, while the female stereotype was higher only in Agreeableness (Williams, Satterwhite, & Best, 1999). In a recent study of gender stereotypes of personality, Löckenhoff and colleagues (2014) asked individuals across 26 nations to rate the five- factor personality traits of typical women and men. They found that women were seen as slightly higher in openness, agreeableness, and conscientiousness along with some aspects of extraversion and neuroticism. 
Within the general cultural similarities, Williams and Best (1990a) found there was also variation between countries. For example, strength and activity differences between male and female stereotypes were greater in socioeconomically less developed countries, in countries where literacy was low, and where the percentage of women attending the university was low. Perhaps economic and educational advancement are accompanied by a reduction in the tendency to view men as stronger and more active than women. However, the effects were merely reduced, not eliminated. Consistent with this notion of men as stronger and more active than women, across 16 nations, Glick and colleagues (2004) found men were viewed less positively but as more powerful than women (hostile as well as benevolent attitudes), suggesting stereotypically that men were “designed for dominance.” 
The high degree of cross- cultural similarity in gender stereotypes leads to the conclusion that the psychological characteristics differentially associated with men and women follow a pan- cultural model, with cultural factors producing minor variations around general themes (Figure 9.8) (See Williams & Best, 1990a, pp. 241– 244, for a more detailed description of such a model.) In brief, Williams and Best’s model proposes that biological differences set the stage (e.g., females bear children, males have greater physical strength) and lead to a division of labor, noted earlier, with women responsible for childcare and other domestic activities and men for hunting (providing) and protection. Gender stereotypes evolved to support this division of labor. Stereotypes contend that each gender has or can develop characteristics congruent with the assigned role. Once established, stereotypes serve as socialization models that encourage boys to become independent and adventurous and girls to become nurturant and affiliative. Thus, the model demonstrates how people in widely different cultures come to associate one set of characteristics with men and another set with women, with only minor variations around these central themes.
262 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Recent literature points out the process through which such variation may take place. Cuddy and colleagues (2015) looked at how core cultural values, such as collectivism and individualism, moderate gender stereotypes. In their fourth study, they reanalyzed Williams and Best’s (1990) gender stereotype data from 26 countries and found that stereotypes of males reflect those constructs that were more highly valued in a given culture. In more collectivistic nations, the more masculine collectivistic traits were rated, and in more individualistic nations, the more masculine individualistic traits were rated. Thus, in some cultures, men may be considered more collectivistic than women if (and only if) collectivism is culturally valued. However, across cultures, individualistic traits are considered more masculine than are collectivistic traits. Countries where men are stereotyped with collectivistic traits, such as being less selfish, more considerate, and more helpful, should not be considered a utopia for women, as there is greater gender inequality in collectivistic nations relative to individualistic ones. Cuddy et  al. (2015) point out that the Williams and Best (1990) data were published in 1990, and globalization and Westernization have increased across nations since that time. Yet rankings of nations on individualism– collectivism (Hofstede, Hofstede, & Minkov, 2010) and gender inequality (United Gender Inequality Index; United Nations Development Program [UNDP], 2013) have remained stable across the years, although changes would have attenuated the relation between the variables. It is apparent that culture moderates gender stereotypes, with stereotypes of men being more closely linked to core cultural values than those of women. 
In spite of women being evaluated more positively than men across cultures (i.e., the “women- are- wonderful” effect), Glick and colleagues (2004) found that, across 16 nations, gender egalitarian views were negatively correlated with explicit measures of hostile and benevolent attitudes toward women and men. Masculinity– Femininity of Self- Concepts Manlike or womanlike are the essential meanings of the paired concepts of masculinity/ femininity (M/ F). A person might be masculine or feminine in a variety of ways including dress, mannerisms, or tone of voice. Here, the definition is restricted to self- concepts and the degree to which they incorporate traits that are differentially associated with women or men. Within this restricted concept of masculinity– femininity, researchers have used different measurement techniques. Some have used self- descriptive questionnaire items (Gough, 1952), some analyze only socially desirable characteristics (Bem, 1974; Spence & Helmreich, 1978), and others examine gender- associated characteristics without reference to social desirability (Williams & Best, 1990b). 
In contrast to these explicit measures of masculinity– femininity and gender stereotypes, implicit measures have been one means of dealing with the social desirability concern in explicit measures of gender concepts. Perhaps the best known of the implicit measures is the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which assesses the strength of people’s cognitive associations between themselves and gender stereotypic traits (Greenwald, Poehlman, Uhlmann, & Banaji; 2009; Puzio & Best, 2016). The IAT looks at speed of response to words one categorizes as self- words (e.g., me) with non- self words (e.g., others) when paired with gender stereotypical traits (e.g., tender, competitive). Faster reaction times suggest a closer cognitive association with the concepts (Banaji & Greenwald, 2013). Researchers continue to investigate the validity of these measures as well as the comparability of implicit and explicit measures of gender concepts. 
Regarding measurement, for cross- cultural studies of masculinity– femininity, an important consideration are emic or culture specific considerations. Problems arise when a masculinity– femininity scale (e.g., Spence & Helmreich, 1978) developed in one country, often the United States, is translated into another language and administered to persons in other cultures. Scores are interpreted as if they represent comparative degrees of masculinity– femininity in the different cultures, and there is little emic consideration. Cross- culturally, some items in translated scales may be inappropriate due to content, whereas others may be poorly translated (see Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver for an extended discussion of methodological issues). 
Williams and Best (1990b) employed culture- specific measures of masculinity– femininity in a study with university students in 14 countries. Each participant described him- or herself and his or her ideal self using the 300 ACL adjectives, and these descriptions were scored relative to the local gender stereotypes determined in an earlier study (Williams & Best, 1990a). Men in all countries were found to be more masculine than women, hardly a surprising result. In contrast, for the ideal self, both gender groups wished to be “more masculine” than they thought they were. 
 
264 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
While some cultural variation in self- concepts was found, there were no substantial associations with cultural comparison variables, such as economic or social development. Across cultural groups, relative to their own culture’s definition of femininity and masculinity, there was no evidence that women in some societies were more feminine than women in others or that men in some societies were more masculine than men in others. 
In contrast, when self- concepts were examined in terms of affective meaning scores, there were substantial differences across countries in self and ideal self- concepts, and these correlated with cultural comparison variables. For example, the differences in the self- concepts of men and women were smaller in more developed countries, when women were employed outside the home, when they constituted a large percentage of the university population, and where a relatively modern sex role ideology prevailed. 
Thus, an interesting paradox occurs. When using the masculinity/ femininity scoring system, which seems methodologically superior due to its reliance on culture- specific definitions, there is scant evidence of cross- cultural variation and greater evidence of pan- cultural similarity in definitions of masculinity/ femininity. On the other hand, when using the affective meaning scoring system, which is based on ratings by persons in the United States and may be culturally biased, there are a number of robust relationships with cultural comparison variables. This paradox cannot be resolved easily. 
Relations Between Women and Men This section reviews cross- cultural studies dealing with the relationships between men and women. Readers interested in cross- cultural variations in human sexual behavior are referred to Davis and Whitten (1987); Hatfield and Rapson (1993, 1995); Hatfield, Luckhurst, and Rapson (2010); and Reiss (1986). 
Mate Preference The most extensive investigation of mate preferences was conducted by Buss and his associates (1989, 1990b, Shackelford, Schmitt, & Buss, 2005)  who gathered data from 37 samples totaling more than 10,000 respondents from 33 countries. Buss notes that although social scientists often assume that mate preferences are highly culture- bound and arbitrary, his findings are contrary. On two similar lists of potential mate characteristics, Buss asked participants to indicate their preferences by rating or ranking the items. The most striking finding was the remarkable degree of agreement in preference for mate characteristics between men and women. Both genders ranked “kind and understanding” first; “intelligent” second; “exciting personality” third; “healthy” fourth; and “religious” last. Despite the overall gender similarity, women generally valued good earning capacity in a potential mate slightly more than did men, whereas men generally valued physical appearance slightly more than did women, providing modest support for sociobiological views (e.g., Wilson, 1975). 
 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  265 
Conversely, cultural differences were found for virtually every item, and on some items there was great variation across cultures. The greatest cultural effect occurred for chastity, with Northern European groups viewing it as largely unimportant while groups from China, India, and Iran placed great emphasis on it. Men valued chastity in a prospective mate more than did women. Buss (1990b) concluded that there were considerable commonalities among all samples, suggesting substantial unity in human mate preferences that may be regarded as “species typical.” On the other hand, no sample was exactly like any other sample; each displayed some uniqueness in the ordering of mate preference characteristics, thus reflecting modest degrees of cultural variation. 
While a considerable degree of universality has been documented among core components of mate preference criteria, recent work suggests that gender ideology may be an important determinant of mate preference in some cultures. Eastwick et al. (2006) investigated the relation between traditional gender ideology and sex- typed mate preferences in a nine- nation study using samples from Germany, Mexico, Italy, Spain, Singapore, Syria, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United States. Sex- typed mate preference refers to the seeking of qualities in a partner that will likely elicit a homemaker– provider division of labor within the household, such that women perform domestic duties while producing and rearing offspring and men are primarily concerned with providing resources for the family. Components of sex- typed mate preference include “(a) men desiring a mate younger than themselves, (b) women desiring a mate older than themselves, (c) women placing more importance than men on a mate with good financial prospects, and (d) men placing more importance than women on a mate who is a good cook and housekeeper” (Eastwick et al., 2006, p. 606). In accordance with their hypotheses, traditional gender ideology was associated with sex- typed mate preferences across cultures. Moreover, the authors concluded that those with traditional gender ideologies were more likely to have strict, idealized desires about their potential mates. 
Romantic Love and Intimacy As with mate preferences, romantic love and intimacy are assumed to be influenced by culture (Broude, 1987). Generally, romantic love is valued highly in less traditional cultures with few strong extended family ties and is less valued in cultures where strong family ties reinforce the relationship between marriage partners. Past research has shown that Japanese university students value romantic love less than do West German students, with American students between the other two societies (Simmons, Kolke, & Shimizu, 1986). However, recent studies have sought to discover the ways in which the cultural “lines” regarding love attitudes have been blurred by an increasingly globalized and industrialized world (Wang, Lawler, & Shi, 2010). 
Much of the literature on romantic love has questioned whether it is, in fact, a universally celebrated and valued phenomenon across cultures. In a 1992 study, Fischer and Janowiak documented romantic love in 146 of 166 cultures, suggesting that assigning value to passionate and compassionate love between partners is not isolated to Western 
 
266 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
cultures. There is, however, considerable variation in views toward romantic love and its necessity in eliciting marriage. Interestingly, Vaidyanathan and Naidoo (1990/ 91) found that Asian Indian immigrants to Canada show generational changes in attitudes toward love and marriage. Although 63% of first- generation immigrants had arranged marriages, a large proportion of them believed that “love marriages” were an option for their offspring. More than 70% of the second generation wanted more freedom in mate selection and believed that love should precede marriage. 
Bejanyan, Marshall, and Ferenczi (2014) examined the concepts of love and intimacy in a highly individualistic culture, the United States, and a highly collectivistic culture, India. Their findings oppose earlier research suggesting that attitudes toward romantic love bifurcate along collectivistic and individualistic lines. Rather, the authors found that Indians had stronger beliefs in romantic love than Americans, and this difference was explained by their higher collectivistic values. This finding may point toward greater influence and blending of Western and Indian culture, as romance and intimacy are typically discouraged as Indian adolescents approach adulthood. Although attitudes about the value of romantic love may be shifting, the class structure known as caste still dictates mergers between many families (Dhar, 2013). Culture seems to play a critical role in the interpretation of cross- gender close relationships, and an increasingly modernized world may be facilitating culturally blended attitudes regarding love and partnership. 
Harassment and Rape Violence against women affects almost every society around the world and remains a major problem in developed nations (Rozeé, 1993). In the United States, nearly one in five women experience some form of sexual assault or rape between the ages of 18 and 24 (Krebs, Lindquist, Warner, Fisher, & Martin, 2009). 
According to the World Health Organization (2016), one in three women around the world will experience some form of gendered violence, be it domestic or sexual assault, within her lifetime (Figure 9.9). Victimization rates differ by country, as 15% of women in Japan experience intimate partner abuse and/ or rape between the ages of 15 and 49 compared with 71% of Ethiopian women (World Health Organization, 2005). 
Victimization rates are tightly bound to cultural attitudes regarding gender roles. A comprehensive cross- cultural study of attitudes toward rape victims was conducted with university students in 15 countries by a network of researchers led by Ward from Singapore (Ward, 1995). Relatively favorable attitudes toward rape victims were found in the United Kingdom, Germany, and New Zealand, whereas relatively unfavorable attitudes were found in Turkey, Mexico, Zimbabwe, India, and, particularly, Malaysia. Attitudes toward rape victims mirror attitudes toward women more generally, with more favorable attitudes in countries with more modern sex role ideologies and less favorable attitudes in countries with a lower percentage of female labor force participation and lower literacy rates.

Masculine Work- Related Values In the area of more general values, Hofstede (1980) compared work- related values in 40 countries using attitude survey data collected from thousands of employees of IBM, a large, multinational, high- technology business organization. One scale derived from Hofstede’s factor analysis concerned the extent to which values of assertiveness, money, and things prevail in a society rather than the values of nurturance, quality of life, and people. While the scale might have easily been named “Materialism,” this was the only scale for which scores differed based on the gender of respondents. Hofstede named the scale “Masculinity” (MAS) because male employees assign greater weight to the first set of values, whereas females assign greater weight to the second set. Calling the scale Masculinity leads to the expectation that variations on these values might be associated with cross- country variations in other gender- related concepts, such as those discussed earlier in this chapter. 
Hofstede computed a MAS index for each of the 40 countries in his study. The five countries with the highest MAS indices were Japan, Austria, Venezuela, Italy, and Switzerland; the five countries with the lowest MAS indices were Sweden, Norway, Netherlands, Denmark, and Finland. Hofstede (1980) made extensive comparisons between country MAS scores with data from other sources and found a large number of interesting relationships. For example, in high- MAS countries there is greater belief in in-dependent decision- making as opposed to group decision- making, stronger achievement motivation, higher job stress, and work is more central in people’s lives. 
Recently, examination of MAS scores in 76 countries indicated that Masculinity was high in Japan, in German- speaking countries, and in some Latin countries (Italy, Mexico); moderately high in English- speaking Western countries; low in Nordic countries and the Netherlands; and moderately low in some Latin and Asian countries (France, Spain, Portugal, Chile, Korea, Thailand; Hofstede et al., 2010). Two additional dimensions of Hofstede’s work- related values (long- term orientation vs. short- term orientation and indulgence vs. restraint) from World Values Survey (WVS) data indicated that these scores were independent of respondents’ gender (Hofstede, 2016). 
While it is clear that the MAS dimension is a significant one, the appropriateness of designating this value system as “Masculinity” remains somewhat doubtful. Best and Williams (1984, 1994, 1998) found no relationship between the cross- country variations in their sex- stereotypes and masculinity– femininity scores and the cross- country variations in Hofstede’s MAS scores. Likewise, Ward (1995) notes that while Attitude Toward Rape scores co- vary with Hofstede’s Power Distance scores, they are unrelated to his MAS scores. Interestingly, Barry (2015) found that when regional differences were controlled across 60 nations, Masculinity was highly correlated with national individualism. 
It is easy to see the role of culture in the relationships between women and men. The choice of mates, the role of romantic love and intimacy in relationships, and views of undesirable sexual behaviors such as rape and harassment are guided by how cultures 
 
gender and CulTure  |  269 
define masculinity and femininity. These relational behaviors are also affected by broader cultural variables and practices that are discussed next. 
Cultural Practices that Influence Behaviors of Males and Females This section examines broader, more distal cultural influences on gender mentioned briefly in earlier sections of the chapter: the status of women, gender division of labor, religious beliefs and values, economic factors, and political participation. These cultural characteristics and practices enculturate children into their cultural niche (Super & Harkness, 1986), interacting with the more proximal socialization practices, discussed earlier, to shape gender expectations, attitudes, and behaviors. 
Status of Women Lindsey (2015) defines status as a position or rank within a social system that determines how an individual will be treated, including any injustices (e.g., gendered violence) and inequality (e.g., unequal access to education) that an individual may experience throughout the lifespan simply for belonging to a particular group. In every society around the world, women hold a lower social status in comparison with men. Ethnographic evidence suggests that the status of women is multidimensional, including economic indicators, power, autonomy, prestige, political participation (Eagly & Diekman, 2006), and ideological dimensions (Mukhopadhyay & Higgins, 1988; Quinn, 1977). Proposed determinants of such widespread asymmetry, or social stratification, in status between men and women include women’s reproductive roles, secondary sexual characteristics, greater male aggression and strength (Wood & Eagly, 2010), sexual division of labor, complexity of the society (Berry, 1976; Ember, 1981), socialization, education, cultural values (Greenfield, 2016), and religious beliefs. In other words, the advancement of women is dynamically and inseparably linked to biosocial, cultural, economic, and political factors. Recent years have seen marked advances in the overall status of women around the globe, particularly in the West, as a result of greater access to education and contraception (Upadhyay et al., 2014). For example, see Figure 9.10, which shows women’s educational attainment in the United States. It is essential to note, however, that progress is not equally felt among women in the West, as many women face additional structural barriers to their advancement, such as racism, homophobia, and classism (May, 2015). 
The status of women is highly complex, as women may gain status in some areas and not others. In addition, a rise in gender equality and women’s status is not evident in all cultures, particularly in developing nations (United Nations International Conference of Population and Development, 2014). Hvistendahl (2011) recently reported that more than 160  million girls are “missing” from several Asian populations due to increased 
 
 
 
270 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
rates of female infanticide since the 1950s. Despite increasing access to education globally, UNESCO (2014) estimates that 40% of the world’s nations provide less education at a primary level for girls than boys. Additionally, the World Health Organization (2016) reports that nearly a third of women in the world will experience sexual or domestic violence in their lifetimes, as noted earlier. While women are making large strides toward advancement and equity, there is still a long way to go. 
Gender Division of Labor What is considered masculine and feminine may be culturally variable, but the literature suggests two possible cultural universals:  to some degree, every society assigns traits and tasks on the basis of gender (Munroe & Munroe, 1975/ 1994) and in no society is the status of women superior to that of men, while the reverse is quite common (Eagly & Wood, 2016; Hoyenga & Hoyenga, 1993; Population Crisis Committee, 1988; Whyte, 1978). This is particularly evident in the gender division of labor, which is sometimes thought to be “the engine of sex- differentiated behavior, because it summarizes the social constraints under which men and women carry out their lives” (Eagly & Wood, 1999, p. 409). While there is still major inequality in the types of roles that men and women occupy, unequal compensation for labor in equally skilled positions remains an issue in many cultures, such that women are often paid less for their work (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2017; Weichselbaumer & Winter- Ebmer, 2005) (Figure 9.11). 
As mentioned earlier, men have historically occupied more external roles in providing resources for their families whereas women have occupied nurturing, domestic,

and care- oriented roles. D’Andrade (1966) analyzed ethnographic records of jobs and tasks in 244 different societies and found that men were involved with hunting, metal work, weapon- making, and travel further from home while women were responsible for cooking and food preparation, carrying water, caring for clothing, and making things used in the home. Women participated in subsistence activities consistent with childrearing responsibilities (Brown, 1970; Segal, 1983), and men had major responsibilities for childrearing in only 10% of the 80 cultures examined (Katz & Konner, 1981). 
Social, educational, and technological advancement in recent decades has brought about shifts in the occupational structure in industrialized cultures in both labor participation and types of labor. Although women’s participation in the labor force has risen in most countries around the globe, dramatic increases are evident in the United States and the Netherlands. In the 1970s, only 28% of adult women participated in paid labor in the Netherlands, a number that has since grown to more than 60%. Similarly, only 43% of adult women in the United States were part of the labor force in the 1970s. Today, the majority of women participate in paid labor: 61% as compared to 75% of men, a figure that is likely to have risen since the time of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics survey in 2009. Women’s labor participation is on the rise, although less dramatically, in other countries such as Italy, Germany, and Canada. Only one country surveyed, Japan, showed relative stability near 50% from 1970 to 2009 (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2009). 
The type of work that men and women engage in may also be shifting in accordance with women’s rising participation in the labor force, decreased childbearing and childrearing activities, and greater access to and attainment of higher education. In the United States, more women have been entering historically male occupations in management and corporate leadership, although men still dominate these fields (Eagly & Wood, 2010). The reverse cannot be said for men entering historically female occupations as there has 
272 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
not been a marked change in the gendered labor of care- oriented positions (e.g., nurses, preschool teachers, administrative assistants) (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2009, 2017). 
Paid employment, however, does not provide a full picture of women’s economic contributions to the family as women still disproportionately engage in unpaid domestic labor. This extra and largely undocumented labor is often referred to as the “second shift,” as many women attend to housework and childrearing after their workday (Crompton, 2006; Hochschild, 1989; Sayer, England, Bittman, & Bianchi, 2009). Even in societies where women have moved actively into the labor force, there has not been a commensurate reduction in their household duties, underscoring that greater equality at work does not necessarily elicit greater equality in the home (Bianchi, Sayer, Milkie, & Robinson, 2012). Interestingly, Charles and Höpflinger (1992) found that in Swiss families, the strongest predictor of a husband’s participation in domestic activities was the presence of children. Contrary to findings in the United States, sex role patterns were more traditional in Swiss families with children, and the longer they had been married, the less men shared in domestic chores. 
The degree to which a nation’s labor is divided by gender is often predicted by sex- role ideology— in particular, benevolent and ambivalent sexism (Glick & Fiske, 2001; Wood & Eagly, 2010). Although it cannot be said that sexism causes the gender division of labor, several cross- cultural studies have demonstrated that gender inequality and cultural ideologies regarding the roles of men and women are highly associated. Using the United Nations two indexes of gender equality, the Gender Development Index and the Gender Empowerment Measure (UNDP, 1998), Glick & Fiske (2001) found that higher sexism scores in men predicted higher levels of gender inequality across 19 nations. Their findings point to the interconnectedness between gender role attitudes and the gender division of labor. In order to shift systematic differences in occupations and compensation, views about gender must change. 
Religious Beliefs and Values Religious beliefs and culturally based views of family honor also influence views of women and their work outside the home (Rapoport, Lomski- Feder, & Masalia, 1989), as well as the role models that children have access to throughout their development. For instance, ideals of personal and family honor in Latin America and the Middle East link the manliness of men (e.g., machismo, muruwwa) with the sexual purity of women (e.g., verguenza, ‘ird). Ideals and values such as these can be powerful determinants of behavior, influencing the division of labor within and outside the home. Some religious communities prescribe proper roles and behavior for males and females, and children are often brought up in ways consistent with such views. 
Economic Factors Economic factors appear to influence gender- related cultural practices. Bride price or bridewealth, a compensation for the loss of a daughter’s economic contributions to her 
 
 
gender and CulTure  |  273 
family (Heath, 1958), is found in many Asian countries, parts of Africa, and in some Pacific Island societies where her contributions are substantial. Dowry accompanies the bride when her economic contributions to her family are relatively small, and she is expected to live near husband’s relatives. Dowry is a traditional practice in South Asia and several Middle East and North Africa countries. Cronk (1993) theorized that, relative to females, the reproductive success of males is affected more by socioeconomic factors, particularly in societies where men may have more than one wife and must also pay a bridewealth. Consequently, when parents have high socioeconomic status so that sons can pay for wives, males are favored. However, when parents have low socioeconomic status, females are favored because of their ability to marry wealthier, higher status neighbors. For example, the Mukogodo in Kenya are at the bottom of the regional hierarchy of wealth, prestige, and ultimately marital and reproductive opportunities. Due to their low status, it is hard for the Mukogodo men to find wives because they do not have bridewealth to pay for a bride. Because men can have as many wives as they can afford, Mukogodo women are easily able to find husbands and increase their socioeconomic status. 
Economic conditions also may influence sex- biased parental investment in children. Among the Mukogodo, the birth ratio of males to females is typical, but the 1986 census recorded 98 girls and 66 boys under 4 years of age. While there is no evidence of male infanticide, it is likely that boys’ higher death rate is due to favoritism shown toward girls. Compared with sons, daughters are breastfed longer, are generally well- fed, and visit the doctor more often, suggesting that parents may invest more in offspring who provide opportunities for greater economic or reproductive success. 
In sharp contrast, in many other traditional parts of the world (e.g., India, China, Turkey, Korea), cultural practices favor boys. Indeed, boys are highly valued by their families, who rejoice greatly over the birth of a new son (Kağıtçıbaşı, 1982). Female infanticide (Hvistendahl, 2011), wife beating (Flavia, 1988), and bride- burning (Ghadially & Kumar, 1988) are cultural practices that attest to the lack of concern for women in some traditional cultures. Preference for boys continues to be strong in the United States (Pooler, 1991; Puri, Adams, Ivey, & Nachtigall, 2011) and in non- Western countries (Bandyopadhyay, 2003) even though many of the religious traditions and economic circumstances that created the preference for sons no longer apply in contemporary society. 
Female Political Participation Across cultures, men are more involved in political activities and governing bodies than are women (Coffé & Bolzendahl, 2010; Ember, 1981; Ross, 1986). The long- standing stereotyped dichotomy of public/ male versus private/ female suggests that men are in the public eye, active in business, politics, and culture, while women stay at home, caring for home and family (Peterson & Runyan, 1993). However, cross- cultural studies do not support this dichotomy as women are involved in public domains and men are becoming more active in the home (del Mar Alonso- Almeida, 2014; Meil, 2013) (Figure 9.12).

Both children’s and adolescents’ concepts of women’s roles in domains such as business and politics reflect the change in conditions and attitudes toward women around the world (Figure 9.13). Moreover, young girls now conceptualize the female gender role to encompass both homemaking and employment outside the home, especially when there is a more egalitarian distribution of labor among their parents (Croft, Shmader, Block, & Baron, 2014). Research on adolescent girls’ perception of women in politics suggests that increased exposure to female politicians is associated with higher rates of anticipated political involvement and that the effect of role models is mediated by political discussion within the family context. 
Looking at literature exploring women’s status in relation to social institutions, including economic and governmental aspects, it is clear that the liberation and equality of both genders is linked to how gender is perceived within both macro- and micro- level
