Significant progress has been documented in recent years with respect to women’s political, economic, and social advancement despite the persistence of inequalities and systemic barriers in some domains (US Department of Commerce Economics and Statistics Administration, 2011). As May (2015) points out, a major challenge for future generations will be ensuring that the economic and political rise of women is felt by all women, not just select privileged groups. 
Questions and Challenges for the Future The question of sex differences has fascinated social scientists for decades, and, with the growing interest in culture, it seems safe to assume that questions regarding the joint effects of these variables will continue to intrigue researchers. In spite of the fact that females and males are biologically more similar than different, persons in traditional or modern, industrialized societies can expect to live qualitatively different lives based on whether they are male or female. Consequently, psychologists will continue to explore the reasons for these differences both within and between cultures. 
Theories and Methods for Studying Gender Future research concerning the interface of gender and culture will need cogent theories and new methodologies to examine the complexities of gender in various sociocultural systems. In the United States, recent theories addressing masculine and feminine attributes have become multifactorial (Ashmore, 1990; Lemaster, Strough, Stoiko, & Donato, 2015; Spence, 1993), and empirical research has supported such an approach by showing little or no relationship between different aspects of gender (Twenge, 1999). At present, the multifactorial approach has not been examined in other cultural groups to see how the relationships between various aspects of gender, such as personality traits, occupational choices, leisure activities, and personal and social relationships, may be influenced by culture. 
The importance of a multifactorial and multimethod approach (Campbell & Fiske, 1959)  is apparent in Best’s (2001) examination of the links between the Munroes’ observational and qualitative studies (e.g., Munroe & Munroe, 1997) of gender in less developed societies (e.g., the Garifuna or Black Carib of Belize, the Logoli of Kenya, the Newars of Nepal, and the Samoans of American Samoa) with the quantitative, experimentally oriented self- report studies in more developed countries of Best and colleagues (Williams & Best, 1990a, 1990b). Blending studies of behaviors, attitudes, and concepts assessed with varied methods and in contrasting populations can demonstrate the convergence and complementarity in findings and provide a richer, more complete understanding of the relation between gender and culture. 
Furthermore, large- scale comparative surveys, such as the International Social Survey Program (ISSP Research Group, 2016)  and the WVS (World Values Survey, 2015) are now widely used in cross- cultural research, and many of these surveys include 
 
 
 
276 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
questions about gender roles and equality. For example, the WVS includes seven waves (1981– 2014) of representative national surveys on people’s values and attitudes in economically and culturally diverse countries containing almost 90% of the world’s population, with samples averaging around 1,400 respondents. Recent WVS data have shown that high levels of economic and physical security have brought increasing acceptance of gender equality, homosexuality, and other behaviors discouraged by agrarian societies that require high fertility rates to maintain their populations (Inglehart, Ponarin, & Inglehart, 2017). Such large- scale studies, with their broad range of countries, languages, and cultures, invariably lead to questions about scale equivalence, a continuing concern in cross- cultural comparisons (Constantin & Voicu, 2015). 
Looking at personality assessment methodology may suggest another way to examine gender- related concepts across cultural groups. The Five Factor Model of personality (McCrae & Costa, 1990, 1997)  proposes that most significant variation in human personality can be explained by five dimensions: Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Openness to Experience. The model has been applied successfully in a variety of other societies (Church & Lonner, 1998; McCrae & Terraciano, 2008) and has been used to study sex differences in adolescent personality in 23 countries (De Bolle et al., 2015) and sex stereotypes in 27 countries (Williams et al., 1999; Williams, Satterwhite, Best, & Inman, 2000). Indeed, the model could be used to examine other gender- related concepts, such as self and ideal self descriptions of men and women, ideal wife and husband, or father and mother. Using a method from general personality research to study gender concepts provides links with existing theory and permits comparisons across different studies and across different conceptual domains. 
Another method with wide applicability across conceptual areas that has been used in 23 language/ cultural groups is the semantic differential devised by Osgood and his associates (Osgood, May, & Miron, 1975; Osgood, Suci, & Tannenbaum, 1957). This procedure assesses affective or connotative meaning associated with a particular target (e.g., person, concept, event, object), yielding scores on evaluation (favorability), potency (strength), and activity, aspects of conceptual meaning that supersede language differences. 
Finally, the Adjective Checklist (Gough & Heilbrun, 1980), a collection of 300 person- descriptive adjectives which has been translated into more than 20 languages, was used by Williams and Best (1990a, 1990b) in their research described earlier. This method has broad applicability for cross- cultural comparison of gender concepts. Indeed, in their reanalysis of the Williams and Best (1990a) gender stereotype data, Cuddy and colleagues (2015) constructed individualistic– collectivistic and competence scales from Adjective Checklist items. These new scales were used to examine relations with culturally defined masculinity– femininity. Given the broad range of characteristics included in the adjective list, a number of gender- related concepts could be readily explored.

Evaluating Cultural Effects Individual cultures, like individual persons, are unique— no two are exactly alike. Indeed, cultures are not static but changing continually. Beyond description or ad hoc speculation, conventional science does not deal well with uniqueness, focusing instead on commonalities, such as systems of classification. In order to study the effects of culture as an antecedent or independent variable, researchers have categorized societies in a number of ways. For example, societies have been classified according to residence patterns (e.g., patrilocal, neolocal), cultural values (e.g., individualism– collectivism, Hofstede, 1980, 2001; autonomy– conservation, hierarchy– mastery, Schwartz, 1990; 2011), and interpersonal relations (e.g., horizontal– vertical, Triandis, 1995; tightness– looseness, Gelfand, et al., 2011). Using such classifications, culture can be treated as an overarching explanatory framework for a number of phenomena or as a set of values, norms, or beliefs. In either case, culture is assumed to have direct or indirect effects on behavior (Lonner & Adamopoulos, 1997) with intracultural variation. 
Cultural classifications systems have been criticized for being too simplistic, general, and failing to consider situational variables. For example, a person may behave individualistically in some situations (e.g., at work) and collectivistically in others (e.g., with family), which demonstrates the importance of the situation. Matsumoto and his colleagues (Matsumoto, Weissman, Preston, Brown & Kupperbusch, 1997)  have responded to this objection by combining the examination of culture and situation, evaluating an individual’s behaviors relative to individualism– collectivism in four different social contexts. Similar refinements in defining culture are needed to understand better how culture and specific cultural practices may influence behavior. Indeed, a serious flaw in some studies that pretend to be “cultural” is that they treat participants’ country of residence as analogous with cultural context, rather than recognizing that not all persons in a particular country share the same cultural experiences. 
Developmental Questions Future studies of gender concepts across cultural groups should address how social relationships and behaviors change with age. In the United States, Maccoby reports that by 33 months of age, boys were unresponsive to the vocal prohibitions of female partners (Maccoby, 1990). She speculates that girls find it aversive to interact with unresponsive partners so they avoid them. This leads to same- sex playmate preferences, a finding that has been demonstrated across a variety of cultural groups (Munroe et al., 2000). However, the reasons for such preferences have not been examined in a cross- cultural context. 
Furthermore, Maccoby reports that male social groups are more concerned with dominance and competitiveness, and boys frequently use threats, commands, and boasts of authority. Girls, in contrast, are more likely to express agreement and to pause to give their partner a chance to speak. Maccoby speculates that familial processes have been given too much credit or blame for the relational aspects of sex- typing, and she emphasizes 
 
 
278 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
the importance of peer group influences. The range of variation and diversity in familial and peer relationships seen across cultural groups provides an exceptional opportunity for examining gender- related social development. Cross- cultural researchers have only begun to explore these social and behavioral issues with children in other societies. 
Future research should also be concerned with increasing evidence that suggests that both sex and gender can operate on continua rather than as binaries (Joel et al., 2015). The ways in which gender nonconformity is expressed within and between cultures, as well as how nonconforming individuals are treated, remains a relatively unexplored territory. In order to understand the needs of these individuals, further research must document and examine their experiences. 
Conclusion In view of the amount and variety of material reviewed in this chapter, any final observations must be very general. Most striking is the central finding that pan- cultural similarities in sex and gender across cultural groups greatly outweigh cultural differences between them. Indeed, the manner in which male– female relationships are organized are remarkably similar across social groups. The relatively minor biological differences between the sexes can be amplified or diminished by cultural practices and socialization, making gender differences in roles and behaviors generally modest but in some cases culturally important. To use an athletic metaphor, gender does not constitute a new ball game in each culture, but rather some relatively minor variations on a very old ball game. Hence, it is reasonable to think in terms of a pan- cultural model with degrees of variation created by various cultural influences. As globalization brings cultures into greater contact, gender understanding will likely change as a result. Moreover, it will be interesting to see how gender roles and concepts are perceived by future generations. 
It is somewhat surprising that more of the gender- related cross- cultural research is not theory- driven, although there are some studies that are consistent with various hypotheses generated from existing theories. To further refine understanding of sex and gender, future research should examine theoretical concerns relevant to cultural influences on behavior. Indeed, longitudinal studies— such as Gauvain and Munroe’s (2012) study of cognitive development— in societies undergoing rapid socioeconomic development could address whether gender concepts change in theoretically expected directions. 
Finally, studies in the various areas of social and behavioral science often seem to have evolved in isolation. Few researchers have studied the relationship between cultural practices, such as initiation rites— a typical topic for anthropologists— and the development of the individual— a topic usually confined to the psychological domain. In their efforts to understand the impact of culture on behavior, anthropologists and psychologists must learn more from each other. Perhaps the growing field of cultural 
 
gender and CulTure  |  279 
psychology, together with cross- cultural psychology, will provide a bridge between disciplines, recognizing that culture serves as both an independent and an organizing variable.
