Culture and Moral Development 
Joan G. Miller, Matthew Wice, and Namrata Goyal 
A major challenge in studying moral development is accommodating both universal and culturally variable aspects of morality. Whereas early theories of moral development treated morality as a unitary and universal construct centered on justice, recent theories have embraced more pluralistic conceptions of the moral domain. This broadening of conceptions of the moral may be seen in contemporary theories that conceptualize the content of morality in more diverse and culturally inclusive terms. The attention to cultural variability in moral content is an exciting trend in research on moral development and one that can continue to benefit greatly from the insights of cultural psychology. 
Our chapter examines the role of culture in the development of morality. In the first section, we review the major theoretical approaches to moral development. We give attention to the conceptual assumptions informing these theories and to their empirical support, as well as to ways in which the theories are benefitting from giving greater weight to cultural considerations. In the second section, we identify directions for future theory and research on culture and moral development. 
Theoretical Approaches to Moral Development In this section, our focus centers on core assumptions and central empirical findings associated with both classic and contemporary perspectives on moral development. We organize the discussion based on the moral content addressed. 
 
 
 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  293 
Morality of Justice 
Cognitive Developmental Model In one of the earliest psychological approaches to moral reasoning, Lawrence Kohlberg formulated a justice model of morality (Kohlberg, 1969, 1971). Challenging earlier social learning accounts that treated morality in terms of social standards acquired through socialization, Kohlberg defined morality as based on what he argued constituted natural law (i.e., objective standards of moral good that transcend societal norms or personal preferences). In adopting this type of approach, Kohlberg formulated a theory of morality that could explain, for example, why a practice such as slavery always constitutes a moral breach. Even if such a practice is both legally and socially accepted in a particular society, it infringes on human rights that, in this view, are assumed to be of higher priority and not dependent on rules or laws. In drawing on philosophical assumptions (e.g., Kant, 1797/ 1964; Rawls, 1971), Kohlberg defined a behavior as moral only if it meets the formal criteria of being universally applicable, prescriptive, and capable of being applied in an impartial and impersonal manner. Furthermore, in Kohlberg’s view, the content of morality constituted a unitary construct centered on justice: 
Virtue is ultimately one, not many, and it is always the same ideal form regardless of climate or culture . . . The name of this ideal form is justice. (Kohlberg, 1971, p. 232) 
Kohlberg forwarded a model of moral development that involved a three- stage (six- level) sequence of progressively more advanced types of moral understandings, with each stage divided into two levels (Carter, 1980). The first and most basic stage of moral reasoning, referred to as preconventional, is characterized by an egocentric focus on avoiding punishment (Level 1) and benefitting through instrumental exchange (Level 2). In turn, the conventional stage involves a focus on complying with social role expectations (Level 3) and upholding the social order and rule of law (Level 4). The third and most advanced stage is postconventional, which entails reasoning on the basis of abstract ethical principles of justice and human rights (Level 5) and respect for the dignity of individual human beings (Level 6). It is only at the postconventional stage that, in the Kohlbergian view, an individual achieves a fully moral outlook. At the preconventional stage, the individual’s outlook is seen as based on his or her own subjective preferences, while at the conventional stage it is seen as based on the subjective preferences of the social group. In contrast, at the formal operational stage, the individual’s reasoning represents a self- chosen ethical principle centered on the abstract requirements of justice. 
What has been striking about research in the Kohlbergian tradition is not only the findings of marked cultural variation in the highest stages of moral development achieved in different societies but Kohlberg’s interpretation of this variation as compatible with his 
 
 
294 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
claims about the universality of a morality of justice and individual rights. In his early research, Kohlberg (1969) uncovered evidence that postconventional levels of moral judgment are linked to Westernization, urbanization, and socioeconomic status and tend to be absent altogether among individuals living in traditional, small- scale societies. Kohlberg (1981) interpreted the observed cultural variation in developmental terms as supporting a historical progression in which individuals in preliterate peasant communities are assumed not able to cognitively attain the highest stage levels: “My findings that the two highest stages are absent in preliterate or semiliterate village culture . . . suggests a mild doctrine of social evolutionism” (Kohlberg, 1981, p. 128). 
Later Kohlbergian research confirmed these findings while revealing, with refined coding schemes, that the observed incidence of postconventional moral reasoning was even less common than first believed. For example, in a review of research conducted among 45 culturally diverse samples, Snarey (1985) noted that approximately 6% of the responses included a mixture of postconventional and conventional concerns, with only 2% or fewer of the responses purely postconventional. Higher stage responses occurred principally among middle- class Western urban populations, with members of traditional folk societies, such as among village communities in Kenya and New Guinea, failing to use postconventional reasoning. 
Evidence of this marked cultural skewing in the distribution of postconventional moral outlooks had led certain early critics of the Kohlbergian model to argue that the Kohlbergian scheme was culturally bound and reflected a modern Western liberal perspective (Simpson, 1974). Theorists asserted that the Kohlbergian model embodied a secular outlook that neglected religious bases of morality and failed to take into account contrasting cultural views of personhood, such as viewpoints that accord value to all life, not just to all human life (Vasudev & Hummel, 1987). Snarey (1985) also objected to the social evolutionism in the Kohlbergian model in arguing that, even without higher education, individuals can “reason about their customs and norms rather than blindly conforming to them” (p. 227). Sympathetic to the broad agenda of the Kohlbergian approach, Snarey (1985) proposed that the Kohlbergian coding system be modified to include more culturally inclusive content at the postconventional levels, pointing out that, if this change was made, postconventional reasoning would be observed to be much more common cross- culturally. Notably, Kohlberg himself showed some openness to alternative cultural bases for postconventional morality near the end of his career, acknowledging that “general principles at Stage 6 may be one or several,” including not only “universal human care or agape” but also other principles such as “maximum quality of life” (Kohlberg, 1986, p.  497). However, the Kohlbergiacn Standard Issue Scoring Manual, which presented the definitive Kohlbergian coding system, was published without having incorporated any of these various suggestions for greater cross- cultural inclusiveness (Colby & Kohlberg, 1987) and never underwent further revision. 
Later research in the cognitive developmental tradition by Rest (1979) retained the stage assumptions of the Kohlbergian model while assessing moral judgment using a less 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  295 
language- dependent methodology. This work employed a new instrument, the Defining Issues Test (DIT), that used Likert rating scales to assess individuals’ evaluations of the same types of moral issues presented in the original Kohlbergian moral dilemmas. Notably, results observed on the DIT resembled those on Kohlberg’s original moral reasoning interview. A meta- analysis undertaken on more than 400 studies that employed the DIT showed that, as in Kohlberg’s original measure, scores on the DIT showed a positive relationship to education, urbanization, and Westernization (Rest, Narvaez, Bebeau, & Thoma, 1999). 
Another direction taken later in this tradition involved a conceptual revision of Kohlberg’s stage model undertaken by Gibbs (1977, 1979, 2003; Gibbs et al., 1984). Gibbs argued for a universal two- stage developmental progression followed by a higher level that was seen as involving philosophical reflections on ethics and the meaning of life. The early developmental progression included an immature level that was seen as involving cognitive egocentrism (Stage 1) and concrete reciprocity (Stage 2), followed by a mature level that involved an ideal moral reciprocity (Stage 3)  and the mutuality involved in complex social systems (Stage 4). Although Gibbs did not endorse the type of social evolutionist interpretation formulated originally by Kohlberg, his model assumed that the higher stages of moral development would not be observed in less technologically developed societies due to their lesser relevance to ways of life in such societies. 
In addition to the DIT just described, later research in this tradition adopted other types of methods to assess moral reasoning, with these assessment approaches in many cases not based on presenting hypothetical moral dilemmas. For example, the Sociomoral Reflection Measure- Short Form (SRM- SF) that was developed by Gibbs involved eliciting evaluations and justifications of moral issues that were introduced to the research participant in familiar everyday terms (Gibbs, Widaman, & Colby, 1982). For example, to elicit a child’s reflections on issues of contract and truth, the child might be asked to respond to an initial prompt such as “Think about when you’ve made a promise to a friend of yours . . . ” Extensive research has been undertaken assessing reflective moral understandings in these ways, with such research undertaken not only among different age groups but also in different social and cultural communities internationally (for review, see Gibbs, Basinger, Grime, & Snarey, 2007). Although the conclusions drawn from this research avoid the earlier Kohlbergian claim that only certain elite populations ever attain the cognitive ability to reach a purely moral stance, the research findings show similar relationships to cultural background variables as had been observed using Kohlberg’s original approach. Thus, for example, the more recent findings also show that moral maturity is positively associated with age, education, socioeconomic status, and urbanization. 
Research on the Kohlbergian model and subsequent work in this developmental tradition has been groundbreaking even as the field eventually moved in directions that represented a shift away from cognitive developmental approaches. In terms of its major influence, work in the Kohlbergian tradition highlighted the need to distinguish between morality as compared with mere social convention and personal preference. For example, 
296 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
this work challenged earlier emotion- or personality- based models of morality, such as the Freudian model of the superego that portrayed morality as irrational in nature or as a reflection of subjective needs. It also called into question earlier perspectives in social learning theory and in social psychology that identified morality with social standards. In this way, the Kohlbergian approach and later cognitive developmental work captured the sense of morality as a perceived natural law that the individual understands to exist above mere social convention and personal choice. Importantly, work on morality in the cognitive developmental tradition also has stimulated ongoing interest in the developmental emergence of moral outlooks, in recognizing that moral understandings emerge gradually over development (e.g., Gielen & Markoulis, 2001). 
However, the cognitive developmental framework of Kohlberg and other researchers in this tradition built on Piaget’s earlier cognitive developmental stage model and thus has been vulnerable to some of the same theoretical and methodological challenges to such stage models that were directed at Piagetian theory (Gelman, 1978; see also Chapter 7 by Harry W. Gardiner for a broader review of culture and development). Like challenges directed to Piagetian theory, Kohlbergian theory was vulnerable to methodological critiques, with researchers arguing that the use of methods that put a premium on highly reflective reasoning underestimates the knowledge both of children and of populations with lesser formal education. As explained in the next section, a new theoretical per-spective, termed the distinct domain model, emerged as a framework that adopted more child- centered methodologies and provided evidence of earlier moral competence than observed in cognitive developmental research. Interest in Kohlbergian theory also shifted as research turned to newer conceptual frameworks, such as Gilligan’s model of a morality of caring (1982), as well as to exploring new topics, such as the morality of divinity (Shweder, Much, Mahapatra, & Park, 1997). 
Distinct Domain Model Influenced by the cognitive- developmental approach, yet distinct in important ways, the social domain perspective on moral development provided an alternative to Kohlberg’s stage model and put an emphasis on the early- occurring abilities of children to distinguish moral issues from other types of social rules (Nucci, 1981; Nucci & Turiel, 1978; Smetana, 1981, 1983; Turiel, 1979, 1983, 1998). While retaining the universalism of Kohlbergian theory and its assumption that justice and individual rights form the core content of morality, the social domain perspective made contrasting claims regarding the self- constructive processes entailed in moral judgment and adopted a methodology for assessing moral reasoning that has yielded new findings regarding its cross- cultural and developmental distribution. In contrast to the linguistically demanding Kohlbergian approach that required individuals, through open- ended responses, to appraise unfamiliar hypothetical moral conflicts, research in the distinct domain tradition uses more child- centered methodologies. For example, research by distinct domain theorists has employed short- answer questions framed about everyday familiar situations (such as the 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  297 
situation of a child pushing a classmate off a swing or wearing pajamas to a wedding) to assess the abilities of children and adults to distinguish between issues embodying morality, social convention, or personal choice. 
To illustrate, in a study of moral reasoning among preschoolers (Smetana, 1981), children were presented with pen- and- ink drawings of transgressions, such as a child hitting another child or a child not sitting in the designated place (on the rug) during storytime at school. Short- answer questions were administered to assess whether children would categorize the first issue as a matter of morality and the second as a social convention. These short- answer questions assessed such issues as the rule contingency of the issue (“Would it [the depicted event] be OK if there was no rule about it here?”), the relativity of the practice (“Would [the event] be OK at home or in another school?),” whether the issue is legitimately regulated (“Whether or not the teacher should punish the transgressor?), and the judged seriousness of the issue (by rating on a scale how “bad” the behavior is). Strikingly, this type of research has shown that both preschool- age children and adults are able to distinguish between the domains of morality, social convention, and personal choice, with the abilities to make these distinctions observed cross- culturally (e.g., Song, Smetana, & Kim, 1987). 
In contrast to the Kolbergian emphasis on logical deduction in the child’s construction of moral knowledge, the distinct domain perspective stresses the role of everyday social interaction in the child’s construction of morality. In this view, morality is viewed as inductively derived based on individuals observing the intrinsic consequences of actions (Turiel, 1983). Actions which lead to harm or which infringe on another’s rights are interpreted as matters of morality— such as the act of arbitrarily assaulting another person or of taking another person’s belongings without their permission. In contrast, it is assumed that other types of social behaviors, such as dress codes, represent social conventions, in that the behaviors serve to facilitate social coordination and do not involve justice or harm. Finally, it is assumed that a domain of personal choice and prudence exists that is based on the individual’s subjective preferences and does not involve either moral issues of justice or harm or conventional concerns of social coordination (Nucci, 1981; Nucci & Lee, 1993). For example, in research on personal issues conducted by Nucci (1981), personal issues are portrayed as involving an individual engaging in actions that, while they are counter to a stated norm, lead to consequences that are assumed primarily to affect only the actor, such as a girl playing with a friend her parents have forbade her to interact with or a boy wearing long hair in violation of the school’s rules. From this perspective, it is assumed that the content of issues considered in the domain of personal choice is variable, whereas issues considered as moral are universally focused on justice and individual rights. As cultural critiques of this type of stance (e.g., Miller, 2006) have pointed out, however, acknowledging that matters of personal choice are culturally dependent implies that matters of morality are as well, given the mutual dependence of morality and personal choice. For example, a matter of personal choice in one culture (such as violating a parent’s stipulation of whom a child should have as a 
298 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
friend) may be considered a matter of morality in another culture (e.g., based on the importance of respecting parental authority). 
From the social domain perspective, cultural variation in moral reasoning is interpreted as compatible with the assumption that the content of morality is universal. It is argued that what appear to be cultural differences in moral outlook represent merely cultural differences in background knowledge (Turiel, Killen, & Helwig, 1987; Wainryb, 1991). For example, in judging that it is immoral to eat beef, Indians are seen as maintaining a morality of harm. They are viewed as differing from Americans only in their assumptions that a cow is a sacred object deserving of protection from harm and not in their moral assumption that harm should be avoided. In this type of interpretive stance, the position is taken that background epistemological knowledge presuppositions (e.g., assumptions about the existence of a spiritual world of sacred objects) should be held constant or parcelled out in appraising the cultural universality of morality. These cultural knowledge presuppositions are considered as matters of fact whose validity can be ascertained and reconciled rationally, rather than as arbitrary matters of value. 
Cultural Models Work by cognitive developmental and social domain theorists has demonstrated that a concern with justice exists universally. However, even with this universality, culture is found to influence when justice concepts are applied. Such variation, it may be seen, reflects the contrasting adaptive demands of different cultural settings and the relative priority of competing moral obligations, as well as culturally variable theories of the self and associated practices. 
Cross- cultural evidence indicates, for example, that the findings of marked cultural skewing in levels of Kohlbergian moral stage development achieved reflect, at least in part, the contrasting relevance of justice concepts in different social settings. In this regard, Harkness and her colleagues (Harkness, Edwards, & Super, 1981), for example, observed that the moral leaders of a Kipsigis community in Kenya typically score at Conventional Stage Level 3 on Kohlbergian measures, whereas a sample of non- leaders, who were matched on age, education, wealth, and religion with the leaders, tend only to score at Preconventional Stage Level 2. They assume that whereas the concrete individual perspective on morality embodied in Level 2 is most relevant to the everyday concerns of the non- leaders in this community, for the moral leaders, it is important to cultivate the interpersonal systems– oriented perspective of Level 3. More generally, cultural theorists maintain that the understanding of social structure entailed in Levels 4 and higher on the Kohlbergian scheme has relevance primarily in contexts that are closely tied in with state or national governments— a finding that may explain, at least in part, the association observed cross- culturally between higher levels of Kohlbergian moral stage development and processes of modernization (Edwards, 1975, 1978, 1986). 
Cross- cultural work has also shown that, even in cases in which individuals from different cultures agree on the moral status of justice concepts, their application of these 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  299 
concepts in everyday situations may differ depending on other moral values that they hold. Thus, it has been found, for example, that Indians tend to give greater priority to interpersonal responsibilities relative to competing justice obligations than do European Americans because of their contrasting views of such responsibilities (Miller & Bersoff, 1992). In particular, whereas Americans tend to consider interpersonal responsibilities as discretionary commitments, Indians tend to accord them the same obligatory moral status as justice issues. To give an example from the Miller and Bersoff (1992) research, whereas a majority of Indians judged that an agent should commit the justice breach of stealing a stranger’s train ticket if it was the only way to be able to participate as Best Man in a close friend’s wedding, a majority of Americans judged that the agent should not engage in the justice violation in this case. Similar cross- cultural differences have been observed in research contrasting the moral judgments of Chinese and Icelandic children (Keller, Edelstein, Fang, & Fang, 1998). When reasoning about moral dilemmas, Chinese children tend to give greater priority to altruistic and relationship concerns and Icelandic children to give greater priority to contractual and self- interested considerations. 
Judgments of moral accountability represent another area in which cross- cultural differences exist in reasoning about justice morality, even in cases in which individuals from different cultures agree on the moral status of the issues involved. In maintaining more contextually oriented views of the agent, individuals from cultures emphasizing collectivist as compared with individualistic beliefs and practices show a greater tendency to consider behavior as under the control of situational influences (e.g., Miller, 1984; Morris & Peng, 1994) and are less prone in such cases to hold agents morally accountable for their actions. Thus, for example, Hindu Indians have been found more frequently than European Americans to absolve agents of moral accountability for justice breaches performed under the agent’s emotional duress, immaturity, or other potentially extenuating situational factors (Bersoff & Miller, 1993; Miller & Luthar, 1989). Similarly, a greater emphasis on contextual sensitivity has been found in moral codes grounded in Confucian as compared with Judeo- Christian cultural traditions (Dien, 1982). This is reflected, for example, in a greater tendency of Chinese as compared with Americans to stress reconciliation rather than conflict resolution in dispute settlement. 
In addition to variability in accountability judgments in relation to justice breaches, cross- cultural variability has also been observed in the perceived severity of different types of justice breaches. For example, research has demonstrated that individuals in a rural Mayan community did not demonstrate an “omission” bias, assumed to be universal, in which justice breaches involving an agent performing an action (e.g., harming someone) are viewed as more serious than breaches of omission, in which one transgresses through passive inaction (e.g., allowing someone to be harmed) (Abarbanell & Hauser, 2010). Specifically, it was found that although Americans viewed harm resulting from action as more serious than harm resulting from inaction, Mayans did not show this bias and treated each type of breach as equally serious.
300 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Evidence also exists for early- occurring cultural variability in understandings of distributive justice. After collaborating on a joint task, 7- to 8  year- old children from Germany as compared with those from hunter- gatherer cultural backgrounds have been found to distribute the rewards differently depending on their cultural background (Schafer, Haun, & Tomasello, 2015). Whereas German children distributed the rewards in a joint task based on merit, children from a hunter- gatherer society distributed them in an egalitarian fashion, regardless of individual contributions. 
Finally, as has been briefly noted in discussion of the social domain viewpoint, cultural differences in everyday justice reasoning may occur because of culturally based variation in the assumptions which individuals make in determining the applicability of justice concepts. These cultural differences in background premises may lead to marked variation in everyday moral judgment, with individuals from different cultural communities disagreeing in their assessment of such issues as what entities are assumed to have rights and to be entitled to protection from harm, or even regarding what, in fact, constitutes harm. For example, in maintaining a greater cultural emphasis on hierarchy, orthodox Hindu Indian populations consider it as morally justifiable to accord unequal privileges to females relative to males (Shweder, Mahapatra, & Miller, 1987). 
In sum, while cultural research provides support to claims that justice and individual rights represent universal moral concerns, such research also highlights significant cultural variation in everyday moral outlooks. The research indicates that cultural variation is associated with justice concerns being accorded different relevance and accorded contrasting priority relative to other types of moral considerations. Cultural differences in conceptions of the entities entitled to protection from harm and in ideas of what constitutes fair distribution of resources also lead to marked differences in specific moral judgments. 
Morality of Community 
Gilligan Morality of Caring Interest in the morality of caring stemmed from concerns raised by Carol Gilligan about gender bias both in the Kohlbergian model of moral development and in psychological theory more generally (Gilligan, 1977, 1979). A  former student of Kohlberg, Gilligan observed that the dissertation research on which Kohlberg had based his theory included only males. She charged that this contributed to Kohlbergian theory being insufficiently sensitive to the perspective of women and to females tending to score lower than did males on Kohlbergian measures of moral reasoning. It may be noted that, subsequent to Kohlberg’s dissertation, all later research undertaken by Kohlberg and his colleagues included both males and females, and the charge of gender bias on Kohlbergian measures was later shown to be unsupported (e.g., Walker, 1984). However, in expanding her concerns into a new theoretical perspective on the morality of caring, Gilligan developed this criticism of Kohlberg in a direction that took into account what she saw as the distinctive viewpoints and experiences of women. 
 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  301 
The morality of caring perspective of Carol Gilligan and her colleagues presented a major conceptual challenge to both the cognitive developmental and social domain frameworks in terms of a new vision regarding the content of morality, the processes underlying its development, and the impact of gender on its form (Gilligan, 1982; Gilligan & Wiggins, 1987). Gilligan argued that morality needs to be viewed as extending to issues of caring and interpersonal responsiveness. Challenging the assumption that justice forms the exclusive content of morality, Gilligan maintained that caring represents an integral aspect of morality. In contrast to the cognitive emphasis of the cognitive developmental and distinct domain perspectives, Gilligan argued for the need to understand the development of morality in terms of the affectively based development of self— a process that she viewed as gender- related. 
Drawing on psychodynamic and attachment formulations (e.g., Ainsworth, 1978; Chodorow, 1978), Gilligan located the roots of morality in the development of self in early socialization experiences. In naturally identifying with their mothers and in having experiences in family interaction that emphasize interpersonal responsiveness, girls were seen as developing a connected self and associated morality of caring (Gilligan & Wiggins, 1987). In contrast, in identifying with their fathers, boys were seen as developing an autonomous self and an associated morality of justice. The emphasis on gender differences in Gilligan’s morality of caring perspective led to applications of the theory in contexts in which it is seen as more relevant than theories of morality focused on justice. One example of this is nursing education, in which some theorists have adopted Gilligan’s model as a more appropriate framework for moral education given the caring involved in the job of nursing (Harbison, 1992). 
In its attention to gender- related variation in individuals’ sense of self and moral outlook, the morality of caring perspective accords greater weight to social considerations than do either the cognitive developmental or distinct domain perspectives. However, in Gilligan’s model, little or no weight was given to cultural meanings and practices that structure self- related experiences and outlooks. Rather, the claim is made that, whereas cultures vary in their everyday socialization practices, they all embody the same patterns of structural inequalities associated with gender and thus would all lead to fundamentally the same forms of self and morality. 
Whereas there was initial embrace of the claim that males emphasize justice and females emphasize caring, later evidence indicated that moral reasoning tends not to be gender- related (Thomas, 1986; Walker, 1984, 1991). Rather, it appears that any gender- related variation in moral reasoning arose primarily from differences in education, occupation, discourse style, or in the types of issues under consideration (e.g., abortion), rather than from gender differences in moral outlook per se (see Jaffe & Hyde, 2000, for mixed support). 
Although rejecting the claim that moral reasoning is gender- related, contemporary psychological theorists continue to embrace Gilligan’s assertion about the existence of a morality of caring (Jaffee & Hyde, 2000; Walker, 2006). The conclusion is drawn that 
302 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
caring for family, friends, and other individuals in close relationships represents an important aspect of morality for both males and females, with such a morality assuming the same form in all cultural contexts. Interestingly, then, whereas the morality of caring perspective of Gilligan has succeeded in broadening contemporary understandings regarding the content that is considered moral, it remains within a universalistic framework. 
Cultural Models Although Gilligan portrayed the morality of caring as universal, a reading of morality of caring responses cited by Gilligan (1982) illustrates respects in which the type of morality of caring responses identified by Gilligan embodies an individualistic approach to caring. One individualistic aspect of this morality, for example, is in the weight given to individual choice in making the decision about whether or not to be responsive to the needs of others. As 11- year- old “Amy” argues 
If you have a responsibility with someone else, then you should keep it to a certain extent, but to the extent that it is really going to hurt you or stop you from doing something that you really, really want, then I think maybe you should put yourself first. (Gilligan, 1982, p. 35) 
The individualistic tenor of the morality of caring is also reflected in the emphasis placed on acting in a way that is separate from conventional role definitions. Embracing such a stance, college student “Claire” describes how she has rejected societal role definitions and begun to act more autonomously in developing a morality of caring: 
I am not necessarily the type of girlfriend I should be or that I’ve been perceived as, and I’m not necessarily the type of daughter that I’ve been perceived as. You grow up to find yourself in the way other people see you, and it’s very hard, all of a sudden, to start separating this and start realizing that really nobody else can make these decisions. (Gilligan, 1982, p. 52) 
Additionally, the individualistic tenor of the morality of caring is evident in its eschewing of self- sacrifice and promotion of individuality. As Gilligan describes Claire’s adoption of such an individualistic stance as she develops a mature morality of caring outlook, 
 . . . she has come to observe “faults” in her mother, whom she perceives as endlessly giving, “because she doesn’t care if she hurts herself in doing it. . . . Measured against a standard of care, Claire’s ideal of self- sacrifice gives way to a vision of “a family where everyone is encouraged to become an individual and at the same time everybody helps others and receives help from them.” (Gilligan, p. 54) 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  303 
The emphasis on balancing harm to self and other, rather than on self- sacrifice, is also evident in recent research showing that judgments of moral obligation of caring for another are based not only on taking into account the welfare of the individual receiving help but also on the cost incurred by the giver of help (Sorkhabi, 2012). 
In sum, although Gilligan never explicitly linked the form of the morality of caring to the individualistic assumptions of middle- class European American culture, this type of outlook is evident in the morality of caring responses observed among European Americans, with informants emphasizing choice, rejecting role obligations as a basis for moral commitments, and stressing the need to avoid the loss of individuality entailed in stances that appear to involve significant self- sacrifice. 
Whereas the individualism of the morality of caring orientation is thus reflected in the open- ended caring responses cited by Gilligan (1982), more direct evidence that the morality of caring outlook differs qualitatively from the types of outlooks on community maintained in many collectivist cultures is found in a program of comparative studies undertaken among middle- class European American and Hindu Indian populations (Miller, 1994). This research demonstrated that whereas European Americans tend to conceptualize caring as involving freely given commitments that are considered matters of personal choice, Indians tend to conceptualize interpersonal responsibilities as moral duties that extend across a broader range of need and role situations. As compared with Hindu Indians, European Americans also give greater weight to individual tastes and interests in assessing interpersonal responsibilities. Thus, they tend to treat responsibilities to meet the needs of family and friends as dependent on personal affinity and liking, whereas Indians tend to treat such responsibilities as dependent on more immutable role- based obligations (Miller & Bersoff, 1998). For example, European Americans maintain that a person has less responsibility to be responsive to their brother’s needs if they personally share few common tastes and interests with the brother and thus do not enjoy each other’s company than if they share many common tastes and interests and enjoy being together. In contrast, Hindu Indians maintain that a person’s responsibility to his or her brother is unaffected by such self- serving considerations. Furthermore, Indians consider it as morally required, rather than as beyond the scope of morality, to give priority to the needs of others in the face of personal hardship or sacrifice, and they show a greater tendency than is shown by European Americans to experience satisfaction in such cases (Miller & Bersoff, 1995). These cultural differences are illustrated in the following prototypic responses to a situation that was presented to informants involving a wife who remained married to her husband after the husband was severely injured in a motorcycle accident and had become depressed and inactive for the rest of his life. Viewing the wife’s behavior as both morally required and as highly desirable, a Hindu Indian informant noted the satisfaction that she anticipated that the wife would experience in being responsive to her husband’s welfare and fulfilling her duty as a wife:
304 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
She will have the satisfaction of having fulfilled her duty. She helped her husband during difficulty. If difficulties and happiness are both viewed as equal, only then will the family life be smooth. (Miller & Bersoff, 1995, p. 275) 
In contrast, viewing such behavior as a matter for personal decision- making rather than of morality, an American focused on the dissatisfaction that she anticipated that the wife would experience in giving insufficient attention to her personal desires: 
She is acting out of obligation — not other reasons like love. She has a sense of duty but little satisfaction for her own happiness. (Miller & Bersoff, 1995, p. 275) 
The relationship between individualistic concerns and interpersonal moral duties has also been shown to be intertwined in ways that are distinct from the patterns illustrated among European- Americans and Hindu Indians. For example, research conducted among Finnish adolescents has demonstrated an approach to moral reasoning in which concerns with both individual rights as well the greater societal good are viewed as mutually reinforcing one another rather than as in opposition (Vainio, 2015). Specifically, curtailing one’s individual freedoms in order to give greater power to the state was viewed by Finnish adolescents as a means to increase the welfare of individual citizens. Such moral reasoning has been shown to be characteristic of other Nordic countries, such as Denmark (Arnett & Jensen, 1994) and Sweden (Scarr, 1996) and may be seen to be influenced, at least in part, by the Nordic welfare system (Vainio, 2015). 
Recent research has also explored the role that culture plays in affecting caring behavior through addressing variability in norms of reciprocity. This line of research has revealed, for instance, that Americans are more likely to view helping a friend as obligatory when that friend had done some service for them which has not yet been reciprocated, relative to a situation in which the beneficiary has already reciprocated. Among Hindu Indians, however, helping the friend is viewed as a moral obligation regardless of the past pattern of social support exchanges (Miller et al., 2014; Miller, Akiyama, & Kapadia, 2017). 
Cultural research has also begun to explore variability in the motivation to engage in helping behavior, particularly in terms of how individuals respond to expectations to help others. Such research has shown that social expectations to help others in need tend to be more fully internalized among Hindu Indians as compared with Americans. Whereas, among Americans, helping a friend or family member in a situation in which it is socially expected is perceived to be less satisfying, among Hindu Indians high levels of satisfaction in helping family and friends is experienced regardless of whether or not the helping behavior is expected (Miller, Das, & Chakravarthy, 2011). 
Morality of Divinity Part of the impetus for work on moralities of divinity was the success of research on the morality of caring that had challenged earlier views of morality as limited to issues of 
 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  305 
justice and individual rights. The impetus for this work on divinity, however, also stemmed from anthropological research that highlighted nonrational aspects of human inference and the existence of moral outlooks grounded in spiritual concerns (e.g., Shweder, 1984; Shweder et al., 1987). 
Just as role- based responsibilities have tended to be approached exclusively as conventional rather than moral concerns within the classic psychological theories of moral development, religious or spiritual orientations have tended also to be understood exclusively as matters of convention. One of the important insights of cultural research is to document that morality may be grounded in spiritually based issues that are orthogonal to concerns with justice or community (Shweder et al., 1997). Shweder and Much (1987), for example, provided evidence that informants from an orthodox Hindu Indian temple community justify their judgments that it is wrong for the husband to steal in the Heinz dilemma by reference to negative consequences in suffering and spiritual degradation that they believe will ensue. The Heinz dilemma involves a hypothetical situation in which a husband is confronted with the dilemma of whether to steal an overpriced drug in order to save the life of his sick wife. Notably, the arguments made by orthodox Hindu Indian informants in such cases tend to make no mention of considerations of justice, individual rights, or welfare. Condemning stealing as a violation of dharma, the Hindu Indian informants interpret the act of stealing as leading to spiritual degradation and automatic suffering in cycles of future rebirths (for analysis of Buddhist understandings of dharma and related moral concepts, see Huebner and Garrod (1991). These types of culturally based epistemological assumptions, it is documented, inform orthodox Hindu Indians’ moral reasoning about a wide range of everyday social practices, resulting in moral assessments markedly different from those observed among secular Western populations, with their contrasting epistemological presuppositions. Thus, it is shown, for example, that orthodox Hindu populations tend to consider it a moral violation for a wife to eat with her husband’s elder brother or for a widow to eat fish, with their reasoning influenced by such spiritually based epistemological premises and arguments as that “the husband is a moving god and should be treated with comparable respect” and that “the body is a temple with a spirit dwelling in it. Therefore the sanctity of the temple must be preserved. Therefore impure things must be kept out of and away from the body” (Shweder et al., 1987, pp. 76– 77). 
Evidence for moralities of divinity that extend beyond justice and welfare have also been documented in other cultural populations. Haidt and his colleagues (Haidt, Koller, & Dias, 1993) demonstrated, for example, that lower class Brazilian children as well as lower class African American children tend to treat in moral terms certain disgusting or disrespectful actions, such as eating one’s dog, even while viewing such actions as harmless. Reflecting their assumption that humans relate to each other and to the Divine in terms of a hierarchically structured order, fundamentalist Baptist informants consider divorce as a sacrilege, with negative repercussions for the afterlife (Jensen, 1997, 2009). As one informant reasoned:
306 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Divorce to me means [that] you slap God in the face. In other words, you bring reproach upon God. Because Jesus Christ and the church are a form of marriage. What we are saying by divorce is that the bride goes away from the husband. Think about what that means. That means that we could lose salvation. [Divorce] breaks down the very essence of our religion and that’s why I think divorce is shameful. (Jensen, 1997, p. 342) 
Within these spiritual perspectives, the epistemological premises not only differ markedly from the secular premises assumed in the mainstream theories of moral development, but are integrally linked with moral prescriptions regarding right behavior. 
Moral Ethics Frameworks In an influential taxonomy of moral beliefs, Shweder and colleagues (Shweder et  al., 1997) proposed an ethic of divinity as one of the “Big Three” ethics of morality (the other two being autonomy and community). Within this framework, diverse and conceptually distinct moral values were organized into three categories based on their content. The ethic of divinity views morality in terms of a natural sacred order and emphasizes issues of divinity such as spiritual purity and degradation. This ethic of divinity is seen as conceptually distinct from the other two ethics: the ethic of community, which concerns moral beliefs related to one’s membership in a society, and the ethic of autonomy, which emphasizes one’s rights as an individual, autonomous being. 
Shweder’s formulation of the Big Three ethics framework has had great influence on recent, pluralistic approaches to studying moral development. The Cultural- Developmental perspective (Jensen, 2008), for instance, utilizes the Big Three ethics in order to understand how reasoning within each of these moral domains changes over the course of development. Within this framework, moral reasoning is typically assessed through conducting interviews and coding responses in terms of their reference to each of the ethics. Within Jensen’s Cultural- Developmental framework, these three broad categories encompass subcategories which allow for a fine- grained analysis of responses. The larger category of divinity, for example, contains the subcategory of “scriptural authority,” which refers to sacred text as a source of moral truth (Jensen, 2004). 
Although research employing a Cultural- Developmental approach has uncovered use of all of the ethics, including divinity, across many diverse societies (e.g., Jensen, 2008), such research has also demonstrated between- culture differences in the relative emphasis given to each form of morality. Reliance on the ethic of divinity, for instance, has been shown to be higher among Brazilians relative to people living in the United Kingdom and New Zealand (Guerra & Giner- Sorella. 2015). More striking, however, are the robust within- culture differences in reliance on the ethics of divinity, with religious beliefs and practices being a major factor accounting for this variability. Within both the United States and India, for example, use of the ethic of divinity is greater among those who are religiously conservative relative to those who are religiously liberal (Jensen, 1997, 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  307 
2015). These differences in emphasis on divinity also depend on contextual factors, such as whether divinity reasoning is applied to private or public issues. Research conducted among evangelical and mainline Protestants within the United States has found that although evangelical Protestants have been shown to reason in terms of divinity more for public issues, mainline Protestants show the opposite pattern, using the ethic of divinity more frequently when reasoning about private issues specific to their own lives (Jensen & McKenzie, 2016). 
Given its emphasis on understanding the developmental trajectory of diverse aspects of moral reasoning, Cultural- Developmental theory has forwarded a template for the developmental timeline for each of the ethics. Within this template, it is proposed that autonomy reasoning is available early in childhood and remains stable in its usage into adulthood, with community and divinity developing at relatively older ages (e.g., Jensen, 2008). The assumed reason for the delay in divinity reasoning is that a child may not have the cognitive capacity to grasp abstract notions of divinity prior to adolescence (Jensen, 2015). This proposed developmental template, however, is conceptualized as flexible and anticipated to differ across cultural contexts. With regard to divinity, if the child is exposed to concrete practices and routines that are intertwined with notions of divinity at a young age, divinity reasoning may be available early in childhood. Such early divinity reasoning is demonstrated in research conducted among Indian children by Pandya and Bhangaokar (2015), who showed an early use of the ethics of divinity in their reasoning when interviewed about a set of moral scenarios. This emphasis on divinity among young children was seen as reflecting the children’s diverse daily experiences with practices, rituals, and discourse shaping their understanding of divinity. The centrality of divinity in moral reasoning early in childhood may be seen in the following response by an 8- year- old boy: 
If we do good for God, God will also do good for us. But if we have broken his idol by mistake and if we don’t tell everyone, then God will be upset and angry. He will like for us to say the truth and to face the consequences. Even if we did it by mistake, he will be happy that we could let everyone know, he will feel less worried and be so proud of us! (Pandya & Bhangaokar, 2015, p. 31) 
The notion of divinity has also received attention in Moral Foundations theory, which has extended the moral taxonomy beyond the three ethics to five foundations (Haidt & Kesebir, 2010; Graham et al., 2011, 2013). Drawing inspiration from the Big Three ethics, Moral Foundations theory represents an attempt to reconcile both the diversity and commonality of moral beliefs across cultural contexts. Moral Foundations theory seeks not only to expand the moral content studied by psychologists, but also to utilize evolutionary theory to argue for a set of innate moral primitives with roots in natural selection. From the perspective of Moral Foundations theory, cultural diversity in moral values is a function of particular Moral Foundations being more or less 
308 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
elaborated in different cultural contexts. In a pluralistic fashion, Graham, Haidt and their colleagues have proposed as the five Moral Foundations: care– harm, fairness– cheating, loyalty– betrayal, authority– subversion, and sanctity– degradation. The care– harm foundation is seen as rooted in an evolutionarily deep propensity toward caring for the young and vulnerable; the fairness– cheating as based on an evolutionary imperative to avoid being cheated; the loyalty– betrayal foundation and authority– subversion foundations as related to maintaining group cohesion; and the sanctity– degradation foundation as centered on an extension of the human “behavioral immune system” that, it is assumed, evolved to avoid potentially harmful toxins and contaminants. Since the theory was first posited, a sixth potential foundation of liberty– oppression has also been proposed (Graham et al., 2013). 
Moral Foundations theory complements Haidt’s social intuitionist model of moral judgment that views moral judgment as based on intuition, with deliberate, effortful moral reasoning seen as more often functioning as a post hoc justification for moral stances (Haidt, 2001). In contrast to classic approaches to moral reasoning, morality in this view is understood as rooted in subjective perceptions of moral status rather than formal criteria. 
Moral Foundations theory has been applied to the domain of politics, with a particular focus on shedding light on America’s “culture war” (Haidt, 2012). Major empirical findings from this tradition have shown that individuals who identify as politically liberal tend to disproportionately reason based on principles of harm and fairness, giving less attention to loyalty, authority, and sanctity. In contrast, political conservatives tend to utilize all five foundations in their moral reasoning (Graham, Haidt, & Nosek, 2009; Haidt & Graham, 2007; Haidt & Joseph, 2007). 
Whereas work on Moral Foundations theory dominates contemporary work on morality in social psychology and has contributed to an increased interest in the topic of morality in work in the social psychological tradition, its approach to culture has limited cultural sensitivity. The Model is intended to serve as a means of accounting for the broad range of moral concerns cross- culturally while also providing a way to tap cultural variation in moral outlooks in terms of differential endorsement of the various moral foundations. However, the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) developed to tap moral outlooks (Graham et al., 2011) is framed in terms of observer- imposed (etic) considerations that fail to capture the ways that moral concerns are assessed in different cultural contexts. Thus, for example, as discussed earlier, whereas research on caring has highlighted its relationship- dependent bases that distinguish it from justice concerns, the MFQ assesses caring as a component of harm and assesses it by means of a single decontextualized scale item (i.e., “compassion for those who are suffering is the most crucial virtue”; Graham et al., 2011, p. 385). Likewise, in another example, fairness is portrayed on the MFQ in global ways (e.g., by items such as “Justice is the most important requirement for a society”) that provide little insight into ways that norms of justice are applied in different cultural communities and in everyday settings. Notably, whereas research on 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  309 
the MFQ discriminates outlooks based on political affiliation and gender, it has uncovered few cultural differences and thus provides little insight into cultural variation. Also, in contrast to the developmental and cultural models of morality discussed earlier in this chapter, work on the MFQ does not distinguish on formal grounds between matters of morality, convention, and personal choice, but instead treats as “moral” any social standard. In contrast to these earlier models of morality, it then provides no criteria for identifying moral abuse or for avoiding a stance of extreme moral relativism. 
Future Directions In the following section, we consider future directions for theory and research on culture and moral development. Future directions that we address include going beyond taxonomic models of moral content, considering intergroup relations and prejudice, investigating within- culture power dynamics, and exploring moral socialization processes. 
Beyond Taxonomic Models of Moral Content As summarized in the previous section, the range of moral content studied by psychologists has expanded greatly over the past 10– 15 years. Such approaches have been largely inspired by Shweder’s Big Three ethics (Shweder et al., 1997) and have included Graham and Haidt’s Moral Foundations theory (Graham et  al., 2011)  and Jensen’s Cultural- Developmental approach (2008). Although these approaches have contributed greatly to broadening the moral domain in psychology and to creating theoretical frameworks capable of accommodating cultural diversity in moral beliefs, several limitations exist with regard to taxonomic approaches to classifying diverse moral content as they are embodied in scale measures. 
One limitation is the inability of the scale measures relied on in taxonomic approaches to adequately accommodate and address culturally specific concepts. For example, moral reasoning among Indian populations has uncovered individuals’ use of a rich vocabulary of culturally grounded moral terms and concepts with great local sig-nificance. Concepts such as paap, which convey sin or divine punishment, are central to moral reasoning (Kapadia & Bhangaokar, 2015) and are thus necessary for constructing an account of morality within Indian culture. However, such culturally specific concepts are not represented explicitly in the scale measures adopted by taxonomic theories and are glossed over in coding undertaken at the level of the major taxonomic categories, such as autonomy, divinity, and so forth. 
Another limitation is in the lack of attention in taxonomic approaches to contextual variation in the reliance placed on different moral principles. For example, the work cited earlier comparing perceived moral obligations to help others in the US and India revealed cultural differences in the breadth of situations in which the moral obligation to help existed (Miller, Bersoff, & Harwood, 1990). Such meaningful contextual sensitivity 
 
 
 
310 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
is lost, however, when the focus is shifted to the magnitude or emphasis placed on different moral foundations rather than on the scope or contingency of moral judgments. This is most evident in recent attempts to tap ethics across cultures using validated scale measures. For example, using the Community, Autonomy, and Divinity Scale (CADS) (Guerra & Giner- Sorella, 2010), Guerra and Giner- Sorella (2015) observed that Japanese scored lower on divinity relative to individuals from New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Brazil, and Israel. However, the authors noted that this finding may have occurred due to the scale items on the CADS failing to tap aspects of divinity related to the natural world associated with Shintoism. 
Taxonomic approaches are also limited in de- emphasizing the manner in which distinct ethics or moral foundations interrelate to one another and how these patterns of interrelationships vary across cultures. For example, among Hmong families living in Thailand, responses to a moral vignette included an emphasis on role- related community ethics that were framed in terms of divine law (Hickman & Fasoli, 2015). A coding scheme focused on discrete moral foundations, however, does not capture respects in which the outlook observed among the Hmong involve mutually constitutive and not discrete moral concepts. 
Intergroup Relations and Prejudice Understanding the relationship between moral reasoning and intergroup prejudice presents another promising new area of future inquiry (e.g., Killen & Cooley, 2014). Moral reasoning in an intergroup context presents an added complexity in that individuals must balance justice concerns with social group considerations, such as the individual’s social identity. In the case of resource distribution, for instance, children have shown a tendency to favor family and friends when allocating resources (e.g., Renno & Shutts, 2015). However, with age, children have also been found to become more aware of the status of disadvantaged social groups and to be concerned with rectifying inequalities. This has been observed not just in distribution of desirable objects, such as modeling clay (Li, Spitzer, & Olsen, 2014), but also in distribution of valuable resources, such as medical supplies (Elenbaas & Killen, 2016). These findings suggest that, with an increasing understanding of status differences, children are able to adjust their judgments about distributions accordingly and bring to bear justice concerns in an intergroup context. 
Beyond resource allocation, research on intergroup prejudice has also given attention to exclusion based on group membership. This research demonstrates a complexity in terms of the challenge involved in balancing moral concerns with social identity. One example of this complexity concerns how moral judgments of out- group exclusion depend on a variety of factors, including the social status of the person making the judgment (Crystal, Killen, & Ruck, 2008) and the context of the exclusion, such as whether exclusion based on race or gender discrimination prevents a student from participating in school or in a friendship group (Killen, Lee- Kim, McGlothin, & Stangor, 2002). 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  311 
Continued exploration of moral perspectives on how individuals come to interact with others of different cultural backgrounds presents a promising area of future research for several reasons. It allows a test of moral theories in a complex, multifaceted situation in which moral reasoning may conflict with social identity concerns. An additional reason is for its social relevance, such as its having implications for multicultural classrooms in which experiences of exclusion and discrimination have been associated with negative social and academic outcomes (Huynh & Fuligi, 2010). 
Power Dynamics Future research employing a cultural perspective on moral development should also recognize the variation that exists both between and within cultural communities, with particular attention given to ways in which social status and power dynamics shape the experiences of individuals within cultures. Theorists working in the social domain tradition (e.g., Turiel, 2002, 2005) have brought much- needed attention to this issue. Inspired by contemporary work in anthropology (e.g., Abu Lughod, 1993), such research has centered on the heterogeneity of cultural groups, with a particular focus on marginalized members of communities. Such theories have been critical of various cultural psychological approaches to morality based on what is perceived to be their over- homogenization of cultural groups and lack of attention to social justice concerns in the context of hierarchical societies. Although these concerns are valuable in terms of bringing greater attention to the heterogeneity of culture and to the unequal experiences of members of different status in cultural groups, such concerns have also at times been biased by ethnocentric notions of morality. 
One example of such bias may be seen in the attempt by social domain theorists to criticize on moral grounds hierarchical gender norms based on what is perceived to be their inherent injustice. Such critiques, it may be argued, have a tendency to export Western ideals of feminism, which may not be prioritized or even recognized by local populations (Menon, 2002; Menon & Shweder, 1998). Work by Neff (2001), for instance, has sought to provide empirical support for an asymmetry of rights and duties as existing within married couples in India. In her research, responses to a vignette depicting a marital conflict revealed among Indian populations a greater concern for issues related to autonomy when responding to the husband and interpersonal duties when responding to the wife. Neff interpreted these results as providing support for an imbalance in rights and duties as existing within Indian families, which she interpreted as signifying injustice in relationships structured by hierarchical gender norms. However, research by Goyal, Wice, Adams, Chauhan, and Miller (2015) has challenged these claims. Through an analysis of conflicts between married couples in both the United States and India, Goyal and her colleagues demonstrated that concerns with role- related duties expressed by Indian participants did not differ when evaluating the husband and wife. Furthermore, role- related duties were perceived to be greater overall among Indians compared to Americans, for whom there was a greater concern with equality in roles. Such findings challenge the 
 
312 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
notion of an imbalance of duties proposed by social domain theorists and suggest instead the existence of reciprocal role- related duties across genders. 
The preceding research notably does not call into question the existence of dissatisfaction and oppression within hierarchical systems. The research does, however, suggest that hierarchical gender norms do not inherently and invariably involve universal justice breaches. The findings highlight the need to approach non- Western gender norms with a greater sensitivity to local cultural meanings. Future research on power dynamics should continue to strive to understand the moral outlooks of all individuals within a population, with greater attention given to those in lower status positions. However, in considering this topic, great caution should also be taken to avoid exporting unwarranted ethnocentric claims that are out of step with the values of local populations. 
Moral Socialization Processes Cultural research can also provide a greater understanding of how children come to acquire moral reasoning skills through socialization. Understanding moral socialization processes from a cultural perspective is important not just because such processes may align with culturally variable goals, also but because common goals may be reached through culturally variable approaches. 
Parenting practices differ across cultures in terms of the socialization goals and values guiding them. Research conducted among Taiwanese parent– child dyads, for instance, has revealed an emphasis on eliciting shame in the child in order to socialize proper behavior (Fung, 1999). Events in which the parent attempts to shame the child occur frequently and are seen as an essential component of moral socialization, which is viewed by parents as facilitating correction of problematic behavior. However, such shaming practices are associated with parental warmth among Chinese children, but not among Americans, for whom shame is associated with negative outcomes, such as aggression (e.g., Tangney, 1992). 
Parents may also employ culturally distinct strategies to reach common socialization goals. For example, contrasting parenting strategies have been associated with increased helping behavior among Indian in contrast to German toddlers (Torrens & Kartner, 2017). Specifically, corporal punishment was found to be positively associated with helping among Indian toddlers, but negatively associated with helping among German toddlers. Such findings demonstrate how distinct, culturally normative parenting strategies can promote similar outcomes in moral behavior (see also Chapter 8 by Heidi Keller for a related discussion on development and attachment). 
Conclusion As is the case with cultural work in other areas of psychology, cultural research on moral development remains in a peripheral position in the field, with mainstream investigators tending to downplay its importance. Still, there has been substantial movement toward 
 
 
CulTure and Moral develoPMenT  |  313 
embracing more pluralistic and culturally diverse conceptions of the moral and toward recognizing cultural diversity in moral development. Research is uncovering qualitative cultural variation in moral outlooks that speaks to common concerns with justice, community, and spiritual issues. Investigators are also working to formulate approaches to culture and moral development that take into account intergroup dynamics and other socially relevant topics and that examine power dynamics and processes of enculturation. Far from leading either to an extreme relativism or to a view of individuals as merely passively conforming to existing understandings, research on culture and moral development is pointing the way for understanding moral outlooks as creative agentic commitments that reflect culturally influenced processes of meaning- making.
