11 
Culture and Cognition 
Qi Wang and Sawa Senzaki 
At a kindergarten in Beijing, a researcher is playing a game of storytelling with a child, “Winter is coming. Wild geese are leaving for the South. Before they leave, the goose leader tells everybody that the journey will be full of dangers. So everyone should fly closely together. A little goose says to herself, ‘Flying together will be very slow. I’d like to fly all by myself.’ So she leaves the group, starting alone for the South. Tell me what happens next.” 
c: Then she flew and flew by herself and met with an eagle. She was very scared. So she quickly . . . When she met the eagle, she began to regret, because she was not obedient to the adults and she flew alone. Now she met an eagle and thought she would surely be eaten by the eagle. Then she flew and flew quickly and then met the big goose leading the group. She said “Sorry” to the group leader. The big goose forgave her and let her follow the group and fly together. Then the big goose drove away the eagle and they flew to the south together. 
In a kindergarten in a suburb of Boston, a child was telling her version of the story about the same little goose: 
c: She said to the other birds “I’ll try my best to go alone. You should too. We shouldn’t be together. We should be alone.” And she flew off through the air. It was so nice in the breeze, she went . . . [unintelligible]. Then a big eagle came. It was very hungry. It hadn’t eaten any food for 2,000 years. But now the bird flew and flew and got away. And she built a little nest and her little eggs hatched and the little ducks went “honky! honky!” And the mother bird made a little rocker for the nest. And they went to sleep and all their nice little dreams came true. The end. 
 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  319 
In response to the same situation, in which a little goose tried to break away from her group and embark on an adventure on her own, our two storytellers indeed anticipated similar dangerous encounters for the protagonist. Yet they cast different spins on the plot and supplemented vastly different outcomes. In the Chinese version, the little goose went back to her group for help and regretted leaving the group; in the end the group reunited. In the American version, the little goose was able to skip the danger herself and happily built a colony of her own (Wang & Leichtman, 2000). 
Traditionally, cognitive processes have been assumed to be the products of innate neural structures that are universal across cultures (e.g., Tooby & Cosmides, 1992; Fodor, 1983; Pylyshyn, 1999). This trend has been carried forward; for instance, in The Oxford Handbook of Attention (Nobre & Kastner, 2014), although several theoretical models of attention have been thoroughly discussed, not a single chapter is included to discuss cultural differences in attention. Similarly, dominant theories of cognitive development have been mainly based on findings of children from Western family practices and traditions and have paid less attention to the sociocultural contexts where children learn how to think (Gauvain, 2001; Rogoff, 2003; Wang, 2018). 
Bruner (1990) proclaimed that, “the central concept of a human psychology is meaning and the processes and transactions involved in the construction of meanings” (p.  33). Decades of research in cultural psychology has demonstrated that cognitive processes entail active actions of meaning- making in which individuals organize and interpret the world based on their assumptions, beliefs, and goals that are deeply conditioned by the wealth of customs, institutions, and traditions of their culture (Nisbett, 2003; Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Shweder, 1991; Wang, 2013a). Thus, culture, as a system of values and practices, provides an overarching framework to guide individuals when they attend to, perceive, evaluate, explain, describe, and remember events and objects related to themselves and the larger environment. 
Understanding how culture shapes our cognition is critical because one of the striking differences between humans and nonhuman primates is the extent to which human cognition relies on cultural practices (e.g., Richerson & Boyd, 2006; Tomasello, 1999). In this chapter, we discuss the various ways that culture shapes cognition— the processes and products of the human mind. Our coverage ranges from what is traditionally considered to be less purely cerebral components, such as attention and perception, to higher mental processes, such as reasoning and autobiographical memory. These cognitive components may be directed at nonhuman objects or at the world of humans— namely, social cognition. Across our discussion, we highlight socialization practices that mediate cultural influences on the developing mind. 
Attention and Perception We are surrounded by abundant amounts of information. Within a matter of milliseconds, our sensory system registers hundreds of sensations. In order to perceive our surroundings, 
 
 
320 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
however, we can only process a certain amount of information, and the vast majority of other information is filtered out of our attention. It has been proposed that there are two general mechanisms of attention: exogenous (or bottom- up) versus endogenous (or top- down) attention (Chun & Wolfe, 2001; Posner, 1980). While people are likely to attend to visually salient information, such as colorful objects or moving objects (i.e., bottom- up, stimulus- oriented attention), people also perceive their surroundings based on what makes sense to them. Cultural psychologists and anthropologists have long identified the critical role of culture in the latter, top- down attention as people subscribe to culture to derive meaning in their environment (Bruner, 1957). While much of this process occurs without specific intention or awareness, a large body of empirical findings suggests that habituated practices grounded in the cultural meaning system shape our attention. 
A pioneering study demonstrating the role of culture in attention and perception comes from Abel and Hsu’s (1949) comparison between Chinese Americans and European Americans on their performance of the Rorschach test. Notably, Chinese Americans tended to refer to the whole pattern of the Rorschach inkblot, whereas European Americans tended to focus on a specific part within the same inkblot. Earlier researchers have also studied cultural differences in perception as a function of ecological settings and social orientation (Berry, 1966; Witkin & Berry, 1975). For example, Berry and Witkin tested people’s ability to focus on the focal object by decontextualizing it from the field among Canadian Eskimos and Temme people in West Africa. The results demonstrated that Canadian Eskimos were able to decontextualize the focal object from the field, and this was termed the field- independent perceptual style. In contrast, people in Temne communities in West Africa tended to see the focal object as part of the field, thus showing a perceptual style often classified as the field- dependent style. Witkin and Berry concluded that Temme people habitually engage in the field- dependent perceptual style because their ecological setting is based on farming and agriculture, and their social structure emphasizes conformation to the group. Contrarily, Canadian Eskimos live in mobile hunting ecological settings, and their social structure is more oriented toward individual autonomy, which is likely to be associated with the field- independent perceptual style. In addition to these earlier studies, an accumulating number of studies in the past few decades have suggested that ecological, social, and cultural settings shape visual attention and perception (e.g., Nisbett & Masuda, 2003; Nisbett & Miyamoto, 2005). 
Analytic Versus Holistic Cognition According to Nisbett and his colleagues, culturally unique cognitive habits, particularly those found in Western and Eastern cultures, can be classified as analytic versus holistic cognitive styles (Nisbett, 2003; Nisbett, Peng, Choi, & Norenzayan, 2001). An analytic style of cognition has been found predominantly among members of Western societies (mainly the United States, Canada, and Western European societies), and this cognitive style is characterized as focusing on the central object by decontextualizing it from the context. Conversely, a holistic style of thought has been found commonly in East Asian 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  321 
societies (mainly China, Japan, and Korea), in which people are inclined to attend to both focal and contextual information as well as to the relations between the two. 
Nisbett and his colleagues suggest that such culturally unique cognitive styles have been maintained due to particular ecological, philosophical, and social contexts that can be traced back to Ancient Greek and Chinese civilizations (Nisbett, 2003; Nisbett et al., 2001). The Ancient Greek civilization centered around fishing, herding, and small- scale agriculture due to its ecological affordance. As individuals were not required to engage in complicated social relationships in such ecological settings, Greeks had the freedom to maintain personal agency and individualistic mindsets. Another remarkable characteristic of Greek civilization is its philosophical and moral traditions, which claimed that the world is composed of substances that can be detached from the context and separated into individual objects, each of which possesses unique characteristics and properties. Nisbett and his colleagues suggest that such historical contexts fostered mental habits for decontextualizing and analyzing individual components in the field, thus encouraging selective attention focusing on individual objects (Nisbett et al., 2001). 
In sharp contrast, the ancient Chinese civilization centered around large- scale agriculture, which required coordination among groups of people and resulted in a network of complicated social relationships. Nisbett and his colleagues suggest that such environments required close attention to the social environment, leading to attention generally focusing on the field in addition to the central objects (Nisbett et al., 2001). In line with such ecological constraints, traditional religious and philosophical beliefs in East Asian societies, such as Taoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism, promote a more relation- oriented, context- oriented nature, which led historically to the development of holistic thought. In this view, the nature of the world is interpreted as impermanent and interconnected. Holistic thought emphasizes that, in order to understand the focal object (or people), it is critical to understand the context. Because objects and contexts are often perceived as a whole unit in Eastern societies, the idea that attending to contextual and background information in addition to the focal objects is emphasized as necessary in understanding the nature of the world. 
Empirical Supports to Analytic Versus Holistic Attention There has been accumulating evidence showing systematic cross- cultural differences in attention and perception using a wide variety of tasks. For example, in order to examine cultural variations in patterns of attention, Masuda and Nisbett (2001) asked university students in the United States and Japan to observe short videos depicting underwater images (i.e., the Michigan Fish task). Masuda and Nisbett found that when describing underwater scenes, American students tended to focus on the focal objects such as the large fish, whereas Japanese students were more likely to attend to both focal objects and background. For example, an American student would say “Three large fish, one with an orange belly and two with spiky fins, were swimming from left to right,” whereas a Japanese student would describe the same scene as “The water was green so I  think it 
 
322 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
was in the bottom of the river. Fish went behind the seaweed.” When these participants were later asked to complete a recognition task, Japanese participants’ memory was more influenced by the background. That is, when the original fish were presented with the original background, both American and Japanese participants could recognize them well, but when the original fish were presented with a novel background image, Japanese participants performed poorly, suggesting that Japanese participants used background and contextual information to understand the focal objects. These results indicate that Americans are likely to focus on the focal objects and decontextualize them from the scene due to an analytic cognitive style while Japanese are more likely to attend to both focal objects and the background due to their holistic cognitive style. 
Other studies have investigated how people recognize and attend to others’ emotions in social situations. Masuda and his colleagues (Masuda et al., 2008; Masuda, Wang, Ishii, & Ito, 2012) presented participants with a lineup of five faces and asked participants to rate the intensity of the emotion presented by the figure placed in the middle. The stimuli included a congruent condition in which the central and background figures showed the same emotions, and an incongruent condition in which the central and background figures demonstrated different emotions. While the rating was similar across cultures in the congruent condition, Japanese participants were significantly more likely to be influenced by the background figures than were Americans in the incongruent condition. For example, when the central figure showed a happy expression and the background figures presented an angry emotion, Japanese participants’ rating of happiness was lower than that of Americans (see Chapter 12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang for more discussion about emotion). 
Cultural differences in attentional patterns have also been found using a variety of nonsocial tasks, such as the Change Blindness task (Masuda & Nisbett, 2006), Rod- and- Frame task (Ji, Peng, & Nisbett, 2000), and the Framed Line Test (FLT; Kitayama, Duffy, Kawamura, & Larsen, 2003). In the Change Blindness task, participants were asked to find the differences between two images. While American participants found more differences in the foreground main objects than did Japanese, Japanese participants found more differences in the background items than Americans. With the Rod- and- Frame task, participants were presented with a line in a frame that rotated, and the task was to identify when the line was vertical. American participants were better at identifying the angle of the inside line than Asians because they were less influenced by the orientation of the frame (Ji et al., 2000). In the FLT (Kitayama et al., 2003), participants were presented with a square and a target line inside, and then they were shown a differently sized frame and asked to reproduce a line that was identical to one in the first image in either absolute length (absolute task) or proportional length (relative task). While American participants outperformed Japanese participants in the absolute task, Japanese participants did better than American participants on the relative task. 
Cultural products, such as artworks, are another means to reveal how different perceptual styles manifest in society. For instance, drawing a landscape requires techniques 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  323 
to reduce three- dimensional information onto a two- dimensional field. Examining landscape paintings from the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries in Western and East Asian societies, Masuda and his colleagues (Masuda et al., 2008)  identified that the Western artists often employed a linear perspective, which restricts the viewer’s perspective to a single standpoint in order to produce the sense of depth. This type of visual layout reflects an analytic cognitive style, as only a few foreground objects take up space within the imagery, and the background information is not clearly depicted. One characteristic of this style is that the location of the horizon tends to be low, in order to represent the sense of depth. In contrast, East Asian artists have traditionally employed a different technique, such as the bird’s eye view, which depicts the image from multiple viewpoints. While this style allows a rendering to include a large number of objects within the image, there is a tradeoff in that the sense of depth is typically lost. In order to include a larger number of items, the location of the horizon tends to be relatively high in Eastern artwork. This style reflects holistic thought, as the background is emphasized as much as the foreground. Masuda and colleagues (2008) have also found that college students, as contemporary members of given cultures, also demonstrated similar patterns in their landscape drawings, demonstrating that culturally unique perceptual styles are transmitted over generations. 
Research has further shown cross- cultural differences in visual attention using physiological measures. For example, Chua, Boland, and Nisbett (2005) used an eye- tracker to examine patterns of eye movements during scene perception. While participants observed a variety of images including a central, foreground object (e.g., a tiger, airplane) as well as the background, American participants were quicker to attend to the foreground objects and looked at the foreground objects longer than did Chinese participants. Another study, using a modified version of Masuda and Nisbett’s (2001) Michigan Fish task, found that Canadian students looked at the foreground objects (e.g., large fish) longer than did the Japanese students, whereas Japanese students looked at the background area longer than their Canadian counterparts (Senzaki, Masuda, & Ishii, 2014). Importantly, such cultural differences were prominent when participants described their observations afterward instead of just passively following the movements of the fish. This result supports the theoretical assumption that meaning is central in understanding the critical role of culture in shaping attention and perception (Shweder, 1991) even though people often engage in culturally constituted cognition as a habit without a conscious effort. 
Furthermore, researchers have begun to examine neural mechanisms underlying cross- cultural differences in attention and perception. For example, in a study using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), European American and Asian American young adults were compared using the modified version of the FLT (Kitayama et  al., 2003). Researchers found that participants recruited brain regions associated with attentional control, such as the left inferior parietal lobule and the right precentral gyrus, when they engaged in culturally unfamiliar tasks; that is, when Americans needed to attend to the context and when Japanese needed to selectively attend to the target (Hedden, 
324 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Ketay, Aron, Markus, & Gabrieli, 2008). This result suggests that when people engage in a cognitive style that is outside of their tendency, in the case of a culturally unfamiliar FLT task, the area of the brain that is associated with attention requires a larger cognitive load. 
Other studies have employed event- related potential (ERP) methods to study how culture shapes early attentional processes. For example, European American and Asian American’s performance was compared on the Odd- Ball task, which required participants to respond to the target stimuli and not respond to nontarget stimuli while the sequence was infrequently interrupted by task- irrelevant deviant stimuli (i.e., background). In this study, European Americans displayed greater P3 amplitudes than Asian Americans when processing the target stimuli, while Asian Americans displayed greater P3 amplitudes than European Americans when processing task- irrelevant deviant stimuli (Lewis, Goto, & Kong, 2008). The P3 waves are thought to reflect information processing, and the results of this study suggest that European Americans were focusing on processing the information relevant to the central target object while Asian Americans were also processing contextual, irrelevant novelty stimuli. Other studies have examined the effect of semantic congruency by focusing on the N400, which is the negative poststimulus onset usually observed between 250 and 500 ms. The N400 components are usually observed when participants detect incongruent meanings (e.g., “I drink coffee and dogs”). Studies have shown that Asian participants tend to demonstrate a larger N400 amplitude in responding to incongruent images (e.g., a crab against a parking lot, a smiling person surrounded by frowning faces) than congruent images (e.g., a crab against the beach, a smiling person surrounded by smiling people), while this effect is absent in European American and Canadian participants (Goto, Ando, Huang, Yee, & Lewis, 2010; Goto, Yee, Lowenberg, & Lewis, 2013; Russell, Masuda, Hioki, & Singhal, 2015). Another ERP study found that both European Canadians and Japanese demonstrated episodic incongruent effects on the N400, but the amplitude of the N400 was associated with behavioral accuracy only among Japanese participants (Masuda, Russell, Chen, Hioki, & Caplan, 2014). Taken together, these studies provide compelling documentation of differentiated neural responses to attention across cultures (see also Chapter 21 by Joan Y. Chiao and Katherine D. Blizinsky concerning culture and neuroscience). 
The Development of Analytic Versus Holistic Attention An overwhelming body of empirical studies supports the theoretical assumption of analytic versus holistic cognition. As discussed earlier, Nisbett and colleagues have hypothesized that cross- cultural differences in cognition are rooted in different historical, ecological, and social orientations traditionally emphasized in Western and Eastern cultures (e.g., Nisbett et  al., 2001). According to Nisbett (2003), members of a given culture gradually learn cultural ideas and values through socialization, and a culturally unique cognitive practice becomes habituated over time. More recently, there has been a growing interest in examining the developmental trajectories of culturally divergent attention and perception. 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  325 
One of the first studies to compare the development of analytic versus holistic styles of attention and perception was conducted with American and Japanese 4- to 13- year- old children. Using the modified version of the FLT, Duffy and his colleagues identified cross- cultural differences emerging at around age 6 (Duffy, Toriyama, Itakura, & Kitayama, 2009). Similarly, cross- cultural differences in cultural products were found in second- graders’ artworks (at around ages 6– 7) in Canada and Japan (Senzaki, Masuda, Nand, & Ishii, 2014). In this study, researchers asked children in first through sixth grades to draw a landscape image, a similar paradigm used by Masuda and his colleagues with college students (Masuda et al., 2008). They found that when children did not understand the meaning of horizon, there were no significant differences in the location of horizon across cultures. However, when children started to demonstrate an understanding of a horizon, in about second grade, Japanese children drew their horizon significantly higher on the page and included a larger number of objects than did Canadian children. This study provides further empirical support that the influence of cultural meaning on attention and perception takes place early in development. 
Another study (Imada, Carlson, & Itakura, 2013)  suggests that the development of culturally unique patterns of attention and perception is a gradual process from early to middle childhood. In a scene description task similar to Masuda and Nisbett’s (2001) Michigan Fish task, a tendency of cross- cultural variation in visual attention and perception emerged around age 4– 5, whereby Japanese children described more background information than did American children, and the difference reached the levels of adults at around ages 8– 9. Imada and her colleagues (Imada et  al., 2013) have also used the Ebbinghaus illusion task (Doherty, Tsuji, & Phillips, 2008; Káldy & Kovács, 2003), which is a commonly used optical illusion of the size of the target circle when surrounded by either larger or smaller circles. Japanese children were more susceptive to the Ebbinghaus illusion than were American children, and such a cultural difference in attention was amplified as the children’s ages increased. 
Research using nonverbal tasks has provided evidence for an earlier onset of cross- cultural differences in attention. For example, Kuwabara, Son, and Smith (2011) found that 4- to 5- year- old Japanese children were more sensitive to contextual information than American children of the same age group when they judged appropriate facial expressions (e.g., smile vs. frown) in various contexts (e.g., party vs. a scary animal). Similarly, Kuwabara and Smith (2012) examined children’s performance using a relational matching task and a visual search task. They found that 4- year- old American children’s visual attention was more object- oriented, whereas 4- year- old Japanese children’s visual attention was more relation- oriented. Specifically, when the relational matching task was conducted using highly contextual and information- rich stimuli, Japanese children outperformed American children, which suggests that the object- oriented perceptual style limited American children’s performance. In contrast, when the visual search task was conducted using cluttered but organized scenes, American children performed better than did Japanese children, which suggests that the object- oriented perceptual 
326 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
style allowed American children to effectively orient their attention toward the target object. In a more recent study, Kuwabara and Smith (2016) demonstrated significant cross- cultural differences in perception at 3 years of age. Using three tasks to examine how children recognize familiar objects, the researchers found that 3- year- old Japanese children were more likely to use a holistic, configured processing style while American children were more likely to use an analytical, feature- oriented processing style. For example, when a common object was masked and only a few features (e.g., the wings and windows of an airplane) were shown, American children were better at recognizing them than were Japanese children. Also, given their holistic perception, Japanese children performed worse than American children when playing a matching game in which one object in the pair was presented upside down. 
Using an eye- tracker, Waxman and colleagues (2016) examined attentional patterns in 24- month- old American and Chinese infants. They first presented a familiarization phase in which infants were familiarized to a scene, such as a girl petting a dog. In the test phase, then, infants were shown either a new action- familiar object scene (e.g., the same girl kissing the same dog) or a new object- familiar action scene (e.g., the same girl petting a pillow). While infants in both cultures showed predominantly similar attentional patterns, there was a brief period of divergent attentional patterns across cultures at an early phase of stimuli presentation. Particularly, American infants showed more preference toward the new object- familiar action over the new action- familiar object, whereas the Chinese infants showed the opposite pattern. Although the cross- cultural difference was minimal, as it only occurred for less than 1 second, this study provides the insight that children may start to show culturally specific patterns of attention at a very early age. 
These findings add to the current literature in analytic versus holistic attention across cultures by demonstrating the developmental trajectories of acquiring culturally unique cognitive styles. In addition to examining the developmental trajectories, it is also necessary to investigate the socialization practices where culturally unique perspectives are transmitted across generations in order to understand how attention and perception are shaped by cultural contexts. Developmental psychologists, particularly those basing research on Vygotsky’s sociocultural perspective (e.g., Vygotsky, 1930/ 1978; see also Cole, 1996; Gauvain, 2001; Rogoff, 2003), have identified that early parent– child interaction plays a critical role in children’s learning what and how to pay attention in their daily environment (see also Chapter 7 by Harry W. Gardiner and Chapter 8 by Heidi Keller, concerning culture and development, respectively). 
Attention and Perception: Family Socialization Several studies have examined cross- cultural variation in attending to multiple events among European American and Mexican- heritage families (Chavajay & Rogoff, 1999; Correa- Chávez, Rogoff, & Arauz, 2005; Rogoff, Mistry, Göncü, & Mosier, 1993). These studies have found that both mothers and children from indigenous communities of Mexico tend to demonstrate simultaneous awareness, which is evident in more frequent 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  327 
alternations of attention among multiple events at the same time, compared with European American mothers and their children. Rogoff (2003) suggests that simultaneous awareness is a reflection of Mexican ecological settings and cultural socialization of learning styles. Mayan Mexican households tend to have more siblings than European American families. In Mayan cultures, observational learning is expected for children, and this learning style requires the learner to divide attention among multiple events occurring simultaneously. This is in contrast to the dominant learning style in European American cultures, in which the learner is expected to focus his or her attention on the directed goals. This hypothesis is supported by a study that showed a reduction of simultaneous awareness among Mayan children whose mothers had received schooling experience, particularly Western- style schooling (Chavajay & Rogoff, 2002). 
Even when comparing cultural populations with similar economic and educational backgrounds, different socialization patterns have been found pertaining to attention. In an early study, Fernald and Morikawa (1993) observed American and Japanese mothers and their 6- to 19- month- old infants play with toys at home. While both American and Japanese mothers showed similar characteristics such as simplification of language and frequent repartition in their speech to infants, their focus of attention differed markedly. Compared with Japanese mothers, American mothers more frequently and more consistently labeled objects (e.g., “Here is the car!”) and were overall more likely to talk about the objects to their infants. In comparison, Japanese mothers were more likely to emphasize interpersonal relationships and social routines (e.g., “Mr. Doggy said hello to you!”). A more recent study (Senzaki & Shimizu, 2016a) demonstrated similar findings in a laboratory setting with American and Japanese mothers and their 6- to 18- month- old infants. In this study, mothers were asked to read a children’s picture book to their infants that included focal characters (i.e., ladybugs) and background characters (e.g., frog, bird) but did not include any storylines. American mothers predominantly verbalized a focus on the focal characters in the book, as approximately 75% of their discussion centered around the focal characters. On the other hand, Japanese mothers discussed the background (45%) as well as the focal characters (55%). Japanese mothers also discussed more social interactions between the focal and background characters (e.g., “The frog says let’s play together to the ladybugs!”) than did American mothers. Interestingly, the cultural difference was robust regardless of the infants’ age, suggesting that children encounter culturally scripted patterns of attention at as young as 6 months. 
To further investigate the process in which children acquire analytic versus holistic styles of attention across cultures, Senzaki and her colleagues (Senzaki, Masuda, Takada, & Okada, 2016) compared how Canadian and Japanese 4- to 9- year- old children completed the Michigan Fish task either by themselves or with their parents. They found that children did not demonstrate significant cross- cultural differences when they engaged in the task by themselves. However, culturally different patterns were observed when children engaged in the task with their parents, particularly among older children. Regardless of the children’s age, American parents verbalized more about the focal fish and Japanese 
328 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
parents verbalized more about what was going on in the background. Interestingly, only the older children (7– 9 years), but not the younger children (4– 6 years of age), showed cultural differences mirroring those in their parents. This suggests that older children have learned their parents’ perceptual styles in attending to their environments. Together, studies of early parent– child interactions provide a theoretical and empirical demonstration of how culture provides foundations for the shared meanings and worldviews that have been historically transmitted through socialization practices over generations and the close- knit relationship between culture and perceptual- cognitive functions. 
In sum, the large body of research examining analytic versus holistic attention has revealed cultural differences between Eastern and Western, particularly Japanese and North American samples. Several recent studies have further extended their investigations into other cultural groups, as well as within groups. For example, studies have found that individuals from Central and East European cultures (e.g., Croatia, Czech Republic, Romania, Russia) tend to be more holistic than those from Western European countries (e.g., France, Germany, Greece; Grossman & Varnum, 2011; Kühnen, Hannover, & Roeder, 2001; Varnum, Grossmann, Katunar, Nisbett, & Kitayama, 2008). Furthermore, considerable within- culture differences have been observed in Turkey between adults from farming and fishing communities (holistic) and those from the herding community (analytic; Uskul, Kitayama, & Nisbett, 2008). Similarly, Northern Italians, who tended to have more independent self- views, were also more analytic than Southern Italians, who tended to have more interdependent self- views (Knight & Nisbett, 2007). Both in the United States and Russia, working- class adults tended to show more holistic patterns of attention than do middle- class adults (Grossman & Varnum, 2011). Importantly, cultural influences through analytic versus holistic thinking styles extend well beyond attention and perception to higher level cognitive processes like attribution and reasoning. 
Attribution and Reasoning Culturally grounded cognitive processes are also at work during social interactions. Social interactions involve inferring and reasoning about others’ behaviors and making judgments. Traditionally, social psychologists have argued that there is a strong tendency for people to overestimate others’ internal attitudes and dispositions while underestimating situational factors when explaining their behaviors, which is known as correspondence bias. In the classic social psychology research conducted by Jones and Harris (1967), participants were asked to read an essay about Fidel Castro that was either pro- or anti- Castro. Before reading the essay, however, it was explicitly explained to participants that the writer of the essay was instructed to write either a pro- or anti- Castro essay for a debate and that it was not their choice which one they would write. When asked to identify the essay writer’s attitudes toward Castro, participants still tended to assume the writer’s attitudes corresponded to those expressed in the essay. Originally, the 
 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  329 
studies were predominantly conducted with North American participants, and this bias was assumed to be “fundamental” and deeply ingrained in people, thus a fundamental attribution error. However, cross- cultural comparisons, stemming from analytic versus ho-listic cognition, have demonstrated that this tendency to explain other people’s behaviors primarily based on their internal dispositions while ignoring situational influences may not be universal (for review, see Choi, Nisbett, & Norenzayan, 1999). 
Anthropologists have long documented cultural differences in the ways people understand others’ behaviors. For example, people in non- Western cultures tend to explain others’ behaviors by emphasizing the situation, temporal occasion, and social context (Geertz, 1975; Hsu, 1981; Levy, 1973; Mauss, 1938/ 1985; Selby, 1974, 1975; Strauss, 1973). Research from cultural psychology also supports this notion that the ways in which people understand and explain others’ behaviors are shaped by culture. For example, Morris and Peng (1994) found that when participants were asked to explain a social situation (e.g., a group of fish swimming), American participants were more likely to believe that the individual fish’s movement was influenced by internal factors such as the desire to lead the group or to break away from the group, whereas Chinese participants were more likely to believe that the same fish’s movement was influenced by other fish, such as being abandoned by the group. 
Using the original essay paradigm, Miyamoto and Kitayama (2002) found that Asians were more likely than Americans to spontaneously generate situational causal inferences. In this study, American and Japanese participants were asked to read a student’s essay arguing either pro- or anti- capital punishment. After reading the essay, participants were informed that the essay writer was assigned the side (either pro- or anti- capital punishment) of the essay as part of a political science course assignment, and participants were asked to evaluate the essay writer’s true attitude on this issue. When the essay was long and the argument was highly persuasive, both American and Japanese participants made the fundamental attribution error. However, when the essay was relatively short and less persuasive, only American, and not Japanese, participants made the fundamental attribution error. In another study (Masuda & Kitayama, 2004), researchers manipulated the situational constraint for the target’s action. In the high situational constraint condition, participants were told that they would be listening to a student (i.e., protagonist) reading an essay that is either favoring or opposing nuclear experiments. Participants were then given two envelopes, each of which contained either side of the pro- or anti- controversial essay, and they were asked to choose an envelope to be read by the protagonist. Participants then listened to the protagonist reading the essay and evaluated her attitudes. Even in this high situational constraint condition, American participants still inferred that the protagonist’s attitude corresponded to the essay content, whereas Japanese participants attributed the protagonist’s attitude to situational causes. 
Researchers have identified spontaneous trait inference (STI), an automatic, effort-less, implicit process assuming that someone’s personality accounts for their behavior, as an underlying mechanism for correspondence bias (Uleman, Saribay, & Gonzalez, 
330 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
2008; Winter & Uleman, 1984). While STI can be observed across many cultural groups to a certain extent, there are also significant and systematic cross- cultural differences in the level of STI demonstrated in both behavioral and neurophysiological investigations. For example, cross- cultural similarities and differences in STI were tested with the false recognition paradigm (Shimizu & Uleman, 2017). In the false- recognition paradigm (Todorov & Uleman, 2004), participants are asked to remember pairs of a face and behavior (e.g., “He was calm and phoned for help while the others just screamed”; “He told the cashier that she gave him too much change”). They later engage in the recognition task in which faces are paired with previously presented traits (e.g., calm) and those implied but not presented traits (e.g., honest). Both Americans and Japanese were more likely to make errors when previously studied faces were paired with implied but not explicitly indicated traits than when the faces were paired with unrelated traits. However, Americans did so to a greater extent, and their judgments tended to be more automatic than those of Japanese participants. Similarly, in a neurophysiological study, participants were asked to remember a pair of facial photos and a trait- implied behavior, and then later engage in a lexical decision task (Na & Kitayama, 2011). When participants were primed with a previously studied face, lexical decision for the word that was implied in the originally paired behavior was facilitated and recognized quickly by European American participants, while this effect was not significant for Asian American participants. Also, only European American participants showed an N400 waveform when the incongruent trait was presented with the target face, suggesting that European Americans were more likely to spontaneously infer the personality trait of the target face than were Asian Americans. 
Family Socialization in Attribution and Reasoning While the dispositional bias has been consistently observed among Western populations, a pioneering study by Miller (1984) has demonstrated that there is a gradual developmental process in Western children to focus on dispositional qualities in explaining others’ social behaviors. In this study, 8- , 11- , and 15- year old children and adults in the United States and India were asked to describe a recent event when someone they knew well acted prosocially or antisocially and to explain why the behavior was undertaken. American adults made the most dispositional accounts, followed by 15- year- old American children, especially for antisocial behaviors. Whereas the tendency to make dispositional accounts increased with age among Americans, the tendency to make references for contextual factors increased with age among Hindu Indians. Cultural differences were small at younger ages (8 and 11 years) in ways children inferred others’ behaviors. In another study in which American and Hindu Indian children and adults were asked to describe their peers, Miller (1987) found that American adults and older children (at age 15) were much more likely than Hindu Indians to use general psychological attributions to describe the person (e.g., “He is smart and creative”). Hindu Indians, on the other hand, more frequently described their peers in terms of their social roles (e.g., “She is a 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  331 
teacher”) or possessions or behaviors (e.g., “She has a blue bike”; see also Chapter 10 by Joan G. Miller, Matthew Wice, and Namrata Goyal on culture and moral development). 
In addition, earlier research on parental beliefs about their children’s behaviors has provided some insights into different cultural socialization practices regarding attribution. For example, Kurauchi (1987) surveyed American and Japanese mothers’ attributions about their children’s behaviors at school. American and Japanese mothers were asked to imagine hypothetical scenarios where a child got into trouble at school, and they were asked to rate how the child’s mother would feel in that situation (e.g., a 5- year- old boy forgetting to bring paperwork from home to school, and the teacher scolded him in front of other children). When imagining these situations, American mothers were more likely to be upset with the child’s teacher, whereas Japanese mothers were more likely to feel ashamed of themselves about their children’s problems at school. Stevenson and Lee (1990) also found that American mothers generally attributed their children’s academic performance to ability, while Taiwanese and Japanese mothers tended to focus on their children’s effort. 
More recently, Chiang, Barrett, and Nunez (2000) compared the attributions made by American and Taiwanese mothers regarding the causes of children’s positive (e.g., helping others) and negative (e.g., hurting others, breaking objects) behaviors. The researchers found that American mothers typically attributed their children’s positive behaviors to their children’s internal and stable traits and blamed external situations (e.g., luck, fate, or chance) for their children’s negative behaviors. In sharp contrast, Taiwanese mothers attributed their children’s positive behaviors to situations and negative behaviors to both their children’s traits and situations. There are also cultural differences in the ways that parents describe others’ behaviors to their children. In one study, American and Japanese mothers were asked to watch vignettes of social interactions made by puppets and talk about these vignettes with their 6- to 18- month- old infants (Shimizu, Senzaki, & Uleman, 2018). For example, in one scene, a bear helped an elephant by opening a box that the elephant was trying to open (i.e., prosocial action), and in another scene a pig hindered the elephant by closing the box (i.e., antisocial action). Both American and Japanese mothers made more dispositional comments toward an antisocial character (e.g., such as a mean piggy) than to a prosocial character. However, there was also a significant cross- cultural difference, whereby American mothers overall made more dispositional comments than did Japanese mothers regardless of the nature of the character’s behavior. 
These studies demonstrate that there are important cultural differences in the ways that mothers explain their children’s and others’ behaviors. Children are exposed to culturally unique ways of attribution and reasoning in their daily lives and from an early age, which they may later internalize into their own cognitive repertoires to understand themselves and others. It is important to reiterate that cultural differences in dispositional versus situational attribution are closely tied to analytic versus holistic thought. As summarized in aforementioned studies, members of non- Western cultures, particularly those in East Asian cultures, tend to have a more holistic perception of other 
332 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
people’s behaviors that are situated in context, compared with people of Western cultures who tend to focus on inherent features of the agent. Apart from analytic versus holistic thought, other cultural dimensions, such as naïve dialecticism, can also influence how people understand their physical and social environments. 
Naïve Dialecticism The tendency for East Asians to refer to the situational or contextual information in explaining and predicting others’ behaviors may be related to the theory of naïve dialecticism. According to this perspective, cultural lay theories of a good cognitive model in Eastern cultures include the three principles of naïve dialecticism:  the principle of change, the principle of contradiction, and the principle of holism (Norenzayan, & Choi, & Nisbett, 2002; Peng & Nisbett, 1999; Spencer- Rodgers, Boucher, Mori, Wang, & Peng, 2009; Spencer- Rodgers & Peng, 2004). The principle of change refers to the idea that the world is an unpredictable, dynamic, impermanent, and changeable place that is always in constant flux. The principle of contradiction is the belief that two or more contradicting propositions may both be true simultaneously (e.g., yin- yang). Last, the principle of holism refers to the idea that everything is connected, and the part cannot be understood by itself without considering the whole. 
Given this naïve dialecticism, members of Eastern cultures are more comfortable with psychological contradiction both within themselves and in others than are Westerners (Spencer- Rodgers et al., 2009). This tendency, together with the principle of holism, may explain why East Asians are less likely to expect other people’s behaviors to match their internal attributes or attitudes and are more likely to infer to situational information to understand others’ behaviors. Dialectical thinking style has been observed in a number of studies in East Asian samples. For example, Peng and Nisbett (1999) found that Chinese preferred dialectical proverbs containing seeming contradictions (e.g., “Too humble is half proud”), dialectical resolutions to social conflicts, and dialectical arguments over classical Western logical arguments more than Americans did. Choi and his colleagues (Choi, Dalal, Kim- Prieto, & Park, 2003) also showed that East Asians tended to have a more complex causal theory than did North Americans, considering a greater amount of information in explaining others’ behavior (e.g., causes of a murder). 
Other studies have shown that the way people predict the future also differs across cultures due to dialecticism. To examine nonlinear and dialectical thinking in Eastern cultures, Ji, Nisbett, and Su (2001) asked participants to think about a variety of scenarios (e.g., changes in the stock market, the likelihood of a couple who has been dating for more than 2 years breaking up in the future) and then to predict what would happen. American participants were more likely to predict a linear trend in the future, whereas Chinese participants were more likely to predict the opposite direction of the trend (e.g., a stock that is currently making positive outcomes would fall). Dialectical prediction among East Asians has also been demonstrated in predicting social situations (Norenzayan et  al., 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  333 
2002). Participants were asked to read scenarios of hypothetical characters showing certain dispositions (e.g., Jim is being helpful by lending small amount of change to his neighbors) and were given different situations where the character needed to make a decision (e.g., giving change to a stranger). When participants were asked to make predictions of hypothetical characters, Koreans made greater situational inferences than Americans, especially when situational information was salient. 
More recent research has extended the investigation into neurophysiological measures. For example, one study (F. Wang et al., 2016) using fMRI identified that the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), which plays a key role in monitoring and resolving conflict during information processing, is activated when Chinese participants engage in dialectical thinking, particularly in relation to perception of the self (see Figure 11.1). Furthermore, investigation has confirmed that people prefer others who show cognitive styles that are dominant in their own cultural group. For example, Na and his colleagues (Na, Choi, & Sul, 2013) used an impression- formation paradigm by asking participants
