334 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
to compare two targets each demonstrating holistic and analytical thinking styles. In two studies, participants were presented with responses made by two targets completing the exclusion task (Choi et al., 2003) and the prediction task (Ji et al., 2001). To complete an exclusion task, target participants acted as if they were “detectives” investigating a murder case and excluding irrelevant clues from a list of all possible clues (e.g., the number of pets the victims owned, the victim’s history of sexual abuse by his or her parents). In the prediction task, target participants made predictions of events (e.g., the world burglary rate). Researchers manipulated the responses made by two targets so that one of them demonstrated a dialectical (and holistic) thinking style whereas the other demonstrated an analytical thinking style. Americans prefer a less dialectical and more analytical thinker, while Koreans prefer a more dialectical and more holistic thinker. These findings are important in demonstrating that culturally shared cognitive styles may be sustained by neural mechanisms and further reaffirmed in everyday interpersonal situations. 
Like other perceptual and cognitive processes, cultural differences in dialectical thinking style emerge in childhood. In a study on the development of dialectical thinking, Ji (2008) asked 7- to 11- year- old Chinese and Canadian children to predict future academic performances and relationships (e.g., whether good friends continue to be good friends). Cultural variations start to appear at around 9  years of age and reached the adult level at around age 11, whereby Chinese children were more likely than their Canadian counterparts to predict changes. A study by Senzaki and Shimizu (2016b) further revealed culturally unique socialization practices in relation to dialectical thinking. In this study, American and Japanese mothers completed a modified version of the Dialectical Self Scale (Spencer- Rodgers et al., 2008). Specifically, parents were asked to indicate how much they expected their children to develop dialectical thinking characteristics (e.g., “I want my child to believe there are always two sides to everything, depending on how you look at it”). Japanese mothers preferred to a greater extent for their children to develop dialectical thinking than did American mothers. Furthermore, when parents were asked to describe their infants, American mothers made more dispositional descriptions of their infants than did Japanese mothers, and Japanese mothers included more contextual information to explain their infants than did American mothers. Finally, Japanese mothers reported their infants showing more contradicting dispositions (e.g., easy to be soothed, but also showing great distress when there were limitations) in their daily activities than did American mothers. These studies provide support to the theoretical notion that caregivers habitually engage in culturally unique cognitive and reasoning styles in their daily interactions with their children, and such socialization practices play an important role for children to acquire culturally shared ideas and perspectives. 
We have discussed cultural differences in analytic versus holistic thinking in relation to attention, perception, and reasoning, as well as the influence of naïve dialecticism on how people understand their physical and social environments. Another important cognitive domain that has garnered much research attention among cultural psychologists 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  335 
concerns memory, which is further related to people’s construal of the self, others, and the world. 
Memory Memory, no matter whether it is about personal experiences from the past (i.e., autobiographical memory) or objects and events in the world entails an active act of rationalization, interpretation, and transformation, rather than a faithful photocopy of information or a mere recovery of the information stored in the brain. The process of memory construction is further guided by culturally prioritized beliefs, goals, and motivations that influence how individuals perceive, understand, process, and remember information (Ross & Wang, 2010; Wang, 2013a). As such, “social organization gives a persistent framework into which all detailed recall must fit, and it very powerfully influences both the manner and the matter of recall” (Bartlett, 1932, p. 296). 
To capture the pervasive and overarching influence of culture on the constructive process of remembering, Wang (2016) proposes a cultural dynamic theory in which memory is construed as an open system that emerges, develops, and transforms under the multitude of influences of culture. The theory posits that memory in constructed through the dynamic transaction between an active individual and his or her changing environment that constitutes multiple levels of social, cultural, and historical variables. Individual and group differences in memory emerge as a result of the transaction. Furthermore, memory is situated in culturally conditioned time and space over a multitude of timescales from seconds to a lifetime. Culture thus exerts influences over the course of remembering, affecting every stage from perception and encoding, to consolidation and retention, to retrieval. Finally, memory develops in the process of children acquiring cultural knowledge about the self and the purpose of remembering through their everyday actions and interactions with parents and important others. As a result, cultural differences in memory emerge early in ontogeny. By situating memory in context, the theory highlights the adaptive nature of human memory and cognition in response to, consciously or unconsciously, varied cultural expectations. It further provides an explanatory framework to understand cultural influences on various aspects or components of memory, to which we now turn to discuss. 
Accuracy There is little evidence for cultural differences in basic memory capacity or skills that enable accurate remembering (Chua, Chen, & Park, 2006; Han, Leichtman, & Wang, 1998). Yet, as long as memory is an active construction, it is “exceedingly subject to error” (Bartlett, 1932; p. 176). Bartlett (1932) is arguably the first to demonstrate that memory construction through one’s cultural knowledge or schema can result in systematic memory errors. For example, he presented Cambridge students with a Native American folktale of a young man who jointed a war of ghosts and got killed. The story contains many foreign 
 
 
 
336 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
or supernatural elements that are unfamiliar to his “educated and rather sophisticated” participants of an English background. Bartlett found that in subsequent recalls of the story, the participants either omitted the foreign elements of the story or changed them to forms common to their social group. Thus, the phrase “something black came out of his mouth” was later recalled as “he foamed at the mouth,” and “canoe” was replaced with “boat” and hunting seals replaced with “fishing.” The part about the ghosts, which was the central point of the original story, was completely missed by all participants. Bartlett’s findings were groundbreaking at his time. They reveal that memory involves a constructive process that is deeply conditioned by the meaning system of culture. 
Cognitive styles prominent in a culture can also influence memory accuracy and the type of memory errors people tend to make. As noted in a previous section, analytic and holistic attentional focuses can influence how people attend to and perceive objects and events in the environment and subsequently shape memory for the objects and events relative to their background (Masuda & Nisbett, 2001). Another important dis-tinction associated with analytic versus holistic thinking is categorization, which has been shown to contribute to cultural differences in memory accuracy (Schwartz, Boduroglu, & Gutchess, 2014; Yang, Chen, Ng, & Fu, 2013). Western, analytic thinkers often use taxonomic categorization, grouping things based on attributes (e.g., “cat” and “dog” belong to the same taxonomical category), whereas Eastern, holistic thinkers use more thematic categorization, grouping things based on their relationships with each other (e.g., “dog” and “bone” are functionally related; Chiu, 1972; Ji, Zhang, & Nisbett, 2004). Given that Westerners tend to focus on categories and rules and Easterners tend to focus on similarities and functional relationships, different patterns of memory errors may result between cultures. To investigate this question, Schwartz and colleagues (2014) presented their American and Turkish participants with categorically related and unrelated word pairs. Participants were then asked to recall the target word from the pair in response to the cue word. Americans made more categorical errors than did Turks, giving incorrect responses that were taxonomically related to either the cue word or the target word. Turks mistakenly recalled more noncategorically related words than did Americans. These results suggest that Americans more frequently use categories to organize information in memory or to support retrieval strategies than do Turks. Thus, culturally preferred categorization styles influence memory and result in corresponding memory distortions. 
In addition, cultural beliefs and assumptions can motivate memory distortions and false memory. Western, particularly European American, cultures value the pursuit of happiness, where people tend to hold the belief that happiness is central and common to a good and satisfying life. In contrast, East Asians tend to view life as comprising ups and downs, and therefore life satisfaction is not dependent on how many positive emotions one is experiencing (Koo & Oishi, 2009; Suh, Diener, Oishi, & Triandis, 1998). The cultural differences in how happy people think they should feel can shape the way they evaluate and remember their daily experiences, regardless of the actual experiences. To examine this question, Oishi (2002) compared retrospective accounts of emotion with 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  337 
daily diary and online reports of emotional experiences. He found that European and Asians Americans did not differ in daily diary reports of the quality of their day or in online reports of current positive (e.g., pleasant, calm, happy) and negative moods (e.g., unpleasant, sad, worried). However, cultural differences emerged at the end of the week, when participants were asked how good or bad the week was or how often they had experienced different positive and negative moods. European Americans retrospectively reported greater satisfaction with the week and a higher frequency of positive emotions than they did in their diaries or online. In contrast, Asian Americans’ retrospective reports were unchanged from their diary and online reports. Thus, in line with their belief that happiness is common and is the basis of a good life, European Americans reconstructed their memories of their daily experiences to be more positive than they actually were. Such memory distortions were absent in Asian Americans. 
Content Focus Memory content focus refers to the extent to which memory information concerns rememberers themselves versus others and social interactions (i.e., self- focus vs. other- focus). It may reflect the centrally important goals and motivations of the rememberers. Conway and colleagues propose that working self- goals serve an executive role in modulating the process of remembering (Conway & Pleydell- Pearce, 2000). These currently activated and salient self- goals channel cognitive resources to encode and consolidate goal- consistent information into memory and later prioritize selective retrieval of such information at recall, thus profoundly influencing what events and what aspects of the events are remembered. Importantly, fundamental self- goals such as autonomy and relatedness, although universally existing (Deci & Ryan, 2000), are variably emphasized in different cultures (Wang, 2013a). The culturally prioritized self- goals often remain chronically activated and readily available to guide the remembering process. Thus, in cultures that prioritize autonomous self- goals, such as European American culture in particular, people may focus on information concerning their own roles and perspectives that accentuates the uniqueness and agency of the individual. Such information is likely to be elaborately represented in memory and highly accessible during recall. In contrast, in cultures that prioritize relational self- goals, such as East Asia, people may focus on and remember information about social interactions and significant others. 
This is indeed what cross- cultural studies have found. When asked to recall recent or distant personal events, European American adults and children as young as the preschool age often recall memories of unique personal experiences in which they cast themselves as the central character of the story (e.g., “the time I won a prestigious award”). In contrast, East Asian adults and children often recall memories focusing on the roles of others and social interactions, with the self taking a peripheral role (e.g., “a family outing”; Han et al., 1998; Wang & Conway, 2004; Wang, 2001a, 2004). Interestingly, European Americans tend to cast themselves as the central character even when recalling memories of important others. In one study, for instance, European American and 
 
338 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Taiwanese college students were asked to recall earliest childhood memories in response to cue words of self, mother, family, friend, and surroundings (Wang, 2006a). Across all memories, European Americans focused more on their own roles than did Taiwanese, who emphasized more the roles of others. Cultural differences are further reflected in the content focus of memories that are important for the self. When asked to recall memories that help explain “how you have come to be the person you currently are,” Australians recalled a greater proportion and more detailed accounts of personal experiences that did not involve other people, whereas Asians recalled a greater proportion and more detailed accounts of social experiences that they had shared with others (Jobson & O’Kearney, 2008). Notably, the culturally prioritized self- goals that shape memory content focus not only at the group level, but also at the individual level as well. Within the same culture, individuals who exhibit heightened autonomous self- goals tend to recall more self- focused memories, whereas those who exhibit heightened relational self- goals recall more socially oriented memories (Wang, 2001a, 2004). 
Additional evidence for the influence of culturally prioritized self- goals on memory content focus has come from studies that experimentally primed self- goals to increases the retrieval of memory content consistent with those self- goals (Wang, 2008; Wang & Ross, 2005; Wang, Shao, & Li, 2010). For instance, in a study by Wang and Ross (2005, Study 1), European American and Asian American college students were asked to describe themselves as either unique individuals (i.e., autonomous- self prime) or as members of social groups (i.e., relational- self prime). They then recalled their earliest childhood memories. In both cultural groups, those whose autonomous self- goals were activated prior to the recall reported more self- focused memories, whereas those whose relational self- goals were made salient recalled more socially oriented memories. In a follow- up study (Wang & Ross, 2005, Study 2), participants received the same primes as in Study 1 and were asked to read a storybook. They then received a surprise memory test about the story shortly after the reading. Compared with those in the relational- self prime condition, those in the autonomous- self prime condition recalled more information about the protagonist and introduced fewer peripheral characters and fewer social interactions in their story memories. Thus, when remembering both personal experiences and story material, memory content reflected the particular self- goals being primed. These findings provide experimental evidence for the influence of cultural self- goals on memory content focus. 
Importantly, the priming effects did not eliminate or even reduce the magnitude of cultural differences in either personal memory or story memory: European Americans recalled more self- focused and protagonist- focused memories than did Asians, regardless of priming manipulations (Wang & Ross, 2005). Thus, priming and culture exerted independent effects on memory. These findings suggest that the cognitive frame (i.e., activated self- goals) at the time of retrieval is not the sole determinant of recall and that cultural discrepancies in recall may also reflect differences in how information is originally encoded and represented in memory that is relatively resistant to priming. In other words, cultural self- goals may filter the information people retrieve from memory, as 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  339 
reflected in the priming effect. They may also directly act on memory encoding by affecting people’s attention, perception, emotion, and meaning analysis during an ongoing event, resulting in cultural differences in memory representations. Thus, cultural self- goals, along with other cultural factors, may determine how, what, and whether event information is encoded in memory (Wang, 2013a, 2016). This is in line with the cultural differences in attentional and perceptual processes discussed earlier (Nisbett, 2003; Nisbett et al., 2001). 
Valence Memory valence, namely, the extent to which memory information concerns positive versus negative past events, appears to be influenced by self- goals for enhancement versus improvement that are variously emphasized across cultures. Western, particularly European American, cultures endorse to a greater extent self- enhancement goals that motivate individuals to pursue and maintain a positive sense of self. In contrast, East Asian cultures prioritize self- improvement goals that motivate individuals to identify their own weaknesses and further seek actual change and improvement in the self (Heine & Hamamura, 2007; Heine, Lehman, Markus, & Kitayama, 1999). Accordingly, Western individuals may dwell on past events in their memory that boost their positive self- views, whereas East Asians may attend to and remember events that provide opportunities for self- reflection and improvement. Indeed, research has shown that whereas European Americans tend to exhibit a positive bias in memory, East Asians are often even- handed in remembering positive and negative events and sometimes even focus more on negative experiences (Endo & Meijer, 2004; Oishi, 2002; Ross, Heine, Wilson, & Sugimori, 2005). 
In a study by Endo and Meijer (2004), for example, American and Japanese collage students were asked to recall as many incidences as they could of success and failure that they had experienced in their lives. Whereas Americans recalled considerably more success stories than failure stories, Japanese recalled slightly more failure stories than success stories. Similarly, Gelfand and colleagues asked American and Japanese college students to recall as many fair and unfair behaviors as they could think of that were engaged by either themselves or other people (Gelfand et  al., 2002). Americans recalled more memories in which they were fair as well as more memories in which others were unfair than did Japanese. Also, Americans remembered far more fair behaviors engaged by themselves than by others, and they remembered far more unfair behaviors engaged by others than by themselves. Japanese, in contrast, recalled similar numbers of fair and unfair behaviors engaged by themselves and by others. 
Cultural differences in memory valence is also reflected in judgments of subjective distance. Ross and colleagues (2005) asked Canadian and Japanese college students to recall events that either made them feel proud or embarrassed. Whereas Canadians found proud events easier to recall than embarrassing events, Japanese found no difference in recalling proud and embarrassing events. Furthermore, Canadians reported feeling further away in time from embarrassing events than from equally distant proud events. 
 
340 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
This asymmetry reflects the motivation to maintain favorable self- regard: by subjectively distancing an unflattering episode and by feeling temporally close to a pleasing episode, Western individuals can dissociate their current self from blame and yet continue to claim credit for former accomplishments. These biases were absent among Japanese. 
Thus, self- enhancement goals privileged in Western cultures motivate individuals to reconstruct memories to shed positive light on the self, whereas self- improvement goals valued in East Asian cultures motivate individuals to remember and assess their past experiences to position themselves for genuine improvement (Oishi, 2002; Wang, 2013a). In addition to memory reconstruction, cultural differences in memory valence may also reflect different cultural experiences people encounter in their daily lives and thus different types of information they encode in memory. In a study by Kitayama and colleagues (Kitayama, Markus, Matsumoto, & Norasakkunkit, 1997)  using a situation sampling method, Japanese and American participants were asked to recall situations they had experienced in which their self- esteem either increased or decreased. A second group of Japanese and American participants were then asked to judge how much their self- esteem would have increased or decreased if they had been in those situations themselves. Both Japanese and Americans judged the Japanese self- esteem- decreasing situations as more condemning to their self- esteem than American ones and judged the American self- esteem- increasing situations as more enhancing to their self- esteem than Japanese ones. Thus, life experiences people regularly encounter in the United States are particularly effective in boosting positive self- views, whereas life experiences people regularly encounter in Japan afford opportunities for self- criticism. The different kinds of experiences can be subsequently encoded and retained in memory, thus contributing to cultural differences in memory valence. 
Subjectivity Subjective elements such as emotions, thoughts, and desires are considered to be the defining feature of autobiographical memory (Bauer, 2007), as well as critical components of the literary genre of autobiography and other life- writings (Wang, 2013a; Weintraub, 1975). Important from the current perspective, cultures hold different attitudes toward subjective experience and expression, which can, in turn, influence their manifestation in memory. In Western, particularly European American, cultures that place a great emphasis on individuality and agency, inner subjective experiences are often regarded as a reflection of the true self and clear indicators of one’s distinctiveness from the social world. Consequently, individuals are encouraged to attend to and express their inner thoughts and feelings (Halberstadt, Denham & Dunsmore, 2001; Markus & Kitayama, 1991). In contrast, in East Asian cultures, where there is a paramount concern with social harmony and group interests, a great emphasis is placed on moderation of all matters of the heart (Mauss, Butler Roberts, & Chu, 2010). Individuals are encouraged to attend to social norms and regulate their behaviors that may have direct consequences for group functioning and to control and minimize emotions and other subjective experiences 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  341 
because they can be potentially interruptive of social harmony (Halberstadt et al., 2001; Wang, 2013a). 
Cross- cultural studies have revealed differences in memory subjectivity in line with these different cultural beliefs and expectations. When recalling autobiographical events, European American adults and children more frequently refer to their thoughts, feelings, and desires than do their Asian and Asian American counterparts (e.g., Wang, 2001a; Wang & Conway, 2004; Wang & Ross, 2005). For instance, in a study of lifespan retrieval in middle- aged adults from China and the United States (all European Americans), participants were asked to each recall 20 memories from any period of their lifetime (Wang & Conway, 2004). Regardless of which life period the memories came from, Americans referred more frequently to their thoughts and emotions in the memory events than did Chinese. Similar cultural differences in memory subjectivity have also been observed in adults’ memories of recent events (e.g., Chua, Leu, & Nisbett, 2005) and very- long- term memories, such as earliest childhood recollections (Wang, 2001a), whereby European American adults more frequently described their emotions, personal opinions, and agency in the past events than did Chinese and Taiwanese. Similarly, when recalling memories of fictional stories (Wang & Ross, 2005) or vicarious experiences of significant others (Wang, 2006a), European American adults referred more frequently to the needs, desires, and opinions of the story protagonist or those of their own than did Asian Americans and Taiwanese. 
Furthermore, cultural differences in attending to subjective experiences in memory events emerge as early as the preschool age (Han et al., 1998; Wang, 2004). For example, when asked to recall recent and distant autobiographical events, European American 4- , 6- , and 8- year- olds made more spontaneous references to their emotions, personal preferences, and opinions than did their Chinese counterparts (Wang, 2004). In a more recent study, European American and Chinese immigrant 6- year- old children and their mothers were asked to independently recall emotionally salient events that they experienced together (Wang & Song, 2018). European American children recalled more information about their subjective states than did Chinese immigrant children, and European American mothers recalled more information about the subjective states of themselves, their children, and other people than did Chinese immigrant mothers. The cultural differences were larger in mothers’ than children’s memories, reflecting the influence of continuing socialization and enculturation. 
Cultural influences on memory subjectivity may take place not only at memory retrieval but at encoding as well, where individuals differentially attend to and represent subjective information in their memories. In the study described earlier by Wang and Ross (2005) in which European American and Asian American participants were primed to focus on their autonomous or rational self- goals, cultural differences in participants’ references to internal states persisted in both personal memory and story memory, in spite of the priming. These findings suggest that cultural self- goals and the associated cultural attitudes toward subjective experiences may serve as a constructive filter affecting 
342 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
the extent to which individuals attend to and encode their inner thoughts and feelings during ongoing events. Subsequently, cultural differences in the representation of subjective information may persist in memory and resist the influence of priming at recall. 
Specificity Memory specificity refers to the representation and recall of specific, one- time events occurring at a particular time and place in the past as well as the recollection of rich details about the events. In contrast to specific memory, there is generic or general memory for events that happened repeatedly or on multiple occasions and those that took place during an extended period of time. Specific memory and generic memory tend to serve different functions and are thus motivated in varied degrees across cultures, resulting in cultural differences in memory specificity (Wang, 2009a). Specific memories of unique events with idiosyncratic details (e.g., “One time I won a prestigious award”) are a critical ingredient for the individuality and autonomy that are highly valued in Western cultures. In contrast, generic memories (e.g., “My family went to church every Sunday”) often imply social conventions, rules, and regularities and therefore are important for people in cultures such as East Asia that embrace social harmony and collective solidarity. 
Research has consistently revealed cultural differences in the extent to which people remember specific episodes and their details versus general events (for a review, see Wang, 2009a). European American adults and children retrieve more frequently unique, one- time episodes than do their Asian counterparts, who more often recall general or routine events (e.g., Han et al., 1998; Wang, 2001a, 2004; Wang & Conway, 2004). Also, Westerners exhibit easier access to a greater number of specific memories than do East Asians for both distant (e.g., childhood; Peterson, Wang, & Hou, 2009; Wang, 2001a; Wang, Conway, & Hou, 2004)  and very recent events (e.g., yesterday or today; Oishi, Kurtz, Miao, Park, & Whitchurch, 2011; Wang, 2009b). For example, Oishi and colleagues (2011) observed that when asked to list all the activities they engaged in on the previous day, both American retirees and nonretirees reported approximately 30% more activities than did Korean retirees and nonretirees. Furthermore, when recalling specific episodes, European American adults and children often report more event- specific details than do Asians, who often include more general information (Wang, Capous, Koh, & Hou, 2014; Wang, Hou, Tang, & Wiprovnick, 2011; Wang & Song, 2018). These cultural differences in memory specificity are further extended to the construction of future events (Wang et al., 2011, 2014). 
Paralleling cultural differences in specificity have also been observed in memories for fictional stories (Wang & Ross, 2005) and memories about significant others (Wang, 2006a), as well as memories in individuals with psychopathology (Jobson, Moradi, Rahimi- Movaghar, Conway, & Dalgleish, 2014). Furthermore, studies that keep the to- be- remembered event constant across groups have yielded the same pattern of results. For example, in a study to examine European American and Korean preschoolers’ memories for a staged event (Chae, Kulkofsky, & Wang, 2006), a researcher visited children in their 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  343 
classroom and played with them a “Pizza Game” in an identical way for the two cultural groups. Approximately 1 week following the event, a second researcher interviewed children individually about the event in a free recall and a prompted recall task. American children recalled more specific details of the staged event in both tasks than did Korean children. 
That memory specificity is culturally motivated is further reflected at the individual level: within a single culture, people who exhibit a greater autonomous orientation are also more likely to recall specific memories as opposed to generic memories, compared with those who exhibit a greater relational orientation (Wang, 2001a; Wang, Leichtman, & White, 1998). Mediation analysis has provided further evidence for the role of cultural self- goals in retrieving specific memory details. In one study, 3- year- old children from Chinese families in China, first- generation Chinese immigrant families in the United States, and European American families were asked to recall memories of recent events and provide self- descriptions in a storytelling task (Wang, 2006b). Compared with their Chinese and Chinese immigrant peers, European American youngsters recalled more detailed memories; they also exhibited a greater autonomous orientation by describing themselves in more personal as opposed to social terms. Mediation analysis further indicated that the children’s self- goals with an autonomous relative to relational orientation accounted for the cultural differences in the amount of detail of their memories. 
Cultural differences in perceptual styles may influence how people perceive and encode discrete events from ongoing activities (Zacks & Swallow, 2007) and thus shape memory specificity during encoding (Wang, 2009b, 2013b). As discussed earlier, Asians often engage in holistic perceptual processes, attending to relationships and similarities among objects and events, whereas Westerners tend to engage in analytic perceptual processes, focusing on salient features of individual objects and events (Nisbett & Miyamoto, 2005; Norenzayan, Choi, & Peng, 2007). The holistic processing of information in Asians may lead them to view different objects and events as interrelated and thus perceive fewer discrete episodes in a continuous flux of information. In comparison, European Americans attending to salient properties of individual objects and events may analytically segment the information into a greater number of unique episodes. 
This is indeed what has been found. In one study (Wang, 2009b), Asian and European American college students were presented with a narrative text and were asked to segment the text into discrete events. Asians perceived and thus encoded fewer discrete episodes than did European Americans. Correspondingly, at an immediate recall test following reading of the narrative text, Asians recalled fewer event episodes from the text than did European Americans. In another study, cultural influences on encoding and recall were examined using a random sampling method (Wang, 2013b). European American and Asian American participants were sent a text message three times a day during a 1- week period and were asked to record as soon as they received the message what was happening during the past 30 minutes. At the end of the week, they received a surprise memory test for the events that they had recorded. The immediate event entry 
344 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
reflected the amount of specific detail being perceived and encoded, and the delayed recall tabulated retention and retrieval. Among Asians, those who moved to the United States at an earlier age and were therefore likely more Americanized perceived and, subsequently, recalled more event details than those who moved at an older age. 
Function Memory is meant to serve practical purposes, whether it is about gaining knowledge about the world or understanding the self and others. The purposes or functions of memory, in turn, directly affect the organization of and access to the memory system (Baddeley, 1988; Bluck & Alea, 2009; Pillemer, 1998). At a broad level, memory can be viewed as a functional adaptation to one’s social- ecological environment. For example, Australian Aboriginal children and adolescents of the desert regions develop extraordinary visual- spatial memory that enables them to efficiently navigate in their physical surroundings (Kearins, 1981). Furthermore, as Neisser (1982, p. 12) proclaimed, “changes in the social and cultural environment can change the uses of the past.” Thus, people in different cultures may use memory to serve different functions in line with their cultural goals and expectations. 
Cross- cultural studies have examined the extent to which people use their past experiences— namely, autobiographical memory— to understand the self, connect with important others, comfort emotional wounds, or learn valuable lessons (for reviews, see Alea & Wang, 2015; Wang & Ross, 2007). In line with their cultural emphasis on individuality and personal uniqueness, Westerners, particularly European Americans, often use memories to discern meaning and construct a unique personal identity. This use of memory for self- understanding is less prominent in the Asian cultural context, where the self is largely defined by one’s social roles and duties. Paradoxically, memories are also frequently used for relationship purposes in Western cultures that are characterized by high relational mobility, where social relations are often voluntary and unstable and require conscious effort for maintenance (Kito, Yuki, & Thomson, 2017; Schug, Yuki, & Maddux, 2010). Sharing memories with others serves as an effective means to foster intimacy and deepen interpersonal ties (Beike, Brandon, & Cole, 2016; Levinger, 1980). In contrast, in cultures like East Asia that are characterized by low relational mobility, relationships are often by default based on one’s social roles and status and therefore cannot be easily formed or dissolved and require less maintenance through sharing of memories or other means (Kito et al., 2017; Wang, 2013a). Indeed, when asked to describe when and why they had previously thought and talked about their personal memories, European American college students reported more frequent uses of memory for self and social purposes than did Chinese (Kulkofsky, Wang, & Hou, 2010). Similar cultural differences in the use of memory for social bonding have been found between Americans and Trinidadians (Alea, Bluck, & Ali, 2015). 
Furthermore, in Western cultures, there is a general appreciation of memory in regulating emotions, with the belief that thinking about and sharing memories can help 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  345 
individuals cope with negative feelings and capitalize on positive ones (Pennebaker, Zech, & Rimé, 2001; Reis et al., 2010). This belief is not shared in other cultures, such as East Asia, where people tend to believe in fate and readily accept negative events as uncontrollable losses (Bjorck, Cuthbertson, Thurman, & Lee, 2001). People in these cultures often deal with negative experiences and feelings through psychological distancing and avoidance, trying not to think or talk about such experiences (Tweed, White, & Lehman, 2004). Also, given their relationship concerns (such as to avoid losing face or burdening others), Asians and Asian Americans have been found to be less willing than Westerners to disclose emotional experiences (Kim, Sherman, & Taylor, 2008). For instance, whereas Koreans reported that 20% of their emotional experiences were never shared, US participants reported only 5%. French and US participants also reported sharing repetitively a single emotional episode with others on a greater number of occasions and sharing it almost immediately with a shorter delay when compared with Koreans, Singaporeans, and Japanese (Rimé, Corsini, & Herbette, 2002). 
On the other hand, memories are valued for their didactic functions in Asian cultures, where “learning implies full knowledge of the precedents of a past age” (Nakamura, 1964, p. 205). There is a great emphasis on history and respect for the past in this cultural context, and individuals are encouraged to learn from past experiences in conducting their current and future activities (Wang & Conway, 2004). In contrast, Western cultures emphasize “forward thinking,” and individuals tend not to appreciate the intellectual and moral values of the past to the same extent. For example, in a study in which American participants described previous times when they had consulted their memories of personal events, Hyman and Faries (1992) found that although self and social functions were common uses of autobiographical memories, the use of memories to direct one’s current behavior was rarely evident. Also, when asked to recall personal events from their lifetimes (Wang & Conway, 2004), Chinese middle- aged adults were five times more likely than their European American counterparts to spontaneously generate moral lessons (e.g., “Since then, I have realized that there are more nice people than bad ones in this world”). Similarly, in line with their oral tradition, in which cultural knowledge is passed across generations by word of mouth, Indigenous Australians reported more frequent use of memory to “teach and inform” than did non- Indigenous Australians (Nile & Van Bergen, 2015). 
In a more recent study that examined the explicit knowledge of the functional uses of autobiographical memory, European and Asian American adults and school- aged children were asked to indicate their agreement with statements about why people think about and share memories (Wang, Koh, Song, & Hou, 2015). Children were also interviewed for personal memories concurrently with the memory function knowledge assessment and again 3  months later. It was found that European American children endorsed more self- and emotion regulation functions than did Asian American children, whereas Asian American adults endorsed more didactic functions than did European American adults. In addition, children’s endorsement of memory functions, particularly 
346 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
social functions, was associated with more detailed and personally meaningful memories both concurrently and over time. These findings suggest that people in different cultures hold different beliefs about the functional usage of memory, and such beliefs can, in turn, influence how people construct memories of their experiences (see also Chapter 17 by Amir Rosenmann and Jenny Kurman on culture and self). 
Childhood Amnesia Childhood amnesia, also called infantile amnesia, refers to the absence or scarcity of memories about very early life events (Peterson, 2002; Rubin, 2000). Although children as young as age 2 or 3 often exhibit impressive abilities to retain personal event information over extended periods of time, especially with adults’ assistance (Harley & Reese, 1999; Nelson & Fivush, 2004), most adults cannot consciously recall events that occurred before they were age 3 or 4 (Rubin, 2000). This phenomenon deserves separate attention as it is directly related to the mechanisms for memory consolidation, retention and forgetting, and memory development more generally. More important from the current perspective, culture plays a critical role in influencing the expression and extensiveness of childhood amnesia (Wang, 2003, 2013a). 
When asked to recall their earliest childhood memories, Europeans and European Americans report events dating from, on average, age 3½ years, which is more than 6 months earlier than the earliest events reported by Asians (MacDonald, Uesiliana, & Hayne, 2000; Mullen, 1994; Wang, 2001a). Also, Westerners show easier access to early childhood memories than do Asians. For example, in one study (Wang et al., 2004), college students from China, the United States (all European American), and Britain were asked to recall as many childhood memories (of events occurring before the age of 5 years) as they could in a 5- minute period. Participants then dated each memory they recalled. Chinese participants recalled approximately half the number of memories as US and British participants, and they also recalled their earliest memories from about 6 months later than did the two Western groups. Similarly, in a study on children’s early childhood recollections, European Canadian and Chinese 8- , 11- , and 14- year- old children were asked to recall in a 4- minute period as many memory events as they could that took place before they went to school (Peterson et al., 2009). Children then identified their age at the time of each event. Consistent with adult data (Mullen, 1994; Wang, 2001a; Wang et al., 2004), European Canadian children had their earliest memories from a younger age and recalled more memories from their early childhood than did Chinese children, with the cultural differences increasing with age. 
Wang (2001a, 2003)  proposed that, from a cognitive perspective, culturally prioritized self- goals may influence the extent to which cognitive processes and resources are channeled into the encoding, retention, and retrieval of autobiographical memories. Autonomous self- goals, as embraced in Western cultures, may motivate individuals to attend to, encode, and retain information of events that happened to “me” and further drive the early development of an organized, articulated, and durable autobiographical memory 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  347 
system. In contrast, relational self- goals, as nurtured in many Asian cultures, may prioritize instead the retention of knowledge— not necessarily in the form of memory— that is critical for social harmony and collective solidarity. The development of a structured memory system for one’s own experiences may not be accentuated, and this may lead to more prolonged childhood amnesia. 
In line with this proposal, research with individual difference analysis has shown that, even within a single culture, children and adults with more salient autonomous self- goals tend to show greater accessibility to childhood memories— reporting earlier and more detailed childhood memories— than do those with more salient relational self- goals (Wang, 2001a, 2006b; Wang et  al., 1998). In a more recent study of childhood recollections in Mexicans, de la Mata, Santamaría, and Ruiz (2016) found that participants with more school experience exhibited a greater autonomous sense of self and also recalled earlier childhood memories when compared with those with less formal schooling. 
Experimental studies that prompt individuals to focus temporarily on either their autonomous or relational aspect of the self have provided further evidence for the effect of culturally prioritized self- goals on accessibility to childhood memory. When Asians were primed to focus on their autonomous self- goals, they reported their earliest memories as early as European Americans did, at approximately 3½ years of age, which was 7 months earlier than the earliest memories of Asians, who were primed to focus on their relational self- goals, as well as those in a control condition (Wang & Ross, 2005). Given that cultural differences in accessing early childhood memories emerge early (Peterson et al., 2009) and persist into adulthood (Mullen, 1994; Wang, 2001a; Wang et al., 2004), adults’ retrospective recollections of early childhood memories may reflect the operation of cultural self- goals both in the child at the time of the remembered event and in the adult at recall years later. 
Memory Socialization Socialization is at the root of the cultural differences in memory that emerge early and persist into adulthood. In particular, family memory- sharing practices often reflect parents’ implicit or explicit socialization goals in line with cultural norms and expectations, which are transmitted to and internalized by children into their own memory operations (Wang & Brockmeier, 2002; Wang, 2013a, 2018). Given the importance of remembering personal experiences for establishing an autonomous sense of self and affirming self- esteem in Western cultures, Western parents share memories with their children more frequently, more positively, and in a more child- focused way compared with parents of other cultures (Miller, Wiley, Fung, & Liang, 1997; Mullen & Yi, 1995; Wang, 2001b; Wang, Leichtman, & Davies, 2000). For example, in a study of conversational interactions between mothers and their 3- year- old children, Mullen and Yi (1995) found during a 1 - day observation that European American mothers talked with their children about past events three times as often as did Korean mothers. Similarly, Martini 
 
348 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
(1996) observed that, during family dinners, European American parents asked their children to talk about past events twice as often as did Japanese American parents. 
Furthermore, European American mothers tend to observe a “looking good” principle and frequently position their children in a positive light in the past event, whereas East Asian mothers often adopt a “didactic mode” and discuss children’s past transgressions to explicitly instruct children to follow rules (Miller et al., 1997; Mullen & Yi, 1995; Wang, 2001b; Wang et  al., 2000). Also, memory conversations between European American mothers and children often have the children as the focal point, with mothers frequently referring to the children’s roles and perspectives in the past event. In contrast, memory conversations in East Asian families are often mother- centered and hierarchically organized, in which mothers set the direction of the conversation and frequently refer to social interactions and group activities (Wang, 2001b; Wang et al., 2000). 
Parents also differ in how they incorporate subjective elements of the past into memory conversations. European American mothers more frequently encourage children to discuss their subjective experiences such as thoughts, feelings, and wishes than do Japanese, Korean, and Chinese mothers, who focus more on children’s behaviors in connection with social norms and expectations (Martini, 1996; Miller et al., 1997; Mullen & Yi, 1995; Wang, 2001b; Wang et  al., 2000). Similarly, when reading books together, European Americans mothers focused more on the inner thoughts and feelings of story characters than did Chinese American mothers, who focused more on the characters’ behavior (Doan & Wang, 2010). These different approaches to the subjectivity of memory or story are evident even when the event under discussion is highly emotional. For example, Fivush and Wang (2005) examined Chinese and European American mother– child conversations about highly positive and negative events (e.g., birthday parties, conflict with parents or peers). They found that whereas American mothers dwelled on lengthy discussions about the causes of emotions, Chinese mothers quickly switched to pinpoint the social and behavioral implications of emotions to their children. 
Cultural differences in memories of specific past events and their details, as well as the long- term accessibility of such memories from early childhood (i.e., childhood amnesia), can also be traced back to early family socialization. European American mothers frequently engage in high- elaborative memory conversations with their children in which they dwell upon specific episodes, follow- up on children’s responses with rich details, and provide feedback to encourage children to contribute. In contrast, Korean, Japanese, and Chinese mothers tend to initiate low- elaborative memory conversations and often repeat their questions without providing embellished information or following up on children’s responses (e.g., “Who went to the park with us? . . . Who else? . . . And who else?”; Minami & McCabe, 1995; Wang, 2001b; Wang et al., 2000; Wang & Fivush, 2005). Similarly, when telling baby stories with their young children, German mothers told lengthy and detailed stories about specific incidents from the children’s babyhood, whereas Indian mothers tended to talk about general routines of what the children used to do as babies (Schröder, Kärtner, & Keller, 2015).
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  349 
According to the social interactionist account of childhood amnesia, high- elaborative conversations play a key role in facilitating children’s developing memory, whereby young children learn to use linguistic and narrative codes to structure and reinstate memory information so that their memories are likely to be well- consolidated and maintained over a long period of time (Fivush, Haden, & Reese, 2006; Nelson & Fivush, 2004). Indeed, parents’ use of a highly elaborative style early on directly facilitates children’s abilities to recall specific events over the long term (Harley & Reese, 1999; Leichtman, Pillemer, Wang, Koreishi, & Han, 2000; McCabe & Peterson, 1991) and predicts an earlier age of first memories by adolescence (Jack, MacDonald, Reese, & Hayne, 2009). Reese and Neha (2015) further observed that in New Zealand Māori culture, which places paramount importance on oral tradition and memory, mothers who reported greater cultural affiliation also reported sharing memories more frequently with their children, and maternal memory conversations were directly associated with children’s memory skills. This may explain the finding that Māori adults recall earlier childhood memories than do New Zealand European and Chinese adults (MacDonald et al., 2000). 
Conceivably, European American mothers’ use of a high- elaborative conversational style early on, compared with Asian mothers’ low- elaborative style, directly contribute to cultural differences in specificity and long- term accessibility of memory in children (Wang, 2006b, 2007). In a cross- cultural longitudinal study (Wang, 2007), European American, Chinese, and Chinese American immigrant mothers and their children discussed shared past experiences three times at home, when the children were 3, 3½, and 4½ years of age. Across all time points, European American mothers carried out more elaborate conversations than did mothers of the two Chinese groups. Mothers’ provision of specific details directly facilitated children’s memory both concurrently and over the long term, such that European American children recalled more specific details of the past events than did their Chinese peers. Notably, mothers’ provision of specific details during memory conversations was positively associated with their endorsement of autonomy and individuality and negatively related to their endorsement of relatedness. Similar findings have also been obtained in a study of mother– child conversations about the past and future in Turkey and the United States (Sahin- Acar & Leichtman, 2015): American mothers provided more voluminous, descriptive, and elaborative talks than did Turkish mothers, and mothers who endorsed more individuality engaged in more elaborative talks about future events. 
Finally, children develop culture- specific views of memory functions through early socialization. European American parents frequently use memory conversations to facilitate autonomy and positive self- views in children and to strengthen parent– child bonding (Kulkofsky, Wang, & Koh, 2009; Sahin- Acar & Leichtman, 2015; Wang & Fivush, 2005; Wang et al., 2000). They are also eager to play the role of “emotion coaches” and explain and resolve negative affect to help children regulate their emotions (Wang, 2001b; Fivush & Wang, 2005). Asian parents, in contrast, often share memories to situate children in a relational hierarchy, and they use memory conversations to teach children lessons and 
350 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
guide children’s current and future behavior (Miller et al., 1997; Mullen & Yi, 1995; Wang et al., 2000). Over time, children in different cultures may internalize their parents’ usages of memory conversations into their own knowledge of memory functions and further use such knowledge to guide their remembering of the past (Wang et al., 2015). 
In sum, as the cultural dynamic theory posits (Wang, 2013a, 2016), the constructive processes of remembering are thoroughly immersed in the cultural context in which a multitude of influencing variables operate on various aspects or components of memory. The cultural variables influence what information and how much of the information we remember and how we structure our memories in line with our cultural expectations. They shape not only how we recall the past, but also what we perceive as our experiences unfold. The influences of culture on memory manifest early in development, whereby parents, in line with their cultural beliefs, scaffold a communicative context in which they instill, consciously or unconsciously, in their young children culture- specific ways of remembering. This socialization process perpetuates cultural influences on memory across generations. 
Conclusion Like the two little storytellers at the beginning of our chapter, people in different cultures attend to, perceive, evaluate, explain, describe, and remember physical and social events in dynamic, constructive, and interactive processes guided by their cultural beliefs, norms, and assumptions. The processing of information in cognition and memory does not take place merely inside an individual’s mind or brain, independent of content and context. On the contrary, it entails an active construction that is susceptible to the content of the information and is in response to its context that comprises a multitude of social, cultural, and historical influences. As such, cognition is a joint product of individual sentiments and cultural expectations. Socialization practices further sustain and perpetuate culturally preferred ways of thinking, perceiving, and remembering across generations. 
While this chapter largely focused on cultural differences in cognition, it is also important to consider similarities across cultures. For example, a comprehensive analysis of a large variety of color terms across the world has revealed a systematic and universal way that the colors are categorized in groups (Berlin & Kay, 1969). A recent study using computational modeling has provided further evidence to support this theory, demonstrating the hierarchical emergence of basic color terms based on the wavelengths that are more available for humans (Loreto, Mukherjee, & Tria, 2012). However, even such strong universal patterns of color perception can be the subject of cultural differences. For instance, Roberson and colleagues (Roberson, Davies, & Davidoff, 2000; Roberson & Hanley, 2007) compared color perception of Berinmo- speakers from Papua New Guinea, Himba- speakers from Nambia, and English- speakers from the United States. They found that the ways people discriminated colors (e.g., green vs. blue) were different depending on the categories existing in their own languages. A recent study has also observed linguistic 
 
CulTure and CogniT ion  |  351 
differences in color perception at the neurophysiological level (Athanasopoulos, Wiggett, Dering, Kuipers, & Thierry, 2009), demonstrating considerable evidence for cultural variation. Thus, even the most basic cognitive processes are not free from cultural influences. An important line of future research is to examine the interplay between biological dispositions and cultural experiences in producing cultural similarities and differences in cognition. 
Notably, our analysis predominantly focused on the East– West contrast, which reflects the characteristics of the extant body of cross- cultural research. Yet culture is not just about comparisons between Westerners and East Asians. Research that further examines diverse world populations will yield critical findings on how culture shapes cognition. Also, within- culture differences in our increasingly multicultural worlds beg additional attention from researchers. For example, a number of studies have applied cultural models to understand behaviors and values in different social- economic classes in the United States (e.g., Fiske & Markus, 2012; Stephens, Fryberg, Markus, Johnson, & Covarrubias, 2012); for example, that people from lower social classes tend to favor more contextual over dispositional explanations for social events than do those from upper social classes (Kraus, Piff, & Keltner, 2009). In addition to social- economic status, the concept of culture should be broadened to include gender, religion, geographical condition, and so forth, to further our understanding of the interplay between mind and culture (Cohen, 2009). 
A historical perspective is also critical to study cognition and culture in our fast- changing world, both in terms of individual development across the lifespan and societal changes across historical times (Greenfield, 2013, 2018; Varnum & Grossmann, 2017; Wang, 2013a). Given that culture is not static but transitory and evolving, the mutual relation between culture and cognition may change its forms in the course of development. For example, one study found that, when asked to draw landscapes, both Canadian and Japanese adolescents, particularly those in the eighth and ninth grades, were more likely than younger children as well as college students to demonstrate culturally deviant cognitive styles (Nand, Masuda, Senzaki, & Ishii, 2014). Social- political systems may also introduce cultural variables that influence the cognition of an entire generation. For example, China’s one- child policy, initiated in the late 1970s, transformed family dynamics and created a new parent– child interaction pattern that facilitates child- centeredness. Consequently, Chinese adults who grew up as only children exhibited more salient autonomous self- goals and also remembered their childhood experiences in a more “Western” manner (i.e., earlier dated, more specific, more self- focused, and less socially oriented), compared with Chinese adults who grew up as children with siblings (Wang et al., 1998). It will be a fruitful area of research to examine the interplay between mind and culture within individuals over time and across generations. 
Finally, cognitive styles and processes can evolve in response to the unique social- ecological environments of our time and culture. In particular, technological inventions and the associated products (such as the Internet and social media) have introduced 
352 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
new modes of thinking and remembering (Wang, 2013a). Individuals are not just passive consumers of information, but also active disseminators and creators of information. The processing and storage of information is not solely located in the mind or brain, but can be outsourced to an infinite transactive memory system that is both transitory and permanent. As a special form of culture, the Internet and other technological inventions provide researchers with both challenges and opportunities to understand the adaptive nature of human cognition.
