12 
Culture and Emotion 
Integrating Biological Universality  with Cultural Specificity 
David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang 
Humans experience a wide range of affective phenomena, and much of it is called “emotion” by researchers and laypersons alike. Emotion is an aspect of our lives to which we all have a lifetime to access as well as to contemplate about the proper words to describe its experience. Emotions give meaning to life, serve as important motivators for our behaviors, and color our thoughts. They are a fuel for growth, development, and action (see Chapter 8 by Heidi Keller, for example, on the function of emotion in development across cultures). 
Since findings documenting the universality of facial expressions of emotion (reviewed later), research from the past few decades has flooded the literature with evidence for both cultural similarities and differences, supporting both biological and cultural determinants of various aspects of emotion. This literature has lent itself to debates about the universality versus cultural specificity of emotion and the roles of biology and culture. These debates continue until today. 
In this chapter, we integrate this seemingly disparate literature by providing a biocultural model of emotion that integrates a biologically based core emotion system that is calibrated, regulated, and elaborated by culture. (The model we present here updates a model previously published in Matsumoto and Hwang [2012].) We describe three premises underlying the model that help to organize and understand disparate findings in emotion research. Given these premises, we believe that the seemingly contradictory literature on culture and emotion can be understood in a cohesive manner and somewhat neatly integrated into a coherent whole and that future research questions 
 
 
362 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
should focus on the relative contributions of biology and culture. Our position is that the relative contributions of biology and culture, and thus findings of universality or cultural specificity, differ depending on the type of emotion examined and the specific domain of emotion assessed. 
We begin this chapter with a brief description of the study of emotion and culture in historical perspective, beginning with Darwin and the original studies documenting the universality of facial expressions of emotion. We also review briefly subsequent research documenting both universality and culture- specificity. We then present our biocultural model, beginning with its underlying premises, including our working definitions of emotion and culture. We then re- review selected studies in the literature in light of the premises and our model. Our review and framework does not include judgments of emotional expressions, as we believe this aspect of emotion involves a different cognitive system related to emotion (see Matsumoto & Hwang, 2017, for more discussion of this area). 
The Study of Emotion and Culture in Historical Perspective The Influence of Darwin Emotion and culture have been objects of study and fascination by philosophers and other thinkers for centuries. Emotions played a large role in the thinking and writing of Aristotle and Socrates (Russell, 1994) and were well represented in the third- century Sanskrit text Rasadhyaya (Shweder & Haidt, 2000). Emotion was also central to many who were influential to modern psychology, such as Freud, Darwin, Erikson, Piaget, Bowlby, and others. 
Contemporary studies of emotion and culture, however, find their roots in the work of Darwin. Much of this work was about instinctive behavior ranging from the supernatural and theological to the natural, and his theory of evolution via natural selection has made three notable contributions (Dewsbury, 2009). First, he introduced a viable mechanism for evolutionary change and natural selection, explaining the continuum of humans’ involvement over time. He proposed that individual variations in heritable appearances and populations are capable of increasing exponentially. Second, he claimed that evolutionary change occurs by natural causes and is totally explicable without any inherent purpose or predetermined direction. In other words, environmental changes such as weather, drought, or earthquake forced species to develop certain or newly modified functions and features better fitting for survival. This theory of naturalism has influenced many developing disciplines, including not only psychology but also biological and natural sciences. Third, he accumulated much supporting evidence across phylogenetic lines, such as beetles, barnacles, and people from different cultures (Dewsbury, 2009). 
 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  363 
Darwin’s endeavors helped us to understand humans in relation to animals as outcomes of nature and his arguments concerning the continuity between human and nonhuman animals have had strong impact on understanding emotions. According to Darwin, humans share fundamental, core properties with nonhuman primates, including emotions, in addition to unique traits and characteristics that individuals are born with and that were essential for natural selection to work. Darwin’s thesis concerning emotions was summarized in his work, The Expression of Emotion in Man and Animals (Darwin, 1872), in which he posited that emotions and their expressions had evolved across species, were evolutionarily adaptive, biologically innate, and universal across all human and even nonhuman primates. Darwin believed that all humans, regardless of race or culture, possessed the ability to express emotions on their faces in similar ways. He engaged in a detailed study of the muscle actions involved in emotion and concluded that the muscle actions are universal and that their antecedents can be seen in the expressive behaviors of nonhuman primates and other mammals. 
Darwin believed that emotions and their expressions were functionally adaptive, and he purported three principles that explained the nature and functions of emotions and expressive behaviors. His principle of serviceable associated habits suggested that fa-cial expressions are the residual actions of more complete behavioral responses. For example, he suggested that humans express anger by furrowing the brow and tightening the lips with teeth displayed because these actions are part of an attack response. His prin-ciple regarding direct actions of the nervous system posited that humans and animals had acquired certain stimulus- response connections that aid in their survival through natural selection. This was exemplified in his description of responses toward suffering (e.g., pain or choking), in which he explained that when humans are suffering, their expiration becomes violent, which in turn influences the circulation of blood. Because the vascular system within the eyes is sensitive, the gorging of the blood would damage the system. In order to protect the eyes from the gorging of the blood, the orbicular and corrugator muscles involuntarily contract to reduce the amount of the blood flow into the vascular system in the eyes. This contraction of the muscles results in firmly tight eyelids with wrinkles around the eyes. Darwin argued that this response occurs in humans regardless of cultures and races and that individuals with this response would be more likely to survive than those who did not. 
Darwin also posited the principle of antithesis, in which an opposite state of mind produced opposing characteristics in expressive behaviors. For example, happiness and sadness are opposite states of mind and are expressed by two opposing movements— zygomatic major, which pulls the lip corners up, and depressor anguli oris (triangularis), which pulls the lip corners down. These contrasting movements are invaluable in interpersonal communication as they quickly communicate contrary mental states. In addition to the three main principles just listed, Darwin also proposed an inhibition hypothesis in that people are unable to perfectly simulate facial expressions in the absence 
364 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
of a genuine emotion and are unable to completely suppress their true expressions when feeling strong emotions, resulting in emotional leakage on the face. 
 Post- Darwin Darwin’s work, while influential and provocative, was not without criticism. One main concern about his ideas was the lack of hard evidence that supported his claims. Many of Darwin’s original ideas were supported only through his observations and descriptions of emotional expression in humans and other animals. Albeit done in painstaking detail, such descriptions would not be accepted as scientific proof for his universality thesis. (He did, however, conduct the first judgment study of emotions.) 
Darwin’s claims were also challenged by some anthropologists such as Margaret Mead, Gregory Bateson, and Ray Birdwhistell (see reviews in Ekman, Friesen, & Ellsworth, 1972). These scholars claimed that facial expressions of emotion could not possibly be universal because they had observed many cultural differences when conducting their fieldwork. Just as every culture learned a different verbal language, they argued, every culture must have a different language of facial expressions. 
Unfortunately, early research on this topic was rare and did not resolve the conflicts between these two viewpoints. Between the time of Darwin’s original writing and the 1960s, only seven studies attempted to address this gap. They did not, however, produce unequivocal data speaking to the issue of the possible universality of emotional expression (reviewed in Ekman et al., 1972). Thus, for the first half of the twentieth century, the question of whether facial expressions of emotion, and emotion in general, were universal or culture- specific was unresolved. If anything, the general zeitgeist of the times leaned toward viewing emotions and faces as culture- specific. 
The Original Universality Studies It was not until the mid- 1960s when psychologist Sylvan Tomkins (1962, 1963), a pioneer in modern studies of human emotion, joined forces independently with Paul Ekman and Carroll Izard to conduct what has become known today as the original universality studies. In the first of these studies, these researchers obtained judgments of faces thought to express emotions pan- culturally by members of a number of different cultures (Ekman, 1972; Ekman & Friesen, 1971; Izard, 1971). The findings from these studies demonstrated the universal recognition of six emotional expressions— anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, and surprise— as judges all around the world agreed on what emotion was portrayed in the faces. 
One possible criticism of the initial set of studies was that all of the cultures involved in those studies were relatively literate, urbanized, and modern. To address this potential criticism, Ekman and his colleague Wallace Friesen conducted two studies in two preliterate tribes in the highlands of New Guinea (Ekman & Friesen, 1971; Ekman, Sorenson, & Friesen, 1969). These were cultures that were living essentially in primitive ways, with no formal systems of writing. In the first study, the researchers demonstrated that the 
 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  365 
New Guinean tribe members, who had never seen Westerners before, recognized the same facial expressions of emotion as did members of the cultures in the earlier studies. In the second study, Ekman and Friesen demonstrated that expressions posed by the preliterate tribe members as they reacted to emotion- eliciting stories were reliably judged by US Americans who had never seen preliterate tribespeople before. These two studies were influential in demonstrating that the previous findings had not occurred because of shared visual input (e.g., mass media, television, movies, magazines). 
The next study was a production study, in which emotions were elicited in participants who reacted spontaneously to the elicitors and whose produced facial expressions were directly measured. The first study that documented the universal production of facial expressions of emotions was Friesen’s (1972). In that study, 25 American and Japanese participants watched highly stressful films (body mutilation and sinus surgery) while their spontaneous facial reactions were recorded. Coding of the facial behaviors that occurred indicated that the American and Japanese participants displayed emotions such as disgust, fear, sadness, and anger similarly when the participants of the two groups watched the stimuli alone. The study was meaningful because it marshaled the first cross- cultural evidence for the production of facial expressions of emotion when emotions were spontaneously elicited. 
The initial studies described here are known as the “original universality studies” as they were the first to document that certain facial expressions of emotion were universally expressed and recognized. This initial discovery of the universal basis for emotional expression had an enormous impact on contemporary psychology as expressions provided an objective and reliable signal of emotion. Using universality as a platform, methods of measuring facial behaviors validly and reliably were developed, which have been a boon to subsequent research and the empirical literatures. 
Subsequent Research on Emotions Across Cultures: Documenting both Cross- Cultural Similarities and Differences Findings documenting the universality of facial expressions of emotion and the development of emotion coding systems led to a plethora of research, theory, and application in psychology in the past half- century. These studies have made enormous contributions to studies in all areas of psychology and particularly in social, personality, and developmental psychology, with applications in clinical, forensic, industrial, and organizational psychology. All of this was made possible through the contributions of the original universality studies. 
More relevant to this chapter, subsequent cross- cultural research on emotion blossomed. Much of this research continued the initial line of facial expressions of emotion and documented both cultural similarities and differences. For example, studies of congenitally blind human adults and children, kin versus non- kin, infant development across cultures, and nonhuman primates have all provided strong evidence for the 
 
366 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
universality of facial expressions of emotion (for a comprehensive review, see Hwang & Matsumoto, 2016). 
But cultural differences in facial expressions of emotion were also documented. They were initially observed in a second condition of the Friesen (1972) study. When the American and Japanese participants viewed the stressful stimuli alone, they displayed the same expressions of disgust, anger, fear, and sadness. When with a higher status experimenter, however, there were dramatic differences. While the Americans tended to continue to show their negative feelings, many Japanese smiled, concealing their negative feelings. These findings led to the concept of display rules, which are culturally prescribed rules, learned early in life, that dictate the management and modification of the universal expressions depending on social circumstance (Ekman, 1972; Friesen, 1972). Since then, many other studies have also demonstrated cultural differences in facial expressions and display rules (Edelmann et al., 1987; Matsumoto, 1990, 1993; Matsumoto & Kupperbusch, 2001; Matsumoto, Takeuchi, Andayani, Kouznetsova, & Krupp, 1998; Matsumoto, Yoo, Hirayama, & Petrova, 2005; Waxer, 1985). 
Cultural similarities and differences have also been observed in many other domains of emotion, including studies of the antecedents of emotions (Boucher & Brandt, 1981; Brandt & Boucher, 1985; Buunk & Hupka, 1987; Galati & Sciaky, 1995; Scherer, Matsumoto, Wallbott, & Kudoh, 1988; Scherer, Summerfield, & Wallbott, 1983; Scherer & Wallbott, 1994), appraisal processes (Mauro, Sato, & Tucker, 1992; Roseman, Dhawan, Rettek, & Naidu, 1995; Scherer, 1997a, 1997b), subjective experience (Kitayama & Markus, 1994; Kitayama, Markus, & Matsumoto, 1995; Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Matsumoto, Nezlek, & Koopmann, 2007; Scherer et al., 1983; Scherer & Wallbott, 1994; Wierzbicka, 1994), and concepts, language, attitudes, beliefs, and values about emotion (Levy, 1973, 1983; Lutz, 1983; Romney, Boyd, Moore, Batchelder, & Brazill, 1996; Romney, Moore, & Rusch, 1997; Russell, 1991; Schwartz, 2004; Schwartz & Bardi, 2001; Tsai, 2007; Tsai, Knutson, & Fung, 2006). 
Collectively, studies from the past five decades have flooded the literature with evidence for both cross- cultural similarities and differences, supporting both biological and cultural determinants of various aspects of emotion. But despite the continuing emergence of overwhelming amounts of evidence, our theoretical understanding of the relation between culture and emotion has not progressed much and disagreements concerning universality versus cultural specificity still exist, as well as concerning the contributions of biology and culture. To be sure, previous reviews have led to substantial insights (e.g., Mesquita, 2003; Mesquita & Frijda, 1992; Shweder, Haidt, Horton, & Joseph, 2008; van Hemert, Poortinga, & van de Vijver, 2007). But, even today, many contemporary authors argue about whether emotions are either universal (and biologically based) or culture- specific (and thus learned and constructed), as if they are mutually exclusive dichotomies (e.g., see Barrett, Mesquita, Ochsner, & Gross, 2007; Feldman Barrett, 2006a, 2006b). Despite the fact that concepts like display rules allow for models of emotion that posit the coexistence of a biologically innate, genetically encoded system and cultural learning in 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  367 
the use and modification of the system, the field has not progressed much beyond such either/ or theoretical dichotomies, which may be created by limitations in our ways of theory- building. 
In the next section, we present a model that goes beyond previous reviews to explain disparate research findings and integrate universality with culture- specificity and biological innateness with cultural construction. We suggest the simultaneous coexistence of both universality based on a biological substrate and cultural differences based on learned constructions and we argue that such frameworks are possible, more realistic, and better account for the data to date. 
The Simultaneous Coexistence of Universality and Cultural Specificity: Integrating Biology and Culture The Main Proposition We offer a biocultural model of emotion that posits five propositions and tenets (see Table 12.1): 
 1. Humans possess an innate, biologically based, core system of emotion that allows for the elicitation of certain emotional responses that have universal physiological, psychological, and social components. We call this the Core Emotion System (Levenson, 1999, 2003, also did so). This core system is biologically resident, a product of our evolutionary history, and provides the platform for universality in the production of immediate reactions when these emotions are elicited, which we call Universal Priming Reactions. 
TABLE 12.1 Propositions and Main Tenets of the Biocultural Model of Emotion 
Proposition Label Main Tenet 
1 Core Emotion System Humans possess an innate, biologically based, core system for emotion elicitation that produces Universal Priming Reactions. 
2 Front- End Cultural Calibration 
Cultures regulate what elicits emotions. 
3 Back- End Cultural Calibration 
Cultures regulate the expressive reactions and instrumental behavioral responses that occur when emotions are elicited. 
4 Cultural Elaboration of Emotional Experience 
Cultures facilitate the self- report of experience (feelings). 
5 Cultural Elaboration of Emotion Meanings 
Cultures elaborate on emotions to construct culturally based emotions and culture- specific attitudes, values, and beliefs about emotion. 
 
 
368 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
 2. Cultures regulate the Core Emotion System to calibrate what we become emotional about in the first place. Cultural learning and knowledge play a large role in this calibration. We call this process Front- End Cultural Calibration. 
 3. Cultures also regulate the Core Emotion System to modify and adapt the expressive reactions and instrumental behavioral responses that occur as a result of emotion elicitation. We call this Back- End Cultural Calibration. 
 4. Cultures (through language) facilitate the self- report of experience, which is partially culturally constructed. We call this the Cultural Elaboration of Emotional Experience. 
 5. Unique human cognitive abilities including language, memory, and abstract thinking allow cultures to elaborate on human emotions by facilitating the construction of culturally based emotions and their associated meanings. We call this the Cultural Elaboration of Emotion Meanings. 
We assume that humans have a biologically innate, core emotion system that allows for the elicitation of emotions (LeDoux, 2000; LeDoux & Phelps, 2008; Panksepp, 1994, 2008a). When certain emotions are triggered, they produce Universal Priming Reactions. Culture regulates this core system by calibrating it to culturally available events so that individuals learn what to become emotional about in the first place. Culture also regulates the priming reactions and behavioral responses after an emotion so that individuals learn what kinds of expressive behaviors to display and instrumental behaviors to engage in once emotion is elicited. Culture elaborates subjective experience, affecting the relative intensity of emotional experiences and facilitating the emergence of culturally constructed emotions, which are unique to human cultures and require cultural knowledge for elicitation. These emotions may be universal but not necessarily biologically innate and they may be somewhat different in different cultures. Shame, guilt, jealousy, and love, for instance, may exist all around the world, but there are likely major cultural differences in what specific cultural events elicit them, their form, function, and meaning. Cultures also elaborate emotions by creating specific emotional meanings, which are attitudes, values, and beliefs about emotions requiring higher level cognitive skills including abstract thinking, memory, and language, guiding how individuals should think about emotions. All of these are more highly influenced by culture. 
Three Premises About Emotion and Emotion Research In order to integrate the seemingly disparate literature briefly introduced earlier into a more cohesive whole provided by the above- mentioned theoretical framework, we offer three premises that underlie our model: (1) emotions should be distinguished from other affective phenomena; (2) different types of emotions exist; and (3) within an emotion different domains exist, some more influenced by biology and some by culture. Given the premises and the preceding theoretical framework, dichotomous, mutually exclusive questions concerning whether emotions are universal or not, or biologically innate or 
 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  369 
not, should be replaced by questions concerning the degree of relative contribution of biological and cultural factors. We contend that the relative contribution of biological and cultural factors to emotion depends on what emotion is being studied and the specific domain of emotion assessed. Given that previous literature has not made such distinctions, it is no wonder that controversies have existed. 
Premise 1: Emotions or Not? Studies involving emotions need to distinguish them from other affective phenomena. Doing so requires a definition. Researchers study emotion with many different implicit definitions and differences in what researchers call emotions may account for many of the differences reported in the literature. Although it is difficult to arrive at a consensual definition of emotion that encompasses all possible types of emotion and distinguishes emotion from other affective phenomena, we believe that researchers need to make explicit their working definitions so that others can understand what part of the affective world they call emotion. We do so here. 
We define emotion as transient, bio- psycho- social reactions to events that have consequences for our welfare and potentially require immediate action. They are biological because they involve physiological responses from the central and autonomic nervous systems. They are psychological because they involve specific mental processes required for elicitation and regulation of response, direct mental activities, and incentivize behavior. They are social because they are often elicited by social factors and have social meaning when elicited. The key characteristics of emotion in our definition is that it is a state not a trait; a mental condition, not just physiological or cognitive; the product of an appraisal process; and involves multiple components including affect, physiological response, mental changes, and expressive behavior. 
Many studies conflate any affective phenomenon with emotion, probably because our awareness of emotion is represented in affect (although we recognize the existence of unconscious emotions; see Winkielman & Berridge, 2004). But humans experience a broad range of affective phenomena, some of which are emotions (in our definition), others not (e.g., tiredness, hunger). For example, Kitayama, Markus, and Kurokawa (2000) examined feelings of superiority, being on top of the world, moody, friendly feelings, respect, and calmness. Clearly these are affective phenomena and important mental states, but we would not call them emotions. If emotions are different from other affective phenomena, then findings about non- emotions may not be generalizable to emotions. 
Other researchers may have different definitions of emotion and different definitions may lead to different conclusions about what to include as emotions, and we encourage such viewpoints. Our point is that emotions may be different from other affective phenomena and that researchers should have an explicit working definition of emotion and evaluate the literature or conduct research accordingly. 
 
370 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Premise 2: Different Types of Emotion All emotions are not the same; that is, different types of emotions may exist and recognizing these differences may be necessary for understanding the relations between culture and emotion. In the past, different types of emotions have been proposed, including basic emotions (Ekman, 1992, 1999; Izard, 2007), self- conscious emotions (Keltner & Buswell, 1997; Tangney & Fischer, 1995; Tracy & Robins, 2004), positive emotions (Fredrickson, 2001; Fredrickson & Losada, 2005), prosocial emotions (McCullough, Bono, & Root, 2007), and moral emotions (Haidt, 2001). A comprehensive treatise on a taxonomy of emotions is beyond the scope of this chapter. For our purposes here, we propose a very gross distinction between emotions that evidence indicates are biologically innate (reviewed in more detail later; Buck, 1999; Ekman, 1992, 1999; Izard, 2007; LeDoux & Phelps, 2008; Panksepp, 2007, 2008a) and those for which there is no or insufficient evidence. We call the former biologically based emotions and the latter culturally constructed emotions. 
There is strong evidence for emotions such as anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise to be classified as biologically based emotions (Buck, 1999; Ekman, 1999; Izard, 2007), but there are disagreements about others. And the status for some emotions is unclear; expressive behaviors typically associated with shame, embarrassment, or pride, for example, have been observed in nonhuman animals (De Waal, 1989), but evidence for their cross- cultural expression, physiological signatures, and antecedents and reactions is still lacking. We do not argue for the inclusion of any specific emotion into either category; instead we argue that a classification should exist and may be useful in understanding the literature. Our propositions here can be understood regardless of what specific emotions are considered biologically based or culturally constructed. Furthermore, we do not argue that our distinctions are the only available or best. We encourage future theorizing to produce better categorizations and eventually a more accurate taxonomy of emotions. 
Premise 3: Different Domains of Emotion Different domains of emotion exist and have different implications for our understanding of the associated biological and cultural contributions. For example, some studies have examined immediate expressive reactions such as facial expressions, vocal utterances, physiological reactions, or mental changes (Levenson, Ekman, Heider, & Friesen, 1992; Tsai, Levenson, & McCoy, 2006). Others have examined self- reported subjective experiences at the time of emotion elicitation or in recall (Kitayama, Mesquita, & Karasawa, 2006), the meaning of emotion (via descriptions of different aspects, features, or effects of an emotion; see Uchida & Kitayama, 2009), the pleasantness of the events that elicit emotion (Mesquita & Karasawa, 2002), concerns about emotions (Mesquita, 2001; Mesquita & Karasawa, 2002), or concepts about emotion (Russell, 1990, 1991). All of these were called “emotion” but actually sampled what we consider to be different domains of emotion. 
It is important to distinguish the domain of emotion being studied. We call the im-mediate responses that occur when emotion is elicited Universal Priming Reactions; these 
 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  371 
include physiological responses, expressive behavior, and cognitive gating, all of which typically occur within seconds (or fractions thereof) of an emotion- eliciting event and require precise measurement with quick resolution. Priming Reactions do not require language or conscious deliberation. We call the overt behaviors that represent adaptations to the environment Instrumental Behaviors. We call the self- reported experience or feelings part of emotion Subjective Experience; this requires language and some higher order thinking (such as introspection). Finally, we call attitudes, values, beliefs, lay theories, and concepts of emotion Emotion Meanings. These require language and higher order cognition. These distinctions are important because different findings can be obtained depending on the specific domain of emotion studied. 
Culture Like emotion, writers have attempted to define culture for years and it is difficult to arrive at a consensual definition of it. We offer our working definition so readers can evaluate our interpretations of the literature vis- à- vis our definition. We define human culture as a unique meaning and information system, shared by a group and transmitted across generations (Matsumoto, 2007; Matsumoto & Juang, 2013). Cultural meanings and information enhance social coordination, allowing for greater differentiations among social groups, institutionalizing cultural practices and customs, and prescribing social norms and expectations for all important aspects of social life such as mating, aggression, and cooperation. Because groups communicate their solutions across generations, each generation need not create entirely new solutions, thus ensuring efficiency for survival. 
Culture is a response to ecological and environmental context (DeKay & Buss, 1992; Georgas, van de Vijver, & Berry, 2004). It is the complex of ways that emerges when groups address ecological problems to meet biological needs and social motives. Culture is a set of time- tested solutions for the problem of how to survive and reproduce. Human cultures are evolved potentials, albeit likely more recent in evolutionary history than the emotion system. The emergence of human cultures coincides with the evolution of a host of complex cognitive abilities including language (Premack, 2004), self– other knowledge, the ability to know that other people not only are intentional agents but can share intentions (Tomasello, 1999; Tomasello, Carpenter, Call, Behne, & Moll, 2005), and the ability to continually build on improvements and discoveries (ratcheting; Tomasello, Kruger, & Ratner, 1993). Many of these coincide with the development of the higher cortical areas of the brain and the language areas compared to the location of the emotion system, which is in the older, subcortical areas. 
Cultures create norms concerning the regulation of emotion to facilitate social coordination because emotions are primary motivators of behavior (Tomkins, 1962, 1963) and have important social functions (Keltner & Haidt, 1999). Norms are guidelines for expected behaviors, thinking, and feelings derived from the cultural meanings ascribed to contexts, relationships, and events. They identify the range of permissible behavior that allows groups to function effectively. Cultures encourage adherence to 
 
372 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
norms and create sanctions against infractions, which aids their members and groups in negotiating the complexity of human social life. By regulating emotions in socially desirable ways, cultures ensure that expressive and instrumental behaviors follow culturally prescribed scripts, increasing social coordination and decreasing social chaos and conflict (see Figure 12.1; see also Chapter 5 by Yoshihisa Kashima on the functions of culture). 
Summary We propose that it is necessary to distinguish among different types (e.g., biologically based vs. culturally constructed emotions) and domains (e.g., Priming Reactions, Instrumental Behaviors, Subjective Experience, and Emotion Meanings) of emotion in furthering our understanding of the relation between culture and emotion. Based on these delineations, we hypothesize that the relative contributions of biology and culture to emotion differ depending on what type and domain of emotion is studied. The contribution of biology is greatest (and the relative contributions of culture least) when Priming Reactions of biologically based emotions are studied, driving universality in these reactions. When Emotion Meanings are studied, the relative contributions of culture are greatest (while the contributions of biology least), producing large cultural differences in this aspect of emotion. Studies of Subjective Experience and Instrumental Behaviors should occupy intermediary positions, with contributions from both biology and culture (Figure 12.2). Here, we describe in more detail the specific propositions and hypotheses that flow from this model and research that supports this framework.

The Core Emotion System and Universal Priming Reactions The Proposition Emotions are reactions produced by a rapid, biologically innate information processing system that helps us act with minimal conscious deliberation (Cosmides & Tooby, 2000; Ekman, 1992; Lazarus, 1991; Tomkins, 1962; Tooby & Cosmides, 2008). Levenson (1999) called this the “core emotion system” and suggested that it evolved to deal with species- constant problems related to survival in a time- tested, predictable, and automatic fashion. These problems could occur in interactions with nature or with other humans. Problems associated with birth, battle, death, and seduction have occurred throughout our evolutionary history, and emotions aided in adapting to those problems rapidly and with minimal conscious deliberation. If humans didn’t have emotions, they could not make rapid decisions concerning whether to attack, defend, flee, care for others, reject spoiled food, or approach something useful. And babies would have to wait to acquire language to communicate with their caregivers. For instance, drinking spoiled milk or eating rotten eggs has negative consequences for our welfare. Disgust helps us immediately take action by rejecting them, which is adaptive because it aids in our ultimate survival and allows us to adapt immediately without much thinking. In some instances, deliberately thinking about what to do might cost one one’s life especially in imminent, potentially life- threatening situations. 
The core emotion system is hard- wired, fairly impermeable to modification by experience, and relatively unchanged throughout the lifespan. It resides in the subcortical

areas of the brain in and around the amygdala (LaBar & LeDoux, 2003; LeDoux & Phelps, 2008; Panksepp, 2008a, 2008b). When emotions are triggered, they orchestrate other systems such as perception, attention, inference, learning, memory, goal choice, motivational priorities, physiological reactions, motor behaviors, and behavioral decision- making (Cosmides & Tooby, 2000; Tooby & Cosmides, 2008). They simultaneously activate certain systems and deactivate others in order to prevent the chaos of competing systems operating at the same time, allowing for coordinated responses to environmental stimuli (Levenson, 1999). Emotions initiate a system of components that includes subjective experience (feelings), expressive behaviors, physiological reactions, action tendencies for instrumental behavior, and cognition; the term “emotion” is a metaphor for these reactions. All of these occur because emotions help prime action, preparing individuals to engage in instrumental behaviors to adapt to the environment. 
We call the reactions that occur immediately as a direct consequence of the triggering of emotions and that help to prime behavior Priming Reactions. These consist of nonverbal expressions, physiological reactions, and cognitive gating. Our proposition concerning the existence of a core emotion system leads to the hypothesis that when examining Priming Reactions of biologically based emotions, we expect relatively less contribution of culture and greater contribution of biology, producing universality in response. 
The Evidence Evidence for the universality of immediate priming reactions in facial expressions comes from multiple sources of data. Since the original universality studies described earlier, many cross- cultural studies have demonstrated that a set of facial expressions of emotions are universally produced (Matsumoto, Keltner, Shiota, O’Sullivan, & Frank, 2008; Matsumoto & Willingham, 2006) and recognized (Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002; Matsumoto, 2001). For instance, the immediate facial expressions of emotion of judo athletes from 35 countries in medal matches at the Olympic Games differentiated winners from losers, and there were no cultural differences (Matsumoto & Willingham, 2006). Congenitally blind adults and children produce the same facial expressions when the same emotions are triggered as do sighted individuals (Charlesworth & Kreutzer, 1973; Dumas, 1932; Eibl- Eibesfeldt, 1973; Freedman, 1964; Fulcher, 1942; Galati, Scherer, & Ricci- Bitti, 1997; Goodenough, 1932; Ortega, Iglesias, Fernandez, & Corraliza, 1983; Thompson, 1941). The facial expressions of blind judo athletes from 23 countries at the Paralympic Games were at near- perfect concordance with the expressions of sighted athletes (Matsumoto & Willingham, 2009). Because congenitally blind individuals could not have possibly learned the expressions visibly, they must be the products of a biologically resident ability. The studies of sighted and blind athletes at the Olympic Games were notable because they examined facial expressions produced spontaneously by individuals from many different cultures in a real- life setting. Other evidence for universality of priming reactions in facial expressions comes 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  375 
from studies of kin versus non- kin, infant development of emotional expressions across different cultures, and nonhuman primates (for a comprehensive review, see Hwang & Matsumoto, 2016). 
Another source of evidence for universal priming reactions comes from studies of physiological signatures of emotion. When emotions are aroused and facial expressions are used as markers of those emotions, discrete physiological signatures occur in both the autonomic and central nervous systems (Davidson, 2003; Ekman, Davidson, & Friesen, 1990; Ekman, Levenson, & Friesen, 1983; Levenson, Carstensen, Friesen, & Ekman, 1991; Levenson & Ekman, 2002; Levenson, Ekman, & Friesen, 1990; Mauss, Levenson, McCarter, Wilhelm, & Gross, 2005; Rainville, Bechara, Naqvi, & Damasio, 2006; Tsai & Levenson, 1997). These patterns exist in people from cultures as widely divergent as the United States and the Minangkabau of West Sumatra, Indonesia (Levenson et  al., 1992). Other studies testing different ethnic groups in the United States reporting no ethnic differences in either expressive behavior or physiological reactions also provide further support for universal priming reactions (Soto, Levenson, & Ebling, 2005; Tsai, Chentsova- Dutton, Freire- Bebeau, & Pryzmus, 2002). 
Studies documenting the effects of facial expressions of emotion on cognitive gating provide further evidence for why immediate priming reactions are universal (for a comprehensive review, see Hwang & Matsumoto, 2016). Facial expressions of emotion gate attention and regulate respiration, augment subjective experience, and regulate interpersonal relationships. Facial expressions of emotion are also linked with appraisal processes and subsequent behaviors across cultures. Additionally, there is evidence for universality in vocal utterances associated with emotions (Sauter, Eisner, Ekman, & Scott, 2010; Simon- Thomas, Keltner, Sauter, Sinicropi- Yao, & Abramson, 2009). All of these functions are part of the anatomical and physiological hardware with which humans are born with, and thus universal. 
Cultural Calibration of the Core Emotion System Front- End Cultural Calibration of Eliciting Events 
The Proposition Emotions are elicited as we scan our environments and evaluate (appraise) objects, events, or situations for consequences to our welfare (Ekman, 2003; Ellsworth & Scherer, 2003; Frijda, Kuipers, & ter Schure, 1989; Roseman, 1984; Roseman et al., 1995; Scherer, Schorr, & Johnstone, 2001). If events do not have such consequences, we continue scanning; if they do, they trigger emotion in order to prime action and incentivize behavior (Frijda et al., 1989; Tomkins, 1962, 1963). One way for cultures to regulate emotions is via front- end calibration of the emotion system to culturally available events (Figure 12.3). Human cultural lives are replete with culture- specific events that require appropriate behavioral responses for adaptation but that need to be learned. Cultures ascribe meanings that are 
 
 
 
376 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
drawn from the collective pool of cultural wisdom to those events; those meanings facilitate the triggering of emotions in the first place. 
Cultural calibration of the emotion system can result in both universality and culture- specificity, consistent with previous conclusions of this aspect of emotion (Mesquita & Frijda, 1992). Because biologically based emotions are universal and have the same intra- and interpersonal functions, emotions such as anger and disgust are potentially destructive emotions in any culture (Rozin, Lowery, Imada, & Haidt, 1999). For these reasons, people of all cultures minimize the expression of these emotions toward higher status others or to in- group members (Matsumoto et al., 2006). Similarly, a gun is not something that existed in our evolutionary history. Yet, during enculturation, people of many cultures learn to associate guns with death, harm, crime, and threat to safety and well- being. Thus, a gun can be encoded with the same psychological themes across cultures, producing common but learned responses to the same stimulus event. 
Cultural differences in emotion triggers arise when culture- specific meanings are attributed to objects, events, and situations, which is consistent with previous reviews of this aspect of emotion (Shweder et al., 2008). For instance, while the minimization of destructive emotions toward higher status others may be universal, exactly who is a higher status person and how those emotions are minimized may be culturally variable. In many cultures, age is a status marker; in other cultures, it can be wealth, occupation, or gender. Death rituals are associated with vastly different meanings across cultures, from celebrations of life to events of grieving and mourning (Mead, 1943). Different cultural meanings of these events become associated with different emotion- eliciting themes and produce different culturally based emotional reactions to the same event; this would

explain the vast differences in original debates of universality versus cultural specificity of emotion described earlier. Cultural differences can also occur by limitations of culturally available events. That is, if an event occurs in one culture but not another, then it cannot be an event to which emotions are elicited in a culture in which it doesn’t exist. If a gun doesn’t exist in a culture, it is likely that it won’t elicit an emotional reaction. 
The Evidence Data support the contention that many of the same types of events trigger biologically based emotions across cultures, providing evidence for cultural similarities in emotion triggers. The most prominent work is that of Scherer and colleagues, who conducted a number of studies assessing the quality and nature of emotional experiences in many different cultures. One study involved approximately 3,000 participants in 37 countries on five continents (Scherer, 1997a, 1997b). Respondents reported about situations that elicited anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, shame, and guilt. The situations were coded into categories such as good news and bad news, temporary and permanent separation, and success and failure in achievement situations. The resulting events included both events that are found in nature (death) and those that are culturally learned (watching television news). No culture- specific antecedent category was necessary, indicating that all categories of events generally occurred in all cultures. In addition, there were many similarities across cultures in the relative frequency with which each of the events elicited emotions. The most frequent elicitors of happiness across cultures were “relationships with friends,” “temporary meetings with friends,” and “achievement situations.” The most frequent elicitors of anger were “relationships” and “injustice.” The most frequent elicitors of sadness were “relationships” and “death.” 
But there are also considerable sources of evidence for cultural differences in emo-tion triggers (Scherer, 1997b). Cultural differences occur in the relative frequencies of different events to trigger emotion and many of these are related to cultural limitations in the available events or in the meanings of those events. In Matsumoto and colleagues’ (Matsumoto, Kudoh, Scherer, & Wallbott, 1988) study based on the Scherer et al. dataset described earlier, world news was a more frequent trigger of sadness for Europeans and Americans than for the Japanese; problems in relationships, however, produced more sadness for the Japanese than for Americans or Europeans. Strangers and achievement- related situations elicited more fear for Americans, whereas novel situations, traffic, and relationships were more frequent elicitors of fear for the Japanese. In Japan, crime is relatively low and it is not uncommon for people to walk outside safely at night; thus, walking in the dark would elicit less fear there than in the United States. Finally, situations involving strangers were more frequent elicitors of anger for the Japanese than for the Americans or Europeans. Situations involving relationships brought about more anger for Americans than for Japanese. 
These data support the idea that the same types of events and the same underlying themes in all cultures elicit emotions. But there are cultural differences in the relative 
 
378 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
frequencies of events that trigger emotions and the existence of culture- specific triggers. Thus, eating a dog may be a luxury in one culture, resulting in joy, but a revolting thing in other cultures, eliciting disgust. All of these reactions are enabled because of a core emotion system. 
Back- End Cultural Calibration of Emotional Reactions and Responses 
The Proposition Cultures calibrate the core emotion system on the back end (i.e., once emotions are elicited) via display and behavior rules, which are norms to help manage and modify priming reactions and instrumental behavioral responses to what is appropriate in specific situational contexts (Figure 12.3). We distinguish between reactions and responses; the former refers to immediate, relatively unconscious manifestations of elicited emotions and the latter to more conscious, deliberate instrumental actions that aid individuals in adapting to their environments. 
Display rules serve to amplify, deamplify, neutralize, qualify, or conceal immediate priming reactions (Ekman & Friesen, 1969), creating a complex and elaborate range of expressive behavior when emotions are aroused. Individuals can also simulate emotions when they are not elicited. Display rules are guidelines for expressive behavior that are consistent with social roles and norms. They serve an important function in culture by helping to regulate emotional expressions, which aids social coordination and group survival. 
Behavior rules are culturally based rules that dictate the range of appropriate instrumental behaviors in any given context given an elicited emotion. These rules are learned throughout the lifespan and facilitated by culturally laden meanings infused in each context. That is, although emotions provide the impulse for behavior (related to the concept of action readiness; Frijda et al., 1989; Frijda & Tcherkassof, 1997), whether individuals engage in instrumental behavior, and how, is determined in large part by context, which derives meaning from cultures. Thus, while anger may provide the impulse for aggression, whether one yells, hits, steams about, sits and fumes internally, or even cooperates is all dependent on culturally based rules for specific contexts (see Matsumoto & Wilson, 2008, for more discussion). 
Because people of all cultures must deal with the same problems of social coordination and generate much the same meanings for the same social relationships, some display and behavior rules should be universal. For example, because mothers and fathers play much the same roles across cultures with regard to childbirth, childrearing, and family dynamics (Georgas, Berry, Van de Vijver, Kagitcibasi, & Poortinga, 2006), some meanings of self– father or self– mother relationships may be universal and thus lead to similar rules across cultures. Likewise, family and close friends likely have very similar meanings across cultures, producing cultural similarities in rules toward these relationships. 
 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  379 
But cultural differences in the meanings ascribed to context, events, social roles, and relationships may produce different display and behavior rules. For example, while the social roles of “mother” and “father” exist in all cultures, in some cultures the father may be seen as a revered authority figure; other cultures may view mothers and fathers as equal partners. “Being a good research participant” may mean “to be yourself and to act as if you were alone” in some cultures but it might mean “maintain a good impression regardless of how you truly feel” in others. The social role of “being a good daughter- in- law” may require a woman in certain contexts to endure snide comments or to be dealt with as a second- class citizen. In order to enact this social role correctly, women need to regulate their expressive reactions and instrumental behaviors in those situations. 
Thus, we hypothesize that display rules will produce universality in Priming Reactions of biologically based emotions when there is cross- cultural consistency in the meaning of context, events, or social roles, but cultural differences when there is cultural variation in those meanings. Behavior rules will produce greater cultural differences in instrumental behaviors when emotions are elicited because they are largely moderated by context. 
The Evidence Consistent with our hypothesis for expressive behaviors, several studies have shown cultural similarities in expressive behaviors in different contexts. Friesen’s (1972) classic study of Americans and Japanese viewing stressful films when alone (described earlier) was the first to provide such evidence. Other studies have demonstrated cultural differences in expressive behavior, likely due to cultural differences in the meaning of context. Matsumoto and Kupperbusch (2001) showed that allocentric participants masked their negative feelings to a higher status experimenter while idiocentric individuals did not, replicating Friesen’s (1972) findings in their second condition. Allocentric participants masked positive feelings as well, suggesting the existence of display rules that prescribed the suppression of all emotions, not just negative ones. This finding was consistent with other findings that collectivistic cultures are associated with a display rule norm of less expressivity overall than are individualistic cultures (Matsumoto, Yoo et al., 2008), suggesting that expressive regulation for all emotions is central to the preservation of social order in these cultures. Tsai, Levenson, and McCoy (2006) demonstrated that European American dating couples produced more positive and less negative emotional behaviors when conversing about conflicts in their relationships than did Chinese American couples despite the fact that there were no differences in emotional experience or autonomic reactivity. 
In Matsumoto and Willingham’s (2006) study of Olympic medalists, silver medalists did not smile at all immediately at the completion of their final match (which they lost), but they smiled during the subsequent medal ceremonies, regardless of their culture and despite some of them having strong feelings to the contrary just minutes before. Presumably, the athletes all had a display rule to be a good loser in public. People around 
 
380 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
the world have a universal display rule to express more positive emotions when with family and close friends but to suppress their negative emotions with strangers (Matsumoto, Yoo et al., 2008). These display rules correspond to what has been found in studies of actual spontaneous expressive behavior (Buck, Losow, Murphy, & Costanzo, 1992; Fridlund, 1991; Fridlund, Kenworthy, & Jaffey, 1992; Matsumoto & Kupperbusch, 2001; Wagner & Smith, 1991). These universal display rules can be produced by cross- cultural similarities in the meaning of social contexts and social roles. 
Emotional expressions can be both universal and culture- specific for the same person in the same context if displays are examined in sequence across time. This occurs especially when intense emotions are aroused in a context where individuals need to regulate their expressions. When emotions are aroused, impulses emanating from subcortical areas of the brain initiate the emotion response system, including expressive behavior (LeDoux, 2000; Panksepp, 2008a). At the same time, the facial nerve receives stimulation from cortical areas under voluntary control (Matsumoto & Lee, 1993; Rinn, 1991), which would be associated with display rules. Thus, the initial and immediate emotional reactions (originating from the subcortex) may be universal and appear first because their neural connections are lower and closer to the facial nerve. Culturally influenced emotional displays may occur subsequently because of the additional neural work necessary for regulatory needs to drive expressive behavior from the cortex. Matsumoto and colleagues (2009) provided evidence for this in a reanalysis of the expressions of Olympic athletes whose first, immediate facial reactions upon match completion were universal (Matsumoto & Willingham, 2006); their subsequent expressions, however, were culturally variable. Athletes from urban, individualistic cultures expressed their emotions more while athletes from less urban, more collectivistic cultures masked their emotions more. The subsequent, culturally moderated expressions typically happened within 1 second of the initial expression. 
We know of no cross- cultural research that has directly examined similarities or differences in instrumental behaviors when emotions are elicited. There is, however, indirect evidence. For example, a number of studies have shown that people of different cultures engage in different cooperative versus competitive behaviors when playing economic decision- making games (Henrich et al., 2001; Henrich et al., 2006; Osterbeek, Sloof, & van de Kuilen, 2004), and these games are infused with emotion. Also, intercultural dyads playing these same types of games generally have worse outcomes than same- culture dyads, and the latest studies in this area have linked these outcomes with culture- level dimensions and emotions experienced prior to game play (Matsumoto & Hwang, 2011, 2015). Nevertheless, this area is ripe for future research. We anticipate that intensity of emotion, along with context, will moderate the relationship between emotion and instrumental behaviors such that more intense emotions will produce less culturally regulated behaviors. Cross- cultural research that has demonstrated that specific variants of the universal facial expression of anger have been reliably associated 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  381 
with two types of acts of imminent aggression support such notions (Matsumoto & Hwang, 2014). 
Summary The cultural calibration of the core emotion system allows for a multiplicity of uses. Cultures calibrate the emotion system by linking emotion with culturally available events, allowing for emotions to be elicited in a wide range of situations and ensuring that culturally relevant stimuli get a response. When cultural events are identified as worthy of an emotional response, cultural calibration influences the reactions and responses produced, linking emotions with specific repertoires of expressive and instrumental behaviors that each culture deems appropriate and necessary for social coordination. This calibration allows for a complex interplay between evolved biology and cultural learning on reactions and responses (i.e., Priming Reactions and Instrumental Behaviors) that is moderated by context (Figure 12.4). While the “press” of culture may influence Priming Reactions and Instrumental Behaviors, they are also influenced by the “push” of biology. In some contexts, the biological push will be greater than the cultural press, allowing for greater pan- cultural similarity in response; in other contexts, the cultural press will be greater than the biological push, allowing for cultural influences.

The Cultural Elaboration of Emotional Experience The Proposition Subjective experience is created by a host of factors that increase in cultural origin (Mesquita, 2003, made a similar point about emotional experience but did not make the differentiations we do here.) Subjective experience begins with an awareness of sensations that occur because of the physiological reactions associated with emotion and perhaps even the appraisal process by which an emotion- eliciting event is evaluated (Ellsworth & Scherer, 2003). These sensations go through an interpretation and labeling process that is likely influenced by cultural knowledge (including language) and the cultural meanings of context in which the emotions are experienced. Cultural worldviews, for instance, may influence how one’s sensations in the context are interpreted and labeled. Culture- specific meanings about relationships and events are also likely to influence the interpretation and labeling process (and the sensation awareness itself; see Kohler, 1929). Self- reports reflect the verbal output of this process, and they, too, are influenced by cultural factors such as social desirability and response sets (see Figure 12.5). Thus, self- reports of emotional experience are acts that reflect rather complex combinations of biological and cultural processes. 
This process is likely moderated by the type of emotion elicited and its intensity. Biologically based emotions are associated with unique physiological signatures and universal appraisal processes; their sensations should be somewhat discrete and self- reports
