CulTure and eMoTion  |  383 
of those emotions should be somewhat cross- culturally similar, especially if the emotion aroused is intense. Culturally constructed emotions, however, may not necessarily be associated with unique physiological signatures; their sensations may be more diffuse and culturally variable. 
This process is also likely moderated by the time lag between the occurrence of the emotion- eliciting event and the self- report; the sooner introspections are made about an experienced event the more accurate they are (Block, 2007). This notion has implications for interpreting studies vis- à- vis their methodologies in assessing emotional experience. Some studies assess emotions in real time or relatively close to it; others assess recall of experience to events that have occurred in the past. Cultural influences on report are therefore likely to be larger for the latter because of the close relationship between culture and memory (Wang & Ross, 2007; see also Chapter 11 by Qi Wang and Sawa Senzaki). 
For these reasons, we propose that Subjective Experience occupies an intermediary position regarding the relative contributions of biological and cultural factors and depends on the emotion in question and the context in which it is elicited and reports obtained. We hypothesize that self- reports of biologically based emotions are more likely to be universal, especially in terms of their structure and if obtained in real time. Self- reports of culturally constructed emotions, however, and even of biologically based emotions, are more likely to be culturally variable, especially if recalled from previous experiences from memory. 
The Evidence As predicted, there is universality in subjective experiences produced when emotions are aroused. In their large- scale study, Scherer and Wallbott (1994) demonstrated strong cross- cultural similarities in the self- report profiles of the emotions they sampled. In a reanalysis of the Scherer dataset, Matsumoto and colleagues (2007) demonstrated that 95– 99% of the variability in self- reported emotional intensity was attributable to within- , not between- , country factors, and there were no reliable associations with ecological- level cultural dimensions. Similarly, no differences in self- reported emotions were reported by Tsai and colleagues in two studies examining ethnic differences in biologically based emotions assessed in real time (Tsai et al., 2002; Tsai, Levenson et al., 2006). 
Also consistent with our hypothesis, there appears to be universality in the structure of emotional experience. Kuppens and colleagues (Kuppens, Ceulmans, Timmerman, Diener, & Kim- Prieto, 2006) sampled emotional experiences from 9,300 participants in 48 nations and showed that positive and negative affect emerged as universal dimensions. Similar findings were obtained by Scollon and colleagues (Scollon, Diener, Oishi, & Biswas- Diener, 2005). Fontaine and colleagues (2006) reported cross- cultural similarity in emotional reactions of shame and guilt in Belgium, Hungary, and Peru, and Oishi and colleagues (Oishi, Diener, Scollon, & Biswas- Diener, 2004) reported cultural invariance in the cross- situational consistency of affective experiences. 
 
384 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
But a number of studies reported cultural differences in absolute mean levels of emotional experiences for both biologically based and culturally constructed emotions (Kuppens et al., 2006; Matsumoto et al., 1988; Scherer et al., 1988; Scherer & Wallbott, 1994; Scollon, Diener, Oishi, & Biswas- Diener, 2004; Scollon et al., 2005; Tsai, Knutson et al., 2006). As predicted, cultures play a larger role in the construction of the emotional experience of culturally constructed emotions, which are associated with self- construals (Nezlek, Kafetsios, & Smith, 2008; Nezlek, Sorrentino et al., 2008; Singelis, Bond, Sharkey, & Lai, 1999; Singelis & Sharkey, 1995). Kitayama and colleagues (Kitayama et al., 2000, 2006; Kitayama, Park, Sevincer, Karasawa, & Uskull, 2009; Uchida & Kitayama, 2009), for instance, have shown that people in collectivistic cultures report experiencing socially engaging emotions such as friendliness, respect, and sympathy more than socially disengaging emotions such as pride, self- esteem, sulkiness, or frustration. Members of individualistic cultures tend to experience more socially disengaging emotions than engaging emotions. Chentsova- Dutton and Tsai (2010) extended these findings by demonstrating that attention to individual aspects of the self amplified emotional experience for European Americans while attention to relational aspects of the self amplified experience for Asian Americans. 
There are also interesting cultural differences in emotional complexity— the co- occurrence of both pleasant and unpleasant emotions. Early research showed that this co- occurrence is more prevalent in East Asian than in Western cultures (Bagozzi, Wong, & Yi, 1999; Schimmack, Oishi, & Diener, 2002). European Americans who tend to report positive emotions more frequently or intensely also tend to report negative emotions less frequently or intensely, while East Asians are more likely to report the co- occurrence of positive and negative emotions. But Scollon et  al. (2005) indicated that pleasant and unpleasant feelings are rarely reported at the same time across cultures and Leu and colleagues (2010) indicated that cultural differences in dialectical emotions may occur more frequently in positive situations only. Among Western– East Asian bicultural individuals, dialectical emotions are more likely to be reported when the individual identifies with Asian culture or interacts in an Asian language; when the same individual identifies with Western culture or speaks a non- Asian language, dialectical emotions occur less often (Perunovic, Heller, & Rafaeli, 2007). These effects occur partly because of cultural or code frame switching (see Chapter 19 by Ying- yi Hong and Siran Zhan, for a review). 
Different types of cultural knowledge have been proposed to account for cultural differences in emotional experience. Kuppens et al. (2006) suggested that cultural differences in experience were related to nation- level life satisfaction, individualism, and the cultural appropriateness of experiencing emotions. Tsai and colleagues (2006) reported that the cultural differences they observed were due to cultural differences in “ideal affect.” Eid and Diener (2001) reported that cultural norms for experiencing emotions affected reported experiences across cultures. Kitayama and colleagues have suggested that reported emotional experiences are a set of “socially shared scripts” 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  385 
composed of physiological, behavioral, and subjective components (Kitayama & Markus, 1994; Kitayama et al., 1995). Regardless of the mechanisms, these studies are consistent with our notion that cultural knowledge influences emotional experience and that this influence is larger for culturally constructed emotions. 
The Cultural Elaboration of Emotion Meanings The Proposition One aspect of emotion that is uniquely human concerns the fact that we create meanings about emotion via concepts, attitudes, values, and beliefs about emotion, which are constructions that occur because of memory, language, self– other knowledge, and abstract thinking. Because these cognitive abilities are intimately related to culture, these mental phenomena are more highly constructed by culture than are immediate Priming Reactions, Instrumental Behaviors, or Subjective Experience. For this reason, we propose that Emotion Meanings are relatively more cross- culturally variable precisely because they are based on cultural constructions. (Shweder et  al., 2008, made a similar point about emotional meanings but did not make the same differentiations we do here.) Universality is still possible because emotion itself is a universal phenomenon and some emotions are biologically based. Thus, we hypothesize that biologically based emotions provide a platform for universal representations of emotional states in language but that cultures construct specific categories of emotion terms represented in languages and specific attitudes, values, beliefs, and lay theories about emotion. Because cultures evolve, emotion- related language, attitudes, values, and beliefs also change and evolve. 
The Evidence 
Concepts of Emotion Most cultures have a word for the concept of emotion and most words for emotion across languages overlap in semantic space (cf. Brandt & Boucher, 1985). Yet not all cultures have a word for emotion, such as the Tahitians (Levy, 1973, 1983) or the Ifaluks of Micronesia (Lutz, 1982). And even if a culture has a word for emotion, that culture’s word may have different connotations than in English. 
Many emotion terms in one language may not have an equivalent in another. The typical example of this is the German word Schadenfreude, a term that doesn’t exist in English and that refers to joy in another person’s misfortunes. But just because a culture does not have a word for an emotion does not mean that that emotion does not occur in the culture without the term (many English- speakers derive joy in other’s misfortunes). The fact that some emotion words exist in some cultures but not in others represents how different cultures represent their affective worlds in language. The fact that German culture contains the word Schadenfreude suggests that that feeling state or situation has some importance in that language and culture that it does not have in English. But it 
 
 
 
 
386 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
doesn’t mean that the phenomenon of Schadenfreude does not exist outside of German culture. Many other such examples exist, such as the Korean concepts of dapdaphada and uulhada, which have no translation equivalents in English or German (Schmidt- Atzert & Park, 1999). This expression may have evolved because of the cultural need to avoid direct expressions of strong negative descriptions of emotion, which may not be well accepted in the culture. 
Another way in which cultures construct different meanings about emotion is in what the term refers to. In American English, “emotion” refers to an internal state that focuses on affect (cf. Clore, Ortony, & Foss, 1987). In some cultures, emotions are statements about relationships among people or between people and events (Gerber, 1975; Myers, 1979; Riesman, 1977; White, 1980). Cultures also differ in where they locate emotions, such as the heart in the United States, the gut in Japan, the liver for the Chewong of Malay (Howell, 1981), the intestines for Tahitians (Levy, 1973), or “the insides” for the Ifaluk (Lutz, 1982). Locating emotions in the heart is important for American culture because it speaks to the importance of feelings as something unique to oneself that no one else can share and it identifies emotion with an important organ. The fact that other cultures identify and locate emotions outside the body, such as in social relationships with others, speaks to the ideological importance of relationships in those cultures. 
Studies examining the structure of the emotion lexicon across cultures are also relevant. Shaver and colleagues (Shaver, Schwartz, Kirson, & O’Connor, 1987) performed a cluster analysis on emotion terms in American English and indicated that the terms clustered into five basic- level emotion categories (love, happiness, anger, anxiety/ fear, and sadness), two superordinate categories (positive and negative), and 24 subordinate categories. Shaver then examined the structure of the emotion lexicon in Indonesia (Shaver, Murdaya, & Fraley, 2001) and reported the same five basic- level categories and two superordinate categories but 31 subordinate categories. Church and his colleagues also reported cross- cultural similarity in the basic and superordinate categories in their comparison of the English and Filipino emotion lexicons (Church, Katigbak, & Reyes, 1998; Church, Katigbak, Reyes, & Jensen, 1999). 
Wierzbicka (1999) examined emotion concepts across languages and proposed 11 hypotheses that could account for both universality and cultural specificity in emotion lexicons. For example, she proposed that all languages have a word for the term “feel,” and in all languages some feelings can be described as good and some as bad; some may be viewed as neither good nor bad. Her system allows for a mapping of the affective space with the emotion lexicon in any culture, which produces universality, but also for different cultures to produce different numbers of words in any area of that space, which allows for cultural differences. Research on languages such as Native American East Cree has supported Wierzbicka’s claims (Junker & Blacksmith, 2006). 
These studies suggest that the gross structure of representations of the emotion domain across languages is likely similar worldwide but that different cultures make fine- grained distinctions and emphasize different subordinate- level emotion concepts. This 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  387 
conclusion is consistent with our proposition that biologically based emotions provide a platform for universal representations of emotional states in language but that cultures construct specific meanings and categories of emotion terms represented in a language. Cultures may hypercognize emotions, in which many variations of emotions are identified and reified by words, or they can hypocognize emotions, in which relatively fewer emo-tion words exist (Levy, 1973). (This process is similar to how cultures can elaborate universal color perceptions via language; see Rosch, 1973, 1977; Rosch & Lloyd, 1978). The type of words that different cultures use to identify and label the emotion worlds of their members is a product of cultural construction (and influence subjective experience). 
Attitudes, Values, and Beliefs About Emotions Consistent with our hypothesis, cross- cultural research on attitudes, values, and beliefs related to emotion typically report large degrees of cultural variability. For instance, some high- level cultural value dimensions are based on emotion, such as Hofstede’s (2001) Uncertainty Avoidance or Schwartz’s (2004) Affective Autonomy, and there are large cultural differences on both (see also Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith on cultural dimensions). Cultural values about how people want to feel— ideal affect— are different from how people actually feel— actual affect (Tsai, 2007; Tsai, Knutson et  al., 2006):  European Americans and Asian Americans value high arousal positive affect such as excitement more than do Hong Kong Chinese who value more low arousal positive affect such as being calm. But the cultural construction of values about emotion does not necessarily correspond to the emotions people actually have; temperament and personality traits predict actual affect better than cultural values, whereas cultural values predict ideal affect better (Tsai, Knutson et al., 2006), consistent with our delineations concerning different domains of emotion. 
Similarly, Mesquita and Karasawa (2002) reported that reported emotional experiences of Japanese were predicted by interdependent concerns but the reports of Americans were predicted by both independent and interdependent concerns. In a related study, Mesquita (2001) asked Dutch, Surinamese, and Turkish respondents to rate social worth, appraisals, source of appraisals, action readiness, social sharing of emotions, and belief changes. Surinamese and Turkish respondents perceived their emotions as relational phenomena, grounded their ratings in assessments of social worth, and reflected more of a subjective reality; Dutch respondents perceived their emotions as much less reflective of the social environment, focused more on the inner world of the individual, and blended objective and subjective reality. These all tap Emotional Meaning and thus are culturally variable. 
Uchida and colleagues (2009) reported four studies in which they demonstrated cultural differences in lay theories about emotional expression and inference, suggesting that emotions are understood as phenomena that occur between people in Japan, whereas they are understood as within people in the United States. In our view, assessing understandings about other people’s emotions is a cognitive task that is highly influenced by culture. Thus, it makes sense that such understandings are more culturally variable. 
 
388 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
The literature is peppered with numerous other studies documenting cultural differences in Emotional Meanings, including cultural differences in the meaning of and narratives related to shame, guilt, or embarrassment (Bedford, 2004; Bierbrauer, 1992; Ho, Fu, & Ng, 2004; Hong, 2004; Lebra, 1983; Liem, 1997), the social sharing of emotions (Singh- Manoux & Finkenauer, 2001), comfort in expressing emotions (Stephan, Stephan, Saito, & Barnett, 1998), folk theories of emotion and expression (Ye, 2004), beliefs about verbal expressions about emotions (Wilkins & Gareis, 2006), beliefs about self and other emotions (Johnson, 2007), and desires for emotions (Diener & Lucas, 2004). These cultural differences occur because the dependent variables in these studies were ratings of attitudes, values, beliefs, or lay theories about emotion, thus sampling Emotional Meanings. Because Emotional Meanings are culturally constructed in the first place, it is no wonder that major cultural differences occur when they are studied. 
Conclusion We have tried to integrate the seemingly disparate literature on culture and emotion by providing a biocultural model of emotion that integrates a biologically based core emotion system that is calibrated, regulated, and elaborated by culture. Based on this integrated, multifaceted model, we believe that the seemingly contradictory literature can be understood in a cohesive manner by distinguishing emotions from other affective phenomena, among different types of emotion, and the specific domains of emotions assessed. If the premises underlying our model are accepted, then universality and cultural differences can be somewhat neatly integrated into a cohesive whole and questions can focus on the relative contributions of biology and culture. Our position is that the relative contribution of biology and culture should differ depending on the type of emotion examined and the specific domain of emotion assessed, which in turn produce universality or cultural differences in findings. 
To be sure, we do not argue about the specific boundaries between emotions and other affective phenomena or biologically based versus culturally constructed emotions. And we acknowledge that the distinctions we have drawn are somewhat artificial because there is likely no emotion that is entirely biologically driven without cultural influence and vice versa. More research and theorizing is needed to make better delineations concerning which affective phenomena are emotional and which are not, and which emotions are part of a biologically innate set and which are not. Furthermore, we acknowledge that our delineations may not be the only or the best delineations that can or should be used. We contend that some kind of delineations should be made and can help to synthesize and integrate a large and seemingly disparate, contradictory literature. We offer ours as a step in this effort. 
We also have not dealt with the important question of what constitutes “universality.” How many studies across how many cultures with what kinds of samples need 
 
CulTure and eMoTion  |  389 
to be conducted? What effect sizes are necessary to make reasonable conclusions about universality? Is universality demonstrated when 100% of the samples in our studies all provide the same data, without individual differences? If not, what’s the cutoff? These questions have been discussed in the literature (Ekman, 1994; Izard, 1994; Russell, 1995) but deserve attention periodically as the literature grows. 
Although the model we presented herein is supported by the literature we cited, there are parts of the model that deserve research attention in the future. For example, we do not know much about the Back- End Calibration of the core emotion system beyond the existence of display rules. How do display rules kick in? Where do they exist in the brain? How does context or emotion intensity affect them? Likewise, we know little about behavior rules. What are these rules? In which contexts will an angry person fight or not? Why? These and other areas of the model are ripe for future studies. 
We also need to give food for thought to alternative methodologies in the study of emotion. Cross- cultural studies of priming reactions tend to involve only a few cultures, probably because of the labor- intensive nature of measuring such reactions. Are there ways to collect data on priming reactions across more cultures? And, most importantly, how do the different emotion domains we have highlighted in this chapter interact with each other? Assessing multiple domains of emotion within the same individuals across cultures is a topic worthy of future research (see also Chapter 2 by Michael Harris Bond for a similar call for more multilevel cross- cultural research). In- depth, indigenous research on these issues will also make contributions in the future. 
Although the literature reviewed herein appears to fall somewhat neatly into the theoretical framework we proposed, one of the limitations of most of the previous research is that the studies generally tested only one dependent variable related to a single emotion domain (e.g., facial expressions, emotional experiences, etc.). Recent cross- cultural research examining multiple emotional domains, however, has provided additional support for the framework presented here, demonstrating cross- cultural similarities in emotion perception (i.e., judgments of immediate priming reactions) but cultural differences in emotion understanding and emotion regulation beliefs in the same participants (Shao, Doucet, & Caruso, 2015). Future studies examining multiple emotion domains in the same participants across multiple cultures and subcultures are needed to examine the relative contributions of biology and culture to emotional processes. Such studies will help push the field from either/ or debates about universality versus culture specificity to more constructive ways of understanding and studying emotion across all its domains.
