PA R T  I V 
Personality and Abnormal Psychology 
 
13 
Culture and Personality 
Jüri Allik and Anu Realo 
Introduction In this chapter, we discuss the relationship between culture and personality. According to some researchers, the distinction between the two concepts makes little sense because personality is believed to be entirely produced, controlled, and sustained by cultural forces. No culture, no personality! Particularly for researchers who were working in the field of culture and personality in the first part of the twentieth century, all adult behavior was “culturally patterned” (mostly by culture- specific childhood experiences), and, as a result, people living in the same culture who had been through a similar socialization process would also develop a certain “modal” personality type that was common to most people in that culture (LeVine, 2001). In a rather similar manner, personality was seen by many, particularly members of the Marxist sociohistorical school, as a product of sociohistorical development, just like any other social institution or practice. Therefore, to understand introspection, which is a prerequisite for answering self- report personality questionnaires, one should seek its social roots in the stages through which it is shaped in society (Luria, 1976). Early studies carried out by researchers from this school of thought have been seen as precursors to the contemporary field of cultural psychology, which places great emphasis on the interrelatedness between people and their cultural environments (Cole, 1996). 
It seems quite self- evident that people’s customs and habits are more civilized than they were only a few hundred years ago (Elias, 1939/ 2000). Also, despite defining personality traits as “enduring tendencies to think, feel, and behave in consistent ways” (Allik & McCrae, 2002, p. 304) that are surprisingly stable and resistant to external influences, most contemporary personality researchers also agree that personality traits can and do change, to some extent at least, across the lifespan, not just because of intrinsic maturation, but also due to significant life events and, possibly, other environmental influences 
 
 
402 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
(Bleidorn, Hopwood, & Lucas, 2018; Specht, Egloff, & Schmukle, 2011). For example, it has been proposed that normative changes in personality— that people become universally more socially adapted as they become older— can be explained by the social investment theory (Helson, Jones, & Kwan, 2002; Helson, Kwan, John, & Jones, 2002; Roberts, Wood, & Smith, 2005), which states that societal differentiation in social roles based on age is one of the driving mechanisms of personality development. Thus, environmental influences on personality change are not disputed:  the question concerns their relative size compared to other factors. For example, the Second Law of Behavior Genetics, which pertains to social (family) and biological (genetic) factors, maintains that the effect of being raised in the same family is always smaller than the effect of genes (Turkheimer, 2000). 
In this chapter, we discuss different approaches to the study of personality and culture that have emerged in the distinct yet related fields of psychology and anthropology over time, and that have helped enhance our understanding of the complex and dynamic relationship between the two constructs. We discuss the struggle between universality and specificity (or relativity) and how this has influenced our understanding of cultural similarities and variations in personality over time. We also try to broaden the range of discussion about the relationship between culture and personality by introducing new topics— domestication, civilization, moral statistics, and psychopathology— that have not traditionally been discussed in this context. 
The Question of Universality Versus Specificity The boundary between anthropology and psychology, as Gustav Jahoda (2014) in his brief yet insightful history of the relationship between the two fields described, has always been rather fuzzy. Anthropology (including ethnology) is the study of customs, institutions, and human- made artifacts from past and present societies, which are often, but not always, quite exotic. Psychology, on the other hand, studies the mind, feelings, and behavior of people who predominantly, but not always, happen to live in the so- called WEIRD— white, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic— societies (Arnett, 2008). Yet ethnographic descriptions of peoples have often not only included their customs or social structures, but also their psychological features and characteristics, and there have been many attempts made to use ethnographic material in order to draw conclusions about the human mind and human behavior (Jahoda, 2014). In a similar vein, psychologists have tried to show how certain patterns of values or societal norms may have an important impact on institutional arrangements, policies, and everyday practices (e.g., Gelfand et al., 2011; Hofstede, 2001). 
Another similarity between the fields is their quest to answer the question of universality versus specificity. The postulate of “the psychic unity of mankind,” which states that all human beings, regardless of their culture or race, share the same basic psychological and cognitive make- up, excludes the possibility of people in one culture having 
 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  403 
abilities or psychological mechanisms that are totally different or absent in some other cultures. In its extreme form (universalism), the relevance of cross- cultural variation is mostly denied. At the same time, there is a myriad of details that vary from one culture to another. This variety creates the impression that everything around us is produced by culture, which penetrates even the deepest layers of the human mind. It seems reasonable to argue that the human mind exists only in relation to a culture and cannot be separated from it (see also Chapter  1 by Walter J.  Lonner, Kenneth D.  Keith, and David Matsumoto for more discussion of the issue of universals vs. cultural specificity). Therefore, it is entirely understandable that many researchers in both disciplines have been interested in describing, cataloguing, and systemizing this complex world of cultural differences (Allik & Realo, 2017b, 2018; Realo & Allik, 2008) via a tangible set of cultural dimensions. 
The American anthropologist George Peter Murdock (1897– 1985) was among the first to notice that the seemingly vast cultural variation across the globe can be reduced to a relatively small set of underlying dimensions. In 1957, he published his first cross- cultural dataset, the World Ethnographic Sample, consisting of 565 cultures, which were categorized along 30 basic economic, ecological, social, and political variables (Murdock, 1957). These 30 variables were designed, as he formulated it, to be as representative as possible of the entire known range of cultural variation. He rated nearly all of the ethnographic material himself, and, in general, these ratings were replicable by other raters. Sawyer and LeVine (1966) applied a factor analysis to Murdock’s data and found nine dimensions that summarized the original 30 characteristics. The dimensions were primarily characterized by the means of subsistence (e.g., agriculture, fishery) and dominant family structures (e.g., patrilinearity, matrilienarity) of these cultures. Later, Sawyer (1967) applied a similar approach to the 82 modern nations that had been described by the 236 social, economic, political, and other characteristics in 1955 and found three dimensions— size, wealth, and politics— that accounted for 40% of the total variance in the cultural differences across those nations. 
However, Sawyer’s dimensions of cultural variation did not appeal to many researchers who were working in the field of cross- cultural psychology, which emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s as an independent, separate discipline from its intellectual predecessors, such as mainstream psychology, anthropology/ ethnography, and sociology (Jahoda, 2011; Van de Vijver, Chasiotis, & Breugelmans, 2011). Indeed, although societies seem to have followed a similar path from a “band” through to a “tribe” and a “chiefdom” to a “state” (Service, 1971), with a tendency to expand, the size of a state tells us very little about its culture. Fortunately, it was realized that there is another way to describe and account for cultural differences apart from analyzing basic economic, ecological, social, and political variables, and that is through what people believe. One group of these beliefs is called values; these express cultural ideals and shared understandings about what is good and what is bad. In cross- cultural psychology, values are seen as the central axis or theme of culture around which shared beliefs, symbols, and norms are 
404 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
grouped. Cultural values shape and justify people’s goals, habits, and actions, and are reflected in everyday practices and institutional functioning (Schwartz, 1994). 
In his pioneering work, Hofstede (1980) analyzed survey data for 17,000 IBM employees from 40 countries. Although the survey focused only on work- related values, Hofstede was able to derive dimensions characterizing the cultures as a whole. Indeed, for several decades, researchers exploited Hofstede’s (2001) four dimensions— power distance, individualism– collectivism, masculinity– femininity, and uncertainty avoidance— as the main, if not the only possible, typology of cultures. Because of its pivotal role in social discourse, it was individualism– collectivism that overwhelmingly appealed to psychologists, and, as a result, Hofstede’s study triggered a massive amount of research on individualism– collectivism in the following decades (Allik & Realo, 2004; Realo, Koido, Ceulemans, & Allik, 2002). It was only after a considerable period of enthusiasm that several eminent cross- cultural researchers started to argue that perhaps the dimensions were used too readily as an explanation for almost every difference in values, attitudes, and behavior between the so- called individualist and collectivist cultures and that we should look beyond individualism– collectivism to explain cross- cultural differences in behavior (see Realo & Allik, 2008; Realo & Allik, 2009, for a review). Hofstede himself extended the list by adding two dimensions: first long- term versus short- term orientation (Hofstede & Bond, 1988) and later indulgence versus restraint (Hofstede, Hofstede, & Minkov, 2010). Other researchers have proposed their own candidates for universal cultural value dimensions (e.g., Inglehart & Baker, 2000; Schwartz, 1994; Welzel, 2013), for dimensions underlying cultural norms (e.g., tightness– looseness; see Gelfand et al., 2011; Mandel & Realo, 2015), for beliefs or so- called social axioms (Bond et al., 2004; Stankov & Saucier, 2015), and for social relations (Fiske, 1991, 1992). In all cases, however, it is believed that a relatively small number of dimensions is sufficient to describe a large amount of cross- cultural differences. Although researchers are still disputing which dimensions deserve a place on this short list (de Mooij, 2013; Minkov, Bond, & Blagoev, 2015), Hofstede’s cultural value dimensions (Hofstede et al., 2010), as well as those based on the World Values Survey (WVS) and the Schwartz Value Theory (Borg, Bardi, & Schwartz, 2017), appear to be the most dominant (see also Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith for an extended review of cultural dimensions). 
Similarly to early anthropological studies which focused on examining and understanding cultural differences, there was a fascination with the enormous variation in personality traits in the early years of personality psychology. When Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert scrutinized Webster’s dictionary of English in 1936, they were able to identify approximately 18,000 unique terms used to describe personality or behavior out of about a half- million words (Allport & Odbert, 1936). Even 30 years later, Allport was quite pessimistic and had very little hope of understanding this “incredible complexity” of personality traits: “Since traits, like all intervening variables, are never directly observed but only inferred, we must expect difficulties and errors in the process of discovering their nature. The incredible complexity of the structure we seek to understand is enough 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  405 
to discourage the realist, and to tempt him to play some form of positivistic gamesmanship” (Allport, 1966, p. 3). And yet, personality researchers were able to reach the preliminary consensus that five independent dimensions are usually enough to describe the entire richness of personality traits, not only in English, but supposedly in many other spoken languages as well (Goldberg, 1993; John, Angleitner, & Ostendorf, 1988; John, Naumann, & Soto, 2008). 
Another line of research, distinct to the lexical approach, stems from clinical practice and is used to classify mental disorders into distinctive categories. These categories have often resembled discrete personality types, such as extraverted versus introverted (e.g., Jung’s typology) or viscerotonic versus cerebrotonic (e.g., Sheldon’s typology) (Eysenck, 1947/ 1998). This fascination with distinctive types of personality made psychologists similar to cultural anthropologists, who believed that culture has a great impact in de-veloping and “molding” the individual personality. Patterns of Culture by Ruth Benedict (1887– 1948) became one of the most popular best- sellers in its field, promoting the idea that each culture chooses from “the great arc of human potentialities,” and only a few traits from this spectrum become the leading personality traits of the people living in that culture (Benedict, 1934/ 1959). For example, the Dobuans of Melanesia were described as suspicious and paranoid, the Kwakiutl were autocrats and despots, and the Pueblos of New Mexico were typically unemotional and passive (Benedict, 1934/ 1959). Later, a cultural anthropologist, Abram Kardiner (1891– 1981), formulated his theory of “basic personality structure,” which was further developed by Cora Du Bois (1903– 1991) in her concept of the “modal personality” (Du Bois & Kardiner, 1944). According to the concept of the modal personality, there are many different personality types in each culture, not just one, as was initially suggested by Kardiner, and, out of the many, one appears to be the most frequent or dominant (“modal”) and usually represents the nation or culture as a whole (Inkeles, 1997). 
The most fundamental change in the history of personality psychology was undoubtedly the replacement of the categorical approach with dimensional systems. While previously researchers had talked about traits or categories that apply to some of the people some of the time, Hans Jürgen Eysenck (1916– 1997) was the first to argue that universal dimensions are applicable to all individuals all of the time (Eysenck, 1947/ 1998). Personality is determined by an individual’s position on each of these personality dimensions, of which two— neuroticism or emotional stability and extraversion— are present in every modern personality taxonomy. These dimensions also accommodate both normal and disordered populations because mental disorders are often associated with extreme positions on these dimensions (Widiger, Gore, Crego, Rojas, & Oltmanns, 2017). 
Although personality researchers still debate the exact number and content of personality dimensions (Block, 1995; Eysenck, 1991; Thalmayer & Saucier, 2014), they generally agree that there is a relatively small number of independent themes around which all personality traits can be organized (Allik & McCrae, 2002; Goldberg, 1993; McCrae & Costa, 2003). These personality traits are not, however, an accident of evolution, as some 
406 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
researchers had tried to portray them (Tooby & Cosmides, 1990). It seems more realistic to understand personality traits as a genotypic reaction to different environmental demands (Penke, Denissen, & Miller, 2007). Thus, even though the origins and exact meaning of personality traits are still debated, it is obvious that personality researchers have finally found a common language that helps to make sense of the cacophony of the literally thousands of personality tests and the traits they are supposed to measure. 
Linking Dimensions of Personality and Culture For many researchers working in the field of cultural psychology, as we noted in the introduction, personality is a product of social construction and, consequently, a cultural phenomenon in the first place. If culture is understood as socially shared information that is encoded in symbols, then practically the only tools for the study of personality— questionnaires— exploit the most distinctive and founding feature of human culture: language (Toomela, 2003). Specifically, it was proposed that a coherent Big Five personality structure emerges only for those individuals who have moved from one dominant structure of word meanings and thinking in “everyday concepts” (concrete categories) to another level of thinking in “scientific concepts” (abstract categories) (Toomela, 2003). However, a reanalysis of the reported data found no evidence of structural differences between adults classified as “concrete” or “abstract” thinkers (Allik & McCrae, 2004). Thus, the use of cultural tools, such as language, does not automatically mean that the object of description— personality traits— is affected by what we usually call culture. 
As noted earlier, the Five- Factor Model (FFM) emerged from the consensus that five broad personality dimensions can characterize the largest amount of variance across many types of personality data (Goldberg, 1993; John et al., 2008; McCrae & Costa, 2003; McCrae & John, 1992). The Five- Factor Theory (FFT), however, first formulated by McCrae and Costa (1996, 1999), was a completely different story. The FFT was perceived as a dissident theory, one that challenged many established theories and doctrines. It originated in efforts to understand the remarkable stability of personality traits across long periods of time: At the time, longitudinal research had shown that decades of life experience appeared to have only a moderate impact on basic personality traits (McCrae & Costa, 2003). Combined with findings from behavior genetic studies that had shown a powerful effect of genes and a small effect of the shared environment on personality traits, these observations led to the proposal that traits are endogenous dispositions, relatively untouched by life experiences (including culture). That theory certainly explains the findings of longitudinal stability and heritability, together with an immunity to cultural influences (Allik & McCrae, 2002). 
The authors and supporters of the FFT did not believe that their main postulate— that culture never has any effect whatsoever on personality traits— was literally true. But they did believe that it is a parsimonious first approximation to the truth (Allik & McCrae, 2002; McCrae & Costa, 2003). Many characteristic adaptations such as values, 
 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  407 
attitudes, self- concept, and the like, as discussed earlier, are undeniably shaped by culture; but they need not be confused with basic dispositions, which may stay relatively unaltered across the lifespan. From the available evidence, two effects have emerged that are particularly informative about the FFT: the cohort effects of secular trends and the effects of acculturation on personality traits (Allik & McCrae, 2002). When these questions were revisited more than 10 years later, there was little support for a strong and unquestionable effect of culture on personality (Allik & Realo, 2017b). This is not to say that personality traits do not change across the lifespan, be it due to significant life events (Bleidorn et al., 2018; Specht et al., 2011), intrinsic maturation (Roberts & Delvecchio, 2000), or clinical intervention (Roberts et  al., 2017), but the effects of these are relatively small (Costa, Herbst, McCrae, & Siegler, 2000). Moreover, personality traits also predict life experiences (Jeronimus, Riese, Sanderman, & Ormel, 2014), and, therefore, it probably makes more sense to talk about the corresponsive principle, which suggests that “the most likely effect of life experience on personality development is to deepen the characteristics that lead people to those experiences in the first place” (Caspi, Roberts, & Shiner, 2005, p. 470). 
However, the independently developed taxonomies of personality traits and cultural values created a new possibility to explore the link between these two domains. There is a highly remarkable paper by Hofstede and McCrae (2004) that examines these possible links. This influential paper advances two apparently incompatible explanations that are supported only by one of the two authors. Hofstede (the first author) believes that culture, as a collective programmer of the mind, affects the process of socialization and, as a result of this, minds take forms that are determined by culture. For example, higher levels of masculinity and uncertainty avoidance produce higher numbers of people who are prone to neurotic tendencies. In contrast, McCrae (the second author) supports a radically different interpretation of these associations between personality and culture. His reverse causation hypothesis implies that there are innate temperamental differences between various populations that give rise to cultural differences. 
In order to find support for the reverse causation hypothesis, it is important to understand the mechanism that could produce changes in the frequency of gene variants. For instance, it was already noticed some time ago that newer nations like Australia, Canada, and the United States, whose populations are largely made up of relatively recent immigrants, tend to have higher extraversion scores than those European countries from which the immigrants largely came (Lynn, 1981). Later research has repeatedly shown that both extraversion and openness to experience are strong predictors, not only of people’s voluntary migration intentions (Pungas, Täht, Realo, & Tammaru, 2015), but also of them actually undertaking migration (Camperio Ciani & Capiluppi, 2011; Camperio Ciani, Capiluppi, Veronese, & Sartori, 2007; Jokela, 2009; Jokela, Elovainio, Kivimäki, & Keltikangas- Järvinen, 2008). Consequently, this could lead to a gene drift, or changes in the frequency of allele variants: explorers carry genes for extraversion and openness. Having different personality dispositions could lead, in turn, to the adoption 
408 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
of different social and cultural practices. As a possible scenario, consider a population that has a relatively high concentration of neurotic and not- so- agreeable people. They will, in general, be tense, irritable, and conflict- prone, and interpersonal interactions will be difficult. Each new decision will be a potential source of distress and conflict. Such people may find that they can coexist only if they adopt a rigid set of rules and screen out new situations that would require new decisions. In other words, they would develop the values and institutions that typify high uncertainty avoidance countries (Hofstede & McCrae, 2004). 
However, the choice between the two alternative explanations put forward by Hofstede and McCrae (2004) is even more difficult because the direct and reverse causation hypotheses are not mutually exclusive. It is possible, as the corresponsive principle suggests, that certain personality traits dispose people to adopt certain social and cultural practices. At the same time, cultural norms can suppress and/ or express personality dispositions that provide a better match to a particular culture. 
Challenges to Universality Strictly speaking, “universal” means that something is characteristic of all members of a class, without any limits or exceptions (Allik, Realo, & McCrae, 2013). In fact, little in nature meets this absolute criterion, but many characteristics appear to be relatively invariant, suggesting that they could be near- or semi- universals. As such, universalism and relativism are not two mutually excluding alternatives. In reality, we can speak about degrees of universality. Nevertheless, both programs— universalist and relativist— seem to have their own challenges. 
The FFT (McCrae & Costa, 1996, 1999, 2003), which claims that personality traits are relatively immune to environmental influences, including culture, is a good example of a universalist theory (Allik & McCrae, 2002; McCrae & Costa, 1996, 1999), and those who oppose this theoretical position have been in search of evidence against it. We have summarized the most salient challenges to the universality of personality traits elsewhere (Allik & Realo, 2017b) and, therefore, only provide a very brief summary here of the most important challenges. 
First, researchers have eagerly tried to find unique personality traits or exceptional combinations of common traits that are specific to one culture alone (Cheung, van de Vijver, & Leong, 2011). However, most of these attempts to establish unique or indigenous traits have failed because what was believed to be a trait unique to one culture was later found to be applicable to other cultures as well, although perhaps not exactly to the same degree of salience (Church, 2016; Church & Katigbak, 2005). 
Second, if acculturation of personality traits existed, this would be an indisputable example of cultural influence. Indeed, recent data have supported the view that acculturation shapes personality traits (Güngör et al., 2013; Söldner, 2013; Zimmermann & Neyer, 2013). For example, Japanese Americans become more “American” and less “Japanese” 
 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  409 
in their personality as they report higher participation in the US culture (Güngör et al., 2013). However, these studies have also shown that a more sophisticated methodology is needed to study the effects of acculturation on personality traits. To draw firm conclusions about acculturation effects on people’s personality traits, it is necessary to measure their personality traits before they move to another country or cultural environment. As we have already argued, many acculturation effects can probably be explained by self- selection because it is open and extraverted people who are more likely to migrate and, through this experience, often become even more open and experience more positive emotions (Söldner, 2013; Zimmermann & Neyer, 2013). 
Third, if a small change in personality accompanies switching from one language to another, then we can take this as evidence for relativity. For example, when German and Spanish versions of the NEO Five- Factor Inventory were administered to two groups of bilinguals of these two languages, in both groups, regardless of the individual’s first language, respondents scored higher on Extraversion and Neuroticism when Spanish was the test language (Veltkamp, Recio, Jacobs, & Conrad, 2013). Although it is possible that bilinguals may have two slightly different personalities that they can switch between with a change in language (Ramírez- Esparza, Gosling, Benet- Martínez, Potter, & Pennebaker, 2006), these differences are usually too small to have wide- ranging practical consequences (Lönnqvist, Konstabel, Lönnqvist, & Verkasalo, 2014). 
Fourth, when the same questionnaire is used again over a considerable time interval, it is possible to determine whether different cohorts living under various conditions have similar personality scores. The results of Twenge and colleagues’ meta- analyses have shown dramatic cohort effects (Gentile, Twenge, & Campbell, 2010; Twenge, 2000, 2001; Twenge & Campbell, 2008; Twenge et al., 2010; Twenge & Im, 2007)  in many personality characteristics, such as self- esteem, self- liking, anxiety, extraversion, and even in various forms of psychopathology. Albeit impressive, the interpretation of all of these cohort effects requires caution. For example, some of the trends reported by Twenge and colleagues were difficult to replicate in samples that are more representative of the general population (Terracciano, 2010; Trzesniewski & Donnellan, 2010). Also, it is often very difficult, sometimes impossible, to disentangle age, cohort, and period effects (Realo & Dobewall, 2011) due to a lack of longitudinal datasets gathered from the same or in different countries in different periods of time. Moreover, these generational differences in personality characteristics may also be explained, as one possibility, by response style. Until we are unable to differentiate between substance and style, it is always possible that changes in mean scores indicate not substance but a variation in response style (Mõttus, Allik, Realo, Rossier, et al., 2012). 
Let us assume that younger cohorts in the United States indeed shifted toward substantially higher levels of neuroticism and extraversion over a 30- to 40- year period, as was shown by Twenge (2000, 2001) in a series of meta- analyses. One possible cause for these cohort effects is self- domestication, with the suppression of negative feelings being an example of this (Hare, 2017). Social scientists have observed that people change, as 
410 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
a rule, relatively little over the individual life course; it is mainly a new generation that assumes new values, attitudes, and habits (e.g., Putnam, 2000). Historians have admitted that certain events in human history cannot be explained only by changes in economic conditions or social institutions. For example, in order to explain what happened economically in the world around 1800, it is not enough to point to climatic, technological, or even political conditions. It seems that changes in people’s attitudes toward work and cooperation may have impacted the whole economic system to such an extent that these generated an unprecedented boost in wealth (Clark, 2007). 
Another example is the decline in violence. If we rely on statistics, not TV news alone, we are currently living in the most peaceful period in human history (North, Wallis, & Weingast, 2009; Pinker, 2011). It is very difficult to explain, for example, the decline of homicide by social and political conditions alone. It seems that we need to en-gage a method that Norbert Elias (1897– 1990) referred to as the civilizing process (Elias, 1939/ 2000). For example, to explain the drop in violence, Pinker (2011) proposed that human nature is becoming less aggressive, more pacified, feminized, and rational. Many of these changes accompany domestication, in the way that Charles Darwin described the process. When domesticating animals, humans domesticated themselves at the same time (Hare, 2017). 
The process of domestication can be illustrated by one of the most fascinating studies in the history of science. In early 1950s, a Russian biologist, Dmitry Belyaev (1917– 1985), decided to study domestication experimentally using wild silver foxes as a model species. To hide his research project from Trofim Lysenko, who killed genetics in the Soviet Union both figuratively and literally, he went to Kohila— a small town about 30 km from the Estonian capital Tallinn— to ask Nina Sorokina, a leading breeder of silver foxes, to carry out the planned experiment in complete secrecy. The idea was to determine the least aggressive foxes and breed them to produce a new generation of tamer foxes (Dugatkin & Trut, 2017; Trut, 1999). Surprisingly, it took only 20 or so generations to transform a wild silver fox into a domestic dog. Although aggressiveness toward humans was the only criterion for selection, the appearance of tame foxes also changed. Their head became smaller, white spots appeared in their fur, their tails rolled, and their ears became floppy. They even started to bark the way that dogs usually do (Gogoleva, Volodin, Volodina, & Trut, 2008). In other words, although a specific behavioral trait was chosen for selective breeding, the observed rapid changes also included changes in the foxes’ physical appearance and reproductive cycle (Dugatkin & Trut, 2017; Hare, 2017). 
Because nobody has been able to domesticate, for example, zebras, Belyaev proposed that the fact that foxes share genes with dogs could be responsible for their tame behavior. Twenty- plus generations is, of course, too short a period for change in a whole genome. One thing, however, that breeding tameness can do is to “silence” one set of genes and “switch on” another set (Kukekova, Temnykh, Johnson, Trut, & Acland, 2012). Although the mechanism of gene expression is more often assumed than demonstrated, its role in domestication is irrefutable.
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  411 
To sum up, differences in personality traits between generations are not only possible but also likely, yet, for their reliable description, we need sound theories about how and why differences between birth cohorts evolve and what the role of culture in this process is. 
Challenges to Relativity In a certain way, the FFT (McCrae & Costa, 1996, 1999, 2003) also provided a challenge to theoretical perspectives emphasizing cultural relativity and specificity of personality. The first challenge was the finding that age differences in personality traits show pan- cultural patterns (McCrae et al., 2004; McCrae et al., 1999). In other words, relatively similar patterns of age differences have emerged in a large number of different cultures, with people being likely to become less extraverted and less open to new ideas and values, but generally more responsible for their own actions and more agreeable as they age (McCrae et al., 2004; McCrae et al., 1999). Even dramatic changes in society and political life, like those that happened in the Soviet Union and after its dissolution in Russia, do not seem to leave detectable traces on personality development when analyzed at the aggregate level (Allik et al., 2009). 
The second challenge concerns the apparent lack of societal or political influence on people’s personality traits. In addition to the experiments on fox domestication described earlier, there have been (and still are) other large- scale social experiments, one goal of which was to breed a “new type” of human being, sometimes called the Homo sovieticus (Zinoviev, 1985). The artificial split of Germany into East and West Germany at the end of 1940s was carried out, seemingly, by almost perfect experimental design. After reunification in 1989– 1990— that is, after approximately half a century of complete isolation— it was interesting to observe the consequences of the two very different ideologies and political practices on people’s personalities. It certainly came as a big surprise that, when studying thousands of participants from the former East and West Germany, researchers were able to discover only a few significant differences in respondents’ personality trait levels (Angleitner & Ostendorf, 2000), most notably in A5: Modesty and O6: Openness to Values, with participants from former East Germany scoring higher on the former and lower on the latter, facet scale. However, these differences accounted for less than 1% of the total variance, and they may indeed be due to measurement error. Nevertheless, the values of the people living in the two regions of Germany were still notably different in 1997, despite having gone through substantial changes over the previous 20  years (Inglehart & Baker, 2000). Thus, values, but not personality traits— as measured by contemporary personality questionnaires— seem to be affected by social and political conditions. 
A similar example is the division between North and South Korea, which was the result of the Allied victory in World War II in 1945. Differently from former East and West Germany, an ethnically and linguistically similar population has now lived under 
 
412 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
two radically different social, economic, and political systems for more than 70 years. This has taken a heavy toll on the North Korean population, where children are up to 13 cm shorter and 7 kg lighter than children brought up in South Korea (Schwekendiek, 2009). There is no known comparative study of personality in North and South Korea, but it would be very interesting to know about the consequences of such failed social experiments. Indeed, it would be shocking if personality differences between these two countries, for example, were smaller than expected. 
Researchers tried to make the distinction between temperament and character as representing biological and social personality traits, respectively (Cloninger, Svrakic, & Przybeck, 1993). However, a comparison between homo- and heterozygote twins revealed that all personality traits (Jang, Livesley, & Vernon, 1996; Riemann, Angleitner, & Strelau, 1997; Yamagata et al., 2006) have approximately equal heritability. In addition to isolated traits, the FFM structure was also strongly heritable, and, as such, it was possible to conclude that it is predominantly biology which controls personality (McCrae, Jang, Livesley, Riemann, & Angleitner, 2001). 
These are serious challenges that relativists need to take seriously. Any complete theory should accommodate this evidence, too. 
Different Ways of Doing Cross- Cultural Research The WVS proudly maintains that its surveys are conducted in almost 100 countries, which contain almost 90% of the world’s population.1 Unfortunately, personality traits were never regarded to be of such importance as to establish a global organization for collecting personality data. Nevertheless, there are several models for carrying out cross- cultural research in psychology (Allik, Massoudi, Realo, & Rossier, 2012). One of these data collection models was borrowed from anthropologists who, at least in the early years of the discipline, liked to send well- prepared expeditions to locations of interest. A serious limitation of this model is its low productivity in terms of cross- cultural comparisons: obviously, these in- depth and valuable expeditions can cover only a limited number of ethnic groups and geographic locations (Allik & Realo, 2018). An even more serious obstacle, however, lies in the fact that many anthropologists and cultural psychologists believe that cross- cultural comparisons are in fact not meaningful or even possible (see Berry, Poortinga, Breugelmans, Chasiotis, & Sam, 2011, for a review). Nevertheless, many cross- cultural psychologists have adapted the anthropological research model by applying it in two cultures, most often comparing some exotic or a far- away culture with their own, and there is no doubt that this approach has produced some spectacular results. For example, Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) theory of independent 
1. www.worldvaluessurvey.org 
 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  413 
and interdependent self- construals, which aimed to explain and characterize the general differences between Western (i.e., American) and Asian (i.e., Japanese) views of self and the consequences of these for emotion, cognition, motivation, relationships, and group processes, had a major impact on the field. It took nearly 25 years for researchers to come up with a more refined seven- dimensional model because “a simple contrast between independence and interdependence does not adequately capture the diverse models of selfhood that prevail in different world regions” (Vignoles et al., 2016, p. 968). 
However, the most influential recent developments in cross- cultural psychology can be attributed to an alternative model of data collection, which has its roots in the so- called missionary model. Already in 1867, Charles Darwin (1809– 1882) circulated a printed leaflet entitled “Queries About Expression” among his acquaintances who were in touch with “primitive” peoples all around the world (very often missionaries) in order to study how emotions are recognized and expressed in different cultures. The answers to these queries formed the basis of his book, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (Darwin, 1872/ 1989), where, on pages 19– 22, he even gave the names of the 29 correspondents who had kindly replied to his query (Freeman, 1977)  (see also Chapter 12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang for a discussion of the influence of Darwin’s work on studies of emotion and expression). 
Instead of writing to Christian missionaries, contemporary researchers recruit collaborators among their academic colleagues from different parts of the world, asking them to translate questionnaires into their native languages and then collect data in their countries. Such international research consortiums are often held together by the promise that the first one, two, or three papers will be co- authored by all those who participate in the data collection. This model has led to a true revolution in cross- cultural research. It likely is only a small exaggeration that the most valuable personality datasets have been collected using this more productive “technology” (Allik et al., 2009; Guillaume et al., 2016; McCrae, Terracciano et al., 2005; Schmitt et al., 2007). One serious shortcoming of this method is that participants are usually recruited based on convenience rather than representativeness. Another problem is that not all places of interest have colleagues who are sufficiently trained and motivated to be able to take part in the project. Finally, the translated questionnaires typically assess constructs developed in Western countries with little, if any, attempt to identify indigenous constructs in the target cultures (see Zecca et al., 2013, for an exception). 
Instead of actively seeking out collaborators from different countries, cross- cultural data can also become available not because the author of a certain measurement instrument was interested in cross- cultural comparisons, but simply because researchers in different countries found the instrument useful and relevant and wanted to adapt it to their culture. In personality psychology, the Eysenck’s Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) was apparently the first instrument to enjoy truly international popularity (Lynn & Martin, 1995). Other examples include Cloninger’s Tridimensional Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) and the Temperament and Character Inventory (TCI), which have been translated 
414 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
into many languages (Miettunen, Kantojärvi, Veijola, Jarvelin, & Joukamaa, 2006). In 1992, Paul T. Costa, Jr. and Robert R. McCrae published their Revised NEO Personality Inventory (NEO PI- R; Costa & McCrae, 1992). Ten years later, it was possible to report the use of the NEO PI- R in 27 different languages and 36 different cultures or regions (McCrae, 2002, 2017). Currently, NEO PI- R/ 3 profiles have been compared across more than 62 countries and 37 languages (Allik et al., 2017). 
Sometimes, as we know, large multinational corporations also contribute to cross- cultural personality research. Despite some criticisms about its approach, it is impossible to overestimate the impact of Hofstede’s (1980) pioneering study of work- related values in 40 IBM national subsidiaries, which was later expanded to different populations in 76 countries. Recently, results of a giant study were published involving more than 1 million participants from 31 countries who responded to a particular personality questionnaire (Bartram, 2013). 
In the age of the Internet, it would be foolish to ignore new, more cost- effective methods of data collection. During a relatively short period, it is possible to recruit huge numbers of participants from one country (Rentfrow & Jokela, 2016; Rentfrow, Jokela, & Lamb, 2015)  or, indeed, from all over the world (Gebauer et  al., 2015; Srivastava, John, Gosling, & Potter, 2003) without even leaving one’s office. Again, an obvious limitation is recruitment method— most often, participants nominate themselves for the study— so that participation is dependent on motivation and access to the Internet (Pullmann, Allik, & Realo, 2009). Despite this and other problems (e.g., attention and compliance, ethical issues, etc.), the Internet nevertheless holds great promise and offers great benefits over “traditional ways” of recruiting participants to collect diverse samples from different parts of the world with relatively little effort and cost (Maniaci & Rogge, 2014). 
Finally, it is possible to learn about personality without sending out any questionnaires. It was the studies of two Dorpat, now Tartu, professors, Adolf Wagner (1835– 1917) and Alexander von Oettingen (1827– 1905) that established what is usually referred to as moral statistics (Lederer, 2013). In his prize- winning book entitled Moral Statistics, Alexander von Oettingen (1868), who was a professor of evangelical theology, examined the statistics of suicide, homicide, and other social events that could shed light on people’s moral principles. However, it was not until 1971 that Richard Lynn published his Personality and National Character in which he used certain statistics— smoking, con-sumption of coffee, and the like— as indicators of certain behavioral characteristics related to personality traits (Lynn, 1971). (See also Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver for more discussion about cross- cultural research methods). 
Large- Scale Studies of Personality We compiled a list of the large- scale personality surveys that involve at least 20 countries or districts and at least a thousand participants (Allik & Realo, 2017a). Selecting 20 as 
 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  415 
the threshold was a choice of convenience rather than a profound theoretical deliberation. Albeit using this relatively modest threshold, it turned out that only a surprisingly small number of studies (n = 32) was able to surpass this by the end of 2016. The largest sample had nearly 3 million participants (Gebauer et  al., 2015), but even the smallest study in terms of its number of participants (N = 2,480) was large when compared with the usual sample sizes of studies published in major journals in social- personality psychology (Fraley & Vazire, 2014). The studies included in the review either analyzed one particular trait (e.g., depression or subjective well- being) or the whole spectrum of personality traits according to a particular taxonomy (e.g., Cattell’s 16 personality factors, Eysenck’s Big Three, the Big Five, or the Big Six). The border between personality traits and some other constructs, such as well- being and values, was not clear. We included the few studies of well- being and emotional experience that involved some other explicit personality measures (Fischer & Boer, 2011; Tay & Diener, 2011). Some of these data were collected during surveys carried out simultaneously in various study sites, while other studies are compilations of previously published data. Most of the studies used the self- report format:  participants were asked to complete questionnaires describing how they think, feel, or act in some typical situations. Other studies used informant- reports: participants were asked to describe the personality of someone they know sufficiently well. In several studies (Allik, Mõttus, & Realo, 2010; Terracciano et al., 2005), participants were instructed to describe not a particular individual, but a prototypical representative of the whole nation (i.e., national stereotypes). 
What can be concluded based on this information? Most importantly, that the number of the large- scale surveys of personality is too small to arrive at far- reaching conclusions (Allik & Realo, 2017a) and that country- level personality mean scores are sometimes tricky and should be handled with caution (Mõttus, Allik, & Realo, 2010). 
How Large are Cross- Cultural Differences in Personality? One derivative of the postulate of the psychic unity of humankind is that all cultural or national differences in personality are small relative to individual variation within each culture or nation. An obvious way to test this postulate is to compare the variance in national mean scores with the variance of the same trait within these nations. Based on published data using either the NEO PI- R (McCrae et al., 2005) or the Big Five Inventory (Schmitt et al., 2007), it turns out that the variance in personality trait scores at the national (aggregate) level is about nine times smaller than the standard deviation of individual- level scores within cultures (Allik, 2005). Recently, we analyzed NEOPI- R/ 3 scores collected in 62 different countries or cultures and 37 different languages (Allik et al., 2017) and were able to confirm previous findings: mean differences in personality traits across countries and cultures were about 8.5 times smaller than differences between any two individuals randomly selected from these samples (Allik et al., 2017). 
 
416 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
It could be argued that personality judgments are not special and that people are quite similar all around the world, not just in terms of their personality traits, but also their values, attitudes, beliefs, and the like. However, this is clearly not the case. For example, the WVS (2005– 2008), which collected answers from 82,992 participants in 57 different countries asked, among other questions, “How important is God in your life?” (World Values Survey Association, 2014). The ratio of country- level variance to mean within- country variance on this question is only 1.28. This indicates that the differences between means of any two randomly selected countries in the importance of God in people’s life is practically as large as the difference between any two individuals who live in the same country. Thus, while there are substantial differences between countries in values and social norms, as we showed earlier, cultural differences in personality traits appear to be relatively small (Allik et al., 2017). 
For this reason, it is not particularly easy to establish the ranking of mean scores of countries or cultures on these traits. Researchers have even questioned the reliability of country mean scores because of relatively low convergent correlations between different sets of data (Meisenberg, 2015). Another reason for questioning the trustworthiness of country- level mean scores is that country rankings on personality traits sometimes look implausible. For instance, counterintuitively, Mõttus and colleagues (2010) found that country rankings on Conscientiousness suggested that the most disciplined and methodical people live in relatively poor African countries, whereas the most lackadaisical and easygoing people live in highly developed East- Asian countries. These and other puzzling rankings led some researchers to question the credibility of national mean scores of personality in general (Heine, Buchtel, & Norenzayan, 2008; Heine, Lehman, Peng, & Greenholtz, 2002; Perugini & Richetin, 2007). One seductively simple reason why we should not trust culture- level aggregate personality scores is the frame- of- reference theory. Already some time ago, Leon Festinger (1954) proposed that people who complete self- report surveys compare themselves with the implicit standards of their culture. Because standards are different across cultures, the same level of a trait may score low in a high- standard society but relatively high in the low- standard society. Obviously applicable in some fields of studies such as health- related research or political attitudes (Hopkins & King, 2010; King, Murray, Salomon, & Tandon, 2004), the frame- of- reference theory does not seem to work well with personality traits. Because personality mean scores— but also social standards— differ much less than is usually expected, we were not able to register any significant reference- level effects when it came to personality ratings (Mõttus, Allik, Realo, Pullmann, et al., 2012). 
There is another popular myth that could be discredited by relatively small personality differences between cultures; namely, the accuracy of national character stereotypes. In his famous book, The Nature of Prejudice, Gordon Allport (1954/ 1978) defined a stere-otype as an exaggerated belief associated with a category that has a kernel of truth. Indeed, certain stereotypes are accurate because they reflect reality, at least to a certain extent (Jussim et al., 2016). For example, it is generally believed that men are more dominant 
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  417 
and women more friendly and complaisant (Löckenhoff et al., 2014), and this is true because there are indeed objectively measured differences between men’s and women’s personality traits that are quite similar almost everywhere in the world (Costa, Terracciano, & McCrae, 2001). Even more interestingly, these differences seem to be increasing with human development (Schmitt, Realo, Voracek, & Allik, 2008). Another group of stereotypes concerns age differences in personality traits. With age, people are believed to become more law- abiding and less open to new experiences (Chan et al., 2012). Again, this seems to be true because age stereotypes of these personality traits correlate with both self- and observer- ratings of these traits across different age groups (Chan et al., 2012). However, national character ratings, although being highly agreed upon by participants in the survey, do not converge with objectively assessed personality traits (Terracciano et  al., 2005). Indeed, national character stereotypes of Canadians and Americans are polarized to the extreme (Adams, 2003), although there are very few, if any, significant differences between Canadians and Americans in their personality traits (Terracciano et al., 2005). This is a well- replicated finding (Allik, Alyamkina, & Meshcheryakov, 2015; Allik et al., 2010; Allik et al., 2009; McCrae, Terracciano, Realo, & Allik, 2007; Realo et al., 2009), which is most likely due to the fact that national mean scores on personality traits differ so little that it is almost impossible to detect differences between the countries. 
How Replicable are Personality Data? In 2015, a large collaborative study by the Open Science Collaboration (2015) was published in Science; it showed that about two- thirds of psychological studies failed to replicate. Before this revelation, there was a similar claim that the majority of biomedical research may not survive the replication test (Ioannidis, 2005). In psychology, the replication crisis has hit some fields more severely than others, with social psychologists being “more vulnerable than most other scientists to such accusations of pervasive wrongness” (Baumeister, 2016, p. 153), and, therefore, they have felt the need to defend themselves and their field against the claim that most published research findings in social psychology are false (Stroebe, 2016). Spurred on by similar concerns, personality psychologists issued a warning to increase the replicability of their research findings (Asendorpf et al., 2013). 
In a special issue of the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology on “Rigorous and Replicable Methods in Social Psychology” (Stangor & Lemay, 2016), Roy Baumeister, one of the most influential psychologists of our time (according to his Google Scholar profile, his works have been cited more than 160,000 times at the time of writing this chapter), defended doing “risky science,” which has worked, he believes, so well for social psychology (Baumeister, 2016). Social psychology, Baumeister maintains, has discovered many important phenomena and created a broad basic understanding of human nature and human social behavior that has been interesting and useful to other disciplines as well as to the general public. By adopting more restrictive research protocols, however, there is the danger for scholars to be “caught up in a highly rigorous but narrowly focused 
 
418 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
style of research” (p. 155) that is simply boring to colleagues in other fields. An alarming example, Baumeister says, is personality psychology with the Big Five, which is “far more solidly based in data than, say, Freudian psychoanalytic theory— but its influence on thinkers in other fields is far less, and indeed it has failed to capture the imagination of the intellectual community” (p. 155). In his closing statement, Baumeister (2016) emphatically called on social psychology to think carefully about how much to follow in personality psychology’s footsteps, or the entire field of social psychology “might end up being one of the losers” (p. 158). Obviously, not everyone shares Baumeister’s (2016) passion for Freudian psychoanalytic theory, which perceives personality as something that only highly trained professionals after years of exhausting practice can determine. If personality traits are not well- kept secrets but banal facts that can be registered by virtually any bystander, then Baumeister’s appeals to return to Freudian psychology have already been obsolete for quite some time (Allik, de Vries, & Realo, 2016). 
There was a period when the use of psychoanalytic theories in culture and personality studies largely prevailed (Inkeles, 1997; LeVine, 2001). For example, cultural anthropologists were eager to take the Rorschach ink- blot to exotic cultures (Searls, 2017)  and ask natives what they see and what they believe makes it look like that in order to learn about their personality, emotions, cognition, and interpersonal tendencies. Very little, if anything at all, changed in our understanding of personality or culture as a result of these studies. It is even surprising that, on many important variables, such as the average number of responses, for instance, there were relatively few cross- cultural differences. From the point of view of contemporary personality psychology, including the FFT, the Rorschach test is vague and uninteresting (Costa & McCrae, 2005). 
One explanation why personality psychology may look boring from the point of view of a social psychologist, which Baumeister (2016) seems to identify as, is that the two disciplines have adopted rather different goals and principles. Like physicists, personality psychologists have consistently sought simplicity and a smaller number of underlying principles, whereas social psychologists more resemble chemists, who seem to be fascinated by the challenges of complexity (McCrae, 2009). If your goal is to discover, for example, the hundreds of tricks your mind plays during cognition— cognitive biases— then the discovery of only five personality dimensions may look like a complete failure. However, to our knowledge, nobody has annulled the essential function of science to seek universals. As we have mentioned in another paper, when Galileo dropped objects of different materials and weight from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, he was looking for a property that is common to all matter (Allik et al., 2013). This is why personality psychologists are primarily interested in what is common to personality descriptions in all (or at least in most) cultures and societies, without dramatic exceptions. Cross- cultural differences are also certainly interesting and, at times, even entertaining, but only universal features, it seems, could provide a satisfying answer to the question of why some people are happy and others feel miserable, why some are hard- working and others are lackadaisical, and why some are inquisitive while others are satisfied with what they already have (Allik et al., 2013).
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  419 
Cross- Cultural Psychopathology Moral statistics were an attempt to observe how social aberrations, as they were understood by the founders of the discipline, are spread across human societies. Sooner or later, the question about the prevalence of mental disorders across cultures was bound to be raised. Indeed, it was shown that, like personality traits, the prevalence of mental disorders and disabilities across cultures and societies is not uniform (Ormel et al., 1994). Because mental disorders are believed to be characterized by the same set dimensions as the normal personality, it is almost axiomatic to assume that mental disorders somehow indicate the distribution of personality traits (Lynn, 1971). 
Usually, Emil Kraepelin (1856– 1926) is identified as the founding father of modern scientific psychiatry (Decker, 2004; Engstrom & Kendler, 2015; Healy, Harris, Farquhar, Tschinkel, & Le Noury, 2008; Hippius & Mueller, 2008; Hoff, 1994; Jablensky, Hugler, Voncranach, & Kalinov, 1993; Steinberg, 2015). He is known for his contributions to many other areas, too, such as psychopharmacology (Müller, Fletcher, & Steinberg, 2006; Saarma & Vahing, 1976; Schmied, Steinberg, & Sykes, 2006; Vahing & Mehilane, 1990), sleep research (Becker, Steinberg, & Kluge, 2016), and psychology (Eysenck & Frith, 1977; Steinberg, 2015). He is also credited with founding cross- cultural psychiatry (Jilek, 1995; Machleidt & Sieberer, 2013). Even before his ground- breaking studies in Indonesia (Kraepelin, 1904), he was appointed to the chair of psychiatry in Estonia where two out of three most spoken languages (i.e., Estonian, Russian, and German)— were beyond his comprehension (Allik, 2016; Allik & Tammiksaar, 2016). He needed assistance to talk to his patients who, in fact, provided his first cross- cultural experience. 
Summarizing his clinical work in the asylum at Buitenzorg (Bogor) on the major Indonesian island of Java, he noted, about the frequency of dementia praecox— the name he gave to a disease discovered by him and known today as schizophrenia— and other mental disturbances that these were occurring with approximately the same frequency as in European countries. In his Memoirs, Kraepelin wrote about his Javanese observations: 
A hasty examination showed that most of the patient population had [no] dementia praecox to a greater extent than in Germany and that therefore race, climate and living conditions had no decisive influence on the origin of this disease. . . . The auditory hallucinations in case of dementia praecox are considered unimportant, probably because language and speech only have a lesser influence on the thinking process in Java. Delusions were also remarkably scarce. From these and other experiences, I became convinced that my attempt to prepare the way for comparative psychiatry could be successful and intended to follow- up these ideas as soon as possible. (Kraepelin, 1987, pp. 115– 116) 
Thus, although Kraepelin observed approximately the same frequency of mental diseases in Java as in Estonia and Germany, the symptoms of these diseases might have 
 
420 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
peculiarities influenced by race, climate, or even culture. This universalist conclusion was somewhat against the dominating view that some mental disorders must be endemic. One of the greatest naturalists of the nineteenth century, Karl Ernst von Baer (1792– 1876), observed in his doctoral dissertation, On Endemic Diseases of Estonians (1814), which was defended in Dorpat many years before Kraepelin’s arrival, that Estonians, who were predominantly peasants, suffer from diseases that are rare or unknown among Germans. At the same time, Baer spotted that, for instance, cramps and mental diseases are quite rare among Estonians. However, we are not aware how Kraepelin’s psychiatric experience in Dorpat influenced his later views on comparative or cross- cultural psychiatry, but we still have clinical cards of Estonians filled in by Kraepelin himself (Rotzoll & Grüner, 2016). 
Kraepelin wrote a sympathetic review of Lombroso’s L’uomo delinquente (1884). Criminality is caused, as Kraepelin argued, seemingly in agreement with Lombroso, by biological, not social factors (Lees, 2002, p. 151). Kraepelin’s views about mental disorders, which he so brilliantly discussed in his inaugural lecture in Dorpat (Engstrom, 2016; Engstrom & Weber, 2005), did not relate mental illnesses automatically with brain illnesses, as was the dominant view in psychiatry, but biological factors still played an important role. Therefore, it was expected that mental disorders could be caused, at least partly, by physical constitution, which was very different for Estonians. The link between Estonian and Uralic languages had just been discovered, which was fruitful ground for the idea of the existence of a Mongoloid substrate in the Estonian physical makeup (Kalling, 2016). 
The current understanding of the prevalence of common mental disorders in various cultures is not very different from that of Kraepelin’s initial and limited observations. The findings confirm that common mental disorders are highly prevalent globally, affecting people across all regions of the world (Steel et al., 2014). Although globally uniform, some regional variation in the prevalence of common mental disorders can be noticed. For example, countries within North and South East Asia display consistently lower 1- year and lifetime prevalence estimates than other regions. One- year prevalence rates are also low in Sub- Saharan Africa, whereas English- speaking countries return the highest lifetime prevalence estimates (Steel et al., 2014). 
Very often, eating- disordered behavior is perceived as a direct consequence of Westernization of society and culture. It seems quite untenable, for example, that the prevalence of symptoms of anorexia and bulimia nervosa would be higher in countries where a considerable proportion of the population suffers from malnutrition. Nevertheless, a recent analysis demonstrated that non- Western participants scored higher than more affluent Western participants on virtually all Eating Disorder Inventory subscales, both in normal and eating- disordered samples (Podar & Allik, 2009). This is a surprising result because eating- related behavior is very often involved in culture- specific practices and symbols. Nevertheless, eating- disordered behavior appears to be more prevalent in the less Westernized societies (see also Chapter 14 by Junko Tanaka- Matsumi for more discussion of abnormal psychology and culture).
CulTure and Personal iTy  |  421 
Conclusion Personality psychologists like to think about their field as the core that brings the different parts of psychology together (Allport, 1961). At times, it has simply been wishful thinking, not endorsed by sufficiently relevant findings or theoretical insights. However, personality psychology has spread across the borders of countries much more easily than many other areas of psychology. If it is sometimes feared that many generalizations in psychology are relevant only to those who attend Psychology 101 classes in North American universities (Arnett, 2008), personality psychology has been, from the very beginning, an international enterprise. Although personality psychology has been very fascinated by all kinds of cultural differences and unique details, it has predominantly been the psychic unity of humankind that has emerged from cross- cultural studies.
