Abnormal Psychology and Culture 
Junko Tanaka- Matsumi 
The Global Landscape of Culture and Psychopathology Research on culture’s interplay with human behavior and experience has made notable progress since the publication of the initial edition of this Handbook (Matsumoto, 2001). Important societal developments and global population movements have contributed to an increasing interest in investigating the dynamic cultural contexts of “human adaptation and its failures” (Phillips, 1968). Advanced epidemiological studies have contributed to estimating the prevalence of mental disorders and rates of mental health service utilization around the world (Kessler & Üstün, 2004)  and among representative samples of ethnic and racial groups (Holzer & Copeland, 2013). The World Health Organization (WHO, 2017) has identified depression and anxiety disorders as common mental disorders affecting the lives of 322 million and 264 million people, respectively, around the world. Depressive disorders are ranked as the single largest contributor to nonfatal loss of health and functioning, affecting particularly people in low- income nations (Alonso, Chatterji, He, & Kessler, 2013). Proponents of “a new architecture of global mental health” have encouraged transdisciplinary approaches to assess, design, implement, and evaluate intervention programs to help distressed persons, with implications for community- based policy- making (Kirmayer & Ryder, 2016; Mendenhall, 2018). With an upsurge in migration around the world, there has been increased interest in the mental health status of migrants within the acculturation context (Berry, 2006; Neftci & Barnow, 2016). Furthermore, globalization demands new ways of thinking about culture in terms of “hybridization, turbulence and virtual exchange” (Kirmayer, 2006, p.138). Across these evolving scenes, culture has come to the fore of mental health research, 
 
 
432 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
practice, education, and policy- making (Collins et al., 2011; Marsella & Yamada, 2007; Tanaka- Matsumi, 2018). 
The Goals of the Chapter In this chapter, psychopathology refers to “the distress, disability, and helplessness of human beings in the face of important problems, challenges, and tasks of living” (Draguns, 2017, p. 343). Culture is defined as “a unique meaning and information system, shared by a group and transmitted across generations, that allows the group to meet basic needs of survival, pursue happiness and well- being, and derive meaning from life” (Matsumoto & Juang, 2008, p. 12). Functions of culture include (1) the adjustment function, (2) the ego- defensive function, (3) the value expressive function, and (4) the knowledge function (Triandis, 2007; see also Chapter 5 by Yoshihisa Kashima on the functions of culture). The major goal of this chapter is to appraise the current state of knowledge of the relationship between culture and psychopathology. More specifically, this chapter aims to (1) identify the contribution of different conceptual and methodological approaches to investigating the relationship between culture and psychopathology, (2) seek integration of universal and culture- specific approaches to cross- cultural psychopathology, and (3) promote the development of linkage studies in the field of cross- cultural psychopathology in the age of globalization. In this chapter, these aims are pursued with a focus on major psychiatric disorders and their assessment methods that have generated a large amount of literature from both emic and etic perspectives. 
Emic and Etic Perspectives to Psychopathology Formulations of and findings on the relationship between psychopathology and culture are rooted in one of three general orientations, which have been described as absolutist, universalist, and culturally relativist (Berry, Poortinga, Segall, & Dasen, 1992; see also Chapter 1 by Walter J. Lonner, Kenneth D. Keith, and David Matsumoto for more discus-sion of these orientations in historical perspective). The absolutist orientation would ad-vocate the biological model of psychopathology, with invariant symptoms across cultures. However, the literature is in agreement that culture exerts varying degrees of influence on psychopathological processes and manifestations (Draguns, 1980; Draguns & Tanaka- Matsumi, 2003; Marsella & Yamada, 2007). Therefore, the most plausible positions from which to study psychopathology and culture are the etic and emic positions. The universalist and cultural relativist viewpoints overlap greatly with the etic and emic positions (Berry, 1969; Berry, Poortinga, Breugelmans, Chasiotis, & Sam, 2011). Cross- cultural psychologists “typically expect both biological and cultural factors to influence human behavior, but, like relativists, assume that the role of culture in producing human variation both within and across groups (especially across groups) is substantial” (Segall, 
 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  433 
Lonner, & Berry, 1998, p. 1104). The etic and emic approaches differ markedly in terms of the recognition of the nature of the mutual embeddedness of culture and mental illness (Sam & Moreira, 2012), with the etic or universalist view emphasizing the comparability of cross- culturally or even globally applicable dimensions or categories. These categories are generally equated with the major entries of the Western Kraepelinian diagnostic system. 
Historical Origins of Cross- Cultural Psychopathology Kraepelin’s Pioneering Questions on the Universality of Psychopathology. Historically, Emil Kraepelin’s (1904) observational accounts from Java of the universality of mental disorders (such as “dementia praecox” and “manic- depressive psychosis”) inspired psychiatric researchers to study the relationship between culture and psychopathology. These pioneers include Lin (1953), Devereux (1961), Leighton et  al. (1963), Wittkower and Rin (1965), Brody (1967), J. Murphy and Leighton (1965), Yap (1967), J. Murphy (1976), Kiev (1972), Draguns (1973, 1980), H. B. M. Murphy (1982a), Pfeiffer (1970/ 1994), and Fabrega (1974), among others (see Marsella, 1993). Kraepelin was inspired by the experimental psychologist Wilhelm Wundt, who was formulating Volkerpsycholgie (folk psychology or anthropological psychology), first at the University of Heidelberg since 1851 and later at the University of Leipzig in Germany (Jilek, 1995). Throughout the major part of twentieth century, cross- cultural researchers pursued the same questions posed originally by Kraepelin (1904): Are there universals in psychopathology? What are the sources of “very remarkable differences” in the forms of psychopathology? For more than a century, answers to these questions have reflected both emic and etic perspectives. 
Cross- cultural research is believed to enhance our understanding of psychopathology with regard to prevalence rates, risk factors, protective factors, and the possible etiology of particular disorders (Al- Issa, 1995; Draguns, 1990; Leff, 1988). To this end, the universalist or etic perspective has inspired research on the cross- cultural validity and reliability of psychiatric diagnoses. The culturally relativist or emic investigators, on the other hand, eschew comparison and categorization. The word “emic” has, in fact, come to mean “culture- specific” (Brislin, 1983, p.  382). Emic researchers focus on the local context of a phenomenon within a culture and investigate indigenous, culturally based meanings of concepts, such as idioms of distress (Nichter, 1981; Weiss et al., 1992). The key to conducting emic research is collecting ethnographic or culturally grounded data without imposing a priori definitions and the ideas of the researcher. Emic researchers believe that the dialectical interaction of biological and cultural processes shapes abnormal behavior and its communication (Jenkins, 2015; Kleinman, 1988). 
 
 
434 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Emergence of Cultural Relativity Perspectives on Psychopathology Historically, Sarbin and Juhasz (1982) have analyzed the broadening of theoretical approaches to mental disorders leading away from the ethnocentrism of the colonial era to a cultural relativism beginning with the contributions of anthropologists such as Mead (1935) and Benedict (1934). Much later, in the 1960s, some aspects of cultural relativism were strongly reflected in the works of Foucault (1965), Goffman (1961), Scheff (1966), Sarbin (1969), Szasz (1961), and Ullmann and Krasner (1969, 1975). These scholars advanced a view that the standard of what is normal and abnormal is culturally variable. Many people who would be considered abnormal in one culture would be considered quite normal in another culture due to differences in values and norms for certain behaviors. 
By the mid- 1960s, the majority of abnormal psychology textbooks published in English introduced cultural relativity views of abnormal behavior (Tanaka- Matsumi & Chang, 2001). Culture- relevant topics covered in introductory psychology textbooks have also increased steadily since the 1960s (Lonner & Murdock, 2012). Rejecting the psychiatric- medical model of abnormal behavior, Ullmann and Krasner (1969, 1975) viewed psychiatric diagnosis as a value- laden social act involving the patient and the observer in a specific context. Rosenhan (1973) demonstrated the context effect of psychiatric labeling in his paper titled “On Being Sane in Insane Places,” published in Science. Tanaka- Matsumi and Chang (2001) noted, however, that the authors of contem-porary abnormal psychology textbooks have almost invariably followed the major disorder categories (e.g., depression, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders) based on successive editions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association. 
Draguns (1980) cautioned that, historically, three factors have complicated the problem of identifying cultural universals and cultural particulars in psychopathology: (1) the application of Kraepelinian categories throughout the world, (2) the exportation of Western psychiatric institutions to other cultures, and (3) the imitation of Western symptoms and complaints by patients in cultures undergoing modernization. In this chapter, I apply a combined emic- etic perspective (Brislin, 1983; Chen, 2010) with a hope of illuminating derived- etics (Berry, 1989) and cultural particulars in the content of human distress and its antecedents, communication, and social consequences. Throughout this chapter, etic and emic perspectives are both emphasized in order to derive cross- culturally common themes of psychopathology. 
Culture and Psychiatric Diagnosis Etic Approaches and Emic Critiques As a starting point for modern, prototypical cross- cultural research on psychopathology, I  examine the US- UK Diagnostic Project (Cooper et  al., 1972). This project provided 
 
 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  435 
an important impetus toward identifying sources of cultural variation in diagnostic outcomes and the subsequent development of standardized assessment methods to compare abnormal behavior patterns across cultures. There were three parts to the project. First, Cooper et al. (1972) confirmed earlier reports that comparisons of hospital diagnoses of first admissions to the mental hospitals in New York and London revealed striking contrasts for nearly every major diagnostic category. Most notably, there were far more patients with the initial diagnoses of schizophrenia in the New  York sample and more patients diagnosed with depressive psychoses in the London sample. Second, Cooper et al. (1972) demonstrated that these diagnostic differences disappeared greatly when British and American project psychiatrists diagnosed the patients with the WHO’s standardized diagnostic system ICD- 8 (International Classification of Diseases- Version 8). Finally, the US- UK Project examined whether American and British psychiatrists used different symptom criteria when evaluating videotaped interviews of both American and British patients. Cross- national agreement was high for prototypical cases. However, for mixed cases, American psychiatrists had a broader concept of schizophrenia and British psychiatrists had a broader concept of manic- depressive disorder. Furthermore, both groups of experienced raters expressed confidence in their conflicting diagnoses. 
Questions raised by the results of the US- UK Diagnostic Project have led to two competing pathways in research on psychopathology and culture. The first is the development and field testing of standardized diagnostic instruments across cultures. The second is refocusing on each individual culture and avoiding cross- cultural comparisons. In the first etic pathway, cross- cultural variability due to diagnosticians was to be controlled or eliminated since it interfered with a reliable assessment of patient differences. In fact, ever since Kraepelin introduced the two major psychiatric concepts of schizophrenia and manic- depressive disorder, the predominant approach has been bio- medical in nature, without systematic attempts to observe the patient’s social surroundings. Accordingly, major efforts went into the development of explicit diagnostic criteria and standardized diagnostic systems based on biomedical models of mental illness (Sartorius & Janca, 1996). 
In contrast, those who were intrigued by cultural- contextual factors in the practice of psychiatric diagnosis have gone on to develop a separate and emic path of cultural research. Arthur Kleinman’s (1977) paper on the “category fallacy” marked the beginning of the “new cross- cultural psychiatry.” Kleinman (1977, p. 4) stated that psychiatric categories (e.g., schizophrenia) are bound to the context of professional psychiatric theory and practice in the West. Eschewing the predetermined, Western- derived diagnostic categories, more contextually oriented scholars promoted the cultural relativist position and produced descriptive and ethnographic studies relevant to psychopathology. The themes of these pioneering studies included cultural idioms of distress (Nichter, 1981), contextual descriptions of culture- bound syndromes (Simons & Hughes, 1985), and cultural interpretations of major disorders, including depression (Kleinman & Good, 1985a), anxiety (Hinton & Good, 2009), and schizophrenia (Jenkins, 2015). An overall theme of the new cross- cultural psychiatry is describing the context and experience of human distress 
436 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
rather than developing categories of disorders (Littlewood, 1990). Consistent with the emphasis on the indigenous information, these researchers focused on collecting narrative data expressing the illness experience of the distressed persons rather than imposing theoretical models and categories of mental illness. 
In sum, this section reviewed the seminal US- UK cross- national diagnostic study in order to illuminate the conceptual and methodological questions in studying the relationship between culture and psychopathology via both etic and emic lenses. 
Mental Health Professionals and Healers as Culturally Embedded Nearly five decades after the landmark US- UK diagnostic study (Cooper et al., 1972), cultural variation in diagnostic practice and clinical decision- making persists. That is, clinicians use different criteria for the local diagnosis of psychiatric disorders. James et al. (2014) conducted a cross- national comparison of hospital discharge rates from 2000 to 2010 for pediatric bipolar disorder in the United States and England. After controlling for cross- national differences in length of stay, they found that discharge rates for pediatric bipolar disorder were 12.5 times higher in the United States than in English hospitals. The authors attributed these differences to differences in community diagnostic practices reflecting local norms. More standardized epidemiological surveys produced comparable prevalence rates in pediatric bipolar disorder (James et al., 2014). Incidence rates for pediatric bipolar disorder were not reported in these studies. The cross- national disparities in diagnosis were minimized when the clinicians used standardized diagnostic systems such as the ICD- 10 (World Health Organization, 1992; see also Clacey, Goldacre, & James, 2015). The researchers noted that the cross- national variation was likely due to differences in professional judgments within the local hospital setting. 
The standardized systems have contributed to investigating the universality of mental disorders across different cultures and have produced a large amount of new literature on cross- cultural psychopathology. However, the assessment of the culture of the diagnostician has received minimal research attention, as has the cultural context of abnormal behavior (Angel & Williams, 2013; Fabrega, 1987; Kleinman, 1988; Rogler, 1999; Thakker & Ward, 1998; Whaley, 1997). As a consequence, cross- cultural mental health research has lacked specification of cultural factors and culture- relevant hypotheses in its research design (Betancourt & López, 1993; Canino, Lewis- Fernández, & Bravo, 1997; López, 1989; Phinney, 1996). Matsumoto and Yoo (2006) called for more “linkage studies” in order to test culture- relevant hypotheses in cross- cultural research by empirically linking specific cultural factors to observed differences among selected variables. 
The act of identifying, describing, labeling, and developing a treatment plan involves a complex sociocultural process (Draguns, 1980; Kirmayer & Young, 1999; Westermeyer, 1987). Empirical research on cross- cultural psychopathology must therefore consider the 
 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  437 
three interactive factors of the patient, observer, and assessment context as being relevant to the process and outcome of clinical diagnosis (Draguns & Tanaka- Matsumi, 2003; de Haan, Boon, Vermeiren, & de Jong, 2014). In studying race differences in psychiatric diagnoses, Whaley (1997) clarified diagnostic questions as harboring two different propositions:  (1) the clinician bias hypothesis and (2)  the cultural relativity hypothesis. Similarly, López (1989) proposed specific factors contributing to overdiagnosing and underdiagnosing of certain psychiatric disorders such as “paranoid schizophrenia” in African Americans. These views suggest that diagnosticians have their own baselines for psychopathologies for different ethno- cultural groups and that they are influenced by their own normative judgments (Adebimpe, 1981; Clacey et  al., 2015). Therefore, indigenous diagnostic practices do continue to differ across cultures, while the more standardized project diagnoses increase reliability in judgment. Both the clinician bias hypothesis and cultural relativity hypothesis remain plausible in cross- cultural research on clinical assessment of psychopathology across cultures. 
Methodological Innovations in Epidemiology: Standardization of Assessment Instruments The US- UK Diagnostic Project (Cooper et al., 1972) stimulated the development of (1) explicit diagnostic criteria to define specific psychiatric disorders, (2) standardized structured interview schedules by trained diagnosticians, and (3) face- to- face interview protocols for large- scale community surveys (Holzer & Copeland, 2013). The Epidemiological Catchment Area Study (ECA) in the United States used the advanced epidemiological method and involved five centers, located in St. Louis, Baltimore, New Haven, Durham, and Los Angeles (Robins & Regier, 1991). The ECA survey generated epidemiological research data according to ethnicity, age, gender, and socioeconomic status. More than 20,000 randomly selected community residents were interviewed using the Diagnostic Interview Schedule (DIS) for case identification (see Table 14.1 for instruments cited in this manuscript). The DIS assesses major psychiatric disorders described in the DSM- III to determine lifetime and current diagnoses based on a set of explicit diagnostic criteria (Robins, Helzer, Croughan, & Ratcliff, 1981). The DIS was translated into Spanish. The ECA also included African Americans (n = 4,649), Hispanics (n = 1,428), mostly Mexican Americans, and small samples of Asians (n = 238) and Native Americans (n = 148). The ECA results suggest the importance of assessing the direct and indirect effects of ethnicity and acculturation status on the prevalence of affective disorders. For example, the lifetime prevalence of affective disorders was 11.0% for Non- Hispanic whites and 7.8% for Mexican Americans (Karno et al., 1987). In comparison with Mexican American women, the rate of major depressive episodes was 2.5 times higher for Non- Hispanic white women under 40 years of age. However, Mexican Americans born in the United States resembled non- Hispanic whites in exhibiting increased rates of specific symptoms of major depression (e.g., dysphoria, appetite disturbances, sleep disturbances, etc.) (Golding, Karno, & Rutter, 1990). The rates for Mexican Americans born in Mexico were lower in eight of 
 
438 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
the nine symptom categories of major depression examined. Some of these ECA findings may be the result of interactive effects of ethnicity with acculturation and acculturative stress. In the ECA study, birthplace and language served as the index of acculturation status. With acculturation, Mexican Americans may have learned to experience and/ or express depression through more cognitive and affective symptoms rather than through the somatic channel. Subsequently, a methodologically and conceptually more advanced community household survey called the National Latino and Asian American Study (NLAAS; Alegria, Takeuchi et  al., 2004)  estimated the prevalence of mental disorders and rates of mental health service utilization of representative samples of Latinos and Asian Americans in the United States. Alegria, Vila et al. (2004) conducted a systematic evaluation of the measures used in this psychiatric epidemiological survey by combining etic and emic measures to establish cross- cultural equivalence. Using the NLAAS dataset,
