abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  439 
Lorenzo- Blanco and Unger (2015) developed a model to evaluate the mediating role of acculturation stress in the depressive symptoms and smoking behavior of Latino youth. Perceived discrimination and family conflict were both related significantly to increased stress, which predicted the severity of depressive symptoms and cigarette smoking. Empirical assessment studies of perceived discrimination and psychopathology in ethnic minority groups have consistently shown adverse effects of discrimination (e.g., Chou, Asnaani, & Hofmann, 2012). Another major field survey of mental health is the National Comorbidity Survey (NCS) conducted in the United States (NCS; Kessler et al., 1994). The NCS has conducted four surveys, including the initial survey, a 10- year follow- up survey, a replication survey, and an adolescent supplement survey. The NCS used the Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI) based on the then most current DSM- III- R (American Psychiatric Association, 1987). The NCS sample comprised 8,098 persons, including white (75%), black (12.5%), Hispanic (9.1%), and other (3.3%). The prevalence rates of any disorder were higher in the NCS than in the ECA in all groups. 
Internationally, the interview- based method such as the DIS used in the ECA was widely translated into different languages and used in major psychiatric epidemiological surveys of general populations of different countries in the 1980s. Epidemiological studies hold the promise of establishing normative baselines for different disorders across cultures. Baselines in general populations can serve important functions when we compare the thresholds for abnormal behavior in different cultures. Methodologically, the investigators reported developing both linguistically and culturally reliable and valid Spanish version of the DIS based on a comprehensive cultural adaptation model (Bravo, Canino, Rubio- Stipec, & Woodbury- Fariña, 1991). Specifically, these authors addressed the cultural validity of the instrument in terms of semantic, technical, content, criterion, and conceptual equivalence. Hwu and Compton (1994) compared the outcomes of six major epidemiological surveys conducted in Puerto Rico (Canino et al., 1987), the United States (Karno et al., 1987), Canada (Bland, Orn, & Newman, 1988), Korea (Lee et  al., 1990), Taiwan (Hwu, Yeh, & Chang, 1989), and New Zealand (Wells, Bushnell, Hornblon, Joyce, & Oakley- Browne, 1989). Hwu and Compton (1994) made post- hoc cross- national comparisons of the lifetime prevalence rates of different disorders according to such variables as gender and urban versus rural area. Cultural variations were evident for major disorders as defined by the DSM- III. The lifetime prevalence rates for the majority of disorders, except alcohol abuse/ dependence in Korea, were generally lower in Asian samples (Korea and Taiwan) than in American, Caucasian, and Hispanic samples. 
Helzer and Canino (1992) compared DIS data involving 48,000 respondents from 10 cultures in North America, Europe, and Asia. They found that, in every culture investigated, men had higher rates of alcohol abuse/ dependence than did women, particularly in Taiwan, China, and Korea. Within the United States, only 10% of men and women who met the DSM- III diagnosis of alcohol abuse/ dependence in the ECA study sought treatment (Robins, Locke, & Regier, 1991). This alone suggests that the differentiation of 
440 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
normal and abnormal drinking is difficult to establish both within and across cultures (Bennett, Janca, Grant, & Sartorius, 1993). The World Mental Health Survey Initiative (WMHSI) of the WHO conducted general population surveys that estimated the prevalence of mental disorders in a total of 26 countries, including 6 countries in the Americas, 10 in Europe, 4 in the Middle East, 2 in Africa, and 4 in Asia or the Pacific (Kessler, Haro, Herringa, Pennell, & Üstün, 2006). The WMHSI employed the WHO- CIDI, which is a structured face- to- face interview method that generates diagnoses based on the definition and criteria of both the ICD- 10 and the DSM- IV (American Psychiatric Association, 1994; Kessler & Üstün, 2004). Results of CIDI interviews with more than 200,000 community residents were analyzed for lifetime prevalence, age- of- onset distributions, projected lifetime risk, and cohort effects. Among the results, lifetime prevalence rates for “any disorder” were highest for the United States (47.4%) and lowest for Nigeria (12%). 
In sum, the development of a standardized face- to- face interview instrument such as the fully structured CIDI enabled worldwide epidemiological surveys of major mental disorders, enhancing our understanding of not just the prevalence but also of sociodemographic factors possibly associated with differential rates of mental disorders across cultures. In discussing the discrepancies in the prevalence of mental disorders across cultures, Kessler et al. (2006) stated that differential stigmas attached to admitting emotional problems are culturally variable. They also acknowledged the potential differences between the fully structured CIDI administered by trained lay interviewers and semi- structured clinical diagnostic interviews carried out by experienced local clinicians. Kessler et al. (2006) evaluated the WMHSI as producing an “unprecedented amount of high quality data on the general population epidemiology of mental disorders around the world” (p. 165). Hwu and Compton (1994) provided plausible explanations for cross- cultural differences in the prevalence rates of mental disorders. They included such factors as biological vulnerability, culturally determined protective factors, thresholds for reporting symptoms, social stigma, and demographic risk factors (e.g., divorce). In the next section, the question of incorporating cultural factors in diagnostic work is answered affirmatively. 
Developing Cultural Formulations for Standardized Diagnostic Systems Cultural competence in diagnostic assessment requires knowledge of the patient’s culture, including the language, cultural modes of expressing distress, and meanings of subjective experiences as well as coping and social support networks (Sue, 1998; Sue, Zane, Nagayama, & Berger, 2009) and ability to engage in a dynamic, culturally informed interaction process with the patient (Kirmayer, 2012; Tanaka- Matsumi, Seiden, & Lam, 1996). The diagnostic system itself must be able to gather culturally salient information regarding the patient. To increase the cross- cultural applicability of the DSM- IV, its authors 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  441 
took several new steps: (1) presentation of information in the text regarding cultural variations in the clinical manifestations of disorders, (2) a description of 25 culture- bound syndromes in an appendix, and (3) an outline of a cultural formulation for the evaluation of the individual’s cultural context. These are important cultural factors introduced into the DSM- IV. However, they were not regarded as integral parts of the diagnostic system, as, for example, “culture- bound syndromes” were put in an appendix. 
In other words, cultural- contextual information was not infused in the main assessment work in the DSM- IV. DSM- 5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013)  was published in 2013 with some major changes in the system, including a part- dimensional approach instead of an all- categorical approach (Blashfield, Keeley, Flanagan, & Miles, 2014). A  major advancement is the publication of the Cultural Case Formulation Interview (CFI) with specific procedures and guidelines (Lewis- Fernández et al., 2014). The CFI describes 16 interview questions supplemented by 12 modules for further assessment (Lewis- Fernández, Aggarwal, Hinton, Hinton, & Kirmayer, 2016). The 16 questions of the CFI cover four domains of culturally relevant assessment: (1) cultural definitions of the clinical problem (3 questions), (2) cultural perceptions of cause, context, and support (7 questions), (3)  cultural factors affecting self- coping and past help- seeking (3 questions), and (4) cultural factors affecting current help- seeking (3 questions). These correspond to contextual questions regarding explanatory models, the patient– clinician relationship, coping and help- seeking, cultural identity, spirituality, religion, and moral traditions, psychosocial stressors, social networks, and level of functioning. 
International Psychologists’ Perspectives on Standardized Diagnosis What do international psychologists think about classificatory diagnosis? Evans et  al. (2013) conducted the WHO- IUPsyS (International Union of Psychological Science) Global Survey of 2,155 psychologists’ perspectives on the diagnostic classification of mental disorders in 23 nations. The results revealed a wide variation in the responses to questions regarding the difficulty with cross- cultural applicability, bias toward the United States and Europe, and the need for a national classification of mental disorders. These cross- national differences may be related to discrepancies between rationally derived diagnostic systems such as the DSM and the WHO- ICD- 10, and clinicians’ folk taxonomies of mental disorders (Flanagan, Keeley, & Blashfield, 2007). Evans et al. (2013) reported that international psychologists showed high agreement regarding such items as “informing treatment decisions” and “facilitating communication” as the most important purposes of diagnostic classification. The majority of these psychologists, however, indicated that they did not necessarily adhere to the DSM or ICD in clinical practice. Mental health professionals hold their own models of mental illness that do not necessarily correspond to the conceptualizations of disorders defined in standardized diagnostic 
 
442 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
instruments such as the DSM and ICD (López & Guarnaccia, 2000, 2016). Flanagan, Keeley, and Blashfield (2008) analyzed these issues conceptually and empirically to explain disparities between rationally derived categories of mental disorders in the DSM- IV and folk taxonomies of mental disorders. Kleinman (1988), Rogler (1999), and many others argued that the standardization of categories is itself a form of “cultural suppression” because category contents are selected by rational decision to conform to the procedural norms of scientific and professional guidelines rather than indigenous, local norms. 
In conclusion, the development of standardized diagnostic instruments has dramatically altered the nature of cross- cultural research by attempting to use the same criteria for case identification across cultures. The cultural backgrounds of both the clinician and the patient affect diagnostic judgments. The CFI developed for DSM- 5 is a promising tool for integrating cultural elements into the interactive diagnostic process between the patient and the clinician. Its status in terms of reliability and validity, however, will depend on the demonstration of culturally informed case formulation and acceptance for use by local or community clinicians (Lewis- Fernández et al., 2014). 
Indigenous Approaches to Diagnosis and Assessment of Illness Indigenous views and concepts of distress are considered fundamental to understanding the cultural context of illness behaviors (Kirmayer, 1984). Emically oriented investigators have studied psychopathology in relation to sociocultural context (Hinton & Good, 2009; Hofmann & Hinton, 2014; Jenkins, 2015; Kleinman, 1980, 1986; Marsella & White, 1982; Sam & Moreira, 2012). These researchers investigated (1) the meanings of indigenous idioms of distress, (2) culture- specific taxonomies of disorders, (3) the role of culture in identifying and shaping the form and meaning of antecedent risk factors, and (4) attributions for consequences of illness. 
The Explanatory Model Interview Catalogue As an alternative to standardized diagnostic assessment, Weiss et al. (1992) developed the Explanatory Model Interview Catalogue (EMIC) to identify culture- specific idioms of distress, perceived causes of illness, and help- seeking behavior. The EMIC provides an operational framework for semi- structured interviews to gather data in order to systematically clarify the experiences of an illness from the point of view of the person affected. The EMIC was originally used in a cultural study of leprosy and mental health in India. Reported interrater agreement of EMIC items using kappa ranged from .62 to .90. Weiss et al. (1992) described five areas of inquiry for EMIC interviews: (1) patterns of distress, (2) perceived causes, (3) help- seeking and treatment, (4) general illness beliefs, and (5) disease- specific queries. EMIC has been used to formulate explanatory model interviews to investigate various disorders such as leprosy, depression, ataque de nervios, 
 
 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  443 
alcohol abuse and dependence, depression and somatoform disorders, neurasthenia, and chronic fatigue syndrome, in various parts of the world (Weiss, 1997). To illustrate, Lewis- Fernández et al. (2009) examined the clinical profiles of 66 Hispanic persons with experience of ataque de nervios at the Hispanic Treatment Center in New York City. First, they used the EMIC; second, the standardized interview by SCID (Structured Clinical Interview); and third, an integrative interview that considered the results of the qualitative EMIC and standardized SCID methods using the DSM- IV criteria for panic dis-order. The main finding was that the overlap between folk criteria of ataques de nervios and DSM- IV diagnostic criteria for panic attacks was only 17%. The emic- etic combined methods show the importance of probing the narratives of each person seeking treatment in a culturally informed context. As the authors stated, “Ultimately, ataque de nervios and panic disorder are labels for overlapping categories of experience rather than mutually exclusive sets” (Lewis- Fernández et al., 2009, p. 155). In sum, culture- specific data generated by the EMIC may contribute to identifying universals in contextual factors associated with major disorders and folk illness taxonomies. 
In the next section, I review the major findings on the interplay between culture and human distress defined specifically as mental disorders. 
Issues and Findings on Major Disorders Depression 
Values and Conceptualization of Depression Historically, themes of personal and communal loss, role disruption, and sudden changes in one’s environment have been linked to states of dejection, anger, and even severe melancholia (Jackson, 1986). The cross- cultural literature on depression has been noted for value- laden observations of colonial, ethno- medical investigators (Fabrega, 1974; Marsella, 1980). For example, Carothers (1953) wrote that African natives did not have the capacity to feel depressed because the size of their frontal lobe was much smaller, hence inferior to that of Westerners. During this time, cultures were identified with qualifiers such as “simple” and “primitive” in the literature (McCulloch, 1995). Prince (1968) then published a major review article on depressive syndromes in Africa and questioned whether the sudden increase in the prevalence of depression in sub- Saharan Africa after the mid- 1950s reflected a “fact or diagnostic fashion.” The anthropologist Field (1960) issued a definitive statement, based on her fieldwork in rural Ghana with Ashanti women, that depression was actually common in Africa. Her anthropological fieldwork suggested that the Western bio- medical model and its ethnocentric method would miss depressed Africans because the investigator was not informed about indigenous cultural practices of depressed roles in traditional Ashanti communities. 
 
 
 
444 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
In the twenty- first century, depression is recognized as one of the most common and most debilitating mental health problems throughout the world (Kessler & Bromet, 2013). The Global Burden of Disease Study by the WHO identified depression as the fourth leading cause of global burden in terms of Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs). Furthermore, it was estimated that depression would rank second in DALYs in 2020 and first by 2030 worldwide (Alonso, Chatterji, & He, 2013). After more than 60 years since Carothers’s (1953) colonial psychiatry work, the prevalence of depression in African regions, particularly North Africa, was reported to be “high” (Ferrari et al., 2013). 
Marsella (1980) integrated the literature on “depressive experience and disorder across cultures” and concluded that the conceptualizations of depression are culturally variable. He further stated that “there appears to be no universal conception of depression” (p. 274) and “even among those cultures not having conceptually equivalent terms, it is sometimes possible to find variants of depressive disorders similar to those found in Western cultures” (p.  274). Although different cultures may have different words describing subjective experiences of what is called depression in English, connotative meanings of these words can be widely different (Chentsova- Dutton & Tsai, 2008; Manson, Shore, & Bloom, 1985; Tanaka- Matsumi & Marsella, 1976). 
To investigate sociocultural differences in conceptions of depression, Karasz (2005) presented a vignette describing DSM- IV– based depressive symptoms to working- class South Asian (SA) immigrants and affluent upper- middle- class European Americans (EA) and asked them to generate “representational models of illness” in a semi- structured interview. The SAs endorsed a “situational stress model” in social and moral terms. In contrast, the EAs presented biological explanations. Conceptions of depression also differed in similar ways among primary care patients of EA, SA, and Hispanic American (HA) ethnic groups in New York City (Karasz, Garcia, & Ferri, 2009). In Uganda, Johnson et al. (Johnson, Chin, Kajumba, Kizito, & Bangirana, 2017) conducted mixed- method studies to investigate explanatory models (EMs) of depression held by patients seeking treatment in traditional healing and psychiatry clinics. They also assessed differences in EMs of patients and their providers in dyads. Both patients and “healers” differed in conceptions of depression, and the patients’ depressive symptoms included a range of psychological, affective, and somatic symptoms. In Uganda, traditional healers include a diversity of specialists including herbalists, spiritualists, diviners, pastors/ sheiks, faith healers, and midwives. Psychiatric approach takes a Western- derived biomedical perspective, with a focus on the individual patient and reduction of symptoms (Johnson et al., 2017). 
Epidemiology and Cross- National Studies A number of international studies have published prevalence estimates of “major depression.” Lifetime prevalence estimates using the DIS varied across studies, ranging from a low of 3.3% in Seoul to a high of 12.6% in Christchurch (Hwu & Compton, 1994). However, even within the United States, the estimates of lifetime prevalence varied depending on the instrument used. For example, the ECA study estimated the lifetime prevalence at 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  445 
5.8%, while the National Comorbidity Survey (Kessler et al., 1994) estimated it at 17.1%. These differences might be explained by methodological factors such as the specificity and sensitivity of the diagnostic instruments used and age compositions of the samples studied. Thus, a better research design is a simultaneous case finding and assessment using the same instrument with demonstrated reliability. 
A prototypically etic study of depression is the WHO international project on the diagnosis and classification of depression in Switzerland, Canada, Japan, and Iran. The goal was to test the feasibility of using standardized instruments (WHO, 1983). Patients (N = 573) were diagnosed using the Schedule for Standardized Assessment of Depressive Disorders (WHO/ SADD) by project psychiatrists. The WHO/ SADD examines 39 symptoms of depression. Its overall reliability was .96, with no specific item reliability falling below .90. The study indicated that more than 76% of the depressed patients reported core depressive symptoms that included “sadness, joylessness, anxiety, tension, lack of energy, loss of interest, loss of ability to concentrate, and ideas of insufficiency” (WHO, 1983, p. 61). Suicidal ideation was present in 59% of patients. The WHO project also discovered cross- cultural variation in the expression of depression. Specifically, 40% of patients displayed “other symptoms” such as somatic complaints and obsessions that were not listed among the original 39 symptoms of depression measured by the WHO/ SADD. Variations existed both within and across cultures. Marsella, Sartorius, Jablensky, and Fenton (1985) interpreted these findings as a strong demonstration of cultural factors. Thornicroft and Sartorius (1993) reported 10- year follow- up results of this WHO project on clinical course, service contact, suicidal acts, and social function outcomes among the available 79% of the original patient sample. More than one- third (36%) were readmitted at least once in the follow- up period, and death by suicide occurred in 11% of patients, with a further 14% making unsuccessful suicide attempts. 
Weissman et al. (1996) reported the first cross- national comparison of major depression from 10 population- based surveys that administered the DIS based on the DSM- III to representative community samples in the United States, Canada, Puerto Rico, France, West Germany, Italy, Lebanon, Taiwan, Korea, and New Zealand. The lifetime prevalence of major depression varied widely, from 1.5% in Taiwan to 19% in Beirut. Insomnia and loss of energy were universal symptoms of major depression. Persons with major depression were also at increased risk for comorbidity with substance abuse and anxiety disorders in all 10 national locations. In every country, the rates of major depression were higher for women than men. Furthermore, the WHO International Consortium in Psychiatric Epidemiology (ICPE) coordinated comparative analyses of WHO data. The results demonstrated considerable variability in lifetime prevalence, from a low of 3% in Japan to a high of 16.9% in the United States, with the majority in the range of 8– 12% (Andrade et al., 2003). The results suggested that depression is a very chronic disorder with recurrent episodes among nearly 75% of respondents. 
Moving away from standardized instruments, Haroz et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review of the literature to investigate folk symptoms of depression across cultures. 
446 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
The researchers reviewed only qualitative studies of depression worldwide on 170 different study populations representing six regions of the world, including sub- Saharan Africa. They identified the most frequently mentioned DSM- 5– prioritized features of depression across diverse populations:  depressed mood/ sadness (68.8%), fatigue/ loss of energy (58.8%), problem with sleep (58.2%), and social isolation (54.1%), among other features. Other higher relative frequency features were more indigenous and not prioritized in DSM- 5. These results demonstrate the cross- cultural variability of depressive symptoms and the importance of considering indigenous expressions of depression that are not covered by the standardized instruments to avoid underdiagnosis of clinically relevant cases (Kleinman, 2004). 
More specific comparisons of types of depressive symptoms reveal further culture- relevant findings. For example, guilt has been considered one of the symptoms of depression that is predictive of suicidal ideation and acts in the literature. Its subjective contents revealed remarkable differences in Kimura’s (1967) clinical interviews of depressed patients in Germany and Japan. When primed, Japanese patients expressed guilt as being centered on more specific interpersonal themes, whereas German patients expressed guilt spontaneously in terms of more religious content. Personal guilt is historically associated with the development of individualism in the Judeo- Christian tradition in the West (Jackson, 1986). Kuittinen et al. (2014) conducted a comparative study of depressive symptoms and their psychological correlates among native Finns and older Somali refugees in Finland. They reported that Somali refugees tended to report more frequent somatic symptoms (e.g., insomnia, fatigue, and loss of appetite) than cognitive- psychological symptoms (e.g., self- blame, guilt, sense of failure), while native Finns expressed more cognitive- psychological symptoms. Ryder et al. (2008) conducted a comparative study of Chinese and Euro- Canadian depressed outpatients using three different methods. Their work revealed the importance of distinguishing spontaneous expressions of somatic versus psychological symptoms and responses to “imposed” questions regarding these symptoms. In China, cultural regulations may not permit communication of psychological symptoms but reinforce somatic complaints to provide medical support. Stewart et al. (2004) conducted a 6- month interval cross- cultural assessment of the role of cognitive errors in depressive symptoms in large community samples of adolescents in Hong Kong and the United States. In both samples, they found that current depressive symptoms predicted depressive symptoms 6 months later, thus suggesting cross- cultural commonality in the predictive power of current depressive symptoms inclusive of affective, cognitive, and somatic symptoms. 
Social Origins of Depression Pioneering work by Brown and Harris (1978) on the “social origin” of depression among working- class women in London found significant predictors of depression in a prospective study. The experience of a loss of parent(s) early in life, not having someone to confide in, and husband’s unemployment status were all risk factors for depression of their 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  447 
spouses. Lorant et al. (2003) confirmed a significant relationship between socioeconomic inequity (lower SES) and depression based on a meta- analysis of 60 studies. The authors reported that SES is a moderate to strong correlate for the prevalence of depression. Low SES increases the risk of episode onset and moderately increases the risk of persistence of depression. The results of meta- analysis continue to support Dohrenwend and Dohrenwend’s (1969) landmark report on the relationship between lower social status and depression. In Japan, Kitanaka’s (2011) medical anthropological study of depression revealed a psychiatric- medicalization process of this concept and subsequent institutional and societal approval of depression as a legitimate illness for employed men but not necessarily for women staying at home. Kitanaka’s culturally informed discourse analyses demonstrated value- laden, gender- linked roles and treatment of depressed experience and communication in contemporary Japanese society (Hitokoto & Tanaka- Matsumi, 2014). In the United States, Crowder and Kemmelmeier (2014) found that higher rates of depression were related to higher levels of suicide in “honor states” but not in non- honor states. Furthermore, higher levels of antidepressant medication prescription were associated with lower suicide rates in honor states but not non- honor states. 
In sum, empirical research studies indicate that the subjective experience and reporting of depression is closely related to varying social contexts across cultures. 
Folk conceptions of depression vary across cultures. Every culture investigated reported experiencing “depression.” A  variety of instruments, including standardized diagnostic interview schedules, self- report scales of depressive symptoms, or more open- ended Explanatory Model (EM) interviews, have contributed to accumulating evidence for cross- cultural similarities and differences. Empirical research demonstrated the role of the sociocultural contexts in predicting subjective experiences of depression and causal attribution for different types of preferred treatments. 
Schizophrenia Schizophrenia is a concept applied to a cluster of socially debilitating symptoms involving disorders of thought, perception and attention, motor symptoms, and affective symptoms (Kring, Johnson, Davison, & Neale, 2015; Murphy, 1982b). Kraepelin’s original concept, dementia praecox, literally meant early onset (praecox) and progressive intellectual deterioration (dementia). He focused on both course and symptoms of this disorder. Later, Bleuler coined the term “schizophrenia.” He believed that the disorder did not necessarily have an early onset and did not follow a degenerative course requiring life- long institutionalization as Kraepelin did. 
Epidemiology The ECA study (Keith, Regier, & Rae, 1991) using the DIS based on DSM- III diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia estimated a lifetime prevalence rate of 1.3% for the general population in the United States, with the highest concentrations of schizophrenia among 18- to 29- year- olds and without significant gender difference. Schizophrenic disorder was two 
 
 
 
448 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
to three times more prevalent among the never married (2.1%) and divorced/ separated (2.9%) than among the married (1.0%) or widowed (0.7%). More people diagnosed with schizophrenia were unemployed than those without this diagnosis in the community. In the United States, schizophrenia was almost five times more common at the bottom of the socioeconomic ladder than at the top. As for race- ethnicity, the lifetime rate for blacks (2.1%) was significantly higher than that found for both white/ Anglo (1.4%) and Hispanic (0.8%) groups. However, when controlling for age, gender, marital status, and, most importantly, SES level, the significant difference between black and white prevalence rates disappeared. The correlations between SES and the diagnosis of schizophrenia were consistent without making causal interpretations. Thus, both the sociogenic hypothesis and the social drift theory of schizophrenia (Kring et al., 2015) might offer plausible explanations in this epidemiological study. 
International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia In the cross- cultural domain, the idea of comparing traditional versus modern or developing versus developed societies reached a high point with the WHO’s (1973, 1979) International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia (IPSS). WHO conducted three major studies on the course and outcome of schizophrenia at 20 research centers in 17 countries. Prominent features of the WHO schizophrenia program include (1)  simultaneous case finding and data collection, (2) standardized instruments, (3) trained project psychiatrists, (4) combined clinical and computer- based reference categorization of the case, and (5) multiple follow- up assessments (Jablensky, 1989). 
In the IPSS (WHO, 1973)  1,202 patients were evaluated at nine centers in Africa (Nigeria), Asia (India, Taiwan), Europe (Czech Republic, Denmark, Russia, the United Kingdom), Latin America (Colombia), and North America (the United States). The purpose of the IPSS was to develop and test a standardized method of diagnosis using the Present State Examination (PSE: Wing, Cooper, & Sartorius, 1974). WHO (1973) reported universality in the core symptoms of schizophrenia. These symptoms included lack of insight, predelusional signs (such as delusional mood, ideas of reference, perplexity), flatness of affect, auditory hallucinations, and experiences of control. In a 2- year follow- up study (WHO, 1979)  that investigated the course and outcome of schizophrenia, project psychiatrists interviewed 75.6% of the patients. Across most centers, the participants lacked positive psychotic symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations. However, they exhibited negative psychotic symptoms such as flatness of affect, lack of insight, and difficulties with cooperation. Acute undifferentiated and catatonic cases of schizophrenia were more prevalent in developing countries. The IPSS also conducted 5- year and 25- year follow- up studies. The overall report clearly indicated tremendous variability in the outcomes of schizophrenia across settings and times (Harrison et al., 2001). The dual hypotheses due to genetics and environment reflect the interplay of culture and biology. The results also confirmed more positive outcomes for early diagnosis and intervention across cultures.
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  449 
The prognosis for schizophrenia was operationalized as the percentage of the follow- up period characterized by psychosis. Prognoses were better for patients in developing countries (Colombia, Nigeria, and India) than for those in developed countries (the United States, Great Britain, and Denmark). During the follow- up period, 48% of the participants in Aarhus, 47% in Washington, and 36% in Prague were still psychotic more than 75% of the time. During this same period, only 7% and 19% of the participants in Cali and Agra were judged to be psychotic. Social isolation and unmarried status were associated with a poor outcome in both developed and developing countries (WHO, 1979). High educational status was predictive of chronicity in non- Western and developing countries, but not in the West. For example, in rural Agra, India, outcomes for schizophrenia were worse among the better educated. Warner (1994) explained that educated men in the Third World are affected adversely by greater labor market stresses. Although Jablensky (1989) concluded that “schizophrenia is highly malleable by internalized or extrinsic environmental influences (or both)” (p. 521), the researchers offered only tentative suggestions that better outcomes might stem from the community support and family ties found in rural settings. 
In a more ambitious project, the WHO conducted a prospective epidemiological study to compare the true prevalence of schizophrenia across cultures (Jablensky et al., 1992). In this case- finding project, 1,379 participants were evaluated at 12 centers in 10 countries: Aarhus (Denmark); Agra and Chandigarh (India); Cali (Colombia); Dublin (Ireland); Ibadan (Nigeria); Moscow (Russia); Nagasaki (Japan); Nottingham (UK); Prague (Czech Republic); and Honolulu and Rochester (United States). The project identified all individuals who contacted “helping agencies” for the first time over 2 consecutive years in specified geographical catchment areas. Identified persons were then screened for symptoms of a functional psychosis. The helping agencies included indigenous healers and religious institutions. The incidence rates were found to be comparable in developed and developing countries. However, more patients in the developing countries had an acute onset of schizophrenia. Another purpose of the WHO case- finding study was to investigate the role of stressful life events occurring 2– 3 weeks preceding the development of schizophrenic episodes (Day et al., 1987). The results suggested that specific events described by participants from developing countries might not be easily classified into predetermined categories. 
Methodological critiques of the WHO schizophrenia project concern patient selection and differences in access to hospitals across countries. Cohen (1992) attributes the differences in prognosis to differing rates of hospital contact rather than to illness. In Cohen’s view, the greater proportion of acute cases in developing countries merely reflects differing access to modern psychiatric centers. Waxler- Morrison (1992), however, found that differential access could not account for prognostic findings in her 5- year follow- up study of hospitalized schizophrenics in Sri Lanka. Other researchers (e.g., Hopper, 1992)  have pointed to the standardized procedures and exhaustive follow- up 
450 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
evaluation of the patients in the WHO study as safeguards against contamination by artifacts. Jablensky and Sartorius (1988) concluded that “the position of cultural rela-tivism vis- à- vis the identification of schizophrenia in different populations finds little support” (p.  68). Kleinman (1988), however, cautioned that the sample’s homogeneity based on the imposed case identification criteria eliminated those who did not fit the category criteria; thus the WHO project was designed to identify universality and systematically eliminate important cultural variations. Finally, the controversy regarding prognosis of schizophrenia gained a new momentum in policy- making aimed at reducing service disparities in developing countries (Cohen, Patel, Thara, & Gureje, 2008). Readers are referred to the WHO report to review the scope and issues and the findings of this major project (Hopper, Harrison, Janca, & Sartorius, 2007). 
Cultural Interpretation of Schizophrenia Empirical cross- cultural studies of schizophrenia suggest that the course of the disorder is highly variable depending on the social environment. In an attempt to account for the prognostic differences, Lin and Kleinman (1988) compared Western and non- Western societies according to a number of factors, including family structure, social support, work environment, communication styles, and attribution of mental illness. These cultural explanations remain plausible because contrasts in culture were not based on a priori, verifiable hypotheses or ethnographic assessment of cultural differences. 
Expressed Emotions and Familial Context Expressed Emotion (EE) by the family of the schizophrenic patient has offered a promising lead into the prediction of relapse in the West (Leff & Vaughn, 1986). Specifically, the best predictor was the number of critical remarks made about the schizophrenic patient by a relative when the relative was interviewed alone (Leff & Vaughn, 1986). The authors compared the WHO’s Indian data from Chandigarh center and similar data collected in London, Los Angeles, and Pittsburgh. They identified large differences between the Chandigarh relatives and the Anglo- Americans. The Indian relatives made a mean of 3.6 times fewer critical comments than the Los Angeles relatives of schizophrenic patients did. One major concern regarding the EE measurement for cross- cultural research purposes is the cultural validity of using the frequency of negative verbal remarks as EE. Based on the cross- cultural research literature on emotion and its communication, cultures differ greatly in the perception and expression of negative emotions verbally or nonverbally (Matsumoto & Hwang, 2012). Furthermore, Jenkins and Karno (1992) argued that the EE construct itself taps primarily into cross- culturally variable features of family response to an ill relative. López et  al. (2004) studied the role of the family for Mexican American and Anglo American families with patients who return home in the context of schizophrenia. The authors found that family warmth was a protective factor for Mexican Americans. For Anglo Americans, family criticism was a significant risk factor for relapse. These differential outcomes were related to culturally construed self- orientations of interdependence and independence (Markus & Kitayama, 1991), 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  451 
respectively. Jenkins (2015) thus stated:  “Attitudes, affects, and actions on the part of family members toward their ill relative are the culturally constituted features indexed by EE” (p. 137). 
Desjarlais, Eisenberg, Good, and Kleinman (1995) advanced several hypotheses about how social and cultural factors might contribute to a better course of schizophrenia. Among them, conceptions of the cause and course of schizophrenia held by the members of a social group should influence the course of illness. Internal versus external attribution of illness should also predict chronicity, such that attributing cause of illness to the self should lead to chronicity. When internal attribution is combined with the nuclear family environment in a highly competitive, technologically developed society, lack of firm support should also increase chronicity. As Jenkins (2004) stated, “the subjective experience of individuals with schizophrenia invariably involves culture and agency” (p. 52). In conclusion, core features of schizophrenia as conceptualized by Kraepelin have persisted for more than 100  years across diverse cultural contexts and generations (Jablensky, 1997). Beyond the core features of schizophrenia as a major psychiatric disorder, sociocultural environmental factors are associated with variable course and outcome of schizophrenia. Future agenda should address reduction of disparities in service utilization across developed and developing nations with divergent backgrounds. 
Anxiety Disorders Good and Kleinman’s (1985) review of the literature on culture and anxiety stated “anxiety and disorders of anxiety are universally present in human societies” (p. 298). They also cautioned that “the phenomenology of such disorders, the meaningful forms through which distress is articulated and constituted as social reality, varies in quite significant ways across cultures” (p.  298). Individualistic and collectivistic cultures may differ in antecedents and consequences of specific emotions, emotion regulation, the specificity and quantity of direct communication (Matsumoto, Yoo, & Nakagawa, 2008; Triandis, 1994). The languages of emotion words and their natural taxonomies are of enormous variety across cultures (Mesquita & Frijda, 1992; Russell, 1991; see also Chapter 12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang on for more discussion of culture and emotion). Barlow (2001) has proposed a biopsychosocial model of anxiety disorders with contributing factors of cue- provoked physiological arousal, cognitive interpretation, and approach– avoidance coping behavior and its consequence. Investigating anxiety disorders thus poses a major challenge for cross- cultural researchers even though probably nobody would disagree that anxiety and fear are human universals. In fact, the literature is in agreement that there is great cross- cultural variability in anxiety disorders as defined by cognitive, somatic, and affective symptoms (Hunter & Schmidt, 2010; Tanaka- Matsumi & Draguns, 1997). 
Epidemiology Hwu and Compton’s (1994) comparison of the six major epidemiological surveys suggests that the lifetime prevalence rates of the DIS- derived specific anxiety disorders 
 
 
 
452 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
vary greatly depending both on the disorder (e.g., generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, etc.) and ethnic culture. The greatest prevalence ratios varied from a low of 2.9% for generalized anxiety disorder to a high of 7.3% for panic disorder when the DIS data from Taiwan, Korea, the United States, Canada, New Zealand, and Puerto Rico were compared. These indicate that cultures define different thresholds for symptoms of anxiety disorders (Hofmann, Asnaai, & Hinton, 2010). Tseng et al. (1990) investigated the symptomatology of patients with “neuroses, situational adjustment reaction or acute emotional reaction” (p. 252) at five research centers in Asia. The sites included Chiang- Mai (Thailand), Bali (Indonesia), Kao- Hsiung (Taiwan), Shanghai (China), and Tokyo (Japan). The study assessed the similarities and differences between normal and clinical populations within the same culture and then compared their data across cultures. Symptom profiles of the patients in each city deviated from the profiles of the normal participants toward exaggeration. In addition, there was cross- cultural variability across the five centers, together with a greater similarity between the Taiwan and mainland China groups than between any other centers. Differences in diagnostic practices accounted in part for cross- cultural differences in reported symptoms of “neurosis.” Tseng, Xu, Ebata, Hsu, and Cui (1986) had psychiatrists in Beijing, Tokyo, and Honolulu diagnose six videotaped Chinese patients undergoing a mental status examination. Psychiatrists from Beijing diagnosed them with neurasthenia when their colleagues in Tokyo and Honolulu diagnosed them with adjustment reactions. Tseng, Asai, Kitanishi, McLaughlin, and Kyomen (1992) compared diagnostic judgments of Japanese psychiatrists in Tokyo and American psychiatrists in Honolulu. Patients with the project diagnosis of social phobia were presented on videotape. The diagnostic agreement of the Japanese psychiatrists was greater than that of the American psychiatrists for the Japanese cases of social phobia (taijin kyofusho). The agreement rate of the Japanese psychiatrists for the two American cases was only 6.5%. Tseng’s two international studies demonstrate that diagnostic practices contribute to cross- cultural variability in observed symptoms. For this reason, researchers endorse the use of a standardized diagnostic system to control for differences in diagnostic practice. 
Cultural Context of Expressing Anxiety To the extent that anxiety disorders reflect an exaggeration of a culture’s baseline (Draguns, 1980; Hunter & Schmidt, 2010; Lambert et al., 1992; Tseng & Hsu, 1980), standardization of diagnostic criteria may miss culturally unique deviations and meanings ascribed to the subjective experiences of anxiety and fear in cultural contexts. Culture- bound disorders such as taijin kyofusho in Japan (Russell, 1989; Tanaka- Matsumi, 1979)  and koro (Tseng et al., 1992) in Southern China and Southeast Asia demonstrate the impor-tance of assessing the cultural values of specific symptoms and cultural responses to the individuals exhibiting these anxiety- based disorders. Similarly, the cultural idiom of dis-tress, ataque de nervios in Latin American populations (Guarnaccia, Rivera, Franco, & Neighbors, 1996), is reported to occur in culturally stressful and familiar settings, such as during a funeral or at the scene of an accident. As Kirmayer (1991, p. 26) stated, “cultural 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  453 
beliefs or rules and patterns of interaction are constitutive of the disorder . . . there is no way to intelligibly describe the problem without invoking cultural particulars” (p. 26). 
Heinrichs et al. (2006) investigated cultural differences in perceived social norms for tolerating shy and reticent behaviors presented in vignettes and self- reports of social anxiety among nonclinical students in eight individualistic and collectivistic countries based on Hofstede’s (2001) individualism scores. Perceived social acceptability for reticent social behaviors was greater among samples from collectivistic countries (e.g., Japan, South Korea, and Spain) than those from individualistic countries (e.g., Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands, and the United States). Participants from collectivistic countries reported higher social anxiety and fear of blushing symptoms. Schreier et al. (2010) replicated these results except for Latin American countries (Costa Rica and Ecuador). Participants from collectivistic versus individualistic countries reported significantly different levels of acceptance of socially withdrawn behaviors and fear of blushing. These studies show different cultural norms for socially reticent behaviors across the dimensions of individualism and collectivism. In sum, anxieties are pan- human experience. Cultural differences in the prevalence of anxiety disorders are expected due to differences in individuals’ perceived cultural norms for expected behaviors. Epidemiological surveys further support cross- cultural differences in rates of anxiety disorders. 
Somatization and Neurasthenia Somatization is a common problem across cultures and is associated with significant health problems including chronic disease, anxiety disorders, depression, and occupational or social disability. The question concerns the cultural meaning of somatic complaints. It may be ethnocentric to view bodily complaints as the simple result of a lack of “psychological mindedness” (Draguns, 1996; White, 1982). Different cultures may selectively encourage or discourage the reporting of psychological or physiological components of the stress response (Arens, Balkir, & Barnow, 2013; Chentsova- Dutton Chu, Tsai, & Rottenberg, 2007; Su, Lee, & Oishi, 2012). The focus on psychologization versus somatization has been particularly salient in the literature on Chinese mental health (Cheung, 1989; Draguns, 1996; Kleinman, 1986; Ryder et al., 2008). 
Neurasthenia is a very common diagnosis in China. In China, neurasthenia is called shenjing shuairuo, literally meaning “neurological weakness.” Symptoms of neurasthenia include bodily weakness, fatigue, tiredness, headaches, dizziness, and a range of gastrointestinal and other complaints (Kleinman & Kleinman, 1985b). Kleinman (1982), with the assistance of a Chinese psychiatrist, interviewed 100 Chinese patients with the di-agnosis of shenjing shuairuo. He used the Chinese- language version of the Schedule of Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (SADS) modified to yield DSM- III diagnoses. Kleinman reported that 93 neurasthenic patients met the criteria for depressive disorder, and 87 of them further met the criteria for major depressive disorder. Patients spontaneously complained of headaches (90%), insomnia (78%), dizziness (73%), pain (48%), and loss of or poor memory (43%), among others. However, when Kleinman specifically 
 
454 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
asked the patients about psychological and affective symptoms, they acknowledged dysphoric mood (100%), trouble concentrating (84%), anhedonia (61%), hopelessness (50%), and low self- esteem (60%). In Shanghai, Zhang (1989) demonstrated that the pri-mary “Western” diagnostic status of Chinese- diagnosed neurasthenia (shenjing shuaiuro) varies between depressive and anxiety disorders depending on the particular Western- derived standardized instruments employed. These observations have been supported by more recent empirical research on symptom- level variation in Han Chinese and Euro- Canadian depressed outpatients (Dere et  al., 2013). In this case, content validation of the standard Western diagnostic instruments and criteria, such as the DSM- 5, should accommodate somatic symptoms as one mode of expressing depression. 
From an emic standpoint, the discrepancy between spontaneous expression of so-matic complaints and elicited symptoms (e.g., dysphoria) suggests that cultural meanings of symptoms are altered by interpretations based on Western- derived standardized instruments and imposed criteria. Elicited symptoms may not conform to culturally accepted ways of expressing distress. Somatic complaints are less stigmatized among Chinese, and somatization justifies an acceptable medical intervention. Chinese in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and China do not readily recognize psychological symptoms as problems that justify seeking help in a medical setting (Cheung, 1989). The setting (e.g., general medical vs. psychiatric clinic) and problem conceptualization are meaningfully related within a cultural context. Ryder, Yang, and Heine (2002) remarked that the issue of somatization versus psychologization of emotional distress is a paradigmatic example for cultural psychopathology. Ryder et al. (2008) provided support for this position through the use of combined emic- etic methods of clinical data- gathering with Chinese patients and Euro- Canadian patients regarding cultural shaping of depression according to differential reinforcement of somatic and psychological dimensions. 
Summary of Issues and Findings on Major Disorders This section focused on four major disorders represented in most textbooks of psychopathology and abnormal psychology by introducing some of the seminal studies and following up on the issues generated by such studies. This extended review of the empirical literature demonstrated the substantial role of culture in the expressions of symptoms, course of the disorder (e.g., schizophrenia), and predictors of outcome for all major disorders. 
Research has accumulated empirical findings with regard to social constructions of illness. Causal explanatory models predicted preferred treatment types (e.g., biomedical, herbal medicine, counseling). The emic and etic perspectives are both active movers of this stimulating field of research. The field of culture and psychopathology has moved toward unpacking culture and developing more specific hypotheses with regard to the types of relationship between culture and abnormal behavior. The next section provides initial evidence for linkage studies with implications for cross- cultural psychopathology research. 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  455 
Toward Developing Linkage Studies: Unpacking Culture Culturally informed researchers have incorporated the following four concepts more actively in research on culture and psychopathology: (1) cultural self- construal, (2) values, (3) family structure and social support, and (4) individualism and collectivism orientations. These concepts have been the direct targets of empirical investigations in cross- cultural and cultural psychology (e.g., Kitayama & Cohen, 2007; Matsumoto & Juang, 2008). The findings offer normative assessments of human adaptation and help predict and explain failures of adaptation in dynamic cultural contexts. In recent years, particularly in the area of anxiety- linked problems, we can identify some exciting developments in linkage studies (Matsumoto & Yoo, 2006) that have tested specific hypotheses regarding the relationship between cultural factors and empirically measured responses. 
As a promising start, Matsumoto et  al. (2008) developed theoretically based hypotheses to test the relationship between emotion regulation (reappraisal and suppression) and adjustment in 23 countries. Country- level results provided empirical support for the cross- cultural linkage between emotion regulation strategy and positive and negative indices of adjustment. To operationally measure cultural values, this study applied data from both Hofstede (2001) and Schwartz (2004). Suppression strategy was positively correlated with power distance, hierarchy, and embeddeddness and negatively correlated with individualism and egalitarianism (Matsumoto et  al., 2008). Krieg and Xu (2015) conducted a meta- analysis to investigate the relationship between social anxiety and cultural self- construal of independence and interdependence based on 32 published studies from the United States, Canada, and Australia. Supporting Okazaki’s (1997) conceptually derived hypotheses developed earlier, the results indicated that independent self- construal was indeed a significant mediator for social anxiety in Asian- heritage individuals. 
Among social anxiety disorders, DSM- 5 defines taijin kyofusho (TKS, fear of in-terpersonal relations) as a cultural syndrome with prominent symptoms of fear of interpersonal situations due to the thought, feeling, or conviction that one’s appearance and actions in social interactions are inadequate or offensive to others. Vriends, Pfaltz, Novianti, and Hadiyono (2013) examined the role of independent and interdependent self- construal (Singelis, 1994)  as mediators of the association between cultural background (Indonesia, Switzerland) and the measures of TKS. The Indonesian sample scored higher on self- report measures of both TKS and social phobia. The effect of cultural background was partially mediated by an interdependent self- construal for both TKS and social phobia. The results suggest that TKS symptoms are common outside Japan and Korea and that elevated levels of these symptoms are seen as clinically relevant by Indonesian and Swiss participants. Hong and Woody’s (2007) research with community samples of Koreans and Euro- Canadians also found independent and interdependent self- construal to be a significant mediator of the relationship between their ethnic background and self- report of social anxiety. 
 
456 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Cross- cultural research using nonclinical samples has reliably demonstrated the relevance of cultural self- construal as a significant predictor of TKS and social phobia (Dinnel, Kleinknecht, & Tanaka- Matsumi, 2002; Norasakkunkit, Kitayama, & Uchida, 2012; Zhou, Lacroix, Sasaki, Peng, Wang, & Ryder, 2014). TKS is variable with regard to types of interpersonal situations, suggesting higher prevalence in collective cultures as in Japan, Korea, Indonesia, and China. Relational mobility and a context- dependent communication style in Japanese society are prone to reinforce social avoidance and fear of rejection (Sato, Yuki, & Norasakkunkit, 2014). Fear of social rejection and behavioral inhibition are associated more strongly with interpersonally stressful situations for Japanese than for American individuals (Hashimoto, Mojaverian, & Kim, 2012). These various findings are relevant to functions of intersubjective cultures (Chiu, Gelfand, Yamagishi, Shteyberg, & Wan, 2010), where the perception of cultural norms regulates adjustment of members of cultural groups. If cultural differences in perceived norms were available, predictions of psychopathology would be more culturally salient because researchers would not be imposing uniform criteria for mental disorders (Chentsova- Dutton & Tsai, 2010; Chentsova- Dutton, Tsai, & Gotlib, 2010). 
Conclusions and Future Directions for Research More than a century of research on culture and psychopathology has shown that culture exerts a major influence on the identification, labeling, course, and outcome of maladaptive behaviors. This chapter provided further, abundant, empirically derived answers to each of the seven following questions posed earlier (Tanaka- Matsumi, 2001): (1) What is the phenomenon under investigation (e.g., depression), and how is it defined by the profession and by indigenous cultures? (2)  What words and concepts are used to describe the phenomenon? (3)  Are different words and concepts equivalent? (4)  What aspects are known to be culturally similar and variable? (5)  What would account for cultural similarities and differences? (6) How does one express different types of distress to others in the same culture? (7) What are the implications of universality and cultural relativity for the theory of psychopathology? These are dynamic questions because they call for contextual assessment of psychopathology involving the researcher, the study participants (patients), and the community to achieve triangulation of data inclusive of quantitative and qualitative information (Creswell & Miller, 2000). 
To answer these fundamental questions based on the combined emic- etic perspectives, this chapter devoted much space to demonstrating the importance of considering the sociocultural context of clinical assessment and those trained to use the various instruments, including psychiatric diagnosis. Culturally informed investigator asking these questions would refrain from imposing diagnostic categories and criteria developed in one culture on another (Haynes, Kaholokula, & Tanaka- Matsumi, 2018; van de Vijver & Tanaka- Matsumi, 2008). Therefore, advanced clinical research strategies are expected in 
 
abnormal PsyChology and CulTure  |  457 
order to culturally adapt and/ or develop various clinical instruments to establish equivalence across cultures. Accelerated progress is expected in the development and dissemination of culturally informed, contextually oriented assessment and intervention across diverse cultures. Finally, emerging linkage studies hold promise for identifying theoretically based thresholds for human adaptation and its failure.

Culture and Psychological Interventions 
Cindy Y. Huang and Nolan Zane 
Introduction Research has consistently identified disparities in mental health treatment utilization and quality of care for ethnic minority populations (Institute of Medicine [IOM], 2003; US Department of Health and Human Services [USDHHS], 2001). For decades, presidential commissions have found that these racial and ethnic disparities were due to problems in accessing treatment, as well as to the lack of effective treatments for ethnic minority groups such as African Americans, American Indians, Asian Americans, and Latino/ as (Commission on Mental Health to the Surgeon General, 1978; President’s New Freedom Commission, 2003). Ethnic minority clients often saw therapists or were administered treatments that did not properly take into account their cultural backgrounds, linguistic preferences, and life circumstances. 
This chapter aims to provide a deeper understanding of the current literature on mental health treatments and interventions for ethnic minority communities. It also provides a synthesis of a long- standing program of research examining how cultural issues affect mental health utilization and treatment outcomes. The objectives of this chapter are to: 
 1. Identify mental health disparities for ethnic minority populations, including disparities in the engagement and utilization of treatments and in treatment outcomes 
 2. Discuss the cultural factors relevant for mental health treatments, with an emphasis on racial/ ethnic match between client and therapist, face concern, and social validity and their influences on treatment processes and outcomes 
 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  469 
 3. Apply the Proximal– Distal Model, an empirically supported framework that serves as a guide in cultural intervention research 
 4. Examine the ways in which researchers are translating culture and mental health research into culturally adapted and community- centered interventions 
 5. Highlight the challenges still involved in addressing cultural issues in mental health intervention research 
 6. Provide suggestions for future directions in the field of culture and mental health treatments 
Disparities in Psychotherapy Ethnic minority groups have different patterns of mental health service use depending on the ethnic group being examined (Sue, 1977; Sue, Fujino, Hu, Takeuchi, & Zane, 1991). A  5- year study of more than 13,000 Asian American, African American, and Latino clients found that 20.5% of African Americans were in the mental health system, compared to their Los Angeles County representation of 12.8% (Sue et al., 1991). In contrast, Asian American and Latino clients made up 3.1% and 25.5%, respectively, in the LA mental health system, while their populations in the County were much higher (8.7% and 33.7%, respectively). Similar patterns were found in another large- scale study of 14,000 clients in the Seattle mental health system (Sue, 1977). Studies on ethnic minority youth also demonstrate similar patterns (Ho, Liang, Martinez, Huang, & Yeh, 2006). 
For immigrant populations in the United States, such as Asian Americans, disparities in mental health use deserve particular attention. Many of these ethnic minority individuals may not be mental health literate and therefore less familiar with mental health care and treatment. The Asian American population increased by 43% from 2000 to 2010, making it the fastest growing population in the United States (Hoeffel, Rastogi, Kim, & Shahid, 2012). The disparities experienced by Asian Americans and other immigrant groups may become an increasing public health problem as the current trends in population growth continue. Additionally, these ethnic minority groups are diverse, with different languages, cultures, and immigration histories. For example, Asian Americans are considered to be one racial/ ethnic group, but the majority of Vietnamese, Chinese, and Asian Indians were born outside of the United States. This is not true for other groups of Asian Americans, such as the Japanese and Hawaiians, who tend to be born in the United States (Zane, Hall, Sue, Young, & Nunez, 2004). The intragroup diversity within the Asian American population poses a unique challenge for mental health researchers. Non- US born Asians may experience difficulty in acculturating or adapting to mainstream US culture, while this process may not be as relevant for US- born Asians. 
Immigrants in the United States who experience serious mental health disorders underutilize mental health services. In a nationally represented sample of Asian American 
 
470 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
adults, individuals with diagnosable mental disorders still underutilized mental health services at half the rate compared to individuals with mental health problems in the general population (28% vs. 54%; Meyer, Zane, Cho, & Takeuchi, 2009). US- born Asian American participants were almost 15 times more likely to use mental health services than non- US born participants. Those born outside of the US were more likely to use mental health services if they emigrated at a younger age. In addition, English- language fluency moderated the use of alternative services (e.g., services performed by a religious/ spiritual leader, doctor of Oriental medicine, chiropractor) on mental health service utilization. Specifically, Asians with poor or fair English proficiency who sought alternative services were less likely to utilize mental health services. However, individuals who were proficient in English and used alternative services were almost seven times more likely to also use mental health services. From this research, it is clear that cultural factors such as acculturation, beliefs about mental health problems, and social stigma impact the disparity in mental health use rates among ethnic minorities. 
There also are disparities in the quality of mental health care for ethnic minority clients, which are reflected in poorer psychotherapy processes and outcomes (Zane et al., 2004). Premature termination serves as a proxy for client satisfaction and, as such, is considered an indirect indicator of treatment outcome. An unsatisfied client is more likely to drop out before the treatment ends. The length of treatment (i.e., dosage or the number of treatment sessions a client received) also serves as an indirect indicator of treatment outcome. Clients receiving mental health services tend to report more improvement in their symptoms with increased number of therapy sessions (Hansen, Lambert, & Forman, 2002; Lambert & Hawkins, 2001). A systematic review of clinical trials for mood disorder (e.g., anxiety, depression) treatments determined that the average number of sessions needed for patients to demonstrate clinical improvement was 12.7 sessions (Hansen et al., 2002). National databases of clients receiving mental health services in naturalistic settings (e.g., community mental health centers) showed patients receiving an average of fewer than five sessions (Hansen et al., 2002). 
Since the 1970s, studies have found higher dropout rates for ethnic minority clients, and this dropout occurs early in outpatient treatment (Sue, 1977). Clients in other service settings show similar rates of premature termination. For example, 29% of African American veterans receiving treatment with a White therapist failed to return for a second session (Rosenheck, Fontana, & Cottrol, 1995). For those clients who remained in treatment, they averaged 17 sessions compared to the 25 sessions of African American clients paired with an African American therapist (Rosenheck, Fontana, & Cottrol, 1995). In other studies, Latino and Asian American clients for whom English was not their primary language were more likely to prematurely drop out if their therapists were White (Russell, Fujino, Sue, Cheung, & Snowden, 1996; Sue et al., 1991; Yeh, Eastman, & Cheung, 1994). Similar disparities have been found in recent studies. In a study with 300 adults receiving mental health services at a university counseling center, approximately 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  471 
36.8% of ethnic minority clients dropped out of treatment compared to only 24.9% of the White clients (Owen, Imel, Adelson, & Rodolfa, 2012). 
Premature dropout and treatment duration serve only as proxies for actual treatment outcomes, but few studies have directly examined racial/ ethnic disparities in treatment outcomes for clients who remain in treatment. For example, we assessed the treatment outcomes of White and Asian clients at a community mental health center in the first and fourth treatment sessions (Zane, Enomoto, & Chun, 1994). Asian clients were more depressed and hostile after four sessions of treatment after controlling for pretreatment levels. Compared to White clients, Asian American clients were also less satisfied with their treatment progress, therapists, the overall service received, access to services, and the fee charged. In other words, Asian American clients were less satisfied with all aspects of their treatment experience compared to their White counterparts. In addition, therapists were more likely to evaluate Asian clients as having lower levels of psychosocial functioning than White clients after short- term treatment. Of particular note is that these disparities were apparent after just a short period of treatment (i.e., four sessions). 
These disparities in treatment outcomes are concerning as they highlight the need to better understand how ethnic minority clients respond to mental health treatments. Mental health treatment researchers have long worked to develop empirically supported treatments (ESTs), which are treatments that have been shown to be more efficacious compared to a placebo or another treatment control (Chambless & Hollon, 1998). Clinical trial studies comparing the effectiveness of an intervention relative to a treatment control group form the scientific basis for ESTs. However, few clinical trials have focused on establishing empirical support of ESTs for ethnic minority populations. Chambless and colleagues (1996) were unable to find a single study that implemented the rigorous standards needed to establish efficacy for treatments for ethnic minority clients. Furthermore, the US Department of Health and Human Services (USDHHS) (2001) found that clinical trials used to generate professional treatment guidelines did not include data for any minority group. Specifically, these studies did not report race or ethnicity information, and, if the information was available, minorities were categorized as “non- white” without additional information. None of the studies used to establish treatment guidelines analyzed data to determine efficacy by race or ethnicity, much less the diversity found within racial and ethnic minority groups. This is problematic because these guidelines are used widely in the mental health profession and applied to people from all backgrounds. 
A study indicated that even the most current treatment research programs are not producing “best available evidence” on minority populations or issues. A review of 379 clinical trials funded by the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) published between 1995 and 2004 revealed that less than half of these studies included information on the specific ethnic composition of their participants (Mak, Law, Alvidrez, & Pérez- Stable, 2007). When the studies did specify ethnic composition, most ethnic minority groups 
472 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
were underrepresented compared to their representation in the US population. This was most apparent for Asian Americans, Hispanics, and Native Americans. White Americans continued to be the most sampled ethnic group in clinical trials, with 61% representation in studies that provided specific ethnic information. Few studies examined ethnic or cultural effects in their clinical trials. Research with children and adolescents showed similar patterns. Huey and Polo (2008) conducted a meta- analysis of this research and found an increase in the number of clinical trials including ethnic minority youth compared to previous years. However, the majority of studies still included underrepresented samples and inadequate sample sizes, thus limiting the generalizability of findings from this research to ethnic minority youth clientele. 
The limited empirical base on ethnic minority issues is primarily due to difficulties in defining and articulating “culture” in consistent and useful ways (see Chapter  1 by Walter J. Lonner, Kenneth D. Keith, and David Matsumoto and Chapter 4 by Evert Van de Vliert and Dejun Tony Kong for more discussion about this issue). While the research on cultural diversity has grown substantially in recent decades, it has been difficult to make use of this knowledge for mental health treatment (Sue & Zane, 1987). The challenge lies in knowing which cultural factors should be addressed in the specific processes and components of treatments as cultural experiences are sometimes difficult to incorporate directly into research designs. This challenge is further exacerbated by the distal nature of ethnicity. Culture is often assessed by ethnicity and race, making them proxies for culture (Walsh, Smith, Morales, & Sechrest, 2000). The use of these proxies may obscure important, culturally relevant psychological variations that may be related to treatment outcomes within both ethnic minority and white groups. These cultural variables usually mediate the influences of the client’s ethnicity and important clinical processes and outcomes. There is an overwhelming number of cultural factors that can affect treatment processes which, in turn, can affect outcomes. Figure 15.1 depicts some of the key cultural factors that may influence psychotherapy processes and outcomes. These cultural factors serve to link treatment procedures and outcomes by identifying key therapeutic elements necessary for culturally responsive treatment. The following sections discuss these factors in relation to their influence on the psychotherapy experiences, processes, and outcomes for ethnic minority clients. 
Cultural Factors in Psychotherapy Our research focuses on examining how certain cultural variations may affect the process and/ or outcomes in mental health treatment for ethnic minority clients. For example, researchers have long studied the effects of a racial or ethnic match between client and therapist and its impact on treatment process and outcomes. A client’s first impressions of a therapist are critical in determining the client’s responsiveness to the therapist over the duration of their interactions (Spiegel, 1976). For many ethnic minority clients, this

474 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
initial perception may be impacted by the therapist’s race or ethnicity, which may evoke in clients certain impressions, attitudes, stereotypes, or judgments. 
Racial and Ethnic Match Ethnic and racial issues are often assumed to be important and salient for ethnic minority clients. These issues influence the cultural preferences and experiences of psychotherapy for minority clients. In a sample of 102 clients using outpatient mental health services, one study examined racial and ethnic match and how they relate to three important culture- specific elements of mental health care (Brach & Fraserirector, 2000; Leong & Lau, 2001): racial match between client and therapist, care provider knowledge of prejudice or discrimination (i.e., therapist’s knowledge base about how client prejudice or discrimination experiences may affect the therapy experience), and care provider discussions of race and ethnicity (i.e., therapist’s ability or willingness to openly discuss issues of race and ethnicity in treatment). There were significant ethnic group differences on two of the three cultural elements, with ethnic minority clients placing greater importance on having racial match and provider knowledge of prejudice/ discrimination experiences of their group than whites (Meyer & Zane, 2013). In particular, African Americans had the strongest preferences for racial/ ethnic match, which was associated with positive perceptions of their therapists and positive treatment outcomes (Meyer & Zane, 2013). 
The cultural elements also were associated with the clients’ experiences in treatment. We used discrepancy scores of the cultural elements as predictors to examine their influence on four types of service evaluations: access, quality of care, general satisfaction, and treatment outcomes. Discrepancy scores reflected the difference between the importance of an element and the extent to which that element was included in the service. Larger discrepancy scores indicated higher value from clients for an element but less inclusion of that element in their treatment. The findings indicated that when clients considered a cultural element important to their care but perceived it to be absent, they were less satisfied with various aspects of their treatment. However, this was only true for ethnic minority clients, not for white clients. For white clients, the cultural element discrepancy scores were not significantly related to the four types of service evaluations. In contrast, for minority clients, discrepancies between importance and experience in racial match and provider history of discrimination/ prejudice were significantly related to three of the four outcome variables (access, quality of care, and general satisfaction). These clients who had considered racial match important but were not matched with a therapist of the same race rated their services as less satisfactory, less accessible, and of lower quality of care. When ethnic minority clients considered provider knowledge of discrimination and prejudice important but perceived their therapists as lacking in this knowledge, they were also less satisfied with the quality of care they received. 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  475 
The findings demonstrated that issues surrounding race and ethnicity are important to ethnic minorities in mental health treatment, and, in fact, these clients are less satisfied when such elements are not included in their care. In general, ethnic minority clients prefer to be seen by therapists of the same race/ ethnicity and tend to be more satisfied with their treatment experience when their therapists are knowledgeable about certain life experiences associated with being an ethnic minority individual, such as experiences with discrimination and prejudice (Cabral & Smith, 2011; Meyer & Zane, 2013; Meyer, Zane, & Cho, 2011). These findings highlight the significance and clinical utility of addressing racial and cultural issues in treatment when working with ethnic minority clientele. 
Our investigation into the premature dropout of ethnic minority clients suggests that ethnic match between client and clinician plays a significant role in the early stages of treatment for these clients. Clients whose therapists were of the same ethnic background were less likely to drop out prematurely; this was true for all clients except African American clients (Sue et al., 1991). These findings remained significant even when controlling for the influences of sex, age, marital status, socioeconomic status, gender match, and diagnosis. Other factors were also associated with premature dropout for different ethnic groups: a client– therapist gender match decreased the likelihood of dropout after one session, as did higher social class status, being female for Mexican Americans, being older for whites, and having a psychotic diagnosis for African Americans and Whites.
