This research suggests that ethnic match is often a critical factor for Asian American, Mexican American, and White clients at the beginning of treatment. 
Of particular interest in this study was the dropout rates among Asian and Mexican American clients for whom English was not their first language. Research has shown that these clients tend to be less acculturated, less familiar with mental health care, and less inclined to use mental health treatment (Sue et al., 1991). Ethnic match was significantly associated with lower odds of premature dropout for non– English proficient Asian American and Mexican American clients. When these clients were ethnically matched with their therapists, they were less likely to drop out prematurely. Ethnic and language matches (i.e., the client and therapist speak the same language) were also associated with decreased odds of dropout, especially when different combinations of ethnic and language match were found. Thus, ethnic match emerged as an even more important factor in the positive outcome of treatment for clients who did not speak English as their primary language. For Asian clients, having both matches (i.e., ethnic and language match) or having one type of match was critical in reducing the likelihood of premature dropout. For Mexican Americans, having both was important. 
A recent study extended the examination of ethnic match by investigating therapist characteristics that included ethnicity, birthplace, and acculturation level (Suarez- Morales et al., 2010). Clients and therapists were matched based on their place of birth (i.e., Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, or United States) and acculturation level to American and Hispanic cultures. Matches in birthplace and acculturation were associated with 
476 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
increased client participation in treatment for Hispanic outpatient clients, suggesting that client– therapist matches on variables related to ethnicity and race (such as nativity, acculturation level, and enculturation level) may be a more informative way to examine how ethnic and cultural matches affect treatment processes and outcomes. 
Despite its salience in treatment for ethnic minority clients, previous studies are inconsistent in their findings on racial or ethnic match and treatment outcomes. Some studies have found positive effects for match in terms of increased utilization, decreased substance use, and lowered treatment dropout (Dana, Gamst, Der- Karabetian, & Kramer, 2001; Flaskerud, 1986; Flaskerud & Liu, 1991; Flicker, Waldron, Turner, Brody, & Hops, 2008; Ibaraki & Hall, 2014; O’Sullivan & Lasso, 1992; Suarez- Morales et al., 2010; Sue et al., 1991; Wu & Windle, 1980), while others have found null or minimal effects (Fiorentine & Hillhouse, 1999; Gamst, Dana, Der- Karabetian, & Kramer, 2004; Watkins, Terrell, Miller, & Terrell, 1989). Ethnic and demographic matches are distal and structural variables that affect attitudes, values, and expectancies, which, in turn, are presumably more proximal to treatment outcomes (Sue & Zane, 1987). Even when clients and their therapists are ethnically similar, their cultural attitudes and levels of acculturation may differ. Ethnic matches do not ensure psychological matches or similarities, so that therapists and clients from the same ethnic background may not necessarily share attitudes, beliefs, and expectancies that may affect treatment outcomes (Maramba & Nagayama Hall, 2002). These inconsistencies highlight the need to better understand the psychological processes that may mediate the racial and ethnic match effect. 
Match on personal characteristics between two individuals may imply that they share some commonalities or are similar in certain respects. The perception of similarity has been linked to a variety of positive psychological outcomes. People are attracted to similar others and also prefer to interact with them compared with dissimilar others (Cushman, Valentinsen, & Dietrich, 1982). Interactions with perceived similar others also can create an expectation of mutual understanding and provide a sense of security and predictability. It seems reasonable to assume that perceived similarity could be critical in influencing interactions between a therapist and client. Mental health clients, in particular, want to be validated and to feel secure in treatment, and they may search for and attend to cues of similarity, such as racial or ethnic matches, to obtain this reassurance and support. 
One study sought to determine how racial match effects impacted important treatment processes and how perceptions in similarity mediated these effects. Using an experimental design, we tested if racial match affected the treatment processes of therapist credibility and the working alliance (Meyer et al., 2011). Asian American young adults were randomly assigned to a racially matched or racially unmatched condition based on the counselor’s race. Photographs of the counselor and their patient were shown to each participant, along with an audio recording of a brief counseling session. This allowed us to directly test whether racial match affected counselor credibility and the working relationship between therapist and the client.
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  477 
Findings suggested that similarity in personal values and beliefs (i.e., attitudinal similarity) affected perceptions of support, which then impacted both therapist credibility and the working alliance. Asian Americans who felt similar to the therapist in personal attitudes, values, and/ or personality also perceived the therapist to be more supportive, and this resulted in a stronger working alliance and greater therapist credibility. Owen and colleagues found that having a strong therapist– client relationship moderated the negative association between experiences of microaggressions and psychological health (Owen et  al., 2011). Clients who reported more experiences of microaggressions reported poorer psychological health, but clients who had positive relationships with their therapists experienced better outcomes than those who experienced microaggressions but had poorer relationships with their therapists (Owen et  al., 2011). Another study found that therapists who had greater multicultural awareness had better counseling relationships with their clients, regardless of racial/ ethnic background (Berger, Zane, & Hwang, 2014). These findings suggest that while racial or ethnic match is one important pathway to culturally competent treatment, there are other alternatives so that such matches are not always necessary. Even counselors not matched to their clients on race can capitalize on other types of similarities (attitudes, values, personality) that they share with their clients to enhance the counseling relationship. 
The cultural values and value orientations of clients also may affect their initial response to treatment. The client’s interpersonal value orientation may be especially pivotal because treatment often focuses on one’s interpersonal relationships and problems, and change in treatment is often achieved through the working relationship established between therapist and client. Cultures can vary greatly in the interpersonal values and orientations that guide and regulate social interactions and social relationships. 
Face Concern Face has been identified as a key and often- dominant interpersonal dynamic in Asian so-cial relations (Sue & Morishima, 1982), especially when the relationship involves seeking help for personal issues (Shon & Ja, 1982). Asian American clinicians have regularly pointed to face concern as an important interpersonal issue that affects Asian American clients in the treatment process. “Face” refers to a person’s set of socially sanctioned claims concerning their own social character and integrity; this set of claims is largely defined by certain prescribed roles that they carry out as a member and representative of a group (Zane & Yeh, 2002). Processes in traditional, Western psychological treatment can often lead to experiences of face loss. Face is defined as a person’s own claims about his or her social character and integrity, and one’s face is strongly tied to the roles one effectively carries out as a member of a specific social group (Zane & Yeh, 2002). Face concern may affect critical processes associated with mental health treatment. First, many clients experience shame and stigma associated with mental illness. Second, therapists are typically trained to elicit self- disclosure from clients in order to achieve catharsis, which is believed to help release suppressed emotions. This process may lead to great face loss for 
 
478 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
certain clients, especially those who are not accustomed to sharing private thoughts and feelings with a stranger. Finally, clients from more collectivistic cultures also may feel that they have caused face loss to their family members and partners after disclosing interpersonal problems about significant others. Consequently, these experiences may negatively impact treatment processes (e.g., poor working alliance and constrained or minimal self- disclosure) if therapists are unaware or insensitive to these issues. 
To better examine face concern within the context of psychological treatment, we developed and validated a measure assessing concern over loss of face (LOF; Zane & Yeh, 2002). Following an extensive literature review coupled with a behavior analytic assessment approach to the face construct, 21 items were developed to assess face concern. The criteria used to determine item inclusion were: 
 1. The item involved a face- threatening behavior in either one or more of these factors: social status, ethical behavior, social propriety, or self- discipline. These areas have been suggested by the literature to be the most common face- threatening situations (Ho, 1976; Hu, 1944; Hwang, 1987) 
 2. The item was not highly related to maladjustment.  3. The item could be easily translated into Japanese and Chinese for cross- national re-
search purposes. 
The validity of the LOF measure was tested with White American and Asian American young adults. The measure was internally consistent with an alpha of .83. The measure demonstrated both concurrent and discriminant validity. As predicted, face concern correlated positively with other directedness, private self- consciousness, and public self- consciousness and negatively with extraversion, acting (the desire to perform before others), and White cultural identity. Face concern was only correlated moderately with social anxiety and social desirability. However, it was not significantly related to response acquiescence, and, more importantly, it was not related to maladjustment. Similar results were found when Asians and whites were analyzed separately. 
We assessed for incremental validity and determined if face concern could account for ethnic variance above and beyond personality variables in Western psychology. Asian Americans had significantly more face concern than did White Americans. Ethnic differences between Asians and Whites were also found on social anxiety, acting, other directedness, social desirability, and White cultural identification. However, the Asian– White difference on face concern persisted even after controlling for ethnic differences on these other personality variables. An effect size analysis provided another way of examining the sensitivity of the LOF measure to ethnic differences. The effect sizes for the ethnic differences included the following: acting = .31, other- directedness = .27, social anxiety = .38, Asian cultural identity = .83, and face concern = .64. The effect sizes associated with ethnic differences on most of the other personality variables were somewhat larger than what Cohen (1992) considers to be a small effect size, whereas the effect size 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  479 
associated with ethnic differences on face concern was somewhat larger than a moderate effect size according to Cohen’s standards. 
These findings strongly suggest that ethnicity plays an influential role in determining how important face concern may be for different individuals. The only effect size larger than the face concern effect size was the one involving Asian cultural identity, which is a large effect size based on Cohen’s standards. However, this was expected since we did not expect to find much overlap in the cultural identities of whites and Asian Americans on Asian cultural identity. These results supported the reliability and construct validity of this measure of face concern. They also provide strong evidence that the measure is especially sensitive to ethnic and cultural differences for Asian and white Americans and may be useful in research on cultural issues in treatment. 
Self- disclosure is an important process variable in psychological treatment and a critical component of the treatment process. Clients must share important, private, and confidential concerns with their therapists to receive appropriate care and treatment. Many clients may be hesitant to provide this type of information since doing so may cause guilt, embarrassment, or shame. This is especially true for ethnic minority groups, where stigma and shame are often associated with mental health problems. To examine the effects of face on self- disclosure, we experimentally varied ethnic match and gender match and assessed acculturation, cultural identity, and face concern prior to the experiment with American and White American college students (Zane & Ku, 2014). Face concern was a negative predictor of all of the following types of self- disclosure: disclosures of personal values/ feelings, private habits, close relationships, and sexual issues. That is, participants with higher face concern were less likely to disclose personal information than were those with lower face concerns, regardless of ethnicity. Gender match affected disclosure about sex life, whereas ethnic match did not affect any type of self- disclosure. Acculturation was a negative predictor of disclosure concerning close relationships, but this effect was mediated by face concern: less acculturated individuals were more concerned about face, and those concerned about face tended to disclose less about their close relationships. 
Face concern and its influence on treatment credibility also was investigated. Credibility refers to the client’s belief that the therapist is an effective, trustworthy, and expert helper (Kazdin & Wilcoxon, 1976; Sue & Zane, 1987; Tracey, Glidden, & Kokotovic, 1988). Therapists can use more direct counseling styles in which they provide specific advice and more straightforward strategies to resolving conflict and difficulties. Therapists using an indirect style tend to encourage clients to develop their own interpretations and insights into their emotional experiences, which involves using more open- ended questions and reflecting on how the client feels and is experiencing the situation or relationship. Existing literature points to Asian American clients preferring a more direct counseling style by the therapist than a nondirect one (e.g., Kim, Li, & Liang, 2002). In one study, we examined the counseling styles of therapists and hypothesized that face concern would moderate this relative preference for a direct versus nondirect counseling style 
480 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
(Park, Kim, & Zane, under review). We also tested an alternative hypothesis that counseling expectations would account for this preference. Findings showed that Asian American participants did prefer the direct style to the nondirect one. Face concern moderated this effect, while counseling expectations did not. More specifically, Asian Americans with high face concern had greater preference for the directive approach over the nondirective one, whereas this preference was not found for individuals with low face concern. 
Establishing credibility in treatment and intervention is related to treatment effectiveness, especially for ethnic minority clients who may be less familiar with psychotherapy and counseling (Sue & Zane, 1987). This is even more relevant when the individual is a first- time client as this person may be experiencing discomfort with the expectations of disclosing private matters to a stranger. Since face concern refers to an interpersonal dynamic that is determined by the presence of others (Choi & Lee, 2002; Ho, 1984; Hu, 1944; Hwang, 1987), it is possible that those who are relatively high on face concern are more role- oriented and may view the therapist as an authority figure who provides advice and directives. It is also possible that direct counseling styles are more credible for those with greater face concern because the role of the therapist is more clearly defined, leaving less ambiguity in the client– therapist interaction. The fact that Asian Americans with high face concern prefer more direct therapeutic approaches strongly suggest that face concern may affect client responses to different types of treatments. This also highlights the utility of “unpacking” ethnicity to examine culture in social and psychological variations such as face concern. 
Social Validity Our recent studies focused on investigating ways to improve treatment credibility and engage ethnic minority and immigrant clients in treatment. Social validity is defined as the perception of the social importance and acceptability of an intervention by a specific cultural group (Wolf, 1978). Mental health treatments validated with mainstream clientele often may not be socially or ecologically valid for ethnic minority clients (Bernal, Bonilla, & Bellido, 1995). Researchers have suggested that people are less likely to engage in treatments that they find to be socially invalid (Kazdin, 1977). There are three aspects of social validity that can be considered with respect to an intervention: (1) clients from a particular cultural group must perceive the clinical problem addressed by the intervention as significant or important, (2) clients must find the major procedures or activities of an intervention to be culturally acceptable or appropriate, or (3)  the treatment goals or the outcomes targeted for change by the intervention must be valued by the clients (essentially, these goals are considered to be functional and have adaptive value). The following studies focused on the second aspect of social validity by examining if the major procedures in two evidence- based treatments were culturally valid or acceptable for a particular ethnic minority group. 
One study examined the social validity of an evidence- based family intervention, the Family Check- Up (FCU; Dishion & Stormshak, 2007), in a sample of Asian immigrant 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  481 
parents (Huang & Zane, 2016a). The FCU is a brief, assessment- driven intervention focused on assessing parenting behaviors, family relationships, and family strengths in order to reduce child mental health problems. The parenting behaviors that are assessed include positive reinforcement to increase desired behaviors in children, higher levels of parental monitoring to decrease children’s negative behaviors (e.g., substance use, gang involvement), and conflict resolution skills (i.e., setting limits and consequences). The FCU takes place over three meetings and follows this format: 
 1. A  semi- structured, intake interview and the administration of self- report measures on child behaviors, parent mental health, parenting behaviors, and family relationships 
 2. Videotaped observations of parenting behaviors and family relationships, assessed though five distinct tasks that are completed by the parent(s) and child 
 3. A final feedback meeting in which parents are given a summary of their family’s assessment findings. Findings from the two previous meetings are presented to the parents, and the feedback focuses on the specific parenting behaviors and family- related factors that may be relevant for addressing the child’s presenting problems. Families are also presented with specific treatment recommendations based on the FCU findings. The information is presented in a strengths- based manner using motivational interviewing strategies. The ultimate goal is to foster family involvement in the treatment process and follow- through with the treatment recommendations. 
We compared social validity evaluations of the FCU in a sample of 101 Asian immigrant parents and 87 white, middle- class parents with children aged 9– 13  years. Parents were presented with a thorough description of the FCU, including its meetings, procedures (as just outlined), targeted goals, and intended outcomes. We adapted the Treatment Acceptability Rating Form- Revised (TARF- R; Reimers et al., 1992), a measure that assessed for social validity in five ways:  (1) understanding of the intervention, (2)  acceptability of the intervention, (3)  willingness to participate in the intervention, (4) perceived effectiveness of the intervention, and (5) disruptiveness of the intervention in the family’s daily activities. 
Compared to white parents, Asian immigrant parents found most aspects of FCU to be less socially valid. Asian immigrant parents had lower understanding of the FCU, found the videotaped tasks and feedback meeting to be less socially acceptable, were less willing to participate in the FCU, and rated the feedback meeting as less effective compared to white parents. Regression analyses also found that the social validity of the three FCU sessions predicted lower overall ratings of the FCU by Asian immigrant parents. Furthermore, more enculturated Asian parents evaluated FCU as less socially valid, suggesting that parents who maintain higher levels of affinity with their culture of origin may find this family intervention to be less acceptable and relevant for them. As a whole, these findings strongly suggest that a frequently used evidence- based family 
482 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
intervention may be problematic for an ethnic group for which it has not been validated— in this case, Asian immigrant parents. 
In a young adult sample, we examined the social validity of cognitive behavior therapy (CBT; Cheng et  al., 2016). This study deconstructed CBT into nine essential treatment components:  (1) learning the relationship between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors; (2)  identifying emotions; (3)  identifying harmful and helpful thoughts; (4)  challenging harmful thoughts; (5)  changing and replacing harmful thoughts with helpful ones; (6)  understanding healthy activities; (7)  generating healthy activities; (8) selecting realistic healthy activities; and (9) setting future goals. 
A sample of 392 Asian American and 135 white American college students evaluated the social validity of these CBT components. Asian Americans found seven of the nine CBT components of CBT to be less socially valid than did white Americans. Asian Americans found understanding how thoughts affect feelings and behaviors, identifying harmful and helpful thoughts, changing and replacing harmful thoughts, understanding healthy activities, selecting realistic healthy activities, and setting future goals to be less socially valid. These striking ethnic differences in social validity of CBT may reflect cultural variations in how psychological problems are manifested with respect to depression. Research has indicated that Asian Americans tend to express depression more through somatic symptoms (e.g., headaches, stomachaches) than through cognitive and affective indicators (Chun, Enomoto, & Sue, 1996; Hsu & Folstein, 1997). As such, interventions such as CBT that focus on cognitive changes may not be as credible for these clients who may be expecting a more physical health approach to ameliorating their depression. 
From this body of research, it is clear that cultural considerations are necessary in effective psychotherapy. Ethnic match is an important factor in determining positive treatment outcomes. In addition, treatment outcomes and related precursors, such as treatment credibility and the working alliance, are also influenced by factors that can account for important between- and within- ethnic group variance. Perceived relevance (e.g., social validity) of a treatment’s procedures, goals, and processes to a cultural group may also influence how much ethnic minority clients are willing to engage in a treatment. These findings strongly demonstrate that cultural variables are salient for ethnic minority clients, and they can be informative to developing more effective evidence- based treatments for ethnic minority clientele. 
A Systematic Approach to Studying Cultural Influences in Psychological Interventions The field of culture and psychology has grown tremendously in the past few decades, and this research has provided critical and informative knowledge on understanding the impact of cultural factors on mental health. However, this body of work has been challenged by the lack of systematic approaches to explaining how culture affects treatment 
 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  483 
processes and outcomes. With some exceptions (e.g., Gallimore, Goldenberg, & Weisner, 1993), few models that were developed to explain cultural influences in mental health have been empirically tested. The Proximal– Distal Model was developed to address this need and to serve as a guide for researchers seeking to better capture important cultural variations in treatment processes and outcomes for ethnic minority clients (Sue & Zane, 1987). 
This framework allows for researchers to better investigate culture by articulating how cultural differences in treatment cause/ exacerbate problems for ethnic minority clients (Sue & Zane, 1987). This model allowed us to organize the existing knowledge on cultural differences into testable research hypotheses. The model proposed that ethnicity is more distal to treatment outcomes than other variables, such as client attitudes. Thus, outcomes may be more directly affected by attitudes (proximal variable) than ethnicity (distal variable) because ethnicity affects attitudes that, in turn, impact outcomes. First, we hypothesized that ethnic and cultural variations affect treatment credibility, a critical process in treatment that often predicts positive outcomes. In other words, cultural differences may have direct effects on how much clients believe psychological treatment will be effective and that their therapists will help them with their emotional problems. Treatment credibility has been a powerful and consistent predictor of treatment effectiveness (Kazdin & Wilcoxon, 1976). The model was one of our major efforts to be more definitive about the impact of culture on processes and outcomes in treatment. 
The Proximal– Distal Model reflects the movement in the field of culture and mental health away from population- focused (i.e., group differences) studies and toward an examination of ethnic or cultural group differences on therapy process and outcomes. While understanding group differences has provided important information about ethnic minority treatment experiences, it also has obscured variations among individuals in a particular minority group. This is due to the descriptive nature of these studies, which neglects to determine exactly how culture affects the treatment experience of minority clients and their treatment outcomes. A shift in the past 10– 15 years has led to a research emphasis on variable- focused studies (i.e., research examining specific psychological variables associated with cultural and group differences) and how these variables impact treatment effectiveness. This includes variables such as cultural value orientation, cultural identity, control orientation, shame, and stigma, which allows for improved explanations and understanding of the specific effects of cultural influences. These constructs also refer to individual- level variables and can capture important variations among majority individuals as well as among minorities. This method of studying culture fosters research that enhances our general understanding of human behavior by expanding the array of psychosocial constructs that can be used as explanatory models. 
The Proximal– Distal Model identifies three domains that posit how cultural variations may adversely affect treatment credibility and outcomes. The framework articulates three areas where treatment- relevant cultural differences can occur: (1) problem conceptualization, (2) means for coping with or solving the problem, and (3) goals for treatment. 
484 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Research in each of the areas is presented, along with a discussion of their impact on treatment processes and outcomes. 
Culture and Problem Conceptualization The ways in which a client’s presenting problems are conceptualized can affect how a therapist approaches treatment (e.g., through treatment selection, targeted goals). If the client’s problems are conceptualized in a culturally incongruent manner or in a way that conflicts with the client’s belief systems (Frank, 1961), the credibility of the therapist and/ or treatment may diminish. Cultural differences in mental health beliefs can result in differing perceptions of the problem between client and therapist (Sue, Wagner, Ja, Margullis, & Lew, 1976; Lum, 1982). Asian Americans are more likely than whites to believe that mental health problems are influenced by organic or somatic factors, while whites are more likely than Asians to believe that mental health is caused by avoiding morbid or negative thinking patterns (Sue et al., 1976). Yet, most cognitive therapies assume that negative thoughts and beliefs are at the core of emotional problems, which would be more consistent with how white clients conceptualize mental health. If psychotherapy requires clients to engage in painful or negative thoughts and de- emphasizes somatic interventions, many Asian American clients may find the process of psychotherapy to be inconsistent with their beliefs about what keeps them healthy. 
Using the Proximal– Distal model, we tested the hypothesis that cognitive matches (defined as therapist– client matches in attitudes, beliefs, and expectancies about treatment- related outcomes) on treatment- relevant factors such as perception of the problem, coping orientations (i.e., the preferred ways of dealing with the problem), and belief in the effectiveness of treatment (i.e., treatment credibility) would affect treatment outcomes. We studied white and Asian clients at a community mental health center after their first and fourth sessions of treatment (Zane et al., 2005). Outcome measures included client psychological distress and psychosocial functioning. Findings indicated that various types of therapist– client cognitive matches predicted short- term treatment outcomes from both client and therapist perspectives. Specifically, with respect to problem perception, when therapists and clients perceived similar amounts of distress associated with a certain mental health problem, this similarity positively predicted psychological functioning after four sessions of treatment. 
Cultural variations in problem perception may also involve the types of symptoms that clients present to their therapists in treatment. Research has consistently shown that Asians and Asian Americans experiencing clinical levels of depression tend to present with more somatic symptoms (Cheung & Lau, 1982; Chang, 1985; Yen, Robins, & Lin, 2000; Ryder et al., 2008). Somatic symptoms can also be the culturally “sanctioned” ways in which Asians and Asian Americans seek help for psychological distress. East Asian cultures traditionally emphasize a more holistic view of body and mind that may socialize them to focus on physical symptoms rather than just emotional ones when seeking help (Hwang, Myers, Abe- Kim, & Ting, 2008; Lin & Cheung, 1999). In a clinical study of 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  485 
Asian and white outpatients, we determined whether somatic symptoms and other client tendencies predicted clinical outcomes after short- term treatment (Kim, Zane, & Blozis, 2012). We found that clients with more somatic tendencies had poorer functioning even after four sessions of treatment. The tendency to present with somatic symptoms was a negative predictor of treatment outcome, and this may have occurred because orthodox approaches to psychotherapy seldom address somatic symptoms as a focus of treatment. 
Cultural Differences in Coping and Problem- Solving The Proximal– Distal model also posits that clients and therapists may differ in the ways they prefer to cope with or solve the client’s problems. Therapeutic procedures and the client– helper roles adopted as the means for problem resolution also may run counter to a client’s preferred ways of coping with problems or may violate certain behavioral norms considered important in his or her culture. For example, asking clients to respond in culturally unacceptable ways may decrease the credibility of the therapist or the treatment. Earlier studies consistently documented that Asian Americans preferred structured, unambiguous tasks and wanted immediate, pragmatic solutions to psychological problems compared to White Americans (Arkoff, 1959; Meredith, 1966). Traditional insight- oriented psychotherapies, however, often use an open- ended problem- solving process to help clients gain insight into their problems. For Asian clients, these ambiguous questions may lead them to perceive therapy as inefficient or not relevant to their immediate concerns. Thus, expectations concerning the therapist’s role, coping preferences or orientations, and beliefs about the types of help to be received may affect the problem- solving process in therapy. 
Psychological treatment typically involves teaching clients adaptive ways to cope with stressors in their lives. We examined the coping styles of Asian and white American young adults who were coping with interpersonal conflict and stress (Lam & Zane, 2004). This study specifically examined ethnic variations in both primary control coping (i.e., directly changing the nature of the stressor) and secondary control coping (i.e., changing the individual’s feelings and thoughts in reaction to the stressor). The findings indicated that both white and Asian Americans preferred primary control coping more than secondary control coping. However, white Americans were more oriented toward primary control than were Asian Americans, whereas Asian Americans were more oriented toward secondary control than were white Americans. Ethnic effects were also found on independent and interdependent self- construals. Asian Americans were significantly less oriented toward independent self- construal— and significantly more toward interdependent self- construal— than were white Americans. 
Given these differences in self- construals, we investigated whether self- construals mediated the ethnic differences in primary and secondary control orientations. Findings showed that independent self- construal fully mediated the ethnic difference in primary control orientation. In essence, whites were more independent- oriented than Asians, and independent- oriented individuals tended to be more oriented to primary 
 
486 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
control. Western cultures typically emphasize independence, self- reliance, and autonomy (Markus & Kitayama, 1991), and individuals seem to exercise direct control over their environment in order to meet their personal needs (Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995; Morling & Fiske, 1999). Conversely, interdependent self- construals partially mediated the ethnic difference in secondary control orientation. Asians were more interdependent- oriented than whites, and individuals who were more interdependent tended to be more oriented to secondary control. Individuals with strong interdependent self- construals tend to emphasize a relational self in which a person’s self- definition and self- concept are predicated on the nature and quality of his or her relationships with others. The motivation to enhance or minimize discord in these relationships often socializes people more toward secondary control coping strategies that involve an individual’s attempts to accommodate or adapt to existing circumstances (Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995; Morling & Fiske, 1999). 
Ultimately, cultural variations in coping orientation are only salient for treatment issues if the cultural variations are empirically related to treatment outcomes. Some of our research has found that cultural differences in coping can affect treatment processes and outcomes. In the cognitive match study mentioned previously, coping orientation match predicted less dysphoria after four treatment sessions (Zane et al., 2005). Clients with therapists who shared similar expectations of avoidant coping at pretreatment demonstrated less discomfort and less dysphoria after short- term treatment than clients with therapists who were less similar on this coping orientation. We also found that avoidance coping was predictive of more negative outcomes after short- term, outpatient treatment for Asian American clients (Kim et al., 2012). Clients who were more likely to use an avoidant coping style experienced more negative symptoms (e.g., blunted affect) and psychological discomfort (e.g., anxiety, depression) at posttreatment. In addition, non– English- speaking clients were more likely to have negative treatment outcomes, which were mediated by an avoidant coping style. 
Cultural Differences in Treatment Goals and Outcomes Even when cultural congruence exists between therapists and ethnic minority clients in problem conceptualization and the preferred methods for problem resolution, the client may still leave therapy because she feels that the therapy has not adequately addressed her major needs. Murase and Johnson (1974) compared East Asian and Western psychotherapies and noted that, from the beginning of treatment, the primary goal of Eastern psychotherapies is to recover and improve the client’s functioning so the client can resume productive roles in life (e.g., better work productivity, enhanced ability to function as a parent and/ or spouse). They suggested that the goal of Eastern therapies is social and objective rehabilitation due to the emphasis on social functioning and the fact that one can observe these changes in the person’s life. However, they considered the primary initial goal of Western therapies to be personal and subjective restoration. Western therapies tend to emphasize the reduction of the personal distress and emotional suffering clients have experienced so that they feel as they did prior to the onset of their mental health 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  487 
problems (Murase & Johnson, 1974). With respect to treatment goals, the Proximal– Distal model posits that certain ethnic minority clients may be using different criteria to judge the effects of therapy than those commonly used by therapists. Take the example of a recent Asian American college student who reflected on her initial psychotherapy experience with one of the authors. She described her first therapy sessions as an amazing and cathartic experience that helped her learn about herself. Yet the student only stayed for three sessions. When asked why her treatment duration was so short, she replied, “Oh, it did not help my grades.” This conversation demonstrated several things: (1) the positive associations with therapy were insufficient in keeping the student engaged in treatment because its goals (i.e., decrease stress, psychological distress, and burden) were incompatible with her own criteria for a positive outcome (i.e., improve grades). 
In our study on cognitive match, we found that similarities in treatment goals between client and therapist predicted better outcomes in the treatment sessions (Zane et al., 2005). Clients reported how affected they were by the therapeutic work (session depth), how relaxed or comfortable they felt in sessions (session comfort), how good they felt about their progress in the sessions (session positivity), and how emotionally stimulated/ interested they felt in the sessions (session arousal). Treatment goal match was a positive predictor of three of the four session outcomes. Specifically, when clients and therapists agreed on the goals in treatment, clients experienced the sessions as more impactful, felt more comfortable in sessions, and were more positive about the progress made in sessions. 
Other Factors Affecting Treatment Credibility We investigated other cultural variables that may affect treatment credibility, which is the major treatment process identified in the Proximal– Distal model. We examined ethnic differences in treatment credibility (Wong, Beutler, & Zane, 2007). As indicated earlier, therapists can vary in the extent to which they are direct or indirect by how they work with the client. Direct therapists generally provide more structured feedback and specific suggestions to clients on how to manage their problems. Conversely, nondirect therapists use more reflection and reframing of the problem to allow clients to independently solve their problems. Both approaches have merit and are effective in treatment. Our experiment varied therapeutic approach by having Asian American and white American participants observe prominent experts in the field conducting therapy using either a direct or nondirect style. Across both therapeutic styles, Asian Americans evaluated these sessions as lower in counselor credibility and working alliance than white Americans. Counselor understandability (i.e., how much they understood the counselor when they spoke) was a significant mediator of the relationship between ethnicity and intervention credibility. Asian Americans found the counselors more difficult to understand, which in turn was related to lower counselor credibility and lower working alliance. These findings suggest that Asian American’s experiences with treatment credibility may be influenced by how familiar they are to the counseling or therapy process. 
 
488 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Factors related to ethnicity or culture have been found to moderate the relationship between treatment approach and credibility. We examined the credibility of cognitive therapy (CT) and time- limited dynamic psychotherapy (TLDP), which are two widely used and empirically supported interventions (Wong, Kim, Zane, Kim, & Huang, 2003). The study conducted a comprehensive analysis of culturally based variables and their related effects on credibility perceptions. Variables assessed included cultural identity, self- construals, values, and mental health beliefs. Asian American participants were randomly assigned to read either a CT or TLDP treatment rationale for depression and then rated the credibility of the intervention. Results indicated that cultural identity and self- construals moderated the differences in credibility between CT and TLDP. Participants with low levels of white identity rated CT as significantly more credible than TLDP, whereas participants with high white identity did not rate the two treatment rationales differently. Individuals with high independent self- construals found CT to be significantly more credible than TLDP, whereas less independent individuals did not find one intervention approach to be more credible than the other. These findings underscore the importance of examining the treatment effects of specific variables, which often capture important and salient psychological variance between ethnic or cultural groups such as cultural identity, acculturation, and self- construals. 
In summary, the Proximal– Distal Model identified specific cultural factors that influence treatment processes and outcomes, and it allowed researchers to test and provide evidence for the clinical relevance of these factors on treatment and intervention processes. These processes are particularly important because they impact the credibility of mental health treatments, which influences the treatment process and eventual mental health outcomes. One pattern emerging from this body of work is the notion of cognitive match— on problem perception, problem- solving preferences, coping styles, and treatment goals. Similar goals and expectations of treatments between client and therapist yield better treatment outcomes. Mismatches between client and therapist on these key processes negatively affect the credibility of the treatment and that of the therapist delivering the treatment. In light of this knowledge, new ways of thinking about client and therapist match are important to fully address the needs of ethnic minority clients. One potential avenue to addressing and improving congruence in the treatment process is through intake interviews and assessments. By assessing and inquiring about clients’ cultural beliefs related to mental illness, their attitudes (and doubts) about the treatment procedures, and their own personal goals for treatment, therapists may be able to better modify their approach to treatment to optimize treatment credibility and, ultimately, treatment outcomes. 
Culturally Informed Mental Health Interventions This review clearly demonstrates that a substantial amount of research has been conducted to better understand how cultural factors affect treatment processes and outcomes. 
 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  489 
However, the extent to which this research has been effectively translated into culturally informed intervention strategies is often unclear. How are these findings used to inform ESTs and other psychological interventions? This section discusses the progress made in culturally informed intervention research. 
ESTs are considered “best practices” in mental health care and have become the standard in mental health practice and research. ESTs have been shown to significantly outperform placebos or other treatments (Chambless & Hollon, 1998; Huey & Polo, 2008). The availability of ESTs for ethnic minority clients, unfortunately, continues to lag behind that for white clients (Atkinson, Maruyama, & Matsui, 1978; Sue, 1977; Sue & Zane, 1987). This gap is mainly due to a lack of research on ESTs for these clients. This gap is particularly salient for clients who are less familiar with psychological practices, such as Asian immigrant populations (Lee, 1982; Leong, 1986). Over the past 10 years, numerous efforts have been made to modify orthodox ESTs so that they can better address the mental health needs and cultural issues of ethnic minority clients (Huang & Zane, 2016b). A related but separate field of research is the movement to develop culturally sensitive treatments for specific communities based on the community’s articulated needs. These two efforts share a common goal of reducing disparities in mental health quality of care for ethnic minorities. 
Culturally Adapted Interventions Significant progress has been made in developing culturally adapted interventions to enhance mental health care for ethnic minorities. Adaptations vary in form, content, and the manner by which they are implemented. A cultural adaptation is defined as the systematic changes made to the protocols of ESTs that consider culture, language, and context in a way that is sensitive to the client’s worldview, cultural meaning, and values (Bernal, Jiménez- Chafee, & Domenech Rodríguez, 2009). 
An impressive increase in studies examining the effectiveness of culturally adapted interventions has occurred in recent years. This includes randomized control trials and quai- experimental studies of adapted ESTs. The outcomes targeted are varied (e.g., phobias, anxiety, depression), as are the targeted ethnic minority populations and communities (e.g., migrant farmworkers and Hispanic and Asian Americans). These studies and research reviews tend to corroborate the effectiveness of culturally adapted ESTs in decreasing distress and symptoms and enhancing psychosocial functioning (Benish, Quintana, & Wampold, 2011; Chowdhary et  al., 2014; Hovey, Hurtado, & Seligman, 2014; Huey & Polo, 2008; Pan, Huey, & Hernandez, 2011; Smith, Domenech Rodriguez, & Bernal, 2011; van Loon, van Schaik, Dekker, & Beekman, 2013). For example, one study examined the pretest- posttest levels of depression, anxiety, and stress in a sample of female migrant farmworkers who received a culturally tailored cognitive- behavioral therapy (CBT) support group (Hovey et al., 2014). At 6- month follow- up, the women experienced a significant reduction in depression, anxiety, and stress from pretreatment to posttreatment. Asian Americans less acculturated to mainstream American 
 
490 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
culture had better outcomes after receiving a culturally adapted, brief exposure therapy for phobias compared to less acculturated Asian Americans who received the standard exposure therapy condition (Pan et al., 2011). In addition, high effect sizes were found for culturally adapted psychotherapies over conventional psychotherapy for ethnic minority clients, with standard mean differences ranging from .72 to 1.06 (Chowdhary et al., 2014). These findings were found for both adult and child psychotherapies, though effect sizes were higher for the adult therapies (Jackson & Hodge, 2010). 
A challenge, however, is that there is often little consistency in how the adaptations were made (Huang & Zane, 2016a). There is a diversity of guidelines and approaches for developing cultural adaptations to an EST. Without one specific framework, it is difficult to determine which adaptation approach should be applied to which EST, clinical problem, and client group. This has resulted in cultural adaptations that varied greatly in type, form, and treatment focus. 
A content analysis study was conducted to better understand what types of adaptations have been made and the treatment process or processes that adaptations addressed (Zane, Kim, Bernal, & Guotaco, 2016). This study specifically focused on the form and content of the adaptation, rather than on the effectiveness of an EST over a nonadapted EST. The analysis found 41 relevant studies, which ranged from delineating the development process of culturally adapting an evidence- based treatment, to describing case studies or case examples, to reporting on results from randomized controlled trials. The majority of the adaptations were made for the Hispanic or Latino populations (58.5%); 17% of the adaptations were made for Asian Americans; 12.2% were culturally adapted for African Americans; and 12.2% were adapted for use with Native American populations. 
Adaptations to treatments can also address changes in surface structure or deep structure (Resnicow, Baranowski, Ahluwalia, & Braithwaite, 1999). Surface structure changes refer to changes in the structural aspects or the contextual aspects of the treat-ment. Examples include changing the type of personnel who provided the treatment (e.g., linguistically compatible therapist) or using materials in the client’s native language (e.g., translating study materials into the client’s language). Deep structure changes refer to changing a treatment’s purported core components to stimulate or produce psychological changes in the client. For example, changing the procedures of a treatment to be more culturally congruent with certain coping styles reflects a deep structure change. The content analysis found that only four types of adaptations were used in the majority of the adapted interventions: use of appropriate language and metaphors, provision of education and information, acquisition or practice of new behaviors, and the types of participants engaged in the treatment. Three of these four most frequent adaptations focused on surface- level structural changes to the treatment. Interventions also applied adaptations in four other areas:  (a) development of working alliance, (b) relabeling or destigmatizing, (c) provision of rationale for treatment or explanation of the problem, and (d) healing setting characteristics. In contrast to the four most frequent adaptations, most of these adaptations focused on deep structure changes.
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  491 
The pattern that emerged from examining the most frequent type of adaptations strongly suggests that changes to both surface and deep structure of the treatment appear needed if treatments are to be optimally effective with ethnic minority clientele. On average, 63% of the adaptations involved some type of surface structure modification. In contrast, when we examined the four most frequent deep structure changes, on average, only 43% of the adaptations involved these changes. The lack of emphasis on deep structure changes may have limited treatment impact because deep structure changes tend to affect treatment processes most often linked to treatment outcomes. Our findings also indicated that adaptations did not often address basic treatment processes that are essential to effective therapy. For example, a strong therapeutic or working alliance has been consistently linked to positive treatment outcomes (Martin, Garske, & Davis, 2000; Orlinskey, Ronnestad, & Willutzki, 2004), as has client self- disclosure (Jourard, 1964; Stricker & Fisher, 1990). Less than half of the adaptations addressed working alliance in their adaptions and only a few studies focused on enhancing client self- disclosure. 
Even when the adaptations have addressed deep structure changes, it was unclear if the adaptations actually achieved their goals due to the lack of empirical evidence showing changes in the treatment process targeted by the adaptation. More specifically, the areas of focus for the adaptations occurred because researchers assumed or nominated these domains based on some empirical evidence that substantial ethnic and/ or cultural variations existed on the variables. As the basis for documenting these cultural variations, investigators primarily used findings from focus groups or systematic literature reviews to determine if there were important cultural and ethnic differences on the variables they selected for adaptation. None of the investigations provided any type of evidence that empirically demonstrated the adaptation actually had changed a critical treatment process related to outcomes. Consequently, there appears to be a major disconnect between research on cultural adaptations to treatment and research on what makes psychotherapy effective. This disconnect may contribute to the measured progress in reducing disparities in the quality of mental health care for ethnic minority clients. 
To address some of the challenges identified in the adaptation- content study, we proposed the Critical Process Approach (CPA) as a guide to help researchers sort and select the most relevant variables that need to be addressed by a particular adaptation. The CPA emphasizes the need to have an empirically grounded approach to developing adaptations for ESTs so that these adaptations can be developed in a way that systematically links them to important treatment processes. The CPA has four conditions that must be met: 
 1. Empirical evidence demonstrating substantial variation on the variable being adapted must exist between different cultural or ethnic groups. This means that the effect size associated with group differences on this variable needs to be sufficiently large so we are confident that the adaptation is addressing a stable and salient cultural issue for that ethnic group.
492 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
 2. The variable adapted also must be empirically linked to some type of critical process in treatment or directly to a treatment outcome. This is to ensure that adaptations that are selected and used or applied have a greater likelihood of actually contributing to the effectiveness of the treatment. 
 3. There must be a rationale that explains how the adaptation is culturally significant. Cultural significance refers to the extent to which an intervention (i.e., an adaptation) has features that align with, or fit with, the cultural tendencies of clients from a specific culture. 
 4. There must be some empirical evidence that the adaptation is considered or perceived as culturally appropriate, or socially valid, by the stakeholders of that cultural or ethnic group. An adaptation is only successful if there is empirical evidence demonstrating social validity by the specific cultural or ethnic group for whom an adaptation was made. 
By using the CPA as a guiding framework, researchers have a way to systematically adapt interventions for ethnic minority and cultural groups. We are using the CPA to develop and pilot test an adapted intervention of CBT for depression among Asian Americans. Given the previous research and following the CPA, the adaptation uses face- saving strategies to enhance self- disclosure and client engagement as well as specific CBT procedures for pain management to address the somatic tendencies of Asian American clients. For the former, the adaptation focuses on reframing personal issues into solving specific problems as opposed to reducing “personal” symptoms or managing a “personal” disease (Littlejohn & Domenici, 2006). In this way, the orientation fosters demonstrations of mastery and competence that can enhance face restoration and minimize further face loss. For the latter, the adaptation capitalizes on empirically supported behavioral medicine procedures in pain management, such as relaxation training and biofeedback to reduce the pain caused by somatic symptoms so that the intervention directly addresses one of the major presenting problems for Asian American clients. 
Community- Centered Cultural Interventions Increasing awareness of the importance of community- centered research has led to the acknowledgment that empirically validated treatments may not always address the critical mental health needs of a specific community. As such, there is an ongoing debate on the need to develop interventions from within a community (i.e., ground- up approach) rather than adapting ESTs, which is perceived as a top- down approach in intervention development. A  ground- up approach to intervention development is consistent with the community- based participatory research (CBPR) approach, where the needs of the community and its members drive the development, procedures, and implementation of an intervention. CBPR is a collaborative research approach that involves all partners (e.g., researchers, community stakeholders) equitably (Wells, Miranda, Bruce, Alegria, & Wallerstein, 2004) and has emerged as a gold standard for working with ethnically diverse 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  493 
communities. CBPR begins with a research topic that is important to the community and has an aim of combining knowledge with action to promote social change, particularly for the community. The CBPR approach has been instrumental in reducing disparities in the quality of healthcare and mental health care and access to care for certain ethnic minority communities (Alegria et al., 2011). Furthermore, the CBPR approach may serve as a useful framework in informing the development of culturally valid interventions for ethnic minority communities. 
Using CBPR and an interdisciplinary team of researchers from psychology, nursing, and theater and dance, we collaborated with a community- based organization that serves Asian immigrant communities. The collaboration determined that elderly Asian adults were in need of a safe space where they could engage in health- and mental health- enhancing activities. We developed a 10- week cultural movement intervention based on a traditional form of Chinese exercise called Lishi with a sample of elderly Vietnamese American immigrant adults. Lishi is an arts- based movement that has been used to promote mental and physical health for centuries. Its movements are similar to those of Tai Chi, a commonly practiced form of exercise around the world. Lishi integrates regulated breathing, alignment postures, and movement exercises to improve balance, flexibility, and mobility, and it is intended to be a holistic approach to health, including mental health. 
The stigma surrounding psychological issues and mental health treatments, especially among older generations, may act as a barrier for engaging Asian immigrants in mental health care. Since Lishi was developed in Asian cultures and has been used for centuries among these cultures, the cultural challenges were minimized for these participants. Furthermore, the focus on physical activity also improved the intervention’s acceptability for this group. Attrition from this pilot study was less than 6% for those participants who received the intervention (Huang & Zane, under review). Findings indicated that elderly Asian immigrant adults who received the intervention had better balance and energy level and less bodily pain at posttest compared to no- treatment control group participants. They also had significantly higher levels of self- efficacy compared to control group participants at posttest, indicating an improved sense of self- worth and competence. In addition, dosage (i.e., number of sessions attended) was negatively associated with depression at posttest for the participants who received Lishi, suggesting that this intervention also was effective at decreasing psychological distress. This study demonstrated the effectiveness of a culturally valid, culturally acceptable intervention at engaging and retaining a difficult- to- reach immigrant population. 
The development and use of cultural interventions are increasing in popularity among other ethnic minority communities. Rowan and colleagues (2014) conducted a review of prevention and treatment interventions for indigenous communities in the United States and Canada, and found 17 different studies that were designed with culturally specific interventions for these communities. Examples of cultural interventions included dancing, fasting, storytelling, ceremonial practice, and sweat lodges. More than 
494 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
74% of the studies found reduction or elimination of substance use problems through the cultural interventions (Rowan et al., 2014). Among Native Hawaiian communities, research on the effects of hula, a traditional Native Hawaiian dance form, have found positive psychological and physical effects for patients rehabilitating from cardiac events and/ or surgeries (Maskarinec et al., 2015). Community- centered research provides a viable alternative and/ or complement to the orthodox evidence- based approaches in developing more culturally informed interventions that can better address the mental health needs of specific ethnic minority communities. 
In conclusion, the inclusion of ethnic minority populations in treatment research has improved drastically in recent decades. The prevalence of culturally adapted ESTs is increasing, and evidence points to its effectiveness over orthodox, nonadapted mental health treatments for ethnic minority populations. A pervasive issue in this research remains the variability in adaptation types (i.e., surface- or deep- level changes) and the dearth of empirical frameworks to guide the intervention adaptation process. The CPA model was developed to tackle this issue by providing researchers with a framework to manage and conduct intervention adaptation research. Another major problem in this field is the low representation of ethnic minority clients in studies examining mental health treatments, especially clinical trials. As such, effect sizes of ethnic and racial status on treatment outcomes are often lacking. The use of CBPR in research and intervention development has grown in popularity as the field struggles to engage hard- to- reach and underserved communities. CBPR ensures that the treatment engagement involves developing and designing treatments in close collaboration with key stakeholders in ethnic minority communities (Kataoka, Novins, & DeCarlo Santiago, 2010), thus allowing the stakeholders to provide regular and ongoing feedback on the relevant cultural issues for the target community. This process can be more effectively and systematically integrated into the context of treatment, which improves the likelihood that the intervention is culturally informed in a proactive manner. The growth in the development and use of community- centered cultural interventions can promote the inclusion of these interventions in rigorous research (i.e., clinical trials). 
Research Challenges and Future Directions The field of culture and mental health intervention research has made significant progress in the past few decades. There is growing knowledge about which specific cultural factors and cultural variations are important in mental health treatment processes and outcomes. There is also continued growth in the number of ESTs for ethnic minority groups and communities. Despite these improvements, challenges remain in research on culturally informed interventions for mental health care. Addressing many of these challenges should provide future opportunities for more impactful research in this field. 
 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  495 
One major challenge in research on cultural and mental health intervention is that culture can be difficult to define. Inconsistencies and variations in operationalizing culture can lead to methodological and conceptual challenges that complicate efforts to examine ethnicity and culture on psychotherapy processes and outcomes (see also Chapter 6 by Jia He and Fons J. R. van de Vijver for more discussion about cross- cultural research methods). For instance, selecting the right research questions is guided by the conceptualization of culturally related variables and can vary dramatically from study to study. Ethnic affiliation is assumed to be representative of cultural variation. However, ethnicity and ethnic differences are not necessarily synonymous with cultural differences. Ethnic differences represent group membership that implies differences in culture, whereas cultural variations refer to actual differences in attitudes, values, beliefs, and lifestyles resulting from different cultural experiences. Ethnic affiliation often maps onto cultural differences, which are more proximal to psychotherapy processes and outcomes. Often the research questions asked include “Does a specific ethnic group benefit more from a treatment compared to another ethnic group?” It may be more useful for researchers to ask whether differences between ethnic groups on culturally relevant variables, such as stigma beliefs about mental illness, affect a specific process or outcome in treatment. 
In addition, ethnicity and cultural background are often confounded by various factors such as socioeconomic status, education level, community environment, and English proficiency. Neglecting to account for these variables creates problems in interpretation of study effects and also misses opportunities for increasing design sensitivity (Luborsky, Auerbach, Chandler, Cohen, & Bachrach, 1971). Another challenge in this research is the heterogeneity within each ethnic minority group (Leong, 1986). Country of origin, immigration history, education level, socioeconomic status, and language preference are some examples of differences that occur within one group (e.g., Asian, Latino). Despite this diversity, studies rarely assess these within- group variations (e.g., Vietnamese vs. Japanese, Mexican vs. Puerto Rican) as carefully as they should. The focus is often on the investigation of intergroup differences (e.g., Asian vs. Latino, Asian vs. white). There can be substantial gains for researchers who examine and capitalize on this within- group diversity. For instance, Puerto Rican and Mexican college students in both Latino and Anglo American cultures varied in their responses to counselor styles (Pomales & Williams, 1989). Enculturated Latino students rated the nondirect therapist as more credible than did the bicultural students. In contrast, the acculturated Latino students rated the therapist as more trustworthy than did bicultural or enculturated students regardless of therapist style. This sampling challenge continues to be a problem due to the relatively small number of minority group individuals who are available or accessible for research studies, especially in clinical trials. The CBPR approach in culture and mental health research may be one way to better address this challenge— proactively collaborating with community stakeholders beginning with the study development process (e.g., research questions and design, participant recruitment) will ensure the inclusion of critical factors relevant to the community for which the research is targeted.
496 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
A fourth challenge that impacts mental health intervention research on cultural issues involves the selection and use of appropriate measures. Cultural and ethnic differences may not be assessed reliably if the measures used are invalid or insensitive to these differences. This includes the use of clinical assessments that either overpathologize or underpathologize symptoms of ethnic minority clients or measures that were normed on white populations. Additional problems include having measures that are limited to English- speaking clients only, inadequate translations, and cultural differences in approaching the assessment tasks (Okazaki & Sue, 1995). Despite concern over the cross- cultural validity of assessment measures, there is limited information on how to combat these issues. This is due to the lack of available research on cultural bias in measurement. Moreover, as measures are being translated and validated for use with ethnic minority samples, newer versions of a measure or a new gold standard measure are being developed in English. This results in a continuous cycle in which the development of appropriate assessment instruments for ethnic minorities often lags behind the most contemporary measures used in the field. One way to prevent this cycle is for cultural and mental health researchers to develop measures that assess specific cultural variables, such as the loss of face (Zane & Yeh, 2002) measure. 
Finally, in clinical outcome research, what actually happens to the client in the intervention is often unclear. It is often difficult to observe the extent to which therapists and clients have complied with or carried out the therapeutic tasks (Collins, Martin, & Hillenberg, 1982). This source of treatment ambiguity involves problems in procedural reliability, which refers to the degree to which the treatment has been implemented in accordance with the experimental plan. This problem is a critical one that can occur for both clients (Taylor, Agras, Schneider, & Allen, 1983) and therapists (Billingsley, White, & Munson, 1980). In addition, defining the end- point of therapy tasks (i.e., what the client should have learned/ completed in treatment) is often ambiguous. What are the insights, emotional catharses, or skills that clients are supposed to experience during the course of psychotherapy? Core therapeutic learning experiences represent the key variables required for identifying change mechanisms in psychotherapy. These concepts and learning experiences are often insufficiently defined by theories of psychotherapy. These theoretical and methodological inadequacies in clinical outcome research perpetuate the limitations in defining models of change. If mechanisms underlying change in psychotherapy are unclear, it is especially difficult to identify which aspects of treatment that can be adapted or modified to be culturally responsive. As such, these limitations in treatment process and outcome research have impeded progress in the development of culturally informed treatment. 
One way to approach this limitation centers on distinguishing between ultimate criteria (i.e., ultimate goal of therapy) and instrumental criteria (i.e., condition required) for attaining goals in treatment (Fiske et al., 1970). Outcome studies typically have focused on assessing ultimate criteria to determine treatment effectiveness. It is important that studies also incorporate instrumental criteria into the research design 
CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  497 
as this provides the critical empirical link between treatment procedures and outcomes needed to identify aspects of important therapeutic elements for culturally responsive treatment. Figure 15.2 shows how instrumental criteria are incorporated into outcome research and the concomitant methodological issues that need to be addressed. For example, CBT is the most frequently used treatment for major depression. With respect to therapy content, one of CBT’s core treatment procedures involves cognitive or rational restructuring. Essentially, the client learns to (a) understand that feelings, especially extremely negative reactions, often are affected by one’s thoughts and beliefs; (b) identify the irrational beliefs or thoughts about the world and oneself that generate or exacerbate these maladaptive, negative feelings; (c) challenge and understand the irrationality of these self- statements and thoughts; and (d) replace the irrational thoughts with more realistic and rational cognitions that alleviate and/ or reduce the negative feelings. Effective cognitive restructuring attains the instrumental goals of belief change and the development of a cognitive skill. In turn, these major cognitive changes should result in the significant reduction of the client’s depressive symptoms, which is the ultimate outcome criteria. 
Based on this approach, treatment effectiveness for ethnic clientele becomes multifaceted and involves at least two questions: Did the treatment have the desired impact on ethnic minority clients by achieving its instrumental goals (impact)? Also, did the achievement of these instrumental goals produce the expected ultimate outcomes that indicate the treatment’s effectiveness for ethnic minority clients (relevance)? This approach allows for a refined, more nuanced interpretation of outcome results that considers cultural influences in treatment. By measuring both instrumental and ultimate goals, researchers can determine which should be adapted in order to facilitate a treatment’s effectiveness with culturally diverse clients. In addition to impact and relevance, a third issue can be considered: How efficient is the treatment? Treatment efficiency essentially involves a cost- effectiveness analysis of the intervention. These costs include the difficulty level of the therapeutic tasks and the level of skill required to implement these tasks. Therapeutic tasks may often be influenced by cultural differences between client and therapist, while skill level may be affected by the cultural sensitivity skills of the therapist. These costs are weighed against the improvement in the client’s mental health problem. 
In developing and adapting culturally informed interventions, the issue of cultural significance warrants special attention. Often there is little rationale or justification articulating how the intervention’s adaptations are culturally appropriate and valid for a particular cultural group. Gallimore and colleagues (1993) addressed cultural significance by indicating that when an intervention’s activities or procedures are similar to the form and function (i.e., isomorphic) of those activities that typically occur in a client’s cultural setting (e.g., within family or community), cultural fit has been occurred. Essentially, the intervention must be culturally meaningful and fit with the values, attitudes, or coping styles of the clients being served. Yet interventions are often presented and tested with little explanation of cultural
