CulTure and PsyChologiCal inTervenT ions  |  499 
fit or match underlying the culturally informed strategy or intervention. Researchers must make the argument for how each adaptation makes the intervention more culturally appropriate or ecologically valid (Bernal et al., 1995). We need better models to explain how the interventions are clinically significant for a certain cultural group as well as ways to operationalize cultural significance to determine if it has been achieved. 
With growing recognition of the need to address cultural differences in interven-tion research, adaptations and changes are often assumed necessary rather than proved necessary. This has led some researchers to de- emphasize the step of presenting adequate evidence to show which specific adaptations are needed. Studies on social validity are needed to assess for the significance and cultural relevance of the core components of a mental health treatment or intervention (Reimers & Wacker, 1988; Reimers et al., 1998). Yet few studies are utilizing this approach in their adaptations of interventions for cultural and ethnic minority groups and therefore do not collect or present social validity data as part of their adaptation process. Many studies continue to rely solely on focus group data and fail to systematically collect data that can provide a strong empirical basis for designing their adaptations. Researchers need to provide more empirical evidence that the specific adaptations they are testing are, in fact, needed in cultural interventions with ethnic minority populations. 
Conclusion The disparities experienced by ethnic minority clients are largely due to cultural variability in the ways people perceive mental health problems, cope with distress, and value mental health outcomes. Factors involving cultural, ethnic, and racial variations influence the ways in which ethnic minority clients perceive the validity and credibility of the treatments and their therapists, which ultimately can negatively affect treatment outcomes. While significant progress has been made in contributing to this cultural knowledge base, the actual systematic application of this knowledge to develop and implement more culturally informed mental health interventions lags behind. 
Currently, there clearly are some promising ways in which cultural considerations can be applied to intervention development and adaptation to help move the field toward reducing disparities for people from diverse cultural and ethnic backgrounds. Our current work on social validity provides a systematic approach for determining the specific aspects of an EST that may be especially problematic for certain ethnic minority clientele. The CPA is a promising systematic framework for guiding cultural adaptation psychotherapy research. Finally, the use of CBPR approaches in psychotherapy research is growing. Underutilization rates are expected to decrease as community- centered interventions grow in use and recognition, and researchers begin to include more of these interventions in clinical trial research. 
 
500 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Clinical research addressing cultural issues has important implications for international clients and those who need psychological services outside of the United States. Worldwide, community- based statistics show that prevalence rates of mental illness range anywhere from 12.8% to 48.6% (World Health Organization [WHO], 2000), with many people not seeking treatment at all or postponing treatment until years after symptoms become severe and disabling (Olfson, Kessler, Berglund, & Lin, 2000). These disparities are often attributed to logistical barriers such as lack of access to services or financial considerations (Kessler et al., 1997). Studies also point to lack of awareness of mental health problems, perceptions of treatments as ineffective, and a desire to deal with the problems without outside help (Frank & McGuire, 1986; Kessler et al., 2001) as other causes for treatment disparities. In essence, the cultural issues that contribute to mental health disparities among international populations most likely are the same or similar to those found with ethnic minority populations within the United States. Applying a systematic approach to identifying and addressing culture in psychotherapy can be equally applicable for international populations. For example, researchers from outside the United States or those who conduct research with non- US populations can use the CPA approach to culturally tailor ESTs from the United States by applying the norms and values of that host country. Using CBPR to develop community- driven cultural interventions can be one method of engaging people in services in countries or areas where psychotherapy is not commonly used, difficult to access, or viewed as ineffective. This especially applies to rural communities where stigma associated with mental illness may be particularly high (e.g., rural China, indigenous communities). 
The goal of eliminating racial/ ethnic disparities is challenging, but not unrealistic. As more researchers develop approaches that better integrate treatment process and outcome research with ethnic minorities, CBPR, and cross- cultural psychological research, substantial reductions in disparities in the quality of mental health care may occur. Essentially, this involves embracing diversity in all its cultural forms as it relates to mental illness and to psychological rehabilitation and recovery.

 Social Behavior 
 
16 
Control Orientations in the East and West 
Susumu Yamaguchi and Takafumi Sawaumi 
At fifteen, I set my heart on learning. . . . 
At seventy, I followed my heart’s desire without overstepping the line. 
— Confucius/ Lau, Analects, 1979, p. 63 
It is a Confucian ideal that individuals can naturally fit well with the environment. Confucianism views humans as integral parts of an orderly universe, with an innate moral sense to maintain harmony. According to this view, matured individuals such as Confucius can live a comfortable life without experiencing conflicts between their inner demands or wishes and the external world, thus representing the Asian value of maintaining harmony with the world. In North American culture, on the other hand, an individual’s autonomy, independence, and self- sufficiency have been valued to a greater extent than harmony with the environment (Sampson, 1977, 1988). In the North American value system, individuals attempt to acquire an ability to keep important societal and material resources under their control so they can verify and enjoy their autonomy, independence, and self- sufficiency. Thus, an ideal relationship between the self and the environment in North America would take a quite different form from that which Confucian philosophy would preach (Kim, 1994; Triandis, 1994). 
Specifically, here, we focus on the cultural values of autonomy and harmony, both of which are broadly defined in this chapter. Autonomy entails the capacity to behave according to one’s own will (Deci & Ryan, 2000). In addition, because individuals often need mastery over the social and physical environments for their autonomy, mastery is an essential part of autonomy. Thus, we include mastery when we refer to autonomy. Harmony refers to a harmonious relationship with the physical environment as well as with other people. To maintain harmony, individuals usually need to respect social order 
 
 
510 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and traditions and thus often conform to norms. In this sense, harmony is associated with social embeddedness. Thus, we include social embeddedness when we refer to harmony.1 The main purpose of this chapter is to understand how these differences in the core values of North America and Asia can affect the way that individuals adjust their relationship with the environment. Although individuals universally subscribe to autonomy and harmony (Schwartz, 2014), we argue that North Americans tend to behave in ways consistent with the value of autonomy, whereas Japanese and the other East Asians tend to behave in ways consistent with the value of harmony when those values come into conflict (see also Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith on cultural value dimensions). We will discuss how those cultural values affect individuals’ control orientation, which is defined as people’s tendency to choose specific kinds of control strategy over the environment and/ or themselves. 
More specifically, we will focus on how the two cultural values affect individuals’ choice regarding who acts as an agent of control and what becomes a target of control. As to the agent of control, it does not have to be the self. It can be another person or a collective of which one is a member. For example, suppose an individual needs to make her lazy business partner work harder for their project. There are three options in terms of the agency of control. First, she can directly press the partner to work harder. Second, she can ask their supervisor to press him to work harder. Third, she along with other members of the team can press him to work harder. We will argue that one’s choice of agent is affected by the two cultural values that we have introduced. 
The target of control is also affected by cultural values. Individuals’ target of control can be either themselves or the environment (Rothbaum, Weisz, & Snyder, 1982). Researchers have claimed that East Asians attempt to change themselves rather than the environment, whereas Westerners attempt to influence existing realities (e.g., Weisz, Rothbaum, & Blackburn, 1984). We will conceptually analyze Rothbaum and Weisz’s contentions and then review relevant literature, including our recent study, which presents a different picture from the one they propose. The conceptual framework will be expanded to better understand the relation between cultural values and control orientations. 
Before proceeding to the details of the cultural effects on individuals’ control orientations, we digress briefly to verify that East Asians actually subscribe to harmony with the environment to a greater extent than autonomy, whereas the reverse is true with Westerners. 
Harmony Versus Autonomy Not only do people in East Asia endorse harmony, but the maintenance of harmony also serves as an important guiding principle in their daily life, as in teaching, filial 
1. Indeed, autonomy and mastery are close to each other, as are harmony and embeddedness in the value mapping by Schwartz (2014).

piety, advertisements, discussions, and conflict resolutions. Shigaki (1983) found that the most important value among Japanese nursery school teachers is to foster harmonious relationships. Sung (1994) compared filial motivation among Korean and American caregivers of elderly relatives. For a Korean family, harmony was an important motivation for caregiving to elderly relatives, whereas it was not mentioned by Americans. Han and Shavitt (1994) analyzed advertisements in representative magazines in the United States and Korea. They found that magazine advertisements in the United States appealed to individual benefits and preferences, whereas in Korea the advertisements appealed to in- group benefits, harmony, and family integrity. They also demonstrated in a follow- up experiment that ads emphasizing family or in- group benefits were less persuasive in the United States than in Korea. Kim and Markus (1999) found the same cultural trends in the area of magazine ads. In their study, more interestingly, magazine ads in the United States were more likely to emphasize uniqueness whereas those in Korea tended to focus on conformity across four magazine categories (i.e., business, cultural, women’s, and youth). Prunty, Klopf, and Ishii (1990a, 1990b) found that Japanese university students were less argumentative, valued group harmony, and shunned controversy more than did their American counterparts. According to Trubisky, Ting- Toomey, and Lin (1991), Taiwanese students prefer to resolve a conflict within an in- group by obliging (e.g., going along with the suggestions of the group member), avoiding (e.g., staying away from disagreement with the group member), integrating (e.g., integrating ideas with the group member or coming up with a decision jointly), and compromising (e.g., trying to find a middle course to resolve an impasse) than do American students. Leung and Lind (1986) also showed that undergraduates in the United States preferred the adversarial procedure to the nonadversarial procedure in conflict resolution, whereas such difference was not found for Chinese undergraduates. Similarly, Ohbuchi, Fukushima, and Tedeschi (1999) asked American and Japanese college students to recall an experience of conflict (defined as “overt and covert opposition or disagreement with others”) and rate the episode on dimensions such as goal orientation, goal attainment, and tactics in their attempts at conflict resolution. Japanese students tended to avoid a confrontation with the other party, whereas American students tended to strongly assert their request. They found further that the most important goal for the Japanese students was to maintain a positive relationship with the other party, whereas restoration of fairness was the most important goal for the American students. In addition, Ohbuchi and Fukushima (1997) found that, among a Japanese university sample, relational goals in interpersonal conflict situations contributed to their employment of a conciliatory resolution strategy. Leung (1988) showed that Hong Kong Chinese tended to pursue a conflict less than did Americans when a potential disputant is an in- group member. Also, Leung (1987) demonstrated that Hong Kong adults tended to perceive that mediation and bargaining could reduce animosity between disputants and to prefer those procedures to a greater extent than American adults. Indeed, Kwan, Bond, and Singelis (1997) showed that relationship harmony is a more important determinant of college students’ self- esteem in Hong Kong than in the United States.

The foregoing brief review suggests that a core behavioral principle in East Asia is the maintenance of harmony rather than autonomy, whereas the opposite appears to be the case in North America. Now we are ready to discuss how control orientations are affected by those cultural values. 
Concept of Control Although control appears to be a very simple concept, there has never been a consensus among researchers regarding its definition (for a review, see Skinner, 1996). For example, it is defined cognitively by Thompson (1981) as “the belief that one has at one’s disposal a response that can influence the aversiveness of an event” (p.  89), whereas Skinner, Chapman, and Baltes (1988) defined control as the extent to which an agent can produce desired outcomes (p. 118). As Skinner (1996) concluded after a comprehensive review of the control- related constructs, the prototype of control is personal control, in which the agent of control is the self. Apparently most researchers in this area imply “personal control” when they simply refer to “control.” However, because the agent of control is not limited to the self, we mean “causing an intended event” (Weisz et al., 1984, p. 958) when we refer to control in this chapter. This definition is applicable to an agent other than the self as well. 
Agent of Control An agent of control, in the present context, refers to a person or a collective who can cause a particular outcome. As such, the agent can be the self, powerful other(s), or a collective, such as a group or an organization. We will discuss how considerations of autonomy and harmony would affect one’s choice of the agent. 
Personal Control People who value autonomy are assumed to prefer personal control, in which the self acts as an agent. Individuals would especially feel themselves more self- efficacious when their agency is made explicit and thus feel their autonomy to a greater extent than otherwise. We will refer to this type of control as direct personal control, as contrasted with indirect personal control, in which one’s agency is hidden or played down (Table 16.1). 
Direct personal control. Previous theoretical and empirical research in North America has emphasized the importance of self- efficacy, which can be attained by successful direct personal control and serve as the basis for one’s sense of autonomy. White (1959) argued that people have an effectance motivation, which is satisfied by the production of effective changes in the environment. His theory posits that individuals attempt to be agentic toward the environment, and, when they are successful as an agent, they can feel satisfaction, a process which is called a feeling of efficacy. Bandura (1977) advanced this line of thought and argued that expectation of self- efficacy affects one’s coping behavior. 
 
 
 
 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  513 
If one has confidence in his or her self- efficacy, he or she will initiate and persist in coping behavior and consequently attain autonomy. More generally, one’s beliefs in self- efficacy, which is defined as “people’s beliefs about their capabilities to exercise control over events that affect their lives” (Bandura, 1989, p. 1175), determines subsequent motivation, affect, and action (Bandura, 1989). In the cognitive domain, beliefs in self- efficacy lead one to set a higher goal and commit oneself to the attainment of that goal (e.g., Wood & Bandura, 1989). Motivationally, the belief in self- efficacy leads one to put more effort into one’s enterprise (e.g., Bandura & Cervone, 1983), whereas in terms of emotion those with high belief in self- efficacy feel less anxiety in a stressful situation (e.g., Averill, 1973). Furthermore, Langer and Rodin (1976; Rodin & Langer, 1977) demonstrated that a feeling of control can contribute even to longevity. In their field study at a nursing home, mortality was found to be lower among aged residents who had been given the freedom to make choices and the responsibility of taking care of a plant, relative to those who had not been given such choices and responsibility. 
Not only do people bolster beliefs in their ability to control in response to successful control of an event, but they can, in some circumstances, hold an unwarranted belief that they can control chance events. Langer (1975) showed that people perceive an illusion of control over chance events, which are uncontrollable by definition. In one of her experiments, adult male and female office workers were asked if they wished to purchase a lottery ticket costing $1, by which the winner could earn $50. After having agreed to enter the lottery, participants in the choice condition were allowed to select the ticket that they wanted, whereas the other participants in the no- choice condition were not given such a choice. On the morning of lottery drawing, the participants were asked if they would like to sell their ticket to someone who wanted to get into the lottery. The mean price the participants named was $8.67 in the choice condition and only $1.96 in the no- choice condition. This result indicates that participants in the choice condition had an illusion of control that they could choose the winning lottery ticket. 
Given the compelling theoretical reasons and overwhelming empirical evidence indicating the prevalence of direct personal control attempts, there remains little room for questioning a strong orientation among Westerners toward direct personal control of

the environment. Indeed, as noted earlier, personal control of one’s physical and social environment is thought to be a prototype of control (Skinner, 1996). When it comes to East Asians, however, the story becomes more complicated due to the importance of interpersonal harmony. 
Indirect personal control. Direct personal control attempts often cause interpersonal confrontations that East Asians attempt to avoid (Ohbuchi et al., 1999; Trubisky et al., 1991). For this reason, people who value interpersonal harmony would prefer indirect personal control to direct personal control when direct personal control of the environ-ment is undesirable but there is still a need or wish to control the environment. In indirect personal control, individuals hide or play down their agency by pretending that they are not acting as an agent while they are actually doing so. Kojima (1984) provided an excellent example of this kind of control attempt: 
Suppose that a rakugo (comic story) master is annoyed by his disciple, who is singing a song too loudly. Instead of issuing a direct reprimand to stop it, he says, “How well you sing a song!” For a moment, the disciple is proud, taking his master’s statement at its face value, but soon he becomes aware of the true meaning of the message. (p. 972) 
In this episode, the rakugo master pretended that he was not acting as an agent, al-though he actually attempted to stop his disciple from singing. He hid his real intention and praised how well his disciple was singing. The rakugo master’s indirect attempt to stop his disciple from singing has the merit of maintaining their close relationship by letting him become aware of his master’s displeasure by himself. The disciple was not forced to stop his singing and thus could maintain his face. 
The prevalence of such attempts at indirect control can be seen in explicit self- evaluations among Japanese. Because of a modesty norm in Japanese culture, Japanese people hesitate to show their positive self- evaluation explicitly, although their positive self- evaluations are revealed by the Implicit Association Test (Yamaguchi et al., 2007). Thus, for example, Japanese attempt to indirectly enhance self- evaluation by group- serving attributions rather than self- serving attributions (Muramoto & Yamaguchi, 1997). In the previous research, it is well known that people make self- serving attributions, in which they attribute success to their ability and attribute failure to an external cause such as luck or task difficulty (Bradley, 1978; Miller & Ross, 1975), in order to attain positive self- evaluation. Muramoto and Yamaguchi found that Japanese make self- effacing attributions about their own performance, whereas they make group- enhancing attributions about their group performance. This result indicates that Japanese do not always make self- effacing attributions. Rather, the result can be interpreted as an attempt to indirectly raise their self- evaluation by praising their in- group while maintaining harmonious relationships with others through self- effacing attribution. As the social identity theory (Tajfel, 1982) posits, evaluation of one’s in- group affects one’s social identity, 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  515 
which is defined as “that part of an individual’s self- concept which derives from his knowledge of his membership of a social group (or groups) together with the value and emotional significance attached to that membership” (p. 255). Because one’s social identity is equivalent to one’s self- conception as a group member (Abrams & Hogg, 1990), one can enhance one’s self- evaluation by favorable evaluations on one’s in- group. In this way, individuals can raise their self- evaluation without disrupting group harmony. Consistent with this interpretation, Muramoto and Yamaguchi have found that Japanese participants tend to evaluate their personal contribution to group success as equal to or greater than that of the average group member, although they may not express this self- evaluation to their in- group members. This finding suggests that Japanese attempt to enhance self- esteem, albeit indirectly. This result also indicates that Japanese pretend that they are not acting as an agent, although in actuality they are acting agentically to enhance their self- esteem. Such pretension is necessary in Japan because the cost of direct personal control of self- evaluation is high. Sawaumi and Yamaguchi (2013) have revealed that Japanese hold negative impressions about those who exert direct personal control (i.e., uncompanionable and imprudent). When it comes to group performance, one’s agency is diluted among in- group members; thus attribution of group success is less agentic than attribution of personal performance. Muramoto and Yamaguchi’s findings indicate that Japanese do strive for higher self- evaluation but through another route in which one’s agency is played down and thus disruption of interpersonal harmony is less likely. It is quite conceivable that, in Japanese culture, one’s need for higher self- evaluation is masked by an even stronger need for maintenance of harmony and is fulfilled indirectly through other means such as group enhancement rather than self- enhancement. 
Self- effacing attribution for one’s performance is not limited to Japanese. Researchers have maintained that humility is a norm in Chinese societies as well (for a review, see Leung, 1996). Farh, Dobbins, and Cheng (1991) have found, in line with Muramoto and Yamaguchi (1997), that Chinese employees in Taiwan rated their job performance less favorably than their supervisors did, even when the self- ratings were revealed only to researchers. In addition, Wan and Bond (1982) found that such self- effacing tendencies among Chinese disappeared in a public situation as far as luck is concerned, suggesting that the self- effacing attribution is related to impression management. 
This empirical evidence suggests that, despite recent arguments by Heine and his colleagues for lower self- concept among Japanese relative to North Americans (Heine, Lehman, Markus, & Kitayama, 1999; Heine, Takata, & Lehman, 2000), expressed low self- concept among Japanese and Chinese needs to be taken with reservations. They may be just following the modesty norm prevalent in their societies and attempting to heighten their self- evaluation indirectly by showing that they are competent enough to understand and follow the cultural norm. Indeed, more recent studies have demonstrated that Japanese people show self- enhancement in a different way (e.g., Sedikides, Gaertner, & Toguchi, 2003)  (see also Chapter 17 by Amir Rosenmann and Jenny Kurman on self- effacement and self- enhancement).
516 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
The previous research suggests that, as a whole, those who value interpersonal harmony would tend to choose indirect personal control in the fear that direct personal control attempts may cause interpersonal confrontations. For those who value autonomy, on the other hand, indirect personal control would not be an attractive choice because it is not conducive to their sense of autonomy even when it is implemented successfully. It will become their choice, however, when direct personal control is unavailable. Lopez and Little (1996) reported that US military- dependent children in Germany tended to use indirect coping strategies (i.e., indirect control attempts) when they are faced with uncontrollable events. 
Proxy Control When exercise of personal control is neither readily available nor encouraged, one might well relinquish direct control attempts and seek “security in proxy control” (Bandura, 1982, p. 142). Proxy control means control by someone else for the benefit of the person (Table 16.1). 
For example, in third- party interventions, intermediaries are called in to regulate interpersonal relationships between parties with potential or actual conflict of interests. With the help of those intermediaries, people can gain desired outcomes without acting agentically. In this sense, they are thought to use proxy control in third- party interventions. As the foregoing analysis on East Asian’s reluctance to use direct personal control suggests, third- party interventions would be preferred to a greater extent in East Asia than in the West. Indeed, according to Bian and Ang’s (1997) survey of 1,008 Chinese workers and 512 Singaporean workers, intermediaries play an important role when a worker changes his or her job, bridging the job changers and their new employer in both countries. 
Proxy control is essential to the survival of those who are in a weaker position and thus unable to change their environment to their liking by themselves. Because they don’t have enough skills, knowledge, and power to bring about their desired outcomes or avoid undesired outcomes in the environment, they cannot afford a means to control their environment other than proxy control. Thus, it would be of paramount importance for those in a weaker position, such as children and subordinates in an organization, to develop an ability to locate powerful others who can be induced to act for their benefit. For example, parents are powerful persons who can bring about desired outcomes for children. Thus, a child would ask his or her parents to buy him or her an expensive toy. Likewise, a subordinate may ask his or her boss to negotiate with the CEO of the company for his or her promotion. In those situations, people who seek for proxy control are unable to exercise their direct personal control. The child cannot afford to buy an expensive toy by herself, and the subordinate cannot negotiate directly with the CEO regarding his promotion. Thus, these individuals need to use proxy control if they wish to bring about a desired outcome in their environment. 
Prevalence of proxy control in Asian contexts is reflected in a Japanese indigenous concept, Amae, which has been suggested by a Japanese psychoanalyst, Doi (1972), to be a 
 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  517 
key concept to understand Japanese mentality. In everyday use, Amae involves a person’s behavior that is not necessarily acceptable (Taketomo, 1986). More precisely, individuals can presume that their inappropriate behavior would be acceptable if they are in a close relationship with a counterpart. This presumption is called Amae among the Japanese (Yamaguchi, 1999). For example, the child may expect his or her parents to buy an expensive toy because the parents love the child. The subordinate who wishes to be promoted may expect his superior to accept the request because they have been in a friendly relationship, even if the subordinate is not qualified for promotion. In those examples, the requests are normally perceived as inappropriate by the counterparts. Nevertheless, the requesters or solicitors are attempting to get what they desire through a powerful other, such as parents, spouse, or superordinate, because the counterparts are in a close relation-ship with them. It is important to note here that Amae typically involves a close relation-ship, such as a child– parent, husband– wife, or a close friend type of relationship. In close relationships, even inappropriate behaviors are often accepted, albeit within some limits. Thus, Amae among Japanese can be considered as an attempt at proxy control, in which a benefactor accepts an inappropriate behavior or request that would barely be acceptable in other relationships (for a more detailed discussion, see Yamaguchi, 2004; Yamaguchi & Ariizumi, 2006). 
Obviously, Amae or other types of proxy control will not foster a sense of self- efficacy in attaining the goal of control. Individuals in a proxy control situation have to relinquish their direct control over the environment and also forgo an opportunity to acquire requisite skills (Bandura, 1982). A resulting low self- efficacy may well “foster dependence on proxy control, which further reduces opportunities to build the skills needed for efficacious action” (Bandura, 1997, p. 17). Thus, as far as one subscribes to the value of autonomy, proxy control is definitely undesirable because of its deteriorating effect on one’s autonomy. However, if one gives priority to maintenance of harmony, a bright side of proxy control, including Amae, will emerge: proxy control can have a beneficial effect on interpersonal relationships. If the benefactor successfully handles the situation for the requester’s benefit, it will foster a feeling of trust in the requesters. The benefactor will also feel that he or she is valued and trusted by the requester because the requester relinquished control and asked the benefactor for a favor. Even in terms of self- efficacy, proxy control may not necessarily be detrimental. It can foster a feeling of self- efficacy in managing interpersonal relationships because proxy control entails social skills to locate a powerful other and induce the person to work on behalf of the requester. In this sense, proxy control should be distinguished from a mere relinquishment of control. It can be conceived as a control attempt in which the real agent (i.e., self) is hidden. In proxy control, individuals know what they want and they often use well- developed social skills to induce a potential benefactor to work on their behalf. For this reason, the situation is typically under the requester’s control rather than the benefactor’s. By using proxy control, individuals may get even what they normally cannot afford when they attempt personal control, as in the case of Amae.
518 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Indeed, Kim and Yamaguchi (1999) have found that Japanese understand the double- edged- sword nature of Amae: a detrimental effect on autonomy and a facilitative effect on interpersonal relationship. We asked more than 1,000 Japanese, including junior high, senior high, and college students, as well as adults, to answer questions about Amae in an open- ended questionnaire. The results indicated, as expected, that Japanese acknowl-edge both positive and negative aspects of Amae and consequently have an ambivalent attitude toward it. Japanese respondents associated positive feelings with Amae, such as like/ love, acceptance, or trust, as well as negative feelings such as dependent, unpleasant, selfish, or childish. The respondents also answered that, in allowing Amae, there are posi-tive aspects such as a closer relationship and reciprocal benefit, as well as negative aspects such as immaturity and trouble for the provider of benefit. The Japanese respondents ac-cepted Amae only in certain situations. As Taketomo (1986) maintained, Amae would be welcome and accepted only when both interactants agree. That is, acceptability of Amae would depend on the closeness of the interpersonal relationship and the context in which Amae is made. Amae appears to be a useful way to control individuals’ physical and social environments, at least in Japan. Successfully implemented, Amae will enable powerless individuals to change their environment to their liking while maintaining interpersonal harmony. 
Collective Control In addition to indirect personal control and proxy control, there is another type of con-trol that does not come into conflict with interpersonal harmony. In collective control, one attempts to control the environment as a member of a group or collective, which serves as an agent of control. Thus, members do not have to worry about maintenance of interpersonal harmony among in- group members because they share the goal of control (Table 16.1). 
In East Asia, the unit of survival has been a group or collective rather than isolated individuals or nuclear families (Triandis, 1994). As the unit of survival, groups or collectives may well be autonomous agents. Indeed, Menon, Morris, Chiu, and Hong (1999) argue that East Asians perceive collectives as autonomous. They demonstrated, consistent with their argument, that East Asians tend to more readily attribute the cause of various events to group properties rather than personal properties. Chinese in Hong Kong attributed the cause of organizational scandals to group properties rather than individual properties, whereas their American counterparts showed the opposite tendencies. 
In collective control, responsibility as well as agency will be diffused among actors (Latané & Darley, 1970). If everyone in a collective is responsible for the outcome to the same extent, no one will have to take personal responsibility for a negative outcome. Although no one can claim responsibility for a positive outcome either, this is exactly what East Asians prefer. Muramoto and Yamaguchi (1997) showed that Japanese prefer to attribute success to their group members, indicating that Japanese do not claim personal responsibility for their successful performance in a group. People can maintain harmony 
 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  519 
among in- group members by sharing responsibilities for the outcome regardless of its valence. 
Not only are groups perceived as agents, but East Asians also have a belief that they are more efficacious as a collective rather than as a person (Earley, 1989, 1993). Earley (1989) asked managerial trainees from the United States and the People’s Republic of China to work on an additive task (Steiner, 1972), such as writing memos and prioritizing client interviews. He predicted and found that social loafing (i.e., reduced effort in a collective task as compared with individualized task) appeared among individualistic Americans as shown by Latané, Williams, and Harkins (1979), whereas it did not appear among collectivistic Chinese. It was also found that the Chinese participants worked harder in a group than when working alone, especially in high shared- responsibility settings in which the participants were given a specified group goal. He interpreted the results as indicating that Chinese give priority to group goals and collective action rather than to their self- interests, whereas the opposite is the case with Americans. Earley (1993) advanced this line of interpretation and further demonstrated that nonoccurrence of social loafing among Chinese is related to an individual’s perceived group efficacy, which is defined as a person’s expectation about a group’s capability. In this experiment, managers from the United States and China were asked to perform simulated managerial activities, as in Earley (1989), under one of three conditions of group membership: alone, in- group, or out- group. In the in- group and out- group conditions, the participants were led to believe that they were working either with in- group members or out- group members, as the case may be. For the Chinese participants, performance was significantly higher in the in- group condition than in the out- group or alone condition, whereas for the American participants, performance was significantly higher in the alone condition than in the other two conditions. Corresponding to the result on performance, the Chinese participants perceived group efficacy in the in- group condition was higher than that of the American participants. Hence, the results suggest that the Chinese participants worked harder in the in- group condition because they have a belief in in- group efficacy. In a similar vein, Iyengar and Lepper (1999) showed that Anglo Americans worked harder on a task of their own choice than on a task that was ostensibly chosen by others, whereas Asian Americans put more effort into a task that was ostensibly chosen by their in- group members than on one they chose for themselves. 
Such beliefs in collective efficacy may well lead people to create an illusion of collective control among them. Yamaguchi (1998) hypothesized that Japanese would tend to estimate risk unjustifiably lower in a collective setting than when they are alone. In the first experiment, Japanese female participants were asked to estimate a risk level in fictitious situations described in a vignette, with a varied number of risk companions who are exposed to the same risk source. For example, the participants were asked to estimate the probability of getting cancer assuming that they were drinking water contaminated with carcinogens either alone, with a small number, or with a large number of risk companions. There is absolutely no normative ground to expect that the number of risk companions 
520 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
affects the probability that one gets cancer. Nevertheless, the participants estimated that the risk level would be lower with more risk companions. In the second study, the finding was successfully replicated in a laboratory setting in which participants were exposed to a real risk of electric shocks. This group- diffusion effect of risk perception has been replicated in Hong Kong using essentially the same vignettes (Amy & Leung, 1998). 
Yamaguchi, Gelfand, Ohashi, and Zemba (2005) examined more directly if Japanese overestimate their collective efficacy and Americans, especially males, overestimate self- efficacy. Japanese were predicted to hold a belief that their collective control is more efficacious than their personal control, whereas Americans, especially males, would hold the opposite belief that their personal control is more efficacious than their collective control. In the experiment, participants were told that the experiment was concerned with the effect of an unpleasant experience on the subsequent task performance. Ostensibly for this purpose, the participants were told that they would be assigned either to a control condition or an unpleasant experience condition depending on the result of lottery drawings. It was explained that they would be asked to take a bitter drink in the unpleasant experience condition, whereas they would not have to take the drink in the control condition. Actually, there were two conditions: alone and group conditions. In the alone condition, each participant was asked to draw four lottery tickets, each carrying a one- digit number. In the group condition, on the other hand, the participant was told that he or she was a member of a four- person group, with the other three participants in other rooms. An experimenter explained that each of the four members of the group would draw one lottery ticket. It was explained both in the alone and group conditions that the participant’s assignment to the conditions would be determined by the sum of the four numbers on the four lottery tickets. That is, the experimental situation was controlled so that both in the alone and group conditions the chance of getting into the unpleasant condition was the same. The participants in the alone condition drew four tickets alone, whereas the participants in the group condition were led to believe that each of the four group members would draw one lottery ticket. As in Yamaguchi (1998), there was no normative ground for the participants to believe that the sum of the four digits would be affected by who drew the lottery tickets. The dependent variable was the participant’s estimate of the likelihood that they would eventually be assigned to the unpleasant condition and have to take a bitter drink. The results indicated, as predicted, that the Japanese participants in the group condition estimated their likelihood of being assigned to the unpleasant condition lower than those in the alone condition, whereas the reverse tendency was the case with American male participants. The American female participants showed the same tendency as their Japanese counterparts: they overestimated their collective efficacy relative to their self- efficacy. Although the result for the American females may appear perplexing, it can be explained in terms of the values that American females subscribe to. Gilligan (1993) argued that females in the United States value interpersonal relatedness to a greater extent than do males, and they are less psychologically separated from others as compared with American males. Consistent with Gilligan’s (1993) argument, 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  521 
Beutel and Marini (1995) reported that, among US high school seniors between 1977 and 1991, female respondents were more likely than male respondents to express concern and responsibility for the well- being of others and less likely than male respondents to accept materialism and competition. It is conceivable, therefore, that females in the United States are more like East Asians in the sense that they value maintenance of interpersonal relationships and care for others. Such orientations may well lead American females to foster general beliefs in collective efficacy. 
Developmentally, a sense of self- efficacy is fostered in one’s socialization process (Bandura, 1989, 1997). When a baby is born, the baby does not have any sense of self- efficacy. Infants gradually develop a sense of self- efficacy based on the contingency between their behavior and its outcome. Because the contingency between behavior and its outcome is often influenced by parents, teachers, or other powerful adults, one’s sense of self- efficacy is thought to be influenced by the cultural milieu in which one is raised. If the contingency between infants’ behavior and outcome is constructed or emphasized, as in the United States, they will grow up with a high sense of self- efficacy. On the other hand, if adults stress and construct a contingency between collective behavior and outcome, children will develop a relatively stronger sense of collective efficacy (i.e., that collectives are more efficacious in influencing the environment). Once established, this sense of collective efficacy functions as a self- fulfilling prophecy. Thus, Chinese tend to believe in collective efficacy and put more effort in collective settings than when alone (Earley, 1993), which makes the collective more efficacious than the individual (see also Chapter  7 by Harry W.  Gardiner and Chapter  8 by Heidi Keller on culture and development). 
In sum, it appears quite reasonable for East Asians to prefer collective control over personal control for at least three reasons. First, in collective control, individuals are not perceived as agents and thus they can avoid interpersonal conflicts. Second, they hold a self- fulfilling belief that a collective effort is more efficacious than the effort of the individual. Third, collective control can facilitate interpersonal harmony with in- group members because their personal goals are compatible with the group goals. Like indirect personal control, it would be safer in terms of interpersonal harmony that people exercise collective control indirectly (indirect collective control). 
As to the agency of control, we proposed four possibilities in addition to direct personal control (i.e., indirect personal, direct collective, indirect collective, and proxy), which has been claimed to be important in Western cultural milieus. As summarized in Figure 16.1, emphasis on the maintenance of interpersonal harmony would lead individuals to adopt the lower route through indirect personal control, proxy control, and collective control strategies. On the other hand, emphasis on autonomy would encourage one to adopt the upper route through direct personal control strategies. Previous research and present discussions suggest that the upper route is more prevalent among people who value autonomy, whereas the lower route is preferred among people who tend to value interpersonal harmony more than individual autonomy.

Target of Control Individuals in any culture need to adjust their relationship with the physical and social environment for their physiological and psychological well- being. In doing so, individuals attempt to change either the physical and social environment or themselves. Rothbaum et al. (1982) and Weisz et al. (1984) proposed an important distinction be-tween two kinds of control attempts: primary control and secondary control. In primary control, the target of control is existing external realities in one’s physical and social environment. Individuals attempt to “enhance their rewards by influencing existing realities (e.g., other people, circumstances, symptoms, or behavior problems)” by means of “personal agency, dominance, or even aggression” (Weisz et al., p. 955). In secondary control, on the other hand, the target of control is oneself. Individuals attempt to “enhance their rewards by accommodating to existing realities and maximizing satisfaction or goodness of fit with things as they are without changing the existing realities” (Weisz et al., p. 955). By extending the meaning of control to include secondary control, the authors made a seminal contribution to the advancement of conceptual and empirical research in this area. Specifically, in the present context, they applied the distinction to cultural differences in control orientations. Weisz et al. argued that primary control plays an important role in everyday life in the United States, whereas secondary control does so in Japan, corresponding to differences in cultural values of autonomy and harmony. 
Available empirical evidence, however, shows a more complicated picture than Weisz et al. (1984) initially assumed. In the following sections, we will elaborate the meaning of the two kinds of control and clarify etic and emic of control orientations. Individuals need to control their environments for their survival, which would lead to the universal preference for primary control. On the other hand, when affordable choices are available, individuals behave consistently with the cultural values they subscribe to.

Primary Control According to Rothbaum et al. (1982), both primary and secondary control include four types of control: predictive, vicarious, illusory, and interpretive (Table 16.2). In predictive primary control, individuals attempt to predict events so that they will succeed at them. An example of this type of control would be to predict the next move that one’s opponent will make in a chess game. By predicting the opponent’s move correctly, one will have a better chance to beat the opponent. Vicarious primary control is equivalent to proxy control in that it includes an attempt to manipulate powerful others. In illusory primary control, individuals attempt to control an uncontrollable event like a chance- determined event. The superstitious behaviors of gamblers would be included in this category. A gambler may continue to wear a dirty hat that he or she wore 10 years ago at the time of a big winning bet believing that the hat brings good fortune. Last, interpretive primary control refers to attempts at understanding problems to solve or master them. 
In discussing primary control, it needs to be noted that proxy control, or vicarious primary control in Rothbaum et  al.’s (1982) terminology, is included in their original classification of primary control attempts. Proxy control is unique in that the agent is a powerful other rather than oneself. Because proxy control is detrimental to the development of skills required for personal control and thus would neither be valued nor preferred in the United States (Bandura, 1997), Weisz et al.’s (1984) argument that primary control is more prevalent in the United States than in Japan appears logically untenable. Indeed, available empirical evidence indicates that Weisz et al.’s suggestions face a serious problem when examined empirically. Seginer, Trommsdorff, and Essau (1993) compared control beliefs of Malaysian students with those of North American and German students using their scale of primary and secondary control. Their Malaysian sample consisted mostly of Iban and Malay students whose religions emphasize the importance of harmonious interpersonal relationships. Thus, their Malaysian participants are thought to endorse the value of harmonious relationships. However, their result did not provide support for Weisz et al.’s suggestion. In terms of total primary control beliefs, contrary to the researchers’ expectation, Malaysians scored higher than Germans and no difference was found between Malaysians and North Americans. Furthermore, it was found that the Malaysian students scored higher than both the North American and German students on the vicarious primary control (i.e., proxy control) dimension. This result indicates,

Strategy Example 
Predictive Predict one’s opponent’s move to win a game 
Vicarious (proxy) Manipulate a powerful other to obtain something 
Illusory Behave superstitiously 
Interpretive Understand a problem to solve it 
 
524 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
as the foregoing discussion suggests, that Malaysians tend to control the environment through someone else (proxy control) rather than directly. 
In one of Weisz’s empirical studies, McCarty et al. (1999) compared stress coping strategies of 6- to 14- year- olds in Thailand and the United States. Because the Thai child is taught from an early age not to “disturb their personal equilibrium by expressing one’s own feelings or wishes overtly” (p. 810), the results from Thai children are thought to be suggestive of East Asians’ coping strategies. Regarding primary control, they found no difference between children in the two cultures. One important difference, again, was that Thai children reported more than twice as much covert (i.e., indirect) coping as their American counterparts. This result indicates that Thai children exert indirect personal control rather than giving up their influence on realities, just as Japanese students enhance self- evaluation indirectly (Muramoto & Yamaguchi, 1999). Such results led McCarty et al. to conclude: 
Thai youngsters were more likely than Americans to use covert coping methods when interacting with adults, but they were not more likely than Americans, in these situations, to adopt secondary control goals or to relinquish control. In other words, it would not be correct to assume that the deferent, subtle, indirect forms of coping employed by Thai youth in these situations imply a lack of investment in exerting influence or causing events to turn out as they wish. A more accurate view may be that Thai youth were following the social norms of appropriate outward behavior towards adults while maintaining goals that involved just as much primary control as those of American youth. (p. 816) 
On the other hand, Nakamura and Flammer (1998) compared control orientations of Swiss and Japanese students. When it comes to active problem- solving strategies, which can be classified as interpretive primary control, Swiss students tended to adopt them more than did their Japanese counterparts. This result indicates that, in a specific primary control strategy such as interpretive primary control, Japanese are less inclined to use primary control relative to Westerners. 
Overall, previous empirical research is scarce and has not demonstrated that Japanese or East Asians are motivated to use primary control in general to a lesser extent relative to Americans or Westerners. Although undoubtedly cultural milieus affect individuals’ choice of control strategies, we should not ignore the fact that individuals in any culture need to pursue control over the environment for their subsistence. Hence, it is not surprising that the concept of primary control cannot appropriately differentiate control orientations in the East and West. 
We will discuss how the primary- secondary control distinction matches differences in cultural values after reviewing research relevant to secondary control.

Secondary Control The second component of Weisz et  al.’s (1984) arguments was that secondary control would be more prevalent in East Asian cultures relative to American culture. To appropriately examine the validity of this hypothesis, it is again essential that we take a closer look at the nature of secondary control. Weisz et al. suggested four kinds of secondary control, as he did for primary control (Table 16.3). 
Predictive secondary control refers to accurately predicting events and conditions so that one can control their psychological impact on the self. For example, one may attempt to know how a dentist will treat his or her decayed tooth before visiting the dentist so he or she can reduce the negative impact of the treatment. In this case, the target of control is fear or other negative feelings that may accompany a dental treatment. Generally, the target of predictive secondary control is the psychological impact of external events. In vicarious secondary control, on the other hand, individuals attempt to gain a feeling of self- efficacy by aligning with powerful others or groups that can accomplish things that the individuals cannot afford. In this type of control, the target is one’s feeling of self- efficacy. Cialdini et al. (1976) provided a good example of this type of control. He demonstrated that college students tend to show their associations with successful others. In one of his experiments, college students were found to wear school- identifying apparel after a victory of their school’s football team. By basking in reflected glory, these college students could foster a sense of self- efficacy, albeit illusory. This type of control can be considered proxy control of internal states; in this case, a feeling of self- efficacy. As to illusory secondary control, Rothbaum et al.’s (1982) and Weisz et al.’s (1984) definitions are not consistent. In Rothbaum et al., this type of control was defined as a person’s attempt to “align themselves with the force of chance so that they may share in the control exerted by that powerful force” (pp. 16– 17). According to this definition, the control target was once again one’s sense of self- efficacy, as in vicarious secondary control. On the other hand, illusory secondary control was defined by Weisz et al. as an individual’s “attempts to associate or get into synchrony with chance so as to enhance comfort with and acceptance of one’s fate” (p. 957). According to this new definition, the target of control is one’s feelings associated with acceptance of one’s own fate. For example, a dying cancer patient may accept his or her fate and stop fighting against it. By doing so, the patient will be able

Strategy Target 
Predictive Psychological impact of external events 
Vicarious (proxy) One’s feeling of self- efficacy 
Illusory One’s feeling of self- efficacy (Rothbaum et al., 1982) One’s feelings associated with acceptance of fate (Weisz et al., 1984) 
Interpretive Psychological impact of one’s experience 
 
526 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
to control emotions such as fear of death and restore his or her peace of mind. If illusory secondary control refers to this type of coping, it would be more appropriately termed accommodative secondary control because it does not involve any illusion about control, and the most likely goal of control is to restore one’s peace of mind. Finally, in interpretive secondary control, individuals attempt to derive a meaning or purpose from existing realities and thereby enhance their satisfaction with those realities. An extreme case of such control is the attempt by Kaisen, a Japanese Zen priest of the medieval period. When he was executed by fire, he reportedly uttered, “If you train your mind to disregard agony, you will find even fire cool.” In more ordinary life, when we make a mistake or fail at something, we attempt to derive a meaning from the mistake or failure and justify it. For example, a student who failed a final exam may think, “It is all right that I did not get credit for the course. I have learned a lot in the class anyway.” Thus, in interpretive secondary control, the target of control is the psychological impact of one’s experience. 
The extant empirical evidence on cultural differences in secondary control is again scarce, and the results are mixed. Seginer et al. (1993) found that secondary control beliefs are stronger among Malaysian adolescents than German or North American adolescents. In Nakamura and Flammer’s (1998) comparison between problem- solving strategies by Swiss and Japanese students, reinterpretation strategies, which can be classified as interpretive secondary control, were found more often among Japanese students than Swiss students. However, McCarty et al. (1999) did not find any consistent secondary control attempts among Thai youths compared to American youths. 
In an attempt to directly compare control orientations among Americans and Japanese, Morling (2000) asked questions of participants in aerobics classes in Japan and the United States. Being asked what they would do in a class when the moves get too difficult, both Japanese and American participants answered that they were most likely to try harder to keep up with the instructor. Because this response is operationalized by the author as a secondary control attempt, the result indicates that secondary control was dominant in the aerobics classes in both cultures. The second most reported response, however, was more frequently primary control (i.e., to change the move to something they like) among Americans than Japanese. 
In all, the previous research on cultural differences in secondary control strategies provides mixed results and thus does not allow us to draw any conclusions. Perhaps the conceptual ambiguity of secondary control and resulting diversity in its operationalization are responsible for the mixed results. Because the specific target in the four types of secondary control is diverse (see Table 16.3), we need to examine which cognitive or emotional component of the self individuals would wish to control in each culture. In response to such situation, Morling and Evered (2006) pointed out that secondary control has dual purposes: adjustment of the self to the existing realities and acceptance of the realities. However, Kurman, Hui, and Dan (2012) proposes a new control type that is a hybrid of primary and secondary control. In that control strategy, the control agent first aims at self- improvement (i.e., secondary control) in order to heighten her potential 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  527 
to make changes to the environment (i.e., primary control) in the future. This control strategy indicates that secondary control can be used as a means to exert primary control. 
According to Morling and Evered (2006), Heckhausen and Schulz (1995) and Weisz et al. (1984) have focused on different roles of secondary control: control- focus and fit- focus, respectively. However, Skinner (2007) maintains that fit- focused secondary control should be classified as another related but different concept, such as accommodation, and thus should not be treated in control research (see also Morling & Evered, 2007, for their rebuttal). 
In all, although Weisz et  al.’s (1984) distinction between primary and secondary control is conceptually clear, this dichotomy does not match cultural differences in control orientations. As we have seen, their claim that “primary control is more valued and prevalent in the US, whereas in Japan secondary control has been more central in everyday life” (p. 955) cannot be sustained conceptually nor empirically. It is not primary control per se that is valued in the United States. Nor is it secondary control per se that is valued in Japan particularly or in East Asia in general. We should not confuse primary and secondary control with cultural values. 
Indeed, more recently, Sawaumi, Yamaguchi, Park, and Robinson (2015) demonstrated that Japanese prefer primary control to secondary control just as do Westerners. In this study, the Japanese participant was presented with a description of six fictitious situations and asked how he or she would solve a conflict. For example, a protagonist needed to ask an important job partner to work harder for their project. The participants preferred to exert primary control more than secondary control. In addition, direct personal control was most preferred among primary control strategies. Contrary to what is expected from Weisz et al. (1984), this study shows Japanese preference to direct personal control over secondary control. This finding has an important implication for a debate regarding the primacy of primary control or secondary control. 
Primacy of Primary Control or Secondary Control There have been debates on the primacy of primary control over secondary control (Heckhausen & Schulz, 1995, 1999; Gould, 1999). Heckhausen and Schulz (1995) argued in their theory of lifetime development that primary control has functional primacy over secondary control. Because the target of primary control is one’s environment, they maintained that “it enables individuals to shape their environment to fit their particular needs and developmental potential” (p. 286). On the other hand, they argued, the adaptive value of secondary control is limited to its compensatory function. For example, when people experience a threat to self- esteem or self- efficacy due to failed or unavailable primary control, secondary control is assumed to ameliorate the negativity of this threat and “preserves and rekindles the individual’s motivational resources for maintaining and enhancing primary control in the future” (p. 286). According to their view, “the primacy of primary control is invariant across cultures and historical time” (p.  286), which is supported by Sawaumi et al. (2015). 
 
528 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
 Gould (1999) criticizes Heckhausen and Schulz (1995), arguing that they constructed their theory “largely in biologically driven terms” (p.  600) and ignored cultural perspectives. Obviously, control over the environment is essential for human survival. Hence, one can legitimately advance an argument that primary control is indispensable for human existence. It does not follow, however, that direct primary control is more adaptive than secondary control in any cultures or in any situations. 
The debates between Heckhausen and Schulz (1995) and Gould (1999) suggest that both primary and secondary control can be adaptive depending on the situation. It is obvious that primary control provides the most straightforward way to heighten one’s psychological well- being if it does not disrupt harmony. On the other hand, there can be situations in which people can be rewarded by taking secondary control. Gould and our foregoing analysis suggest that secondary control can be more adaptive than direct personal control of the environment (which Hechhausen and Schulz meant by primary control) in East Asia for at least two reasons. First, secondary control can contribute to the advancement of an individual’s mental and biological strength. For example, Chang, Chua, and Toh (1997) have found that the tendency to use secondary control is associated with lower test anxiety among Singaporeans. It is quite conceivable that successful control of one’s emotions is associated with lower test anxiety. In addition, when individuals have some specific goal, they may attempt to improve their abilities to catch up with the standard set by an expert. American and Japanese participants in an aerobics class who attempted to catch up with their instructor (Morling, 2000) must have improved their ability in aerobics over those who exerted primary control and moved to a lower level class that matched their present aerobic exercise ability. Undoubtedly, results of secondary control such as improved ability, resilient personality, mental stamina, and increased physical strength would be beneficial for one’s adaptation in the future. Second, secondary control would also make a contribution to the advancement of psychological well- being by fostering a sense of self- efficacy in terms of controlling oneself and maintaining interpersonal harmony. When individuals have successfully controlled their internal state, such as their desires or emotions, it may well foster a sense of self- efficacy in terms of controlling oneself, which would heighten one’s psychological well- being. In addition, if one can maintain harmonious relationships with the environment as a result of successful secondary control, the sense of self- efficacy in maintaining harmony will also be fostered and thus would advance one’s sense of psychological well- being. That is, an individual’s psychological well- being can be heightened by the sense of self- efficacy in self- control and maintenance of harmonious relationships with the environment as far as he or she subscribes to the value of harmonious relationships with the environment, which will be arguably facilitated by secondary control. Indeed, in Korea, Kim and Park (1998) developed a scale to measure the sense of self- efficacy in maintaining interpersonal relations and social harmony based on Bandura’s (1997) conceptualization. They found that their Relational Efficacy and Social Harmony Efficacy Scale is positively correlated with life satisfaction and negatively correlated with stress among Korean 
ConTrol orienTaT ions in The easT and WesT  |  529 
high school students. It is important that psychological well- being can be gained without the risk of direct confrontations by using secondary control. Thus, in a culture in which people value harmonious interpersonal relationships, secondary control can be more adaptive as long as immediate biological needs are not at issue. 
In a recent study, Sawaumi, Kurman, Park, Robinson, Sagie, and Yamaguchi (2017) provide supportive evidence for the above- mentioned eclectic view: individuals prefer to exert primary control rather than secondary control if it is affordable. To test this view, we introduced a distinction between ideal choice and actual choice of control strategies. We asked undergraduate students in Israel, Korea, New Zealand, and Japan to indicate their ideal and actual choices in hypothetical conflict situations. The participants were given a detailed description of primary and secondary control strategies in conflict situations. Then they were asked to answer how much they would ideally like to employ and how likely they would actually employ each control strategy. Regarding their ideal choice, the results supported Heckhausen and Schulz’s (1995) view: the participants preferred primary control to secondary control in all four cultures. However, the support for primacy of primary control was limited to ideal choice. When it comes to actual choice, their preference varied across cultures. In Japan, primary and secondary control strategies were chosen to a similar degree, whereas in Israel primary control strategy was significantly preferred to secondary control strategy, indicating that Japanese hesitate to actually exert primary control strategy. This finding points to the complexity of the choice of control strategies in cultural contexts. In some cultures, pressure to maintain interpersonal harmony is stronger, and thus the aggressive control strategy of direct personal control is not adaptive. 
Probably the most important assumption in Heckhausen and Schulz’s (1995) theorization is that psychological well- being is solely dependent on one’s sense of autonomy, which is closely related to one’s sense of self- efficacy and self- esteem. Although they did not state this explicitly, it appears, at least to us, that their argument makes use of an assumption that is shared by many Western researchers. If a theorist stipulates the indispensability of the sense of autonomy for psychological well- being, it would follow that individuals’ psychological well- being can be enhanced only in response to their direct and personal control attempt that has brought about desired outcomes in the environment. On the other hand, if a theorist assumes only that a sense of successful adaptation is enough for one’s psychological well- being, any primary or secondary control strategies can be claimed to bring about one’s psychological well- being. Figure 16.2 illustrates the two alternative routes to psychological well- being. The upper route describes a route that would be chosen by those who value autonomy. Alternatively, the lower route describes a route to psychological well- being through a strategy of successful adaptation that does not require autonomy. The lower route does not entail changes in one’s environment for higher psychological well- being, although it does not exclude primary control. As long as direct control attempts do not disrupt harmony, individuals who value harmony would also exert direct control, as shown in Sawaumi et al. (2017). For example, an individual 
530 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
will not hesitate to open a window in a classroom when he or she is alone and feels hot, although the same person may hesitate to do so when he or she is not alone in the classroom and is uncertain about how others feel about the room’s temperature. 
Primary control would have functional primacy over secondary control only when individuals’ biological or social needs are urgent or in a culture in which their psychological well- being depends largely on their sense of autonomy, which can be bolstered by their capability in exerting direct and personal control over the environment. On the other hand, when individuals’ biological or social needs are not urgent or in a culture in which their psychological well- being is determined primarily by their ability to fit well with the environment, secondary control would heighten one’s psychological well- being if one values harmony with the environment. Consistent with this reasoning, Sawaumi et al. (2015) have revealed that Japanese prefer primary control more with a greater extent of urgency, as when an important work partner does not work hard for a project. 
Future Agenda for Empirical Research We believe many important empirical questions are still awaiting our research attention. We will highlight some of those questions in the following section. 
Agency and Target of Control The conceptual analysis and empirical evidence reviewed in this chapter point to the importance of strategies other than direct personal control. One of our suggestions is that indirect personal control, proxy control, and collective control strategies are available and actually used in place of direct personal control when individuals attempt to control the environment. Based on the foregoing discussions, one can predict cross- cultural as well as individual differences in the choice of control strategies: (a) East Asians, who
