The Culturally Situated Self 
Amir Rosenmann and Jenny Kurman 
The truism that “there is no ‘I’ without a ‘we’ ” (Scheler, 1967) serves as the basis for any discussion of the self from a cultural perspective. All of us, without exception, are shaped by our sociocultural surroundings, which we in turn also shape. A cross- cultural perspective thus touches on the most fundamental unit of psychological inquiry— the self. This point has not been lost on the generations of researchers who have delved into the ways different cultures construct and inform the varied aspects of selfhood. Doing justice to this voluminous body of theory and research would be impractical in a single chapter. Therefore, in this chapter, we have chosen to introduce several key areas of research representative of central aspects of selfhood, including some that have been subject to change as globalizing and consumerist processes transform sociocultural conditions. 
James (1890) defined the “I” self as the thread of subjective continuity between one moment and the next that links our past, present, and future selves. Because this “I” is always present in our minds on this most basic phonological level, this stream of consciousness creates an experience of ourselves as possessing a consistent individual identity. This core sense of self is universal even when the experiences through which it unfolds are often culture- specific. The effects of culture are even more observable in the “me” self, which, according to James, includes the material, social, and spiritual selves. Among the many contemporary definitions of the “me” self, this chapter employs Brehm and Kassin’s (1993) conceptualization, which draws attention to the “ABCs of the self ”— that is, its affective, behavioral, and cognitive components. The affective aspect pertains to self- esteem, or to the valence attached to individuals’ perceptions of themselves; the behavioral component refers to the ways the self and self- concerns affect observable behaviors; and the cognitive facet pertains to the components, content, and organization of the self- concept. 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  539 
All three components have been researched from a cross- cultural point of view. In this chapter, we describe demonstrable cultural effects on these facets of selfhood while paying special attention to the underlying universals of self- processes. Specifically, we review the cultural variations in drives for self- consistency and positive self- regard, as we concomitantly argue for a substratal psychological resemblance that underlies them. 
Beyond the polemic integration of some selected aspects of this vast literature, we also aim to point out avenues for future research. Late in the chapter, we thus explore how the self may be changing as a result of contemporary globalizing and consumerist processes. Before addressing these contemporary issues, however, we introduce historical trends in research on cultural modalities of selfhood (primarily Markus & Kitayama’s work from 1991). These are presented first to contextualize and historicize the reviewed literature. Additionally, seeing that much of the field grew around these conceptualizations, they are indispensable to its understanding even today, more than 25 years later. 
Self- Construal: A Historic Perspective The cross- cultural perspective on the self has gained momentum as part of (Western) psychological science’s wider fascination with the very different cultural constructs native to East Asia (Matsumoto, 1999). This cultural distinction became codified into Hofstede’s (1980) individualism– collectivism dimension, later developed by Triandis (e.g., Triandis, Bontempo, Villareal, Asai, & Lucca, 1988; see Chapter 1 by Walter J. Lonner, Kenneth D.  Keith, and David Matsumoto for historical perspectives, and Chapter  3 by Peter B. Smith for a review of cultural dimensions). It was in this form that the “East versus West” distinction was adopted and elaborated in relation to modes of selfhood. Against this backdrop, Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) characterization of independent versus interdependent variations of self- construal became prominent. 
According to this interpretation, a minority of (individualist, Western) cultures encourage individuals to define themselves as bounded, unitary entities, complete unto themselves and clearly separable from others. While interpersonal relationships, social roles, and membership in groups are obviously important to individuals everywhere, those with an independent sense of self define themselves in terms of their internal attributes, individual goals, and uniquely integrated personalities. This self is perceived to be stable across time as the essence of the individual’s personality encapsulated within the self remains unchanged. Furthermore, this self should exhibit a great deal of stability across situations and social roles as the same inner attributes are expected to manifest themselves consistently in an individual’s actions, habits, and interpersonal behaviors. 
In the context of these sociocultural systems that have been constituted by and for autonomous individuals, each person is afforded a measure of inalienable dignity and inherent worth. This basic sense of dignity is not contingent on others as the dignity of a particular individual can be jeopardized only by failing to live up to her or his own 
 
 
540 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
internal standards (Leung & Cohen, 2011). Because of this emphasis on an individual’s immutable core, epitomized by idioms such as “to thine own self be true” (Shakespeare, trans. 1994, 1.3.78– 82), self- actualization and self- expression become primary mandates (Illouz, 2007). Within these contexts, people aim to increase their sense of self- worth by asserting their uniqueness and relishing their personal achievements (e.g., Oishi & Diener, 2001). 
According to Markus and Kitayama (1991), however, in much of the world, self-hood is construed in a very different way that manifests the wider cultural emphases of collectivism. Those with an interdependent self- construal view themselves as inherently embedded within a network of interpersonal relationships and assumed social roles. This widespread cultural understanding of selfhood does not rest on some illusive essence to be discovered and expressed. Instead, the self is uniquely defined by its specific constellation of relationships, roles, and social obligations. Hence, this selfhood is never “an island unto itself,” as representations of significant others and their relationships with the individual comprise an indispensable part of the self. Later research had demonstrated that this inseparability of self from other exists on a neurofunctional level. For example, self- referential regions of the brain (the medial prefrontal cortex and rostral anterior cingulate cortex) were similarly activated among Chinese and American participants who had been instructed to think about themselves. However, Chinese (but not American) individuals showed the same pattern of activation when thinking about their mothers as well (Zhu, Zhang, Fan, & Han, 2007), suggesting that “mother” was included as an integral part of Chinese participants’ selves. 
Within these collectivist contexts, individuals are not expected to express their uniqueness, but rather to fit in and adapt their behaviors to the changing demands of the situation. If consistency between inner attributes, expressed opinions, and observable behavior is valued in the independent self, the interdependent self is valued for its flexible ability to accommodate different social expectations. An individual’s self- worth is put in the hands of others who judge whether an individual’s behaviors are appropriate to her or his place in the social hierarchy and network of social obligations. This notion of face gives others the power either to affirm or to repudiate an individual’s worth and stands in sharp contrast to the internality of dignity- based worth. For these reasons, self- restraint and humility are encouraged for the sake of preserving the interpersonal harmony on which an individual’s worth is dependent (Leung & Cohen, 2011). 
Adding South to the original East versus West dichotomy, Cohen and colleagues (e.g., Cohen & Nisbett, 1994) identified a third type of culture arranged around the prin-ciples of honor. Honor cultures typically originate in frontier societies, where lawless-ness and low or absent governmentality necessitate effective alliance building in order to secure resources and ensure safety. In these highly stratified contexts, individuals (and mainly men) put on airs of resolute assertiveness and unflinching willingness to defend their ground against any encroachment. If this projected image wins the respect of wards and serves to deter competitors or would- be aggressors, it validates the individual’s claim 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  541 
for status and social power. While this type of cultural arrangement is clearly evident in many regions of the world and is markedly different from both previously described cultural archetypes, its implications on selfhood have not been thoroughly researched. Hence, it is mostly absent from the following discussion. 
Subsequent Elaboration, Refinement, and Critique of Self- Construal Models Not only do differences in self- construal shape the content and structure of individuals’ self- schema, they also influence attentional focus, awareness, and mentalization. Those with more interdependent self- construal are generally more attuned to contextual features and tend to process scenes holistically. In contrast, independent self- construal is associated with a narrower focus of attention that concentrates on the figure while neglecting its background (Nisbett, Peng, Choi, & Norenzayan, 2001; Oyserman, 2017). 
These differences in cognitive processing carry over to attentional biases found in Western contexts. For instance, the mere prospect of owning an item is enough to shift the attention of (presumably independent) American participants toward it. This self- reference effect also yields better recollection of such an item. In contrast (presumably interdependent) Chinese participants evince no such effect. Moreover, their recollection is best when an item is associated with a close other (mother in this case; Sparks, Cunningham, & Kritikos, 2016). Studies of autobiographical memory show discrepancies as well. Americans are more likely than those from non- Western cultures to remember events from a self- centered point of view, assign greater importance to these events, and vividly recall their individual emotional reactions (in contrast to, e.g., Chinese individuals [Wang, 2001] or Turkish individuals [Sahin & Mebert, 2013]). These patterns of recollection plausibly follow from what individuals attend to in real time and from the type of self- narrative into which these memories are integrated. 
In light of these fundamental differences in processing self- relevant social information, it is no wonder that they affect social cognition and judgment of others as well. A review of this extensive literature is beyond the scope of this chapter (but see Chapter 11 by Qi Wang and Sawa Senzaki for a discussion of cultural influences on social cognition). Here, it suffices to say that East- Asians approach situations as if they are social psychologists who are trying to understand the social context in which behavior occurs. Westerners, in contrast, act as if they are personality psychologists, tirelessly attempting to extrapolate from behavior (of the self or of another) to the individual’s internal characteristics (Gilovich, Keltner, & Nisbett, 2010). 
As this short discussion illustrates, Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) theory of cultural variation in self- construal became exceedingly influential, first among cross- cultural psychologists and then in growing circles within psychological science. In the process, however, many nuances and qualifications present in the original theorization were omitted. Perhaps this simplistic understanding of the theory became popular because it reproduces many preconceptions about the exceptionality of the West and its 
 
542 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
stark contrast to the “Orient,” as exemplified by Japanese and other North- Eastern Asian cultures (Matsumoto, 1999; Vignoles et al., 2016). It also confuses between individual- level analyses (i.e., type of self- construal) and larger scale societal and cultural variables (e.g., collectivism vs. individualism; Vignoles et al., 2016) or simply assumes that a specific nationality corresponds with a particular type of self- construal (Matsumoto, 1999). Indeed, after careful examination of existent research, Matsumoto concluded that the theory is not supported by empirical findings. 
In light of such critiques, researchers began noting variations in self- construal within cultures rather than only between them (as was already suggested by Markus and Kitayama, 1991). This led to the development of scales designed to measure self- construal on an individual level, typically mapping each form of self- construal onto a single, corresponding scale (e.g., Singelis, 1994). Nonetheless, many studies failed to record the expected patterns of associations between culture and members’ self- construal scores or between self- construal scores and their various hypothesized correlates (Matsumoto, 1999). Even core predictions, such as those associating interdependent self- construal with spontaneous descriptions of the self in terms of its relations to others and membership in social categories, received only equivocal support at best (see our later discussion of this finding; e.g., Oyserman, Coon, & Kemmelmeier, 2002). 
In response to these empirical and theoretical issues, scholars offered refinements to the dichotomy of independence– interdependence. One approach taken by Kagitcibasi (2005) suggests the possibility of admixtures between the two. Her construct of the relational self thus combines relatedness (the interdependent construal) and autonomy (the independent construal). Others employed a more refined cultural macro- distinction as the basis for their inquiries into forms of selfhood. Specifically, Singelis, Triandis, Bhawuk, and Gelfand (1995) crossed the individualism– collectivism dichotomy with Hofstede’s dimension of power distance to create a distinction between vertical (hierarchical) and horizontal (egalitarian/ leveled) cultures. 
The resultant four cultural typologies were subsequently elaborated into four matching types of self- construal. Within individualism, this yielded a distinction between a horizontal variant that stressed autonomy and self- direction (typical of Scandinavian cultures; Thomsen, Sidanius, & Fiske, 2007)  and a vertical variant that corresponded with interpersonal competitiveness (Singelis et al., 1995; Vignoles et al., 2016) and self- enhancement (e.g., the United States; Thomsen et al., 2007). Within collectivism, these were mapped onto the self- construal types suggested by Güngör, Karasawa, Boiger, Dinçer, and Mesquita (2014). Here, the horizontal variant takes the form of a relatedness- oriented interdependence, found, for instance, in Turkey, where “the sheep that separates from the flock is devoured by the wolf.” The vertical counterpart, in contrast, emphasizes conformity, as is the case in Japan, where “the nail that sticks out gets hammered down.” In both cultures, autonomy was negatively associated with conformity but positively (albeit modestly) associated with relatedness. This suggests that, in the context of collectivistic cultures, independence and interdependence are not opposites, harking back to the relational self of Kagitcibasi (2005).
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  543 
 The association between independence and interdependence varies across these different measures and tends to be modest in size regardless of direction. If measures yield relatively orthogonal construal dimensions, they do not support the interpretation of self- construal as a unidimensional variable spanning the range from complete independency to complete interdependency. The fact that independent and interdependent self- construals can no longer be conceptualized as polar opposites suggests that multiple forms of self- construal may coexist in a single individual. This opened up the possibility, now empirically validated, that a specific self- construal can be primed and its effects tested regardless of an individual’s culture or trait- level scores (Oyserman, 2017). 
Given the great distance between Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) original conceptualization and these subsequent refinements, Vignoles et  al. (2016) proposed a new operationalization of independence and interdependence self- construals. This systematic cross- cultural project, however, did not confirm predictions derived from the original theorization. In this work, the researchers developed seven scales, each of which contrasted a specific facet of independent versus interdependent construal. While these scales demonstrated psychometric robustness, they did not coalesce into a higher order structure corresponding to independent versus interdependent self- construal. This suggests that the two archetypal forms of self- construal are not unitary concepts, thus again refuting the notion of a unified, bipolar continuum of self- construal. Furthermore, the population- level scores of cultures did not identify a “pure,” uniformly independent (or uniformly interdependent) culture. In fact, these findings did not conform to common sense expectations, nor did they reproduce the earlier cross- cultural findings that informed Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) original theorization. 
These issues notwithstanding, the basic dichotomy between independent and interdependent forms of selfhood has proved very fruitful. Indeed, it continues to inform both theorization and measurement of much cross- cultural research. In the absence of a widely accepted alternative theoretical framework, the perspective offered by Markus and Kitayama (1991) is indispensable. Thus, even as more work is needed to reconcile the described conceptual and empiric discrepancies, the heuristic value of this binary perspective cannot be overlooked. We therefore refer to this dichotomous conceptualization of selfhoods in reviewing the scholarly work which sprung out of it. In the following sections, we discuss some of the topics relevant to the ABCs of the self from this influential perspective, beginning with cognitions related to the self- concept. 
The Cognitive Aspect of the Self and Culture: The Self- Concept The self- concept is the collection of self- referent knowledge, including characteristics and abilities as well as the important beliefs, attitudes, and values that a person considers to be self- defining (Brehm & Kassin, 1993). Prior to the late 1970s, most research on self- concept was based either on self- ratings of predetermined inventories or on the widely used Twenty Statement Test (TST; Kuhn & Mcpartland, 1954). In the TST, participants 
 
544 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
are asked to fill in 20 statements continuing the stem “I am _ _ .” In line with earlier data obtained in India (Shweder & Bourne, 1984), Cousins (1989) showed that, upon standard administration of the TST, people from Asian cultures report more social roles than psychological attributions, in sharp contrast to Westerners. These findings were taken to imply the existence of systematic cultural differences in the content of the self- concept. This conclusion, however, was later qualified by an additional condition of the test. When the context was specified (e.g., “me at home”; “me at work”), Japanese people reported more psychological attributes than Americans. It thus seems that these cultural differences are less a matter of the self- concept’s content than the way this self- referent knowledge is organized and activated. 
Second- generation research on the self- concept focused on how self- knowledge is organized. Within this literature, the work of Linville )1985) gained prominence. Linville developed a model and a method to measure self- complexity. In these studies, individuals were asked to sort characteristics into groups that define them. In this Q- sort design, participants can create as many categories as they want and can recategorize each characteristic multiple times. The number of categories and the degree to which they do not overlap (i.e., the number of unique characteristics in each category) are combined to form a complexity index. Self- complexity was demonstrated to relate to better adjustment (Linville, 1987), probably due to superior ability to regulate negative feelings: more self- aspects provide more opportunities to reappraise negative outcomes and to compensate for weak self- aspects by using stronger ones (McConnell, Rydell, & Brown, 2009). A Chinese study supported the buffering role of self- complexity, showing that it moderated the relations between daily hassles and negative affect as well as between critical life events and self- esteem (Gong & Zhang, 2015), suggesting universality in the buffering ability of self- complexity. 
Addressing possible cross- cultural variances, Brown, Shilling, and Park (2017) found that, in comparison to Americans, three different samples of South Koreans generated significantly more self- aspects (resembling the number of categories in Linville’s complexity index). The authors presented further data from previous studies that used similar tools to measure the number of self- aspects in Western or European countries (United States, Poland, Germany, and England), as well as in other Asian countries (China and Japan). These data confirmed that the number of self- aspects was consistently lower in Western cultures relative to Asian cultures. These findings can be interpreted in light of the greater inclusion of others in the interdependent self because close relationships may lead to self- expansion (Emery, Walsh, & Slotter, 2015). The larger number of close relationships and the greater commitment to them found in non- Western cultures (e.g., Schug, Yuki, & Maddux, 2010) may lead to more self- expansion and concomitantly, more self aspects. 
Another structural aspect of the self- concept is its clarity. Similar to any other clustering of cognitive and evaluative responses to an object, those related to the self- concept may be more or less internally consistent, exhibit differing degrees of stability 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  545 
over time and be endorsed with higher (vs. lower) levels of certainty. Campbell et  al. (1996) developed self- concept clarity as an index of self- concept integration across these structural domains. Individuals who possess a clearer self- concept also tend to exhibit higher levels of self- esteem and better psychological adjustment. 
The emphasis on the congruent stability of the self over time and across situations would seem most compatible with the Western, bounded conceptualization of the independent self (Markus & Kitayama, 1991)— a self that is situated within the wider Western intolerance of ambiguities and internal contradictions (Spencer- Rodgers, 2004). Indeed, in East Asian samples, this and other measures of self- system congruence seem to have less of an impact on self- esteem and overall psychological adjustment (Cross, Morris, & Gore, 2002). Nonetheless, even in such contexts, these structural elements of the self are still important, as supported by data demonstrating their relevance to the psychological adjustment of individuals from East- Asia (e.g., Wu, Watkins, & Hattie, 2010). 
Spencer- Rodgers (2004) used the “East- West” difference in cultural worldviews as their point of departure in developing the dialectical self. This form of self- system expresses the East- Asian cultural tradition of Confucian tolerance of ambiguity, internal contradictions, and expected malleability. Thus, the concept of the dialectical self seems to be almost antithetical to self- concept clarity as these concepts evince opposite worldviews and hence opposite views of the self (Boucher, 2011). Yet, regardless of this divergence in theoretical underpinnings, findings regarding the dialectical self are nearly a mirror image of those reported for self- concept clarity. That is to say, even in East- Asian contexts, where dialectism is valued, higher measures of dialectical selfhood are associated with decreased self- esteem and subjective well- being (Chen, Benet- Martínez, Wu, Lam, & Bond, 2013). 
Across measures and conceptualizations, then, it seems that individuals are better off (at least with regard to their self- esteem, subjective well- being, and other indices of psychological adjustment) if they possess a highly internally congruent and stable sense of who they are and what characterizes them as individuals. While cultures differ greatly in their expectations for such self- system integration, the general principle holds (albeit to different degrees) on the individual level across cultures (Church et al., 2008). 
The preceding literature review points to a more clearly defined, yet less complexly structured self in Western cultures than in non- Western ones. These trends are incongruent with the finding that self- concept clarity within Western contexts is positively associated with self- complexity (Campbell, Assanand, & Di- Paula, 2003). While the relatively lower stability and internal congruency of the self in non- Western cultures has received empirical and theoretical support, more data are needed to better understand cross- cultural differences in self- complexity. Some early refinements in the study of self- complexity that were abandoned may be relevant in the cross- cultural context. For example, the distinction between the complexity of positive versus negative aspects of the self (Morgan & Janoff- Bulman, 1994) may prove to be relevant to a cultural understanding of self- complexity. Another potential issue is the interpretation of degree of 
546 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
overlap between categories. Linville (1985) understood this overlap as undermining complexity, while others (e.g., Donahue, Robins, Roberts, & John, 1993) saw it as decreasing self- differentiation and thus positively related to adjustment. This issue of overlap between categories of self- aspect has not yet been fully explicated, let alone in a cultural context. The same is true for the wider question of self- complexity and culture, which still requires a great deal of empirical as well as theoretical research. 
The Affective Aspect of the Self and Culture: Self- Esteem and the Universality of Positive Self- Regard Selves differ not only in content and organization, but also in valence and affective tenor. Probably the most studied construct within self- psychology, self- esteem, is an emotional component of self in that it reflects the basic feeling and overall evaluative tone an individual holds toward himself or herself (Goodman & Coopersmith, 1969; Rosenberg, 1965). As such, self- esteem is a part of the core self (Judge, Erez, Bono, & Thoresen, 2002)  and an important index of overall psychological adjustment (Rosenberg, 1965; Sowislo & Orth, 2012). Hoyle, Kernis, Leary, and Baldwin )1999) pointed to the distinction between genuine positive self- esteem and artificially inflated self- esteem. While the former is the fully internalized, relatively stable, and underlying sense of an individual’s self- worth, the latter is a more defensive construct and, as such, is marked by instability, uncertainty, and vulnerability. According to these and other researchers, only genuine self- esteem is indicative of and conducive to individuals’ psychological adjustment (e.g., Kernis, 2003). 
Cross- cultural research has demonstrated cultural influences regarding several aspects of self- esteem. Here, we discuss these cultural influences as they relate to population- level differences in self- esteem scores, the anchoring of self- esteem, and the closely related question of the universality of the self- enhancement motive. 
Population Levels and Anchoring of Self- Esteem Level of self- esteem is not entirely dependent on the content of the self- schema or what people hold in high esteem about themselves. The average level of reported self- esteem (i.e., population mean scores on Rosenberg’s widely used scale; Rosenberg, 1965) varies across cultures, with East- Asian and other face cultures demonstrating markedly lower reported levels of self- esteem compared to Western and Westernized cultures (e.g., Bond & Cheung, 1983; Tafarodi, Lang, & Smith, 1999). Tellingly, while in Western contexts the distribution of reported self- esteem scores on the Rosenberg scale typically has a pronounced left tail (i.e., scores tend to cluster near the maximal point of the scale), in Japan the distribution of scores is very close to normal (Heine, Lehman, Markus, & Kitayama, 1999). 
 
 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  547 
This question of overall self- esteem may also relate to what is held in esteem by different cultures. Given the extent to which cultures modulate individuals’ levels of self- esteem, it is not surprising that cultures also direct individuals to base their self- esteem on different domains. On the most fundamental level, each culture sets a different gold standard for human behavior. Individuals’ self- esteem is thus derived from their evaluation vis- à- vis this culturally defined “ideal person.” Chiu (2006) described this ideal in the United States as an autonomous, independent, and positively unique person, whereas in Japan the ideal is a conforming person who fits into important groups and strives for social harmony. This distinction can be easily applied to other dignity versus face cultures and again harks back to Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) conceptualization of independent versus interdependent selfhood. Less is known about the gold standard defining the ideal person in honor cultures beyond the basic mechanism that attaches self- esteem to the degree of respect one receives from others (Leung & Cohen, 2011). 
This cross- culturally informed perspective has unfortunately remained largely isolated from the mainstream of psychological research examining individual differences in the anchoring of self- esteem. This large body of research traces the contingencies of self- worth theory as developed by Jennifer Crocker and colleagues (e.g., Crocker, Luhtanen, Cooper, & Bouvrette, 2003; Crocker & Park, 2012). Based on work with American college students, the theory specifies seven discernable yet interrelated domains (others’ approval, appearance, competition, academics, family support, virtue, and God’s love; Crocker et al., 2003). The theory also posits that these domains do not all supply equally viable anchors for self- worth. Some are more external and unstable as they require constant feedback from the environment (e.g., others’ approval, appearance, and competition), while others offer more stable, internal anchors for self- worth (e.g., virtue and God’s love). Studies from several cultural contexts demonstrate that individuals whose self- worth is less anchored in external contingencies generally exhibit better psychological adjustment and enhanced well- being (see Crocker & Park, 2012, for review). 
A relatively rare integration of self- worth theory with the cross- cultural perspective provides empirical support for the rationale we have presented. In line with presumed differences in self- construal, the generally lower self- esteem and subjective well- being of Taiwanese students (relative to a comparable American sample) were found to be at least partially attributable to their sense of self- worth being highly contingent on the approval of others (Liu et al., 2017). This is in line with the contention that the judgments of others are very important to the self and to self- esteem in East- Asian interdependent contexts. Nevertheless, the externality of these judgments supplies a less favorable basis for self- worth across cultural contexts. 
From our cross- cultural perspective, however, it is surprising that this operationalization has remained unchallenged. The seven domains of contingencies of self- worth probed in this measure (Crocker et  al., 2003)  seem appropriate mainly for samples resembling those used in the original work. Academic competence is an unlikely anchor for the self- worth of nonstudents, while God’s love is a dubious anchor 
548 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
in relatively secular settings (such as Germany [Schwinger, Schöne, & Otterpohl, 2015] or China [Cheng & Kwan, 2008]). As we have seen, extant literature suggests that culture plays a significant role in shaping the anchors of self- worth available to individuals (Cheng & Kwan, 2008). For instance, the concept of “face,” which is central to individuals’ self- worth in many East- Asian cultures, does not map onto any of these American- generated domains. Yet research suggests that, for Chinese students, academic achievement in and of itself is less important than its recognition as a source of pride or shame for the student’s family (i.e., its face implications; Liao & Wei, 2014). Indeed, while many researchers use simple translations of the original scale outside of its original cultural context, others have developed comparable measures of anchors informed by the local culture (e.g., Uchida, 2008). 
Additionally, the oft- repeated bifurcation of anchors into external versus internal contingencies seems to be somewhat imprecise. Thus, academic competence could represent both types of motivations (e.g., competitive superiority or self- improvement), and any form of acceptance from others (including family members) could reasonably be categorized as external (Crocker & Luhtanen, 2003). Nonetheless, considering that empirical analyses have repeatedly clustered academic competence with other “external” anchors and family support with “internal” ones (Crocker & Park, 2012), this division appears to be based on the stability of the anchor and its exposure to perpetual outside feedback, rather than on externality– internality per- se. This conceptualization explains why academic competence is clustered with other unstable, external anchors while family support offers a more stable source of self- worth, akin to anchors based on God’s unconditional love or inherent human dignity. 
From our perspective, this argument suggests that culturally specific anchors may determine population- level differences in self- esteem. Western cultures, in which the prevailing notion of dignity assigns inalienable value to individuals (Leung & Cohen, 2011), are also where population- level self- esteem is highest. This default high regard is not granted either in face or in honor contexts, where self- worth is contingent on social judgments that are neither unconditional nor unfaltering. The dignity afforded in Western contexts may thus provide an especially durable anchor for Western individuals’ higher overall sense of self- worth. Research has yet to explore this possibility or adequately measure dignity’s role in self- worth. Nonetheless, this suggestion is congruent with Crocker and Park’s (2012) later claim that self- worth is always based on something and that adjustment and well- being are affected by the stability of these anchors. Perhaps, then, dignity cultures do afford their members a genuinely higher and more stable sense of self- worth. 
Against the backdrop of these cultural differences, we next discuss the robust cross- cultural difference in self- esteem as it relates to the ongoing debate regarding the universality of the need for positive self- regard. This need for positive self- regard manifests in one of the best studied motivational processes of the self: the motivation to self- enhance.
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  549 
The Self- Enhancement Motivation The prevailing tendency of individuals to self- enhance (i.e., to hold unrealistically positive views regarding the self) was originally introduced as a positive illusion— a cognitive distortion that aids psychological adjustment (Taylor & Brown, 1988, 1994; Taylor, Lerner, Sherman, Sage, & McDowell, 2003a, 2003b). Self- enhancement is generally inseparable from the underlying feeling of self- worth (Dunning, 1999), seeing that self- enhancement and the self- enhancement motive are intimately related, and individuals with high self- esteem reveal more self- enhancing biases (Falk & Heine, 2015; Hamamura, Heine, & Takemoto, 2007). Alongside self- consistency, self- assessment, and self- improvement, self- enhancement is often considered to be one of the basic motivations of the self (e.g., Brown, 1998; Sedikides & Strube, 1995). Self- enhancement is hence both common and adaptive, while unbiased realism regarding the self is typically found only in those who suffer from depressive disorders (i.e., in “depressive realism”; Alloy & Abramson, 1988). 
The self- enhancement motive is postulated to drive a number of very robust psychological phenomena. Research has repeatedly shown, for instance, that the proportion of people who rank themselves as average or above on any given trait far exceeds 50% (e.g., Sedikides & Gregg, 2003). In some cases, as many as 80% of members of a group rate themselves as being above the group’s average (College Board, 1976– 1977, as cited in Dunning, Meyerowitz, & Holzberg, 1989). This above- average effect appears to be a straightforward manifestation of the self- enhancement motive. Nevertheless, the above- average effect was found not only in self- evaluations, but in evaluations of other people as well. Klar and Giladi (1997) revealed that any member of a group is likely to be perceived as being above average (so- called everyone is better than average effect). The existence of this effect challenges the notion that the above- average effect reflects self- enhancement as it may reflect a more general bias. In Western contexts, however, this bias is smaller in size than the comparable bias in self- evaluations. Even after the general above- average effect is parceled out, self- evaluations still evince a better than average bias. This is not the case in Japan, where self- serving biases disappear after controlling for other- serving biases (Hamamura et al., 2007). 
Indeed, the above- average effect, even in its simplest form, is much weaker or absent in East- Asian cultures. A meta- analysis conducted by Heine, Kitayama, and Hamamura (2007) on 91 relevant cross- cultural comparisons revealed evidence for much higher self- enhancement behaviors among Westerners as compared to East- Asians (average effect size of d = .84). Cultural differences in self- enhancement were found in real- life behaviors as well. For example, in an analysis of 1,346 academic journals published between 2009 and 2014, self- citations were shown to correlate positively with the individualism index of the author’s country (Deschacht & Maes, 2017). Notably, self- citations were twice as common in articles written by authors from individualist countries (the United States, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Canada, Denmark, Sweden, Ireland, Norway, and Finland) than in those written by authors from collectivist countries (Japan, Singapore, China, South Korea, and Taiwan). 
 
550 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
In congruence with this documented cultural difference in level of self- enhancement, the use of self- enhancement mechanisms is generally less frequent in East Asia than in the West. Psychological science has identified many such mechanisms of self- enhancement, including downward social comparisons (e.g., Aspinwall & Taylor, 1993; Wills, 1981), self- serving attribution biases (Bradley, 1978; Greenwald, 1980; Miller, 1976), and idiosyncratic definitions of desired traits (Dunning & Cohen, 1992; Dunning et al., 1989), as well as elaborate maneuvers used to justify failures (Snyder, 1985). Many of these mechanisms, however, may be specific to dignity cultures and not appear as often or in the same way outside of these contexts. Thus, for example, self- serving attributions were less prevalent in Japan (Kitayama, Takagi, & Matsumoto 1995), and self- serving biases were evident only for ability attributions (Kashima & Triandis, 1986). Conversely, Japanese people were found to be more responsive to failure feedback than Canadians (Heine, Kitayama, & Lehman, 2001) and, unlike Americans, considered failure as more meaningful than success (Kitayama, Markus, Matsumoto, & Norasakkunkit, 1997). 
A comprehensive theoretical analysis of this literature (Hepper, Gramzow, & Sedikides, 2010)  suggested the distinction within self- enhancement between positive self- enhancement and self- protective strategies. The structure of this model (later integrated as the “extended self- enhancement tactician model”) was cross- validated in China and the United States (Hepper, Sedikides, & Cai, 2013). This cultural comparison yielded the expected finding that Chinese individuals, relative to Americans, employed more self- protective strategies to safeguard self- esteem when failure was expected or had occurred (e.g., self- handicapping beforehand or attributing failures to external and localized causes). Within the positive strategies of self- enhancement, however, the cultural patterns were less consistent. While Americans tended to “embrace positivity” (e.g., spending time with people who think highly of the individual) more, the two groups did not differ regarding “self- affirming reflections” (e.g., attending to strengths and capabilities and not to failures or areas of incompetence). Furthermore, “favorable construals,” a cognitive cluster which includes the use of self- serving attribution biases, were more prevalent among Chinese participants than among Americans. 
In summary, manifestations of self- enhancement vary greatly between cultures. Despite some contradictory results, the general consensus also holds that the overall levels of straightforward, direct self- enhancement are lower in face (e.g., East- Asian) cultures than in dignity (e.g., Western) cultures. While most scholars agree that this cross- cultural difference is meaningful and robust, its underlying reasons continue to fuel a hotly debated controversy, to which we turn next. 
The Debate Regarding the Universality of the Self- Enhancement Motive Two groups of scholars clearly emerged surrounding the question of the variability of the self- enhancement motivation. According to the universalists, the underlying motivation for self- enhancement exists in all cultures even though its manifestations differ radically 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  551 
from one culture to the next. Initially, these scholars claimed that self- enhancement is not detected in face cultures because it is measured by the above- average effect in reference to characteristics valued in Western cultures (Sedikides, Gaertner, & Toguchi, 2003). Subsequently, researchers argued that while the self- enhancement motive is universal, its manifestations in face cultures are more subtle and tacit, necessitating appropriate measurements and research designs (e.g., Brown & Kobayashi, 2003; Kurman, 2003; Sedikides, Gaertner, & Vevea, 2005; Yamagishi et al., 2012). The relativists, on the other hand, claim that self- enhancement does not serve any major function in the selfhood of individuals from face cultures. The measured difference in self- enhancement and levels of self- esteem are therefore taken at face value— as indicative of a fundamental cross- cultural difference in self- related motivations. According to these scholars, the need for high self- esteem (and, consequently, for self- enhancement) is culturally specific and is largely limited to dignity contexts (e.g., Heine et al., 2001; Kitayama et al., 1997). 
Suggested Reasons for the Apparent Lack of Self- Enhancement Motive in Face Cultures The relativist argument against the universality of the self- enhancement motivation was already present in Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) seminal account of the relative importance of self and others in interdependent selfhood. In the following, we describe and discuss four implications of this model: the importance of self- success for people from face cultures, the presumed contradiction between self- enhancement and self- criticism, the claim equating desire for uniqueness with self- enhancement, and the theory of relational mobility. 
The Importance of Self- Success in Face Cultures The centrality of others in interdependent self- construal raises the possibility that, in this context, self- worth is entirely contingent on self– other relationships. Here, the desire for personal excellence is substituted by the need to maintain harmony within the in- group and to fit- into it (Markus & Kitayama, 1991; see also Chapter 16 by Susumu Yamaguchi and Takafumi Sawaumi). Meeting such interpersonal demands may increase self- esteem. Additionally, if the self is intertwined with the in- group, then esteem can be bolstered by the in- group’s achievements, thus replacing the need for personal successes (Heine & Lehman, 1997). In these contexts, to excel and outperform other in- group members could plausibly jeopardize in- group harmony and thus incur social costs. In sum, Heine et  al. (1999) claimed that the demand to fit in makes self- enhancement redundant as individuals’ capabilities and qualities, in and of themselves, are mostly irrelevant. 
As a counterargument, we suggest that the distinction between self- success and successfully fitting in may very well reflect distinct paths through which self- worth should be acquired. Nonetheless, the question of who succeeds and in what has little bearing on the need for and level of individuals’ genuine self- esteem. In face cultures, people may assign 
 
 
552 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
worth to themselves because they believe they fit in well and contribute to the community and not because they outperform others. They are likely still motivated by the desire to deem themselves worthy based on the prevailing cultural criteria. Such anchoring of self- worth in communal interdependencies also manifests in the mechanisms of self- enhancement which are prevalent in face cultures. We discuss this issue further later. 
Self- Enhancement and Self- Criticism The Japanese tendency to scrutinize and self- criticize following failures in order to self- improve is well documented (e.g., Heine, Takata, & Lehman, 2000; Kurman, Hui, & Dan, 2010). Indeed, following failure, Japanese individuals try harder than following success, whereas the opposite is true for Canadians (Heine et al., 2001). Self- criticism thus seems to be stronger in Japan, and perhaps in other face cultures as well, compared with dignity cultures. Several studies by Kitayama (Kitayama et al., 1997; Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Heine et al., 1999) posited this propensity for self- criticism as the antithesis of self- enhancement and as evidence to its absence. 
We question this view of self- criticism as the opposite of self- enhancement. Self- enhancement often amplifies positive affectivity and increases coping resources (Taylor et al., 2003a, 2003b) including self- efficacy (Felson, 1984; Taylor & Brown, 1988). These augmented resources likely underlie the positive relationship between self- enhancement and self- improvement. They also potentiate other adaptive coping behaviors in face of adversity, including the ability to learn from failures, which is the constructive facet of self- criticism. Some self- enhancement and positive regard for the self, then, are required if self- criticism is to lead to self- improvement. 
In line with this explanation, in studies where self- enhancement correlated negatively with self- criticism, this relationship was limited only to emotional self- criticism (i.e., experiencing a strong negative emotional reaction to failures). Contrarily, both in Israel and in Japan self- enhancement was unrelated to constructive self- criticism; that is, to taking proactive actions following failures (Kurman, Yoshihara- Tanaka, & Elkoshi, 2003). Therefore, the East- Asian tendency to attend to failures in service of self- improvement does not imply corresponding low self- enhancement. The need for positive self- regard (self- enhancement included) seems largely orthogonal to the East- Asian tendency to self- criticize and self- improve following failures. 
Self- Enhancement and Self- Uniqueness The proverbs “the nail that stands out gets pounded down” as opposed to “the squeaky wheel gets the grease” were cited by Markus and Kitayama (1991) to illustrate the value of uniqueness in collectivist versus individualist cultures. Kim and Markus (1999) drew on this comparison in their famous study showing that European Americans preferred unique figures (e.g., a triangle among squares) and chose the less common colored pen (green or red— whichever was rarer). This preference was significantly weaker for Asian Americans and even less prevalent among native Koreans (but see Yamagishi, Hashimoto, & Schug, 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  553 
2008, described later). Despite the illustrative appeal of this study’s findings, it is important to note the complete lack of social comparison or self- relevance of the measured preferences. Thus, the demonstrated preference for uniqueness does not necessarily carry over to self- uniqueness, let alone to meritorious uniqueness achieved by outperforming others. 
Nonetheless, self- uniqueness may be more appealing outside of face cultures. When asked to recount events that decreased their self- esteem (Kurman et  al., 2003), Israeli participants described events where their perceived uniqueness was threatened (e.g., “when I had to wear uniforms and everyone around me looked alike”). Contrarily, Japanese participants recounted instances in which behaving uniquely threatened their self- esteem (e.g., “when I was the only one who ordered a specific dish in a restaurant”). An aversion to personal uniqueness is well- rooted in the theoretical cross- cultural literature, which emphasizes the importance of conformity in face cultures (e.g., Chao, 1994; Yamaguchi, 1994). 
This type of personal uniqueness, however, does not directly map onto the need for self- enhancement. Despite the resemblance suggested by Markus and Kitayama (1991), self- uniqueness may emerge from adopting an idiosyncratic, nonconforming identity and thus be unrelated to the need to outperform others and self- enhance. Empirical support for the independence of these two constructs was provided by Thomsen et al. (2007). This comparative study of Danes and Americans demonstrated that while Danes value uniqueness and autonomy more than Americans, they have a lower tendency to self- enhance. In sum, we argue that self- enhancement cannot be reduced to a desire for uniqueness, and, consequently, the face aversion of uniqueness does not necessarily imply the absence of self- enhancement. 
Relational Mobility Theory Another framework related to the apparent lack of a self- enhancement motive in non- Western cultures is based on the theory of relational mobility. Relational mobility was defined by Yuki and colleagues (Falk, Heine, Yuki, & Takemura, 2009; Schug et  al., 2010)  as the freedom to choose and change one’s relational partners frequently in response to changing circumstances or needs. These researchers further suggested that, in a free market of relationships, people should maintain their attractiveness in the eyes of others by engaging in self- enhancement. People in face cultures do not have to promote themselves and emphasize their attractiveness in the eyes of others as these cultures have low relational mobility. Others, and especially members of the extended family, are likely to stay in the relationship regardless of individual attractiveness. In such contexts, the benefits of self- enhancement are moot, as is the motivation to self- enhance. 
The opposing universalist perspective would posit that relational mobility is a compelling explanation for cross- cultural differences in self- presentation (see later discussion), but not for differences in actual self- worth or motivation to self- enhance. In other words, there is no reason to equate the pressure to present oneself very favorably— and thus to maintain relational attractiveness— with genuine self- esteem. 
 
554 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
To summarize, the relativist position rests on evidence showing that face cultures discourage certain forms of direct self- enhancement (e.g., basking in individual achievements) or their presumed correlates (e.g., great desire for uniqueness, aggrandizing self- presentations, or, contrarily, lack of self- criticism). While we do not dispute these findings, they do not convincingly support the conjecture that people in face cultures do not possess a self- enhancement motivation. Instead, we contend that these findings illustrate the dramatic role of cultural norms in shaping how people present themselves to others and the mechanisms they use to self- enhance. 
Because self- worth is inseparable from the notion of selfhood, and selfhood itself carries the cultural underpinnings of individuals’ psychology, issues of self- worth are embedded in a complex web of sociocultural contingencies. This issue is thus a nexus of sociocultural, interpersonal, and psychological considerations. As such, it requires a nuanced approach specifically designed to disentangle cultural mandates from psychological needs. Next, we present work from scholars who employed this perspective in support for the universalist position vis- à- vis the self- enhancement motive. 
Support for the Universality of the Self- Enhancement Motive Support for the universality of the self- enhancement motive is anchored in the claim that normative restrictions are especially salient in face cultures. The study of tightness supports this claim: face cultures are also the tightest cultures and are characterized by a maximal level of social control and surveillance (Gelfand et al., 2011). In the same vein, Yamaguchi (1994) describes a closely controlling social system in Japan that encourages conformism and obedience as it fosters interdependent self- construal. These normative restrictions plausibly include societal control over self- reported level of self- esteem. If indeed cultural restrictions prohibit direct expression of the self- enhancement motive, indirect findings could be called upon to indicate its existence. The following section describes empirical support for the possibility that culturally appropriate forms of self- enhancement become observable once cultural restrictions are lifted (see also Chapter 16 by Susumu Yamaguchi and Takafumi Sawaumi for extended discussion of control orientations). 
Type of Trait ⁄Characteristic Personality theorists and the trait literature point to a distinction between agentic and communal traits (after Paulhus & John, 1998). In the current context, agentic traits refer to characteristics that emphasize self- distinction and personal excellence (valued most in individualistic- independent cultures), whereas communal traits refer to qualities that support the social group and its inner structure (valued more in collectivistic- interdependent contexts). 
Sedikides et  al. (e.g., Sedikides et  al., 2005; Sedikides, Gaertnesr, & Vevea, 2007)  claimed that individuals would invariably self- enhance on the traits and characteristics valued most by their respective culture. Indeed, Japanese individuals were 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  555 
as biased as their Canadian counterparts in their positive evaluations of the quality of their interpersonal relationship (Endo, Heine, & Lehman, 2000). Evincing a better than average effect, participants from both countries evaluated their own relationships as better than the relationships of their peer. Even though the authors claimed that this bias contributed to feelings of belonging and not to self- enhancement, our alternative, self- enhancement interpretation seems plausible as well, especially given that relationships with others are included in the interdependent self and determine its worth (Markus & Kitayama, 1991). 
In regard to personality traits, these divergent cultural emphases suggest that, in Asian and other non- Western cultures, self- enhancement should be evident for communal traits. This line of reasoning further suggests that the Western focus on agentic traits had limited the operationalizations of self- enhancement mainly to these traits and subsequently created an artifactual cultural difference in self- enhancement (e.g., Sedikides et  al., 2005; Sedikides, Gaertnesr, & Vevea, 2007). Kurman (2001) indeed found in a within- culture comparison that self- enhancement in Singapore was stronger for communal (e.g., generous) than for agentic (e.g., intelligent) traits. In a between- culture comparison, the finding of greater self- enhancement in a Western culture (Israel) than in Singapore was only replicated for agentic traits. No such cultural difference emerged regarding communal traits. Possibly, then, the constraints placed by face culture on self- enhancement of agentic, self- focused traits are much weaker for communal traits and ratings of the self ’s relationship as those do not threaten group or interpersonal harmony. 
However, studies conducted by Heine, Kitayama, and other notable scholars who adhere to the relativist position had consistently failed to replicate these trends. Based on a meta- analysis of the literature, this group of researchers concluded that East- Asians do not self- enhance regardless of the type of trait measured (Heine et al., 2007). Nonetheless, Church et al. (2014), for example, more recently reported on different findings. In their study, self- enhancement was measured using a round- robin design. All participants in a group of four rated each other as well as themselves on several traits. This design produced measures of the perceiver effect (an individual’s evaluations of others in the group) and the target effect (an evaluation of a target individual by all others). From these, an index of self- enhancement was calculated by subtracting the target and perceiver effects from individuals’ self- evaluations. Ratings were gathered for both agentic and communal traits and in the United States and China (additional factors and cultures are not discussed here). Analyses of individuals’ self- evaluations showed the expected pattern of trait type by culture: relative to Americans, Chinese participants rated themselves lower on agentic traits but no differently for communal traits. Regarding the self- enhancement index, there were no significant differences between the studied cultures. This study thus replicated the finding that East- Asians tend not to overevaluate themselves on agentic traits while demonstrating the propensity to self- enhance once cultural norms on how to rate others are taken into account.
556 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Enhancement by Others Culutral differences point to the need to conceptualize self- enhancement not only from the narrow perspective of the self, but also to examine the way the attributions of others are used to enhance one’s self. For example, Endo et  al. (2000) found that Japanese participants gave their relationship partner a higher rating than they gave themselves. Such other- enhancement was not present in the West. These findings appear indicative of a culture- specific mechanism of enhancement in which each actor enhances her or his partner, thus accruing self- worth without directly engaging in enhancement of the self. 
This notion of vicarious self- enhancement also finds support in studies of individuals’ expectations from significant others. For example, Muramoto (2003) reported that Japanese individuals expected significant others to attribute the self ’s successes to internal factors but failures to external factors. At the same time, Muramoto found that individuals conformed to the cultural norm when asked to judge their own performances, attributing success to external factors and failures to internal ones. Therefore, positively biased attributions are not made by the actors themselves, but rather by others close to them. Muramoto further demonstrated that these expectations from close others were not the result of perceiving others to have understood the situation differently. On the contrary, the expectations of positively biased attributions by others were positively correlated with the actor’s belief that they understand the actor and the situation well. This sophisticated mechanism allows people in face cultures to have their cake and eat it too: they conform to their culture’s norms (and do not self- enhance themselves) but nonetheless maintain their high self- evaluation through the biased eyes of significant others. 
Relying on Muramoto’s work, Dalsky, Gohm, Noguchi, and Shiomura (2008) later suggested that people with interdependent selves rely on a mechanism of “mutual self- enhancement.” This mechanism operates to enhance one’s self- worth by the exchange of compliments between partners in close relationships. If close others are an extension of the self, enhancing them also indirectly enhances the self. These others are furthermore expected to enhance the self by communicating their favorable judgments of it. This dynamic of reciprocally biased attributions and evaluations allows individuals to retain positive self- regard without engaging in blatant self- enhancement, which is culturally inappropriate. In accordance with this notion, these researchers showed that mutual self- enhancement was related to inclusion of others in the self, measured by overlap between circles representing the self and “others in general” as well as by scores on the relational interdependent self- construal scale (Hong, Morris, Chiu, & Benet- Martínez, 2000). This pattern of relations was found both in Japan and in the United States. Note that cultural differences in mutual self- enhancement or differences in level of inclusion of others in the self were not reported. Future studies should explore whether mutual self- enhancement is more pronounced in East- Asian cultures than in the West. 
The expectation that important others will provide the self with enhancing feedback was demonstrated in additional work by Gaertner, Sedikides, and Cai (2012). These researchers focused on the preferred feedback from important others. American 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  557 
and Chinese participants rated their preference regarding four types of feedback operationalized by sentences such as “I want (parent, teacher, friend, or classmate) to tell me: (a) that I am a great student (self- enhancement); (b) how to be a better student (self- improvement); (c) that I am an average student (self- effacement); (d) nothing about the kind of student I am (no feedback).” A similar pattern was revealed for desired feedback among Chinese and American participants. Self- enhancement and self- improvement feedback responses were preferred to the same extent, while in both cultures participants rejected the options of no feedback and self- effacement feedback. 
These findings suggest that once cultural restrictions on direct enhancement of the self are bypassed, East- Asians do in fact engage in self- enhancing strategies (Gaertner et al., 2012; Muramoto, 2003). This again supports our contention that while mechanisms of self- enhancement are highly culturally bound, the motivation for self- enhancement is not (see also Chapter 16 by Susumu Yamaguchi and Takafumi Sawaumi on different types of agentic control). 
The Norm of Modesty in Face Cultures Modesty refers to public understatement of one’s favorable traits, abilities, and characteristics (Cialdini, Wosinska, Dabul, Whetstone- Dion, & Heszen, 1998). As mentioned earlier, according to Markus and Kitayama’s (1991) theoretical description of the inter-dependent self, ostentatious personal success may interfere with the demand to blend into the in- group. In these context then, modesty is expected, and a lack of modesty is highly criticized. In a theoretical analysis, Lee, Leung, and Kim (2014) suggested such a “humility bias” as one of the factors that could explain cross- cultural differences in self- enhancement. Individuals who overstate their claim for face (which, as noted earlier, is bestowed by others) incur social penalties. To avoid such a social penalty, modest self- evaluations become habitual and the individual internalizes a humility bias. 
Empirical findings lend support for this idea. For example, Chinese children who modestly lied about their own good deeds were judged to have acted in a moral way (Lee, Xu, Fu, Cameron, & Chen, 2001). Additionally, Yoshida, Kojo, and Kaku (1982) found that socialization toward modesty resulted in a dramatic increase of criticism of self- enhancers among Japanese children between grades 2 and 5.  The complimentary negative judgment of self- enhancers was also illustrated by a field study (Cullen, Gentry, & Yammarino, 2015) that relied on archival datasets of managers who attended leadership development programs. These data from face cultures (China, South Korea, Taiwan) and from the United States included self- ratings of leadership capabilities, as well as three external evaluations of the same qualities from respective trainers. In face cultures, but not in the United States, those who overestimated their capabilities were more likely to receive a negative evaluation from their workplace supervisors, presumably because their immodesty had disruptive effects. 
Therefore, a norm of modest self- presentation was empirically demonstrated in East- Asian cultures. It has been suggested that the cultural variation in demands for modesty 
 
558 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
may create a corresponding variation in self- enhancement between cultures. In line with this notion, when cross- cultural differences in modesty were parceled out, differences in self- enhancement between Israelis and Singaporeans became nonsignificant (Kurman & Sriram, 2002). 
The role of modesty in self- enhancement in face cultures again points to the need to distinguish between self- enhancement manifestation and the self- enhancement motive. Differences in the observable manifestation of self- enhancement do not nec-essarily imply parallel differences in the underlying self- enhancement motive. In practical terms, this suggests that studies should endeavor to measure self- enhancement in ways that bypass the endemic forms of social surveillance and control found in face cultures. 
Facilitating Self- Enhancement One way to elicit genuine self- evaluation from individuals is to encourage precision. Yamagishi et al. (2012) did exactly that and showed that when Japanese participants were offered a small incentive for providing accurate self- estimations, the rate of “above average” self- evaluation increased. This suggests that, by default, Japanese people do not report their genuine self- evaluations but rather a downplayed version of them, more in line with norms of modesty. Nonetheless, their genuine (and self- enhancing) evaluations are highly accessible and easily reported once accuracy is incentivized and rendered normative within the study’s context. 
Another approach to facilitate the expression of self- enhancement is to reduce social scrutiny, thus lessening the hold of humility norms. Leeriness of the scrutiny of others among East- Asians is evident even on a neural level. Their error- related negativity (ERN) increased after they were primed with watching faces, but this was not the case for Americans (Park & Kitayama, 2014). The mere image of a watching face created an automatic social evaluative threat. Hence, reducing the salience of perceived social control could be meaningful. Such a reduction can be achieved by solitary, anonymous settings. If self- restrictions on expression of blatant self- enhancement are actively employed in face cultures, it follows that individuals would be more forthcoming with their genuine self- reports when placed in isolation from others. 
Relying on this assumption, Kanagawa, Cross, and Markus (2001) manipulated the setting in which American and Japanese students gave self- descriptions:  alone, with a large group of students, with a peer, or at a professor’s office. Japanese students gave more positive self- descriptions in the solitary setting than in the other settings. Americans, on the other hand, were not affected by setting condition. Other studies have similarly shown that, in Japanese samples, reducing the salience of others induced more self- enhancing attributional biases (Kudo & Numazaki, 2003). Even the Japanese aversion to being perceived as unique disappeared under such conditions. Yamagishi et al. (2008) replicated Kim and Markus’s (1999) experiment (see earlier discussion) with an added condition in which Japanese participants made their choice while alone. While 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  559 
the standard replication yielded the expected cultural effects, these disappeared in the solitary condition. 
Another way to learn about genuine self- evaluations without engaging desirability biases is to use implicit measures instead of self- reports. 
Implicit Measures of Self- Esteem One of the most popular measures of implicit attitudes is the Implicit Association Test (IAT; e.g., Greenwald, Poehlman, Uhlmann, & Banaji, 2009). Purported to measure the strength of nonconscious associations, the IAT relies on comparing response latencies to a target- positive pairing with response latencies to a target- negative pairing. The IAT can also be used to measure automatic attitudes toward the self (contrasting self- positive vs. self- negative pairings) and has become a widely used operationalization of implicit self- esteem (Greenwald & Farnham, 2000). 
Studies that used the IAT to measure self- esteem generally have shown that East- Asian participants have positive self- regard comparable to that found in Westerners (Hetts, Sakuma, & Pelham, 1999; Kobayashi & Greenwald, 2003). Yamaguchi et  al. (2007) sampled American, Japanese, and Chinese students in a study that convincingly demonstrated this pattern. In their study, the traditional category of “general other” against which the pairings of self- positivity/ negativity are usually measured was supplemented by another contrast category of “best friend.” In light of the conceptualization of the interdependent self, this is an especially stringent test of positive self- regard. The results revealed that, in all three countries, implicit self- esteem was positive in comparison both to the general other and to the best friend. These results were later replicated by Falk et al. (2009) who found no effect of culture in a cross- cultural comparison of implicit self- esteem measured by the IAT, using best friend as the “other” category. 
Yet these researchers later favored findings from implicit measures which show lower self- enhancement in face cultures while questioning the validity of the self- IAT (Falk & Heine, 2015). Their criticism is based on three grounds: relatively low correlations between explicit and implicit self- esteem, low convergence validity of different implicit measures of self- esteem, and lower predictive ability of various implicit measures of self- esteem regarding a large array of criteria in various cultures (Falk, Heine, Takemura, Zhang, & Hsu, 2015). These researchers had gone on to argue that implicit self- esteem is not a meaningful cross- cultural construct and that implicit associations with the self are not formed through the same process by which other implicit attitudes developed. Such an explanation, however, disregards other studies that clearly showed implicit association of the self with specific characteristics (e.g., math: Nosek, Banaji, & Greenwald, 2002; shyness: Asendorpf, Banse, & Mücke, 2002). 
We believe that, despite a possible weakness of the IAT measurement of the self, the presented findings are suggestive of some careful conclusions. In general, implicit measures of self- esteem support the existence of a basic positive self- regard among Japanese and Chinese individuals. Furthermore, several studies found positive implicit attitudes 
 
560 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
toward the self even when the contrast category was not an abstract, general other, but rather a best friend or in- group member. When this line of research is integrated, the finding of positive implicit self- regard in East- Asian samples further supports our contention that the general lack of explicitly expressed self- enhancement in these cultures stems from socially desirable responses (see Lalwani, Shrum, & Chiu, 2009). 
We thus find converging evidence to support our universalist position, according to which people are motivated to perceive themselves as worthy, well- regarded individuals regardless of their culture. Because cultures differ greatly in what constitutes the “ideal individual,” this motivation to self- enhance takes very different forms in different cultural settings. Specifically, blatant and direct self- enhancement runs contrary to the face culture’s emphases on in- group harmony and relational interdependence. Because of this, the straightforward manifestations of self- enhancement seen in dignity cultures are eschewed on a social level and suppressed on an individual level. Nonetheless, in studies where research design and operationalization take these cultural factors into earnest consideration, self- enhancement is detected outside of dignity cultures. The polemic described earlier is summarized in Table 17.1. If indeed self- enhancement is present in
