one form or another in all cultures, then cross- cultural similarities should also be apparent in its function in psychological adjustment and its contribution to subjective well- being. 
Relations Between Subjective Well- Being and Self- Enhancement The literature on the adaptivity of self- enhancement to psychological adjustment across cultures reveals mixed results. The issue is further complicated by the different operationalizations of self- enhancement (not all of which may be equally cross- culturally valid; as reviewed earlier) and of psychological adjustment. Many of the relatively early studies showed the expected positive relations between high self- regard and well- being in face cultures as well. Kwan, Bond, Singelis, and Kwan (1997) reported self- esteem to be a significant predictor of life satisfaction in Hong Kong. Likewise, Anderson (1999) showed that depressive symptoms and loneliness are linked to attributions that are not self- serving, with this pattern emerging both in China and in the United States. Additionally, Kurman (2003) showed that self- enhancement is associated with more positive and less negative affectivity in Singapore and Japan, much like in Western samples. Piccolo, Judge, Takahashi, Watanabe, and Locke (2005) found that, in Japan, positive self- regard (measured as the “core self- esteem”) was a strong predictor of happiness and job satisfaction. More recently, Church et al. (2014) reported that self- enhancing biases predicted self- rated adjustment in all studied cultures, including the United States and China. 
A study conducted in the United States and China manipulated self- esteem by describing a desirable trait as possessed by others more than by the self, or vice versa (i.e., self- effacement vs. self- enhancement, respectively) while participants were instructed to reflect on the past week. The manipulation generated a meaningful effect on subjective well- being, with those in the self- enhancement condition showing increases in well- being compared to their baseline level (measured a week before). A notable finding is that this effect did not interact with culture, indicating that the self- enhancement manipulation was as meaningful in China as it was in the United States (O’Mara, Gaertner, Sedikides, Zhou, & Liu, 2012). Another study used a similar procedure to manipulate self- enhancement, with the additional condition of self- protection:  people had to mention negative important traits and then reflect on the extent to which these traits characterize themselves as compared to others. The dependent variable was life satisfaction. Results showed manipulated self- enhancement had equal positive effects for both Chinese and American participants, whereas self- protection contributed to life satisfaction for Chinese but not for American participants (Lafrenière, Sedikides, & Lei, 2016). 
In yet another study, Tsai, Chiang, and Lau (2015) compared the negative affectivity of European Americans and Asian Americans after receiving negative feedback, followed by an intervention designed to produce either self- enhancement or self- improvement. In the self- enhancement condition, participants were asked to write an essay describing the negative feedback as not credible, while in the self- improvement condition the essay 
 
562 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
was directed at what can be learned from the feedback. This study yielded a culture- by- condition interaction: reduction of negative affectivity that was more pronounced in the self- improvement (vs. self- enhancement) condition for Asian Americans, whereas the opposite was true for European Americans. Nonetheless, the simple effect of culture by self- enhancement was not significant, with the self- enhancement intervention mitigating negative affectivity in both contexts. 
These findings do not imply that different cultural groups necessarily have similar determinants of happiness. Indeed, relationship harmony was found to be more important to the happiness of people with interdependent selves than for those with independent selves (Kwan et al., 1997; Lu et al., 2001; Stewart et al., 2003; Uchida & Kitayama, 2009). Nevertheless, these studies do indicate that (culturally appropriate) self- enhancement and positive self- regard are tied to East- Asians’ subjective well- being, at least to a certain extent. Moreover, across cultures, personal achievement is considered a feature of happiness (about 25% with no significant cultural variation; Uchida & Kitayama, 2009). Therefore, even in this most independent domain of self- achievements, the motivation to have a positive self- view (and thus, the drive to self- enhance) exists and is linked with perceptions of happiness. 
Another group of studies had nevertheless shown that culture moderated this link between self- enhancement and well- being. For example, Arnault, Sakamoto, and Moriwaki (2005) found a significant link between the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) and negative self- descriptor for American but not Japanese women. 
The inconsistencies in this literature suggest the need for further research into possible moderators of these effects. Such moderators are likely related to differences in research design and operationalization. First, as we discussed earlier, the operationalizations of self- enhancement used in different studies are not all equally valid in face cultures. Second, well- being was operationalized in a variety of ways as well, conceivably influencing the studied relation. Nevertheless, a positive relationship between self- enhancement and well- being has been supported by a large variety of studies, methodologies, and research groups. Furthermore, available experimental evidence supports the proposed causal relations between self- enhancement and well- being in face cultures as well as in dignity cultures. It therefore seems likely that high self- regard is predictive of well- being and psychological adjustment across cultures. It follows that culturally appropriate forms of self- enhancement contribute to psychological health and individual adjustment outside the limited context of dignity cultures. If self- enhancement is universally adaptive (albeit through culturally specific mechanisms), the motivation to self- enhance should likewise be universal. 
Based on the preceding body of evidence, we believe that there are core commonalities across cultures regarding the affective aspect of the self, the universal need for positive self- regard, and the underlying self- enhancement motive (see polemic summary in Table 17.1). Certainly, cultures have a great deal of impact on these aspects of the self, but their influence stops short of changing what individuals want and need. The culturally specific 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  563 
ways that these needs manifest in observable behavior is nonetheless an issue of great importance, which we next discuss from another perspective, that of self- presentation. 
The Behavioral Aspect of the Self and Culture: Self- Presentation With the increasing prominence of research into executive functions (e.g., Barkley, 2012), some scholars refer to self- regulation as the self ’s behavioral aspect (Brehm & Kassin, 1993). Cross- cultural differences in self- regulation, however, have already been thoroughly investigated, discussed, and integrated by numerous authors. In light of this, and in keeping with the current focus on issues of self- regard, we offer a limited discussion of cultural variations in self- presentation behaviors to provide a cultural perspective on the self ’s behavioral aspects (following Osborne, 1996). 
Self- presentation was first introduced and defined by Goffman (1959) in his classic work, The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life. In his book, Goffman focused prima-rily on strategic self- presentation, through which individuals deliberately create certain impressions and guises as part of their pursuit of personal interests. This perspective was later extended to include the viewers of these displays of self, so that self- presentation (and its close companion, impression management) was defined as the act of negotiating identities with an audience (Schlenker, 1980). Indeed, all self- presentations carry the potential for social influence and are thus only enacted within some kind of social interaction. While self- enhancement may remain entirely private (e.g., as the story individuals tell themselves to account for their successes and failures), self- presentations are public acts that are behavioral by their very nature. Furthermore, because the possibility of social judgment is inherent to self- presentation, it stands to reason this construct would evince observable cultural variations. 
These differences are again expected to conform to the cultural considerations discussed earlier: Outside the context of dignity cultures, different forms of social judgment and scrutiny are emphasized over individual self- expression, leading to more extensive use of strategic self- presentation. This should be especially true in face contexts, where self- restraint is mandated for the sake of maintaining social harmony. In such contexts, individuals are directed to fit in, conform, and constantly mind their social station— a mandate wholly incompatible with unfettered self- expression and the individual uniqueness it establishes (e.g., Hemert, Vijver, Poortinga, & Georgas, 2002; Lalwani et al. 2009; Triandis & Suh 2002). 
Building on these premises, Riemer and Shavitt (2011) suggested that, in collectivist cultures, the ubiquitous demand for presentation of a normative, socially appropriate image would render the self- presentation process relatively automatic and thus less effortful. Consequently, the depletion of ego resources associated with strategic self- presentation in the West (Vohs, Baumeister, & Ciarocco, 2005)  should be weaker when collectivism is dominant. To test these hypotheses, Reimer and Shavitt instructed 
 
 
564 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
participants to remember an 8- digit number as they filled out an impression management questionnaire. As expected, the cognitive load created by keeping the number in mind affected the impression management abilities of those with low collectivism at the personal level (Study 1) and of those whose culture is noncollectivistic (Americans; Study 2). It did not affect impression management among those with high collectivism or those from an Asian culture (from Hong Kong or Singapore). 
Turning from the lab to natural organizational settings, Lu, Cooper, and Lin (2013) investigated what they called “presenteeism” and showed it was more prevalent among Chinese than among British employees. Unlike the results reported earlier, presenteeism was positively related to exhaustion for both Chinese and British employees, especially for those who had supervisory support. These incongruent results may reflect the universal costs of presenting an artificial self- image within long- term relationships as opposed to short- term episodes (e.g., Paulhus, 1998). In the context of a supportive atmosphere where unmanaged authenticity is presumably more of an option, strategic self- presentation may tax an individual’s resources, even in cultures in which self- presentation is prevalent. 
 Another relevant in vivo setting is that of job interviews. These afford an appealing setting for the study of self- presentation because individuals seeking jobs have a relatively uniform motivation— to present an appealing, highly hirable image of themselves (Leary & Kowalski, 1991). In their large- scale study (N = 3509), Sandal et al. (2014) asked students from 10 countries to indicate how they present themselves in job interviews. Endorsements of four self- presentation tactics (assertiveness, emphasizing individual differences, accommodation, and pointing out obstacles) were then related to country- level value priorities (Schwartz, 1999, 2006). In line with hypotheses, individuals from countries high on embeddedness (assigning great importance to conformity and tradition; i.e., Malaysia, Iran, Ghana, Hong Kong, and Turkey) endorsed more self- presentation tactics overall in comparison to those from countries relatively low on embeddedness (Germany, Norway, the United States, Italy, and the Russian Federation). This difference was greatest for the tactic of pointing out obstacles, as well as for the accommodation tactic, though to a lesser degree. The authors interpreted the especially pronounced difference regarding pointing out obstacles as indicative of embedded individuals’ strategic self- protection. Within embeddedness- oriented cultures, recruiting external factors as possible explanations for future failures may help the candidate save face later. Needless to say, preparing for the possibility of future failure was not considered to be an effective self- presentation tactic by low- embeddedness participants. 
The findings just reviewed point to the greater overall reliance on self- presentation tactics in face cultures. Given the modesty and humility norms in these cultures, it is not surprising that the preferred tactics adopted for self- presentation do not include straightforward self- promotion. Work conducted on perceptions and judgments of explicitly positive self- presentation in different cultures further illustrates this point. 
Chen and Jing (2012), for instance, asked participants to read a (fictitious) self- presentation of a student who is competing for an award. Participants’ collectivism was 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  565 
predictive of greater liking and higher perceived competence of the candidate with the more modest self- presentation. In contrast, individualism of the raters was related to higher ratings for the boastful presenter. In another study, competence and likability of professors as a function of self- enhancing versus self- effacing presentations were studied in the United States (continental and Hawaii), as well as in South Korea (Kim, Berger, Kim, & Kim, 2014). Students read a hypothetical professor’s self- introduction at the beginning of the semester; these self- presentations were either self- enhancing or self- effacing. Not surprisingly, in all three locations, professors who self- enhanced were perceived as more competent than those who self- effaced. Likability of self- effacers (as opposed to self- enhancers) was increased in the American contexts but not in South Korea. Correlational analyses showed that independent self- construal was positively related to greater competence assigned to the self- enhancing presentation in the United States and to both greater competence and likability in Korea. The varying degree of likability among self- enhancers in the two studies can be explained by the different targets used. In a context where self- enhancement is expected and competence is guaranteed, as in the case of the professors, a modest self- presentation can perhaps humanize the superior and signal her or his approachability, thus incurring greater likability. 
It can be concluded that, in non- Western cultures, individuals engage in more extensive and strategic self- presentation. Mirroring the previous discussion on self- enhancement, however, the face that is displayed is not necessarily the boastful self- promoting one commonly associated with impression management in the West. Figure 17.1 offers a schematic description of our major claims up to this point. It relates dignity versus face cultural settings to issues of self- enhancement (summarizing our position, as presented in Table 17.1) and integrate them with cultural variances in self- presentation. 
In recent years, online life has emerged as a central sociocultural setting for impression management. This sociocultural shift has piqued the interest of researchers, such that much of the scholarly attention has shifted to the study of self- presentation carried out in online settings. Specifically, many researchers have been attracted to social media as a new platform consisting almost entirely of displayed images and evoked impressions. 
Self- Presentation on Social Media Information technology, and specifically the emergence of social networking sites (SNS), has changed human communication and self- expression dramatically (Bazarova, Taft, Choi, & Cosley, 2013; Weiser, 2001). Because of the immediacy and centrality of SNS- mediated social interactions, many people around the world routinely dedicate valuable time and attentional resources to creating, maintaining, and managing their online image. While “the (SNS) medium is the message” to a certain degree (see Reese, Rosenmann, & Cameron, 2019), impression management on SNS generally demonstrates the cultural variations found in other media. 
Qiu, Lin, and Leung (2012) demonstrated the interaction between national culture and cultural elements embedded within SNS media. In their study, they adopted a

natural priming approach, documenting the differential use of Facebook and Renren (the Chinese- language SNS) by the same individuals. They further distinguished between two ways of using SNS. The first is self- focused, with activities aimed at self- disclosure or self- promotion. This usage is typical to Facebook and related to narcissism. The second form of use, “benevolent sharing with the in- group,” is other- centered and includes such activities as sharing information that may be useful for others (e.g., travel tips). They found that Chinese- speaking users flexibly switched between platforms, conducting more in- group sharing behaviors on Renren and acting in a more self- focused way on Facebook. 
 Studies conducted in the West revealed that intensive social activity on SNS in and of itself is predictive of self- promoting presentation tactics. Buffardi and Campbell (2008), for example, revealed a positive correlation between narcissism and numbers of social interactions on Facebook. Ryan and Xenos (2011) investigated a large sample of Australian Facebook users (N = 1,324) and showed that extraversion, significantly related to narcissism, exhibited a significantly positive correlation with preferences for all of the communicative features in Facebook. 
As both extraversion and narcissism are traditionally lower in face cultures, it can be postulated that SNS would be less appealing to those who live in such cultural contexts than to Westerners. SNS technology was also originally developed within Western settings and clearly manifests the cultural sensitivities of its origins (Reese et al., 2019). On the other hand, we have already reviewed evidence showing that strategic self- presentation is more endemic to face cultures. If SNS interactions are intrinsically linked with deliberate self- presentation (e.g., by narrowing the bandwidth of social cues and omitting nonverbal signals that may belie attempts to strategically self- present), then perhaps those most adept at keeping face would take to SNS more eagerly. The cultural perspective on SNS self- presentation is still a developing area of research, but one that has already yielded some interesting insights, which we report next. 
In line with well- established cultural differences from Americans, South Koreans reported they care more about the impression they make on other Facebook users and thus self- disclose less freely (Yoo, Kim, & Moon, 2012). Chen and Marcus (2012) similarly reported that collectivist individuals who are low on extraversion disclosed the least candid and the most audience- relevant information online. In contrast, authentic self- expression was a leading guide in SNS presentation in Finland (Uski & Lampinen, 2016), supporting the general findings of lower use of strategic self- presentation in European countries (Sandal et al., 2014). Indeed, Ghanaians and Turks engaged in more comprehensive impression management relative to Norwegians and Germans (Bye et al., 2011). Most recently, experimental studies supplied further support for these same trends. Lee- Won, Shim, Joo, and Park (2014) reported that a prime of interdependent self- construal decreased subsequent behavioral intentions to engage in positive self- presentation on SNS. 
 Other aspects of self- presenting behavior in SNS settings reveal familiar cultural differences as well. For instance, Merkin (2012) found that Israelis used more direct forms 
568 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
of impression management than Syrians. A study that investigated willingness to post and actual posting of pictures depicting “improper” behavior (e.g., drinking at a party) revealed significant differences between Turkey and the United States, with Americans being less reserved than Turkish participants (Günsoy, Cross, Saribay, Ökten, & Kurutaş, 2015). In addition, individual endorsement of honor considerations predicted a lower number of improper pictures posted in both cultural settings. 
In summary, cultural norms regarding self- presentation are consistent in SNS and other interactions. Figure 17.1 points to less use of self- presentation strategies but more self- promotion in the West compared with other parts of the world. This nascent research also suggests that SNS may facilitate specific culturally informed behaviors. SNS have become central sociocultural arenas, governed by formal and informal norms and regulations, as well as by specific cultural emphases codified into their technological infrastructure. We conclude with a more general discussion of contemporary selfhood and its vectors as related to the transformative processes of globalization. 
Selfhood in an Age of Globalization and Consumerism In the preceding discussions, we have mapped some ways in which cultures structure different aspects of individuals’ selves as individuals simultaneously enact, transmit, and transform their respective cultures. As demonstrated, this reciprocal relationship has long captured the attention of researchers and theorists who have developed a rich and highly diverse body of psychological literature. While the dynamic nature of cultures is a repeatedly mentioned axiom within this literature, it seems that it has largely neglected the changing dynamics introduced by globalizing processes and their profound effects on cultures and societies around the world (for exceptions, see, e.g., the works of Chiu, 2006; Kashima et al., 2011; Matsumoto, 1999; also see Chapter 23 by Huajian Cai, Zihang Huang, and Yiming Jing on changes in cultures across time). 
Providing a comprehensive introduction to the economic, political, and sociocultural phenomena characterizing this globalizing age is beyond the scope of this chapter. Therefore, we will simply define globalization as a set of interlocking processes that dramatically increase the mutual dependency and interconnectedness of economies, societies, and cultures around the world (see Rosenmann, Reese, & Cameron, 2016). Indeed, even within lay public discourses, the impact of globalization on nations’ socioeconomic arrangements and culture looms large (e.g., Griva & Chryssochoou, 2015; Kashima et al., 2011). 
Because cultural exchange is unavoidable within this global context, the processes of globalization evoke an acculturative response even in those who are not counted among the growing numbers of immigrants, refugees, and sojourners. As an acculturative process, globalization presents both opportunities and challenges to individuals’ selves. 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  569 
Many have heralded this globalizing age as marking the emergence of new, more tolerant forms of selfhood as people around the globe are exposed to new cultural worldviews and systems of meaning (Hermans & Dimaggio, 2007). Indeed, never before have so many undergone this type of acculturation and at such a fast pace. Whenever a new cultural worldview is acquired, it reveals that the default, mono- cultural understanding of the world as “just the way things are” is in fact saturated with specific cultural structures and biases (Chiu, 2006; Oyserman, 2017). Thus, in a world where simple mono- culturalism becomes less common, cultures may lose some of their taken- for- granted quality. Instead, multiculturalism facilitates and intensifies a critical evaluation of cultural dogma and thus affords the vantage point required for cultural choice (Hermans & Dimaggio, 2007). 
Hermans’s (1996) influential account of the dialogical self captures this notion of the self as incorporating multiple voices representing differing positions, narratives, and cultural perspectives. Functioning as an intraindividual democracy (Hermans, Konopka, Oosterwegel, & Zomer, 2016), dialogical selfhood is required if individuals are to be able to adapt successfully to the multiplicity of perspectives engendered by globalization (Hermans & Dimaggio, 2007). Unfortunately, an abundance of research, some of which was reviewed earlier, has demonstrated that such multivocal selfhood may not be a viable, or indeed an adaptive, psychological position for many. Moreover, even in cultures that foster a form of decentralized selfhood (i.e., in face settings), the degree to which the self is thus unintegrated is linked with lowered self- worth and well- being. This evidence suggests that self- decentralization may not be fully compatible with psychological adjustment regardless of an individual’s culture of upbringing. If this is indeed true, then globalization’s decentralized, multivocal perspective may challenge the well- being of those born into its clamor. 
Additionally, if the manifestations of selfhood are inseparable from the surrounding cultural context, then wherever culture is headed, selfhood inexorably follows. Thus, the spread of globalizing transformations of cultures and societies around the world requires us to consider possible changes to prevalent forms of selfhood. Because cultural change occurs over time and modes of selfhood are internalized slowly through socialization, direct empirical investigation of this intriguing issue is not readily available. Nonetheless, scholars have suggested different— at times conflicting— theoretical predictions. These are discussed next in terms of theories of modernization. 
Retention and Transition of Culture and Selfhood It seems that the most theoretically developed response to this question emerges from the controversy between proponents and critiques of theories of modernization. According to these theories, individualism, and hence independent selfhood, is driven primarily by economic and technologic advances (e.g., Hamamura, 2012). As societies adjust to new levels of affluence and technological sophistication, smaller social units become functionally superior. For instance, whereas in premodern agricultural settings survival could not be guaranteed without the safety net provided by reciprocal reliance on an extended 
 
570 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
kinship group, this is no longer the case for most of those living in contemporary, economically developed settings. With increased affluence, subsistence ceases to be a preoccupation for many, freeing people to pursue the interests of the smallest social unit of all— the individual (e.g., Fukuyama, 2006). 
According to such a perspective, globalization, with its increasing affluence and distancing technologies, would inevitably lead to less communal social structures and thus more independent forms of selfhood (Matsumoto, 1999). In response to these predictions, critics cite the perseverance of core cultural differences as evidence for the resilience of local cultural syndromes, even within nations that are fully developed economically (e.g., face in Japan). If economic development does not invariably lead to cultural homogenization, as simplistic modernization theories imply, then the evolutionary cultural process of modernization is not universal (e.g., Chiu, 2006). Indeed, data suggest that cultures’ contemporary value profiles are based mostly on their histories and traditional worldviews and not on their current level of economic development. These same sources, however, also show that while cultures differ in their starting points, they mostly follow the same trajectory, leading to more self- centric and rationally organized societies (i.e., a vector of modernization; see Inglehart & Baker, 2000; Chapter 23 by Huajian Cai, Zihang Huang, and Yiming Jing also discusses increasing individualism around the world as a result of modernization). 
These complexities were illustrated in Hamamura’s (2012) attempt to empirically address this overarching question by conducting an extensive analysis of cross- temporal trends of indices of collectivism versus individualism in the United States and Japan. While for the period examined (between 1950 and 2008), this analysis yielded somewhat inconsistent patterns (between nations and between indices analyzed), some consistencies were observed. These commonalities were mostly found regarding demographic trends (e.g., diminishing size of households). Attitudinal indices yielded less coherent patterns, with the notable exception of importance of effort to success, which demonstrated a consistent increased over time in both countries. This belief had been theoretically and empirically linked with collectivism. The increasing levels of an indicator of collectivism in the presumably individualistic United States was not congruent with either a modernization trend toward individualism or the persistence of cultural heritages (see also Chapter 23 by Huajian Cai, Zihang Huang, and Yiming Jing). 
In the current context, we suggest that while this pattern is not consistent with a uniform trend toward individualism per se, it is highly consistent with the spread of consumerism in both nations. Within consumerist contexts, belief in personal effort is crucial— individuals have to believe that if they would only apply themselves and commit fully to the pursuit of material success, they will achieve the sought- after “good life” they so richly deserve (Dittmar, 2007). Even as the role of effort is appreciated primarily in collectivistic settings as a means of maintaining social and interpersonal harmony, it perhaps has a different function in contemporary contexts, where it spurs individuals to persist in their consumeristic pursuits.
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  571 
Relatedly, because the explicitly individualistic Westernized content of globalized culture is highly contested and often resisted (e.g., Chiu, 2006), globalization’s vectors of cultural homogenization may be more strongly based on the widening cultural infrastructure of consumerism (Ram, 2004). Because consumerist forms can easily coopt local heritage and thus accommodate local preferences (e.g., traditional Chinese mooncake vs. American Christmas cookie latte at the respective Starbucks branches), they appear culture- neutral or disappear from sight altogether. This perception notwithstanding, these consumerist forms are in fact required for the globalized socioeconomic order to function and thus are becoming the standard template for societal and psychological realities (Kasser, Cohn, Kanner, & Ryan, 2007). Hence, consumerism becomes a central cultural theme which prescribes, organizes, and legitimizes a myriad of social and individual behaviors— that is, a cultural syndrome (Triandis, 1995). 
Space limitations preclude a full exploration of this emergent cultural syndrome of global consumerism. Nevertheless, it can be described briefly as a constellation of beliefs, practices, and systems of valuation that define proper consumption as the basis for individuals’ claims to identity, status, and group affiliation. It channels manifestations of personal autonomy and self- expression into consumer behaviors, which are now needed to achieve and maintain coherent selfhood (Featherstone, 2007). Within this framework, an unprecedented variety of human needs and desires are shaped and then satisfied by the acquisition and use of commodities (in the form of material goods or services) that are sold for profit in the marketplace (see Reese et al., 2019). In this way, consumerism as a globalizing cultural syndrome is necessary for the continued stability of today’s globalized, corporate capitalism (Kasser, 2016). 
The Psychology of Consumer Selfhood In order to elaborate on the self- psychology corresponding with this emerging cultural syndrome, we first turn to research on the United States. In the past half- century, with consumerism rising to become an endemic cultural syndrome, individuals’ sense of self- worth has increased. Based on a recent HLM analysis specifically designed to identify cohort effects, Twenge, Carter, and Campbell (2017) report that self- esteem has been increasing in later cohorts of their representative national sample. This finding supports similar conclusions from earlier meta- analytical and large- scale studies demonstrating an inflation of self- esteem ratings among Americans (e.g., Twenge et al., 2017). 
Contrary to evidence from individual- level analyses (see earlier discussion), however, these increases in self- worth have not been associated with a comparable rise in individuals’ psychological wellness or mental health. Quite the contrary. Meta- analyses have documented, for example, a general rise in pathological personality tendencies (Twenge et al., 2010) and especially narcissism (e.g., Twenge, Konrath, Foster, Campbell, & Bushman, 2008; see Ahuvia & Izberk- Bilgin, 2013, on the wider question of consumerism and well- being). We interpret this as a decline in genuine self- worth, with compensatory defensive dynamics taking its place. This seems to be the case because consumer 
 
572 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
cultures instill individuals with an insatiable hunger for validation, which in turn feeds a porous, structurally fragile sense of self- worth (Cushman, 1990). 
This is not an unintended side effect of increased consumerism, but rather a product of direct and (at least at times) conscious efforts by marketers. As early as the 1930s, marketers’ trade literature suggested that “advertising helps to keep the masses dissatisfied with their mode of life, discontented with ugly things around them. Satisfied customers are not as profitable as discontented ones” (Dickinson, 1930; as cited in Ewen, 2001). If individuals’ lives, selves, and possessions are always unsatisfactory and not up to the media- propagated ideal, people could easily be persuaded to spend their resources on the newest commodity offered for consumption in the marketplace (Cushman, 1990). Consumer selfhood is thus fragile by definition. It is contingent on the constant external validation of others whose function is to “like,” admire, and envy the individual for his or her consumer lifestyle (Reese et al., 2019). Coincidently, these dynamics of consumerism are remarkably similar to those described in relation to narcissistic personality tendencies. 
The inherent incompleteness of consumer selfhood is the backdrop against which consumerist pursuits are set. Different products are offered on the market to supply symbolic scaffolding for the self, now needed to shore up individuals’ sense of coherent selfhood and identity. Given the psychological meaning attached to these products and their indispensable symbolic functions, they become extensions of the self (Belk, 1988). Research has supported this contention by demonstrating, first, that consumer goods play a role in many self- functions. Thus, experimental studies have demonstrated that individuals consider brand choices as expressive of their personal and social identities (Cătălin & Andreea, 2014). Other studies have shown the importance of brand consumption as a vehicle for the expression and reification of self- worth (Shachar, Erdem, Cutright, & Fitzsimons, 2011). Moreover, research has also demonstrated that the symbolic link between self and consumer products is such that threats to a cherished brand are experienced as threats to the self, eliciting defensive reactions from those whose self is structurally fragile (Lisjak, Lee, & Gardner, 2012). Conversely, consumption of high- status goods was shown to mitigate the effects of threats to the self by affirming self- worth or compensating for its loss (Sivanathan & Pettit, 2010). Indeed, researchers have recently argued for the inclusion of brand ownership as an integral part of the conceptualization and thus the measurement of contemporary self- worth and deserving of a new subscale in self- worth measures (in a sample of British adolescents; Isaksen & Roper, 2016). 
If we employ the terms discussed earlier, this consumer selfhood is externally contingent as self- worth becomes anchored in the vagaries of others’ judgments of the self and its presented consumer lifestyle (Kasser, 2016). Note that this externalization of self- worth is counter to the individualist emphasis on dignity as an internal and inalienable source of basic human worth. Such an externally derived sense of self is also unstable and low in clarity (Kernis, 2003). This structural instability is again adaptive from a market 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  573 
perspective as it renders individuals highly susceptible to the influence of advertisements and other marketing ploys (Mittal, 2015). 
These marketing efforts, which permeate every corner of consumer societies, incessantly evoke an image of a better, happier, more worthy self (Hockley & Fadina, 2015). They thus direct the individual to constantly seek higher self- esteem, greater happiness, a better life— all ostensibly achievable by consumption. As part of these pursuits, individuals are always called on to make personal choices— of which brand to identify with and which version of the consumerist “good life” to aspire to. This seemingly autonomous decision- making serves to strengthen individuals’ engagement and commitment (Moller, Ryan, & Deci, 2006; Thompson, & Loveland, 2015) while never actually affording them the option of opting- out of consumerism (Holt, 2002). Ironically, this motivational focus on increasing self- esteem (as opposed to self- improvement) is detrimental to psychological, relational, and societal well- being (Bushman, Moeller, Konrath, & Crocker, 2012; Crocker & Park, 2004), as is the everlasting pursuit of happiness itself (Schooler, Ariely, & Loewenstein, 2003). Furthermore, decades of research have invariably demonstrated that this type of psychologically aimed consumption does not lead to sustainable increases in genuine self- esteem or general well- being. In fact, those who buy into this prevailing consumer myth that a better self and a better life is just around the corner in a store that sells the coveted product du jour are worse off for it (see for review, e.g., Kasser, 2016). 
In all of this, consumer culture creates a feedback loop between its macro socioeconomic structures and individuals’ selfhood. The commercial interests that govern the macro- level structures in consumer cultures profit from instilling a fragile, consumption- dependent sense of self. This consumer selfhood is also structurally unsound, as the ever- changing standards propagated by marketers feed a constant pursuit of a better, more complete self that is never to be found. This flux may be evident not only on an individual level, but also on the wider cultural level as well. Consumerism and globalizing processes more generally disrupt individuals’ sense of cultural clarity and continuity (Kinnvall, 2004). The mere perception that one’s culture is no longer stable, coherent, and clearly defined has been linked with lowered individual self- concept clarity and, through it, with lesser well- being (Usborne & Taylor, 2010). This consumerist turn of culture and its accompanying forms of selfhood in turn guarantee the willing participation of individuals in the consumption cycle, as well as their continued support for the macro system and its legitimacy (to the extent that there seems to be no viable alternatives to it; Kasser, 2016). Without viable options for dissent or opting- out, consumer culture becomes further entrenched as the organizing principle of both societal and psychological dynamics (i.e., a globally prevailing cultural syndrome). 
This cultural syndrome is expanding in all directions (Reese, Rosenmann, & Cameron, 2019): vertically, by encompassing more socioeconomic classes, including the world’s poorest— the so- called bottom of the pyramid (Wood, Pitta, & Franzak, 2008); horizontally, by permeating new cultural settings as globalization opens up new markets; 
574 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and in depth, by incorporating previously noncommodified resources and forms of social exchange. The examples that most readily come to mind for this globalizing cultural syndrome likely involve the adoption of Western brands and consumer lifestyles in distinctly non- Western settings (e.g., Chiu, 2006) as individuals around the world develop cosmopolitan consumer identities (Cleveland, Laroche, & Papadopoulos, 2009). Nonetheless, even people whose consumer practices are diametrically opposed (e.g., only buying goods produced and tailored for the local market as a way of asserting a traditional or national identity; Cleveland et al., 2009) similarly yoke their identities, claims for status, and group allegiances on consumption and are thus no less consumerist. Stated more generally, even though the coupling of a self- identity and a specific consumer lifestyle is context- dependent, within consumerist societies, the need for such an association remains constant and largely uncontested (Holt, 2002). 
Therefore, as consumerism and the language of consumer selfhood become the one truly global vernacular, these effects can be expected to increase elsewhere around the world (Rosenmann et al., 2016). For example, recent research demonstrated that Chinese individuals are increasingly likely to engage in self- enhancement the more they identify with contemporary (i.e., globalized vs. traditional) Chinese culture. Self- enhancement also increased when such identification was experimentally primed as opposed to simply measured (Zhang, Noels, Guan, & Weng, 2017). Correspondingly, individuals from more globalized sections of Chinese society (i.e., wealthier, more urbanite, and endorsing of individualist values) were found to exhibit more narcissistic tendencies when compared with their more traditional counterparts (Cai, Kwan, & Sedikides, 2012). Within the rapidly globalizing context of Chinese society, some research has already documented what appear to be cohort effects associated with this transition. In a recent study of Chinese secondary school students (N = 1,364), Hu, Zhang, and Ran (2016) showed a strong trend of self- serving attributional biases such that positive outcomes were attributed to more internal, stable, and general sources than negative outcomes (effect size for the composed score: d = 1.23). This is in stark contrast to the abundance of findings (see earlier discus-sion) traditionally associating face cultures with much lower levels of such self- serving biases. 
Conclusion In this chapter, we discussed topics pertaining to the influence of culture on individuals’ selfhood. We reviewed influences regarding the content and organization of the self- schema (a part of the self ’s cognitive aspect), self- regard and how it is anchored (the affective facet of the self), and, finally, how these cultural emphases shape the way individuals present their selves to others (a behavioral component). Throughout, we argued that while these observable cultural influences are often profound, they do not change the core processes of the self or the ways in which these relate to wider issues of psychological adjustment and well- being. 
 
 
The CulTurally s iTuaTed self  |  575 
Whereas no consistent cultural differences can be pointed out regarding the content of the self- concept, some such findings emerge with regard to the structure of the self- concept. It appears that self- complexity (and especially the number of self- aspects) is higher in face cultures in which the inclusion of others in the self expands it. Contrarily, greater self- clarity is more typical of dignity cultures, which encourage a selfhood encapsulating inner, noncontextualized, personality characteristics. Even as cultures impact levels of self- complexity and self- clarity, their effects seem universal. Thus, people everywhere draw benefits from having a stable, congruent sense of self (as in higher self- clarity) and from the buffering against self- threats which is afforded by high self- complexity. 
The debate about the universality of the desire for positive self- regard was extensively discussed. We reviewed the restricted manifestations of self- enhancement in face cultures as well as some empirical findings and at times compelling theoretical arguments cited by those who posit that self- enhancement is a culturally bound motivation, largely irrelevant outside of dignity cultures. Nonetheless, we argued for the universality of the self- enhancement motive and reviewed supporting evidence and theorizations. This polemic is schematically summarized in Table 17.1. More specifically, we pointed to the role of modesty norms and other forms of social scrutiny within face contexts in forcefully discouraging manifestations of “Western- style,” blatant self- enhancement. When these face concerns are alleviated, however, self- enhancement in face culture increases and resembles self- enhancement in dignity cultures. 
The same normative concerns of face versus dignity cultures inform the closely linked behavioral aspect of the self:  self- presentation. The use of self- presentation tactics is more endemic to face cultures, and, as a result, they become less cognitively consuming. Notably, these self- presentation tactics are not aimed at overt positive presentation of the self given the social norms and sanctions against such practice. Recent data on self- presentation in SNS follow the same pattern: in comparison to dignity contexts, face cultures foster less genuine and less positive self- presentations. These patterns are presented in Figure 17.1. 
The Culturally Situated Self: Looking Ahead We began by reviewing the classic model of Markus and Kitayama (1991) and demonstrated how it reflects the social and scientific zeitgeist of its times. We believe that today it is important for cross- cultural psychology to engage in the zeitgeist of the current era and to devote more systematic attention to the emerging conditions of globalization and consumer culture. 
As globalization causes consumer culture to expand and engulf new locales, more varied socioeconomic classes, and more forms of social exchange, we predict that it may propagate its brand of selfhood, with its built- in vulnerabilities and structural fragility. We thus certainly agree with Hermans’s analysis of the self- destabilizing effects of globalization, but perhaps we are less optimistic about the prospects of this process. Indeed, 
 
576 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
in his work, Hermans recognizes human “biological needs” for stability and security and the power of these needs to limit the degree to which we are receptive to the beneficial potentials of this cultural change (Hermans & Dimaggio, 2007). 
These needs and core processes of the self are what may become increasingly strained by globalization’s consumerist turn. As the mediums of consumerism shape the cultural messages individuals receive (e.g., Qiu et al., 2012), this societal sea change will inevitably find expression in individuals’ selves. Within this context, individualism and collectivism are gradually being reduced to marketing ploys— ways to optimally frame marketing messages. Stripped of both dignity and meaningful connection to others, the self is thus made contingent on these manipulated externalities. Within this frame, self- presentation becomes tantamount to self- worth, and even authenticity represents another desirable image to be maintained through proper consumption (Featherstone, 2007).

Social Representations of History as Common Ground for Processes of Intergroup Relations and the Content of Social Identities 
James H. Liu and Dario Páez 
The past two decades have witnessed an explosive advance in culture- rich theory for the study of intergroup relations and social identity. The concept of social representations of history or collective remembering has enriched process- oriented psychology with content, or culturally constructed common ground (Kashima, 2014) that moderates and provides mediators for the operation of culture- general theories and social processes. This chapter first introduces and reviews the toolkit of concepts enabling theorists to diagnose how culture- general processes of intergroup relations and social identity may have been adapted to function in specific contexts, including the pervasive globalization of the twenty- first century. It emphasizes narrative as a core representational concept facilitating the formation and legitimation of states— particularly, romantic nineteenth- century narratives which were at the heart of nineteenth- century European historiography. Following from this, it reviews some important studies in this area (first global then country- specific), illustrating more precisely how content inflects or underpins process and how process changes content in the work of applying psychological theory on history to intergroup relations and social identities changing over 
 
 
soCial rePresenTaT ions of hisTory  |  587 
time. The take- home message is that social representations of history serve as symbolic resources enabling a society or culture (including global culture) to communicate what has worked for it in the past as a means for dealing with its intergroup relations in the present and future. 
While there is considerable global common ground in representing history around the world (with World War II providing the base), there is also considerable variability in the meaning of the lessons in different parts of the world, with young people from developed, Western nations taking a less romantic and more postmodern view of warfare as calamity, and people from developing nations taking a more stoic view of warfare and suffering as part of the process of nation- building. Using social representations of history as grist for the mill of communication within and between groups in society, the content of the national identity of a people is constructed as a dialogue between past and present, in building an agenda for the future. Through use of historical symbols, the heroes and villains, calamities and triumphs of not only global culture, but also of specific nationalities is communicated in an emotionally resonant manner to different groups that interact with one another to form societies and cultures. 
A Toolkit for Conceptualizing Groups as Meaningful Entities Extending Through Time At the core of a representational approach to intergroup relations is shared meaning: the idea that human beings are actively socialized into systems of meaning that not only define who they are and how they relate to the people and institutions around them, but that also allow them a degree of agency to maintain continuity amid change. Liu and Sibley (2009) wrote that “social representations are defined as a shared system of knowledge and belief that facilitates communication about social objects, and culture is conceptualized as a meta- system of social representations mediated by language, symbols, and their institutional carriers” (p. 22). According to such a symbolic approach (see Geertz, 1973), culture is conceived of as an interlocking series of communications repertoires, with particular systems of meaning invoked to maintain the political order or legitimacy prevalent in various institutions, ranging from family or neighborhoods to government. In particular, history is able to communicate a form of legitimacy that Malinowski (1926) describes as the “warrant of antiquity” using tradition and the lessons of history to justify the way things are done here and now (Liu & Sibley, 2015). Groups that aspire to immortality over time by attempting to maintain cultural traditions and claims to sovereignty over a land (e.g., the right to decide questions of life and death) are those most in need of the warrant of legitimacy that history provides, because history is the embodiment of peoples enduring through time, with the rights, privileges, and responsibilities this implies. 
 
588 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
The Role of the State and Other Institutions/ Groups in Shaping Historical Representations as “Common Ground” Controlling narratives of history is one way a state exerts control over dissident groups (Nora, 1989) who may in turn challenge state legitimacy by producing alternative historical accounts (Kus, Ward, & Liu, 2013). The state typically constructs a top- down narrative of history to justify itself and erase alternative accounts. Alternative accounts typically accord with the collective memories of groups aspiring to greater autonomy and a different grasp of the facts than the state (see Liu & Robinson, 2016, for a historical analysis of the Aotearoa/ New Zealand’s Māori). In addition to the state and other sovereign collectives, smaller groups like families or companies may also use a warrant of antiquity to inspire adherence to a charter that articulates the group’s values (or creed/ code of conduct, see Malinowski, 1926). Informal communication, the horizontal social sharing of information and social emotions also feed collective memory (Rimé, 2007). 
Successful state control over the process of historical representation would be described by Moscovici (1988) as hegemonic; the state has to harness informal communication, social emotions, and popular media.1 Establishing a widely consensual narrative of origin is regarded by Malinowski (1926) as essential to group stability. Hilton and Liu (2008) elaborated on Malinowski’s idea of a historical charter “as a widely shared and iconic representation where selective elements of group history, its causes, and consequences have been elaborated into a quasi- legal form that gives moral and sometimes legal implications for group action . . . providing a common understanding through which dialogue flows  .  .  . used to justify certain privileges and social arrangements in society, and [is] perceived as part of the fabric of social reality” (p.  345). A  historical charter would therefore contain widely shared (but selective) knowledge that comes to be regarded as part of the political culture of a people (or smaller group) defining rights, obligations, and roles; invoked to justify political arrangements; and used to settle or make arguments. It is often called to account to refresh or reaffirm basic principles of the group described in its narrative of origin (see Sibley, Liu, Duckitt & Khan, 2008). It is not history itself, but a narrative of history containing ideological (or mythological) elements and selected facts (see Wertsch & Roediger, 2008, or Schwartz, 1997, for discussion of the differences between history and historical representations). 
Compared to other elements in the repertoire of culture- oriented psychology, such as values, axioms, implicit theories, or beliefs, historical representations are more concrete. They include specific events and stories about individual figures, often cast in the 
1. Works of art can provide dramatic accounts of history, with an artistic license that allows them to deviate from “official history” (e.g., the movie JFK sustains a conspiracy theory view of Kennedy’s assassination (Paez & Igartua, 1997). We shall not attempt to address such dynamics in this chapter, but see Winter (2006) for an overview of these issues. 
 
soCial rePresenTaT ions of hisTory  |  589 
roles of hero and villain (see Hanke et  al., 2015). The logic of verisimilitude (truth- seeming) governs historical narratives more than an exact adherence to the historical truth (Bruner, 1990; Liu & László, 2007). Typically, research has focused on nation- states or aspiring states and groups with charter roles within them, where the historical charter (or, less authoritatively, historical narrative) should include a narrative of origin and the ongoing story of a people moving through time (see Huang, Liu, & Chang (2004) for the interesting case of Taiwan and its historical struggle to define itself relative to mainland China). 
More recently, the World History Survey (WHS) has enabled theorists to describe how beliefs about history form the common ground on which young educated people around the world build an understanding of how the political culture of their planet and home culture came to be (see Hanke et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2005, 2009, 2012). The social representations of history described by the WHS can be thought of as both the raw materials (e.g., less well- known elements of history can be revitalized; Liu & Robinson, 2016) and the schema- induced results for collective remembering (e.g., narratives; see Pennebaker, Paez, & Deschamps, 2006). Schwartz (1996) describes collective memories as simultaneously a model of society and a model for society, serving both descriptive and normative functions creating continuity between past, present, and future. 
Representations of History as Narratives Following historiographers like White (1987), Janos László (2008) highlighted that history can be studied as a form of narrative, a story with action templates that form a beginning, middle, and end, populated by heroes, villains, and helpers that make the story a morality play (see also Schwartz, 1996). Such stories provide people with templates to cast their selves and their ingroups (or some other person or outgroup) into meaningful roles. This provides prototypical content for self- categorization processes involving the division of people into ingroups and outgroups (Turner, Hogg, Oakes, Reicher, & Wetherell, 1987). For example, Japanese can easily be cast as the evil villains in the story of the making of the People’s Republic of China (Liu & Atsumi, 2008). Young Japanese people are aware that this role is disadvantageous for them. They may seek to avoid the cast by claiming ignorance or by denying Japanese war crimes (Atsumi & Suwa, 2009). But, given the causes and outcomes of World War II, this position may be difficult to sustain outside of Japan, for historical facts can be invoked to challenge historical representations as part of the dynamic of intergroup relations (Liu & Hilton, 2005). 
The burden of history placed on the main “villains” of World War II, Germany and Japan, can be considered a problem of narrative, history, and identity, as attempts by Germans to “draw a line between the present and past” illustrate (see Hanke et al., 2013; Roth, Huber, Jünger, & Liu, 2017). Thinking of history as a narrative also implies perspective (e.g., of the narrator), and attempts to engender empathy (or disgust) for characters 
 
590 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
in the story (László, 2008; Liu & László, 2007). These enable social roles originating in canonical cultural narratives and lessons from history useful in articulating lessons about cultural continuity (Jetten & Wohl, 2012; Sani et al., 2007) or discontinuity (Roth et al., 2017). Over repeated crises, the specific challenges of history can be societally engineered to become a generalized cognitive narrative template for dealing with future crises (Wertsch, 2002). 
Representations of History as Collective Memories Sociologists studying collective remembering following Halbwachs (1950/ 1980) have emphasized more the institutional forces responsible for producing social memories. In this literature, the canonical narratives mentioned by Liu and László (2007) would be linked to cultural productions like museum displays, commemorations (Olick & Robbins, 1998), collective memories of heroes and martyrs (Schwartz, 1996, 1997), or maps, journalistic practices, and vernaculars (Anderson, 1983; Schwartz, 2014). 
More recently, educationists, especially educational psychologists, have focused their attention on the production of textbooks and history curricula in schools, especially in their relationship to state building and nationalism (Carretero, Berger, & Grever, 2017). This focus on material elements in the production of national culture should be welcomed by psychologists who do not recognize these elements to the extent of other social scientists. It should be recognized that intergroup conflict is produced by institutional forces, particularly those harnessed to producing the nation- state and its discontents (Nora, 1989; Wertsch, 2002). 
In summary, there are multiple sources of social representations of history leading to different forms of representation that may exist side by side in a given society: Moscovici (1988) distinguishes between hegemonic (widely shared, relatively undisputed in terms of meaning), polemical (disputed between different segments of a society), and emancipated (with different versions of history prevalent in different parts of the population, but each with its own accepted sphere of influence) representations. A central process in representation is how individuals appropriate widely- known stories, social facts, rituals, monuments, and canonical works of art to form their own representational profile (Hanke et al., 2015; Sibley & Liu, 2013). People not only assimilate, but also reuse and take agency in revising these cultural toolkits in the process of attributing meaning to their own experiences. For instance, the first studies on public opinion showed that the minute of silence observed for World War I fallen soldiers, which from the perspective of officialdom was supposed to transmit a set of epic and positive nationalistic collective emotions and beliefs, was actually associated to personal recollections of missing relatives and low- arousal negative emotions, like sadness and nostalgia, among individuals (Winter, 2006).

Processes of Social Representation Social representations might be considered as a more dynamic conception of Durkheim’s idea of collective representations, put forward by Moscovici (1976). Importantly, social representations enable persons to assimilate new information about social objects into existing cultural frameworks, to cope with social issues and dilemmas (Moscovici, 1976; Sibley & Liu, 2013; Wagner & Hayes, 2005). Anchoring (Moscovici, 1988) implies a cognitive process wherein new social objects are integrated into the preexisting patterns of representation. For instance, September 11 could be likened to Pearl Harbor, and Saddam Hussein to Hitler through analogical reasoning (see Spellman & Holyoak, 1993). Second, anchoring involves social aspects in which a group gives meaning to their representations through processes of communication (e.g., the “War against Terror” is a just and necessary war, just like World War II; see Jodelet, 2006; or, for explication of the general processes involved, Wagner & Hayes, 2005). 
The process of objectification turns something abstract into something more concrete (Jodelet & Haas, 2014; Wagner & Hayes, 2005). These processes of objectification are present in historical understanding: events are reified in figures (like Columbus, who represents “Discovery,” or Hitler, Nazi evil) and images (Columbus’s three ships are the figurative image of Discovery, Lautier, 2001). Flags, statues, gestures, and emblems are prototypical tools that afford the objectification of representations, symbolizing important meanings and evoking collective emotions. Empirical evidence suggests that people learning about historical issues anchor the information they receive in their experience, group membership, and values. 
For instance, young migrants in the West are typically less interested in European nations’ history than majority youth. Muslim young migrants are more critical about Holocaust issues; they construct analogies between Crusades, World War II conflicts, and the current Israel– Palestinian conflict, whereas Western youth usually lack this perspective (Grever, 2012). Hanke et al. (2015) found further that many young Muslims are indifferent to figures in world history from other cultures. Historical representations may thus anchor meaning in conflict (see Páez & Liu, 2012). 
Individualized Features of Collective Remembering At the micro- end of the continuum between society and the individual, social and cognitive psychologists emphasize individual- level and intraindividual- level features of the remembering or forgetting of historical events (like flashbulb memories, Hirst & Meksin, 2008), historical analogies in decision- making, and making attributions for historical events (Hegarty & Klein, 2017). The experimental methods used by these scholars contrasts sharply with the more qualitative and archival work referenced in the previous 
 
 
592 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
paragraph, but the results are consistent with core ideas of this chapter: that content and representation of the past deeply influence how people deal with current intergroup relations (including decision- making and recognition/ recall tasks). Showing the convergence of these different traditions, evidence suggest that, for instance, both flashbulb memories and collective memories are formed during the formative years of identity- making; they are partially similar in content; elicited by novel, unique, and surprising events when these events are emotionally loaded; relevant for social identity (i.e., being related to a central attitude and to previous knowledge of the person); involve changes to central aspects of social life (“are consequential”); and are rehearsed interpersonally and collectively (Hirst & Meksin, 2008; Páez et al., 2018). Wertsch and Roediger (2008) provide a useful high- level summary of the tensions and linkages in this area. 
As an example of these, attribution theory has defined three main causal factors in defining events requiring explanation as those that are negative, surprising, and self- relevant. Bruckmuller, Hegarty, Teigen, Bohm, and Luminet (2017) argue that unexpectedness and self- relevance are not inherent properties of events but an expression of the relationship between events and people’s expectations. Thus, content influences process, and processes carried out in time reconfigure content. Liu, Fisher- Onar, and Woodward (2014) have theorized that drastic content reconfigurations are more likely to occur in moments of societal crisis. 
Toolkit Summary In summary, a short list of the theoretical premises structuring the toolkit that historical representations bring to studying intergroup relations and social identity are (1) the character of the “common ground” (or representations of history) is crucial to shaping the quality and quantity of intergroup conflict within or between societies; (2) even when elements of a representation of history are consensual (e.g., form a common ground of shared knowledge), there is still contestation in interpreting the meaning of history for current events; and (3) through this process of interpretation, where representations of history are put to the test as lenses (with such properties as culturally inscribed social roles) to examine present- day challenges, cultural continuity can be maintained or it can fail. The collapse of a historical charter is associated with a cultural collapse where the meaning system of a people is compromised (Liu, Fisher- Onar, & Woodward, 2014). 
Together, these premises enable the theorist to view political culture as a system of meaning that is capable of anchoring (providing interpretations of current events that maintain the basic premises of its historical charter, see Moscovici, 1988), change (where the interpretations characteristic of a society are transformed through communication processes and institutional change), or even rupture or collapse (Liu & Pratto, 2018). A representational approach to culture encourages theorists to think of culture not as given (as a values- based approach implies), but consisting of structures of shared meaning located in time and place and subject to sometimes chaotic periods of change.

The group, particularly a nation and its subgroups, moves through periods of time that produce changes operating at a micro- level (e.g., individual remembering, judgment, and decision- making) and at the macro- level (e.g., institutional state building, mass media productions) linked by a mid- level of conversational engagement (moderated by organizations and technology; see Bennett & Liu, 2018; Sibley & Liu, 2013). 
Having introduced the conceptual toolkit for a representational approach to culture, identity, and intergroup relations, we now describe seminal research in defining first the content of global representations of history that structure intergroup relations and social identity in our times, before proceeding to specific case studies of particular peoples. Among this family of nations, a variety of social processes can be seen to operate according to the representational ground on which the legitimacy of the society stands. 
Defining Global Common Ground: Two World History Surveys as a Global Charter of Collective Remembering The past 100– 200 years could be described as an era of accelerated globalization (Ritzer, 2011). Two world history surveys, the first primarily qualitative and the second one quantitative, conducted in the last years of the twentieth century and the first years of the twenty- first century, provide illustrations of how the content of social representations of world history are keyed (Schwartz, 1997)  to understanding this era. Our era is one where the global experiences of the past 200 years influence intergroup relations around the world as an interconnected whole. The specific representations formed by university students around the world provide a cogent and powerful illustration of how the different sources for historical representations are manifested as the products of global society and individual nations. 
The First World History Survey The first WHS used two open- ended, fill- in- the- blanks questions: (1) “Write down of the names of the 5 people born in the last 1,000 years whom you consider to have had the most impact, good or bad, on World History,” and (2) “Imagine that you were giving a seminar on world history. What 7 events would you teach as the most important in world history?” Data were collected from samples of university students in 24 countries around the world and reported in two major publications (Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2005). 
The results of the first WHS were surprising in terms of the regularity of the representations of history collected from educated young adults around the world (see Tables 18.1 and 18.2): (1) there was historical foreshortening, with the recent past being emphasized over the distant past; two- thirds of events nominated and 72% of figures named were from the past 100 years, and almost 80% of events and 90% of figures came

anchored in personal memory. For example, Britons were more likely to remember World War II than were Americans probably because the British experienced the war much more directly and personally (Scott & Zac, 1993). Second, people emphasize recent events because they feel “they are living during the most important and innovative period of world history” (Golec de Zavala, Cichocka, Eidelson, & Jayawickreme, 2009). This recency effect has been also linked to the idea of communicative history (Assman, 1997) or that three generations is the maximum for people to retain vividly historical events. The span of communicative memory is about 80– 100 years, three or four generations. This idea could explain why World War II is so important for collective memory. Studies have confirmed that when asked about important political events lived by relatives (Pennebaker, Páez, & Rimé, 1997) or about genealogical knowledge and relatives’ information, most people provide information about the experience of two or three generations (Attias- Donfut & Wolff, 2003; Candau, 2005): these intergenerational topics touch on experiences of war or social unrest, and fresh wars reignite social memories of World War II (Schuman & Rieger, 1992). This tendency in conversation to focus on recent (negative) events may be adaptive because recent events are more informative and require more rapid reactions than distant and/ or positive ones (Bar- Tal, 2013; Taylor, 1991). It is also highly adaptive in an era of continuous change, in contrast to a premodern view of history keyed to antiquity, as in the era of Imperial China or precolonial India (or tribal cultures), where the intergenerational transmission of memory would presumably be stronger across many generations. (See also Chapter 11 by Qi Wang and Sawa Senzaki concerning culture and recency effects on memory.) 
Young educated people in India and China did not name a single event earlier than the nineteenth century among the 10 most important events in world history, and Confucius was the only figure from antiquity named (number 10 in China2) (see Tables 18.1 and 18.2). Similar results can be seen for India and Turkey. The warrant of antiquity has been withdrawn from the empires that ruled much of the world prior to the rise of the nation- state. In terms of representational power, historical foreshortening privileges the accomplishments of the West in the past 200 years and positions World War II (and the Industrial Revolution) as makers and breakers of human civilization and the units within them. 
Eurocentrism Tempered by Ethnocentrism The first WHS and other surveys using a similar methodology (based on open- ended nominations) to determine the most important figures and events in world history found a large degree of cross- national consensus that Western history and cultural events are considered to be the most historically significant by lay people (Glowsky, Ellerman, Kromeier, & Andorfer, 2008; Liu et al., 2009; Pennebaker et al., 2006). Events recalled as 
2. Confucius was nominated by Chinese even though he broke the 1,000- year rule in the questionnaire protocol; Jesus and Mohammad broke through as well for Christian and Islamic societies, respectively. 
 
598 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
important for world history around the world have Europeans exerting agency (e.g., New World Discovery) or Europe and North America as major actors (e.g., the World Wars), or simply are European events, such as the French Revolution, Industrial Revolution, or Protestant reformation (Pennebaker et al., 2006). Historiography (Goody, 2007) and news are focused on the United States and western events, and similar findings are described in flashbulb memories (Wang & Aydin, 2009). 
Together, such findings suggest that the dominant representations of history are the representations of world- dominant cultures. They are a product of historical foreshortening and demonstrate the current representational power of the West. Given this global common ground, it is no wonder that late but quick developers like China have in many domains elected to simply to follow the cutting edge of the West (e.g., in science and industry). The WHS and others like it have not identified a global “warrant of antiquity” for resisting globalization. Representations of events in world history are very much focused on the agency of Western civilization in the past 200 years. These results augment those from the much larger World Values Survey, where Inglehart and Baker (2000) report that all countries are moving toward modern values like secularism and self- expression. Globalization is thus associated with Westernization in constructing the common ground of human societies today. 
The major exception to this rule of Western- centrism in the first WHS was the very new nation of East Timor, where the educational curriculum was unstable and less developed. Data from East Timor were collected from students soon after independence, and it seemed for them that recent events affecting East Timor formed the entire content of world history (Liu et al., 2009). Thus, education is implicated in these patterns (see Carretero et al., 2017). 
Outside of East Timor, ethnocentrism was typically more common among Western than non- Western nations: people from Russia and the Ukraine to Hungary and Portugal (among others) mentioned events important to their national history that were not mentioned by any other nation. Events important in the making of the national ingroup were disproportionately regarded as important in world history. This is congruent with studies that suggest in relatively open form (in the Americas) or in a more sophisticated and politically correct form (in Europe) that the contents of history books are focused on the ingroup and mainly Western history (Carretero et  al., 2017; Paez et  al., 2018; Wang, 2009). 
There was more ethnocentrism in free recall nominations of the most important figures in world history. People important in the making of the ingroup were frequently considered to be important to world history. Every nation except 1 (the British Commonwealth of New Zealand) among the 24 surveyed named at least one ingroup member among its top 10, and many named several. Thus, agentic roles for ingroup heroes and villains in nation- building were retained even though the overall narrative might be one of progress or conflict emanating from the West.
