A Story of Politics and War Among educated young lay people, revolutions and wars were most frequently mentioned in world history (Liu et al., 2009) or in the past millennium (Pennebaker et al., 2006) as important events, whereas science and technology, including the Industrial Revolution, were of secondary importance. In the first WHS, warfare and collective violence accounted for 48% and politics accounted for 27% of events nominated, whereas 45% of leaders named were known for their roles in collective violence (Liu et al., 2009). Even though wars produced only 2% of the twentieth- century death toll (Layard, 2005), people tend to stress the role of political violence in world history because of the catastrophic impact of extreme and negative events like wars, and their narratability (Liu & László, 2007). 
This lay belief is congruent with nineteenth- century historiography, where academic historians followed a romantic approach based on German idealistic philosophy, rejecting the principle of laws and causality in history and concentrating more on idiographic descriptions of events triggered by “Great men” (Iggers, Wang, & Mukherjee, 2008). These social representations are also congruent with the dominance of violence and drama in mass media and historical textbooks, as wartime periods often receive more attention in these venues (Zerubavel, 2003). 
World War II is frequently associated with world history and was overwhelmingly the most remembered event in free- recall (see Liu et al., 2005, 2009)— two characteristics indicative of events forming the central nucleus of a social representation (Abric, 1994). Unlike national histories, which typically are anchored by a foundational event at the formation of the nation, World War II is the most likely anchor for the process of representing world history for lay people. World War II not only forms part of the main nucleus of social representations of world history but also serves as an “anchor” or central point when generating new meanings for more current events entering into public life. Perceiving World War II as a necessary war could anchor a stoic view of history (see Iggers et al., 2008), which implies a higher acceptance of social and natural calamities (World Wars I and II, the Great Depression, the Tsunami, etc.). The experience of much of the developing world was that World War II was a part of the process for them to achieve national independence and therefore a necessary evil (Liu et al., 2012). 
Two large- scale collective- level studies at the country- level showed that there is a positive association between the percentage of people willing to fight in a war for their nation or a culture of war and national means of Hofstede’s (2001) power distance, collectivism, and post- materialism, and values of hierarchy and low autonomy (Basabe & Valencia, 2007; Fischer and Hanke, 2009). Together, these findings suggest that the more hierarchical, collectivistic, and materialistic values are in a society, the less negative are the representations of historical calamities and the more positive are attitudes toward fighting for one’s country. At the opposite end, societies emphasizing individualistic, egalitarian, and postmaterialistic values are expected to share a disenchanted view of past collective violence as well as future war. That is, the shift from an industrial and 
 
600 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
materialistic to a postmaterialist society (Inglehart, Basáñez, Díez- Medrano, Halman, & Luijkx, 2004) appears to be reflected in a shift from a relatively positive and romantic social representation of war focused on heroes and martyrs toward a more critical view of war emphasizing suffering and the meaninglessness of war (Páez & Liu, 2012). Postmaterialistic values probably erode “heroic war” narratives and attenuate positive attitudes toward collective violence. (See Chapter 3 by Peter B. Smith for more discussion about cultural dimensions.) 
Unlike most narratives that have a beginning, middle, and end, the story that may be inferred from social representations of world history does not have a tidy beginning, but it does have a recent technical climax. The world wars may provide what Wertsch (2002) describes as cognitive narrative templates, or what Hilton and Liu (2008) have called historical charters for dealing with intergroup relations between states. In the developed world, Hilton and Liu (2008) suggest the global charter is a narrative where the civilized nations of the world have a mandate to band together to protect human life and human rights and maintain civilizational progress against tyranny and dictatorship. This story privileges the winners of World War II, particularly countries like the United States, Britain, and France3 whose roles as winners are built into structures like the United Nations, where they are permanent members of the Security Council. A study based on 20 nations from the first WHS found vicarious collective remembering contributing to the legitimization of war: young people in victorious nations reported higher recall of World War II memories, a less negative evaluation of this event, and expressed more willingness to fight in a new war (Páez et al., 2008). For example, Singapore had the highest open- ended recall of World War II in the WHS (at 94%), was on the winning side (as a colony of Britain with bad memories of Japanese invasion), is relatively high in power- distance, and its young people reported the greatest willingness to fight in a future war on behalf of the nation (Paez at al., 2008, p. 376); Spain was neutral in World War II, its young people had only 50% recall of World War II, and it reported the lowest level of willingness to fight in the survey; France with 64% free recall of World War II and a winner is somewhere in between these two. 
A second narrative can be inferred from putting together the overall global story with country- specific nominations from developing countries. These frequently concern nation- building and are more like national than global charters. For example, Ataturk (Mustapha Kemal) is collectively remembered as the most important figure in world history in Turkey, Mao is number 1 in China and Hong Kong, and Gandhi is the most frequently free- recalled figure in world history in India (Liu et al., 2005, 2009) (see Tables 18.1 and 18.2). In this second, complementary narrative, World War I and World War II are regarded as necessary evils where, by courage and fortitude, great men were able to 
3. This narrative eminence is, of course, balanced in fact by that China and Russia were also winners of World War II, but with a different set of values.

engineer the course of history to give birth to new states that have revitalized the promise of the great civilizations that came before them. 
In accord with Wertsch (2002), who developed the idea of a cognitive narrative template, these narratives lack measurement precision. To address issues of measurement precision, the second WHS was designed to augment and go beyond the first. A list of 40 of the most important events and figures in world history was extracted from the first WHS to serve as source rating materials for the second WHS. 
The Second World History Survey The first WHS based on the free recall of important historical events showed that revolutions and war- related events were more salient than other historical events, whereas leaders were frequently nominated for their roles in wars and other events involving collective violence (Liu et al., 2005, 2009). However, the hegemony of politics and war in free recall of important events and leaders was not replicated in the second WHS using closed- ended quantitative ratings. Warfare and politics- related events and people were not rated as more important than cultural or economic events related to progress (Bobowik et al., 2010, 2014). War leaders were evaluated less positively than civil rights leaders (Hanke et al., 2015). Even if wars are more vivid in free recall, social- structural factors are recognized as important and prevail in more reflexive and evaluative thinking about history when lay people are asked to evaluate lists of specific events and people on ratings scales. 
Universal Heroes, but Villains are Less Consensual Quantitative ratings also revealed a new pattern in the ratings of heroes and villains. There was far greater consensus with respect to the evaluations of the heroes compared to the villains of world history (Hanke et al., 2015). Hanke et al. (2015) argued that historical figures play an important role on the objectification of social representations of history because they can symbolize and embody national and civilizational political cultures, whereas critical events like World War II are more like cultural schema that may be invoked as historical lessons to justify action. Events impart lessons, whereas “heroes” embody values and inspire. 
In the second WHS, the 10 most positively evaluated historical figures across all countries were (in descending order) Albert Einstein, Mother Theresa, Mahatma Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Isaac Newton, Jesus Christ, Nelson Mandela, Thomas Edison, Abraham Lincoln, and Buddha (Hanke et al., 2015). These are scientists, humanitarians, and religious figures with the one exception of a political leader (Abraham Lincoln). It seems reasonable to argue that Abraham Lincoln was perceived as a humanitarian, since he abolished slavery in the United States (see Schwartz, 1997). It might be good news for humanity that, across 40 societies, young educated people around the world had relatively similar views of which figures constituted the most positive figures in world history. These heroes are rooted in humanitarianism, including non- Westerners calling the global system to account for failing to meet its own humanitarian ideals. 
 
 
602 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
The second WHS using closed- ended questions also confirmed the recency bias:  World War II was rated as more important than the Thirty Years’ War and eighteenth- and nineteenth- century wars and revolutions. The current 2005 Iraq War was rated as more important than the American Civil War (but not the World Wars or French Revolution) (Bobowik et al., 2010, 2014). In general, time has a dampening effect, where extreme evaluative views (e.g., the strongly negative views of people like Hitler, Osama, Bush, and Saddam) become more neutral over time (e.g., Genghis Khan being close to the mid- point). 
Lack of Universality in the Dimensionality of Events in World History The greater precision afforded by analysis of a closed- ended questionnaire with Likert scales revealed that 40 of the most important events in world history were not evaluated in a universally shared way (Liu et al., 2012). Liu et al. (2012) found no empirical support for universal dimensions in the evaluation of important events in world history but were able to define theoretically meaningful historical events that adhered together. “Historical Calamities,” “Historical Progress,” and “Historical Resistance to Oppression” were identified as specific latent factors (or concepts) carrying discrete forms of evaluative meaning about historical events across cultures. 
Willingness to Fight Liu et al. (2012) found that “Historical calamities” and “Historical progress” were both able to predict willingness to fight for one’s country by the samples of university students around the world (N = 5,800). The more negatively calamitous historical events were rated (e.g., horrific; and this was typical of the educated young people in Western societies), the less willing they were to fight for their country. To the contrary, the more positively “Historical progress” was rated (typical of developing societies), the more willing they were to fight. These appear to be the fears and hopes drawn from historical lessons and applied to the possibility of future conflict and future nation- building. 
The size of the relationships between evaluation of historical events and willingness to fight in a war for the nation varied across cultures (Liu et al., 2012), with this association higher among developing nations, reflecting a more stoic view of history and greater value attributed to the nation and to valuing progress (Bobowik et al., 2014). At the cultural level, a less negative evaluation of historical calamities (with or without the world wars) is associated with collectivistic and high power distance values, low social development, high religiosity, and partially with low postmaterialist values (Bobowik et al., 2014; Paez et al., 2016). 
Time Heals Historical Trauma Studies based on free recall or the first WHS show that old or long- term negative events were better evaluated than similar recent ones (Pennebaker, Páez, & Deschamps, 2006; 
 
 
 
soCial rePresenTaT ions of hisTory  |  603 
Bobowik et al., 2010). As previously described, evaluation ratings of the second WHS also confirmed this long- term positive bias. In some cases, a midpoint evaluation can reflect lack of information or familiarity (e.g., Western students rating the Qin emperor). But positive evaluations also prevailed for distant wars and military leaders that should be familiar to American and European samples. For instance, the Industrial Revolution and both Napoleon and the French Revolution were evaluated positively, suggesting that either people “forgot” about the poverty and social crisis associated with industrialization, and the terror, Napoleonic Wars, and massacres associated with the French Revolution, or that enough time had passed allowing individuals to reinterpret these events and this figure in a more moderate way. 
This is congruent with the psychological long- term tendency to minimize negative stimuli. People remember a higher proportion of positive events than negative events in the long- term and reinterpret negative events to be at least neutral or even positive (Taylor, 1991). Studies that compare autobiographical memories of younger and elder people or analyze within- subject comparisons between recent and more distant events also confirm a positive bias: increased age or longer periods between the event and recall are associated with more positive appraisals of events (Paez et al., 2016). 
Latent Profile Analysis: Western Culture Versus East Asian and Muslim Culture Latent profile analysis was carried out to identify typologies of persons, distinct groups, or types of people who may have a different set of beliefs or evaluations of figures in world history compared to other groups, profiles, or clusters. The best solution was a four- group typology. Hanke et al. (2015) labeled these historical representational profiles “Secular Idealists” (42.7% of the total sample rated heroes highly, villains negatively, and religious figures moderately), “Religious Idealists” (31.4% rated religious heroes extremely high, secular heroes highly, and villains extremely negatively), “Political Realists” (15.6% of the total sample rated close to the midpoint powerful but villainous figures and rated communist dictators and violent conquerors somewhat positively), and “Historical Indifferents” (10.3%, rating all figures except Hitler and Bush between 3 and 5, near the midpoint of 4). 
Based on multidimensional scaling (MDS), cultural clusters were created and a typology of the evaluation of historical figures was compared. Countries in the Western and Catholic/ Orthodox clusters tended to contain almost entirely (88%) “Secular” and “Religious Idealists.” Countries in the Muslim cluster, by contrast, tended to contain more “Political Realists” (39%) and “Historical Indifferents” (30%). Countries in the Asian zone displayed strong heterogeneity across countries, with a high proportion of “Political Realists” (30%) and a similarly high proportion of “Secular Idealists” (34%) overall. The Chinese sample consisted almost entirely of “Political Realists.” 
This analysis reveals substantial cross- cultural differences in the political psychology of people from different parts of the world. People from Muslim countries were 
 
604 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
relatively indifferent to famous figures from other civilizations, not seeing them as heroes and villains. People in China and in some other parts of Asia followed ethno- nationalist narratives where people like Mao, Stalin, and Lenin “made mistakes,” but also made hard choices required for nation- building. This stoic view of history appears more characteristic of the developing world and may afford its citizens representational power to endure the suffering associated with rapid societal change. 
There may be inferred from these findings a balance of representational power. In the developed world, ordinary citizens see war and other calamities as something to be avoided. This tempers their societies’ appetites for conquest even if they have technological superiority. Developing societies, on the other hand, have a more stoic view of history, are more optimistic about historical progress, and have more collectivistic styles of nationalism which, together with recent experience, make them more likely to conceive of warfare as part of the evolution of human societies (including their own). It therefore suits neither side today to engage in warfare, as was characteristic of the colonial era and the early stages of nationalism. 
We now shift from the global common ground to case studies of nation- states with culture- specific features built on top of the common ground. 
The Operation of Historical Charters for  Nation- States: Culture Specific Processes from Europe to Aotearoa/ New Zealand and the United States of America From its origins in modern nation- states, the teaching of history at schools is one of the principal instruments to legitimate a narrative about the origins of the nation and to encourage national feelings (Carretero, 2011). Hence, school teaching is used to install nationalism as a form of common sense (Billig, 1995). Moreover, as Hobsbawm (1990) pointed out, history can include intentional distortions to construct a tradi-tion in the service of national unity. Carretero (2011) has identified a romantic master narrative of nation- states to achieve the aims of a positive evaluation of a national group’s past and present, as well as identification with its national heroes, who are presented as moral exemplars. According to these romantic narratives, nations and nationals are the main historical subjects. The nation is a natural, timeless, and immutable reality, grounded in territorial and cultural components, and actions of the national group are presented in a simple and morally positive way (Carretero et al., 2017). But the specific form and function of national narratives are worth illustrating in concrete terms for the degree of variability in how they shape intergroup relations across cultures. 
 
soCial rePresenTaT ions of hisTory  |  605 
A Schematic Narrative Template for Expelling Invaders from Mother Russia and for Not Recognizing a Potentially New Era in Hungary On the basis of the analysis of both student surveys and societal accounts of events (e.g., Napoleon’s invasion in 1812 and the German invasion during World War II), Wertsch (2002) developed the idea of a schematic narrative template for Russians called the “expulsion of foreign enemies” narrative. Its premises are as follows: (1) Russia is peaceful and minding its own business; (2)  without provocation, Russia is viciously attacked; (3) Russia suffers greatly and almost loses everything; but (4) through heroism and exceptional bravery, Russia triumphs in the end. 
In contrast, László, Ehman, and Imre (2002) arranged frequently nominated historical events in chronological order for young Hungarians, to find a preponderance of positive initial events and negative later events in Hungarians’ representations of their history. This was surprising given that data collection occurred after the collapse of the Soviet block and after Hungary had achieved national independence for the first time since the 1500s. 
László et al. (2002) found that Hungarians have a historical narrative that emphasizes a glorious (but distant) past followed by a troubled recent 500 years that may lead them to underestimate the promise of their present and future. Unlike many nation- states, the shape of Hungarian collective remembering does not follow a U- shape, where foundational events in the distant past are complemented by seminal events in the near past that renew the promise of the collective for the future. Perhaps this is because Hungarians are an ancient people but Hungary is a new state. 
The schematic narrative template for Hungary (first victory, then defeat) is the exact opposite for that of Russia (first defeat, then victory). Though we have no empirical evidence for this, we theorize that these narratives may serve the function of self- fulfilling prophecies that are not only keyed to objective realities (e.g., surviving the Russian winter is an extremely difficult test for any invader), but also predispose a particular people to be able to draw on culturally sanctioned resources (in the case of Russia, a historical charter to be vigilant against threats to their borders and to have confidence of ultimate victory when faced with a powerful invading enemy) to fulfill their historical charter (in this case, defense of the motherland). We may speculate that Russians would be more resilient when faced with a powerful invading adversary than Hungarians and that this would be an effect of not only objective circumstances (e.g., its size, its winter, its armed forces) but a historical charter giving its people psychological resilience in the face of adversity. 
Following László et  al. (2002), we believe that Hungary may have a narrative of history, but, as a newly re- institutionalized nation- state, it lacks a historical charter. The cultural resources necessary to construct a historical charter can include museums, 
 
606 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
educational curricula, national celebrations, popular historical novels, maps, and borders (in Hungary, one still observes maps of greater Hungary, drawn prior to the outcome of World War I, when its territory was at a zenith), but also successful shared experiences crystallized as historical events in collective remembering. Hungary has experienced many defeats since the Battle of Mohacs in 1526 (the most recent of which were World War I and II and then the failure of its uprisings against the Soviets in 1948 and 1956). It will take time to heal the scars of this historical experience. History must be interpreted, debated, and formulated by different segments of society to impact on a national psyche (see Sibley & Liu, 2013; Winter, 2006). Measurement and psychological consequences of a historical charter are described in our next case study. 
The Bicultural State of Aotearoa/ New Zealand Most nation- states follow the French model and strive to be homogeneous (see Nora, 1989, for the sometimes brutal processes by which cultural variability in France was destroyed following the Revolution). However, others, like Switzerland or New Zealand, have built ethno- cultural variability into the historical foundations of their states. 
A strong body of empirical evidence in psychology has emerged to describe the indigenous people of New Zealand, Māori, as partners of the Crown (or state). Most interestingly, even as process- oriented a feature as the implicit associations between this ethnic group and the state are moderated by historical representations. In the United States, people will explicitly claim to be accepting of multiculturalism but implicitly think of white people as the national prototype. Even in domains like Olympic track and field, where another ethnic group is more frequently representative, Americans will react faster to the coupling of the rare successful white athlete like Bruce Jenner and symbols of the state than the more typical African American champion athlete with the same symbols of the United States (Devos & Banaji, 2005). By contrast, young educated New Zealanders of both European and Māori origins see exemplars of the two groups as equally representative of the nation, implicitly and explicitly (Sibley & Liu, 2007). History can thus be seen to train the habits of the heart and mind: implicit associations can be read as signals of a historical charter as they are relatively less influenced by social desirability compared to explicit measures. 
Drawing from social representations of history, Liu, Wilson, McClure and Higgins (1999) argued that two narratives exist side by side in Aotearoa/ New Zealand, one based on British enlightenment discourses (Liu & Robinson, 2016) and the other anchored in the foundational event of New Zealand history— the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840. Many of the 10 most important events in New Zealand history can be configured in a narrative emphasizing either the rise of enlightenment values/ liberalism (e.g., women’s suffrage, the world wars) or biculturalism (e.g., the Treaty, the Land Wars) involving Māori and British settlers in a U- shaped curve of collective remembering combining foundational and recent events. 
 
 
soCial rePresenTaT ions of hisTory  |  607 
The most direct evidence of a bicultural historical charter is consensus among New Zealanders of both Māori and European origins that the Treaty of Waitangi, which guaranteed Māori rights as British citizens and rendered to the British Crown governorship of the land, is the most important event in New Zealand history. This foundation affords Māori a position of being equal to New Zealand Europeans as a symbolically founding people for the nation. By treaty, Māori have the right not to be assimilated, even though commitment to this ideal was forgotten by the settler group (Bennett & Liu, 2018) during the high water mark of colonization (Liu & Robinson, 2016). The Treaty is what Ricoeur (1974) describes as a symbolic reserve: forgotten by the dominant ethnic group from about the 1850s to the 1970s, but always available to the subordinate group and revived after the 1970s to become nationally relevant through a Māori renaissance indicative of a shift to a postcolonial phase (see King, 2003; Orange, 2004; for histories, Liu &Pratto, 2018, for critical junctures in history and the making of New Zealand identities). 
Furthermore, an ideology developed out of the study of New Zealand discourses, termed historical negation by Sibley, Liu, Duckitt, and Khan (2008), was found to strongly predict political behaviors like supporting bicultural policies (e.g., affirmative action). The variance accounted for by historical negation (where historical wrongs are acknowledged, but deemed irrelevant to current situations involving resource distribution) was far greater than for variables like social dominance orientation and right- wing authoritarianism. This is because historical negation is keyed to the New Zealand dilemma of colonization and its discontents: it is purpose- built to explain bicultural politics, which have been central to intergroup politics in this land over the past 200+ years. Culture- specific variables, which may operate in other contexts (e.g., New Zealand is not the only postcolonial state where indigenous people are important) but are purpose- built from the historical experience of a people, are particularly useful as mediators of political behavior and are excellent functional indicators of the presence of a historical charter. New Zealanders are obligated by historical charter to refer to the Treaty of Waitangi in their collective political discourses and decision- making even if some subgroups among them believe the Treaty should not be relevant to the distribution of value (e.g., reparations for historical injustices, affirmative action) in the present day (Sibley et al., 2008; Sibley & Liu, 2013). 
Historical Symbols as Changing in Time Liu and Robinson (2016) content- and discourse- analyzed 160 years of elite New Zealand political discourses called the Speeches from the Throne (indicating the legislative agenda of a newly elected government). They found that while bicultural discourses were evident in every historical period, they became more pronounced with World War II (where the Māori battalion particularly distinguished itself) and exploded into prominence in the 1970s when the United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community and erected trade and citizenship barriers against New Zealand. The Treaty of Waitangi, interpreted today as the foundational event in New Zealand sovereignty, was never mentioned in the 
 
608 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Speeches from the Throne from 1854 (New Zealand’s first Parliament) through the 1920s (it was declared as null and void by a judge in the 1880s). 
Long durée studies like this are more typical in social sciences that more commonly use qualitative analyses of archives than psychology. New Zealand history is rich in biculturalism, but not so strong in terms of culture heroes, in contrast to the United States, whose cultural prototypes are white (Devos & Banaji, 2005), but one of whose heroes has over time come to be represented as the “Great Emancipator.” 
Culture Heroes as Part of the Symbolic Reserve of Social Representations: The “Great Emancipator” of the United States of America The work of sociologist Barry Schwartz has been seminal in showing how a historical figure like Abraham Lincoln may be transformed as a symbol (or social representation) to suit the needs of the political agendas of a nation evolving over time. Using newspaper accounts, Schwartz (2014) has documented how Lincoln’s Gettysburg address did not become part of the American cultural canon until more than a half a century after his death. Similarly, not one biography of Lincoln in the nineteenth century depicted him in favor of racial equality or a “multiracial society” (Schwartz, 1997). Both Frederick Douglass (a great Negro leader and thinker of that time) and the proponents of segregationist laws interpreted Lincoln’s speeches and acts in a manner consistent with their own political agendas, recognizing well- known facts at the time (e.g., Lincoln did not argue for racial equality, and he was prepared to defend a constitution which allowed slavery until late in the Civil War). Nineteenth- and early twentieth- century commemorations of Lincoln “reinforced the public record of his commitment to a racially divided society” (Schwartz, 1997, p. 482). Selective emphasis and selective interpretation to serve present- day political needs are typically the way in which a historical symbol is constructed and reconstructed (Liu & Hilton, 2005, pp. 539– 540). 
The tide of selection for Lincoln’s deployment as a symbol began to turn during the Great Depression, where analogies were drawn between Roosevelt’s New Deal and Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation; as “slavery symbolized economic want, emancipation became a precedent for state activism” (Schwartz, 1997, p. 484). Social justice as a value came to be squarely on the American national agenda in the 1930s, and this would grow even stronger during World War II, as Lincoln was invoked to mobilize cultural values established during the Civil War to cast America’s reluctant entry into the war as a sacred mission (Schwartz, 1996). During the Civil Rights movement, the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC, became the site of major speeches by Martin Luther King, Jr. and President Lyndon Johnson. Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation had evolved into the symbolic centerpiece of a call for racial equality. By the late twentieth century, Lincoln had been transformed by journalists, biographers, and politicians from defender 
 
soCial rePresenTaT ions of hisTory  |  609 
of the Union to Great Emancipator— icon of the civil rights movement and symbol of equality between whites and blacks. 
Lincoln is a hero of the American state and forms part of the symbolic resources used to warrant one of the key planks of the current state that has evolved over time— that of racial equality. Thus, history is a symbolic reserve, a “moveable feast” of emotionally resonant cultural symbols than can be mobilized (and transformed) by political elites and cultural trend- setting communicators who use elements of the past as warrants of legitimacy for their current political agendas. 
Conclusions: Future Directions for a Representational Approach to Intergroup Relations and Social Identity According to the sociologist Maurice Halbwachs, collective memory “retains from the past only what still lives or is capable of living in the consciousness of the groups keeping the memory alive” (Halbwachs, 1950/ 1980, p. 80). Similarly, Frederic Bartlett, who introduced memory studies in psychology, stated that “with the individual as with the group, the past is continually re- made, reconstructed as a function of present interests” (1932, p. 309). There is ample evidence to show these principles in operation, but there still needs to be more evidence and better theory connecting macro- and mid- level societal phenomena to individual- level phenomena, like flashbulb memories, recognition, and recall memory, and the cognitive and motivational factors driving decision- making. 
Social representations of history are helpful to people for a variety of reasons. First, they define the group and preserve a sense of continuity for the group that endures through time (Sani et al., 2007). Second, they maintain a positive image of the group to which they belong and enhance group cohesion. Third, they provide guidance to group values and norms by prescribing behaviors and contributing to what characterizes or should characterize the group. Fourth, social representations of the past are a symbolic resource that can be mobilized politically to face current challenges (Páez & Liu, 2012; Schwartz, 1996); they provide cognitive narrative templates, ideologies, and other socially shared resources that influence emotions, cognition, and behavior (Jodelet & Haas, 2014; Liu & Hilton, 2005; Pennebaker, Páez, & Rimé, 1997) in a flexible way that connects past, present, and future. 
This chapter has reviewed the conceptual toolkit for applying a social representations approach to intergroup relations and social identity. It has summarized the historical common ground on which global society today rests, as well as reviewing some seminal studies of societies where a historical charter appears to operate, generating culture- specific behavior that changes while maintaining continuity with the past. This approach encourages us to think of culture as something that is constructed and not given as 
 
610 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
peoples move through time and apply the lessons they’ve learned from role models they follow to face present- day challenges that periodically transform society.
