(e.g., how stressful are x, y, and z?); it is not equivalent to psychological symptoms or decrements in well- being. Unfortunately, the boundaries between stress and maladaptive outcomes have been blurred in many studies of acculturation, causing some authorities such as Rudmin (2009) to advocate the discontinuation of investigations that position acculturative stress as an intervening variable in the stress and coping process. It is suggested here, however, that it is more fruitful to increase precision in the operationalization of acculturative stress by refining our measures and distinguishing between stress and its psychological outcomes, rather than by dispensing with the construct. 
 Valid measures of acculturative stress are just that— measures whose items are clearly rooted in the acculturation experience and assess perceived stress. There are measures that capture common threats and challenges arising from intercultural contact, such as discrimination and cultural isolation, and assess exposure to these events, but do not take into account an individual’s appraisal of these experiences (e.g., Miller, Kim, & Benet- Martínez, 2011). On the other hand, there are measures that effectively capture “stressfulness,” with respondents using rating scales anchored to responses such as “not at all tense/ worried to extremely tense/ worried” for each item, but extend the stress domains to a much wider range of threats and challenges (e.g., Cervantes, Fischer, Córdova, & Napper, 2015). Two instruments that are appropriately rooted in the acculturation experience and also incorporate the assessment of stress are the Bicultural Stressors Scale for Hispanic Youth (Romero & Roberts, 2003) and the Multidimensional Acculturative Stress Inventory (MASI) for people of Mexican origin in the United States (Rodriguez, Flores, Flores, Myers, & Calderon Vriesema, 2015). Both measures contain a range of events, ask respondents if the event has occurred or is applicable to them, and, if so, ask respondents to rate the stressfulness of the event. We suggest that these types of measures provide the most robust assessment of acculturative stress. 
This is not to suggest that all stressors experienced by sojourners, immigrants, and refugees are rooted in cross- cultural transition and intercultural contact. Indeed, research by Ritsner, Modai, and Ponizovsky (2000) indicated that immigrants rank material problems as more stressful than cultural ones. Many stressors are normative, and studies have shown that both generic stress, including daily hassles, and acculturative stress contribute to mental health outcomes in immigrants (Kiang, Grzywacz, Marín, Arcury, & Quandt, 2010). Still, we recommend that researchers distinguish stress and stressors and are more precise in their conceptualization and measurement of acculturative versus generic stress in studies of intercultural contact and psychological adaptation. 
Stress and Coping Processes and Outcomes 
Acculturative Stress, Appraisal, and Coping Although earlier research has demonstrated that life changes are linked to mood disturbance and psychosomatic symptoms during cross- cultural transition (Searle & Ward, 1990; Ward & Kennedy, 1993), effect sizes have generally been small, supporting Lazarus’s 
 
 
644 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
(1997) contention that individual differences in the appraisal of stress must be taken into consideration. A  wide range of factors underpins individual differences in stress appraisal; these include personality and temperament (Lechuga & Fernandez, 2011), cultural orientation and background (Szabo, Ward, & Jose, 2016; Wang, Schwartz, & Zamboanga, 2010), and acculturation strategies (Berry, 2006a). However, in terms of the stress and coping process, expectations, which provide the yardstick against which subsequent experiences and behaviors can be measured, appear to be particularly important. There is empirical evidence that “undermet” expectations are associated with greater acculturative stress and poorer adaptive outcomes in expatriates and immigrants (Caliguiri, Phillips, Lazarova, Tarique, & Bürgi, 2001; Negy, Schwartz, & Regi- Ferrer, 2009); however, with few exceptions (e.g., Rogers & Ward, 1993), these studies are constrained by the retrospective reporting of expectations. This deserves greater attention in future research. 
 Given the measurement issues associated with the concept of acculturative stress, it is fair to say that there are fewer studies about stress appraisals than resultant coping responses. Lazarus and Folkman (1984) distinguished two major types of coping:  problem- focused and emotion- focused coping. The former refers to active, strategic cognitive and behavioral responses designed to diminish, control, or eliminate stress; the latter involves the management of affective responses with the objective of decreasing emotional distress. Although operationalized in different ways across studies, problem- focused and emotion- focused coping responses have been the most commonly investigated strategies in studies of acculturative stress. For the most part, research has demonstrated the positive influence of problem- focused coping and the detrimental consequences of emotion- focused responses, although the latter trend may be more robust (Kosic, 2004; Wei, Ku, Russell, Mallinckrodt, & Liao, 2008). Avoidant types of coping have also been identified in research (e.g., denial, disengagement, wishful thinking) and linked to negative outcomes (Capielo, Delgado- Romero, & Stewart, 2015; Kosic, 2004). Beyond this, seeking social support, coping with humor, and cognitive reframing (Suanet & van de Vijver, 2009; Ward & Kennedy, 2001; Yoo & Lee, 2005) are associated with better psychological adaptation in acculturation contexts. 
Research suggests that coping responses also moderate and mediate the effects of acculturative stress on psychological adaptation. Mediational analyses of stress and coping address the “how” and “why” of predictive models while moderation deals with the “when” or “for whom” stress and coping lead to adaptive outcomes (Frazier, Tix, & Barron, 2004). Both are important in understanding the dynamics of stress and coping in the context of intercultural contact and change. Mediation models position coping as an interim process between stress and well- being. This is illustrated in research by Lee and Liu (2001) with Asian American youth. Their study found that acculturation- related family conflict led to ineffective coping strategies, such as denial and venting, and these, in turn, predicted greater symptoms of psychological distress. In contrast, moderation models examine the ways in which coping responses may exacerbate or buffer the negative impact of acculturative stress on well- being. Along these lines, Crockett and 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  645 
colleagues found that active coping, such as problem- solving, planning, and positive reframing, buffered the negative effects of acculturative stress on anxiety and depression (Crockett et al., 2007). The stress moderation hypothesis has also been tested in studies of religious coping in minority groups. Studies have shown that positive religious coping attenuates the link between discrimination and depression as found in Fernandez and Loukas’s (2014) research with Mexican Americans, and it buffers the negative effects of acculturative stress on life satisfaction as reported by Adam and Ward (2016) in their work with New Zealand Muslims. 
Although support has been provided for both mediation and moderation effects of coping, the discussion thus far has not addressed the issue of cultural variations in stress and coping processes and coping preferences across cultures. Kuo, Roysircar, and Newby- Clark (2006) have argued that traditional stress and coping research, including studies of acculturation and adaptation, has not adequately captured the range of strategies employed across diverse cultural groups and contexts. They specifically suggested that Asians use collectivist coping styles that reflect group- referenced strategies, interpersonal interactions, and value- based responses, including conformity, interdependence, humility, social harmony, and respect for hierarchy, and this was largely borne out in their research with Chinese in Canada. Lam and Zane (2004) have also discussed cross- cultural differences in coping styles and highlighted the distinction between primary, task- oriented control strategies designed to change stress- provoking features of the environment and secondary control strategies characterized by cognitive reframing of stressful events and situations. Their research has shown that Asian Americans rely on secondary strategies to a greater degree than their European American counterparts. The extent to which the strategies are effective in dealing with acculturative stress and the degree to which the outcomes are context- bound, however, are uncertain. To address this issue, Szabo et al. (2017) examined secondary coping as a function of cultural background and context in their longitudinal research with Asian and Western international students in China and New Zealand. The results showed that secondary coping buffered the negative effect of acculturative stress over time in China; however, it exacerbated the negative impact of acculturative stress on psychological adjustment in New Zealand. As cultural background did not significantly interact with stress and adaptation, the results point to the importance of context in understanding the dynamics of stress and coping with the experience of acculturation. 
Factors Affecting Stress, Coping, and Adaptation As has been seen in the previous section, the core stress and coping process involves the appraisal of culture- crossing experiences, the presence of acculturative stress, and resulting coping strategies implemented to manage stress, restore equilibrium, and lead to positive adaptive outcomes. Studies of psychological adaptation in acculturating groups and individuals, however, have examined a wide range of factors that influence well- being and related outcomes. Some of the studies link these variables explicitly to stress 
 
646 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and coping, examining direct, mediating, and moderating effects, whereas others are implicitly embedded in a stress and coping framework and focus on adaptive outcomes. Four key variables will be discussed in this section— acculturation orientations, personality and individual differences, social support, and cultural distance— although this is not an exhaustive list. Mention will also be made of some demographic, situational, and contextual variables that affect adaptive outcomes. 
Berry (1997, 2005) has long maintained that integration (i.e., maintenance of heritage culture and intercultural contact with members of the wider society) is associated with positive psychological outcomes. Underpinning this contention is the assumption that ethnic and national cultural orientations act in an additive fashion to bolster well- being, and this has been supported in a comprehensive meta- analysis by Nguyen and Benet- Martínez (2013). Despite the evidence that both heritage and national cultural orientations contribute to positive adaptation, few studies have considered the mechanisms by which these outcomes are achieved or how acculturation styles and strategies fit into a stress and coping framework. There is some evidence that integration and assimilation predict lower levels of acculturative stress (Scottham & Dias, 2010) and that retention of traditional culture can buffer the negative impact of intercultural threats, such as racism, on the severity of acculturative stress (Araújo Dawson, 2009). Mediational models of acculturation, stress, and coping have also been tested, but the models have been so diverse that it is difficult to draw firm conclusions (Ayers et al., 2009; Hwang & Ting, 2008; Kosic, 2004). As is the case in general for stress and coping approaches to cross- cultural transition and adaptation, longitudinal research is needed to elucidate the direction of relationships among key variables. 
Personality and individual differences also influence the process and outcomes of stress and coping. On the side of resources are traits, abilities, motivations, and expectations, such as an internal locus of control (Ong & Ward, 2005), hardiness (Ataca & Berry, 2002), personal and social self- efficacy (Rahman & Rollock, 2004), perspective- taking, honesty- humility (Demes & Geeraert, 2015), mastery (Diwan, Jonnalagadda, & Balaswamy, 2004), decisiveness (Kosic, 2004), a sense of coherence (Jibeen & Khalid, 2010), self- determined motivation (Chirkov, Vansteenkiste, Tao, & Lynch, 2007), and cultural intelligence (Ang et al., 2007). The Big Five personality dimensions have been investigated, showing that Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness are negatively related to depression while the reverse is true for Neuroticism (Ward, Leong, & Low, 2004). Of particular interest in acculturation research is Bicultural Identity Integration (Benet- Martínez & Haritatos, 2005), an individual difference that reflects the degree to which people who have internalized two cultures experience their cultural identities as blended versus compartmentalized and as harmonious versus conflictual (Benet- Martínez, 2012). Research has clearly shown that bicultural identity integration is associated with adjustment (Nguyen & Benet- Martínez, 2013); however, it appears that the harmony, rather than the blendedness, component is associated with decrements in anxiety and depression (Huynh, Nguyen, & Benet- Martínez, 2011).
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  647 
The most comprehensive work on personality and psychological adjustment has been led by van der Zee and van Oudenhoven (2000) in connection with their Multicultural Personality Questionnaire (MPQ; see also Chapter  13 by Jüri Allik and Anu Realo for extended discussion of culture and personality traits). The MPQ has five personality domains: Social Initiative (the tendency to initiate action), Cultural Empathy (the ability to empathize with thoughts and feelings of individuals from different cultural backgrounds), Emotional Stability (the tendency to remain calm under stressful circumstances), Flexibility (the ability to adjust behavioral strategies in a foreign culture), and Openness (the tendency to search out and explore new circumstances). Programmatic research with the instrument has shown that emotional stability, social initiative, flexibility, cultural empathy, and open- mindedness are associated with positive mental health outcomes (van Oudenhoven, Mol, & van der Zee, 2003; van Oudenhoven & van der Zee, 2002). These results have been replicated and extended in various settings with a variety of sojourning groups and in both cross- sectional and longitudinal research (Leong, 2007; Peltokorpi, 2008; Suanet & van de Vijver, 2009; Ward, Fischer, Lam, & Hall, 2009). 
 Individual differences in the availability and use of social support are also important. Social support can be broadly defined as the provision of assistance that engenders feelings of being cared for and valued and enhances a sense of belonging and connectedness for the supported person. Both perceived and received social support have been investigated in stress and coping studies. The structure (e.g., networks such as family and friends) and functions (emotional and instrumental objectives) of social support have also been examined as key predictors of well- being and as buffers of the negative impact of acculturative stress. 
Despite cultural differences in seeking social support (Taylor et al., 2004), research findings on its effects are robust. Social support is associated with lower levels of acculturative stress and predicts positive mental health outcomes for sojourners and immigrants (Baba & Hosoda, 2014; Kiang et  al., 2010; Thomas & Choi, 2006). Social support has been shown to contribute directly to decrements in hopelessness, anxiety, depression, and trauma (Ong & Ward, 2005; Sondregger, Barrett, & Creed, 2004). Conversely, low levels of social support have been associated with poorer general health, including anxiety, psychosomatic symptoms, and social dysfunction (Jibeen & Khalid, 2010). These findings are robust across various sources and forms of social support, including family (Liebkind & Jasinskaja- Lahti, 2000) and friends (Ritsner et al., 2000), traditional and online support networks (Ye, 2006), and across local and overseas ties (Ong & Ward, 2005). 
Social support can both moderate and mediate the negative impact of acculturative stress on well- being (Crockett et al., 2007; Lee, Koeske, & Sales, 2004; Misra, Crist, & Burant, 2003). In these instances, it is important to distinguish perceived social support (i.e., the availability of supportive sources) from received support (i.e., the actual use of social support to ameliorate psychological distress). Perceived availability of social support operates as a functional resource that exerts both a positive direct effect on well- being and buffers the negative influence of acculturative stress. Seeking and receiving 
648 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
social support are more accurately described as coping strategies activated in response to and mediating the effects of acculturative stress. 
Beyond personality and social support, cultural distance can negatively impact psychological adaptation (Babiker, Cox, & Miller, 1980). Research over the past three decades has been largely consistent with Babiker et al.’s (1980) original study with international students, although cultural distance has been conceptualized and assessed in at least three different ways. The first is by assigning ethnic, cultural, or national groups to low and high cultural distance categories based on assumptions about varying degrees of cultural similarity- dissimilarity. For example, reflecting high versus low cultural distance comparisons, Asian international students in New Zealand reported more psychological adjustment difficulties than their European and North American peers (Jose, Ward, & Liu, 2007), and Mainland Chinese students in Australia experienced more acculturation- related adjustment problems than those in Hong Kong (Pan, Wong, Joubert, & Chan, 2008). A second approach involves the assessment of perceived cultural distance. In these instances, sojourners or immigrants are asked to evaluate the similarities or differences between their country of origin and country of residence (Nesdale & Mak, 2003). These studies have shown that perceived cultural distance is associated with increased symptoms of psychological distress and lower levels of psychological well- being (Demes & Geeraert, 2014; Suanet & van de Vijver, 2009). The final approach involves “objective” measures of cultural distance. For example, Jenkins and Mockaitis (2010) constructed cultural distance measures based on national differences in factors such as level of education, religion, language, and political systems from the United Nations Development Program and the World Bank databases. They reported that objective cultural distance had a significant impact on expatriates’ adjustment difficulties while on international assignments. Despite evidence of convergence across these studies, Selmer (2002) has been a critic of the cultural distance hypothesis based on his findings about the adjustment problems experienced by Hong Kong expatriate managers in Mainland China. 
Demographic, group, and contextual factors play a role in stress and coping with intercultural contact. Gender and age are often investigated in the context of stress and coping and as predictors of psychological adaptation, but the findings are mixed. For the most part, it appears that gender differences in psychological adaptation during cross- cultural transition mirror the general patterns found in research on gender and psychopathology. For example, the International Comparative Study of Ethno- cultural Youth reported that males experienced more behavioral problems, but females had more symptoms of psychological distress, such as anxiety, depression, and psychosomatic reactions (Sam, Vedder, Ward, & Horenczyk, 2006). 
Research findings pertaining to age and adaptation are also mixed. Some studies have reported that younger persons cope better with transition while others have concluded that older people have fewer adjustment problems (Selmer, 2001; Yeh, 2003). These seemingly contradictory results are undoubtedly influenced by the age range encompassed in a particular study, as well as by imprecise and variable definitions of “young” and “old” 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  649 
within and across samples. It is possible that a curvilinear relationship exists between age and adaptation, with adolescence and old age representing high- risk periods. In the first instance, the stress of migration may be intertwined with the stress of adolescent identity and development (Kiropoulos, Klimides, & Minas, 2004; Michel, Titzmann, & Silbereisen, 2012). In the latter instance, it may be that acculturation is more difficult for elderly people who have fewer psychological resources to manage a successful transition (Karin & Howard, 2010). 
Similar issues arise when generation is examined as a predictor of psychological adaptation in immigrant groups. In many cases, age and generation are confounded as immigrant parents and their children are included in the same study; however, large- scale epidemiological investigations and national samples can provide insights into generational differences, and studies tend to suggest that first- generation immigrants have a lower risk for mental disorder than their second- generation peers (Breslau et al., 2007; Hjern & Allebeck, 2002); however, this varies by type of disorder and ethnic group (Alegría et al., 2008). 
Finally, contextual factors can impact stress and coping processes. At the national level, immigrant youth in more culturally diverse societies report slightly lower levels of psychological adaptation (Vedder, van de Vijver, & Liebkind, 2006). However, immigrant well- being may be less affected by diversity per se than by how a society tolerates, accepts, or values diversity. Research by Ward, Kim, Karl, Epstein and Park (2019) has shown that normative multiculturalism (i.e., perceptions that one’s society is characterized by diverse cultural groups in contact, a positive valuing of diversity, and policies and practices that support and accommodate diversity) is associated with greater psychological well- being in immigrants and their descendants. Moreover, cultural looseness– tightness impacts psychological well- being, with international students experiencing greater psychological adjustment problems as a function of tightness (Geeraert, Li, Ward, Gelfand, & Demes, 2019). 
Psychological Adaptation Over Time Perhaps one of the most persistent myths about the process of psychological adaptation during cross- cultural transition is that of the normative “U- curve.” Oberg’s (1960) armchair speculation described the emotional reactions associated with cross- cultural sojourns and suggested that the experience of crossing cultures typically commences with a honeymoon phase, followed by crisis, recovery, and adjustment. Although popular and intuitively appealing, both theoretical and empirical bases for the U- curve are lacking. Evidence for its support was appraised by Church (1982, p. 542) as “weak, inconclusive and overgeneralized,” and this remains the case today. 
A major criticism of the purported U- curve model of stress and adjustment is that, for the most part, it has not been adequately tested. First, U- curve studies are often cross- sectional rather than longitudinal. Second, the longitudinal studies that have been published rarely include the earliest stages of cross- cultural transition, which would 
 
 
650 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
ensure that the purported “honeymoon” phase is captured (Bhashar- Shrinivas, Harrison, Shaffer, & Luk, 2005). Third, studies generally report the average pattern of change over time without investigating different patterns and profiles. Although this line of longitudinal research suggests decrements in well- being between pre- departure and post- arrival stages of cross- cultural transition and a tendency for psychological distress to be greatest in the earliest stages of transition, these studies do not capture individual variation (Bikos et al., 2007; Cemacilar & Falbo, 2008; Ying, 2005). The most robust study to date on the experience of stress during cross- cultural transition has been undertaken by Demes and Geeraert (2015). The researchers surveyed almost 2,500 international students at six time points before and during their cross- cultural sojourn (i.e., from 3 months prior to departure to 8½ months overseas). Applying latent class growth analysis to their data to examine changes in baseline stress over time, five patterns of change were observed: reverse J (3.2%), inverse U (4.9%), mild stress (40.6%), minor relief (47.2%), and resilience (4.1%). The two largest classes, mild stress and minor relief, showed very little movement from baseline, and the U- curve hypothesis, in this instance typified by the inverse U as an indicator of stress, received little support, being observed in slightly less than 5% of the sample. 
Moving Forward The stress and coping framework offers insights into the trials and tribulations of crossing cultures and ensuing threats to psychological well- being. The advantages of this approach lie in its roots in the Transactional Model of Stress and in related studies in health and counseling psychology, which have elucidated the nature and process of coping with change. While this has paved the way for the application of a stress and coping framework to the investigation of the outcomes of intercultural contact and the experience of cross- cultural transition and adaptation, significant challenges remain. Discrepancies in the conceptualization and measurement of acculturative stress, the scant attention paid to stress appraisal while crossing cultures, and the scarcity of longitudinal studies have hampered theoretical and empirical advancement in the field. Addressing these issues should be a priority in future research. 
B: Culture Learning Underpinning the culture learning perspective are the core assumptions that cultural novices have difficulties managing everyday social encounters and that the culture- specific skills needed to negotiate a new cultural milieu can be acquired through the learning process. Emphasis is placed on the effectiveness of intercultural behaviors and the acquisition of culturally appropriate skills. Accordingly, in the global arena, the culture learning paradigm has been most commonly applied to the study of cultural novices, such as international students and expatriates; however, it can also be applied to the study of intercultural interactions within national boundaries, including those in multicultural educational, organizational, and clinical settings. 
 
 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  651 
Historically, the culture learning perspective has concentrated on what novices must learn and how they learn it— in short, the acquisition of cultural competence. Appropriate and effective communication skills remain at the core of what should be learned in the cultural learning process, although knowledge about cultural values is also useful as long as this can be translated into culturally appropriate behaviors in intercultural settings. The how component of the culture learning can be understood in terms of general learning processes, including classical and operant conditioning; however, in line with Bandura’s (1977) social learning theory, observational learning is critically important. This involves observation, imitation or modeling, practice, and feedback. Generalization, or the transfer of basic learning to other situations, accounts for the capacity to use previously acquired skills appropriately in new cultural contexts. These learning processes can occur naturally in novel cultural environments or can be integrated into formal intercultural training programs (Knott, Mak, & Neill, 2013). More recently, studies adopting a culture learning approach have moved toward examining the factors that facilitate or impede the acquisition and demonstration of culturally appropriate skills. This line of research typically considers situational factors, such as opportunities for learning and transfer of skills (e.g., contact with members of a new culture, training programs), as well as personal resources, such as language proficiency, intercultural sensitivity, and cultural intelligence (Wilson, Ward, & Fischer, 2013). Figure 20.2 presents an integrated framework for understanding the process and outcomes of culture learning. The framework positions culture learning at the core with key personal and situational factors as antecedents and culturally appropriate and effective skills and behaviors as outcomes of the learning process. The process unfolds over time and in a cultural context. 
FIGURE 20.2 A model of culture learning.
652 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
The framework is not proposed as an empirical model to be tested; it is merely a graphic illustration of one way of understanding the process and outcomes of culture learning. Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that personal and situational factors may act in an additive fashion in the process of culture learning, both exerting direct effects on learning and skills acquisition, or in an interactive manner, with one moderating the influence of the other. For example, cultural intelligence and training may both lead to the more rapid acquisition of new cultural skills, but it may also be the case that the effects of training are stronger for sojourners with higher levels of cultural intelligence. It is also possible for individual characteristics and learning opportunities to play a mediational role. For example, the positive effects of extraversion on skills acquisition may be partially mediated by intercultural contact, as extraverts are more likely to seek out social interactions with host nationals. Additionally, training may improve language proficiency, which in turn leads to more positive learning outcomes. 
Although personal and situational factors are positioned as antecedents to culture learning, it is important to recognize that there are also feedback loops (Chen & Isa, 2003). Successful culture learning should enhance cultural intelligence and language proficiency while unsuccessful learning attempts may decrease motivation or intercultural contact. Most importantly, culture learning leads to the acquisition of skills and the demonstrable ability to perform culturally appropriate and effective behaviors. Skilled performance is typically examined at a general level (i.e., how effective an individual is in negotiating a range of day- to- day tasks required in a new cultural milieu), but it may also be considered in domain- specific areas, such as the academic achievement of an international student, the job performance of an expatriate employee, or the therapeutic effectiveness of a multicultural counsellor. 
Finally, these processes and outcomes occur in a cultural context. The context may be viewed at an institutional or organizational level, such as a school or a corporation, or at the societal level. Clearly, some organizations are more receptive to and prepared for cultural diversity than others (Plaut, Thomas, & Goren, 2009; Thijs & Verkuyten, 2014). Furthermore, there is strong evidence that cultural norms and values affect the degree to which newcomers are welcomed (Gelfand et al., 2011; Hofstede, 2001). These factors, along with cultural distance, can affect the process and outcomes of culture learning (Demes & Geereart, 2014; Kim, Kirkman, & Chen, 2008). 
In the remainder of this section, we draw attention to the behavioral basis of culture learning and the overlapping constructs of cultural effectiveness, competence, and adaptation. We also note that, despite the emphasis on behaviors, for the most part, research has relied primarily on self- report. We then review research on the personal and situational factors that facilitate cultural learning and culturally appropriate skills acquisition. Finally, we describe key challenges to the advancement of the field and suggest ways to move forward.
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  653 
Key Conceptual and Measurement Issues Before elaborating the culture learning framework further, it is necessary to resolve some key conceptual issues. The framework identifies culturally appropriate and effec-tive behaviors as the desired outcome of the culture learning process. What appears to be the essence of this behaviorally defined outcome has been variably discussed as effectiveness, competence, and adaptation across a multidisciplinary literature based on intercultural and cross- cultural perspectives in psychology, communication, management, and training. As we will see, however, there are significant discrepancies in the conceptualization and measurement of these seemingly overlapping constructs, and the imprecise and often inconsistent usage of terminology has hampered the integration and development of the field. 
At the heart of the conceptual controversy are notions about the “attributional versus behavioral” essence of intercultural effectiveness, cultural competence, and sociocultural adaptation (Chiu, Lonner, Matsumoto, & Ward, 2013). Deardorff ’s (2006) study made significant inroads into clarifying these concepts, and extrapolation of her findings go some way to reconciling multidisciplinary strands of research on intercultural contact with culture learning theory. Deardorff employed the Delphi method, inviting recognized experts to share their views with the aim of reaching a consensus, to identify the core characteristics of intercultural competence. Her research concluded that there was a wide variety of definitions of competence across international experts, although the definition that engendered the most consensus was “the ability to communicate effectively and appropriately in intercultural situations based on one’s intercultural knowledge, skills, and attitudes” (Deardorff, 2006, pp. 247– 248). However, Deardorff (2006) noted that the knowledge and skills component of intercultural competence is preceded by requisite attitudes including openness to and respect for other cultures. Accordingly, her pyramid model of intercultural competence distinguishes the base of requisite attitudes (e.g., respect, openness) as the building blocks for knowledge (e.g., culture- specific information, cultural self- awareness) and general communication skills (e.g., listening, observing, interpreting). These, in turn, form the base for desired internal outcomes (e.g., empathy, flexibility) and finally on to desired, culture- specific, external outcomes; that is, intercultural competence, defined as “behaving and communicating effectively and ap-propriately (based on one’s intercultural knowledge, skills and attitudes) to achieve one’s goals to some degree” (p. 254). Deardorff ’s (2006) behaviorally based outcome is in accordance with our conceptualization of sociocultural adaptation as the “acquisition of culturally appropriate skills and the demonstration of functionally adaptive behaviors in culturally novel settings (Wilson, Ward, Fetvadjiev, & Bethel, 2017) and fits well within our model of culture learning. 
The attribute- behavior controversy is also addressed by van Driel and Gabrenya (2013, p. 886) in their discussion of cross- cultural competence. 
 
654 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
"The distinction between cross- cultural competence as an attribute that is antecedent to performance and cross- cultural competence as performance itself is critical given the oft- cited observation that the factors that determine performance do not constitute performance. . . performance is synonymous with behavior. It is something that people do, and it can be observed.” 
This perspective can be taken to acknowledge the importance of traits such as cultural empathy and capabilities such as sensitivity and cultural intelligence, but it does not confuse them with the acquisition of culturally appropriate skills and the performance of effective behaviors in new and unfamiliar settings (i.e., demonstrated intercultural competence; also see Wilson et al., 2017). 
Related to this conceptual issue are limitations in our assessment instruments. Cultural competence or sociocultural adaptation is about skilled behaviors; however, with the rare exception of some early assessment tools that rely on observation and evaluation (e.g., the Behavioral Assessment Scale for Intercultural Communication by Koester and Olebe, 1988), at best, our measures depend on self- reported behaviors and competencies. This raises issues about the ecological validity of commonly used instruments such as the original Sociocultural Adaptation Scale (Ward & Kennedy, 1999), the Intercultural Effectiveness Scale (Portalla & Chen, 2010), and the Brief Sociocultural Adaptation Scale (Demes & Geeraert, 2014).1 
What Facilitates Culture Learning and Skills Acquisition? This section reviews and integrates empirical research within the culture learning framework, examining the correlates and predictors of self- and other- reported culturally competent behaviors and performances. It commences with an overview of personal and situational factors that affect learning outcomes and also considers contextual factors that can influence the acquisition of cultural competencies. 
Situational Factors Culture learning can only commence if there are opportunities to engage in learning processes arising either from naturally occurring day- to- day experiences or from more structured learning activities. Accordingly, studies have demonstrated a positive association between length of residence in a new cultural setting and cultural competency in international students (Wang & Mallinckrodt, 2006), expatriates on overseas assignments (Mol, Born, Willemsen, & van der Molen, 2005), and immigrants (Zlobina, Basbabe, Paez, 
1. The measures of sociocultural adaptation and intercultural effectiveness can be contrasted with instruments that assess personal attributes such as the Multicultural Personality Questionnaire (van der Zee & van Oudenhoven, 2000)  or the Intercultural Adjustment Potential Scale (Matsumoto et  al., 2001). Measures of cultural intelligence (CQ) include self- reported behaviors indicative of cultural competence (e.g., I change my nonverbal behavior when a cross- cultural situation requires it), but as Ng, Van Dyne, and Ang (2009) argue that CQ is an antecedent to learning processes, the measure is not included here. In our framework, we position CQ as an individual difference that predicts cultural competence, which is consistent with the approach generally adopted in research on cultural intelligence. 
 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  655 
& Furham, 2006). Unfortunately, most studies are cross- sectional in nature. Longitudinal studies are relatively rare but demonstrate marked improvement in cultural competency in the first 3– 4 months of a sojourn (O’Reilly, Ryan, & Hickey, 2010) and then a leveling off of skills acquisition over time (Ward, Okura, Kennedy, & Kojima, 1998), approximating a learning curve. But these studies also have shortcomings in that sample sizes are often very small and only the average pattern of change is assessed. 
These issues have been addressed in a recent study by Hirai, Frazier, and Syed (2015), which examined trajectories of sociocultural adaptation in 248 international students surveyed at five time points through the course of an academic year (i.e., during the first month of the fall semester, then on average 1, 2, 4, and 6 months later). The researchers uncovered three trajectories of social difficulties: (1) low decreasing (51%), (2) moderate decreasing (42%), and (3) high stable (7%). The study is important as it demonstrates different trajectories of sociocultural adaptation problems, including a high stable difficulty group that was not identified in the average trajectory. However, the research is not an adequate test of the learning curve hypothesis as the international students had resided in the United States for variable periods of time before the first testing. 
 Culture learners can benefit not only from extended experience in their new environment, but also from past experiences in culturally novel settings. More specifically, experiential learning acquired in one culture may be generalized to another, particularly if the learner has good meta- skills and the cultural environments are similar. Previous international experience is related to greater learning resources, such as increased cultural intelligence (Moon, Choi, & Jung, 2013), more engagement with host nationals (Wu & Ang, 2011), and better sociocultural adaptation (Masgoret, 2006). However, the associations between past experience and current behaviors, while significant, are not strong. 
Intercultural contact affords learning opportunities, and research has shown that sojourners who have more contact with their domestic peers have better social skills (Trice, 2004). There is also clear evidence that intercultural contact is associated with better sociocultural adaptation (Li & Gasser, 2005; Masgoret, 2006; Zlobina et al., 2006). However, if host nationals are not receptive to intercultural interactions, this limits learning opportunities for newcomers. Indeed, sojourners who perceive discrimination have less frequent interactions with host nationals (Leong & Ward, 2000; Ward & Leong, 2005) and have fewer cross- cultural skills (Swami, Arteche, Chamorro- Premuzic, & Furnham, 2010). 
More formal intercultural training also provides an avenue for culture learning and bolsters individual resources such as cultural intelligence (Moon et al., 2013; Rehg, Gundlach, & Grigorian, 2012) and self- efficacy (Mak & Buckingham, 2007). Meta- analyses have demonstrated strong links between training and culturally appropriate interpersonal skills and sociocultural adaptation (Morris & Robie, 2001; Wilson et al., 2013). However, training interventions are not uniformly successful (e.g., Puck, Kittler, & Wright, 2008), and it has been suggested that the relationship between training and positive learning 
656 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
outcomes can be moderated by the type, timing, quality, and objectives (e.g., knowledge, attitudes, skills) of the program (Littrell, Salas, Hess, Paley, & Riedel, 2006). 
Finally, cultural context plays a role in the culture learning experience. Littrell and Salas (2005) maintain that some countries are just intrinsically more difficult to adapt to than others, described as variations in “cultural toughness,” which is likely to be related to the degree of hardship influenced by the level of national development. Cultural looseness– tightness (the degree of behavioral regulation and toleration for deviance from social norms) also impacts culture learning, and research has shown that sojourners experience more sociocultural adaptation difficulties in tight cultures (Geeraert et  al., 2019). Moreover, cultural distance, the degree of dissimilarity between culture of origin and culture of contact, is associated with greater social difficulties and lower levels of self- reported cultural competence (Demes & Geeraert, 2014; Suanet & van de Vijver, 2009; Wilson et al., 2013). 
Personal Factors Four groups of individual difference factors have been linked to positive culture learning outcomes. These are language proficiency, intercultural “mindsets,” cultural intelligence, and personality. 
In an earlier discussion of culture learning approaches to acculturation, Masgoret and Ward (2006) positioned language proficiency at the core and as the key to facilitating intercultural interactions that lead to the acquisition of culturally appropriate and effective behaviors. Indeed, there is an abundance of research that documents the positive role that language proficiency plays in the development of culturally appropriate skills (e.g., Kashima & Loh, 2006; Masgoret, 2006; Zhang & Goodson, 2011). Language proficiency is the first step to gaining entrance to a new cultural community and learning culturally appropriate behaviors in a new cultural environment. Furthermore, the relationship between language fluency and greater participation in the host community is a reciprocal one, with more frequent interactions increasing proficiency and greater proficiency leading to more frequent intercultural interactions (Clément, Noels, & Denault, 2001). 
Beyond language resources, malleable individual differences exert influences on the process and outcomes of culture learning. Key among these are self- efficacy, intercultural sensitivity, and cultural intelligence. The first of these, self- efficacy, refers to individuals’ beliefs and expectations about their capabilities to execute a positive, effective, domain- specific behavioral performance. Although anticipating efficacious outcomes is not sufficient to ensure desired behaviors if abilities are lacking or if situational factors limit the probability of success, expectations are a major determinant of performance. Indeed, research has shown that immigrants’ and sojourners’ pre- departure expectations of social difficulty are significantly related to their subsequent experiences (Mähönen & Jasinkaja- Lahti, 2012; Mähönen, Leinonen, & Jasinkaja- Lahti, 2013; Masgoret, 2006) and 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  657 
that cross- cultural self- efficacy predicts better sociocultural adaptation outcomes (Li & Gasser, 2005). 
A second malleable individual difference is intercultural sensitivity, an individual’s capacity to comprehend and appreciate cultural differences (Chen & Starosta, 2000). Intercultural sensitivity can be seen as an intercultural “mindset” and cognitive antecedent of effective and appropriate culture- specific behaviors. It has been related not only to empathic perspective- taking, but also to intercultural communication effectiveness (Chen & Starosta, 2000). 
More widely researched than either of these is cultural intelligence or CQ, defined as “a person’s capacity to adapt effectively to new cultural contexts” (Earley & Ang, 2003, p. 59). Over the past 15 years, there has been an impressive body of research on CQ, particularly in the context of international business and cross- cultural management. CQ is known to play a significant role in expatriate effectiveness, including successful intercultural negotiations, appropriate cultural judgment and decision- making tasks, and effective performance in multicultural teams (Ang et  al., 2007; Imai & Gelfand, 2010; Moon, 2013). CQ also underpins intercultural communication abilities, and there is robust evidence that it predicts expatriate work performance (Mol et al., 2005) as well as intercultural cooperation (Mor, Morris, & Joh, 2013). 
CQ is multifaceted and assessed in cognitive, meta- cognitive, motivational, and behavioral domains. Of course, some CQ facets may be more effective in predicting performance outcomes than others depending on the sphere of cultural competency. There is evidence that motivational CQ predicts self- reported sociocultural adaptation (Ward et al., 2009). Cognitive and meta- cognitive CQ has been shown to predict culturally appropriate judgment and decision- making, while behavioral CQ and meta- cognitive CQ are associated with better expatriate job performance (Ang et al., 2007). 
Finally, personality is one of the most robust predictors of culture learning and the acquisition of culture- specific skills. There is a rich and abundant literature on learning and performance that can provide the basis for hypothesizing about the links between the Big Five personality domains and the acquisition of culturally appropriate skills. Along these lines, studies have shown that conscientiousness is associated with better learning and performance outcomes (Kappe & Van der Flier, 2010) and better transfer of training (Blume, Ford, Baldwin, & Huang, 2010). Neuroticism is related to lower levels of self- efficacy; as such, it tends to inhibit learning and performance (Schmitt, 2008). In contrast, extraverts and agreeable individuals are likely to create more opportunities for experiential learning because extraverts engage in more outgoing behaviors, and agreeable people relate to others in ways that tend to encourage more supportive feedback (Tams, 2008). Research findings on the Five Factor Model of personality and culture learning largely converge with these predictions. Ward et al.’s (2004) study of expatriates and international students in Australia and Singapore found that extraversion, agreeableness, and conscientiousness were related to less, and neuroticism related to more, social difficulties. The 
658 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
same pattern of correlations was reported by Swagler and Jome (2005) in their study of North American expatriates in Taiwan. 
The MPQ, with its social initiative, flexibility, emotional stability, openness, and cultural empathy subscales, has also been used in studies of intercultural contact and its outcomes (van der Zee & Van Oudenhoven, 2000). Research has shown that MPQ personality traits are positively related to intercultural skills, both in general and in domain- specific areas, such as managing academic demands and job performance (Kagnici, 2012; Leong, 2007; van Erp, van der Zee, Giebels, & van Duijn, 2014; Ward et al., 2009). Open- mindedness and cultural empathy, in particular, foster intercultural insights and contribute to cultural judgment and decision- making skills (Herfst, van Oudenhoven, & Timmerman, 2008). More broadly, there is a robust relationship between MPQ traits and sociocultural adaptation found in both longitudinal (Leong, 2007) and cross- sectional research (Lee & Cifti, 2014; Ward & Fischer, 2008). In general, traits such as cultural empathy and cross- cultural efficacy have stronger relationships with cultural competence than do broader personality dimensions, such as extraversion and openness, as was reported in Wilson et  al.’s (2013) meta- analysis of studies using the Sociocultural Adaptation Scale. 
Moving Forward The culture learning approach provides a second perspective on intercultural contact, emphasizing the necessity for and process of the acquisition of the culture- specific skills required to operate effectively in new cultural milieux. Basic learning processes are at the core of this approach, and the factors that facilitate or impede these learning processes are of primary interest. However, a lack of consensus about the nature and definition of key concepts has hampered conceptual integration of the field (Leung, Ang, & Tan, 2014). Minimally, researchers must be very clear about their conceptual orientations and justify their measurement techniques. Optimally, a consensus about the defining features and appropriate measures of effectiveness, competence, and adaptation should emerge. Whether we can move beyond Van de Vijver and Leung’s (2009, p. 406) characterization of theory and research on intercultural competence as a set of “overlapping, complementary and incompatible models” is the major challenge for the future. 
C: Cultural Orientations and Intercultural Relations The previous sections highlighted affective and behavioral aspects of acculturation, describing the culture learning and stress and coping approaches as frameworks for understanding the challenges and outcomes of intercultural contact. This section focuses on cognitive elements of the acculturation experience, involving questions about identity (how one sees one’s self and one’s ethno- cultural groups) and intercultural perceptions 
 
 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  659 
(how one views and wishes to relate to other ethno- cultural groups). This involves both subtle processes of enculturation and acculturation as well as active decision- making and agentic cognitive and behavioral changes in response to the push and pull of two or more cultural foundations. This approach rests primarily on the acculturation framework originally proposed by John Berry (1980, 1984) and broadly addresses issues of cultural maintenance and participation in the wider society. 
 The roots of Berry’s acculturation framework can be found in his early work on marginality with Australian Aboriginals (Berry, 1970), followed by his theorizing about the retention of heritage culture and the patterns of intergroup relations in plural societies (Berry, 1974). Berry (1984, p. 357) later posed the two core questions defining his model: “Is it considered to be of value to maintain one’s own distinctive identity and cultural group characteristics?” and “Is it considered to be of value to maintain positive relations with my group and others within the society?” The questions form the basis of four acculturation orientations (Berry, 1997, 2001). That is, when individuals wish to maintain both cultural heritage and relations with other groups, integration results. If neither is desired, marginalization occurs. Separation reflects a valuing of only cultural maintenance, while assimilation occurs if only intergroup relations are desired. 
 In this section, we position Berry’s conceptual framework at the center of theory and research on cultural orientations. After summarizing key conceptual and methodological issues, we describe the antecedents of these cultural orientations and their outcomes, placing particular emphasis on adaptation and intercultural relations. We also introduce conceptual challenges and extensions to Berry’s theorizing, including research on the dynamic processes of cultural identity styles, remote acculturation, and acculturating to a globalizing world. Figure 20.3 illustrates the organizational framework for the presentation of this material.

Key Conceptual and Measurement Issues There are two key points to consider with respect to the development of Berry’s theorizing. First, his acculturation framework represents a significant theoretical advance over the unidimensional model of acculturation that was popular in the 1970s and 1980s (e.g., Olmeda, 1979).2 In contrast to the unidimensional approach, Berry regarded the orientations to heritage and contact cultures as orthogonal domains, both of which are important in interpreting acculturative changes. Second, Berry’s theorizing continues to evolve, and a range of modifications and extensions to his basic framework has been introduced by acculturation researchers over time. 
Although the two core dimensions of Berry’s framework are defined in terms of cul-tural maintenance and cultural contact, acculturation researchers have taken a variety of approaches to defining and measuring the second dimension. Some have retained Berry’s original formulation, assessing the desire for cultural maintenance and intercultural contact (e.g., Zagefka, González, & Brown, 2011), while others have examined participation in terms of behavioral indicators of involvement in the customary practices of the national culture (e.g., Kus- Harbord & Ward, 2015). Still others have interpreted the second dimension of Berry’s framework in terms of cultural adoption (e.g., Bourhis & Dayan, 2004), taking on aspects of the national culture, which could be reflected in terms of attitudes, values, behaviors, or cultural identities or a combination of these (Berry, 2009; Schwartz et al., 2015). 
As can be seen from these examples, research has gone beyond the examination of self- and social cognitions, although few programs of research have made clear and consistent distinctions among attitudes, self- reported behaviors, and cultural identities while incorporating multiple domains in their models. Two exceptions to this trend are work by Birman and colleagues, who have systematically distinguished identity and behavioral aspects of acculturation (Birman & Trickett, 2001; Birman, Trickett, & Buchanan, 2005), and studies by Navas and colleagues, who proposed the Relative Acculturation Extended Model (RAEM) that includes real and ideal acculturation responses, highlighting the distinction between acculturation attitudes and self- reported behaviors (Navas, García, Sánchez, Rojas, Pumares, & Fernández, 2005; Navas, Rojas, García, & Pumares, 2007). 
 Despite variable approaches, empirical evidence has supported the conclusion that bidimensional models and measures provide a “more valid and useful operationalization of acculturation” than their unidimensional counterparts (Ryder, Alden, & Paulhus, 2000, p.  49); critical reviews have recommended the use of bidimensional assessment tools (Matsudaira, 2006; Rudmin, 2009), and a recent meta- analysis has supported the psychometric reliability of these measures (Huyhn, Howell, & Benet- Martínez, 2009). Bidimensional measures of acculturation, such as the Vancouver Index of Acculturation (Ryder et al., 2000), and the Acculturation Index (Ward & Rana- Deuba, 1999) have come 
2. This is also the case in comparison with unsophisticated proxy measures, such as nativity and language, still used by public health researchers in epidemiological studies (Ward, Milfont, & Poortinga, 2017). 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  661 
to be regarded as the most robust and flexible assessment tools. First, they can be used to examine the independent effects of heritage and mainstream orientations on adaptation outcomes. Second, they can also be used to delineate the four acculturation strategies proposed by Berry’s (2001, 2006b) theorizing (Snauwaert, Soenens, Vanbeselaere, & Boen, 2003; Ward & Kus, 2012). Third, they can be used as the basis for data- led techniques such as cluster analysis or latent profile analysis to identify different types of acculturation profiles (Fox, Merz, Solórzano, & Roesch, 2013). 
Finally, there is a line of research that involves the “independent” or discrete assessments of the four acculturation categories as originally advocated by Berry (e.g., Berry, Phinney, Sam, & Vedder, 2006). This technique relies on four parallel sets of statements assessing integration, assimilation, separation, and marginalization, respectively, in relation to cultural behaviors or preferences (e.g., friendships, language usage, and media consumption) and generates scores for each of the acculturation categories. This measurement technique has been widely criticized, notably by Rudmin and Ahmadzadeh (2001), who discussed problems arising from ipsative constructs, double- barrelled statements, and acquiescence effects. Moreover, Rudmin (2003; Rudmin, Wang, & Castro, 2017) has argued that a substantial number of studies has shown that the four categories are not independent and, indeed, sometimes intercorrelate in ways that are in conflict with their underlying conceptualization (e.g., a strong, positive correlation between separation and assimilation). 
In the end, the selection of assessment instruments for research purposes will be linked to the overarching objectives of a specific study, and, as discussed by Doucerain, Segalowitz, and Ryder (2017), may involve “methodological tradeoffs.” However, with respect to the use of psychometric scales, there is strong evidence that bidimensional approaches now dominate the field and provide the most robust assessments of acculturation (Celenk & van de Vijver, 2014). There is also good reason to consider carefully the distinction of public and private spheres of activity and between intrapersonal domains, such as identity and values, and interpersonal behaviors. However, the assessment of four acculturation strategies by separate scales to assess integration, separation, marginalization, and integration is not recommended due to psychometric limitations. 
Antecedents and Outcomes of Acculturation Orientations 
Predicting Acculturation Orientations In contrast to the voluminous literature on the acculturation outcomes, relatively little research has been conducted on the predictors of acculturation orientations. Most commonly, personal background factors such as age, gender, generation, length of residence, education, and socioeconomic status have been explored as predictors of both “home and host” cultural affiliations, but, in many cases, the associations between demographic factors and acculturation attitudes and behaviors appear to be sample- specific. Findings on age and gender are mixed, and multigenerational studies often find that 
 
 
662 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
later generations show a stronger affiliation to the national culture (Schwartz, Pantin, Sullivan, Prado, & Szapocznik, 2006), but this does not necessarily involve a weakening of an affiliation to heritage culture. Furthermore, findings are often a function of acculturation domain. For example, ethnic identity often remains strong and relatively stable over generations, but proficiency in ethnic languages often decreases in later generations (Phinney, Berry, Vedder, & Liebkind, 2006). 
For the most part, individual difference measures have been underexplored as correlates and predictors of acculturation orientations, with only occasional studies of motivation, perceptions of cultural distance, and emotional intelligence. Not surprisingly, research has shown that voluntary immigrants are more willing to adapt to and affiliate with the local culture than are forced immigrants (Udahemuka & Pernice, 2010), greater perceived cultural distance is associated with more heritage culture and fewer host culture behaviors (Suanet & van de Vijver, 2009), and emotional intelligence is related to integration (Lopez- Zafra & El Ghoudani, 2014). In addition, greater compartmentalization of bicultural identities is associated with greater endorsement of separation (Benet- Martínez & Haritatos, 2005). 
Personality has received slightly more attention in the acculturation literature, where the focus has been largely on acculturation attitudes. Ramdhonee and Bhowon (2012) investigated the Five Factor Model of Personality as predictors of attitudes toward integration and marginalization in first- generation immigrants in Mauritius. They reported that Openness, Agreeableness, and low levels of Neuroticism predicted favorable attitudes toward integration. In contrast, Neuroticism and low levels of Openness were significant predictors of marginalization attitudes. Benet- Martínez and Haritatos’s (2005) study of Chinese Americans found that Openness predicted opposition to separation, and Luijters, van der Zee, and Otten (2006) reported that low emotional stability was associated with a preference for assimilation over integration. (See also Chapter 13 by Jüri Allik and Anu Realo on culture and personality traits.) 
The only programmatic work that has concentrated on individual differences and acculturation strategies to date has been undertaken by Safdar and colleagues, who proposed the Multidimensional Individual Difference Acculturation Model (MIDA; Safdar, Lay, & Struthers, 2003). The model as a whole draws on a range of theories from social (e.g., Social Identity Theory) and health (e.g., stress and coping theories) psychology and examines acculturation strategies as mediators of the effects of individual differences on intra- and intercultural relations and psychological well- being; however, for our purposes here, emphasis is placed on the relationship between acculturation and individual differences in (1) psychosocial resources such as resilience, mastery, cultural competence, and social support; (2)  co- national connectedness defined by family and co- ethnic relationships and embeddedness; and (3) hassles (i.e., chronic irritants in daily life). Initial research with Iranian immigrants in Canada found that psychosocial resources predicted less support for separation while co- national connectedness predicted more favorable attitudes to separation and less favorable attitudes to assimilation. More 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  663 
recently, Safdar, Calvez, and Lewis (2012) extended their research to Russian and Indian immigrants in Canada and included the assessment of attitudes to integration, separation, and assimilation; however, the relationships between the individual difference antecedents and the acculturation attitudes varied markedly between the samples and for the most part did not replicate the findings from Iranian Canadians. 
Acculturation and Adaptation Berry (2001) has long argued that, under most circumstances, integration is the most adaptive strategy and marginalization the least adaptive, with assimilation and separation falling in between. This suggests that cultural affiliations and participation in both the heritage and contact cultures exert positive influences on adaptation and act in an additive fashion. Along these lines, the International Comparative Study of Ethno- cultural Youth (ICSEY) merits particular attention (Berry et al., 2006). The research examined identity, acculturation, and adaptation in immigrant youth in 13 countries using cluster analysis to generate four acculturation profiles of immigrant youth and comparing psychological and sociocultural adaptation across the integrated, ethnic, national, and diffuse groups (Phinney et al., 2006). 
In line with Berry’s (2001) contentions, the integrated profile was associated with the best psychological and sociocultural adaptation outcomes, and the diffuse profile, similar to marginalization, was associated with the poorest outcomes. In terms of the adaptation outcomes, the ethnic and national profiles fell in between. A  major difference was in connection with psychological adaptation, where the ethnic profile was associated with a higher than average level of psychological well- being and the national profile with a slightly lower than average level of well- being. Conversely, the adolescents in the national group appeared to do somewhat better with respect to sociocultural adaptation. Overall, the pattern of results corroborates the positive contributions that both ethnic and national cultures can make to the psychological and sociocultural adaptation of young immigrants and the dangers of disengagement from cultural ballasts. 
Nguyen and Benet- Martínez’s (2013) meta- analysis provides further support of Berry’s theorizing. The researchers examined 83 studies (N  =  23,197) that examined the relationships between unidimensional, bidimensional, and typological measures of acculturation and measures of psychological and sociocultural adaptation. Their key findings were: 
 1. The mean effect size for integration (referred to as biculturalism in the meta- analysis) was 0.51. 
 2. The relationship between adaptation and integration was stronger than the relationship between either heritage or dominant culture orientation and adaptation. 
 3. The relationship between integration and adaptation was stronger when bidimensional measures of acculturation were used compared to unidimensional or typological measures.

Acculturation and Intercultural Relations Research has shown that preference for integration is linked to more positive intergroup relations for immigrants and members of the receiving society (Zagefka & Brown, 2002). It is often the case, however, that the acculturation preferences of immigrants and minorities do not match the acculturation expectations of members of the receiving society. There is strong international evidence that immigrants consistently prefer integration (Berry et  al., 2006; Ward & Leong, 2006), but the preferences of members of the host community are more variable (Kosic, Mannetti, & Sam, 2005; Rohmann, Florack, & Piontkowski, 2006; Ward & Masgoret, 2008; Zick, Wagner, van Dick, & Petzel, 2001). The significance of the match– mismatch of acculturation preferences and expectations is highlighted in the Interactive Acculturation Model (IAM; Bourhis, Moïse, Perreault, & Senécal, 1997) that links state policies to the dynamic interplay of immigrant and receiving community approaches to acculturation. The model proposes that state immigration policies are intertwined with state ideologies, ranging on a continuum from pluralist to ethnist, and that these policies and ideologies impact the acculturation preferences of immigrants and members of the receiving community. Moreover, it is argued that convergence and divergence of acculturation attitudes and behaviors affect intergroup relations. 
The complexity of the IAM, as well as the variable probability that each match or mismatch actually occurs in contemporary democracies, has prevented a systematic test of all conditions and combinations; however, the underlying principles have been tested in conjunction with the Concordance Model in research that has examined concordance and discordance of immigrant– host views (Piontkowski, Rohmann, & Florack, 2002). Discordance between the acculturation attitudes of the majority and the attitudes they attribute to immigrants is associated with more threatening and less enriching relations (Piontkowski et al., 2002). Furthermore, discordance on the cultural maintenance issue and the contact- participation issue independently contribute to the prediction of realistic threat, symbolic threat, and intergroup anxiety for both majority group members and immigrants above and beyond the effects of negative intergroup contact (Rohmann et al., 2006). 
Re- evaluating the Acculturation Framework: Conceptual Challenges and Extensions Beyond distinguishing real versus ideal acculturation; acculturation in identity, values, attitudes, and behavioral domains; and acculturation in public and private settings to interpret empirical research findings, there have been calls to reexamine the conceptual bases of the framework with a view to extending or modifying it. A fundamental criticism of acculturation research to date has been the widespread emphasis on outcomes, which captures only a static snapshot of acculturation at one point in time (Ward & Geeraert, 2016). Process issues have been largely overlooked. For example, we know that integration is highly desired by immigrants and that it is associated with positive psychological and sociocultural outcomes; however, little is known about how integration is achieved. 
 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  665 
Ward and colleagues considered this issue in their research on identity, integration, and psychological adaptation (Ward, Tseung- Wong, Szabo, Qumseya, & Bhowon, 2018). The researchers introduced the notion of cultural identity styles to describe the cognitive and behavioral strategies that individuals use for identity- relevant decisions. They found that a motivation to integrate activated both hybrid and alternating cultural identity styles in bicultural individuals. The former was defined by blending desirable elements of heritage and national cultures and putting these together in a novel way to form a hybrid cultural identity. The latter style also allowed individuals to retain heritage and national identities but, in this case, by identity- shifting depending on social circumstances. While both identity styles represent attempts to achieve integration, they have different pathways to well- being. More specifically, Ward and colleagues found that the hybrid style was associated with greater cultural identity consolidation; that is, a stronger bicultural, hyphenated identity and, in turn, greater psychological adaptation. The alternating style, in contrast, was linked to greater cultural identity conflict and, in turn, lower levels of psychological well- being. 
Dynamic processes have also been the subject of research by Zhang and Noels (2013) on situated identity and by Doucerain, Dere, and Ryder (2013), whose research using the “cultural day” reconstruction method found that Canadian university students switched cultural identities on average about four times daily. More process- oriented research, including longitudinal studies, is described in the next section, which considers developmental perspectives on cultural contact and change. 
Beyond the issue of process, acculturation research has also been criticized for reducing acculturation experiences to two dimensions, as if heritage and contact cultures are sufficient to capture complex acculturation experiences. The first and simplest response to this criticism has been to “add” cultural orientations depending on the characteristics of the ethno- cultural group under study or the features of their acculturation situation. For example, Verkuyten, Thijs, and Stevens (2012) have examined the dy-namics of ethnic, national, and religious identities in Moroccan Dutch Muslims. At the same time, Ferguson (2013) has discussed how Jamaican immigrants to the United States juggle three cultural worlds, Jamaican, European American, and African American. The crux of these approaches is that constraining cultural orientations to ethnic and national cultures offers only a limited perspective and that multiple aspects of cultural identities need to be considered to gain a more comprehensive and meaningful understanding of acculturative experiences. 
In an era of globalization, it has also been argued that contemporary acculturation experiences transcend national boundaries and that this needs to be taken into account in acculturation theory and research (van Oudenhoven & Ward, 2013). Chen et al. (2016) have proposed the notion of a global orientation, reflecting “the psychological processes involved in acculturating to a globalizing world” (p. 1). Similarly, Kunst and Sam (2013) have shown that a global identity can act as a protective factor for “marginalized” minorities who identify neither with their ethnic nor national groups. At the same time, 
666 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Ferguson and Bornstein (2012) have raised the issue of “remote acculturation.” More specifically, in contrast to the conceptualization of acculturation in terms of continuous, first- hand intercultural contact, they argue that intermittent or indirect contact with geographically or historically distinct cultures, facilitated by globalization, can produce acculturation. Furthermore, in their study of mother– adolescent dyads in Jamaica, they found that 11% of mothers and 33% of adolescents were classified as Americanized Jamaican versus traditional Jamaican. 
More complex and varied considerations suggest that it may be time to think outside the Berry boxes and that the static integration, separation, assimilation, and marginalization categories may not capture the multiple, dynamic ways in which cultural affiliations and orientations may be negotiated. Along these lines, perhaps the most radical position recommends the abandonment of dimensional and categorical frameworks altogether in favor of a network approach, which recognizes that individuals’ cultural engagements are partial, plural, and fluid, whether the engagement is with heritage culture or multiple other cultures. As such, culture’s influence on individuals is also seen as partial and plural. This conceptualization of culture, including its determinants and consequences, is known as the polyculturalist paradigm (Morris, Chiu, & Liu, 2015). Despite the conceptual merits of this theoretical framework, there is little explicit guidance about the practical implications for the measurement of acculturation or the most appropriate methods for conducting polycultural work in the area. (See also Chapter  17 by Amir Rosenmann and Jenny Kurman and Chapter 19 by Ying- yi Hong and Siran Zhan on culture and multiple selves and identities.) 
Moving Forward This section has focused on cultural orientations, how one relates to one’s heritage culture and to other cultures, whether in reference to attitudes, values, behaviors, or identities. The approach is guided by Berry’s (1984, 2001) acculturation framework, which has been extended by researchers beyond two core orientations (e.g., ethnic and national) to three or more (e.g., ethnic, national, religious) and beyond the influence of first- hand face- to- face intercultural encounters to remote acculturation and globalization. These are all positive advancements. The question remains, however, as to whether these models are sufficient on their own to capture the dynamic nature of acculturation in the era of globalization. More attention to process issues and the complexity of multiple cultural orientations is needed in the future. (See also Chapter 23 by Huajian Cai, Zihang Huang, and Yiming Jing on cultural change as a result of globalization, and Chapter 17 by Amir Rosenmann and Jenny Kurman on cultural change due to modernization and consumerism.) 
D: Developmental Processes In this final section of the chapter, we introduce individual development as the fourth pillar of acculturation. We argue that acculturation is inherently intertwined with 
 
 
 
affeCT, behavior, CogniT ion, and develoPMenT  |  667 
developmental processes, and, by failing to consider developmental perspectives, we risk overlooking a crucial element in the changes occurring within individuals as a result of intercultural contact. While we acknowledge that developmental processes influence every aspect of psychological functioning, in this section, we focus on identity development. The study of acculturation from a developmental perspective is still in its infancy, and the empirical evidence is limited in most areas. However, identity has become one of the most intensively researched topics, providing a shining example of how integrating developmental theories into our existing frameworks can expand and enrich our knowledge of acculturation. This includes theoretical frameworks arising from psychosocial and cognitive perspectives on personal identity development (Berzonsky, 1989; Erikson, 1968; Marcia, 1966), developmental work on ethnic identity (Phinney, 1989), and conceptual linkages between personal and cultural identity (Schwartz, Montgomery, & Briones, 2006). Our theoretical framework for synthesizing developmental and acculturative bases of identity development is presented in Figure 20.4. 
In the remainder of this section, we describe the psychosocial theories of identity development that can inform acculturation theory and research and, accordingly, draw attention to key conceptual and methodological issues. We then consider personal and cultural identity development in immigrant and ethnic minority youth and adults. Family influences on acculturation and development and acculturation gaps receive particular attention. We conclude with recommendations to extend developmental perspectives on acculturation.
