Emotion Regulation Cultural differences in display rules affect how people regulate emotions (Mauss & Ford, 2015). Independent and interdependent cultures differ in the importance and significance of expressing emotions to others. Independent cultures value self- expression and social communication that is perceived by others. Interdependent cultures reinforce the importance of social harmony and thinking of one’s self as defined by social relationships and roles. Expressing emotions during social interaction may be perceived as self- focused rather than other- focused. In independent cultures, emotions are regulated through cognitive reappraisal, or thinking about the emotion in a different manner. Cognitive reappraisal assumes that emotions are expressed and experienced to their full extent, and, as the meaning or significance of the emotional event is reconsidered, the emotional intensity of the experience lessens. In interdependent cultures, emotions are regulated through expressive suppression, or an inhibition of the expression of one’s emotions. Through expressive suppression, social harmony across group members is maintained to a greater extent, even throughout emotional events experienced by individuals that may induce mild arousal or perceptions of risk or danger in the social or physical environment. 
Given distinct culture- based strategies for regulating emotions, physiological mechanisms underlying emotion regulation also may differ across cultures. In an ERP study of culture and emotion regulation, Asian Americans showed a greater decrease of the parietal late positive potential (LPP) during expressive suppression relative to European Americans (Murata, Moser, & Kitayama, 2013). The LPP is an ERP component that peaks approximately 300– 400 milliseconds after a stimulus is presented and has been linked to arousal and emotional experience. When regulating emotion in a culture- specific manner, Asian Americans show a reduction in a physiological marker of emotional arousal. These results support the notion that cultural differences in emotion regulation result from distinct physiological mechanisms in the brain. 
Cultural differences in emotional regulation are related to genes. The oxytocin receptor gene (OXTR) has previously been associated with social behavior, including social cognition and empathy (Rodrigues, Saslow, Garcia, John, & Keltner, 2009). In a gene- by- culture study of emotional social support seeking, distressed Americans who carry the G allele of the OXTR rs53576 showed greater willingness to seek emotional social support relative to Koreans (Kim et al., 2010). These findings show that Americans who carry the social sensitivity allele are more likely to behave in a culturally consistent manner. Due to cultural differences in display rules, Americans are expected to express more emotions and to feel emotions more fully. For Americans, emotional experiences are situated in social relationships, with Western European cultural values and a social norm shared by group members (Butler, Lee, & Gross, 2007). For independent cultures, emotional expression is a normative part of the social environment. During emotional experiences, Americans who carry the social sensitivity allele are more likely to seek social support relative to Asians, possibility due to their willingness to share emotionally 
 
 
CulTural neurosC ienCe  |  709 
with others. Similarly, Americans who carry the social sensitivity allele may perceive others as more likely to provide the social resources appropriate for regulating emotions. For interdependent cultures, regulating emotions in a manner consistent with one’s culture reinforces social sensitivity. In a gene- by- culture interaction study of emotion regulation, Koreans who carry the G allele of OXTR rs53576 were more likely to rely on emotion suppression as an emotion regulation strategy, relative to Americans. Koreans who carry the social sensitivity allele show a preference for regulating emotion without reliance on others (Kim & Sasaki, 2012). 
Reward Processing Family obligation as a cultural resource suggests that children play an important role in supporting and providing assistance for their family. For families of Mexican background, family obligation may serve as an important cultural value, buffering adolescent youth from maladaptive behavior. Family serves as an important basis of social identity and as the primary social group for youth. Family obligation encourages youth to provide sustained assistance to their families, thus enhancing interdependence among family members, as well as unity and social support. With a strong societal expectation to care for others in the family, youth gain a sense of self that is defined by close social relationships and fulfillment of duties and obligations. 
Cultural values of family obligation shape the neurobiology of risk and reward during the developmental period of adolescence. In a neuroimaging study of family assistance and reward, white and Latino youth made decisions to contribute money to their family and themselves (Telzer, Masten, Berkman, Lieberman, & Fuligni, 2010). Latino youth showed greater neural activity within mesolimbic reward regions such as the ventral striatum when contributing to their family, whereas white youth demonstrated greater neural response in reward regions when contributing money to themselves. Youth with a strong family identity showed greater reward- related neural activity when making family contributions. These findings show that the cultural resource of family obligation tunes reward neural circuitry during donation. Another neuroimaging study of family obligation and reward in youth found that family obligation values were associated with greater neural activation within the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) during successful behavioral inhibition (Telzer, Fuligni, Lieberman & Galvan, 2013). These results demonstrate the importance of cultural values of family obligation for strengthening the cognitive skills that provide a foundation for preventative health behavior. 
Summary Cultural systems regulate mental and neurobiological mechanisms of emotion. Across distinct models of emotion, cultural systems guide the experience of emotion through the regulation of bodily response and cognitive appraisal. Within social practices, culture guides the recognition and expression of emotion within the body. The content of mental 
 
 
710 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and neural states of feeling reflect the learning of cultural input from the environment. Culture acts as a resource to regulate emotional experience in manner congruent with social norms (see also Chapter 12 by David Matsumoto and Hyisung C. Hwang for more discussion of culture and emotion). 
Cultural Neuroscience of Social Cognition Self- Knowledge Cultural differences affect how people think about themselves in relation to others (Markus & Kitayama, 1991; Oyserman, Coon, & Kemmelmeier, 2002). Independence and interdependence refer to self- construal styles, or how interconnected people feel to each other. Independent selves view themselves as unique and distinct from others. Interdependent selves define themselves by the social context, such as their social relations and roles with others. They perceive themselves as interconnected with close others. 
Early in development, children interact with parents who encourage distinct styles of thinking about the self (Wang, 2006). East Asian parents are more likely to reinforce their children to think of themselves socially, referring to them in conversation by their social roles, relationships, and contexts, while European American parents are more likely to encourage their children to think of themselves personally, referring to them with social attributions, traits, and dispositions. Through cultural construction of the self, children learn from their parents how to remember personal experiences in relation to their social interactions with others or as unitary features of themselves. In storytelling with their children, East Asian parents may reflect on social experiences by describing children’s behavior in relation to social norms and expectations, while European American parents may elaborate on stories with their children by emphasizing details of social events that are related to qualities of their personal actions. As children mature, early cultural experiences coincide with maturational changes in neurobiology such that cultural differences in formation of self- concept are reflected in neural representations of the self. 
By adulthood, neuroimaging studies show that cultural styles of self- construal are reflected in neural representations of self within medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC). East Asians and Westerners in China show distinct neural responses to the self within MPFC (Zhu, Zhang, Fan, & Han., 2007). Across both cultures, people showed greater MPFC activity when thinking about personal traits; however, East Asians also showed greater MPFC response when thinking about a close other, whereas Westerners did not. These findings support the notion of a culture- specific self, such that for East Asian and Westerners, neural representations of the self are interdependent and independent, respectively. In a cross- cultural neuroimaging study of culture and the self, Japanese and Caucasian Americans thought about themselves either by themselves or within a social context (Chiao et al., 2009). For individualistic people, MPFC response was greater when thinking about themselves alone, whereas for collectivistic people, MPFC response 
 
 
CulTural neurosC ienCe  |  711 
was greater when thinking about themselves within a social context. The degree of individualism and collectivism predicts the degree of neural activity within the MPFC when thinking of the self in a culture- specific manner. These findings show that cultural styles of self- construal modulate response within MPFC to self- knowledge. Neural representations reflect variation in encoding of self- knowledge due to culture. Cultural variation in neural representations of the self may illustrate variations in the organization of self- knowledge based on featural dimensions such as the depth and complexity of personal and social experience. 
Cultural influences on neural substrates of the self may vary depending on the type of social knowledge. People acquire social knowledge through encoding of distinct kinds of perceptual and conceptual cues. In a cross- cultural electrophysiological study of culture and self- recognition, British and Chinese participants viewed faces of themselves or personally familiar others and judged direction of head orientation (Sui, Liu, & Han, 2009). British participants showed greater self- advantage in self- recognition relative to Chinese participants. Cultural differences in electrophysiological response during self- recognition were observed within 200 milliseconds. British participants showed greater N2 amplitude when viewing their own face relative to familiar faces, whereas for Chinese participants, N2 amplitude was enhanced for familiar faces relative to own- face. The N2 waveform is typically associated with depth of face processing and greater individuation (Kubota & Ito, 2007). For independent selves, perceiving one’s face may lead to greater attentional processing of the perceptual cue due to the autonomous nature of the in-dependent self- concept. By contrast, for interdependent cultures, perceiving familiar faces may result in greater depth of processing and individuation due to the self- concept as defined by social relationships with others. For interdependent selves, perceptual representations of others expand self- relevant processes leading to greater attentional encoding of other- related social cues, such as familiar faces. 
Cultural differences in self- relevant processing may rely on distinct neurobiological mechanisms of social cognition. Breadth of cultural acquisition and maintenance of self- knowledge depend on independent and interdependent self- concept. In a cross- cultural neuroimaging study of the self, Chinese and Danish participants made judgments of social roles, personal traits, and physical attributes (Ma et  al., 2014). Behaviorally, Chinese showed greater interdependence relative to Danes. Across all kinds of social judgments, Danes showed greater MPFC response during self- processing relative to Chinese participants. Compared with Danes, Chinese participants showed stronger temporoparietal junction (TPJ) response when judging social attributes, but not physical or mental attributes. Furthermore, cultural variation in TPJ response during self- reflection was mediated in part due to the degree of cultural interdependence. Cultural differences in distinct neural substrates of self- processing suggest differential reliance on distinct kinds of social cognition. As an independent culture, Danes may rely more on simulated social inferences when thinking about the self. The MPFC is reliably activated during self- processing and encoding of information relevant to the self. The current findings 
712 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
support the notion that self- relevant processing, irrespective of type of self- knowledge, results in greater activity within regions of MPFC important for encoding and storage of self- knowledge. Consistent with interdependent cultures, Chinese show greater activity within brain regions typically associated with social reasoning and theory of mind. Interdependent cultures define the self contextually, through one’s social roles and relationships. For Chinese participants, greater response within the TPJ when thinking about different social roles is consistent with concept of the interdependent self in which social roles are defined by societal norms that govern the expectations and behavior of self and others. Thinking of the self in terms of social roles may enhance the conceptual processing of the self as defined in context within societal norms and thus strengthen the reliance on neural mechanisms of social cognitive processes that predictively compute rule- based social inferences, such as those associated with the TPJ. Cultural differences in neural pathways of social cognition suggest that the norms and practices of independent and interdependent cultures are encoded differentially at the neural level. 
For people undergoing acculturation, social life is defined by a multitude of cultural experiences. First- generation immigrants are knowledgeable not only of the culture of their heritage, but also of the host culture. Subsequent generations have experience with the heritage culture through interaction with family members and experience with the host culture through interaction with their community. People who are multicultural carry social knowledge about both their heritage and host cultures (Berry, 1997; Hong, Morris, Chiu, & Benet- Martinez, 2000; Oyserman & Lee, 2008). Depending on the social context, bicultural people may think about themselves and others differently, in ways that tunes neural mechanisms of social cognition depending on the culture. In a neuroimaging study of bicultural Asian Americans, people primed with collectivistic cultural values showed greater MPFC and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) response when thinking of themselves in a social context (Chiao et al., 2010). By contrast, people primed with individualistic cultural values demonstrated greater MPFC and PCC response when thinking of themselves without regard to the social context. These results show that neural representations within cortical midline structures encode self- knowledge reflective of the dual identities of bicultural Asian Americans. The flexibility of neural activity within the MPFC to the cultural context illustrates the malleability of brain responses to social experiences of acculturation that require integration of knowledge about the heritage and host culture. 
Social Perception One of the primary social capacities is the ability to perceive and recognize the social signals of others. Humans rely on a range of static and dynamic perceptual cues from the human face and body to infer and reason about other people’s minds. The face, in particular, communicates a wide range of social information, including intentionality and the mental states of others, such as thoughts, feelings, and motivation. Early in development, infants learn to perceive and recognize facial cues, particularly those from 
 
CulTural neurosC ienCe  |  713 
their cultural group, due to variations in neural response early within the perceptual processing stream (Balas, Westerlund, Hung, & Nelson, 2011). When perceiving faces of different races, people show preferential neural response when encoding same- relative to different- race faces. In a neuroimaging study of race and face perception, African Americans and Caucasian Americans showed greater neural response within the fusiform gyrus and medial temporal lobe for faces of the same race, a tuning of neural activity that corresponded to greater subsequent memory for same- race faces (Golby, Gabrieli, Chiao, & Eberhardt, 2001). 
Experiential tuning of neural pathways for social cognition during infancy is later reflected in perceptual biases of mental state reasoning by adulthood. The eye region of the face provides minimal perceptual cues, such as gaze direction, for theory of mind reasoning. Gaze perception plays an important role in the development of the ability to infer mental states (Baron- Cohen, 1995). In a neuroimaging study of culture and theory of mind, Japanese and Americans completed the “Reading the Mind in the Eyes” task, inferring mental states of others from social perceptual cues of the eye region (Adams et  al., 2009). Both Japanese and Americans showed greater accuracy at mental state decoding when viewing social perceptual cues from members of their own cultural group. Neural response within the bilateral superior temporal sulcus was also enhanced when perceiving and inferring mental states from the eye region of cultural group members. The superior temporal sulcus is a brain region important for mental state decoding, particularly from eye gaze (Allison, Puce, & McCarthy, 2000). These findings suggest an intercultural advantage at the behavioral and neural levels when perceiving social cues from faces of members of one’s own cultural group. 
Cultural transmission of social information from group members relies not only on the ability to infer their mental states, but also on the imitation of bodily gestures for social communication. Imitation, a social capacity for learning through the observation of others, relies on a network of brain circuitry including the left inferior frontal cortex and the right parietal lobule. In a neuroimaging study of race and imitation, African Americans and European Americans imitated the gestures of African American, European American, and Chinese American models (Losin, Cross, Iacoboni, & Dapretto, 2014). Both African American and European American participants showed greater neural response within the lateral frontoparietal and visual regions during imitation of dynamic gestures of African Americans relative to Chinese Americans or Caucasian Americans. These findings suggest that culturally acquired associations about different social groups, rather than group membership, affect the magnitude of response within neural pathways of imitation for bodily gestures. 
Empathy Empathy refers to the human capacity to share emotions with others. During empathy, people attend to and perceive the emotional state of another, which automatically generates a representation of emotion in one’s self that is associated with autonomic and 
 
 
714 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
physiological processes and can be regulated (Preston & De Waal, 2002). Perceiving and sharing the emotional experiences of others is an interdependent process and affected by the length and quality of social experienced shared by the self and others. Greater interdependence is more likely to enhance the similarity in emotional representations of the self and others and thus an appropriate response. 
Neuroimaging studies of empathy have identified a matrix of brain regions associated with empathic responding, including the ACC, bilateral insula (AI), and adjacent brain regions, such as the mirror neuron system (MNS), limbic system, and prefrontal cortex (Lamm, Decety, & Singer, 2011). The ACC and AI have been implicated in emotional empathy, or physiological processes associated with a shared representation of emotion with self and other. The MNS consists of the pars opercularis in the inferior frontal gyrus and is active during imitation, action observation, and understanding of intention (Iacoboni et al., 1999). The limbic system, including amygdala and hypothalamus, has been reliably shown to respond during perception and recognition of emotion, as well as during related processes that involve emotion responding, such as emotional memory (Adolphs, 2008). The medial portion of the prefrontal cortex, the MPFC, is typically responsive during cognitive empathy, such as when people infer the emotional states of others through mentalizing and perspective- taking, and it may be relied on as a regulatory mechanism during empathy. Neuroimaging research on culture and empathy have relied on behavioral paradigms that measure neural activity while participants engage in empathy tasks of physical pain (Xu, Zuo, Wang, & Han, 2009), social pain (Bruneau, Dufour, & Saxe, 2012; Cikara, Botnivick, & Fiske, 2011; Masten, Telzer, & Eisenberger, 2011), and emotional pain (de Greck et al., 2012; Mathur, Harada, Lipke, & Chiao, 2010). 
Culture shapes the neural circuitry of empathy. Interdependence is thought to affect the earliest stages of empathy. Other- focusedness, a subconstruct of interdependence, involves sensitivity to others and primacy of the interests of others more than one’s self. When thinking about how to understand and help others, it may be necessary to regulate self- interests for the sake of others. In the healthcare context, the empathy of healthcare workers and family members of patients plays an important social role in effective care. One aspect of contemporary medical care may involve patients undergoing medical treatment that temporarily induces physical pain. In a study of culture and empathy for physical pain, Chinese and Caucasians in China show greater neural response within the ACC and left AI for the physical suffering of group members in a healthcare context (Xu et al., 2009). These findings show that members of one’s cultural group demonstrate greater empathic responding when a group member experiences physical pain during medical treatment. 
Culture also interacts with genes associated with empathy and its neurobiological basis. Prior studies have shown that the oxytocin receptor (OXTR) polymorphism interacts with culture during emotional support- seeking (Kim et al., 2010). The OXTR gene has previously been associated with social sensitivity and empathic behavior. In a gene– culture behavioral study, Americans who carry the G allele of the OXTR rs53576 
CulTural neurosC ienCe  |  715 
and were more distressed showed more emotional support- seeking, whereas Koreans did not. These results show that culture interacts with genes when deciding whether or not to seek social support for one’s distress. People who carry the G allele may be more socially sensitive to societal norms and behave in a manner consistent with their culture. Genetic influences on culturally sensitive behavior may also affect neurotransmission associated with specific neural circuitry. In a gene– culture neuroimaging study, Chinese were shown group members either in physical pain or not (Luo et al., 2015). Interdependent Chinese who are homozygote carriers the G allele of the OXTR gene showed greater empathy, such as perspective- taking and empathic concern, relative to A allele carriers. 
Empathic neural activity within the affective pain matrix, including the bilateral insula and adjacent brain regions such as the bilateral amygdala and superior temporal gyrus, was also heightened for Chinese OXTR rs53576 G allele homozygotes relative to A allele carriers. These findings suggest that Chinese people who are interdependent and carry the social sensitivity allele are more likely to show greater response in neurobiological mechanisms of empathy. Broadly, these studies show that genetic variation of the OXTR gene affects neurotransmission of empathic neural circuitry and behavior in a manner consistent with the societal norms endorsed within one’s culture. 
Cultural differences in the neural basis of empathy may arise depending on the type of emotional expression perceived. For interdependent cultures, maintenance of social harmony is a chief societal goal. Display rules that suppress the expression of emotion in interdependent contexts facilitate this maintenance of social harmony. Facial expressions of anger within an interdependent culture may serve as an important social antecedent for the regulation of emotion. Expressions of anger suggests the importance of further strengthening of social harmony and the necessity of emotion regulation for the maintenance of social harmony within the interdependent cultural context. In a neuroimaging study of culture and international empathy, Chinese and German participants empathized while processing familiar angry, neutral, and unfamiliar neutral faces (de Greck et  al., 2012). Interdependent Chinese showed greater response within a network of brain regions, including the left inferior frontal cortex, left supplementary motor area, and left insula, which have been previously associated with emotion regulation. Independent Germans showed greater response during intentional empathy within the right TPJ, right inferior and superior temporal gyrus, and left middle insula, which are typically activated during social cognition. Neural activity within these regions during intentional empathy for anger was associated with interdependence. These findings demonstrate a cultural difference in empathic neural response for familiar angry expressions, illustrating the importance of the interdependent cultural context for empathic neural processing of anger. 
The cultural sensitivity of group members may be vital not only in the context of healthcare, but also in disaster relief. When members of one’s cultural group show empathy for the pain caused by natural disasters, societal efforts to provide disaster relief and aid for victims are more likely. In a cross- cultural neuroimaging study of interdependence 
716 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
and empathy, Koreans and Caucasian Americans viewed scenes of emotional pain (e.g., group members either in pain due to a natural disaster) or neutral scenes (Cheon et al., 2013; Figure 21.4). Koreans who showed greater “other- focusedness,” or ability to regulate self- interest to attend to others, also demonstrated greater response within the affective pain matrix, including the ACC and insula, as well as the MPFC for group members in emotional pain. These findings suggest that empathic neural circuitry for emotional pain is more responsive for interdependent Koreans. 
Ethnic identity plays an important role in the how people respond to the emotional pain of others. People who identify with their racial or ethnic group may feel a sense of belonging and commitment as well as shared values and attitudes with group members (Phinney, 1990; Sellers, Rowley, Chavous, Shelton, & Smith, 1998). People with a strong ethnic identity, such as members of minority groups within the United States, define themselves as members of their racial or ethnic group and have a sense of emotional significance in belonging to the social group. In a neuroimaging study of ethnic identity in the United States, African Americans showed greater neural response within cortical midline structures, including the MPFC, ACC, mid- cingulate cortex (MCC), and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) when perceiving the emotional pain of group members, while Caucasian Americans demonstrated greater neural response within bilateral parahippocampal gyri (Mathur et al., 2010). Racial identification is positively associated with the magnitude of neural activity within the cortical

Caucasian Americans demonstrated greater neural response within the left orbitofrontal cortex, left putamen, and right interior frontal cortex when perceiving the pain of cultural group members (adapted from Cheon et al., 2013).
CulTural neurosC ienCe  |  717 
midline structures and negatively associated with the magnitude of neural activity with bilateral parahippocampal gyri during empathy for group members (Mathur, Harada, & Chiao, 2012). Degree of MPFC response during empathy for group members was positively associated with motivation to help with donations of time and money. These findings demonstrate the importance of ethnic identity for neurobiological bases of empathy. Belonging and commitment to the social group enhance neurobiological resources for sharing and understanding the pain and suffering of others in the group. Collectively, these findings suggest the importance of ethnic identity for modulating neurobiological correlates of empathy when confronted with the pain of cultural group members. 
Power distance is a cultural dimension that also affects the neural circuitry of empathy. Power distance refers to the societal expectation for hierarchical social interactions (Hofstede, 2001). People living in nations with high power distance, such as Korea, are more likely to expect unequal power distribution, whereas people living in nations with low power distance, such as the United States, may strive for greater equality of power and justification for distributions of power. In a cross- cultural neuroimaging study, Koreans and Caucasian Americans viewed group members in scenes of emotional pain or no pain (Cheon et al., 2011). Koreans showed greater empathy response within left the TPJ (l- TPJ) for group members in emotional pain, relative to Caucasian Americans. Results from this study demonstrate that brain regions for social cognition are recruited when Koreans perceive group members in emotional pain. Koreans may rely on mental state inference for understanding the pain of their group members to a greater extent relative to Caucasian Americans. 
When living in a culture with shared expectations for hierarchical social interaction, Koreans may be more reliant on social inference rather than shared affect representations to demonstrate empathy for group members. Relatedly, group members may perceive, represent, and respond to their conscious emotional state in an autobiographical manner that relies on theory of mind. Thus, when other group members share their emotional state, neural mechanisms for social inference are activated to determine the antecedents and consequences of the state of emotional pain, as well as to infer appropriate strategies for emotion regulation. 
Summary Cultural systems regulate social organization and social practices that guide the metaphysics and epistemology of social behavior. Cultural systems of social knowledge, such as individualism– collectivism and independence– interdependence, guide neural representations and mechanisms of self and others. Mental states of knowledge about self and others, including thoughts, feelings, and beliefs, are stored in neural systems of social behavior. Cultural systems of social thought are represented within the neurobiological mechanisms of social behavior (see also Chapter 11 by Qi Wang and Sawa Senzaki for more discussion of culture and social cognition).

Future Directions in Cultural Neuroscience Historically, research in culture and psychology has illuminated novel ways for thinking about cultural differences in human behavior. Decades of such research show the empirical nature of culture and the importance of rigorous and systematic approaches to the study of cultural differences. Within recent history, the past decades of research on the human brain and genome illustrate the scientific and societal dedication to understanding the biology of human nature. While much of past research endeavors have focused on the universality of the human biology, scientific advances in these fields show the relevance of the human brain and genome for understanding culture and cultural differences. 
Researchers in cultural neuroscience have begun to develop theoretical models for understanding pathways of gene– culture and neuro– culture interactions in mind, brain, and behavior. Coevolutionary models of behavior illustrate the significance of cultural and genetic factors in shaping the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms of behavior. Cultural learning models of behavior predict the cultural system regulation of the mind and brain throughout the lifespan. This systematic approach to cultural differences across multiple levels of analysis emphasizes the advancement of the study of culture through the study of genetic and neurobiological mechanisms of behavior across cultural contexts. By investigating the etiology of human behavior as an interaction of environmental, cultural, and biological factors, scientific efforts to discover cures for complex human diseases become more fully realized. 
Future research in cultural neuroscience may fully embrace the study of culture and human behavior across levels of analysis. Recent empirical advances have demonstrated the importance of cultural context on genetic and neural mechanisms of behavior. Future studies are needed to investigate the organizational and functional significance of multiple genetic and cultural interactions on neural circuitry and behavior. For distinct groups of migrants, including refugees, immigrants, and sojourners, the impact of acculturation on genetic and neurobiological bases of behavior remains relatively less well understood. Research endeavors may begin to explore the malleability and constraints of genetic expression and neuroplasticity across cultural contexts. Expansion of the theoretical and methodological approaches in cultural neuroscience toward the neuroscience of acculturation may benefit efforts to provide evidence- based mental health care for migrants and their families. 
Implications Population Health Disparities Population health disparities refer to group differences in health outcomes of disease prevalence that are unfair or unjust. Racial and ethnic disparities in health and healthcare may result from unequal access to medical care and unfair societal treatment, such as 
 
 
 
 
CulTural neurosC ienCe  |  719 
racial discrimination. Racial and ethnic groups that have been historically marginalized may be at greater risk for negative stereotypes and prejudice that affect physical health and psychological well- being. In healthcare settings, stereotypes and prejudice may alter perceptions between physicians and patients and hinder appropriate or equal access to effective treatment. Immigrants and refugees may also be vulnerable to health disparities due to stereotyping and prejudice associated with minority groups, as well as the acculturative stress of integrating social identities across cultural or ethnic contexts. 
Understanding the etiology of racial and ethnic disparities as an interaction of environmental, cultural, and biological factors allows for advancement in evidence- based healthcare. Negative consequences of racial and ethnic disparities in health and healthcare may be prevented through the development of novel interventions. Healthcare interventions that improve basic medical treatment for members of racial and ethnic minority groups help to close the gap in population health disparities. Increasing awareness of practices that reduce stereotyping and prejudice in the healthcare setting improves the likelihood of equal access to effective healthcare treatment for all. 
Global Mental Health Mental, neurological, and substance abuse (MNS) disorders comprise 13% of the global burden of disease (Collins et  al., 2011). Yet cures and preventative interventions for MNS disorders remain largely elusive due to the limited understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of the human brain. The Grand Challenges in Global Mental Health initiative has identified a number of priorities for scientific discovery of cures for MNS disorders. Toward this goal, one of the chief priorities in global mental health is to identify root causes, risks, and protective factors of MNS disorders across the life course. Research in cultural neuroscience contributes to these scientific efforts at identifying social and biological risk factors for MNS disorders, including the identification of biomarkers of MNS disorders across cultural contexts. Evidence- based advances in cultural neuroscience allow for the identification of the environmental, cultural, and neurobiological determinants of mental disorders, and empirical studies in cultural neuroscience broaden our understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of the human brain across cultural contexts. Through acceleration and expansion of theory and methods in cultural neuroscience, scientists come closer to discovering treatments and cures for global mental health.

Religion and Related Morality Across Cultures 
Vassilis Saroglou 
Religious beliefs, practices, norms, and communities are integral parts of culture and seem to shape most aspects of it. Inversely, culture, at the local, national, and transnational levels, seems to shape religious doctrines, rituals, norms, and groups. By “shaping,” one can envision two major pathways. On the one hand, religion and culture— more precisely, other than religious cultural elements like values, self- concept, emotions, language, and ethnic identity— may parallel and mirror each other, possibly due to long- term bidi-rectional causal influences. Thus, religious universals may parallel cultural universals and cross- religious differences reflect cross- cultural differences in, for instance, self- concepts, emotions, or values. On the other hand, religion and culture may transcend each other. Religion complements, compensates, or changes culture, and culture complements, compensates, or changes religion. At some point, religions may become subcultures or countercultures, and cultures may become quasi- religious alternatives. 
A cross- cultural psychologist is particularly interested in the following basic, pre-liminary question: Do religious differences indeed explain cultural differences? Is religion a sui generis category worthy of being studied on its own, or do religious influences on cultural differences simply reflect the role of socioeconomic factors and value differences among individuals and societies? 
The answer to this question is affirmative. Saucier et al. (2015), analyzing data from 33 countries on almost 50 psychological variables, found that the largest differences between countries did not involve constructs most frequently emphasized in cross- cultural psychology such as values, social axioms, or cultural tightness but instead primarily involved religion and secondarily involved regularity norm behaviors, family roles and 
 
 
rel ig ion and relaTed Moral iTy  |  725 
living arrangements, and ethno- nationalism. The authors concluded that “if a cross- cultural psychologist wishes to focus on variables that generate strong differences between populations, one good strategy is to focus on beliefs connected to religion (or the metaphysical), and especially on practices and behaviors that reflect the everyday impact of religion on persons” (p.  63). Similarly, when it comes to cross- cultural differences, specifically for self- construal, Vignoles et  al. (2016) found that cultural groups emphasize different ways of being both independent and interdependent, depending on (1)  individualism- collectivism and (2)  national socioeconomic development, but also on (3)  religious heritage— that is, the cultural group’s Protestant, Catholic, Christian Orthodox, Muslim, or Buddhist tradition. 
In sum, understanding religion is essential, both theoretically and empirically, to understand cultures, and vice versa. A major area of the religion × culture interaction is individuals’ perception, within their society, of who they are and what they ought to do. 
A Focus on Cross- Cultural Research on Religion and Related Morality Cross- cultural research on religion has a long and decent past, but has exploded in the past 15 years. It simply becomes impossible, even by focusing only on the past 10– 15 years of research, to present a thorough review of the empirical literature within a single chapter, taking into consideration all the cognitive, emotional, moral, and relational- social dimensions of the religion × culture interaction as well as the various outcomes of this interaction across all life domains, from development through health, to social behavior. For a broad global picture on the cross- cultural psychological research on religion in general, the reader may consult earlier introductions (Cohen, 2009; Saroglou & Cohen, 2011) and reviews (Saroglou, 2003; Saroglou & Cohen, 2013; see also Norenzayan, 2016; Wilson, Hartberg, Lanman, & Whitehouse, 2017, for an evolutionary perspective; and Belzen, 2010, Belzen & Lewis, 2010, for qualitative approaches). 
For the purposes of this chapter, I focus on one major area of cross- cultural research on religion: the relationship of religion and religiousness with morality across cultures, and I review primarily research from the past 15 years. This choice was made for several reasons. First, as suggested earlier, religions’ impact on beliefs- and norms- based behavior seems primordial for understanding cultural differences (Saucier et al., 2015). Similarly, knowing how culture influences religious morality might be of primary importance for acquiring a more general understanding of religious differences: the dimensions of religion other than morality (i.e., beliefs, rituals, and group belonging) also have strong moral connotations (Saroglou, 2014). Moreover, in the increased empirical work on religion and culture in the past 15 years, morality is one of the two thematic areas in which researchers have shown the greatest interest; the other is well- being. Furthermore, by focusing on morality, this chapter aims to be unique with respect to previous reviews on 
 
 
726 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
religion and culture.1 Finally, the harmonious coexistence of different cultural groups in today’s globalized world often seems to be undermined by heated moral divides that interfere with various domains such as politics, legislation, or education. It is thus important to dedicate a chapter to the cross- cultural psychological dimensions of the ways religion relates to and influences morality (see also Chapter 10 by Joan G. Miller, Matthew Wice, and Namrata Goyal on culture and morality). 
“Causal” Status of the Religion × Morality × Culture Links Before describing the chapter’s structure and major themes, it is useful to clarify the basic question of the causal— or not— character of the links between religion and morality, and of the role of culture. First, strictly speaking, it is not religion that creates or, more precisely, founds, morality. People’s, even children’s, morality exists partly independently from religion, and children, not only adults, can question religion in the name of moral values (Turiel & Neff, 2000). However, religion shapes morality across cultures in sev-eral ways: it (1) imposes additional values and norms to universal, across cultures, moral principles; (2) elaborates anthropological micro- theories (e.g., a fetus is a human person) that aim to orient universal values toward more narrow domains (e.g., attitudes regarding abortion; Turiel & Neff, 2000); (3) sustains morality through a powerful integrated set of beliefs, rituals, and group authorities; and (4) emphasizes specific hierarchies between values, which may or may not parallel those of the dominant culture (Saroglou, 2014). 
Second, culture, that is, cultural aspects other than religion shapes religion’s relationships with morality. Cultural psychological characteristics and differences on key domains such as self- construal, cognition, emotion, values, and interpersonal and intergroup relations influence (explain or moderate) how religiosity is expressed and how it impacts morality. Similarly, specific characteristics of cultural groups and societies, such as socioeconomic status and development, ethnic and religious diversity, degree of secularization, system of governance, language, and juridical and philosophical traditions, may also shape (explain or moderate) religion’s moral outcomes. 
Chapter Structure In this chapter, I review cross- cultural research from the past 15 years on the way religiosity and religion relate to various aspects of morality— all major domains that people, universally or not, may characterize as relevant for moral judgment. This will include both the interpersonal and non- interpersonal (self- or society- related) domains of 
1. For themes other than morality, the reader may consult specific reviews on cross- cultural psychology of religion as applied to specific major psychological domains such as mental health (Loewenthal, 2007), personality (Saroglou, 2017), development (Holden & Vittrup, 2010; Trommsdorff & Chen, 2012), and emotions (Tsai, Koopman- Holm, Miyazaki, & Ochs, 2013). It is also important, for cross- cultural psychology, to mention acculturation (Saroglou & Cohen, 2013). There also exist reviews of research on the psychology of non- Christian religionists, such as Buddhists (Kristeller & Rapgay, 2013), Hindus (Tarakeshwar, 2013), Jews (Cohen, Gorvine, & Gorvine, 2013), and Muslims (Abu- Raiya, 2013); see also, for an edited volume, Kim- Prieto (2014).

morality. More precisely, I examine both universals (features that hold across religions and cultures) and cultural specifics (aspects that differ as a function of religions, cultures, and cultural/ societal factors) regarding the way religiosity and religion relate to (1) homosexuality, (2) (herero)sexuality, (3) fertility, marriage, family, and parenting, (4) work (job preferences and work ethic) and economy, (5) prosociality, at both the interpersonal and the societal spheres, and (6) citizenship (support for democracy, civic engagement, pro- environmental attitudes, and honesty) (see Chapter 1 by Walter J. Lonner, Kenneth D. Keith, and David Matsumoto for a historical perspective of the study of universals and culture specifics). 
Within each of these sections, the literature review will emphasize evidence from international data, allowing us to disentangle the effects at the individual level from effects at the collective level. More precisely, as far as the religion × culture interaction is con-cerned, one must distinguish between (1) individual religiosity, mostly making distinction between believers and nonbelievers— or between different ways of being religious— both within and across cultures; (2) individuals’ religious denomination (affiliation to specific religious traditions or groups, both within and across cultures); (3)  societies’ religious “heritage” (countries or world regions of Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox, Muslim, Hindu or Buddhist tradition or past); and (4) other countries’ religious characteristics, mainly the mean level of religiousness versus secularization and degree of religious diversity, which may parallel or complement the role of other country- level characteristics (e.g., socioeconomic development). 
In addition, some key comparative studies, and in particular experimental studies that provide methodologically sound information on the “causal” role of religion and/ or culture, will also be examined. Moreover, in all chapter sections, a summary will succinctly synthesize the many individual findings of the studies reviewed within each section. Finally, the chapter will close by offering an integrative synthesis and discussion of the deeper explanatory mechanisms of the religious morality × culture interaction. 
Homosexuality Moral condemnation of homosexuality across religions has been pervasive. Does this translate today into religious intolerance of homosexuality and homosexual persons, and, if yes, is it to the same degree across cultures and religions? Is religious homophobia a simple translation of cultural conservatism, or does religion have a unique and causal role? Do cultural changes in values and related attitudes toward homosexuality influence respective religious attitudes? This section will deal with these questions. 
Individual Religiosity Across Cultures Numerous studies in recent years have focused on religion and attitudes toward homosexuality by analyzing large international datasets, most often from various waves of the World Values Study (WVS), the European Values Study (EVS), and the European Social 
 
 
 
728 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Survey (ESS) (see Table 22.1 for a list of these studies). Each of these analyses has typically included many dozens of countries and many thousands of participants. 
Consistently across all of these studies, individual religiosity is found to predict low tolerance of homosexuality and to do so across countries and across world regions, including Western, secular Europe. This is the case with various measures of religiosity, that is, self- identifying as religious, considering religion to be important in one’s life, religious attendance, and belief in God, thus, not only with religious fundamentalism or religious orthodoxy, orientations known to typically reflect high authoritarianism and conservatism. 
Moreover, religiosity predicts all forms of intolerance of homosexuality; that is, certainly in legal terms (opposing gay rights, marriage, and adoption), but also in moral terms (considering homosexuality to be wrong and unjustifiable), and even in social terms (low acceptance of homosexuals as neighbors or as free to live their lives). In some analyses, the link between religiosity and low social tolerance of homosexuals is weaker if not nonexistent (Hoffarth, Hodson, & Molnar, 2018, Study 2). Similarly, in Western Europe, whereas religious attendance and belief in the superiority of one’s own religion predict both moral and social intolerance of homosexuals, the belief in God (a devotional aspect of religiousness) predicts only a moral but not a social intolerance of homosexuals (Doebler, 2015). 
Importantly, the role of individual religiosity with regard to homophobia seems unique. The effect remains even after controlling for sociodemographic variables, including religious denomination, but also relevant individual characteristics such as income (Jäckle & Wenzelburger, 2015; Malka, 2014), conservatism in values and political orientation (Donaldson, Handren, & Lac, 2017; Hoffarth et al., 2018), endorsement of traditional gender roles (Adamczyck & Cheng, 2015; Janssen & Scheepers, 2018), and intelligence (Souza & Cribari- Neto, 2015). 
Cross- Religious Differences and Country- Level Influences Are all religions equally “homophobic”? Several of the studies mentioned in Table 22.1 offer comparisons between religions in terms of (1)  mean level comparisons between religionists of different denominations; (2)  comparisons, between denominations, of the association between individual religiosity and homonegative attitudes; and (3) comparisons between countries/ world regions of different religious heritages, in particular after controlling for other relevant between- country socioeconomic differences (see, in particular, for the world:  Adamczyk & Cheng, 2015; Hoffarth et  al., 2018; Jäckle & Wenzelburger, 2015; Malka, 2014; and, for Europe: Doebler, 2015; Hooghe & Meeusen, 2013). 
Beyond the key difference between religious believers and nonbelievers, the latter being typically more accepting of homosexuals, these studies generally show a rather consistent rank order on antigay attitudes between religions (see also Figure 22.1). Given the similarly Christian theology of the Orthodox, this relatively high rank may be justified by historical reasons: a communist, sexually conservative past for the East European Orthodox and the long coexistence with Muslims for the Mediterranean Orthodox Christians. Buddhists’ attitudes toward homosexuality are not consistent across studies and may greatly depend on or interfere with the cultural context. Across the world, Buddhists may show stronger homophobic attitudes than nonbelievers (Hoffarth et al., 2018, Study 2) and even stronger homophobic attitudes than Christians if we control for national and household wealth (Malka, 2014). But in European countries, where most Buddhists are converts, they are tolerant of homosexuals (as are Jews), and their tolerance is equal to that of nonbelievers (Hoffarth et al., 2018, Study 2). Moreover, religiosity of Buddhists in East Asian countries (Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan) has been found to predict weaker or null antigay attitudes compared to Catholics and Protestants living in the same countries (Clobert, Saroglou, Hwang, & Soong, 2014; but see Xie & Peng, 2018, for a study in China where Christian beliefs too do not predict homophobia). Finally, in an attempt to disentangle religious effects from other cultural effects at the country level, Adamczyk and Cheng (2015) found that Confucian societies are less tolerant of homosexuality than are European and American societies, and this cannot be reduced to a regional Asian effect. However, a higher proportion of Buddhists contributes to more tolerance. 
Finally, other country- level religious characteristics shape societies’ (in)tolerance of homosexuality, and several country- level features moderate the relationship of individual religiosity with homonegativity. Societies that are more secular and more religiously diverse show, at the country level, a higher mean tolerance of homosexuality, both in legal/ moral and social terms (Souza & Cribari- Neto, 2015; van den Akker, van der Ploeg, & Scheepers, 2013). This effect persists beyond the role of other indicators of societal development such as low perceived corruption and income inequality (Doebler, 2015). 
However surprisingly at first glance, the more liberal a society is, endorsing values of self- expression rather than survival values and demonstrating tolerance by recognizing gay rights, the stronger the association between individual religiosity and the intolerance of homosexuality becomes. Inversely, the religiosity– homophobia link is weaker in size in conservative and religious societies, where homophobia is high (Adamczyck & Pitt, 2009; Donaldson et al., 2017; Hoffarth et al., 2018, Study 2). A similar contrast is observed between Western and Eastern postcommunist Europe, with the former showing statistically stronger links between antigay attitudes and individual religiosity (Doebler, 2015). 
How can these findings be interpreted? In liberal, self- expressive values- oriented societies, variation in moral positions increases. This variation reflects nonbelievers’ more tolerant positions rather than the religious becoming more conservative:  the religious simply “persist.” Variation in religiosity also increases. Consequently, religious ideology offers resources to fuel moral opposition to liberal morality in a context where traditional, cultural homophobia is increasingly reduced. Finally, as suggested by Hoffarth et al. (2018, Studies 4 and 5; see also Batson, Floyd, Meyer, & Winner, 1999; Blogowska, Saroglou, & Lambert, 2013, Study 2), the endorsement of religious rhetoric on the sinner– sin distinction (“love the sinner, hate the sin”) typically applied to homosexual 
rel ig ion and relaTed Moral iTy  |  733 
persons may contribute to legitimize and maintain religious antigay prejudice within liberal societies. 
Experimental Evidence Across Cultures The preceding evidence on religiosity and the low tolerance of homosexuality across the world is correlational, with attitudes toward homosexual people being measured through self- reports. Thus, one could counterargue that this self- report– based evidence is only a translation of moral de- consideration and does not result in real prejudice. However, experimental studies (see Table 22.1) confirm the existence of antigay prejudice also in terms of implicit attitudes and behavioral discrimination and hostility among highly religious participants, at least in Western cultural contexts of the Christian tradition (e.g., Batson et al., 1999, United States; Blogowska et al., 2013, Study 2, Belgium; Jackson & Esses, 1997, Canada; Rowatt, Tsang, Kelly, Lamartina, & Mccullers, 2006, United States). 
Additional experimental studies confirm some “causal role” of religion in implicitly activating prejudice against sexual minorities. This has been attested in various cultural contexts: when passengers were approached by the experimenter in front of a (Christian) church vs. a neutral place (LaBouff, Rowatt, Johnson, & Finkle, 2012, the Netherlands), when students were primed with Muslim words (Yilmaz, Karadöller, & Sofuoglu, 2016, Turkey), and when Christian and Buddhist Chinese students were primed with, respectively, Christian and Buddhist concepts (Ramsay, Pang, Shen, & Rowatt, 2014, Singapore). However, in another study, Buddhist concepts subtly presented to Belgian and French Buddhists (who were mostly converts) activated more positive attitudes toward gay people in comparison to neutral primes (Clobert, Saroglou, & Hwang, 2015, Study 1). 
Summary The religious condemnation of homosexuality as immoral translates, consistently across religions and countries, into associations between personal religiosity— both belief and practice and not only fundamentalism— and low tolerance of homosexuality and people with alternative sexual orientations. This is certainly the case in moral/ legal terms, but often also in terms of mere social tolerance. Even implicit exposure to religious ideas— certainly Christian and Muslim and possibly Buddhist ideas— automatically activates antigay prejudice. Very likely because of the specific religious teachings, the religiosity’s effect on the low tolerance of gays and lesbians is unique and additional to the effects that sociopolitical conservatism and low socioeconomic status have on such low tolerance. For both religious and other cultural reasons, Muslim individuals and countries are the most intolerant of homosexuals, Eastern Orthodox Christianity lies between Islam and Western Christianity, and Buddhism seems to be located at the low end of the religious antigay prejudice continuum. 
At the country level, higher secularism and religious diversity predict a higher mean tolerance of homosexuals. However, in terms of the individual × country- level interaction, whereas in traditional societies and those with a recent communist past (East Europe) 
 
 
734 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
both homonegativity and religiosity are highly normative and their relationship is statistically weaker, the role of religiosity in predicting homonegativity becomes stronger in liberal Western societies. In these societies, self- expressive values allow for higher individual variability in moral attitudes and more conservative reactions against modernity, and the religious rhetoric of the sinner– sin distinction serves to legitimize sexual discrimination. However, in these liberal societies, Catholics and mainstream Protestants tend to explicitly express intolerance of homosexuals more clearly in moral/ legal terms, for instance through opposition to gay marriage and adoption, and less so in social/ personal terms. The preceding findings suggest some internal changes within Western Christianity as it “acculturates” into modernity. Nevertheless, even in such liberal contexts of Christian tradition, religious homonegativity still translates into antigay prejudice and behavior. 
(Hetero)sexuality Why does individual religiosity so pervasively across religions and cultures imply the condemnation of homosexuality and a low tolerance of people of minority sexual orientation? Why is this also the case in liberal societies, which are aware of scientific evidence showing that sexual orientation is determined, at least in part, by genetic and biological dispositions? One possibility is that the intolerance of homosexuality exemplifies, to the highest degree, both a religious mistrust of sexuality in general and the religious emphasis on fertility and family. As will be shown in this and the next sections, religion implies a preference for sexuality that is hygienic, restrictive, and oriented toward survival and fertility. Similarly, religion implies a preference for family- related values and practices that restrict sexuality and intra- sex competition and the related risk for violence and that maximize investment in offspring (see Freud, 1927/ 1961; Kirkpatrick, 2005; Weeden, Cohen, & Kenrick, 2008; Weeden & Kurzban, 2013). These objectives are facilitated by religion’s emphasis on relevant moral emotions (e.g., guilt, disgust), values/ norms (e.g., sublimation, low consideration of hedonism, disapproval of divorce and abortion), beliefs (e.g., women– men differentiation and inequality), and practices (e.g., low premarital and extramarital sex, preference for religious and ethnic homogamy, investment in children). Note that the conflicting links between religion and sexuality are bidirectional, with sexuality also diminishing, experimentally and longitudinally, religious and spiritual aspirations (Rigo, Uzarevic, & Saroglou, 2016; Vasilenko & Lefkowitz, 2014). 
In this section, I examine recent empirical evidence allowing us to answer a series of questions. Is the historical religious mistrust toward (hetero)sexuality still present in attitudes and behaviors, even in liberal and secular societies? Is restrictive sexuality as a function of individual religiosity present across religions and cultures? Are there cross- religious and cross- cultural differences in religious restrictive sexuality? Do the underlying explanatory emotions, values, and beliefs play a role cross- culturally, or are they present only in some religious and cultural contexts?

Individual Religiosity Across Cultures There is strong cross- cultural evidence that religiosity relates to restrictive sociosexuality, as well as to relevant values (low consideration of hedonism), moral emotions (guilt and disgust), and beliefs (gender inequality). 
Schmitt and Fuller (2015) analyzed data from 56 nations (gathered in 10 world regions) from the International Sexuality Description Project. The study included a measure of sociosexual orientation tapping restrictive versus liberal sexual attitudes, desires, and behaviors, as well as a measure of short- term mating interests (desired number of part-ners, time to consent to sex with someone who is desirable, and short- term mate seeking). Across all but one (East Asia) of the world regions, self- identification as religious was negatively related to liberal sociosexuality as well as to short- term mating interests. This was the case for both men and, slightly more strongly, for women, for various age groups, and in world regions of both Christian (Americas, Europe) and non- Christian dominant heritage (Middle East, Africa, Oceania, and South/ Southeast Asia). 
Sexual desire and satisfaction is a major motivation to have sex. Hedonism, defined by Schwartz as pleasure and sensuous gratification for oneself, can be considered a core motivating value for sexual interest. Religiosity is typically found to imply a low consideration of hedonism, and the evidence is strong (religion’s association with hedonism is second in strength only to its association with the value of tradition) and consistent across studies, cultures, religions, genders, and age groups (Roccas & Elster, 2014, a review of 28 studies; Saroglou, Delpierre, & Dernelle, 2004, a meta- analysis of 15 studies; Schwartz, 2012, an analysis of ESS data from 33 countries). 
Moreover, endorsing the moral foundation of disgust– purity sustains attitudes and behaviors typical of restrictive sexuality (Koleva, Graham, Iyer, Ditto, & Haidt, 2012). Religious people across cultures have been found to highly endorse this moral foundation (Azadmanjier & Khalili, 2017, Iran; Bulbulia, Osborn, & Sibley, 2013, New Zeeland; Deak & Saroglou, 2016, Belgium; Koleva et  al., 2012, United States; Nilsson, Erlandsson, & Västfjäll, 2016, Sweden; Yalçındağ et al., 2017, Turkey). In addition, sexual guilt undermines sexual desire and behavior. Specifically, sexual guilt has been found to be related to religiosity and to partly mediate the relationship between religiosity and restricted sexual desire, attitudes, and behaviors. This was the case with different cultural groups within the same country: Euro Canadian and East Asian female students in Canada (Woo, Morshedian, Brotto, & Gorzalka, 2012) and Christian and Muslim men and women in Belgium (Rigo & Saroglou, 2018). 
A subtle explanatory factor of the link between religiosity and restricted sociosexuality could be gender inequality and, relatedly, strong gender differentiation, the latter known to sustain sexism (Glick & Fiske, 2001). Most of the cultural and religious restrictions in norms related to sexuality, marriage, and family target women more strongly than men. Using international data from multiple sources, Schnabel (2016) found that, even when accounting for a country’s human development and gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, gender equality is lower in more religious countries— differences between 
 
736 | The handbook of CulTure and PsyChology 
Christianity, Islam, and Hinduism were smaller than the differences between the religious and the nonreligious. Moreover, priming religious ideas increases subtle sexism even in Western countries of Catholic and Protestant tradition (Haggard, Kaelen, Saroglou, Klein, & Rowatt, 2018: see also Chapter 9 by Deborah L. Best and Angelica R. Puzio on culture and gender). 
Country- Level Influences and Cross- Religious Differences As it will be developed below, there is suggestive evidence that country- level variables may moderate the religiosity– restrictive sociosexuality association. More importantly, religions differ in the degree and the extent to which they imply restrictive sociosexuality, resulting in a kind of rank order similar to that found for religious homonegativity. Finally, experimental and other research shows meaningful behavioral differences between religionists of different religions when confronted with sexual “temptation.” 
In line with evidence reviewed in the previous section showing that the link between religiosity and homonegativity becomes statistically stronger in liberal and secular countries, Jung (2015; WVS data, 47 countries) found that low approval of premarital sex is related to religious attendance and religious importance but that the association is stronger in countries with higher GDP per capita (Jung, 2015). These countries are most often the more liberal ones. This moderating finding again reflects the greater variability in individual differences in morality in societies animated by self- expressive values and, as Jung (2015) suggests, the functional differentiation of religious believers confronted with secularization. 
The preceding study, plus a study on reported behavior of premarital and extramarital sex (Adamczyk & Hayes, 2012; 31 countries, data from the 2012 Demographic and Health Survey) and the previously mentioned study by Schnabel (2016) on gender equality, together provide evidence favoring the idea that Islam, compared to other religions, implies the most conservative attitudes toward premarital and extramarital sexuality, as well as the lowest endorsement of gender equality (Hindus are equally low in premarital and extramarital sex). Importantly, earlier age of marriage, restrictions on women’s mobility, and a country’s human development are not sufficient to explain the highest scores of Muslims on these attitudes and behaviors. Across the world, Christians, then Jews, and finally Buddhists come after Muslims in the rank order of religions regarding their opposition to premarital sex (Adamczyk & Hayes, 2012). This evidence confirms Norris and Inglehart’s (2004) point that the divide between Islam and the West essentially concerns gender- , sexuality- , and family- related norms. 
There may be one exception to this pattern. Islam is considered to favor intramarital sexuality, at least to a greater degree than do other religions, possibly, even if not only, due to the very high value that Islam places on fertility. Interestingly, comparing participants of Christian and Muslim traditions living in Belgium, Rigo and Saroglou (2018) found meaningful similarities. In both groups, religiosity was associated with strong sex guilt and disgust– purity and low disinhibition and sexual fantasy across genders and marital 
 
rel ig ion and relaTed Moral iTy  |  737 
statuses, and this in turn predicted a low frequency of heterosexual behavior among single people. However, religiosity was related to low sexual desire and a low frequency of intramarital sexuality only among Christians but not among married Muslims. 
Finally, there seem to be interesting cross- religious differences in the management of sexual “temptations.” First, Protestants moralize transgressive thoughts, including sexual ones, more than do Jews. Using hypothetical scenarios, Cohen (2003, Study 3; Cohen & Rozin, 2001, Studies 2 and 4)  found that US Jews and Protestants consider having a sexual affair as immoral, but Protestants, more than Jews, report even the mere thought of having a possible sexual affair as immoral. This was not limited to sexuality since Protestants also highly moralized thoughts in other hypothetical scenarios involving cheating on an exam, disrespect of parents, and cruelty to animals. This is because Protestants more strongly perceive thoughts to be controllable (Cohen, 2003, Study 2; Cohen & Rozin, 2001, Studies 1 and 3). 
Second, Kim, Zeppenfeld, and Cohen (2013) argued that if Protestants perceive bad thoughts as immoral more than people of other religions do, they may be partic-ularly prone to adopt the defense mechanism of sublimation. Sublimation is a process by which people take forbidden or suppressed emotions and desires and channel them by displacing them in a nonconscious way toward productive, often creative, ends. Kim et al. (2013; see also Cohen, Kim, & Hudson, 2014; see also Figure 22.2) indeed found that, compared to US Jews and Catholics, Protestants are more prone to choosing creative careers and accomplishing creative achievements if they had, earlier in their lives,
